Dear Ms. Fahey: 

On July 25, 2018, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) issued a proposed rule to revise the 

regulations for prohibitions to threatened wildlife and plants under Section 4(d) of the Endangered 

Species Act (ESA).1 This proposed rule would withdraw the general 4(d) rule and help FWS determine 

the scope of “take” prohibitions to be applied through the issuance of a species-specific “Section 4(d) 

rule.” NASDA supports the issuance of this rule. 

NASDA represents the Commissioners, Secretaries, and Directors of the state departments of agriculture 

in all fifty states and four U.S. territories. State departments of agriculture are responsible for a wide 

range of programs including food safety, conservation, and fostering the economic vitality of our rural 

communities. NASDA members are co-regulators with the federal government on a host of natural 

resource issues and a key partner in land management. 

NASDA supports withdrawing the general 4(d) rule. With this withdrawal, NASDA encourages FWS to 

consult with states when implementing species-specific 4(d) rules for threatened species. Consulting 

with NASDA members will help FWS further understand what conservation is on the ground and what 

habitat exists or can be efficiently improved to help conserve the species. Further, NASDA encourages 

FWS to draw a clearer line between threatened and endangered species. Clarifying this and creating 

more purposeful, species-specific 4(d) rules will create more consistency in implementation of the act.

Dear Tom Vilsack,

I am writing in support of your agency’s proposal to fully reinstate the Roadless Rule on the Tongass National Forest in Alaska. 

Why? Because the world has enough roads. Period.

The Roadless Rule was implemented with unprecedented public support to protect some of our nation’s most pristine public lands, including large parts of the Tongass National Forest. It retains wide bipartisan support, including from 96 percent of people who commented on the recent rollback of the rule in Alaska. 

In the middle of multiple national crises, the Trump administration focused on finalizing its plan to remove crucial protections for Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, serving industry interests aiming to open the forests to clear-cutting. Anything other than a full reinstatement of the Roadless Rule will have far-reaching impacts on indigenous communities, climate, and wildlife, and ignores overwhelming public support for the safeguard, including from Alaska Natives, Alaskans, and taxpayers across the nation. 

President-elect Biden promised bold climate action — and full protection of the Tongass is an integral part of that. It’s already stored over 3 billion tons of carbon — about 15% of what the United States produces in a year — and continues to store more and more each passing year. 

I urge you to fully reinstate the Roadless Rule protection to the Tongass National Forest and put the public interest, environmental justice, our public lands, and taxpayers above corporate profits. 

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Mark Rigney
Evansville, IN 47714

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most effective conservation laws in the United States. Ninety-nine percent of listed species have been saved from extinction, including iconic species such as the bald eagle. The law is also widely popular; polling shows that 90 percent of voters across the political spectrum support the law. The proposed changes to the statute will weaken the law and put thousands of plants and animal species at risk. 

Proposed changes will allow federal agencies to not acknowledge the broad consequences of their actions through changes to the consultation requirements of Section 7 of the Act. Section 7 consultations require that a federal agency that is funding, authorizing, or conducting an activity to consult with the Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service to ensure that the activity does not jeopardize the existence of endangered or threatened species or destroy their critical habitat. The proposed changes will reduce the effects of agency actions required to undergo consultations. For example, the proposed rule seeks comment on changes that would stop consultation for effects like climate change that are manifested through global processes. The changes proposed will also make it harder to protect critical habitat that is being impacted by development. The protection of even small sections of habitat is crucial for species conservation. The proposed changes would allow death by a thousand cuts by ignoring impacts to species critical habitats unless they impacted the entire habitat at once. If the mechanisms for enforcement of the protection of endangered and threatened species and their critical habitats are weakened, species will be put at greater risk. 

I have just returned from a short break, hiking the trails of ancient artwork and petroglyphs created by Native Americans. I appreciate, more than ever, the need to preserve what we still have of our peoples, wildlife, plants and places. We are all earthlings who function better as a whole. Science over economics, please!

I urge you not to move forward these proposed changes and leave the regulations to one of our most effective and popular conservation laws untouched. Please withdraw the proposed changes to section 7 (Interagency Cooperation) rule. CFR Citation: 50 CFR Part 402 / Docket ID: NOAA_FRDOC_0001

To Whom It May Concern: 

The North American Meat Institute (NAMI or Meat Institute) is the leading voice for the meat 

and poultry industry. The Meat Institute has a rich, century-long history and provides essential member 

services including legislative, regulatory, scientific, international, and public affairs representation. 

Together, the Meat Institute’s members produce the vast majority of U.S. beef, pork, lamb, and poultry, 

in addition to the equipment, ingredients, and services needed to produce the safest and highest quality 

products. Many of the Meat Institute’s members operate dual jurisdiction facilities. NAMI appreciates 

the opportunity to provide comment to the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) and Food and Drug 

Administration (FDA; collectively, the agencies) on the above-referenced dockets. 

Food labeling regulations are under the jurisdiction of several agencies. Both FSIS and FDA 

issued separate final rules establishing January 1, 2026, as the uniform compliance date for new food 

labeling regulations issued between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2024. A uniform compliance 

date for labeling changes allows the industry to plan label inventories and resource allocation to 

minimize the economic impact of complying with changes. Frequently changing labels may also confuse 

consumers because they may not be able to compare labels across similar products if the required 

information is not consistent. 

The agencies also reserved the right to establish a different compliance date if special 

circumstances warrant. In that circumstance, the agencies will identify an appropriate compliance date 

and include it in the rulemaking. Should either agency identify label changes that warrant a different 

compliance date, the Meat Institute encourages the agencies to coordinate with each other and other 

food labeling agencies to harmonize compliance and enforcement expectations because a single, 

uniform compliance date benefits both consumers and industry. Separate rulemaking efforts could 

result in a patchwork of different compliance dates, which would be onerous and costly because labels 

would need to be changed frequently to comply with the different standards.

I am glad that the USDA is seeking public input on the "free range" label claim, because consumers are being misled by labels that misrepresent conditions and suggest that animals are being treated better than they are. This is a significant and growing problem, and it is critically important that the public be provided with accurate information in order to make informed food choices. Labels claiming that animals are treated humanely should require meaningful standards and transparency in order to prevent consumers from being taken advantage of as is currently the case. 

I have seen pictures of "free range" factory farm chickens and it is anything but humane. The general public thinks that "free range" means living on a nice little farm with lots of room and sunshine, but that is not the case. 

Please help the public become more informed!

My name is Nicole Howland. I attended ITT Tech from 2002 to 2004. As a member of the Debt 
Collective, I am writing to comment on the proposed regulations concerning borrower defenses 
to repayment, released at 81 Fed. Reg. 39329 (Jun. 16, 2016). 
 
I submitted a defense to repayment application September 2015 with over 50 pages of 
evidence. I saved all my documentation. I have saved all hardcopy proof that I was defrauded 
by ITT Tech. I am a victim of predatory lending. I was 18, very poor, young and naïve when I 
was recruited by an ITT recruiter. ITT Tech asked me for the SSN of my mother and ex-
husband “for FSA purposes”…ITT ran our credit and all were denied. I furnished proof of all of 
this. But that didn’t stop the school from taking out multiple predatory student loans in my name. 
I was one of those statistics likely to default, however, I never have. I have been paying back my 
student debt for 12 years and I OWE MORE TODAY THAN I DID IN 2004 WHEN I 
GRADUATED! The system is broke. I feel that the department of education is failing defrauded 
student debtors on multiple levels. This recent neg reg is very vague and seems as though the 
schools and accreditors are still not liable for restitution…yet, as debtors, we are still forced into 
a life of debt. While that may not seem like much to the decision makers, this debt has ruined 
many lives. I deserve restitution and the Department of Education has failed to even glance at 
the evidence I have submitted to support my claim. 
 
Overall, I am glad to see that the Department of Education finally takes seriously the 
inadequacies of the current system (or lack thereof) for borrower defenses and for holding scam 
schools accountable. Although I am skeptical given the Department’s track record, I am writing 
with the hope that the proposed regulation represents a first step on a new path. In that spirit, I 
offer the following suggestions for improving the rule so that it can truly grant “every dime of 
relief” we are entitled to. 
 
First of all, AS A FFELP BORROWER, I am horrifically distressed at the Department’s proposed 
way of dealing with those loans. FRAUD was not invented in JULY 2010. Of course it is good 
that FFEL borrowers will finally get administrative forbearance like the rest of those who apply 
for relief, but the rest of the rule treats FFEL borrowers as lesser, even though they had no 
choice about the type of loans they took out. There should be an automatic group process for 
FFEL borrowers just as the Department is rightly proposing for Direct Loan borrowers (with 
some modifications discussed below). By requiring FFEL borrowers to make individual 
decisions to consolidate their loans in order to even be eligible for relief, the Department cuts off 
the possibility of automatic group discharges and cuts off the possibility of restitution of amounts 
paid, both of which go against essential elements of the Direct Loan portion of the regulation. 
FFEL borrowers should be treated the same as Direct Loan borrowers—whatever complexity 
may be involved in getting relief to FFEL borrowers, it should be worked out between the 
Department and its contractors. It should not be up to borrowers to navigate the impossibly 
complicated layers of federal student lending just to get relief for being defrauded. 
 
I will state again that FRAUD was not invented by ITT Tech in 2010, which seems to be the year 
that Dept. of Ed likes to focus on with regard to student debt. After all FFELP was the standard 
form of federal student aid prior to 2010. There should be an option for defrauded borrowers to 
consolidate into Direct loan programs to allow their debt to be abolished The Dept of Ed acts as 
if they have no purview over FFELP which is completely irresponsible and untrue.

I am writing on behalf of the American Craft Spirits Association, the only national trade group

Our industry is relatively new. Most of our members have started their businesses in the last 

decade. Craft distillers believe we are bringing back a great American tradition that dates to our 

founding fathers. 

As our growing industry understands it, the excise tax drawback has been a critical tool to 

facilitate growth of American exports and has functioned as intended when it was first created 

two centuries ago and further implemented with Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act 

of 2015 (TFTEA). Drawback is one of the few WTO-sanctioned export incentives that helps 

offset the risk when seeking to develop foreign markets. 

As noted in other comments, beverage alcohol is highly regulated and is often subjected to 

numerous tariff and non-tariff barriers in markets around the world. Further, many foreign 

competitors benefit from large subsidies and marketing support from their governments. As a 

result, we believe the drawback program may become more important to our relatively new 

industry over time and help level the playing field and promote the continued growth of distilled

Exporting our products and importing products, is a vital part of growing our businesses in this 

industry. American spirits are in high demand overseas. And, as market access within the United 

States becomes more difficult because of increased challenges with distribution, exports may 

become a favored option.

 
As noted in the current proposed rule, “CBP currently permits this practice only with respect to 

wine. But as explained, the IRC imposes excise tax and provides exemptions from such tax for 

other goods, including distilled spirits, beer, tobacco products, and certain taxable fuel. Some 

producers have already requested that CBP extend its current treatment of wine to distilled

We concur with the statement in the preamble. This 400 plus page rule is very extensive, and 

noting the current treatment, we wish to comment on two key elements. Tax drawbacks should

America with continued job growth. The drawback provision would similarly support 

manufacturing and job creation within our industry. 

Thank you for your consideration of these comments. 

Sincerely, 

Mark Shilling, Chair Legislative Affairs Committee

Today the Endangered Species Act (ESA) is failing to achieve its primary purpose of species recovery and instead has become a tool for litigation that drains resources away from real recovery efforts on the state, tribal and local level and blocks job-creating economic activities. original goal was to preserve and recover key domestic species from the brink of extinction. Recommends constructive changes in the following categories: 1. Ensuring Greater Transparency and Prioritization of ESA with a Focus on Species Recovery and De-Listing 2. Reducing ESA Litigation and Encouraging Settlement Reform . 3 Empowering States, Tribes, Local Governments and Private Landowners on ESA Decisions Affecting Them and Their Property. 4 Requiring More Transparency and Accountability of ESA Data and Science. The ESA, federal implementation of it, and seemingly never-ending litigation are creating increasing impediments towards reaching that goal. Only by removing these impediments can the ESA be improved for the benefit of saving species. Federal agencies that implement ESA should not list species unless and until they are able to identify actual recovery and numerical goals for healthy species populations upfrontbefore, or at the time of any proposed rule involving listing a species. Recovery plans should be drafted and completed and approved before listing or critical habitat is designated, not as an afterthought, years later, or not at all. Rather than basing decisions on vague trends showing decline or improvement or "professional opinions," ESA listing/delisting petitions should not be accepted by federal ESA implementing agencies unless based on actual data relating to species' condition. Data used for listing decisions should be made public, especially if the data and related studies are being financed by the taxpayer. Federal agencies should have discretion to extend 12 month or 90-day deadlines relating to species listing or critical habitat determinations, without fear of spurious litigation. Rather than force federal agencies to accept petition with equal weight no matter how lacking science and data. Agencies should allow to incorporate the best and most current data. Agencies' Listing Priority Guidance (48 Fed. Reg. 43098) should supersede any conflicting 12-month or 90-day deadline set by rule, settlement or other action. Several terms in the law have become magnets for misinterpretation, conflicting interpretations, or even litigation, and should be clarified, including, for example: "foreseeable future"; "significant portion of the range," "jeopardy" to a species, the technological and economic feasibility of "reasonable and prudent alternatives/measures," and "maximum extent practicable" relating to mitigation. Federal agencies should be required to disclose all details of consent decrees to Congress and an appropriate NEPA process should be applied for settlements to ensure public input in ESA decisions, and to ensure they include best scientific data. Litigious groups and plaintiffs should be discouraged from filing procedural challenges against agencies simply because they do not agree with the agency's decisions, (such as delisting determinations, findings of species listing not warranted). Litigants should be required to pay their own way to curb repeated litigation and foster court cases only on substantive matters. To discourage forum shopping by frequent ESA-litigation-plaintiffs, ESA lawsuits should not be permitted in federal courts other than in a state a species is primarily located. Hourly fees paid by the federal government to litigious attorneys for ESA litigation should be capped like other federal statutes to prevent lucrative payment of attorneys' fees. non-governmental organizations or individuals that file ESA-related lawsuits against the federal government should be barred from receiving federal taxpayer-funded grants. To: 

USDA, Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) 

Subject: 

FSIS Guidelines for Industry Response to Customer Complaints 

In reference to the above subject, the HACCP Consulting Group (HCG), LLC wishes to take this 

opportunity to provide FSIS with constructive comments regarding the above document. 

HCG, based in Alexandria, VA, was founded in 1994 and has provided international and 

domestic HACCP training, accredited by the International HACCP Alliance (IHA), and aligned 

with the expectations and guidance of the National Advisory Committee for the Microbiological 

Criteria for Foods, Codex, and the FSIS. The Guidelines proposed by FSIS are inconsistent with 

key aspects of that long-accepted, proven philosophy. 

Since its inception, HACCP has defined a food safety hazard as “Any biological, chemical or 

physical property that may cause a food to be unsafe for human consumption”. Regarding 

physical hazards, these may include, but are not limited to, glass, metal, stones, wood, etc., that 

may cause injury (cuts in the month, choking, broken teeth, etc.). It is an establishment’s 

responsibility to determine what potential physical hazards may cause the food to be unsafe for 

human consumption. While this should be done using scientific and regulatory guidance, it is our 

opinion the recent guidance from FSIS does not contribute to making appropriate decisions 

regarding hazards and the application of HACCP principles. 

The FSIS guidance document appears to conflate the definition of adulterated within the Acts 

and regulations with HACCP. Adulteration, as defined in the regulations and Acts, is very broad 

and is a legal position as to whether the product can bear the mark of inspection. Something that 

is defined as adulterated by the Acts or regulations may not always be a food safety issue 

associated with a defined hazard. For example, product produced in an unsanitary environment is 

defined as adulterated. This is not the same as product which is known or reasonably suspected 

to pose a specific hazard to the consumer. 

, 

HACCP is intended to address hazards. When FSIS provides guidance stating the HACCP 

system should address any adulterated product from entering commerce, it is problematic as 

there is lack of evidence of a hazard. The Agency is defining the intent of HACCP systems too 

broadly by including safety and quality (or non-hazardous adulteration) concerns. 

HCG disagrees with the statement in the FSIS Guidance document that: “The establishment’s 

HACCP system should function to prevent any adulterated product from entering 

commerce, even if the cause of the adulteration is not a food safety hazard (e.g., it does not 

result in a food to be unsafe for human consumption)”. Foreign material in an ingredient or in 

a finished product that does not meet the definition of a physical hazard should not be addressed

 
in the HACCP hazard analysis or HACCP Plan as a hazard. This is not to say establishments 

should ignore potential foreign material. We recognize the importance of prerequisite programs 

and other standard operating procedures. These aspects of a food safety system are foundational 

but should not be confused with controls necessary to address serious or critical hazards. HCG 

respectfully suggests FSIS should more strongly emphasize the importance of developing other 

plant programs to address control of foreign material concerns to prevent incidents of non-

hazardous adulteration. 

HACCP has been and remains a successful tool for food safety because it focuses essential and 

limited resources toward critical concerns. Incorporating foreign material that does not represent 

a food safety hazard into the HACCP plan obfuscates the definition of a hazard and dilutes the

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I expect food labels to be truthful and not deceptive or misleading. Chickens, pigs, and cows crowded together with little to no access to large grassy fields and abundant sunshine and fresh air is deceptive and misleading.

Thank you for considering my request.

Protecting the Tongass from old-growth logging will not only preserve that capacity, but avoid releasing carbon currently sequestered in its trees. Their way of life is inextricably linked with these lands and waters. They hunt, gather, fish and harvest medicines in the Tongass that their ancestors have stewarded for more than 10,000 years. Restoring full protections will allow their traditional use of the land to continue. Operating in full consultation with Tribal governments and local communities, this program will help the region stoke the already robust fishing and recreation industries that are driving the economy. Again, the Tongass is critical to controlling climate change. We cannot afford to lose it. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Joanne Schneider -PII-

Thank you for allowing public comment on the Conservation and Landscape Health Rule.

I live in Oregon where the BLM has had significant degraded impact on the forests and deserts all over Oregon for many decades. Approximately 10% of Oregon's lands are considered Class 1 or 2 wild lands in conservation; the lowest percentage of the western states! Oregon needs significant new lands put into conservation to have any chance of meeting President Biden's 30x30 goals. Timber plantations and cattle ranch land are not biodiverse forests or deserts and do not meet conservation goals.

The significant amount of Western Oregon BLM land that is logged, along with USFS land, has contributed to drying of the western forests, reduced rainfall, reduced water quantity in watersheds, and hotter landscapes that are challenged to regrow trees. We need to put more of Oregon's western and eastern forests into conservation to combat climate change immediately. This means protecting the largest trees, use of selective logging, avoiding clearcuts, and using longer rotations for more carbon uptake. These will all improve land health for water, biodiversity and fire resilience. It will also produce more timber as proven by Oregon State University's Forest research teams. BLM must reduce soil erosion which holds 40-50% of carbon in forests by avoiding steep slope logging, decommissioning roads, improving culverts to increase the carbon capacity of the land.

On the Eastern dry side of Oregon, much of the dry landscape is fragile and dry desert is still managed by BLM to allow cattle ranching. These fragile plant and animal species can not complete with cattle that kill the plants, consume significant water from creeks/rivers, and out compete the other animals for what little forage exists in these desert ecosystems. Desert range land needs to restrict free-range grazing, require & enforce fencing, rotational grazing on grassland rangelands.

GIVEN OUR CLIMATE EMERGENCY, BLM MUST:
- Immediately put into conservation old growth and mature (MOG) forests, quickly for conservation purposes under the identification of “Areas for Critical Environmental Concern” (ACEC)
- Apply land health standards, based in part on Indigenous knowledge
- Add carbon sequestration in the definition of land health and implement a carbon accounting system
- Identify areas of deforestation and replant them with special attention to riparian zones as a very effective natural climate solution and beneficial to limit soil erosion and in-stream habitat
- change the definition of RESTORATION to include returning the land to a native plant landscape to support other species and improving biodiversity. It should mean land is returned to its natural, native ecological state—and NOT simply replanting a damaged landscape with an invasive plant species for cows as is a practice now
- Define restoration for each ecosystem
- Establish top priority to replant trees in deforested areas

Thank you for giving higher priority to conservation on BLM lands. I hope you will consider adding all of these necessary changes to your rule making. There is no time to lose.

Linda Perrine
Lincoln City, Oregon

As an HR professional, and a former manager, the I-9 verification process is administratively cumbersome, especially now with remote employees. With the onset of COVID it was evidenced by many employers that remote work is possible in many industries, and now employees look for jobs which allow them to work remotely in a state the employer may not operate in. During this time, I-9 document verifications were allowed to be done via electronic format (email, video conference, upload into a HRIS system during onboarding). Many employers and HR professionals are now dealing with how to manage completing I-9's and staying in compliance when onboarding remote employees who will be based from a state the employer currently doesn't have an office location or maybe the office location is a several hours drive to get to. If an employer is allowed to appoint a stranger to the organization as an authorized verifier on behalf of the company, but the company is still held liable for that person's error or omissions, then it would seem verifying these documents remotely would be just as acceptable. Also, the person who physically verifies the document has to complete page 2 of the form, which means the employer either has to explain to them how to complete it, or risk errors being made and having to go back and forth to correct them. 

Another suggestion that seems would work best for all parties involved would be to do away with the I-9 form, or at least the physical verification for remote employees, if that employer participates in E-verify. E-verify is a government system that immediately and electronically verifies that the employee is authorized to work based on the SS# and other documents provided on the I-9 form or the required employee information can be manually typed into the E-verify system. If all employers could move to E-verify it would be much more efficient for onboarding, record keeping, for internal audits, and for ICE audits. Instead of looking for I-9 forms that have extremely particular ways and rules to complete accurately, it would already be in the government system. Maybe like OIG reporting there would be a way to submit a report with new hires or employees that started after implementation date to E-verify for audits to ensure all E-verify are being run for new employees. 

When it comes to Work Authorization docs that expire and need to be renewed, this seems that could also be housed in E-verify and then allow the employer to submit a "reverification" E-verify request to confirm the validity of the renewed work authorization doc - ie visa, I-766, etc. 

We are in a technologically advanced society where so much that we do is now electronic, and it is my opinion that the employment eligibility verification/I-9 process needs to be updated to match where we are as a society. Plus, the technology for creating fraudulent documents has gotten better with these advances in technology, and are so close to the real thing, it would really be best for all to run the eligibility docs through E-verify.

Dear Mr. Kehoe:

Subject: Proposed Rules 15 CFR Part 923 - Coastal Zone Management Program Regulations, Subpart H - Changes to Approved Management Programs

We support the purposes of the proposed rules CFR Part 923 - Coastal Zone Management Program Regulations, Subpart H - Changes to Approved Management Programs, which provide a more effective and efficient process for states and the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to make changes to state coastal management programs. 

The Hawai'i Coastal Zone Management (CZM) Program has reviewed the proposed rules and has the following comments to offer.

1. Under Supplementary Information, the typographical error "VI. Miscellaneous Rulemaking Requirements" should be corrected to "V. Miscellaneous Rulemaking Requirements".

2. We support 923.81(a) that program changes may be submitted to NOAA on a cyclical basis (e.g., quarterly, twice a year, annually) or as the changes occur, which offers the states a flexible timeline to submit their program changes to NOAA for review and approval.

3. The proposed rules should change " 923.81 Program change procedures, deadlines, public notice and comment and application of federal consistency" to " 923.81 Program change procedures, deadlines, public notice and comment and application of approved changes." Pursuant to 923.81(f), the application of approved program changes includes changes to a state's management program and enforceable policies for federal consistency purposes. The phrase "application of approved changes" would be more appropriate to match the title of Subpart H - Changes to Approved Management Programs, and maintain the title consistency from 923.81 to 923.84.

4. Pursuant to 923.81(b), when NOAA receives a program change, NOAA shall notify the state (via email or letter) of the date the program change was received and NOAA's expected decision deadline. NOAA will also notify the state if NOAA determines the submission is incomplete. The proposed rules should include a deadline under 923.81(b) for NOAA to determine and notify the state whether its submission is complete. Otherwise, the program change review timeline, which applies to the review period(s) as indicated by 923.81(c), will not start until the missing information is submitted.

5. A state's public notice is required by 923.81(e)(2)(iii) to indicate that any comments on the content of the program change shall be submitted to NOAA through NOAA's Program Change Web site within 21 calendar days of the date NOAA's review period starts. However, as required by 923.81(e)(1), when the state posts its public notice prior to, or on the same date as, the date the state submits the electronic program change to NOAA, the state does not know the date when NOAA's review period will start. Therefore, when a state posts its public notice on the state's management program Web site, the deadline for comment submitted to NOAA has to be left as "to be determined," which shall be updated when the day one of NOAA's review period is available from NOAA.

6. We support 923.82(c)(4) that the states are not required to submit program changes for local government coastal management programs or plans that do not contain enforceable policies for federal consistency review.

7. We support 923.82(d) that the states are not required to submit as program changes, any changes to state Clean Air Act (CAA) and Clean Water Act (CWA) provisions.

I grew up in Colorado and believed its wilderness areas were the most beautiful in the world. Then, I visited southeast Alaska and met the Tlingit people who view the Tongass as sacred land. This is by far the most stunning land I have ever seen and it is clear the Native peoples treasure this land and use it to gather medicines, fish, and hunt . It is not land that needs to be logged. It needs to be protected to honor their centuries-old way of life. Leaving these forests intact also helps keep the carbon locked in those trees from promoting climate change. 

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

Dear Secretary Purdue,

Please withdraw the proposed rule to 'modernize' swine slaughter inspection. Instead, issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety.

Consumers will be put at risk by the proposed rule. Current regulations protect consumers from foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. 

In your proposal, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide.

The New Swine Inspection System will hand over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter establishment employees. The proposal also removes caps on line speeds, increasing the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination, and other food safety issues. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer, and this proposal will not achieve that. Instead, it has the potential to make food less safe by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

For the sake of public health, please withdraw the proposed rule and design a new rule that prioritizes food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness.

Sincerely,

 Clarification is needed on exactly how "Fiscal Capacity" will be defined and how TTR, GDP and Per Capita personal income by local area will be used in factoring a disaster declaration? 
o There is a 2 year lag in the TTR data, so information cannot be used to show the current fiscal capacity of the state. 
o How much weight will this information carry in a determination of a declaration?
 This skewed information should not be used when making a decision on whether or not to approve a disaster declaration.
 It appears from Table 4-IA "Declarations Factor Marginal Analysis" that FEMA is saying there will be $0 impact on the state in collecting Fiscal Capacity information. However, there will be a cost to the state associated with personnel time utilized in collecting the data.
o The additional time and cost associated with factoring the Fiscal Capacity of an area will put an added strain on state staff. This could lead to a longer time period before requesting a JPDA or a Declaration, which in turn will lead to an additional need in the community, strain to VOAD's and other NGO's who assist with response and recovery.
 Will FEMA consider private resources that could potentially be available (i.e. used in the past)? For example, Lilly, United Way, other NGO's?
o In 2008 & 2012, Indiana received a grant from the Lilly Foundation due to the magnitude of the events in those years. This should have no bearing on the Fiscal Capacity of the state or whether or the resources we have available to recover. A grant of this magnitude is not always available and the state will not always receive assistance in this way. The state also has no authority to direct NGO's to provide funding.
 Will a state's fiscal capacity need to be identified BEFORE requesting a JPDA?
o If a state's fiscal capacity will need to be identified before the state can request a JPDA, much time will have to be dedicated to obtaining this information, thus, leading to an additional need in the community, strain to VOAD's and other NGO's who assist with response and recovery.
 How will FEMA define" technically qualified" individuals who will conduct damage assessments?
o These individuals need to all be trained properly and understand the specifics that surround damage assessments. Will all of these individuals be engineers or otherwise certified professionals?
 Need clarification on how factors will be weighted? Fiscal Capacity and VOAD capabilities.
o Will a state's fiscal capacity carry more weight than the capabilities of the volunteer organizations? Or vice versa?
 How is capacity of the volunteer agencies in the state determined? Federal funding? Past donations and availability of volunteers?
o From year to year, the INVOAD (Indiana Volunteer Organizations Active in Disaster) resources and volunteers can change dramatically. One year, there may be grant funding available and plentiful volunteers, but the next year all this may change. This year, in particular, we have had a shortage in volunteers, but in 2012, the number of volunteers was overwhelming. The states capacity to recover should not be based on past data when factors are constantly changing. An INVOAD's capacity to assist the state is also affected by on-going disasters throughout the country. Therefore, current capacity must be measured in real time.

The

 (EPN) is an organization comprised of almost 500 U.S.

human health, and the environment. We harness the expertise of former EPA career staff and

administration that have a serious impact on public health and environmental protections. 

EPN recognizes that EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) is attempting to accelerate the 

pace of progress in reducing the exposure to lead in drinking water, and supports many of the specific 

changes designed to improve upon the existing LCR.  

To start, EPN strongly supports selected elements of the EPA proposal: (1) the improved public 

lead service line (LSL) inventories, replacement plans, and their public availability; (2) minimization of 

partial lead service line replacements (LSLRs) and elimination of testing out provisions; (3) improved site

corrosion control treatment requirements and monitoring; (5) the explicit prohibition of some forms of 

“gaming”; and (6) faster communication with residents whose water has action level exceedances and 

education of homeowners and residents regarding lead contamination and mitigation.   

Despite these positive changes in the current proposal, EPN is deeply concerned that the proposed 

LCR fails to speed up protection of the public from the harmful effects of lead in drinking water.  

Lead is a highly toxic pollutant that can damage neurological, renal, cardiovascular, immunological, 

developmental, and reproductive systems. The best available science supports EPA’s maximum contaminant 

level (MCL) goal of zero lead in drinking water. Children are at higher risk from the effects of lead than 

adults due to differences in physiology and behavior. The following link shows blood lead levels measured 

in children in recent years as reported in a number of the states by the Centers for Disease Control (CDC):

following link: (

US Fish and Wildlife Services (FWS) must uphold the integrity of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and drop its attempt to weaken it by reducing essential critical habitat.
This proposed rule would reverse FWS' 2016 critical habitat policy position that FWS will generally not exclude Federal lands from critical habitat designations. Instead, it would give permittees and licensees on federal lands the ability to demand FWS review proposed critical habitat designations for potential economic impacts. By stating that FWS shall exclude area when the economic costs of designating them outweigh the benefits, the proposed rule is actually more restrictive than the ESA itself, which states the agency "may" exclude those areas. Such weighing of "economic cost" are distorted because the economic benefits of critical habitat designation usually do not include a full value of the ecosystem services provided by the conserved land. 

The proposed rule would also give undue weight to evidence offered by state, local governments, private interests, and expert or "firsthand" sources. The proposed rule would require FWS to prioritize that information over FWS information unless the agency has information specifically rebutting it. This could allow non-federal entities including those who may not have conservation goals in mind to effectively drive critical habitat designations. 

Protection of habitat is central to the conservation of imperiled species. The purpose of the ESA is to conserve "the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend," as well as to protect and recover endangered species and threatened species themselves. Critical habitat designations advance the ESA's recovery goals by striking a science-driven balance between conservation and economic activity. This proposed rule would hinder, not help, the ability of FWS to protect species and the ecosystems they depend upon.
 The Endangered Species Act is one of our nation's most successful laws. In its current state, it has been more than 99 percent successful at stopping extinction. 
Any weakening of this widely supported law is unacceptable. USFWS must withdraw this disastrous rule. 

Sincerely,

We urge that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety, and that admission for the duration of status remain in effect.

Dear All,

I am submitting comments on the Select Agent status of Brucella abortus. I support the removal of B.abortus from the select agent list. My background and connection to this issue is that I am a strong advocate for wild, free-roaming bison (buffalo).

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

Thank you for this opportunity and your consideration of my comments.

Sincerely,
Marina Mooney

I am a practicing private allergist and academic teacher at Georgetown University School of Medicine. My nurse and I have been preparing allergen extracts in my office and at the Georgetown Allergy Clinic for my patients using aseptic technique for many years. The FDA Draft Guidance would require that allergen extracts now be prepared in an ISO Class 5 environment. Meeting this standard would be prohibitively costly and would make it impossible for myself and most all my colleagues to continue to provide allergy immunotherapy to our patients. In all the years that I have been practicing I have seen no incidence of infections or other problems associated with allergen extracts prepared in my office. I have discussed safety concerns regarding injected allergen extracts/medications and allergen subcutaneous injections have the lowest risks. The Draft Guidance goes beyond what is necessary to ensure patient safety and would threaten patient access to care. There are millions of Americans whose suffering has been alleviated by access to immunotherapy. Not only would this requirement not improve patient safety (as it's already very safe) and cripple access of the common American to an effective therapy for their allergy and asthma, it will drastically eliminate a subspeciality as providing allergen immunotherapy is the focus and financial support of most practices. If this passes without an exception then the already reduced qualified applicants for allergy and immunology fellowship training will drastically reduce and eliminate our speciality. This will in the end hurt our health care system and a patient's access to a currently inexpensive treatment with life long benefit. Obtaining EMRs were already a strain on solo practices. I will not be able to continue to provide allergen immunotherapy if I am required to have an ISO level 5 room in my practice to be able to prepare allergen immunotherapy. USP's proposed guidelines on compounding and allergen immunotherapy is unsafe and very expensive for the patients and will again cut off access to millions of patient, a safe, effective therapy. I strongly urge the FDA to create an exception for allergenic extracts prepared by allergist board certified and allergy fellowship trained physicians in their offices for their own patients as requested in the comments submitted by the Advocacy Council of the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology.

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

There are genuine certification labels that we need to protect; we should not allow them to be overwhelmed by meaningless or deceptive labels that might look good but are not.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

My name is Harry Griffing, Jr. I am the previous owner and now a minority stockholder of Griffing Flying Service, Inc. based at Erie-Ottawa International Airport in Port Clinton, OH. We were recently notified that the exemption for aircraft under 64 passengers will expire this coming June. While I am sorry that we did not know about this rule change sooner, I would like to make my voice heard now. 
The main route we fly into Canada is to Pelee Island, Ontario. Total distance is 20 miles. The surrounding area poses no difference in plants or animals. We have been flying this route since April 7, 1962 and during these 63+ years and tens of thousands of passengers, we have never received a letter from AQI stating they’ve found invasive species on board our aircraft. Using APHIS’s own set of standards, we clearly do not pose a risk. 
While we do fly U.S. residents to Pelee Island for pleasure, we have had multiple occasions where we have had to bring U.S. residents back into the U.S. due to medical emergencies. Eliminating the possibility for air travel for these situations is not fair to our own citizens. 
The aircraft we use carry between 3 and 9 passengers and are only over a short distance. We propose that an exemption is written to account for even smaller passenger numbers than the original rule exempted. Possibly 9 passengers would be a fair number. Additionally, a rule could be set for flying within so many miles of the U.S. border. Making the limit 50-100 miles would keep all plant and animal life within the same geographic range, which would lower the risk that you’re worried about. 
My parents started Griffing Flying Service in 1937. While I know your worry is the threat of invasive species and not small businesses, it’s hard to stand by and watch what my parents built crumble when we do not cause any damage. I have read a lot of the comments written so far and I think there are a lot of option as to how fees could be structured differently while also not killing businesses along the way. 

Harry T Griffing, Jr.
Chairman of Griffing Flying Service, Inc.

Regarding FSIS-2016-0017: I'm writing to oppose the proposed Modernization of Swine Slaughter Inspection rule, which would roll back progress for animals, consumers and workers. The NSIS would place key food safety inspection into the hands of slaughter plants themselves. Compassion Over Killing's investigation of a plant under the pilot high-speed slaughter program, HIMP, revealed pigs covered in feces and pus-filled abscesses being processed for human consumption with a USDA seal of approval. The investigation also showed pigs being dragged, kicked,excessively shocked, and improperly stunned as workers struggled to keep up with the facility's high line speeds. There is widespread opposition to the high-speed slaughter program within the federal government, including USDA whistleblowers and members of Congress. The USDA's own Office of the Inspector General stated that the" HIMP program has shown no measurable improvement to the inspection process." I urge you to protect workers, consumers, and animals and END, rather than expand, this program.

Having worked on all of the single engine models built by American Aviation, Grumman American, Gulfstream Aerospace and American General for the past 25 years as an A&P/IA, it is obvious that there are major differences in the design and structure of the horizontal stabilizer and the attachment of the elevator between the AA-5 failure that prompted this proposed AD and the AA-5A, AA-5B and AG-5B models. While I agree that bond-line separation can be serious (as shown by the AA-5 failure), inspection for such is documented in the Manufacture's Maintenance Manuals and should be performed on a 100 hour and annual basis. But with regard to this AD proposal, one size does NOT fit all and some of the comments in the NPRM justifying the proposal are not correct.

On the AA-5 and AA-1C (and AA-1,-1A,-1B) the outer elevator bearing support bracket is held on to the rather thin stabilizer outer rib with only two MS24694-S53 screws with not a lot of spread to counteract the moment imposed by the elevator force. Such is not the case with the AA5A/B and AG-5B models. On those the elevator is supported with bearing brackets at both mid-span and outer ends with four AN-4 bolts (in each bracket) to the stabilizer rear spar. And the distance from the hinge to the bracket support is far less than on the AA-5. In my opinion (as a mechanical engineer) you could have a hugh length of stabilizer skin delamination to the spar and still have enough strength to support the elevator. Pure speculation, but it is obvious that this design is far more robust than on the AA-5 that failed, probably many times more so. 

Consequently, I feel a failure of the elevator hinge (on the AA5A/B/AG-5B) is extremely remote and does not rise to the level of requiring an AD note, such as AD 2021-14-12, nor is it supported by any failure in this area. I feel a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) would be more appropriate in this instance. And that would apply to inspection of other bond-line joints such as the wings, etc. Here again that is already covered in the Maintenance Manual. 

Finally, why was the AG-5B not included in the NPRM since it has an identical structure as the AA-5A and AA-5B? It is subject to the same possible corrosion and freezing concerns as with any of the other models.

This comment is filed on behalf of the International Trade Surety Association (“ITSA”) in response 
to the above-referenced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. 
 
Our members are customs surety agents who, operating under U.S. Department of Treasury 
certification to secure federal government obligations, provide in excess of 70% of the bonds currently on 
file with U.S. Customs & Border Protection (“Customs” or “CBP”). Our Association and its members have 
long worked constructively with CBP on assuring that customs transactions are properly secured and that 
bond procedures are efficient and effective to protect the interests of CBP, sureties and the trade (i.e., 
importers, drawback claimants, customs brokers, carriers, custodians, et.al.). 
 
We offer the following three comments regarding the Proposed Rule. 
 
 
First, in adopting TFTEA, Congress amended the drawback laws to provide that the importer – in 
addition to the drawback claimant and its surety - would be responsible for satisfying government claims 
against drawback overpayments. The statute specifically states that the importer and the claimant are 
“jointly and severally liable” for the drawback obligations; it does not mention the importer’s surety. 
 
 
The Proposed Rule is the first and only suggestion that the importer’s surety on the import 
transaction should also be “jointly and severally liable” with the importer for the importer’s separate joint 
and several liability with a third-party claimant’s drawback acts. We believe this is unauthorized by statute, 
and in any event, creates an open-ended obligation which cannot be rationally underwritten by sureties and 
is likely to become a substantial impediment to the facilitation of trade which is a most critical purpose of 
the U.S. customs bond surety program. 
 
 
There is no legal authority to add this obligation to the import bond. Congress is well aware of the 
role of sureties in import and drawback programs, and elected to make the “importer” and not “the importer 
and its surety” liable for obligations of a drawback claimant. 
 
 
This is not an unthoughtful choice of words in drafting the statute: it is a logical recognition of the 
fundamental difference between an import transaction and a drawback claim. The surety on an import 
transaction underwrites and secures the obligations of the importer with respect to import transactions; it

I, and most of my fellow citizens, are the descendants of immigrants who were granted a new start in this country. It disappointsme terribly thatU.S. Citizenship andImmigration Services is unwilling to extend the same degree of respect and generosity to immigrants today.

Furthermore, the collection of extensive personal biometric data by a government agency is unnecessaryand, for lack of a better word, creepy. The accrual of biometric data like voice prints and DNA is an overreach on the part of the government into not just the personal lives, but the actual bodies, the physical beings, of its citizenry and prospective citizens.

I'm also concerned that the ruling would allow thisbiometric information to be shared with law enforcement. High-profile instances of police violence within just the last few months show that law enforcement is not - perhaps cannot - be disentangled from personal biases and societal injustices. How can we be certain that the massive amount of data collected will not be turned against well-meaning and perhaps vulnerable people? I don't think we can be sure. The collection of this information strikes me as a threat to the rights of American citizens.

Thank you for your consideration of my comment. I hope it will encourage a withdrawal of this proposed rule.

Sincerely,

Rive Cadwallader
Philadelphia, PA

Under this rule, the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System (NSIS) would place key food safety inspection duties into the hands of slaughter plants themselves, while these facilities operate at dangerously high line speeds, and many problems will likely go unnoticed. 

Compassion Over Killing's investigation of a plant under the pilot high-speed slaughter program, HIMP, revealed pigs covered in feces and pus-filled abscesses being processed for human consumption with a USDA seal of approval. The investigation also showed pigs being dragged, kicked, excessively shocked, and improperly stunned as workers struggled to keep up with the facility's high line speeds. There is widespread opposition to the high-speed slaughter program within the federal government, including by USDA whistleblowers and members of Congress. The USDA's own Office of the Inspector General stated that the "HIMP program has shown no measurable improvement to the inspection process." 

A major cultural shift is happening where consumers more and more are choosing to eat food that comes from humane and natural systems. Nothing about this system is humane or natural. The general public has been learning more and more about programs like high-speed slaughter, and choosing to reject it by eating food derived from other systems. This program will only drive more consumers away and hurt the bottom line for companies.

I urge you to protect workers, consumers, and animals and end, rather than expand, this program.

The DOT should tier the delay standard based on the length of the passenger's flight(s) rather than on its categorization as domestic or international. The purpose of creating differing delay standards seems to be based on the feasibility of delivering a delayed piece of baggage to a customer, not some factor exclusively tied to an itinerary's international or domestic nature. This would resolve some of the DOT's concerns regarding how to categorize single versus multiple-ticket itineraries as well as itineraries involving both domestic and international flights. 
 When a bag is delayed, a passenger has likely suffered two harms: (1) she does not have the contents of her luggage at the time she needs them and (2) she likely must inconvenience herself to retrieve the luggage. The DOT can alleviate the two harms as follows. 
 If the DOT chooses to stay with the 12/15 (or 18/30) hour definition of "delayed" (and not adopt the system proposed above), it should choose the 12-hour definition for domestic flights, rather than the 15-hour definition. If, for example, a flight arrives at 9 a.m., the bag should be "delayed" if it does not arrive by 9 p.m., not 12a.m. By 9 p.m., a passenger has already suffered the inconvenience of not having had her baggage for a full day (of waking hours) once 12 hours have passed. Requesting that she retrieve or be available to receive her luggage between hours 12-15 is arbitrary.
 As for determining when the delay-period ends, the DOT should use all definitions it has proposed and allow the passenger to select which is more convenient for her.
 
 The DOT should also consider ensuring that there is a uniform, online mechanism by which customers can notify the carrier about the delayed or lost baggage.

To whom it may concern:
 
I commend the federal government and the FDA for taking up the issue of breast density notification for women, to help empower patients with more information when they are considering important decisions regarding their breast health care.[1]

The literature is clear: breast density is an important health factor [2, 3, 4]. It is also clear, as evidenced by the 38 notification laws in various states, that women want to know their breast density so they can make informed decisions. However, based on my decades of experience in the science of breast density, I believe there are two areas where the current draft wording could be improved.

Firstly, breast density assessment in clinical practice has traditionally been performed visually. Since the introduction of digital mammography and tomosynthesis, however, readers have been strongly and unknowingly influenced by variations in image processing and imaging mode [5]. This undoubtedly compromises consistency and accuracy, such that some women are provided with results that may not reflect their true breast density; the inter- and intra-observer variability among readers are proof of this [6]. FDA-cleared, automated breast density solutions that work on the raw data from x-ray machines can avoid these problems, and it might be pertinent for the FDA to point this out in its final recommendations [7].

Secondly, the FDAs proposal to establish four categories for reporting breast tissue density in the mammography report perpetuates the use of categorized systems, such as the breast composition assessment portion of BI-RAD [8]. A womans personal breast density does not fall into one of four categories. Rather, her density lies along a continuum. Two women with broadly different densities on that continuum should not be categorized the same because it has been clearly shown that their risk of developing breast cancer and the risk of a mammogram masking a cancer are also continuous values [9]. Again, automated breast density solutions can help resolve this issue by providing a continuous breast density measurement, and in the case of volumetric breast density can provide a measurement which has a sound scientific basis and actual physical meaning (the breast is, after all, a 3D organ). The FDA should consider what breast density scoring system is preferable for a woman.

The FDA has a unique opportunity to help women avoid the scourge of breast cancer. By ensuring that a woman is well informed about her true breast density, the FDA can help her referring physician make sure she receives supplemental screening when necessary and is appropriately advised of her risk of developing breast cancer. Only then can a woman protect herself and her family.

Sincerely,

Dr. Ralph Highnam, PhD
CEO & Chief Scientist, Volpara Health Technologies
Author, with Sir Professor Mike Brady, Mammographic Image Analysis

My name is Hayden Maschmeier, I am a pilot flying for Griffing Flying Service. 

I'd like to start off by saying that I understand the need for agricultural control of what enters the country. I understand the importance of protecting what we have here in the US and not ruining that with any foreign species. However, I think our operation should continue to have some form of exemption from the proposed rule/exemption change that has been outlined here.

Our operation is based in Port Clinton, OH at KPCW airport. We fly to the Lake Erie Islands, including our longest flight which is to Pelee Island, Canada. This flight has a distance of less than 20 miles. On this route, my coworkers and I fly exclusively people and their immediate personal belongings, no cargo is transported. Of all personal belongings that come along for the trip, my coworkers and I will hand load all of it, no machinery is used. The planes we fly have at most 10 seats including the pilot, with our 4 and 6 seat aircraft flying the route most often. The intimacy of the operation paired with the lack of space and complexity of our aircraft likely contributes to the fact that we have been flying this exact route since 1962 and not once have we received any notice that we have transported any invasive specie into the US. 

This operation, and I'm sure there are more that do a similar thing, would be disproportionately affected by this change in regulation while posing a much lower threat to the overall purpose of this more strict enforcement. This increased fee would destroy our ability to offer our services to our Pelee passengers. 
Because of this, we ask that the current exemption remain or a different exemption be put in place. Examples of these could be flights carrying 9 or less passengers. Additionally, a distance exemption could be considered of flights from origin to destination of say 50 miles or a value deemed close enough to pose little risk.

We appreciate your consideration.

Best,
Hayden Maschmeier

This comment is directed toward the section of the proposed fee schedule rule that would transfer over $200 million from USCIS to ICE.
The proposed USCIS fee schedule rule transfers over $200 million in USCIS revenue from customer fees to ICE (Immigration Customs Enforcement). I do not understand the rationale for such a transfer. USCIS is a self-funding agency that operates based on the revenue it receives in fees it charges its customers. ICE is funded by congress. It seems that if ICE requires more money, it should ask congress for more money. Is there any justification for why USCIS customer fees should be increased just to make a gift to a separate government agency?
As enacted in 1988, sections 286(n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1356 (n)) provide that all fee-based revenues deposited into the "Immigration Examinations Fee Account" shall remain available until expended to pay the expenses incurred in providing immigration adjudication and naturalization services. Accessing the IEFA simply to gift funds to ICE would run afoul of the 1988 act and is not lawful.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

This issue is very important to me and my family. Please help consumers to understand what we're buying. We care about animal welfare.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

Like many consumers, I rely on package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised" I assume the claim has substance that is backed by a regulatory agency. 

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) would allow meat and chicken producers to make up their own standards and then self-regulate these "non-standards"--all with the sanction of the FSIS. I find it perplexing and deeply disturbing that companies would still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit. 

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Time and time again industry has shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating and policing itself. Companies are taking advantage of consumers, and grossly overcharging them, by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels to bring in more profits--all while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare. 

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers. 

FSIS owes it to the American public to set a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," take steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensure that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

As recently as October 11, 2017, Hawaii News Now reported four nene were killed on Kauai. The article states that period as a nesting and mating time where the nene are moving around in search of food (HNN, 2017). Increased urbanization decreases the amount of food available and increases the chances of the nene being struck by vehicles as they are searching further for food sources.
