While we understand and agree with a process by which post-secondary institutions demonstrate the value and return on investment of the educational programs they offer, we suggest that the Department consider a replacement to GE that is structured to compare the cost of a program with the salaries that can be earned with that credential, as opposed to looking at actual student debt and actual student earnings of individual cohorts. There are literally hundreds of reasons that the current GE structure will produce false, erroneous, and misleading information. On one hand, by looking at actual student debt information at the time of graduation, there is no accounting for the various ways that students pay for their education.

 A student who pays for their education fully with personal funds while in school has no debt in the GE metric.
 A student who leaves school with debt but pays it off within a few months of graduation is counted as one who has debt in the GE metric, but is truly no different that the first student mentioned aboveboth students payed their cost of attendance and have no debt by the time they begin employment.
 A student who pays using Veterans benefits has no debt. Schools with a higher veteran population, then, are unfairly advantaged with the current GE regulations, and could technically charge as much as they want for their education with no GE ramifications whatsoever. 
 A student who borrows very little money and pays out of pocket while in school wisely limits their debt; students who borrow the exact amount needed to cover tuition might also borrow wisely; those who borrow well more than they need for their education from multiple sources could be considered an unwise borrower. In all three of these scenarios, the students leave school with a completely different debt burden, but the cost of their education was the same. 

With the current GE regulation, the school is being penalized or rewarded on the students' borrowing practices, which are out of the school's control. Using the actual debt burden with which a student leaves school with does not actually tell the Department anything about the cost of the program, the value of the program, or whether that cost can be reasonably offset by employment opportunities. The only thing the current GE formula does is punishes schools for irresponsible student borrowing practices. 

On the other hand, by using student Social Security information to determine actual graduate earnings, the Department is asking for a range of misleading information that does not accurately demonstrate the value of an institution's education. There are many valid reasons that a student might not choose to pursue employment after school:

 Some students are unable to work because of disabilities or family obligations.
 Some students stop working to support their families by raising children at home.
 Students sometimes benefit intellectually from academic programs but decided not to pursue employment in field afterwards, but instead, pursue different interests or further academic study.
 Many students benefit from freelance work, self-employment, or gratuity-earning employment that is not captured in Social Security information.
 Some students fail to fill out their tax returns.

But that is exactly what happens with the current Gainful Employment regulations: if students fail to report earnings on taxes or report earnings incorrectly, our schools are punished! On Inspection Frequency and Cost Burden

Comment: The proposed tap inspection and repair/replacement requirements impose substantial labor and financial costs, especially on small operators and public sector agencies. FAA should consider a tiered or risk-based inspection interval for low-utilization or community-serving operators and provide guidance for financial assistance to those disproportionately affected.

Supporting Evidence: In similar contexts, mandatory equipment upgrades have caused financial hardship and reduced access for rural and nonprofit emergency service providers (GAO, 2015, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-15-98).

On Worker Protections and Training

Comment: All required inspections and repairs should be performed by unionized or properly certified technicians, with clear protections against wage theft, overwork, or misclassification. FAA should require transparency in labor practices and support ongoing worker safety training.

Supporting Evidence: Evidence shows unionized maintenance leads to safer, more reliable aviation outcomes and reduces workforce exploitation (EPI, 2023, https://www.epi.org/publication/union-advantage-new-data/).

On Environmental and Community Impact

Comment: FAA must assess the environmental impact of increased MRB replacements, especially regarding disposal of hazardous composites and metals. Require operators to recycle or safely dispose of MRBs, and encourage development of greener rotor blade materials and repair techniques.

Supporting Evidence: Improper disposal of aircraft parts poses environmental risks, while “green design” standards have cut waste and pollution in the EU aerospace sector (ICCT, 2020, https://theicct.org/publication/sustainable-aviation-eu-sept20/).

On Economic Equity for Small and Public Operators

Comment: High MRB replacement costs threaten economic viability for air ambulance, firefighting, and rural operators, risking loss of vital public services. FAA should publish a socioeconomic impact analysis and consider cost offsets or grants for public-benefit entities.

Supporting Evidence: Emergency service providers in rural and marginalized communities have been disproportionately affected by high compliance costs (NPR, 2018, https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2018/05/30/615359233).

On Safety Reporting, Transparency, and Public Access

Comment: FAA should require reporting and public disclosure of inspection findings, repairs, and failures, broken down by operator type and geography, to foster accountability and help communities advocate for safer air transport.

Supporting Evidence: Public data reporting in transportation safety has improved outcomes and enabled informed oversight by stakeholders (USDOT, 2022, https://www.transportation.gov/data-analysis).

On Labor and Equity in MRB Supply Chains

Comment: The AD should encourage sourcing MRBs and repairs from companies with strong worker protections, nondiscrimination, and local hiring policies. FAA should publish supply chain guidance to prevent exploitation, particularly of workers in global supply chains.

Supporting Evidence: Ethical procurement improves quality and supports community wealth (ILO, 2017, https://www.ilo.org/global/topics/decent-work/lang--en/index.htm).

On Compliance Flexibility for Critical Services

Comment: Critical service operators (air ambulances, disaster relief) should have temporary compliance waivers or rapid repair authorizations when public safety is at stake, with oversight to prevent abuse.

Supporting Evidence: Flexible regulatory pathways for critical infrastructure have prevented service disruptions in health and safety emergencies (CDC, 2020, https://www.cdc.gov/cpr/infographics/emergencyresponse.htm).

On behalf of the undersigned wildlife protection organizations, we are writing to provide 
comments on APHIS’s Proposed Amendments to National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) 
Implementing Procedures. Our members have recreational, aesthetic, moral and professional 
interests in wildlife impacted by Wildlife Services’ “wildlife damage management” programs 
across the country. We seek to ensure that the proposed revised rules will properly implement 
NEPA by helping public officials “make decisions that are based on understanding of 
environmental consequences, and take actions that protect, restore, and enhance the 
environment.” 40 C.F.R. § 1500.1(c). We note that NEPA procedures require that 
“environmental information is available to public officials and citizens before decisions are made 
and before actions are taken,” 40 C.F.R. § 1500.1(b), and to that end, we routinely participate in 
public comment periods opened under NEPA on the actions of Wildlife Services. 
 
Actions Normally Requiring Environmental Assessments 
 
 
In the proposed revision to 7 C.F.R. § 372.6, APHIS identifies “Actions normally 
requiring environmental assessments.” We agree that an action in this category is “typically 
characterized by its limited scope,” but we disagree with the inclusion of “State-wide or district-
wide programs” as examples of actions with limited scope. We are particularly concerned with 
the addition of another category of actions that would require an Environmental Assessment 
(EA) rather than an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), specifically, “Programs . . . to reduce

provided in the proposed § 372.6(e). Despite your assertion that “WS’ use of EAs for this 
purpose has withstood judicial review” (Substantiating Document for Proposed Amendments -- 
June 2016, at p. 7), a federal court has determined that state-wide analysis of Wildlife Services’ 
wildlife killing program in Washington violated NEPA for failure to prepare an Environmental 
Impact Statement (EIS). Cascadia Wildlands v. Woodruff, 151 F. Supp. 3d 1153 (W.D. Wash. 
2015) (“Wildlife Services acted arbitrarily and capriciously and contrary to law by not preparing

Introduction 
 
 
By publication in the February 28, 2022, edition of the Federal Register (87 Fed. Reg. 
11156 et seq.), the Department of Transportation (DOT) has proposed to amend the drug and 
alcohol testing protocols applicable to transportation workers by adding an option for oral fluid 
testing for drugs as an alternative to the current urine sample testing. The Notice of Proposed 
Rulemaking (NPRM) also proposes to harmonize the existing transportation worker drug testing 
standards with the current standards established by the Department of Health and Human 
Services (HHS) for the testing of the federal workplace.

time-definite, scheduled and on-demand delivery needs of their customers around the world.

and have over 1.5 million full-time equivalent employees across the world. 
 
The Association supports the DOT proposal to offer optional oral fluid drug testing as an 
alternative to the urine testing protocols currently in place. Adoption of this alternative will 
provide added flexibility to the drug testing program, may well result in more accurate test 
results, and will potentially result in both time and cost savings. 
Discussion 
 
 Transportation employee drug and alcohol testing is currently regulated by 49 CFR Part 
40 and requires that such testing is conducted through the collection of urine samples. Until 
relatively recently, urine testing was the only acceptable method of testing for banned 
substances. However, as noted in the NPRM, “[w]hile the science supporting oral fluid testing 
did not meet the standards of HHS in 2004, science and research studies have now reached a 
point where HHS is able to determine that oral fluid testing is an appropriate alternative testing 
method for identifying illicit drug use in the Federal workplace. As such, HHS proposed adding 
oral fluid testing to the Federal employee workplace testing program (80 FR 28054, May 15, 
2015) and finalized this proposal, which became effective for Federal employee workplace 
testing on January 1, 2020 (84 FR 57554, Oct. 25, 2019).” 87 Fed. Reg. at 11157. The current 
NPRM would extend the ability to use oral fluid specimen testing to transportation workers 
subject to 49 CFR Part 40.

 
3

in the NPRM. For example, the collection of oral fluids would be observed in all cases, thereby 
virtually eliminating any possibility of adulterating the samples collected. On the other hand,

The watersheds of "America's salmon forest," as the Tongass is commonly known, contribute approximately 50 million fish annually to Alaska's multi-billion-dollar commercial salmon industry. Simply put, Southeast Alaska's economy, culture, and storied fish and wildlife resources are all tied to the health of the Tongass. I also support investments in recreational access and infrastructure, which support Alaska's outdoor recreation and visitor industries, as well as local workforce development. While the Forest Service and community partners ramp up capacity to perform more restoration and recreation-based work, a swift reinstatement of the Alaska Roadless Rule is in order. Comment summary:
Air pollution reduces life expectancy and causes respiratory and heart conditions that limit people's ability to work, exercise and go to school, and the burdens of air pollution disproportionately harm communities of color.

A stronger ozone standard would save lives and protect the health of children, seniors, and other medically vulnerable populations, especially in communities impacted by cumulative exposure. 

Similar to the particulate matter standard, strengthening the ozone standard would incentivize clean tech innovation and boost efforts to invest in renewable energy and cleaner transportation, including low- and zero emission school buses,trucks, and electric passenger vehicles, jump starting our economic recovery and ushering in a green economy strong enough to lift people out of poverty.

Introduction

The currents levels of domestic, human-caused air pollution are killing over 100,000 Americans each year, and disproportionately killing people of color. Before finalizing the rule, APHIS should substantially revise its proposals to revise and update the standards governing the humane care and handling of captive marine mammals. The current proposal ignores a wealth of scientific evidence obtained over the past three decades and essentially maintains a long-outdated status quo for the captive marine mammal industry.

Scientific evidence of the needs of animals of all types is growing exponentially. You must support improvements to increase space allotments for animals contained by human choice and for entertainment to make a horrible life a bit better.

While the agency has proposed several improvements to the standards, such as requiring shade for all outdoor marine mammal enclosures and ramps for older or injured seals, sea lions, polar bears, and sea otters to exit pools more easily, these are minor compared to the significant failures in the proposed rule.

The agency proposes no changes to the space requirements, claiming it is unaware of any science on which to base such changes. In fact, there is a tremendous body of recent research using increasingly sophisticated tagging technology to monitor fine-scale movement patterns of individual marine mammals, especially cetaceans and polar bears. These species travel tremendous distances and dive very deep, making the current minimum space requirements totally inhumane. The best available science for seals, sea lions, and sea otters--even for the slow, plant-eating manatee--also supports major space increases.

The current space standards were set over 30 years ago and have no basis in science or even best practices within the captive display industry. As an example, for up to two orcas, a facility need only provide a circular tank with a diameter twice as wide and a depth half as deep as an average adult orca is long. This standard does not even allow the animal to position itself fully in the vertical plane (its tail would touch and drag on the bottom before the animal reaches full upright orientation). This cannot be considered adequate!

While the rule refers to peer-reviewed papers for proposed changes to some standards (e.g., lighting requirements), it claims the agency is unaware of such papers for other standards (e.g., temperature requirements) and therefore proposes no major changes. Yet a considerable amount of research has been conducted within the past 15 years related to most if not all of the affected standards. 

The proposed rule would still allow pinnipeds to be housed in enclosures with tanks filled with fresh water. Allowing the maintenance of a marine mammal in fresh water is clearly an inappropriate welfare standard.

Several standards have been weakened, particularly regarding interactive programs such as swim-with-dolphin encounters. For example, the standard for the interaction time for each cetacean per day has been increased from two hours to three hours, not based on science or even industry best practices, but simply "on information provided by licensees ... which suggested that the marine mammals would not be harmed by a modest increase in interactive time per day." Facility "suggestions" represent a clear conflict of interest and should never be the sole basis for changes to standards.

The agency asked in previous notices if noise standards should be established. In several instances, noise levels, particularly in air, are extremely high (in theme parks, virtually every night there is a fireworks display directly over the marine mammal enclosures). Noise standards must be established for marine mammal facilities.

In sum, the proposed rule is grossly inadequate and fails to take into account current scientific understanding of the needs of marine mammals. APHIS must substantially strengthen the requirements for keeping cetaceans in captivity before the rule is finalized.

The agency’s proposed rule is well received by many employers, due to increased prevalence of remote employment and the technology advances which make in-person document inspection increasingly irrelevant as an enforcement tool to verify ability of any individual to work in the United States. As context, IRCA was created in the mid-1980s prior to the development of the commercial internet, high definition video and other technological advances. These technological advances have both changed the way Americans work, enabling widespread remote employment as well as providing many potential secure alternatives to in-person document inspection. The model on which IRCA was built—in-person employment at a single bricks-and-mortar worksite—no longer exists for an increasing number of US employers. The proposal is welcome as an attempt to modernize the employment verification process to account for these technological and societal changes.

In my experience both as private immigration counsel for employers coast to coast and as former Assistant General Counsel for the agency, I believe the ideal approach for an alternative to physical document examination entails three key elements: (1) limiting the alternative process to E-Verify employers in good standing, (2) a modified Form I-9 as described in the Proposed Rule, and (3) agency reliance on E-Verify confirmation as fulfillment of the employer’s obligation under the alternative approach. 

The E-Verify system has long been the technological spearhead for the agency’s enforcement of the employment verification requirement, and although it has never been mandatory at the federal levels for all employers, it has been successfully required in various contexts including government contracts and STEM OPT extension eligibility. Significantly, the E-Verify program allows the government to confirm employment eligibility based on electronic transmittal of information, which is exactly what remote verification entails. Although in the mid-1980s in-person document inspect was rightly considered the best way to confirm document authenticity, that is no longer the case in the 50 years since IRCA was conceived. E-Verify successfully provides a superior way to confirm the right of individuals to work in the United States. It requires retention of electronic copies (including photocopies) of the documents presented for inspection and bases its conclusions on those copies as well as the data provided by the employer during the E-Verify process. E-Verify does not depend on physical documents, but on data about those physical documents. As such, E-Verify is already a capable modern twenty-first century approach to employment verification, and can be easily adapted to provide a permanent solution to verification of permanent remote workforces. If E-Verify employers are allowed to permanently rely on electronic inspection of List A, B and C documents, the existing E-Verify system ensures a work-eligible workforce without the need for in-person document inspection because the government’s verification of data from those documents is superior to the employer’s eyes-on-document inspection. Employers have never been forensics experts, a point which historically the government has acknowledged in connection with the Form I-9 process. In other words, the in-person inspection requirement was from the very beginning of IRCA a compromise in a world without the technological advances available today, including E-Verify. By requiring employers with remote workforces to use E-Verify to avoid the in-person document inspection requirement, the government will achieve its mission of ensuring a work-authorized workforce without burdening employers with complex requirements based on the obsolete view that in-person inspection is superior to the verification provided by E-Verify. The proposal to reduce the addition of fluoride in bottled water is not a drastic enough reduction to create tangible change.

It is a long held belief that adding fluoride to community water supplies will prevent tooth decay. But a growing amount of evidence suggests that there are major health concerns. According to the Harvard School of Public Health, the risks of fluoridating water may outweigh the benefits. The Cochrane Collaboration found that most of the initial studies showing the benefits of fluoride were actually deeply flawed. It could be toxic to the developing brain, though. Therefore, much more research is needed to show whether fluoride should be added to water. 

Furthermore, the rule does not account for fluoride already in the source water, meaning that the added amount might be safe but the overall level could be detrimental. In all, this rule needs to involve current research and factor in the calls from public health officials to find more information about the effects of fluoride.

When it was time to PCS, the RFO was essentially held hostage because of our child's EFMP. The gaining post did not have a child psychiatrist (through the town had plenty!) so we either had to PCS to another post or the PCM and psychiatrist would have to sign off on EFMP paperwork that stated our child could be treated by a PCM. Thanks to FDA for keeping patients safe from hospital acquired infection.

 Section VII "Summary of Data Upon Which the Reclassification Is Based," details cases of infection transmission. These involve hundreds of patients around the world over three decades. In many situations, human error facilitated infection transmission.

 As well as the cases cited in this FDA guidance, other evidence points to additional cases of disease transmission. In diabetes, notably glucose meters and other materials can transmit infection. FDA has rasied concern over clinical use meters. CDC has detailed that test strip containers are one such other means of passing infection from one patient to another. FDA should consider the total risk, not piecemeal responces.

 ALL of the evidence presented in the docket is of transmission in professional care facilities. It is clear that healthcare facilities are where FDA should address the problem of lancets infection transmission. Don't fix what isn't broken. The draft presents no evidence to support the proposed up-regulation of personal lancet devices.

 I appreciate FDA efforts to protect people in the clinical setting. That is a setting where we, as patients, have no way of knowing if we are getting fresh blades and disinfected devices. In some cases, we may not even be conscious to ask.

 FDA's 2013 draft meter guidance is instructive to this docket. While the final guidance is not yet out, the draft made a clear distinction between the setting of professional use and individual over the counter home use. Separating devices based on these environments is a logical precedent to follow with lancets.

 FDA should be addressing documented problems. All of the evidence FDA presents is in clinical settings. Therefore, FDA should be using guidance and labeling to address the clinical setting where we need protection and device design that can minimize human factors that contribute to risk.

 Section VII shows that multiple patient devices in-clinic use are a particular risk. The proposed up-regulation to class III of such devices is an indication of FDA's appreciation of that risk. FDA should be clear how unique device identifiers will usefully implement with replaceable blade devices and how both components will be tracked.

 I support FDA taking reasonable regulatory precautions and labeling steps to guide health care providers to use single patient, one-time use, disposable devices. Specifically, those that have blade protection as outlined in section V part B. Multi-patient devices should discourage through regulatory and labeling measures. FDA should address the real risk of transmission and create a clear delineation that safe, single-use, disposable lancets are the best practice.

 Labeling is a tool FDA can use to differentiate between use devices intended for home use and professional settings.

 Devices for a single patient, over the counter, with replaceable blades, should carry a black box label NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. One time use disposable lancets, with blade protection as outlined in section V part B, should be labeled APPROVED FOR CLINICAL USE.

 Price is a driver of purchasing behavior. Third party purchasers, other than the caregiver and patient, may assume that any FDA-approved device is safe in all settings. Clear labeling, as suggested above, will create an economic liability for clinical purchasing agents and insurance payers who require anything for clinical use but lancet devices explicitly approved for clinical use.

 Price driven purchasing is a documented source of safety disruption related to blood testing. The Journal Diabetes Care recently detailed the disruption of testing supplies as a source of increased hospitalization and mortality in diabetes patients served by Medicare. I fear a similar economic driven disruption will occur with lancet access driving use of less expensive devices not intended for clinical settings. FDA labels can protect patients with labels.

been scammed — victimized by predatory, for-profit institutions of higher 
learning for whom profit is the bottom line and educating men and women

ITT Tech and Corinthian are countless. Veterans are left holding the 
proverbial bag: a worthless “degree” and a wasted opportunity to achieve

Dear Ms. Debbie Seguin,

I am writing to express my opposition proposed new regulations described in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. If enacted, these rules would require immigrant children to be held in detention centers indefinitely. The Flores agreement settled decades ago put in place commonsense, humane protections for immigrant children in U.S. custody. These protections included a maximum 20 days in detention and required detained children to be kept in facilities managed by licensed child welfare agencies. 

By removing these protections, already traumatized children will experience more trauma. Already stories of abuse and neglect of children housed in detention centers abound. Family detention has also proven to damage parent-child relationships and puts their physical safety at risk, including for sexual exploitation and abuse.

Prolonged detention involves experiencing a loss of control, isolation from the outside world and detachment from community and culture. These experiences are harmful for people of all ages, but have a higher impact on children because their brains are still developing. The president of the American Academy of Pediatrics said that detention affects children's brain chemistry in a way that is comparable to child abuse. Research has shown much higher rates of depression, anxiety, PTSD and suicidal thoughts in children who have been detained.

Let me ask you how would you feel if this were being done to your children, your nieces, or nephews, or your neighbor's children? If you would not stand to have this done to those you know and love, then there is zero excuse to tolerate this being done to ANYONE. 

We should not use children as pawns! I strongly oppose these new regulations and I believe the US should not expand child detention. 

Sincerely,

I appreciate the FAA's conservative approach to keeping aviators safe, however, I believe this AD is an overreaction to a sample size of one airplane out of a fleet of approximately 19,000 aircraft on which this condition was found. Further, the AD does not site any instances where a PA28 or PA32 has had a wing separate due to a cracked spar. If an aircraft has the factored service life requiring the spar cap inspection, the AD does not adequately capture the costs involved. My own research indicates the inspection alone would cost at least $2000, as opposed to the $295 sited. The AD doesn't describe that this area is not normally accessible for inspection, and that inspection holes have to be cut in the wing skin and access panels installed (this act alone opens the aircraft to future corrosion in a very critical structural part of the airplane). Additionally, the eddy current inspection requires special training and equipment that are not available on the vast majority of general aviation airfields. This AD also has a very negative impact on the value of the aircraft in this fleet. Even if an aircraft does not have the factored service life requiring the expensive inspection, the existence of the AD could possibly knock $10,000 to $20,000 off the value of an airplane. With general aviation being in a precarious state of health, this is a tremendous blow to individual aircraft owners and businesses where the profit margin is close to nil. 

I strongly urge the FAA to reconsider the issuance of this AD due to the scant evidence on which it was based (one aircraft out of 19,000) and the very negative financial impact it will have on the United States' general aviation industry. I would recommend the FAA do more research to determine the validity of the problem (greater sample size of aircraft with the cracked spar, and site mishaps where this has been a finding). I also recommend the FAA does more adequate research into the cost and availability of spar cap inspections (if needed) due to the negative financial impact upon owner/operators).

The International Entrepreneur Rule (IER) is a promising policy that would open the door for 

talented people to come to the United States to build strong teams and innovative products. As 

an international entrepreneur who has personally navigated the immigration system while 

co-founding my cybersecurity company, I believe IER should be implemented rather than 

eliminated. Although IER does not resolve all of the immigration challenges foreign 

entrepreneurs face, it provides crucial time for entrepreneurs to develop their startups in the 

United States. 

On paper, the EB-2 visa might seem like viable pathways for entrepreneurs who wish to stay in 

the country. But in reality, it can be very challenging to qualify for this visa. The requirements set 

a high standard that many entrepreneurs would not be able to meet. For example, the EB-2 

requires an education level above a bachelor’s degree. This is a qualification that does not 

make sense when evaluating entrepreneurs since some of the most successful entrepreneurs in 

the United States did not graduate college, or hold only a bachelor’s degree. Also, the EB-2 

requires a level of experience that a younger entrepreneur with high potential would also not be 

able to meet. I’ve met many entrepreneurs, students especially, who would have been 

interested in IER as an alternative to an EB-1 or EB-2. 

The current existing pathways an entrepreneur might pursue are very costly because of legal 

fees, and the requirements are quite rigid. In contrast, IER was a more flexible option with 

criteria that more clearly relate to an entrepreneur’s chances for success - fundraising, revenue, 

and job creation. 

Overall, I support the International Entrepreneur Rule because it is a policy that makes a lot of 

sense. International entrepreneurs have very limited options to legally be in the United States 

while starting their own companies. The existing options can be quite challenging for 

entrepreneurs, and I like that IER provided clear, reasonable criteria for evaluating applicants.

The Pew Charitable Trusts (Pew) appreciates the opportunity to comment on NOAA Fisheries’ proposed 
2021-2022 Atlantic mackerel specifications. We urge NOAA Fisheries to reduce U.S. Atlantic mackerel 
catch for 2021-2022 in response to the species’ declining populations2 and the recent Fisheries and 
Oceans Canada (DFO) decision to reduce catch by 50%3. 
 
As prey for a wide array of fish, seabird and marine mammal predators, mackerel are an important 
component of the forage base that supports the Northeast Shelf Large Marine Ecosystem (NES LME). A 
broader look at the NES LME forage base reveals other depleted forage species – in fact this very rule is 
recommending a 72% reduction in butterfish due to lower than expected recruitment. Scientists 
increasingly agree4 that catch levels for forage fish like mackerel should be set to maintain high 
abundance to ensure that the species’ predators have plenty to eat. Healthy mackerel stocks would benefit 
the Atlantic ecosystems and the coastal communities that depend on them. In 2018, commercial landings 
of mackerel were valued at $10.7 million in Canada and $4.3 million in the United States,5,6 and these 
values do not consider the additional economic and ecological values that mackerel provide as forage. 
 
In 2019 when the current rebuilding plan and specifications were established, we and others pointed out 
that the fishery has a retrospective pattern. Every time there is a sign of recovery, managers increased 
catch leading to its current overfished and overfishing designations.7 We argued that it was a mistake to 
increase catch on a stock that had just been declared overfished and subject to overfishing based on 
projections from the terminal year of a stock assessment and in such a way that required the Mid-Atlantic 
Fishery Management Council (MAFMC) to adjust its own risk policy8. 
 
Unfortunately, those concerns have been realized as the best available science shows stronger 
conservation is necessary. The 2021 Canadian stock assessment indicates that “the number of spawning-
age mackerel are at a historic low”9. In response to this latest science and to recover the fishery, DFO is 
taking a significant step of reducing catch by 50% as compared to 2020. In this decision, The Honourable 
Bernadette Jordan, Minister of Fisheries, Oceans and the Canadian Coast Guard, stated, “if the spawning 
biomass does not increase over the next two years, we are likely heading towards a commercial Atlantic 
mackerel fishery closure”10.

On behalf of The Arc, I write to comment on Regulation 107431-19. The Arc promotes and protects 
the human rights of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and actively supports 
their full inclusion and participation in the community throughout their lifetimes. 
While we take no position on the state and local tax (SALT) deduction nor the cap itself, we are 
concerned about the proposed regulation that may allow donors to profit from their contributions 
to education programs that are allowed to discriminate against students with disabilities. 
We appreciate the steps that Treasury has taken to curtail taxpayers’ ability to profit on 
contributions to state tax credit school voucher programs. Taxpayers should no longer be able to 
receive financial gain from claiming both a state tax credit and federal charitable deduction for 
donating to private school voucher programs. It was entirely unacceptable that tax credit programs 
in a dozen states were used to pay schools that are allowed to exclude students with disabilities 
while also allowing individual or corporate donors to obtain a tax benefit. 
We have serious concerns about school voucher programs because neither the full rights under the 
Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) nor the accountability under the Every Student 
Succeeds Act (ESSA) outlined below apply to students who are placed by their parents in private 
schools in any state. In addition, these voucher programs typically siphon general state and local 
revenue from public schools that are obliged to accept and serve students with disabilities. 
 
Rights 
Under the IDEA, public schools are required to provide for evaluation, free appropriate public 
education, individualized education plans (IEPs), least restrictive environment, parent participation,

 
2
and procedural safeguards (known as “due process”) to challenge school decisions. Private schools 
have no legal obligation to accept a student with disabilities for admission, unlike public schools 
(referred to as the “zero reject” principle in IDEA). Assuming the student is admitted to a private 
school, the school does not have to accept the student’s IEP or provide special education and 
related services (such as speech therapy, assistive technology, and transportation). 
Accountability 
Under the ESSA, public schools are held accountable for how students - including the subgroup of 
students with disabilities - learn and achieve. Schools must measure and publicly report academic 
achievement, academic progress, English language proficiency, and high school graduation rates. 
ESSA requires that schools look at the performance for all their students, as well as at the 
performance of the disability subgroup, to see if long-term goals and interim measures of progress 
are being met. This means that the performance of students with disabilities is not masked by 
school averages. And, most importantly, ESSA requires that schools take action if students with 
disabilities consistently underperform in: 1) Annual assessments of academic achievement in 
reading, math, and science; 2) English language proficiency; 3) For elementary and middle schools, a 
“measure of student growth” or other academic indicator that allows for meaningful differentiation 
in student performance; and 4) High school graduation rates.

From an employer perspective, I think these proposed changes are a step in the right direction. Having worked in Finance and now Technology, there is a huge need for updating how we file cap-subject petitions given the number of employees that we support from an immigration perspective. By implementing an electronic registration system, we are getting closer to bridging the gap between immigration and technology. Not only will this save resources, including time and money, for employers and their respective legal counsels, but this could free up USCIS resources as well which means they can focus on adjudicating other cases. By decreasing the burden on USCIS, we would hopefully see back logs clear out and fewer instances of suspending premium processing. 

I recognize the potential disadvantages for smaller companies as noted in other comments but I think we can all agree that changes are necessary - the current process is archaic. The unfortunate piece is that there may not be a 'one size fits all' solution. Personally, I'm not looking to create advantages for any company/industry but as stated previously, resources are being wasted on filing these cases regardless of company size. Further, I think we need to think about long-term gains. As previously stated, freeing up USCIS resources could be better in terms of adjudication timescales for other case types.

Separately, I am indifferent on making this process more advantageous for individuals with advanced degrees (even though that would benefit my employee population). That being said, I see the continued need for attracting the world's top talent and creating incentives for those with advanced degrees means that employers can broaden their search for ensuring their open positions are filled by the right/best talent.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this regulatory change. I strongly oppose this change and am troubled by many possible implications of this change. My opposition centers primarily, but not exclusively, on the revoking of maximum line speeds. There are several reasons why I oppose this.

First, I am unpersuaded by the argument that these changes will aide in compliance with HMSA. I am happy with the idea of increasing the number/duration of offline inspections. I am troubled by the idea that this would come at the expense of online inspections. Especially with an increase in line speeds, which will surely lead to greater risk of chaos, I do not see justification for limiting online inspections and allowing industry to essentially police itself. If humaneness is valued, as it should be, and if the spirit of HMSA is to be respected, then we surely want more online inspections, not less. 

Second, I am extremely worried about the consequences for human workers. I already struggle to imagine the horrors of working in a slaughterhouse and have a difficult time understanding how it is acceptable to tolerate the harm that will come to workers when yet more is required of them - that they successfully manage slaughter operations once maximum line speeds have been revoked.

Third, completely independent of the questionable notion that this regulatory change will enhance the humaneness of slaughter, I am troubled by the animal welfare consequences of this regulatory change. Even if compliance with HMSA could be enhanced, revoking maximum line speeds would increase the supply of livestock for slaughter and consumption. Much of U.S. livestock already faces some of the worst living (such as it were) conditions of any living beings on the planet. There is no need to increase line speeds during slaughter unless the volume of animals brought into the slaughterhouse increases. This means yet more animals raised in these conditions. I have a hard time accepting this, because I struggle to identify meaningful distinctions between these animals - especially swine, which are highly-intelligent, sensitive animals - and dogs (which are also highly-intelligent, sensitive animals). American society would be horrified by these conditions being imposed on dogs, so I do not understand why we readily accept this treatment of the very similar pigs. Although this is not directly at stake in this regulatory change, I oppose the change in part because it stands to make the cruel treatment of animals that are very similar to dogs more frequent yet.

In short, I feel empathy for those in chaotic and dangerous working conditions; must, along with other taxpayers, help bear the health care costs of those with stress-related illness made worse by working in an industry moving toward higher-speed (and, inevitably, less-controlled) slaughter; and struggle to identify meaningful distinctions between swine raised for human consumption and our very own canines, which we would never consider slaughtering for consumption in the first place - let alone at higher speeds and with fewer online inspections. For these reasons, this change will cause harm for me and the millions of Americans who are likewise attentive to the problem of harsh working conditions and the prospect of animal cruelty.

Finally, I have an extremely difficult time seeing why the public would be well served by this change. The most notable beneficiaries of this change seem to be a relatively small group of agribusiness stakeholders. Consequently, I have great difficulty understanding why it would be worthwhile to unleash the problems described above, when the overall benefit to the public appears minimal. I am concerned that any cost-benefit analysis that has been completed has not done proper accounting of the harms caused by the problems I identify above.

Thank you again for taking these concerns into account.

Dear Acting Administrator Owens: 

The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) welcomes the opportunity to comment on the National 

Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s (NHTSA's) information collection request concerning speeding. 

Speeding has been a factor in more than a quarter of traffic fatalities for over 30 years, and work to 

address this leading fatal crash characteristic is necessary to reduce deaths on our nation’s roads. 

However, we do not believe that NHTSA’s proposal to examine the effects of a driver education course 

on speeding behavior is an effective use of the agency’s resources in addressing this problem. 

There is no reason to expect that an education intervention like what NHTSA is proposing would reduce 

speeding. A large body of evidence demonstrates that education alone about the dangers of traffic safety 

issues such as alcohol-impaired driving or seatbelt nonuse does not change behavior (e.g., IIHS, 2001 

[attached]; Williams, 1994; Williams & Wells, 2004). Drivers also know the risks of speeding. The AAA 

Foundation for Traffic Safety’s latest Traffic Safety Culture Index (2019) reports that the majority of U.S. 

drivers believe that driving 15 mph over the speed limit on freeways and 10 mph over the speed limit on 

residential streets are very or extremely dangerous, despite nearly as many drivers admitting to these 

behaviors in the past month. 

NHTSA’s (2014) Speed Management Program Plan proposes research and other actions that have more 

promise than driver education to effectively reduce speeding. We recommend that NHTSA direct 

resources towards other components of speed management outlined in the plan, such as automated 

speed enforcement, law enforcement strategies, speed limits, intelligent transportation safety 

technologies, and traffic-calming techniques, rather than towards education courses. The plan 

emphasizes that education associated with speed management should be done in support of 

enforcement, and we agree with that; NHTSA’s own Countermeasures That Work document (Richard, 

Magee, Bacon-Abdelmoteleb, & Brown, 2018) promotes the use of communications in support of 

enforcement as a countermeasure for speeding, but does not endorse driver education alone. 

Incentivizing the fitment of intelligent speed adaptation, as the National Transportation Safety Board’s 

(2017) report on speeding recommended to NHTSA, is another way in which NHTSA could more 

effectively use its resources to reduce speeding.

On behalf of the undersigned participants in the Collaborative for Effective Prescription Opioid 

Policies (CEPOP) we appreciate the opportunity to submit comments on the Center for Disease 

Control and Prevention’s Proposed 2022 CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing 

Opioids. As a diverse group of stakeholders, CEPOP is working to advance a comprehensive and 

balanced strategy to reduce opioid abuse and promote treatment options. We support evidence-

based policies and programs to prevent addiction and overdose, while ensuring patient access to 

safe, effective pain treatment. 

We commend CDC for its actions on the urgent challenges of drug abuse and misuse in America. 

As the agency has helped to identify, 101,035 Americans died from drug overdoses in the 12-

month period ending October 2021, with three-quarters of the overdose deaths linked to opioids.1 

At the same time, according to the agency’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, an 

estimated 50 million U.S. adults had chronic pain and 19.6 million U.S. adults had high-impact 

chronic pain.2 The consequences of inadequate treatment of pain can be severe. We must ensure 

that responses to the opioid epidemic prevent abuse, addiction, and overdose, but do not have 

unintended consequences of depriving patients suffering from pain from appropriate therapies. 

We believe the final guideline must recognize and address both elements of the current 

challenge; misuse and abuse of opioid medications and pain. CDC’s full engagement in the effort 

to confront these public health issues challenges is essential. To that end, we offer the following 

comments.

update process. CEPOP is an organization built on collaboration, and this initiative allows 

stakeholders from a wide array of perspectives to contribute to a comprehensive strategy. We 

encourage CDC to expand collaborations with other federal, state and local agencies to advise 

both on this guideline as it is completed and implemented. In particular, we see a continued need 

for greater coordination across the federal government such as the recently announced HHS 

Overdose Response Strategy. We particularly encourage alignment between CDC, FDA and 

CMS as it relates to prescription opioid medication safe use and abuse prevention. CEPOP is 

focusing on areas such as abuse-deterrent formulations, at-home disposal and deactivation, and 

medication-assisted treatment where the need for such federal coordination is apparent.

includes an incomplete literature review on some aspects of opioid safety (e.g., urine drug 

testing, abuse-deterrent formulations, risk mitigation) and, in some places, includes an emphasis 

on cost containment that is based on outdated information. 

We urge CDC to continue to pursue, in coordination with other public and private sector research

Hello-I am opposed to the USDAs plan to privatize food safety inspection and allow pork producers to operate faster than they already do. These changes put endangered and overwhelmed workers at additional risk of severe injury, increase the chance of contaminated pork making it into the food supply, and will worsen the inhumane handling of pigs.

Existing line speed regulations already make slaughter facilities among the most dangerous and difficult places to work in America. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, meatpacking workers experience injury rates nearly 2.5 times higher and an illness rate almost 17 times higher than the average for all industries. Forcing workers to process the animals faster will only exacerbate these problems, while increasing the risk of contaminated pork being introduced into the U.S. food supply.

Faster line speeds would also inevitably lead to more frequent inhumane incidents, such as pigs being inadequately stunned and therefore remaining conscious during slaughter a violation of the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act. The HSUS works closely with farmers and ranchers across the country who understand the need for humane handling of animals during the slaughter process. These producers uniformly oppose the line-speed rule change as a step backward, especially coming at a time when consumers are more concerned than ever with how their food is produced and how animals raised for food are treated.

Dear Ms. Parker:

This is in response to the Federal Grain Inspection Services April 1, 2020, Advance Notice of Proposed Rule (ANPR) regarding Official Agency (OA) boundary exceptions.

The American Association of Grain Inspection and Weighing Agencies (AAGIWA) is the national association representing official grain inspection and weighing agencies. AAGIWA represents 77 percent of all official agencies. AAGIWA members provided 90 percent of all domestic inspection in Fiscal Year 2019. 

Multiple revisions to the official agency boundary exception provisions in the United States Grain Standards Act (USGSA), and the Federal Grain Inspection Services (FGIS) administration of these exceptions have created uncertainty among both customers and OAs for some time.

Individual AAGIWA members possess differing views on this important issue, however we agree that our customers deserve to receive good service from the official inspection system. 

Two years ago, FGIS requested AAGIWAs input regarding OA boundary exceptions. AAGIWA responded on March 15, 2018, with a letter explaining our position regarding how boundary exceptions should be administered. This letter also included specific suggested changes to FGIS Directive 9290.12, Exceptions and Service Agreements, dated April 14, 2017, to improve administration of the exception program. AAGIWAs comments stressed that exceptions should be administered with a customer focus to ensure all customers receive good service. A copy of our March 15, 2018, letter is enclosed as part of our official comment to this ANPR.

The USGSA was last amended to reinstate the nonuse of service exception as part of the 2018 Farm Bill. Since the 2018 Farm Bill was signed, customers have been prevented from utilizing the nonuse of service provision because regulations to administer this provision have not been promulgated. 

AAGIWA is pleased to see FGIS moving forward to create the necessary regulations that will allow customers to utilize this provision provided by Congress. AAGIWA encourages FGIS to engage with customers and OAs during the regulation development process. AAGIWA also encourages FGIS to prioritize and quickly finalize these important regulations. 

Sincerely,

Thomas Dahl
President

Presently, technical assistance with disproportionality, including significant disproportionality, is available to states via at least three OSEP funded technical assistance (TA) centers – IDEA Data Center (IDC), National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), and Center for Fiscal Reporting (CIFR). 

The advancement of existing technical centers would prove the most effective among states/LEAs and efficient regarding taxpayer funds. Any additional centers would require increased costs related to management of both content and personnel as current resources are shared to minimize expenditures and prevent duplicate efforts of time, communication (e.g., webinars), and content. Notably, separating calculations of disproportionality from the data is impossible as IDC provides technical assistance to states on the collection, reporting, use of child count, educational environments, and discipline data which are in turn used in said calculations. Far be it better to improve upon the established than to create additional TA centers.

Contrarily, should an alternative be deemed necessary, all areas of disproportionality should be integrated into the scope of work. As opposed to one (1) center focused exclusively on significant disproportionality, SPP/APR Indicators 4, 9, and 10 should be incorporated to prevent confusion across methodologies. 

A basic challenge at both SEA and LEA levels when using IDEA data to address significant disproportionality and promote equity is making the distinction between reporting requirements of SPP/APR Indicators 4, 9, and 10 from significant disproportionality. Prevailing centers have been sufficient in developing and disseminating assistance in this area and have supported SEAs in conducting reviews of policies, procedures, and practices as well as root-cause analyses of identifying contributing factors of significant disproportionality via access to toolkits. Furthermore, SEAs receive support in assisting said LEAs in expending IDEA funds on comprehensive coordinated early intervening services (CCEIS) to address causes and contributing factors via the Center for Fiscal Reporting (CIFR).

In conclusion, technical assistance is readily available through several existing centers, several of which already share personnel and/or collaborate on the creation and provision of assistance to states. Developing additional center(s) would, in theory, consolidate resources yet ultimately increase expenses via redundant offerings to states and inflict burden of administering.

We (Oasis Earth) strongly support the expansion of the NPRW critical habitat proposed by the CBD petition. It is scientifically logical that NPRWs transit between the two separate areas presently designated as critical habitat -- east of Kodiak and in the SE Bering Sea. From this standard alone, the expanded, connected critical habitat is clearly warranted. Further, in support of this expanded critical habitat area, it is essential that ship traffic through Unimak Pass be required to adopt a whale-ship strike risk reduction regime (as is in place in heavy ship/whale traffic marine areas elsewhere). This expanded NPRW critical habitat designation will enable this important NPRW protection to be established. Unimak Pass is critical habitat for whale transits between the Bering Sea and the North Pacific. As well, much of the trans-Pacific shipping between North America and Asia transits Unimak (over 4,500 ship transits/year, or 12/day). This poses significant risk of potentially lethal whale-ship strikes in the area, as well as oil (and other hazardous cargo) spills that could significantly impact NPRW survival. To date, there are no sufficient ship speed restrictions in Unimak, or ship casualty prevention and response assets in the area. This must be remedied immediately. The NPRW critical habitat expansion proposed by CBD correctly encompasses Unimak, and would enable enhanced ship safety measures to be enacted for this ecologically important area. This must include ship speed limits of no more than 10 knots, posted bow watches to detect whales, additional whale detection and avoidance measures by transit ships, etc.; as well as the prepositioning of an ocean rescue tug, capable of rendering a save to a ship in distress (loss of power or steering, etc.), on continuous (24/7/365) stand by (and perhaps in escort) at Unimak. Attached is correspondence with NOAA in 2009, requesting its consideration of designating Unimak Pass an IMO Particularly Sensitive Sea Area (PSSA), and/or a U.S. Marine National Monument or National Marine Sanctuary. Consistent with the proposed expansion of the NPRW critical habitat area, additional marine protection for the area, such as that we proposed in 2009, should be adopted. Thanks for considering these suggestions.

I am addressing the benefits to public and worker health and safety provided by the 2017 RMP rule that the proposed rule eliminates.

The new rule:
- Eliminates a requirement that the most dangerous facilities undertake a safer technology alternatives assessment. 
- Removes a requirement that an incident analysis include determining the root cause of accidents and near-misses; that the team investigating an incident include at least one person knowledgeable in the process; and the requirement to include incident investigation reports in hazard reviews. 
- No longer requires qualified, independent, third-party audits to be conducted when a facility has an incident to ensure the cause of the incident is addressed. 
- Strikes a provision that requires facilities to provide the public with information critical to understanding the potential risks from these facilities, including how to communities protect themselves and what potential health risks they might face from an incident. 
- Deletes the requirement that facilities provide emergency planners and first responders with essential information needed for responding to a chemical release allowing companies to claim confidential business information, and either provide limited or no information. 

Also:

- Children are particularly vulnerable to the potential health impacts from exposure to toxic chemicals. (2018/07/11)

- -

In 2020, the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) reported that "it reviewed data in the Synchronized Pre-deployment and Operational Tracker (SPOT) database, ... the database DOD, State and USAID agreed to use to track all contractors working on U.S. funded contracts. SIGAR explained that, while "[t]he SPOT database listed only 127 contractor deaths in Afghanistan recorded from April 17, 2002 to December 31, 2018[,]" the SIGAR "conservatively identified" 2,214 killed (plus 2,921 wounded, plus 1,182 kidnapped or missing). See https://www.sigar.mil/pdf/special%20projects/SIGAR-20-25-SP.pdf
- -
Moreover, DoD should attempt to publicly acknowledge contractor sacrifice and make more of an effort to quantify and disclose the substitution (or outsourcing) of sacrifice from uniformed personnel to the private sector.
- -

- -

I urge the USDA to adopt the strongest possible standards of care for birds used in commercial enterprises and for wild-caught birds used for research. It is unconscionable that for the past 50 years these animals have been denied coverage under the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) and that--even after a court ruled against this exclusion--the department dragged its feet for 20 years. The number of investigations by animal welfare organizations for cruel treatment by bird breeders and others during this time is only the tip of the iceberg of the suffering that could have been avoided had the USDA acted sooner. Now the USDA is finally initiating efforts to promulgate regulations to protect birds under the AWA.

Please include birds for coverage in the AWA. There is no reason to exclude them, and they certainly need & deserve protection!

There should be no double standard when it comes to protecting birds; they should receive the same level of oversight as other animals covered by the AWA, regardless of other laws that may apply to birds. Regulations regarding their welfare should include the following basic elements: 

1. No sale of unweaned or prematurely weaned baby birds. These young, fragile birds are at great risk of succumbing to disease, mishandling, and the extreme hazards of transport. 

2. Environmental enrichment for all birds. Achieving the AWA's goal of ensuring "humane care and treatment" requires that species-specific physical and psychological needs of birds be met. 

3. Health certificates and record keeping for all birds. Records (including but not limited to acquisition and disposition of the birds) and disease testing are essential to prevent disease transmission and illegal trade in wild-caught birds. 

4. Enclosures that enable the birds to express normal behavior, including flight. Confinement in cages causes poor welfare in birds and can lead to destructive habits, including feather plucking. Birds need to be able to fly and express other natural behaviors. The USDA should adopt enforceable standards that don't rely solely on subjective assessments. 

5. No painful physical mutilations. Pinioning (severing of wing muscles or amputation of wings), toe clipping, devoicing, and beak alterations are examples of painful procedures that are typically done for the convenience of keepers and are extremely detrimental to the welfare of the birds. 

6. Coverage of all bird species. There is no justification for exempting certain species because they are addressed in other laws such as the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Many animals covered by the AWA are regulated under state or other federal laws, and such laws do not nullify their protections under the AWA. The same should be true for birds. The ESA does not ensure humane care and treatment.

Reference:
(A) Notice of Proposed Rule Making (NPRM): Docket No. FAA-2015-5814; Directorate Identifier 2014-NM-247-AD 
(B) Service Bulletin (SB) A320-53-1281 Rev01, Dated December 1, 2014
(C) Service Bulletin (SB) A320-53-1281 Rev02, Dated October 9, 2015
(D) Service Bulletin (SB) A320-53-1287 Rev00, Dated July 29, 2014
(E) A318/319/320/321 Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 53-21-11 PB 101

United's Comments

1. UAL requests a statement in the AD to specify the Required for Compliance (RC) paragraphs described in Ref (A) Para (k)(3). The Ref (B), (C), and (D) SB's contain a statement in Paragraph 3 regarding the technical intent but does not define the Required for Compliance (RC) paragraphs:

"The access and close-up instructions, not comprising return to service tests, in this Service Bulletin do not constitute or affect the technical intent of the Service Bulletin. Operators can therefore, as deemed necessary, omit or add access and/or close-up steps to add flexibility to their maintenance operations as long as the technical intent of the Service Bulletin is met within the set parameters."

Therefore, please clarify that Paragraph 3.C and 3.D of Ref (B) (C), and (D) SB's are "Required for Compliance (RC)" for Ref (A). Note that Paragraph 3.D contains no Test requirements.

2. UAL requests the use of the revised Ref (C) SB in lieu of Ref (B) SB, as stated in Ref (A) Paragraph (i). As a result, include Ref (B) as credit for previous action in Ref (A) Paragraph (j). The revised Ref (C) SB includes numerous configuration additions due to factors from MOD 35239P9039.

3. Ref (A) and Ref (D) do not state whether or not the inspection intervals supersede Ref (E) SRM inspections following rework. Ref (A) Paragraph (g)(1) and Ref (D) SB require repetitive inspections not to exceed 12,000 flight cycles or 24,000 flight hours, whichever occurs first. The Ref (E) SRM for Category 'B' rework (as called out by Ref (A) Paragraph (g)(2) and Ref (D) SB) also define different inspection methods, thresholds and subsequent intervals following rework per SRI 53-21-11. Please clarify if the inspections per Ref (A) and Ref (D) supersede defined inspection intervals per Ref (E) SRM. Otherwise, this will cause confusion on which inspection methods and intervals to comply with. In addition, please clarify if the terminating action defined by Ref (A) paragraph (i) and Ref (B) or (C) terminates inspections defined by Ref (E) following rework. 

4. Ref (A) Paragraph (g)(3) states "if any damage detected during the inspection required by paragraph (g)(1) of this AD exceeds the limits defined in [Ref (D)]". This limit relates to the remaining skin thickness as defined by Ref (E). However, the meaning of "remaining thickness out of limits" is inconclusive. The remaining skin thickness following a blend out could become a Category 'B' repair with subsequent inspections or a Category 'C' repair, eventually requiring doubler repair. The Ref (D) SB does not give instruction to accomplish a doubler repair if the remaining thickness is "within Ref (E) limits". Considering the issue at hand, it would not be wise to install an external doubler (unless necessary) if the remaining skin thickness is "within limits". Thus, we propose to clarify the "limit" defined in Ref (A) Paragraph (g)(3) as an allowable rework (blend out) not requiring repair (doubler installation).

5. United has experienced several issues of skin chafing prior to the release of Ref (D) SB. Some aircraft have required doubler repairs due to skin wear beyond remaining thickness allowed. Because repairs may be present, it will not be possible to inspect the skin in the chafing area. Therefore, please include in Ref (A) Paragraph (g) (1) to accomplish a detailed inspection for damage on the "fuselage skin or skin repair (if present)"

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

STEM Success at the University of Arkansas – Pulaski Technical College (UA-PTC) is a 
Title III grant whose primary goal is to increase the number of African American students 
entering STEM careers and majors, as well as a focus on increasing the retention and graduation 
rates of that demographic. A secondary goal of STEM Success also focuses on teacher 
preparation, primarily African American STEM educators. The UA-PTC STEM Success 
program supports students through case management, tutoring, and a variety experiential 
learning experiences. STEM Success is in the final year of a five-year PBI grant, with funding 
slated to end on September 30, 2020. In FY 2017, 24 institutions nationwide were funded 
though the $13.9 million appropriated. 
The grant is funded through Title III, Part F, Section 371 of the amended Higher 
Education Act of 1965, also known as the Predominantly Black Institutions (PBI) Undergraduate 
Program. The PBI funds allowed institutions of higher education to develop programs focused in 
one of the following areas: science, technology, engineering, or mathematics (STEM); health 
education; internationalization or globalization; teacher preparation; or improving educational 
outcomes of African American males. 
All of these mentioned areas are those which Black students have traditionally been 
underrepresented. According to the DOE website, a PBI is defined as an undergraduate school 
that has at least 1,000 students; is at least 40% black; has at least 50% low-income or first-
generation students; and at least 50% of the students are taking courses that lead to an associate’s 
or Bachelor’s degree. The institutions that received grant awards included two-year colleges and 
four-year colleges and universities. 
The UA-PTC STEM Success initiative has been very successful in their four and half 
years at the intuition. The program has retained at least 70% of the students in the program in the 
four years it has been on campus. Additionally, our program graduated 56% and 53% of the 
students in years one and two of the program. These students earned either an Associate’s 
degree or an Associate of Science degree. A majority of the students in cohorts three and four 
are still enrolled, and therefore, graduation information on those cohorts is incomplete. 
The program is making great impacts on the students, and the program has been meeting 
the objectives as laid out in the grant. COVID-19 has hampered the efforts of the program and 
the College during the Spring of 2020. It is hoped that the proposed one-year extension will be 
approved and the program will be able to carry out the grant objectives and provide services to 
the students in the program and on campus. 
Like our colleagues with other PBI programs across the country, it is hoped that this one-
year extension, along with the previous years, will show the need to continue funding of the PBI 
programs. The impacts of COVID-19 on the economy cold show an influx of students returning 
to school for retraining in areas of STEM or teacher education. We aim to be on the forefront of 
the supporting those students as begin reenroll in colleges across the country. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Richard L. Moss, PhD 
Director, STEM Success 
University of Arkansas – Pulaski Technical College

I am writing to express my disappointment with the US Department of Agriculture's decision to withdraw the 2017 final Horse Protection Act rule, which was intended to curb the rampant abuses associated with "soring" (Docket No. APHIS-2011-0009 "Horse Protection; Licensing of Designated Qualified Persons and Other Amendments"). An upgrade to the HPA is desperately needed as horses continue to suffer under a status quo that allows that industry to police itself despite the obvious conflict of interest.

According to the USDA's own review of data in recent years, there remains a persistent and vast discrepancy between violations found by industry appointed inspectors vs. those found by USDA inspectors (despite the latter attending only a small proportion of shows). Unfortunately, it is clear that the industry continues to turn a blind eye to evidence of soring.

Rather than withdraw the rule, the USDA should reissue the rulemaking until the department is prepared to move forward with a new HPA rule containing, at a minimum, all the key components of the 2017 rule. Importantly, the 2017 rule included prohibitions on ankle chains and other "action devices" associated with soring and eliminated the failed industry-run self-enforcement system.

Over 100,000 public comments were submitted in support of the 2017 rule; hundreds of members of Congress voiced their support as well. The 2017 HPA rule would achieve many of the recommendations outlined in the USDA Office of Inspector General audit and the recent National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report, both of which called for an end to the industry self-policing scheme.

In 2021, the USDA announced that the "development of a new and improved HPA proposal [was] a top regulatory priority," but the decision to withdraw the 2017 rule, coupled with the lack of progress on a new rule, suggests satisfaction with the status quo and that the USDA is not serious about fulfilling its legal duty to end soring.

Source to Groundwater 
 
The undersigned organizations appreciate the opportunity to comment on the U.S. 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Interpretive Statement addressing whether the Clean 
Water Act’s (“CWA” or “Act”) National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (“NPDES”) 
permit program applies to releases of pollutants from point sources to groundwater. See 84 Fed. 
Reg. 16810 (Apr. 23, 2019). We strongly support EPA’s conclusion that “the Act is best read as 
excluding all releases of pollutants from a point source to groundwater from NPDES program 
coverage and liability under Section 301 of the CWA, regardless of a hydrologic connection 
between the groundwater and a jurisdictional surface water.” Id. at 16811. 
 
 
The undersigned organizations and our members are deeply interested in the scope and 
administration of the CWA. We represent, own, and operate facilities that are water-dependent 
enterprises. Farmers, ranchers, and foresters need to know whether their day-to-day activities are 
subject to the CWA’s NPDES permitting program or whether they are instead addressed by 
states in accordance with the Act’s nonpoint source programs. Farmers, ranchers, and foresters 
have long had to defend against citizen suit litigation seeking to expand the scope of the NPDES 
permitting program. Likewise, the undersigned organizations have regularly represented their 
members’ interests on the proper scope and limits of the NPDES program before Congress, 
federal regulatory agencies, and the courts. Many normal farming and ranching operations—such 
as crop and forage production involving fertilization and weed and insect pest control, subsurface 
drainage systems, irrigation systems, or the use of lagoons, basins, pits, or impoundments—may 
result in material reaching groundwater from something that fits within the CWA’s broad 
definition of point source and from there being carried to surface waters. 
 
Due to recent expansive rulings by courts such as the Ninth and Fourth Circuits, members 
of the undersigned organizations are at increased risk of citizen suit enforcement. Millions of 
agricultural enterprises could be newly subject to the CWA’s permitting requirements. Equally 
problematic, the Act’s longstanding exclusions for agricultural activities could be compromised 
by erroneously expansive approaches to CWA regulation over releases to groundwater. Given 
the sometimes conflicting EPA statements over the decades regarding whether the CWA’s point 
source permitting requirements extend to releases to groundwater—and an even more confusing 
patchwork of conflicting court decisions—the undersigned organizations appreciate EPA’s 
efforts to provide clarity through the Interpretive Statement.

AAHomecare members include a cross section of suppliers, manufacturers, and other industry

Importance of Coordination of Care 

AAHomecare recognizes that the standard fee-for-service (FFS) compensation methodology for 

health care providers is outdated and inefficient. Under the FFS model, a provider is paid for the 

services/products it furnishes regardless of their effectiveness in treating the beneficiary. 

Further, the FFS model does not encourage coordination among providers. Essentially, each 

provider “operates in a silo.” Too often, the provider does not have a stake in whether (i) the 

overall care to the beneficiary is cost effective and (ii) the care results in improvement to the 

beneficiary’s health.

care providers, DME suppliers have regular communications with beneficiaries and their 

caregivers. These communications allow DME suppliers to report to, and coordinate with, 

treating physicians. 

Health care providers that should collaborate include: physicians, therapists (respiratory, physical 

and occupational), DME suppliers, home health agencies and pharmacies. When such 

collaboration occurs, beneficiaries are treated more cost effectively, beneficiaries avoid 

unnecessary physician and hospital visits, and the Medicare program saves money. 

Coordination of Care and its Relationship to Preventing Fraud 

When health care providers work together in delivering patient care, challenges arise. 

Specifically, any time one provider refers a beneficiary to another provider and there is a sharing 

of reimbursement, then there is a risk of (i) a kickback in violation of the federal anti-kickback

compensation are necessary for there to be effective coordination of care. While it is important 

that the Medicare program encourage coordination, it is equally important that protection 

against fraud be maintained.
