I strongly SUPPORT the proposed critical habitat protections for the five threatened Caribbean coral species and seven threatened Indo-Pacific coral species. 

All of these species have undergone some level of population decline and are susceptible to multiple threats. Notably, the most severe threats are attributed to climate change which NMFS describes as creating a foreseeable likelihood and danger of extinction for these corals throughout all of their ranges. 

An estimated 50% of coral reefs worldwide have already been lost to climate change, and about one-third of reef-building coral species are at risk of extinction. Stressors and risks to threatened coral species include both climate related threats as well as ecological effects of fishing and land-based sources of pollution. 

Impacts of the climate crisis include ocean acidification, which hinders the ability of corals to grow, and ocean warming, which causes corals to expel the algae living in their tissues in a phenomenon known as coral bleaching. 

High-growth conditions for reef-building corals include clear, warm waters with abundant light, and low levels of nutrients, sediments, and freshwater. Critical habitat designations are necessary to reduce and remove threats to these conditions which foster growth and recovery of these threatened species

Coral reefs help support over 25% of all marine life, and designation of critical habitat for these coral species means a chance for recovery and the opportunity to save them from extinction.

Thank you.

Section 296.12 Election of Remedies
“An Injured Person who accepts an award under the Act waives the right to pursue all claims for injuries arising out of or relating to the same subject matter…”

DISCUSSION POINTS
This is a long-term recovery process and the full extent of damages, losses, and expenses may not be known at the time of award and it is beyond anyone’s ability to foretell the future of what those might be so as to claim them on their Notice of Loss.

In order to receive compensation, claimants must sign a release waive all right to pursue additional claims.

Some claimants were very hard hit by this fire and lost all possessions and income sources - thus they may be under duress to sign the Release just to receive immediate financial relief. 

In addition, the Act does not allow any way to re-open a Notice of Loss beyond November 14, 2025 even though additional damages and losses may be experienced due to subsequent damages (flash flooding, mudslides, etc) directly or indirectly related to the fire beyond that date.

Considering this is a long-term recovery event, allow a lump sum payment of 15% of ALL injury, damages, losses, and expenses to be added on to each claim to cover for these future unknown items.

There is no need to list the queen conch Strombus gigas as neither threaten nor endangered at 
this time. Queen conch is not likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future nor is it 
danger of extinction in the majority of its range. The Queen conch FMP (1996) explicitly makes 
a case for sustainability in the US Caribbean and explains the differences between the US 
Caribbean and Florida, the extreme northern range of the queen conch. The EFH and SF A 
Amendments to the FMPs (2001, 2005) explicitly list the HAPCs for queen conch.

management history for the queen conch in the US Caribbean has been established to (1) 
maintain a sustainable fishery (size and bag limits, ACLs, seasonal and area closures and gear 
restrictions) and (2) have been put forth in the international arena for pan-Caribbean 
management of the species (IQCC 1996, Cimo, et al. 2012). The CFMC developed the Queen 
Conch FMP in 1996. When developing the FMP, the CFMC also followed an outstanding 
recommendation of implanting pan-Caribbean management of the species. There have been a 
number of international meetings in the wider Caribbean to address the queen conch, to assess 
the queen conch populations and to evaluate management; an exhaustive search for these data

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

FSA was put in place to protect innocent and vulnerable children. The reasons for the settlement have not changed. These children are still innocent and vulnerable. They are deserving of our protection and our mercy. Please to not implement these proposed regulations.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I am writing to provide comments on the proposed rule FY 2023 Prospective Payment System and Consolidated Billing for Skilled Nursing Facilities (CMS-1765-P).

I am very concerned how the implementation of a 4.6 percent rate cut will impact resident care. Across South Dakota, our members have faced historic hardships during the pandemic, including unprecedented financial hardship. With our members still reeling from the impacts of COVID, this is the wrong time to introduce significant rate reductions. Such a policy at this time would erect a barrier to providing the high quality of care South Dakota Medicare beneficiaries expect and deserve. 

The COVID-19 pandemic profoundly impacted how we provide care and the costs to provide care to residents regardless of a COVID-positive diagnosis. Many of these additional costs will continue due to changes in resident care, infection control, reporting requirements, and other necessary costs. South Dakota providers have still not recovered from unprecedented census declines since March 2020, with the average facility in our state lagging behind 10 percent from their pre-COVID census. 

New admissions are often difficult to accept due to continued struggles to fully staff facilities. While staffing has been a long-time challenge in our profession, the situation is currently more severe than I have seen at any time in my more than two decades with SDHCA. 

Due to historic underfunding in our state, many long term care providers were already in a financially precarious position prior to COVID. After the events of the pandemic, the outlook for our profession, especially for smaller, rural facilities, is uncertain. In the last six months, two nursing homes in our state have closed their doors, and further closures remain a distinct possibility. 

Without a predictable SNF payment rate going forward, it will be difficult, if not impossible, to provide the high-quality care that CMS expects while also improving our care delivery processes.

Given these recent and ongoing challenges, I encourage CMS to proceed in a very deliberate manner and to implement any parity adjustment over the course of three years, rather than in one, giving providers additional time to absorb costs. 

Thank you for your consideration.

Dear Bureau of Land Management,
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule put forth by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) regarding the management of surface resources and Special Areas in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska (NPR-A). While I understand the complexities in balancing resource development and conservation, I believe this proposed rule, as outlined in its abstract, fails to protect the unique and ecologically significant NPR-A adequately.
The National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska is a treasure trove of pristine wilderness, vital wildlife habitats, and strategically important resources. It is paramount that any management framework for this region prioritizes the preservation of its natural beauty, ecological integrity, and long-term sustainability. Unfortunately, as currently presented, the proposed rule does not seem to align with these essential goals.
One of the most concerning aspects of this proposed rule is its potential impact on the significant resource values of Special Areas within the NPR-A. The rule's revisions to the framework for designating and protecting these areas are deeply troubling, as they appear to prioritize resource development over conservation. We must not forget that these Special Areas are home to unique ecosystems and wildlife species that deserve robust protection from adverse impacts.
While the proposed rule claims to enhance access to subsistence activities, it is vital to scrutinize whether these provisions genuinely benefit the local communities. There is a risk that in the pursuit of increased access, we may inadvertently compromise the resources these communities rely on for their sustenance. Any management framework must ensure that subsistence activities continue to thrive without endangering the ecological health of the NPR-A.
Moreover, incorporating aspects of the NPR-A Integrated Activity Plan approved in April 2022 is a matter of concern. As it currently stands, this plan leans heavily towards resource development, potentially at the expense of environmental preservation. The proposed rule should prioritize a comprehensive review of this plan to ensure that it aligns with responsible stewardship and ecological protection principles.
While the proposed rule does not affect currently authorized oil and gas operations in the NPR-A, it fails to adequately address the need for stringent oversight and regulation of these operations to mitigate environmental impacts. This omission raises doubts about the rule's commitment to ensuring responsible resource development within the NPR-A.
In summary, as presented, the proposed rule for the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska is deeply troubling due to its perceived prioritization of resource development over conservation. It fails to adequately safeguard the NPR-A's special areas, protect subsistence activities, and ensure responsible resource development.
I strongly urge the Bureau of Land Management to reconsider this proposed rule in consultation with a broader range of stakeholders and experts to ensure that it aligns more closely with environmental preservation and sustainability principles. Our responsibility is to protect and preserve the NPR-A's unique ecological values for the benefit of current and future generations.
Thank you for considering my concerns on this matter. I implore you to make the necessary revisions to ensure the responsible management of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska.
Sincerely,
Ryan Parrish

After more than four decades of BLM’s bias in prioritizing resource extraction—oil, gas, 
fracking, mining, and livestock grazing—over the protection of public lands and non-
consumptive users, it is urgent for the BLM to rebalance their approach, elevate conservation, 
and prioritize ecosystem health and resilience. 
 
Our nation’s public lands provide clean drinking water and fresh air, offer refuge for wildlife, 
provide public access to nature, encompass iconic landscapes that drive our tourism and outdoor 
recreation economy, and safeguard innumerable cultural landscapes and sites.

Dear Mr. Tosatto; 
 
I write to vehemently object to this Proposed Rule and to request that NMFS immediately withdraw it and 
publish a revised proposed rule that does not financially impact a majority of the U.S. distant water tuna 
purse seine fleet. 
 
NMFS stated objective of the Proposed Rule is to satisfy international obligations with respect to certain 
decisions of the WCPFC. Regrettably NMFS proposals go far beyond what is required to meet those 
obligations and can only be viewed as punitive against the U.S. distant water tuna fleet and supportive of 
foreign flag national fleets and the environmental community. 
 
Specifically, I am objecting to NMFS’s proposal to split the Effort Limit Area for Purse Seine (ELAPS) 
into the US EEZ and High Seas areas, and to assign a separate fishing day limit to each of those areas. As 
you are well aware, for the past 9 years NMFS has combined these two areas with their associated limits 
to provide flexibility to our industry and this process has worked very well. In fact, the objective of 
maximizing operational flexibility has been enshrined in US western Pacific fisheries policy for over 35 
years now under the guise of the South Pacific Tuna Treaty. By creating separate limits for the US EEZ 
and the High Seas, NMFS has effectively reduced fishing opportunities for the U.S. fleet by over 400 
days. NMFS is well aware that the handful of vessels that have fishery endorsements to fish in the US 
EEZ have only utilized an average of 117 days over the past 9 years and there is no plausible scenario 
where those vessels would even use half of those allocated in this or future years. By splitting ELAPS, 
some 440 fishing days that could have been utilized by any vessel in our fleet on the high seas will go 
unused, effectively reducing the allocation of fishing days to the U.S. fleet and making these days 
available to Korea, China, Japan, Island Nations, Taiwan, Philippines, etc. Using the cost of a fishing day 
contained in the South Pacific Tuna Treaty, the loss to most of the US fleet will be over $5 million or two 
hundred thousand dollars per vessel—close to $3.0 million dollars for our fleet vessels alone! There is no 
legitimate reason given by NMFS as to why it has proposed splitting the ELAPS. One can only surmise 
that it is to support or give preference to one sector over another with the actual effect being giving less 
well- managed foreign fleets an advantage or to support the agendas of NGO’s petitioning for reductions 
in effort. Because the U.S. fleet will be required to report daily on its fishing activities, NMFS can easily 
track US EEZ fishing effort without splitting the ELAPS. Therefore, we view this action as arbitrary and 
capricious against the U.S. fleet operators and a direct attempt to further damage Industry.

 
The loss of over 400 high seas fishing days (which will be the result of the Proposed Rule) will have a 
direct negative impact on this nation’s fisheries trade deficit. One of Secretary Ross’s highest priorities is 
to reduce that deficit by exporting more fishery products. Tuna harvested by the U.S. distant water tuna 
fleet and sold into foreign markets is considered an export. The loss of over 400 high seas fishing days 
means that the Proposed Rule will needlessly increase the U.S. fisheries trade deficit by just over $21 
million dollars. 
Again, I respectfully request that NMFS withdraw the Proposed Rule and work with industry to develop a 
proposal that does not financially damage our fleet, while increasing the U.S. fisheries trade deficit 
against the current administration’s position. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sincerely,

I am writing to express my disappointment with the US Department of Agriculture's decision to withdraw the 2017 final Horse Protection Act rule, which was intended to curb the rampant abuses associated with "soring" (Docket No. APHIS-2011-0009 "Horse Protection; Licensing of Designated Qualified Persons and Other Amendments"). An upgrade to the HPA is desperately needed as horses continue to suffer under a status quo that allows that industry to police itself despite the obvious conflict of interest.

According to the USDA's own review of data in recent years, there remains a persistent and vast discrepancy between violations found by industry appointed inspectors vs. those found by USDA inspectors (despite the latter attending only a small proportion of shows). Unfortunately, it is clear that the industry continues to turn a blind eye to evidence of soring.

Rather than withdraw the rule, the USDA should reissue the rulemaking until the department is prepared to move forward with a new HPA rule containing, at a minimum, all the key components of the 2017 rule. On behalf of our 161,000 dentist members, we are pleased to comment on the Centers for 

Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) proposed guidance for the operational control 

range for optimal fluoride concentration in municipal water systems. We offer these 

comments in response to your Federal Register notice of July 13, 2018 (83 FR 32666). 

The ADA supports the proposed operational control range of 0.6 mg/L to 1.0 mg/L for the 

target fluoride level of 0.7mg/L recommended by the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS). 

The low end of the range (0.6 mg/L) will allow for the public to enjoy the decay preventive 

effect of fluoridated water while the high end (1.0 mg/L) will help to reduce the occurrence of 

dental fluorosis. 

This range is feasible and practical for water systems based on historical studies and most 

recently a 2017 study that looked at data from 34 states.1 We appreciate that even the best 

managed water system cannot maintain a perfect level of 0.7 mg/L 24/7/365. The 

operational control range of 0.4 mg/L allows for maintenance of a therapeutic average over 

time. 

The ADA has noted that some water systems have mistakenly interpreted the USPHS target 

of 0.7 mg/L to be highest level of fluoride to be allowed in drinking water at any given time. 

Besides creating anxiety for water system personnel, these systems have set their target 

fluoride level at 0.5 mg/L or lower simply because they do not want to exceed 0.7 mg/L at 

any specific time. 

The proposed operational control range will help to clarify expectations of fluoride level 

management and will aid in states setting regulations for the management of their water 

systems. Once finalized, the ADA looks forward to a revision of the 1995 Engineering and 

Administrative Recommendation for Water Fluoridation,2 as well as increased educational 

opportunities for water system personnel and regulators. 

Fluoridation of community water supplies is the single most effective public health measure 

to prevent tooth decay. The ADA continues efforts to expand access to fluoridation as it 

works to meet the Healthy People 2020 goal of providing fluoridated water to 79.6 percent of 

the U.S. population on public water systems.

2020 Call for Public Comment Dept of 
Education Open Textbook Pilot 
Comments 
I am writing on behalf of the University of Illinois at Chicago Library, in regard to the Open Textbooks 
Pilot Program. The University of Illinois at Chicago Library manages the UIC Open Textbook Faculty 
Incentive Program and distributes nearly $20,000/year in mini-grants to faculty in support of 
converting courses to open access material. The grant program is open to tenure track and non-
tenure track faculty teaching undergraduate courses and can be used to support adopting or 
adapting open educational materials. Through the Consortium of Academic Research Libraries in 
Illinois (CARLI) consortial membership, UIC is part of the Open Textbook Network and has 
representation on the CARLI Open Educational Resources Taskforce. 
Topic 1: Award Size 
The University of Illinois at Chicago Library supports setting an award maximum of 2 million dollars 
to ensure that multiple, smaller scale projects are funded. In previous rounds of funding, the grants 
were awarded to single projects. The UIC Library strongly prefers numerous smaller grants be 
issued to a more diverse group of projects. The UIC Library also supports shortening the project 
period from 48 months to 36 months. The shortened time frame will allow for projects to have a 
larger annual budget and for outcomes to be made available sooner. 
Topic 2: Matching Contributions 
While matching contributions would maximize program impact and encourage sustainability of a 
program or project, a matching contribution requirement might discourage less well-resourced 
consortia from applying for this grant. Moreover, under-resourced institutions and consortia could 
derive the most benefit from open textbook projects. For that reason, matching contributions should 
be encouraged and prioritized but not required. 
Topic 3: High-enrollment 
The UIC Library supports broadening the definition of “high-enrollment courses” to include courses in 
recognized postsecondary credentialing pathways. 
Proposed Priority 4—Using Technology-based Strategies for Personalized Learning and 
Continuous Improvement 
Several high-enrollment courses at the University of Illinois at Chicago rely on technology-based 
learning products such as commercial homework systems and personalized learning products. The 
lack of open source homework systems has been a barrier to adopting open textbooks for high-
enrollment courses. The University of Illinois at Chicago Library supports prioritizing projects with

 
technology-based solutions if projects are open source, rely on widely-adopted, integrated, and 
accessible open standards such as HTML 5 or EPUB, and have a plan for sustainability following the 
grant period. Any technology-based or personalized learning focused projects should also prioritize 
reuse and integration with learning management systems. In addition, these systems are expensive 
to develop and maintain and homework sets need to be updated frequently. Any technology-based 
strategies must include a plan to sustain and update systems and content beyond the grant period. 
Projects that do not have a sustainability component should not be given priority.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

We pay a lot to purchase "free range" and "pasture raised" type eggs. I'm so sad to learn that these descriptions may be inaccurate. Please make sure producers are honest in their descriptions and labeling. Thanks!

Thank you for considering my request.

I am submitting comments on the Select Agent status of Brucella abortus. I support the removal of B.abortus from the select agent list. My background and connection to this issue is that I am a strong advocate for wild, free-roaming bison (buffalo).

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Surveillance Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

Thank you for this opportunity and your consideration of my comments.

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:

Enclosed are my comments on the proposed trapping regulations for the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge Docket Number FWS-R7-NWRS-2017-0058.

I have forty years of experience with the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge as a visitor to hike, fish, canoe, and camp in the refuge and in my capacity as the Alaska Regional Director and Senior Policy Analyst of The Wilderness Society from 1989 to 2002 analyzing and commenting on Kenai Refuge actions, plans, policy, and issues.

I strongly oppose the proposed regulations for several reasons. They are legally flawed and should be entirely rejected.

First, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) did not prepare sufficient analysis and justification for these regulations under law. A Compatibility Determination would show that these regulations are not compatible with the Kenai Refuge purposes as defined by the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) of 1980 PL 96-487 Section 303 (4). The absence of such a Compatibility Determination violates ANILCA and the Comprehensive Conservation Plan (CCP) established under ANILCA, the National Wildlife Refuge Improvement Act, the Administrative Procedures Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). The proposed rule also departs from the 1982 Memorandum of Understanding on wildlife management between the State of Alaska and the U.S. Department of the interior. The proposed regulations basically scrap all federal regulations and adopt the State of Alaska regulations that fail in all legal requirements under federal law. Importantly, the proposed action would also significantly violate the Wilderness Act of 1964 PL 88-577 Section 4. (b) by failing to maintain the wilderness character of the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge Wilderness Area.

Second, the proposed regulations create enormous safety issues by establishing grizzly bear hunting over human food bait stations in recreation areas used for hiking, camping, canoeing, hunting, and fishing that will affect the human safety of these other refuge users by habituating grizzly bears on human foods. The other users would be endangered and totally unprotected from habituated grizzly bears. 

Third, the proposed regulations create wildlife management issues that endanger non target species and offer no protections to beaver, lynx, wolverine, marten, red fox, wolves, river otters, and bald eagles by eliminating the existing protections established under current federal regulations.

Fourth, the proposed regulations have been put forth under a public comment process that is deficient under NEPA and requires a full Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and public comment process because of the significance of the proposed action and its cumulative effects on the legal purposes of the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge and its wilderness and wildlife. 

In summary, I very strongly oppose the proposed rule as outlined by my comments above and urge USFWS to withdraw it in its entirety. It is totally inappropriate for the Kenai NWR, its purposes, its wildlife, and Wilderness Area. 

Please advise me directly of any action USFWS takes on this proposed rule.

Public Comment for Right Whale Regulations 10/6/22
My name is John Moore, I am captain of the F/V Direction, an Area 3 lobster boat. I am
writing this public comment to address concerns I have regarding potential measures the NMFS
may take in order to become compliant within the recent court rulings. I understand the
complexities involved in trying to reach the mandated risk reduction however there are certain
options that are not realistic for the entire offshore fleet. Many of which would hinder our ability
to operate a business.
Over the last 3 years I have tested numerous types of weak ropes. I have yet to test a
single weak rope that breaks at 1700 that would operate in deep waters along the edge of the
continental shelf. The load on these ropes in varying depths and weather conditions will not
permit a 1700 breaking strength. Versions have either parted off due to weather or while hauling
under normal circumstances. Most recently I had two NOAA approved BreakAway release links
break when they entered my hauler. I asked the NEFSC if they had tested these breakaways
under haulers and I was told that they only had put them in the breaking machine but I had yet
to see if they would go through a hauler. I would recommend that NMFS revises plans for
waters that are between 50-100 fathom to have a stronger breaking strength than 1700lbs.
Various load cell data suggests that between those depths a 2000lb breaking strength may be
possible. Additionally it is more likely that a rope manufacturer will be able to develop a 9/16” or
⅝” diameter rope that breaks at this strength. Beyond 100 fathoms I cannot suggest using any
form of weak rope at the current moment.
I have also been part of the ropeless testing program with the NEFSC. I have been
testing both the Edgetech and Smelts units. I want to emphasize to NMFS that I have not had
success using these units. It is important to recognize that what may work for one individual in
one area that they are fishing may not work for another. In the summer I experience extreme
tides that (based on tilt sensor data) continually tilt the ropeless unit on its side causing the rope
inside to become snarled or damage the unit's integrity. For the 2022 fishing year I have
attempted to retrieve a ropeless unit 31 times and I have only been successful 17 times. A 54%
success rate is not going to work for any operation. Coupled with that low success rate there is
about a 10 minute increase to get to my first trap versus traditional buoy systems. The time lost
is something I don’t think NMFS has considered or calculated when looking at the economic
impact ropeless gear would have on the industry. When these units are successful they are also
much more difficult and dangerous to retrieve for crew than a traditional tagline system.
Although there has been progress in ropeless technology there still needs to be further testing
and trials industry wide before they can be approved or mandated. I do suggest that we expand
our efforts in testing ropeless gear. There are not enough individuals testing these units to
determine what may or may not work in certain areas. Additionally, if we were to significantly
expand the program and get units in the water we would be reducing some vertical lines in the
process which would gain risk reduction credit.
The concept of going to one vertical line per trawl is something I am very concerned
about. The ability to haul two different ends is essential for any lobster or crab boat. On a normal
day an individual would choose to haul their gear into the tide and set back fair tide. Only having
one endline would restrict an individual's ability to choose which way to haul their gear. Which
will increase the amount of time it takes to haul and set. In deep water this becomes even more

 
problematic because when an individual has to haul fair tide they often have to circle around the
gear. In certain depths this puts significant strain on the hauler

Re: HS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002 - Public Comment Opposing Proposed Rule

Dear Ms. Sequin, 
As a member of the Boston Bar Association ("BBA"), I fully endorse--and incorporate herein by reference--the comment submitted on November 2, 2018 by Jonathan Albano, President of the BBA, opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement, DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002.

I write separately to underscore my especially strong opposition to the proposed regulations' systematic removal of due process protections for detained immigrants. I am a practicing litigator and a former law clerk to a state appellate judge and two U.S. District Judges, as well as a magna cum laude graduate of Harvard Law School. From my experience as a litigator and a law clerk, I firmly believe that nothing is more fundamental to the fair administration of justice--and the perception of the litigant who ultimately does not prevail that justice has been fairly administered--than an orderly, predictable process where all parties may be heard and the ultimate decision is clearly explained by reference to a neutral set of principles. 

The proposed regulation leaves these principles far behind. Instead, among other flaws ably catalogued by BBA President Albano, it purports to authorize the executive branch to detain immigrants indefinitely with no opportunity to challenge their detention. It purports to permit the executive branch to reclassify--unilaterally--those already determined to be Unaccompanied Alien Children ("UAC") and thereby deprive them of the critical protections this status affords. And it removes the requirement that all minors in a deportation proceeding be afforded a bond hearing, replacing such a critical proceeding with a process wholly confined to political appointees in the executive branch with no opportunity for judicial review.

The fair administration of justice demands more. Immigrants--especially children--must have a full and fair opportunity to make their cases to an impartial decisionmaker in an orderly process. I therefore stand in strong opposition to the proposed regulation.

Very truly yours,
Joshua N. Ruby

I am strongly in favor of using cameras and screens in place of all rear-view mirrors presently required in all vehicles (not just automobiles). The technical and functional benefits have already been discussed at length and are impossible to ignore.

I installed front and rear drivecams in my car after incorrectly being declared at fault in a minor accident. The system I chose also included a full-sized screen that fit over the center mirror that normally displays the rear camera while driving. I was surprised by the number of benefits provided by this system:

1. The wide-angle rear view greatly reduced the size of my left and right blind spots.

2. The wide-angle rear view also made me less agitated by tailgaters.

3. The camera has better night-sight capabilities than my eyes.

4. The camera and screen together serve to eliminate glare from the rear, especially at night.

I believe my benefits would only increase were I to also have cameras and screens to replace my side mirrors.

However, there are risks that must be mitigated: Technology can and will fail (ref: Murphy's Law). In my present system, should the screen or camera fail I can simply remove the screen and use the center mirror.

To mitigate the risk of failure, I would propose that temporary mirrors be provided with every vehicle that can be attached to external and internal mount points when needed. These mirrors should provide the same wide-angle FoV (Field of View) as the cameras, rather than that presently required for OEM mirrors.

These mirrors can also be strictly for temporary use until repair, much like the current reduced-size spare tire, meaning the mirrors may be lightweight and inexpensive. They could be mounted to the forward edge of the front driver and passenger side windows, or to appropriate fixed clip points.

With this mitigation in place, I believe there would be every reason to permit (not require) side and center rear cameras with screens to replace fixed mirrors.

Broadly, this piece of legislation is robust and includes measures that will help standardize the Greenland turbot fishing industry and will improve conditions for those on the boats, killer whales, and the fish residing in this area as well. This regulation includes solid and concrete steps for how fishery operations can comply with these regulations and clearly lays out all of the new exceptions being made to allow hook-and-line C/P vessels to utilize longline pot gear in this new area. Once this proposal has been signed into law, I can imagine that the impacts for all stakeholders will likely be positive, especially for the orca population and the fishery operators that were coming into consistent contact with them. 
While this new regulation is overall strong, one point that needs revision is the admission made in the Background section in reference to the Greenland Turbot Directed Fishery. It is stated that, “the area where the fishery occurs in the BS and AI subareas (…) is very remote, making it difficult to prosecute the fishery.” This admission confirms the BS subarea is not regularly monitored by outside sources due to its remote nature. This raises the question of how the measures in this new regulation, especially regarding equipment marking will be enforced to ensure compliance. There is no compliance measure included in this new regulation, opening to a large question mark on how effective changes will be on a system-scale if individual fishery vessels have no enforcement to use these new pots and label their buoys in specific ways, for example. I would encourage the NMFS to ensure that there are compliance measures in place for this regulation, as well as a plan for how these measures will be monitored given the remote location of the BS fishery subarea. 
Another issue that I fear is potentially being missed in this new regulation is the updates needed to Total Allowable Catch (TAC) amounts for various groundfish. It is stated in the Background section under the heading of “Groundfish Maximum Retainable Amounts (MRAS)” that there are TACs for groundfish and incidental catch, and once those limits are reached all catch of that species must be discarded. However, with the increasing of tunnel limits on pots as an exception to the 9-inch maximum rule to help with the range of Greenland turbot being caught, this also will likely open to more incidental catch of various groundfish taking place. Presumably, the wider the opening in the tunnel, the more fish may be able to swim in both those intended to be caught and incidental catches, so it would be prudent to reevaluate TAC limits and make sure that efforts designed to increase catch of Greenland turbot does not end up increasing incidental take of groundfish and harming their species. Additionally, the removal of gear restrictions preventing the retention of groundfish species by vessels using longline pot gear while directed fishing for Greenland turbot that will allow vessels to retain more groundfish up until the Maximum Retention Amount (MRA) is reached, also implies an increase in take of these groundfish. It is vital to have some measure for monitoring the populations of these groundfish that will be taken more and more between the gear restriction and the widening of tunnels in fishing pots. As a lover of animals and the ocean I agree with this proposed regulation. I like that guidelines are set up for the length, timing, and location of each fireworks display. We are concerned the proposed change from two seats to one seat in the Southeast would severely limit our representation. The Southeast covers a large geographic area covering from Virginia to Louisiana and Puerto Rico. It is an area that includes five separate milk marketing orders in Orders 1, 5, 6, 7, and 33. An area with such diverse geography and variety of producer needs and interests would be incredibly difficult to represent with only one proposed seat. 

The dairy industry in the Southeast has been extremely volatile over the past two decades; it saw both a decline in dairy farms, while also experiencing a rapid increase in population. Due to the Southeast’s increase in population, promotion efforts in the dairy industry will increase in our region as well. Producers from the Southeast region should have a voice in these promotion and education efforts.

We support the USDA considering the population growth and geographic variance of the Southeast with their proposal. When the states were split into different regions, production undoubtedly looked different, and with the change in milk production and population shifts, there may be a need to revisit the distribution of regions. I write to commend NHTSA for taking initial steps to ensure vehicles are safer for people outside cars in its revised New Car Assessment Program (NCAP). Dear Deputy Administrator Wheeler:

On behalf of tens of thousands of members nationwide who are living with and at risk of breast cancer, I am writing to express our grave concern about the damaging impact the proposed Strengthening Transparency in Regulatory Science will have on public health. Restricting the EPAs ability to use the best available science and public health research in rule-making will weaken public health and environmental protections and may result in more people being diagnosed with breast cancer and other diseases.

Breast Cancer Action (BCAction) is a national education and activist organization that works to address and end the breast cancer epidemic. Each year a quarter of a million women are diagnosed with breast cancer, despite the fact that many of these individuals have no known risk factors and engage in healthy lifestyle choices. Extensive scientific research shows that environmental exposures to synthetic chemicals may increase the risk of breast cancer. 

Since our founding in 1990, we have worked for systemic change to stop breast cancer before it starts by understanding and eliminating the root causes of the disease. We recognize that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) plays an essential role in protecting the public from involuntary exposure to harmful chemicals that may increase the risk of breast cancer and may also interfere with breast cancer treatments. 

High-quality, peer reviewed, public health studies and epidemiological studies provide essential information about environmental health and are key to sound, evidence-based policy. We are alarmed that the proposed rule would require that in order for a human-health study to be part of the EPAs rule-making about the health effects of a pollutant or chemical, raw study data, including individual medical records, must be publicly available. This would violate peoples privacy and be both unethical and conflict with existing privacy laws.

The EPA should use the best available science to ensure evidence-based rule making that protects public health. Many disciplines, notably medicine, are able to advance knowledge while protecting patient privacy. It is essential that environmental health studies, even those that include protected health information, are available to the EPA in its decision-making. 

On behalf of everyone living with and at risk of breast cancer, I urge you to reject this proposed rule that would have a devastating implication for public health and environment policy. Public health and epidemiological research is essential to the EPAs ability to safeguard the publics health and well-being.

Moog requests to change the SUMMARY section as shown: 
TO: “It is proposed to adopt an airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Boeing model 757 in 
response to reports from aircraft operators of uncommanded spoiler panel extensions during 
flight. These extensions are the result of a hydraulic system failure, the aircraft flaps extended 
beyond 20 degrees and a failed blocking and thermal relief valve (BTRV) housing, which is a 
part of the the spoiler power control unit (PCU). This AD requires the replacement of certain 
PCUs with ones with replacement BTRVs. Incorporation of the service bulletin will prevent the

proposed AD would require replacing certain power control units (PCUs) with new or changed 
PCUs. We are proposing this AD to prevent an uncommanded extension of spoiler panels in the 
event of a hydraulic system failure, which could result in the loss of control of the airplane. 
 
Reason for change: 
The revised statement adds clarity to these circumstances by identifying the cause(s) and 
provides a corrective action in a single statement. As Boeing indicated in their comments, the 
magnitude of the spoiler float condition at 20 degrres or less is relatively modest and may create 
a rolling moment that is within the airplane capabilities to offset and maintain adequate lateral 
authority. However, with the flaps extended beyond 20 degrees, the magnitude of the angle of 
spoiler increases significantly and the lateral authority is subsequently reduced the in proportion 
to the angle of “spoiler panel float”. The words “single” and “multiple” have been removed 
and replaced with the more general description of “uncommanded spoiler extensions”. This is 
because the proper corrective action summary cannot accurately stated by using both words 
together.

I have a degenerative muscle disease, and so I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

This is an ill thought out rule change. Safety in our mines should always been our first concern, and I do not see how this proposed rule change will make the mines any safer. I do see that it is too ambiguous, it will cause too many issues with uneven enforcement, and it will put additional strain on miners and companies.The current existing work place exam rules work. They allow miners to find and correct issues. 

It will require small operators to put out more expenses than they may be able to afford just to keep up with the record keeping. Larger operations may be able to absorb the costs, but it will hit small operations much harder. What happens with a small operator when the qualified operator is out sick? How does that get addressed? 

The record keeping aspect of this proposed rule change is going to be an nightmare. It puts companies, and individuals at a very high danger of exposure to citations for minor transgressions. It seems to put operators at risk of citations, even if they find them and correct them. The purpose of an inspection is to find things, not to find them, correct them, and then document them for a future inspector to cite, even if they were not there, or did not know the situation. It seems like the mine operator is damned if they do damned if they don't in this case. MSHA itself cannot, or will not indicate to industry if these records will be used to cite operators prior to the rule being implemented. The rule itself is very vague and not a well written rule. It will result in much litigation in the future as it has too many loopholes and issues. People have to pass road tests – so should self-driving cars. Africa Studio/Shutterstock.com

What should a self-driving car do when a nearby vehicle is swerving unpredictably back and forth on the

road, as if its driver were drunk? What about encountering a vehicle driving the wrong way? Before

autonomous cars are on the road, everyone should know how they’ll respond in unexpected situations.

I develop, test and deploy autonomous shuttles, identifying methods to ensure self-driving vehicles are

safe and reliable. But there’s no testing track like the country’s actual roads, and no way to test these new

machines as thoroughly as modern human-driven cars have been, with trillions of miles driven every 

year for decades. When self-driving cars do hit the road, they crash in ways both serious and minor. Yet

all their decisions are made electronically, so how can people be confident they’re driving safely?

Fortunately, there’s a common, popular and well-studied method to ensure new technologies are safe

and effective for public use: The testing system for new medications. The basic approach involves

ensuring these systems do what they’re intended to, without any serious negative side effects – even if

 
researchers don’t fully understand how they work.

Wide-ranging effects

Self-driving cars are expected to improve road safety, freeing up drivers’ time and attention and 

transforming cities and even societies.

The regulations that are created for self-driving cars will have massive effects that ripple throughout the 

economy and society. The rules are likely to come from some combination of the two current automotive

regulators, the federal National Highway Traffic Safety Administration and state departments of 

transportation.

Federal rules focus primarily on safety standards for structural, mechanical and electrical components of

the vehicles, like airbags and seat belts. States can enforce their own safety rules – for example,

regulating emissions and handling driver licensing and vehicle registration, which often also includes

requiring insurance coverage.

Current regulations

Today’s state and federal rules treat drivers and cars as separate entities. But self-driving cars, by

definition, combine the two. Without consistency between those regulations, confusion will reign.

The Obama administration came up with 116 pages of regulations with lots of details, but little

understanding of how self-driving cars worked. For example, they called for each car to have human-

readable permanent labels listing its specific self-driving capabilities, including limits on speeds, specific

highways and weather conditions, all of which would be extremely confusing for users. The regulations

also called for ethical decisions to be made “consciously and intentionally” – which is questionable, if not 

impossible, for a machine.

As a consumer, I'm willing to pay more for high quality organic food. I want to protect my family's health, protect the environment, and support small/medium sized family farms. To accomplish that we need regulations that ensure we truly get organic food and that ensure small organic farmers who use the best practices aren't driven out of business by large agribusinesses that gain advantage by using "loopholes" to provide a lower quality product that is still labelled organic.

We need a Final Rule on the origin of organic livestock and we need it now. At the beginning of the organic dairy movement, one of the big drivers was economic justice for farmers. We have lost thousands of farmers since then. Organic production was intended as an alternative for family-scale producers and it has worked. However, much of the growth in the industry has been usurped by industrial scale operations gaming the system. If it wasn't for the factory farms there could have been thousands of additional dairies saved and converted to organic. The resulting damage to families in rural communities is almost incalculable.

In order to protect the integrity of USDA organic certification and establish a level playing field for a thriving organic dairy market, the Final Rule must:

*Prohibit organic dairy operations from acquiring transitioned animals to expand or replace animals in the organic dairy herd. USDA should prohibit the sales of transitioned animals as certified organic.

*Limit the movement of transitioned animals. Start-up operations should buy organically certified cows. Increased demand for animals raised as organic will create a thriving market for organic replacement animals. This will allow small-to-mid-size organic dairy operations to diversify into breeding replacements whose price will reflect the true cost of organic dairy at their scale of production. 

*Clarify that a "responsibly connected” person who transitions a herd is bound by the same limit as the operation they are connected to. The intent of the rule can be most effectively accomplished by tying the transition to the responsibly connected person(s).

*Be implemented as soon as it is finalized with transitions already in process completed within 12 months. All requirements of the rule should be implemented immediately upon publication of the Final Rule, with the only exception being those dairies that have already started their transition and were already approved by a certifying agent.

*Allow one 12-month transition, and one transition only, per responsibly connected person, with no exceptions. This will prevent the rule from being abused.

Thank you for your consideration,
Kate Pittsley-Sousa

Dear Mr. Hemmersbaugh: 
The Motor & Equipment Manufacturers Association (“MEMA”) submits these comments 
in response to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (“NHTSA”) Federal 
Register notice entitled “Request for Public Comments on Enforcement Guidance Bulletin 
2016-02: Safety-Related Defects and Emerging Automotive Technologies” (referred to 
herein as the “Enforcement Guidance Bulletin”). 81 Fed. Reg. 18935 (April 1, 2016). 
MEMA represents more than 1,000 companies that manufacture motor vehicle parts for 
use in the light- and heavy-duty vehicle original equipment and aftermarket industries.1 
MEMA’s members play a key role in working with vehicle and engine manufacturers to 
improve vehicle safety, efficiencies and emissions. Further, suppliers are often involved in 
or affected by safety-related recalls supervised or adjudicated by NHTSA. 
MEMA shares NHTSA’s interest in ensuring new vehicle technologies are safe for public 
use, and respects NHTSA’s efforts to establish an approach to determining whether a 
software vulnerability poses an unreasonable risk to safety. But, as discussed in more detail 
below, MEMA writes to express concern over NHTSA’s current views on emerging 
technologies and its guiding principles and best practices for vehicle and equipment 
manufacturers to use in developing and implementing new technologies and reporting 
safety-related defects to the Agency. 
 
1 MEMA represents its members through four market segment associations: Automotive Aftermarket Suppliers 
Association (AASA); Heavy Duty Manufacturers Association (HDMA); Motor & Equipment Remanufacturers 
Association (MERA); and, Original Equipment Suppliers Association (OESA). Suppliers are the largest employers of 
manufacturing jobs in the U.S. directly employing over 734,000 Americans with a total employment impact of 3.6 
million jobs. Additionally, the motor vehicle parts manufacturing industry generates over $220 billion in annual 
wages and income, and contributes $355 billion to the U.S. GDP.

 
MEMA Comments RE: Enforcement Guidance Bulletin 2016-02 [Docket No. NHTSA-2016-0040] 
May 2, 2016 Page 2 of 7 
 
MEMA urges NHTSA to forego its traditional enforcement model against manufacturers 
and suppliers of new and emerging vehicle technologies, and, instead, apply a more flexible 
approach for defect determinations. Given the rapid development of these technologies, 
there are currently no applicable performance standards that govern many of them, and it 
may take some time before any detailed guidance can be clearly and reasonably articulated. 
Until then, however, in the absence of such guidance, manufacturers will have difficulty 
identifying and reporting technology challenges that amount to safety-related defects 
under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act (“Safety Act”). MEMA is willing to 
work with NHTSA to establish relevant safety standards as new vehicle technologies 
emerge, but until then, manufacturers of advanced technologies should not be held 
accountable for failure to report within a five-day time frame defects which may have 
safety-implications pursuant to NHTSA’s traditional enforcement model used against 
manufacturers of more established vehicle technology and equipment. 
Further, while MEMA shares NHTSA’s concerns about cybersecurity vulnerabilities in 
software that can connect to a vehicle’s critical safety systems, the proposed guidance is 
impractical given the realities of the vehicle industry.

I am urging you to withdraw the proposed rule to 'modernize' swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety.

The proposed rule puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. In place of these requirements, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide.

The rule also proposes a New Swine Inspection System that hands over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter establishment employees. The proposal also removes caps on line speeds, increasing the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination, and other food safety issues. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer, and this proposal will not achieve that. Instead, it has the potential to make food less safe by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

We urge you to withdraw the proposed rule and design a new rule that prioritizes food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness.

Sincerely,

Marvin Feil
Newton, NJ

Comment on the proposed Queen Conch ESA listing as “Threatened”

The population trajectory of queen conch throughout their range seems to be, sadly, one of decline caused by direct overexploitation by people. Their population has been greatly reduced or has disappeared because of this threat. Therefore, the proposed listing is not only appropriate, but exciting because of the resources (financial and mental) that would be levied to help slow decline and reverse the outlook for an iconic species. I have been studying conch for a rather short time (8 years) but even in that time the magnitude of their decline is apparent. Surveys in exceptionally rare underexploited areas have been completely depressing because of the contrast that they present compared with the majority of the places we visit where few animals and sparse breeding aggregations remain. 

The body of work assembled by the NMFS review clearly demonstrates the uncertain future that queen conch face throughout the Caribbean, and I see no reason to supplement the commendable review with further documentation. However, I will note that the survey that we carried out within the Dry Tortugas National Park this year in August on board the Shedd Aquarium’s research vessel revealed an exceptionally limited population within the well-protected waters of the park. Indeed, we conducted a depth and habitat stratified survey, visiting 178 sites within the park covering approximately 56,000 m2 and found no living queen conch. There were plenty of older shells that indicated a population once existed in these waters, but the only living animals we found were within an (almost literal) stone’s throw of Loggerhead Key and Garden Key. Their fate is uncertain given the hurricane that made landfall weeks later and previous documentation of conch in the area being buried and killed by shifting sands in a silty park. Other rare species were thriving in the park but conch have clearly not been able to recover - attesting to the challenges that conch have once they are depleted to low numbers. Recover will take time and legal protections to grant that time.

I believe that the overwhelming message that has been assembled in the review is an outlook that suggests continued threats to the species because of over exploitation combined with unfortunately lackluster management strategies and low or underfunded capacity for regulation throughout much of the species range. A threatened listing can only help improve the future for an animal that remains widely in decline where it is still found.

Sincerely,
Dr. Andrew Kough

I'm so pleased to see that the Department of Transportation (DOT) is now taking a strong look at the policies regarding emotional support animals. This blatant abuse can easily be considered a form of stealing or fraudulent behavior. 
I feel extremely fortunate to have finally been placed with a highly intelligent Labrador Retriever to help me with a variety of physical limitations. I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

On behalf of the Animal Legal Defense Fund (ALDF), a national nonprofit 
organization dedicated to protecting the lives and advancing the interests of animals 
through the legal system, we submit these comments in response to the U.S. Department of 
Agriculture (USDA) Food Safety and Inspection Service’s (FSIS) proposed Modernization of 
Swine Slaughter Inspection rule (Proposed Rule), 83 Fed. Reg. 4780-4823 (Feb. 1, 2018). 
FSIS’s Proposed Rule, creating the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System (NSIS), would 
have disastrous effects on animal welfare and food safety, in derogation of FSIS’s statutory 
mandates to ensure the humane treatment of hogs at slaughter and the safety of our 
nation’s meat supply. ALDF urges FSIS not to adopt the Proposed Rule, and to end the 
failed HACCP-Based Inspection Models Project (HIMP) immediately. 
 
Statutory Background 
 
FSIS is charged with ensuring that the American meat supply is safe under the 
Federal Meat Inspection Act (FMIA). To that end, FSIS has a complementary duty under 
both the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act (HMSA) and FMIA to ensure that animals are 
treated humanely during slaughter. 
 
The FMIA requires FSIS to ensure sanitary conditions at all establishments in 
which swine are slaughtered; if the conditions are such that the products thereof are 
rendered adulterated, inspectors must refuse to allow such products in commerce.1 FSIS 
regulations require thorough ante- and post-mortem inspections of each animal to ensure 
that only healthy animals and wholesome, non-adulterated meat enter the food supply.2 
 
The FMIA also incorporates the HMSA,3 which establishes a “national policy” of 
slaughtering animals humanely.4 In the HMSA Congress explicitly commanded that “the 
handling of livestock in connection with slaughter shall be carried out only by humane

I write to oppose this proposed regulation removal. I serve on the Parks Commission of my city and have been involved in attempting to keep EAB from affecting our trees. EAB is not (yet) widespread in Minnesota, and transportation can speed up the diffusion of this pest, so removing this regulation would potentially endanger trees in areas where they are not yet endangered. More rapid diffusion of this pest would undercut the efforts associated with past investments in containment & treatment. Tree loss is already a significant problem in my city for various reasons (e.g., construction & development, severe weather), and infestation is an irreversible change that would make the problem worse. Loss of trees can lead to other problems (e.g., flooding) that in turn requires cities to spend more money later (e.g., by planting new trees and upgrading infrastructure). So "saving money" by removing this regulation could well be short-sighted: It could materially damage communities and increase the need for additional money to be spend later. In short, the issue does not only concern bugs and trees; it affects communities, including residents, homeowners, and taxpayers. Funding should be directed both to slowing the spread of the pest and to treatment of affected trees. Thank you for considering this input.

Care can be provided at patient's homes instead of a hospital setting. Home care is more affordable than hospitals.

I am deeply concerned by the proposed, severe cuts to Medicare home health services in the Home Health Prospective Payment System Proposed Rule for CY 2023.

The law requires that Medicare expenditures for home health be budget neutral as CMS implements PDGM, but the new methodology results in significant reductions. In addition to a -7.69 percent permanent payment adjustment starting in 2023, the Proposed Rule forecasts additional cuts of more than $2 billion in 2024 for services provided to Medicare beneficiaries during the pandemic. Over the next decade, these proposed cuts total $18 billion. 

Cuts of this magnitude would be devastating to patients and providers. At a time when both demand for home health and the costs of delivering care are rising significantly, this proposal will significantly limit access to patient-preferred home health, especially among America's rural and medically underserved seniors. 

Further, the proposed methodology in the rule is technically flawed and counter to the intent of budget neutrality of the new payment system. The methodology for annually determining the impact of differences between assumed behavior changes and actual behavior changes on estimated aggregate expenditures and the related proposed permanent and temporary adjustments do not align with the requirements of the statute or its intent to ensure budget neutral rates. The agency also makes no attempt to compare the behaviors assumed by CMS in establishing the initial payment amounts for CY 2020 and the actual behavior observed on aggregate expenditures. Rather, CMS' proposal retroactively re-prices 2020 and 2021 claims payments to establish an artificial target amount and reduces the 30-day payment amounts under PDGM to meet that target. In effect, rather than ensuring the payment amounts are budget neutral, it constitutes an unauthorized rebasing of the 30-day payment amount. 

I hope you will reconsider the methodology to more accurately ensure budget neutrality while avoiding an unauthorized rebasing of the payment system. For the sake of the millions of seniors who rely upon the Medicare Home Health Benefit, please reconsider these cuts before finalizing the Proposed Rule.

I write today as a long time community advocate and also as a family member to two individuals with removal orders. The proposed rule would cause incredible harm to my community, family, friends, and neighbors. I live in a community largely made up of refugees and the children of refugees, like myself. Even though it's not talked about openly too much, I know that many members of my community have Orders of Supervision (OSUP) that came about following old criminal cases. Large numbers are like my cousins, who were in their early 20's and their convictions dating back to the earlly 1990's. My two cousins' experiences have taught me much about the struggles they are facing and how this is impacting their young children and the rest of our very large extended family. The government, through this proposed rule, would be pushing us back toward the poverty that we, as a community, have worked so hard to overcome. My cousins would lose their jobs, and their families would suffer. In fact, our entire community would suffer. We hear all the time about "self-reliance" and "independence," but even when immigrants and refugees are doing just that - supporting themselves, holding down steady jobs, not relying on the government for anything - it isn't enough. This proposed rule is a slap in the face, not just for the individuals working under OSUP, but for our whole community. 
 
With millions of workers out of work due to the ongoing pandemic, now is the worst time to create more layoffs and thrust thousands of diligent workers into unemployment. Millions of families, including my family members with OSUP, are struggling to make ends meet and simply survive the pandemic. By cutting off work options for thousands of individuals, the proposed rule is likely to increase homelessness, hunger, poverty, and mental health issues. 
 
Furthermore, the Department of Homeland Security has decided that certain immigrants and refugees should remain under OSUP because they cannot be removed from the United States. It is unjust to force a status on someone and then prevent them from working to earn a living and support their family. Work authorization has allowed many people on OSUP to support themselves and their families for 10, 15 20 years. Changing the rules now would just punish these individuals again who have already been punished many times over. Changing this policy now would not "encourage [non-citizens] to depart the country," as USCIS claims. Rather, it will only punish people who will remain in the U.S. without the ability to work lawfully. For all of these reasons, I oppose this proposed rule.

actively encourages and challenges the executive and judiciary to support privacy and

environment.

The 1954 Convention on the Status of Stateless Persons (the 1954 Convention) provides that states should identify and protect stateless people on their territory, including the right to wage-earning employment and self-employment.

 Thank you for the opportunity to respond to the International Pricing Index Model for Medicare Part B Drugs. I represent 35,000 retired teachers covered on a Medicare Advantage plan since 2007 and covered on a Medicare Part D EGWP inside a group purchasing alliance since 2012. My role for 17 years now has been to contain costs without shifting costs to the retirees while keeping the Medicare coverage as valuable to the retirees as possible. We have been staunch supporters of fair and reasonable drug prices including the use of generic and biosimilar drugs, where appropriate. This comment is not to be construed as a stance on price controls vs. the free market as both elements already exist within Medicare plans, in that Medicare's regional fee schedules already represent price controls and Medicare Advantage or Part C of Medicare is run by private insurance companies with competition similar to that of the free market.
 Again, we are staunch supporters of fair and reasonable drug prices, and we want to be part of any potential solution instead of perpetuating unfair drug prices by continuing to pay for them. Medicare Part B drugs are those normally administered by a physician, and the physician is reimbursed by Medicare based upon the non-negotiated Average Sales Price (ASP) + a 6% add on. I would like to request that we be considered for participation in any future models or demonstration projects that would include testing alternative pricing models to the existing reimbursement pricing structure of ASP + 6%. This request includes participation in any pricing models that help to fairly share the costs of necessary Research and Development (R&D) for the much needed innovator drugs that patients from all countries benefit yet only patients and health plans in the United States are charged. My contact information is included in this response form.

Dear Dr. Lewis:
 Please extend the comment period to allow an adequate review of all proposed regulations. As an employee in the egg business, I know the challenges we face and a short comment period is not long enough to weigh the benefits or consequences this rule might bring.
 I disagree with the increased outside access proposal. In the desire to give the birds a more humane environment, they will be exposed to predators, weather, and disease such as avian influenza. The mortality will be much greater than the 5-8% that is mentioned. The effect could be as large as avian influenza affecting over 32 million hens in 2015, the majority of which were housed inside.
 I oppose the space considerations being based on kilograms per square foot. As a laying hen ages, her weight increases. Does the rule allow for a house to be stocked with correct density at 18 weeks of age knowing that the hens will get heavier and be overstocked? Or if you stock at the correct density for proposed weight at 80 weeks, how can you be sure that your chickens will reach their expected weight gain? There will be inefficiencies stocking a poultry house using either formula. Stocking based on hen numbers is a much better system.

Supply and demand will force some to close their operations and supplies of organic eggs will be short causing higher egg prices. definition of “rebates, fees, and any other remuneration,” because the statute’s expansive language (“any

reach. Additionally, full disclosure without exemptions is the only way to avoid definitional gaming by the

broad definition of rebates, fees, and other remuneration and believe this will provide the Departments
