There are positive and negative aspects of the proposed modernization rules, but there is also extremely vague and potentially disasterous language that indicates the lack of thinking through the proposed changes The Good change--the elimination of district and automatic granting of national permits. If a Customs Broker is a national license, why does their need to be a district permit in the first place, but also, why should a customs broker have to apply for other permits in the first place. The wording of this change, however, uses the term of "automatically" granting the national permit, but in the same paragraph has language that "CBP will provide guidance...to transition their district permits to a national permit." That does not sound automatic.
The bad changes or suggestions: using Customs Brokers as "force multipliers" for enforcement. In a time when more brokers are needed this will discourage the use of brokers but also put brokers in a position to "advise the client" of noncompliance, errors, omissions but also possible corrective actions. However, brokers are also placed in a position of having to "rat" on their clients. As a Catholic, as a lover of nature, and as someone with deep connections to hunting and farming communities, I urge you to revise this rule to make its emission reduction goals stronger. 

We are facing a time of ecological crisis. As a person of faith, I am called to care for our common home, which includes reducing contributions to climate change and its effects. Currently, the energy demands of our economy are tearing apart the web of life, with disastrous consequences for vulnerable communities and future generations. Across the globe we witness the horrible devastation carbon pollution wreaks on nature and the vulnerable. 

In this face of this global reality, I believe the United States government has a responsibility to provide leadership in the shift to renewable energy. The Affordable Clean Energy rule's weaker emissions standards would expose millions of Americans to more pollution - carrying a multitude of negative effects. Any replacement plan should reduce carbon pollution even more than the original Clean Power Plan standards of reducing emissions by 32% below 2005 levels by 2030. This is in light of the market's rapid shift towards clean energy and the falling cost of renewable energy sources like wind and solar. 

The EPA has a duty to protect us from the impacts of carbon pollution, including the effects of climate change. These include increasing droughts, greater food insecurity, and more severe weather. All this is happening in the United States now. The EPA's mission is to "protect human health and the environment" - I urge the agency to live up to that important responsibility. 

The ACE rule falls short of the EPA's mission and the faithful call to care for creation in the following ways: 

1. Lowering emission reduction ambition for states: The EPA should set increasingly high targets for emissions reductions as a standard for states, instead of providing a range of weaker targets. The ACE rule also allows for too much latitude in state determination of reduction standards, monitoring, and enforcement mechanisms thereby making such benchmarks effectively meaningless. 

2. Incomplete justification for plan: The EPA must take into account all ways carbon pollution affects all areas of society and base target reductions on the most inclusive estimates. 

3. Longer implementing timelines: We are facing an ecological crisis now. The ACE rule limits action on carbon pollution by extending the timeline for states to draft, submit, and implement their plans. We urge the EPA to return to the original timelines from the CPP for state submission of plans (Comment C-53) and the implementation of a federal plan if a state plan is deemed insufficient (Comment C-54). 

I encourage the administration to think creatively about how we can replace fossil fuels with renewable energies. We can take care of our workers, our vulnerable communities, and our environment all at once. What we can no longer afford to do, as Pope Francis says, is ignore the realities before us and place profits over people, the interest of a few over the good of everyone. I urge the agency to revise the ACE rule to provide for the highest amounts of reduction of carbon emissions and to facilitate the movement to renewable energy as quickly as possible.

In Washington, DC where I live, I know people in my community already feeling the impact of climate change. It is making their lives more difficult - it is a burden on their standard of living. Please revise this rule to better care for our common home and the common good of everyone.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. 

Purpose of the settlement was to protect the children and prevent them from facing indefinite detention. Yet this new regulation does not seem to rectify the entirety of the issues which led to the settlement and again endangers our most vulnerable population. 

In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

The United State has been the top educator in the world with high quality advanced education and friendly environment that attract many international students to pursue a degree in a US institute. The current system of tracking the education record of international students has been sufficient to monitor students' performance and stay, and provides students stability and convenience to focus on their school work and research. The proposed rule would add an unnecessary layer of application to international students and may interrupt their education significantly if the applications cannot be processed on time. This would create additional barriers for international students and discourage students to pursue a degree in the US. Eventually, this may harm the educational institutes in the US and the US economy in general, as international students contribute to a large portion of tuition income of US institutes and the prosperity of research and business.

Firstly, the current monitoring system already requires all international students to remain a good standing to continue their education. The educational records are maintained and monitored by each institute, and all activities of students are tracked. Under the current rule, international students have to continue making a progress in their study and file to the school with any change in their study or training. The new rule merely improves this already well-functioning monitoring system, but creates extra burden to students, schools, and government agencies.

Secondly, baccalaureate degrees and doctoral degrees all require at least 4 years of study. Under the new rule, the majority of international students would have to at least file an extension request once. If the applications cannot be processed in time, international students have to experience interruptions to their study or research. In many research fields, such interruptions could be detrimental to students' research.

Thirdly, with potential interruptions of study or research ahead, international students may find it less attractive to pursue education in a US institute, especially when such interruptions can be detrimental to their research. The proposed rule may lead to a decrease in international students, who have been contributing to the diversity and creativity of many research fields in US institutes. If the best students in the world have to choose another destination to study other than come to the US, the advanced education of the US will be significantly harmed.

Last but not least, the proposed rule sends out a discouraging signal to all the international students, with less stability and consistency in the US advanced education. While currently, the brightest minds in every field are willing to choose to contribute to the science, technology, and economy of the US, such discouragement could lead to the flow of these students to other countries with good advanced education, and lend their talents to these other countries. This eventually harms the national interest of the US.

In conclusion, the proposed rule would not be contributing to a monitoring system that currently runs well, but could significantly harm the current and prospective international students that are studying or would like to study in the US, and harm the advanced education, the advanced research, and the economy of the US.

While the agency has proposed several improvements to the standards, such as requiring shade for all outdoor marine mammal enclosures and ramps for older or injured seals, sea lions, polar bears, and sea otters to exit pools more easily, these are minor compared to the significant failures in the proposed rule.

The agency proposes no changes to the space requirements, claiming it is unaware of any science on which to base such changes. In fact, there is a tremendous body of recent research using increasingly sophisticated tagging technology to monitor fine-scale movement patterns of individual marine mammals, especially cetaceans and polar bears. These species travel tremendous distances and dive very deep, making the current minimum space requirements totally inhumane. The best available science for seals, sea lions, and sea otters--even for the slow, plant-eating manatee--also supports major space increases.

The current space standards were set over 30 years ago and have no basis in science or even best practices within the captive display industry. As an example, for up to two orcas, a facility need only provide a circular tank with a diameter twice as wide and a depth half as deep as an average adult orca is long. This standard does not even allow the animal to position itself fully in the vertical plane (its tail would touch and drag on the bottom before the animal reaches full upright orientation). This cannot be considered adequate!

While the rule refers to peer-reviewed papers for proposed changes to some standards (e.g., lighting requirements), it claims the agency is unaware of such papers for other standards (e.g., temperature requirements) and therefore proposes no major changes. Yet a considerable amount of research has been conducted within the past 15 years related to most if not all of the affected standards. 

The proposed rule would still allow pinnipeds to be housed in enclosures with tanks filled with fresh water. Allowing the maintenance of a marine mammal in fresh water is clearly an inappropriate welfare standard.

Several standards have been weakened, particularly regarding interactive programs such as swim-with-dolphin encounters. For example, the standard for the interaction time for each cetacean per day has been increased from two hours to three hours, not based on science or even industry best practices, but simply "on information provided by licensees ... which suggested that the marine mammals would not be harmed by a modest increase in interactive time per day." Re: 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule Dear USDA Forest Service, I am writing to request that you fully restore 2001 Roadless Rule protections on the Tongass National Forest and end large-scale old growth timber sales on the entirety of the forest. The Tongass is a key weapon for fighting climate change, with its old-growth trees effectively trapping and sequestering climate-warming greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Scientists have estimated that the forest accounts for about 8 percent of the carbon sequestered by all national forests. Protecting the Tongass from old-growth logging will not only preserve that capacity, but avoid releasing carbon currently sequestered in its trees. The Tongass is also the ancestral and contemporary homeland of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples, and they have been the driving force of the effort to protect the forest. Their way of life is inextricably linked with these lands and waters. They hunt, gather, fish and harvest medicines in the Tongass that their ancestors have stewarded for more than 10,000 years. Restoring full protections will allow their traditional use of the land to continue. As part of planning for a future beyond old-growth timber, please also make a sustained investment in the Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy. Operating in full consultation with Tribal governments and local communities, this program will help the region stoke the already robust fishing and recreation industries that are driving the economy. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Nathalie Camus - PII -

Dear Director Stone-Manning:

The State of Utah (“State”) strongly opposes the Proposed Rule on Conservation and Landscape Health (the “Proposed Rule”) released by the Bureau of Land Management (“BLM”) on April 3, 2023. This Proposed Rule, if adopted, could fundamentally alter the future management of BLM lands to the detriment of recreation, livestock grazing, mineral extraction, renewable energy production, and other common uses on BLM lands. In 1976, Congress declared in the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (“FLPMA”) that the BLM must manage BLM lands “on the basis of multiple use and sustained yield.” Yet this Proposed Rule seeks to define “conservation” as a “use” within FLPMA’s multiple-use framework. This reframing of the term “multiple use” would contravene FLPMA and violate federal case law in Public Lands Council v. Babbitt, where the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals found that the BLM lacks the statutory authority to prioritize conservation use to the exclusion of other uses. The Proposed Rule would push BLM lands into a protection-oriented management regime more akin to the National Park Service than an agency statutorily obligated to promote multiple-use and sustained yield. 

We find provisions of the Proposed Rule to be ultra vires, inconsistent with principles of Chevron deference articulated by the U.S. Supreme Court, contrary to the very purpose of FLPMA. And we urge the BLM to set aside the Proposed Rule and instead work with states, counties, and tribal governments to truly enhance conservation on BLM lands within the framework of multiple-use and sustained yield.
Of the 22.8 million acres of land the BLM owns in Utah (approximately 42% of our land area) approximately 10.1 million acres are already under a restrictive form of protection such as National Monuments, Wilderness Areas, Wilderness Study Areas, Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, etc. And that’s not to mention millions of acres of other protected public lands such as National Parks, Forest Service Wilderness Areas, and Forest Service Roadless Areas. Of the remaining 12.7 million acres of BLM land still open to multiple-use, there is still a very high bar to clear before any kind of surface disturbing activities can be authorized, as well as many barriers to development in existing BLM resource management plans. In short, the Proposed Rule seems to be a solution in search of a problem when so much of Utah’s BLM land is already under strict Federal protection.

 The Proposed Rule seems to misinterpret the very notion of conservation. Conservation is not a hands-off “use” that excludes more active uses – conservation is an essential element of the regular activities, best management practices, and proper stewardship that occur on BLM land every day. Conservation, by its plain meaning, encompasses the stabilization of eroding stream banks, predator control to protect threatened and endangered species, removal of pinyon and juniper trees to restore healthy sagebrush rangelands, reclamation work on former mining sites, adaptive grazing systems to better conserve native plants, improved fencing to protect riparian areas, controlled burns to reduce fuel loads, installation of wells and pipelines to provide water to native wildlife, enhancements to recreational infrastructure that reduce the impacts of visitation, and so much more. Indeed, the traditional meaning of the word “conservation” encompassed the types of uses that Federal lands were intended for: sustainable timber harvest, responsible livestock grazing, conscientious mineral extraction, and other activities needed to sustain rural economic development. The way to enhance conservation on BLM lands is to promote the multiple-use and active management of those lands and encourage the principles of conservation in all of those uses.

Although the AD references that It was determined that the cracks resulted from fatigue caused by flight loads, a further explanation of how this was determined would be helpful. Were the loads beyond what the aircraft was certificated for?

Additionally, the AD references "loss of control" as a possibility in the event of failure. At the time the aircraft was certified, was the wing spacer considered to be a component integral to the structural integrity of the aircraft? And isn't there a redundant spacer in place already? Was that spacer also found to be cracked? Isn't the structure of the aircraft itself sufficient to maintain the structure of the airplane if the spacer were cracked? 

Is there any analysis what so ever that shows that a cracked wing spacer will compromise the ability of the plane to handle the loads for which it was certified?

About the only thing I agree on with this AD is that a fluorescent penetrant inspection would be prudent. And it would seem to me that if there is a concern, it should be done at the next 100 hour inspection, not waiting until 7,500 hours or 2,000 hours. If it is determined that there is true risk associated with failure, then the decision to replace will be obvious and need not be governed by AD.

Purpose and Need for Proposed Rule 
Currently, the charter fishery is limited to harvesting its percentage of the Area 2C or 3A combined 
catch limit it is allocated under the CSP. Charter catch limits increase or decrease as total halibut 
abundance increases or decreases. When halibut abundance is relatively low, as it has been in 
recent years compared to abundance trends in the 1990s and 2000s, the charter allocations under 
the CSP are lower, resulting in more restrictive annual management measures. 
The only way that charter operators can currently provide more opportunity to charter clients than 
the established management measures allow for in their area is through participation in the GAF 
Program by individual charter operators. Because of the current restrictions on charter harvests 
under the existing charter allocations under the CSP and the limited flexibility for charter operators to 
provide additional harvest opportunities to their clients, the charter fishery has expressed its desire 
to find a market-based mechanism to increase its overall allocation of the halibut resource. 
Based on these concerns, in 2015, the Council initiated the analytic process to develop a “market-
based mechanism” to allow a non-profit entity (similar to a CQE) to purchase and hold a limited 
amount of commercial halibut QS on behalf of charter anglers. The intent of the Council was to 
provide additional harvest opportunity and less restrictive annual harvest measures for charter 
anglers in times of low halibut abundance, while complying with total halibut removals under the 
catch limits established by the IPHC under the CSP. In initiating this effort, the Council sought to 
balance the objectives of participants in the charter fishery without undermining the goals of the IFQ 
Program or creating significant adverse impacts to other halibut sectors. A complete history of the 
development of this proposed action is described in Section 2.2 of the Analysis.

Bear Creek Winery strongly opposes the NPRM to the extent it proposes to eliminate excise tax 

drawback. Not only is it contrary to the statute and congressional intent as explained in detail in a 

separate comment, but if implemented, it would significantly damage Bear Creek Winery’s wine 

export program and reduce Bear Creek Winery’s ability to remain competitive in the global wine 

market. 

Bear Creek Winery is a privately held wine producer in Lodi California. It is owned and operated 

by the Kautz family, a multi-generational grape grower in Lodi and the Sierra Foothills regions.

markets are Denmark, Sweden, Canada, United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, and China.

this number increases to approximately 120. In addition, the Kautz family employs a full team of 

full-time vineyard staff. 

2015 was the first year Bear Creek Winery began utilizing the drawback program. In the 

international markets we compete with origins that have special duty and tariff arrangements that 

favor them over us. As a result, and in combination with factors such as currency exchange, 

California wines are at the higher end of the per unit cost parameters; meaning that we need all 

the help to stay competitive in the global markets. The drawback program has assisted us in that 

direction.

markets. Through a variety of means, such as continuous quality and process improvements,

I strongly urge you to revise the proposed rule in order to keep DACA intact.

Separating DACA’s deferral for deportation and employment authorization benefits weakens the program and exposes it to court challenges that could strip DACA recipients of their ability to be employed.

Over the years, I have had a number of students who were DACA recipients, and I saw how much this program meant to them as they were able to build a life here. They could pursue education and expect to be gainfully employed when they finished, not to mention work to pay for school in the meantime.

The Association of Public Health Laboratories (APHL) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the US 

Food and Drug Administration’s proposed rule to revoke § 2.19, which states that it is FDA policy to use

enforcement programs when the method of analysis is not prescribed in a regulation. APHL understands 

that this regulation states an FDA policy for their own testing methods, and FDA is proposing this action 

because the existing regulation is unnecessary. 

APHL trusts that FDA will continue to rigorously evaluate data to ensure that, no matter the method used, 

the method is fit-for-purpose and meets quality metrics that ensure data accuracy and defensibility. APHL 

also hopes that the revocation of this rule will not impact the FDA’s utilization of defensible state data. 

Many APHL member laboratories that perform regulatory testing on FDA-regulated commodities rely on 

AOAC compendial methods in the absence of a validated FDA method. AOAC Official Methods are 

rigorously evaluated, which makes them ideal to use when running regulatory samples to ensure that 

results are of the highest quality and legally defensible. However, the process for official approval can be 

time-consuming and expensive, and fully approved official methods do not always take advantage of the 

latest technological advances available. It is understandable that FDA would want to remove this specific 

requirement to allow swifter adoption of better technology. APHL hopes that FDA recognizes the states’ 

ability to assist FDA in method development and validation while also taking into consideration the 

technology and equipment available in state laboratories when updating FDA methods. 

APHL trusts that rescinding this regulation does not affect which testing methods state laboratories are 

able to use for regulatory testing. To eliminate potential effects on accreditation, laboratories will need 

to reference the most current method or a method from a specific year on their accreditation scope. While 

the Pesticide Analytical Manual (PAM), Chemical Analytical Manual (CAM), and Bacteriological Analytical

unpublished updates for Laboratory Information Bulletin (LIB) methods that are not offered publicly.

The Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (ODFW) staff have reviewed the Proposed Rule on 
Permitting and Management Regulations for Area 2A Pacific Halibut Fisheries and provide the 
following for consideration. 
 
Permitting for Commercial and Recreational Charter Vessels 
The proposed application deadlines for the commercial fisheries are 15 days to 2 months earlier 
than what has been in place for many years for licesnsing through the International Pacific 
Halibut Commission. There is no indication of how the National Marine Fisheries Service 
intends to inform fishery particpants of these new deadlines. How is NMFS going to ensure that 
fishery participants are aware of the deadline changes? During the transition year, will there by 
an allowance for late applications, given the change in deadlines and permitting agency? Will 
there be any sort of appeals process for late applications or denied applications? Additionally, 
when and where will applications for licenses be available? 
 
Inseason Management 
ODFW staff have concerns about the timing of openings, after the initially announced openings. 
The landugage in the background section of the proposed rule says, “as soon as practicable” in 
reference to additional openings. Is there an estimation on what that time frame may be, days, 
weeks, or month? 
 
Much of the directed commercial fishery landings into Oregon goes to smaller buyers supplying 
local grocery stores and restaurants. They have come to depend on knowing the timing of 
openings (currently every other week) in developing their markets. Especially the first year, 
having an unknown amount of time between openings could be disruptive to those small coastal

My wife and I moved to Alaska for the opportunities it presents in nature, resource development, and the unique ability residents have to balance the two. It's discouraging when federal government policy, developed thousands of miles away by people with mostly outside interests dictate how Alaska should be managed. The Administration did not consult Alaska Native communities, especially those living closest to the NPR-A. Alaska’s federally Recognized Tribes as well as Alaska Native Corporations did not receive invitations to consult on the proposed rule. A letter was sent to these groups to “[inform] them of the rulemaking” seven business days before the rule’s publication.

Responsible development on the NPR-A creates enormous economic benefits. The economic analysis the DOI used ignores benefits like the NPR-A Impact Mitigation Grant program. 
This grant program creates a legal requirement for local communities to receive generous revenues from projects. If project development is slowed or halted by the new rule, Alaska Native communities will lose enormous revenues for public services, health facilities and educational resources, to name a few impacted areas. Diminished oil production from the NPR-A would result in diminished production tax and ad valorem tax revenue for the State and local governments in Alaska. This means less revenue for the State of Alaska to provide services to Alaskans.

If approved, the proposed rule would have significant negative impacts on the permit approval process, even for leases that existed prior to the rule’s implementation. Given the harm to existing lease contracts as well as a clear conflict with the NPR-A’s purpose to develop petroleum, this rule will likely be subject to costly and lengthy litigation. 

The NPR-A was set aside and designated specifically for petroleum development, balanced with conservation, to ensure America’s national security through access to energy. At a time when oil prices are rising and global supply can be easily constricted by foreign governments, investing in domestic oil production is a matter of national and energy security.

I would concur with the comments made by Nathan Dean and Jay Wall. Regardless of what improvements the GAO wanted to make in terms of consistency, it did not mean removing the human element completely. One of the key aspects of Traffic Records is Executive Leadership a dimension of the system that cannot be adequately covered by SMEs reviewing technical documents. The post TR briefing of top level administrators was critical to achieving change in how a State would elect to change its business and always had an impact when properly delivered. While technical content and consistency clearly needed to be improved, relying on an information exchange software platform as the sole tool for assessing progress has been shortsighted. NHTSA appears to be unduly wedded to this software and at last check has demonstrated no signs of changing its basic approach.

I would suggest convening a small group of stakeholders to design a system that captures the best elements of both the old human interaction process and the new documentation driven process (Note: all of the documentation in the world means little if it is not being implemented). Suggested changes could include bringing back an on site team to interview for a week followed up by an electronic documentation in response to fewer but more accurate and clear question. The closeout briefing would take place at the Commissioner level in the form of a Webinar with the NHTSA Regional Administrator on site to offer clarification and technical assistance in developing remedies. States would help pay the expenses of the on site team who would be thoroughly vetted, trained, and advised as to how best to conduct on site panel driven discussions.

Without a return to the human element, NHTSA faces the prospect of losing significant ground in TR progress. While minor technical changes might be made, strategic leadership driven decisions will not be made because policymakers were not part of the process. NHTSA should also note that sister agencies like FHWA still very much retain the human element in its assessment and technical assistance interventions with the States. The agency should consider taking a page from the FHWA playbook to get its TR Assessment process back on track. The Assessments will once again be considered high visibility, important, impactful, and potentially policy transformative events.

This is a comment for the proposed Grades and Standards changes for In-Shell pecans, Publication Date 06/01/2022 Pages 33064-33071 in the Federal Register.

I do not support the proposed changes to Grades and Standards of In-Shell pecans. The proposed standards are more cumbersome and completely unnecessary. This is a change to the standards which has been pushed by the Sheller Representatives on the American Pecan Council since its inception, and serves as a tool for buyers of in shell pecans to push further discounts on American Pecan Growers. Quite simply, a handful of shellers purchase the vast majority of the American Pecan crop, and meticulously sample each and every load, then grade, and pay Growers for their crop. There is no confusion about the quality of the crop that is being moved to the shellers. 

Specifically, the standard for Kernals in the Shell includes language from the original standard "Free from damage by any cause" in the first two grades, U.S. Extra Fancy and U.S. Fancy. This was an unworkable standard even in the original Grades and Standards for In Shell Pecans. Very rarely is any one pound sample of In Shell Pecans ever free completely of an instance of kernel damage--however slight. Automatically this standard puts almost the entirety of the U.S. Pecan Grower's crop in the bottom half of the quality grades.

The real need for transparent standards in the Pecan Industry is certainly in the Shelled Pecan market. The few shellers in the industry move pecan product to thousands of retail and industrial consumers who need this information and quality assurance in their purchase. The impact of sub-par product delivered here and to the end consumer to the entire Pecan Industry cannot be overstated. The unnecessary and unworkable In-Shell Pecan Standards herein proposed do nothing to impact this.

Because of the small number of Shellers in the Pecan Industry, these comments are being submitted anonymously.

Dads, you wouldn't knowingly bring poison into your home, and you certainly wouldn't expose your kids. But you may not realize that if you use at-home hair dyes like Grecian Formula, whenever your children play with your hair, they could be getting a harmful hit of lead.

Lead is highly toxic, especially to children, yet for more than 30 years, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has allowed companies to add a lead-based compound called lead acetate to hair dyes. In 1980, the FDA approved the use of lead acetate in products that restore gray hair to its previous hue. Many of these products are marketed specifically to men.

The lead in these hair dyes poses serious health risks, both to adult consumers and to their children. So Earthjustice, as part of a coalition of health and environmental advocates has petitioned the FDA to ban lead from all hair dyes.

How much lead is in these products? A study by one of the petitioners, Dr. Howard Mielke of Tulane University in New Orleans, showed that samples of hair dyes that listed lead acetate as an ingredient had lead levels between 2,300 and 6,000 parts per million (ppm). The FDA allows lead levels as high as 6,000 ppm in dyes. For perspective, the federal government has banned sales of paint for homes and children's products with lead levels greater than 90 ppm. If a product brushed onto walls and toys cannot have more than 90 ppm of lead, why can a product applied directly to the scalp have more than 66 times that amount?

 If a product brushed onto walls and toys cannot have more than 90 ppm of lead, why can a product applied directly to the scalp have more than 66 times that amount?

The lead in these dyes can contaminate homes and harm childreneven before they ruffle dad's hair. One product's instructions tell adult users to pour the lead-based dye onto their hands and then disperse it throughout their hair. Users then comb and blow-dry their hair. They're told to wash their hands. This process is repeated daily until the desired color is reached, and then weekly after that. Doing this with lead hair dye can contaminate everyday objects in the home, such as combs, sinks, counter tops and bars of soapthings young children are likely to touch too. And because children tend to put their hands in their mouths, they are likely to ingest some of this lead, at which point it enters their bloodstreams.

Lead in blood, even at the lowest levels scientists can measure, harms children. It hurts their brains and nervous systems. It reduces IQ, hinders academic achievement and can cause behavioral disorders such as ADHD. That's why the Centers for Disease Control, the American Academy of Pediatrics and other groups tell parents to eliminate lead from homes before exposure can occur.

In some cases, removing lead can be an expensive undertaking for communities, as they work to replace vital infrastructure or lead plumbing fixtures. But when it comes to lead acetate in a consumer product like hair dye, it should be an easy call. The FDA should simply revoke its approval of lead acetate in dyes.

The State of Alaska (State) has reviewed the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Notice) published in 
the Federal Register (Vol. 86, No. 223, 66498-66505) on November 23, 2022, by the U.S. 
Department of Agriculture (USDA), Forest Service. Please consider the following consolidated 
comments in the final rule. 
 
The State strongly opposes the USDA, Forest Service’s proposal to repeal the 2020 Alaska 
Roadless Rule. The 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule recognized the unique character and history of the 
lands in question and rectified the debilitating economic and socioeconomic consequences from 
misapplication of the 2001 Roadless Rule in Alaska. Numerous existing environmental safeguards 
currently ensure that economic survival is balanced with wise conservation practices and resource 
protection. 
 
Proposed Rule 
The USDA, Forest Service proposes to repeal a final rule promulgated on October 29, 2020 (2020 
Alaska Roadless Rule) that exempted the Tongass National Forest (Tongass) from the 2001 
Roadless Area Conservation Rule (2001 Roadless Rule). Repealing the 2020 Alaska Roadless 
Rule (Title 36, Part 294, Subpart E of the Code of Federal Regulations) would reinstate application 
of the 2001 Roadless Rule to the Tongass; prohibiting timber harvest and road construction and 
reconstruction within designated Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs), with limited exceptions. 
 
The 2001 Roadless Rule remains a national, one-size-fits-all regulation that inappropriately, and 
unlawfully, limits opportunities for Alaskans that live and work in the Tongass. As such, the State, 
along with Alaska’s Congressional Delegation, has worked tirelessly over the consecutive terms of 
six governors (Democratic, Independent, and Republican) to exempt the Tongass from the 
Roadless Rule. 
 
Simply repealing the 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule to reinstate the 2001 Roadless Rule fails to (1) 
meet the stated purpose and need established in the administrative record, (2) adequately respond 
to the State of Alaska’s petition for rulemaking (enclosed), and (3) adequately address 
recommendations from the Alaska Roadless Rule Citizen Advisory Committee.

approach to roadless area management,” nor does the proposed repeal implement adjustments to

My name is Rachel Hale and I am currently an Animal Care Specialist at Busch Gardens (a SeaWorld Park). I have dedicated the past 15+ years of my life to animal care, rescue, training, and overall welfare. My animal experience includes marine animals (dolphins, pinnipeds, manatees, sea turtles), terrestrial animals (small primates, prosimians, gorillas, chimps), and domesticated animals (dogs, cats, small mammals). I worked hard in school to receive a BS with Honors in Biomedical Engineering from Purdue University, and turned down an engineering job ($95K starting salary) to take an -unpaid- internship at the Clearwater Marine Aquarium, where I devoted 50+ hours/week to rescuing, caring for, and training stranded and resident animals. After gaining thousands of hours of experience in animal care/training, I proudly accepted my first full time job working with great apes at Busch Gardens. I am not in this field for the money, nor the glory. I have dedicated my life to the field of animal welfare because it is my utmost passion. 

That being said, myself and my colleagues know our animals better than anyone else. We know what motivates them, what is best for them, and how to make a difference in their lives. I truly hope you take this into consideration when reading the message below. 

After reading the proposed changes for marine mammal APHIS regulations, I strongly disagree with several points. APHIS does incredible work and I want to work together to ensure the best care for marine animals in managed care. However, several of these proposed claims are unjustified and would only be detrimental to the affected animals. After researching, I cannot find any peer-reviewed scientific data to back the need for the proposed amendments and fail to see their benefit for animal welfare. 

For interactive programs defined as "any human-marine mammal interactive program where a member of the public enters a primary enclosure for a marine mammal with the intent of interacting with the marine mammal(s)" - I believe this should EXCLUDE interaction programs where the guest is on a floating platform/ledge or poolside, and programs where trainers bring animals into a public area under their control. These are not the primary enclosure.

I cannot support the rule stating interactive sessions may not exceed 3 hours/day/animal. Marine animals are very social and THRIVE on interaction programs. I urge you to visit a facility and witness this for yourself. Based on my professional experience and knowledge, I believe daily interactions should be determined by the trainers/staff that know each animal better than any governing body. Training sessions enhance an animal's day and animals eagerly look forward to each session. Taking this away from an animal deprives them mentally, physically, and socially and would lead to an INCREASE in stereotypic and undesirable behaviors (as proven from peer-reviewed scientific research). Changes in interactions should be made by the professional staff that works with and knows these animals daily. 
 
The proposed change requiring a minimum of 1 trainer per marine mammal/session and 1 attendant to monitor the session is completely unnecessary. Different situations call for different numbers of attendants, and there have been no recent safety violations with marine mammals. Marine animals, being so social, thrive on group-based behaviors and sessions. Just as walking 2 dogs togethers initiates bonding, so does training 2+ marine animals together. This is not an unsafe practice and would ultimately be detrimental for the animals.

On behalf of The Humane Society of the United States and our members and supporters, thank

you for the opportunity to submit public comment in response to the proposed rule regarding 

recordkeeping and registration provisions for the prevention of Salmonella Enteritidis (SE) in 

shell eggs during production. These comments address the paramount importance of inspections 

of egg farms conducted by FDA, and the availability of inspection reports to the public.

The Federal Register Notice for this information collection requests comments on whether the 

proposed information collection is necessary for the proper performance of FDA’s functions, 

including whether the information will have practical utility. The collection of information 

regarding prevention of SE is vital to ensuring that FDA is able to provide the public the best 

information about production methods that result in lower rates of SE.

This information collection, in addition to FDA on-farm inspections, is the only comprehensive 

nationwide means for the public, as well as for FDA, to know about on-farm conditions that 

impact food safety and public health. We were made aware in a January 4, 2016 letter from Dr. 

Nega Beru of the Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition that egg farm inspections have 

been suspended on the recommendation of state veterinarians in light of the HPAI situation. 

While on-farm inspections are suspended, this information collection is the only way for FDA to 

ensure that farms are in compliance with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and 

regulations, and that adequate control measures for SE are being implemented.

Even with regular on-farm inspections, site visits are only part of the picture, and recordkeeping 

and registration requirements for egg farms ensure that written SE prevention plans and records 

of actions are maintained, that facilities impacted by contamination can be identified, and that 

data and information to support enforcement activities are available.

 
We strongly support continuation of the recordkeeping and registration provisions for prevention 

of Salmonella Enteritidis in shell eggs during production.

Respectfully submitted,

Like many consumers, I rely on on-package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised," I assume that there is value and meaning behind that claim which is backed by a regulatory agency. 

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. Companies will still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit. 

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Time and time again industry has shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating or policing itself. Companies are taking advantage of consumers -- and grossly overcharging them -- by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare. 

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and to ensure that meat and poultry labeling is truthful and not misleading. The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simply perpetuate business as usual, allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for their baseless claims and misleading consumers. 

FSIS ought to serve the American public by setting a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," taking steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensuring that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Concerning Shade requirement:
(b) Shelter. Natural or artificial shelter that is appropriate for the species concerned, when the local climatic conditions are taken into consideration, must be provided for all marine mammals kept outdoors to afford them protection from the weather. Shade must be provided to protect marine mammals from direct sunlight, including during feeding and training sessions. Shade must be accessible and cover sufficient area to afford all animals within the enclosure protection. Shaded areas need not be contiguous and shade structures may be permanent or temporary for easy movement or deployment.

I am strongly in favor of adding this requirement for shade. The clear water we provide for animals in our care provides little protection against ultraviolet and blue light, which have much higher energy than red light. In clear water less than 5% of the energy is lost per meter of water so in the bottom of a 3 meter pool the animals experience an intensity little less than if they were hauled out on the beach. The short wavelengths of blue and ultraviolet light are highly scattered so there is little directionality of this light so even when not looking directly at the sun this light is present. The ultraviolet light is absorbed by the cornea and lens of the eye contributing to keratopathy and cataractogenesis. The blue light reaches the retina and increases the metabolic processes normally occurring there. In natural waters the clarity is often much lower so animals diving below the surface experience much lower levels of this radiation.
A discussion of light in the ocean can be found at: http://www.whoi.edu/cms/files/dfino/2005/4/v43n2-johnsensosik_2383.pdf
A number of factors including: latitude, season, clouds, and structures or vegetation surrounding pool waters will influence the total radiation experienced by the animals. Monitoring the UV Index and providing shade any time the index approaches or exceeds 5 or 6 would be reasonable.
The reflectivity of the pool bottom and surrounding structures will significantly affect the totals. Using sand or darker colors on pool surfaces may be more comfortable for the animals. Pool painters and divers scrubbing bottoms of pools have told me they find bright blue pools to cause much more fatigue of their eyes than sand colored or natural concrete pools. I have spoken to pool painters scraping a blue colored pool who found that painting a sand color over the blue markedly reduced the discomfort they felt looking at the sunlit pool surfaces while completing the work. Preventing the animals looking at the sun during feeding and training sessions is important but it would also be helpful to reduce staring at highly reflective surfaces or the bright blue sky, which actually produces significant blue and ultraviolet radiation due to scattering in the atmosphere of these wavelengths of the direct sunlight. Feeding and training stations where the animals look away from the sun and into shade structures would be ideal.
Shade structures should be designed to drain water falling on them away from the pool. Porous structures may collect dust and other material and if intermittently moistened by rain, the water falling into the pool may contain significant amounts of bacteria.

Marine mammal keepers and trainers care for and train marine mammals in a wide variety of physical 
settings, from inland habitats to ocean enclosures, and engage with the animals in an even wider variety 
of contexts: everything from dynamic stadium performances to intimate interpretive chats, from in-
water guest interactions to educational presentations for schoolchildren, from peer-reviewed research 
designed to enhance understanding of ecosystems and species to veterinary care focused on the 
welfare of an individual patient. No matter the context, the one constant they believe is essential to 
ensure the health and welfare of marine mammals in any managed setting is providing them the 
opportunity for robust, diverse, and positive interaction with a qualified, professional staff with 
knowledge in best-practices and expertise in state-of-the-art animal training and care.

mammals, the additional components specific to marine mammal interactive programs seem unjustified 
based on the strong safety record of these types of encounters. To my knowledge, there is no peer-
reviewed scientific data that demonstrates a need for additional regulation or how further regulation 
would be a benefit to marine mammals. 
 
If interactive programs are defined as “any human-marine mammal interactive program where a 
member of the public enters a primary enclosure for a marine mammal with the intent of interacting 
with the marine mammal(s)” – I believe that the definition should explicitly exclude guest contact 
programs in which the participants may sit/stand on a floating platform or shallow ledge, or remain 
poolside, as well as programs in which trainers bring marine mammals into a public area under stimulus 
control. 
 
Additionally, I cannot support the proposed rule which stipulates that interactive sessions must not 
exceed 3 hours per day per animal. The amount of daily interactive time should be based around the 
best interests and capabilities of the animals as determined by the caregivers that know them best. In 
general, training sessions have proven to be a very enriching part of an animal’s day – providing 
physical/mental stimulation. The notion that somehow limiting or reducing this interaction would 
provide some benefit to marine mammals is not data-driven and has no scientific basis. Any changes to 
the management of the marine animals should build on the high quality of existing animal care and 
training programs, and provide additional opportunities for the animals to engage and interact with the 
professionals to whom their care has been entrusted. At its core, an interactive program session is 
simply a training session – which is a highly beneficial and important component of an animal’s day. 
There is no indication that any restriction in time for interactive sessions is needed, and, is likely not in 
the best interest of the individual animal. 
 
With respect to the proposed changes in attendant/animal ratios, creating a requirement that there 
must be at least one attendant per marine mammal in each session and at least one attendant 
positioned to monitor the session is not necessary. Since the inception of interactive programs in the

attendants based on the situational circumstances. As such, trainers have learned that having the

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable. It is also decidedly un-American.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I write in response to the request for comments regarding query 4, the effects of faster line speeds on worker safety.

Qualificiations:
I am a resident physician living in Forth Worth, Texas. I am licensed to diagnose and manage medical conditions.

Recommendations:
Do not increase line speeds for the NSIS at this time. Records and studies are cited or summarized below. FSIS would be appropriate to grant a limited (<10% of total) number of waivers to establishments that have made binding agreements with NIOSH to evaluate the effects of waivers of line speed restrictions on employee health.

Records and Studies:
Published, peer-reviewed medical research regarding line speeds includes:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25275404: Rosenbaum DA, et al. "Employer differences in upper-body musculoskeletal disorders and pain among immigrant Latino poultry processing workers." J Agromedicine. 2014;19(4):384-94. doi: 10.1080/1059924X.2014.945710.

Of note, this peer-reviewed article remarks that several factors were associated in a statistically-significant manner with worker safety, including monotony of work activity and frequency of activity, which is related to line speed.

Federal research has also been conducted on this topic. CDC and NIOSH research culminated in a report published in 2015 revealed similarly concerning findings:

https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/hhe/reports/pdfs/2014-0040-3232.pdf: NIOSH [2015]. Health hazard evaluation report: evaluation of carpal tunnel syndrome and other musculoskeletal disorders among employees at a poultry processing plant. By Ramsey J, Musolin K, Mueller C. Cincinnati, OH: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, NIOSH HHE Report No. 2014-0040-3232.

This report revealed that " the MSD [musculoskeletal disease] risks remain for many workers, and in some jobs (e.g., live hang line) those risks are likely increased because of production rate increases after our evaluation was completed" (Ibid, p. 19). This was for a production facility whose line speed met or exceeded federal guidelines, and yet nevertheless, due to significant worker injuries, the report recommended that "What the Employer Can Do [... includes] [r]educe cone line speeds and use additional cone lines" (Ibid, p. ii)

Another federal report, this one by GAO, summarizes the extent of research into line speed and worker injury:

https://www.gao.gov/assets/680/676796.pdf: United States Government Accountability Office. Additional Data Needed to Address Continued Hazards in the Meat and Poultry Industry. 2016. GAO-16-337.

GAO identified one NIOSH study that evaluated line speed relationship to worker safety. Unfortunately, the study, due to insufficient design [too short time interval], was not able to assess if line speed was positively associated with worker injury rate. The GAO report does, however, indicate that "USDA data show that its inspectors experience injuries and illnesses
similar to those experienced by other meat and poultry workers [...] including hazards associated with musculoskeletal disorders, chemical hazards, biological hazards from pathogens and animals, and traumatic injury hazards from machines and tools." Another study evaluated by the GAO noted that one test of a doubled poultry line speed did not, due to the fact that twice as many workers were on the line, result in greater injuries. However, "[a]ccording to NIOSH officials, increasing line speed and workers may increase the risk of 'neighbor cuts' due to workers' close proximity. "

As noted in the GAO report, one hog-line specific injury, a neurologic disorder which state and NIOSH officials attributed to carcass splatter, was evaluted. Workers associated the splatter volume with line speed, "because the faster speeds meant they were unable to place the skulls completely on the device before triggering the compressed air, causing greater splatter."

Introduction 
Trichinella spiralis is a parasitic nematode (roundworm) which is found in many warm-blooded 
carnivores and omnivores, including pigs. Trichinella has a direct life cycle, which means it completes all 
stages of development in one host (Figure 1). Transmission from one host to another host can only 
occur by ingestion of muscle tissue which is infected with the encysted larval stage of the parasite. 
When ingested, muscle larvae excyst and enter tissues of the small intestine, where they undergo 
development to the adult stage. Male and female adult parasites mate and produce newborn larvae 
which leave the intestine and migrate, through the circulatory system, to striated muscle tissue. There, 
they penetrate a muscle cell, modify it to become a unique cyst, and mature to become infective for 
another host. The total time required for this development is from 17 to 21 days. Adult worms 
continue to produce larvae in pigs for several weeks before they are expelled. Once adult worms are 
expelled and larvae reach and encyst in musculature, no further contamination can occur. An animal 
that is infected with Trichinella is at least partially resistant to a subsequent infection due to a strong and 
persistent immunity. 
Trichinella and pork 
Trichinella spiralis has a long standing association with pork products, not only in the U.S. but around 
the world. The concept which many people have about the need to cook pork thoroughly is based on 
the risk of becoming infected with this parasite. This concern is well founded in history. At the 
beginning of the 20th century conservative estimates showed a 2.5% infection rate in U.S. pigs. Even 
more alarming were postmortem surveys, conducted in the 1930's. A National Institute of Health 
report published in 1943 found 16.2% of the U.S. population to be infected (1 out of every 6 people). 
This type of information led to considerable publicity on the dangers of eating pork. The historical 
problem of trichinae infection in pigs is responsible for strict federal control of methods used to 
prepare ready-to-eat pork products in the U.S., and expensive carcass inspection requirements in 
Europe. These regulations are still in effect in the Code of Federal Regulations, for processed products, 
and in the Directives of the European Union. 
Despite the historical problems of trichinae and its association with the pork industry, major changes 
have occurred in the last 50 years. Human cases of trichinellosis reported to the Centers for Disease 
Control declined from about 500/year in the 1940's to fewer than 50/year over the last decade. 
Further, many of these cases result from non-pork sources such as bear and other game meats. A 
major decline has also occurred in the prevalence of this parasite in pigs (see Table 1). While 
prevalence has declined considerably in U.S. pigs, the lowest prevalence rates in domestic pigs are

Dear Secretary Purdue,

I am urging you to withdraw the proposed rule to 'modernize' swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety rather than industry convenience. 

The proposed rule puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. In place of these requirements, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide. 

The rule also proposes a New Swine Inspection System that hands over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter establishment employees. The proposal also removes caps on line speeds, increasing the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination, and other food safety issues and increase risk that workers will be injured. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer, and this proposal will not achieve that. Instead, it has the potential to make food less safe by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

We urge you to withdraw the proposed rule and design a new rule that prioritizes food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness.

This current proposal disadvantages conscientious slaughterhouses in a competitive market and can create not only suffering when people get sick, but can cause financial damage to the industry. Your role requires that you consider consumers above industry profit. We are all consumers. Do the ethical thing!

Sincerely,

Dear National Highway Traffic Safety Administration,

I'm the mom of kids who walk and ride bikes in my neighborhood. I'm also the fortunate survivor of a pedestrian accident in which I was hit by a car. For both reasons, I am extremely concerned about traffic safety.

I'm glad to hear that you plan to include pedestrian safety in your proposed changes to the vehicle safety rating system (the New Car Assessment Program, or NCAP). But I believe there need to be even more changes.

First, adopt a “pedestrian risk” framework, versus a “pedestrian protection” framework, for the NCAP’s crashworthiness program. A vehicle that collides with a pedestrian is not “protecting” the pedestrian. While some vehicle design features (i.e., smaller front ends) pose less injury risk to pedestrians, they do not “protect” pedestrians. A vehicle can only provide protection through crash avoidance.

Second, include these testing protocols: test speeds greater than 25 mph; a thorax test; and use of a 50th percentile female dummy in all tests. Fewer than 15% of fatalities occur at or below 25 mph. Test speeds up to 35 mph should be considered, because an additional 13% of fatalities occur between 25 mph and 35 mph. Given that you state, “the head, legs, and thorax are the most common locations of serious injury” when a vehicle strikes a pedestrian, it warrants the addition of a thorax test. Your conclusion that “any countermeasure that is beneficial for a male pedestrian would also be beneficial for a female pedestrian” stands in contrast to your statement, “a female head may be more vulnerable than a male head for the same impact condition.” If female heads are more vulnerable, then countermeasures for males could miss additional vulnerabilities of females. NHTSA should acknowledge and mitigate the gender data gap by using female dummies in all tests. 

Third, a pass/fail score is unacceptable. Like frontal crash star ratings, provide a five-star rating that details the chance of seriously injuring a pedestrian. For example, assign five stars for less than 10% chance of serious injury to pedestrians, four stars for 15% chance of serious injury, and down to one star for greater than 40% chance of serious injury. 

Fourth, I am concerned that NHTSA fails to distinguish between injury risk and fatality risk. Please make this distinction and provide a five-star rating that also details the real risk of a vehicle killing a pedestrian. I was lucky not to have been hit by an SUV, so that I was only injured and not killed. I was lucky the driver saw me and braked in time.

Fifth, as part of the crash avoidance program, include intelligent speed control and think beyond advanced driver assistance system technologies to also consider visibility. Due to NHTSA’s claim that the impact dynamics of high-profile vehicles at higher speeds may reduce the relevance of countermeasures, intelligent speed control should be considered as crash avoidance technologies. Additionally, NCAP should include whether a vehicle can offer better direct visibility of pedestrians from the driver’s seat.

Sixth, conduct physical crash tests rather than rely on voluntary self-reported data from vehicle manufacturers. If NHTSA decides to only rely on self-reported data to select models for verification tests, NHTSA should require actual physical test results rather than predicted response data. 

Seventh, do not wait to update the Monroney Label but begin reporting 5-star injury risk and 5-star fatality risk ratings on the NHTSA website and a supplemental vehicle sticker. 

Eighth, ensure that no vehicle could earn a 5-star safety rating if it receives a failing grade for pedestrian crashworthiness. 

Ninth, avoid comparative ratings for pedestrian risk. I can’t imagine anyone who cares about the risk of injury only compared to vehicles of similar size and weight; people care about the overall risk of injury. Anything less contributes to asymmetry of information. This seems obvious. 

Aga

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I have piloted aircraft for over 43 years and have been on every side of the certification process as a pilot, instructor, and pilot examiner.
Adding an airman's photograph to existing certificates as required by the Intelligence Reform and Terrorist Prevention Act (IRTPA) may be inevitable, but it needn't be a bad thing. 
The FAA's overblown proposal as outlined in this NPRM, borders on the absurd and exacerbates a certification system that is already unmanageable. Issuing pilot certificates with photographs is long overdue and should not require a complete rewrite of 14 CFR 61. As outlined in this NPRM, the additional cost, time, money, and personnel resources would burden the current certification process as never before. The ridiculous time frame currently required for receiving a certificate (usually months from its effective date) would increase exponentially and would entail the continued use of paper Temporary Certificates. Wouldn't this call into question any security benefit of having photographs on a permanent certificate. Surely making things more cumbersome, less effective, less efficient, and not accomplishing the desired outcome was never intended by Congress when they wrote IRTPA.
A simple low cost solution could be to issue a passport-like-document (in book form with similar dimensions) called an Airman Certificate for a period of 8 years that includes a photograph of the bearer. 
This certificate could be issued to students, pilots, mechanics, and flight engineers, ranging from the most rudimentary to the most advanced certificates and would only be reissued every 8 years. 
Additional certificate grades, privileges, ratings and even medical certificate stamps could then be affixed to the inside pages of the certificate by examiners or field office inspectors in the form of a difficult to copy sticker which lists the certificate grade, privileges, ratings, etc. and includes an and includes an imbedded computer chip. The entire process could then be accomplished electronically in minutes rather than months and the airman registry database could be updated in real time.
The airman could then hold the same certificate for 8 years and it would include all of his vital information, qualifications and ratings. 
There would be a one-time cost for the airman every 8 years and eliminate the need for a complete rewrite of the regulation or an ever-increasing cost for every airman every time he renews his CFI, adds a certificate, or category or class or type rating.
In addition, this type of certificate would satisfy long needed modernization of the certification process and reduce rather than increase costs.
Temporary Certificates would no longer exist, and there would no longer be an inordinate wait between a practical test, medical exam, and a new certificate, rating or qualification. 
This IRTPA requirement may actually be a blessing by overcoming inertia and providing an opportunity for meaningful change; a catalyst for long needed improvements in how the government (in this case the FAA) works.
