Dear Madam/Sir,

I am writing to thank you for your excellent work on behalf of the California Current. I write today as a resident of Oregon to ask you to approve the Proposed Rule that would prevent new commercial fishing on currently 'unfished', unmanaged forage fish in federal waters, from three to 200 miles off California, Oregon and Washington. This proposed rule would protect Round Herring/Thread Herring, Mesopelagic Fishes, Pacific Sand Lance, Pacific Saury, Silversides, Smelts, and Pelagic Squids unless it could be shown that fishing for them would not have an adverse impact on the overall ecosystem.

Forage fish are essential components of the ocean food web and are the cornerstone of the California Current Ecosystem off our West Coast, one of the most productive marine ecosystems in the world. Seabirds and other marine wildlife absolutely depend on forage species for food. 

I personally have followed this issue for over three years, along with the Audubon Society of Portland and partner organizations including Pew Charitable Trusts, Audubon California, and Audubon Washington have worked with the Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) to ensure protection of these small, nutrient-rich fish by incorporating them into existing fishery management plans. The PFMC successfully completed this process in 2015. The last step is for NOAA Fisheries to finalize these protections as formal regulations in the Federal Register.

I urge you to approve new drafts of four Fishery Management Plans that include specific language to protect seven species groups of forage fish from unregulated harvest and also limit bycatch of these species in existing fisheries. These amendments have already been approved by the Pacific Fishery Management Council in line with Comprehensive Ecosystem-Based Amendment 1. I ask you to finalize the associated regulations by implementing the Proposed Rule as written.

Restore the Roadless Rule for the Tongass National Forest, Docket #FS-2021-0007-0006 Dear Secretary Tom Vilsack, I strongly support restoring full Roadless Rule protection to the Tongass National Forest. The Tongass is America's wildest national forest, with more than 9 million acres of roadless areas. It provides habitat for a wide range of wildlife, including Alexander Archipelago wolves, grizzly bears and salmon. And it's the ancestral homelands of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. The Tongass stores a vast amount of carbon, with its centuries-old trees serving as a carbon-reserve life raft in this time of climate change. Logging would release most of that carbon into the atmosphere. Closing the door to clearcutting and bulldozing roads will protect the forest's many values. The Tongass belongs to everyone and shouldn't be sacrificed to the timber industry, which provides a small fraction of the jobs and income in Southeast Alaska compared to tourism and fishing - both of which rely on intact forests to thrive. Further, I urge you to swiftly implement your "Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy" announced last year, which for the Tongass would end large-scale old-growth timber sales on roadless and roaded lands, focusing forest management on restoring lands degraded by logging and roads, as well as on recreation, climate health, wildlife habit, and watershed improvement. For wildlands, wildlife, people and our future, the Service should restore full Roadless Rule protection to the Tongass and end commercial old-growth and mature forest logging there. Thank you for this opportunity to comment. Why on earth would a supposed world leader exempt this part of our environment from interference by the industrialized US? Sincerely, Darrel Smith -PII-

I support revising the methionine inclusion of a flat rate 2lb/ton to 2lb/ton of 100% methionine over the life of the flock.
I formulate all of the organic poultry feed for Herbruck's Poultry Ranch.
Methionine is the most important amino acid to poultry in the context of our currently available feed ingredients.
This is because poultry cannot synthesize a sufficient amount of methionine when fed a diet made of the current ingredients allowed for organic poultry production.
The limitation of methionine at key points in a hen's life causes animal health and welfare issues for the birds such as growth issues when they are young which causes feather retention/feather growth and pecking when they are adults.
Chickens need more than 2lb/ton methionine when they are you but need less than 2lb/ton methionine when they are older and laying eggs. In fact, for a majority of the birds' lives they will be consuming less than 2lb methionine (especially when they are laying organic eggs going to the market) if this regulation passes.

There is currently no viable or available alternative to synthetic methionine. When one becomes available, I would love to test and use it and if it succeeds in meeting the needs of the hens, I would support removing synthetic metionine from the list. Until that day, all organic poultry needs synthetic methionine.

GENERAL COMMENTS
We continue to believe that the proposed traceability program is ill-conceived, will cause an economic 
burden on small businesses, will violate existing trade agreements, and will not achieve the result we are 
all seeking – an end to IUU fishing. Further, any attempt to extend the data requirements suggested here 
to domestic fishing operations could undermine international trade and cause our member companies to 
lose millions of dollars.
Enforcement is the key
Rather than forcing U.S. businesses to be the policemen of world fisheries trade, NMFS should assist 
foreign governments and Regional Fishery Management Organizations (RFMOs) in developing their own 
fisheries management and enforcement capabilities. Most import / export firms do not have the ability to 
ground truth claims that the product they are receiving comes from legitimate fishing operations. Yet, if 
the claims are found to be false, they will be held responsible and penalized while the fishing operation 
simply changes its paperwork and exports to some other firm in the U.S. or in a foreign country. The only 
rational way to attack IUU fishing is on the fishing grounds, which means bolstering the management and 
enforcement programs of other countries.
Violating trade agreements
As others have commented previously, there is a question as to whether the proposed rules violate the 
principles of the General Agreement on Tariff and Trade and whether the U.S. would thus be liable to 
action by the WTO. Even worse from the standpoint of our members is that the proposed regulations 
appear to violate the North American Free Trade Agreement. Canada is a major exporter to the U.S. and 
Mexico is the primary source of certain seafood products. Canada is also a major market for U.S. 
products. If Canada decides to retaliate it will significantly disrupt seafood trade and cause extensive 
economic harm to our member companies. Even if Canada simply refuses to comply with the detailed 
requirements of the proposed rule, it will put millions of dollars of trade in jeopardy.

 
Extension to domestic fisheries

fisheries would result in putting our members in violation of state laws and driving up the price of many

EXPORTATION OF FRESH POMEGRANATES FROM PERU TO THE US WITH THE 
USE OF IRRIDIATION 
Currently Peru exports fresh pomegranate arils to the United State (US) and other 
international markets such as the US and Asia. The approval of the advance notice to 
allow for the importation of fresh whole pomegranates to the US with irradiation will allow 
Peru and the US to increase trade, create new jobs and revenue for both countries while 
allowing consumers and retailers to enjoy pomegranates during a period -the spring and 
summer months of the US- when domestic pomegranates are not available. 
On the phytosanitary front the National Phytosanitary Protection Organization of Peru 
(SENASA) has been carrying out control and eradication activities for the purpose of 
achieving free areas for fruit flies (Ceratitis capitata and Anastrepha spp), especially in the 
coastal region where production of pomegranate orchards for export are located. This area 
has very low populations of fruit flies as a result of control and eradication activities that 
SENASA has carried out hand-in-hand with the support of pomegranate producers. Also, 
with the use of a strict phytosanitary irradiation protocol that will be applied in the US, the 
risk of pest introduction will be negligible as it's currently the case with the importation to 
the US of pomegranates with irradiation from other countries such as Mexico and India. 
Gymnandrosoma aurantianum is an insect which was occasionally reported in Cusco {the 
highlands of Peru) in citrus orchards destined for local consumption purposes. This region 
does not have pomegranate production. In addition, such aforementioned this insect has 
not been detected in the coasts of Peru where the pomegranate for exporting is being 
cultivated. Therefore the risk of introduction of this insect to the US is negligible. It's also 
worth noting that the pomegranate is not a preferred fruit host -
a condition that is 
supported by the Official Laboratory of SENASA and its pest surveillance activities. 
The export of this fruit to the US, will be supported by an official phytosanitary certification 
procedure to mitigate the risk of pest infestation; in which the fields will be authorized by 
SENASA on the basis of a phytosanitary management, in harmony with the environment 
and food safety. In addition, the fruit will be subjected to a post-harvest system to eliminate 
defective and damaged fruits, among others, under the supervision of SENASA. 
For many years Peru has exported to the US many fruit products including, among others, 
Hass avocados, grapes, mandarins, mango, lettuce, pomegranate arils. And as noted 
before we export fresh pomegranates to many international markets with strict 
phytosanitary protocols such as those in the US. 
In closing we thank APHIS for the technical collaboration we have had in working together 
to develop the proposed phytosanitary protocol for the exportation of fresh pomegranates 
from Peru to the US. For the aforementioned reasons we respectfully request that it be 
published as soon as possible in order for Peru to be able to export fresh pomegranates 
with irradiation to the US this year.

The National Infusion Center Association (NICA) is a nonprofit organization formed to support non- 
hospital, community-based infusion centers caring for patients in need of provider-administered 
medications. To improve access to medical benefit drugs that treat complex, rare, and chronic diseases, 
we work to ensure that patients can access these drugs in safe, more efficient, and cost-effective 
alternatives to hospital care settings. NICA supports policies that improve drug affordability for 
beneficiaries, increase price transparency, reduce disparities in safety across care settings, and foster 
patient access to the highest-quality, lowest-cost setting. 
 
On behalf of the infusion providers we represent throughout the country, we write to provide feedback 
on the aforementioned rule. 
Method to Control Unnecessary Increases in the Volume of Outpatient Services 
Furnished in Excepted Off-Campus Provider-Based Departments (PBDs) 
NICA strongly supports CMS’s proposal to apply site-neutral payment rates to drug administration 
services furnished in excepted off-campus provider-based departments (PBDs). This policy would 
address long-standing payment disparities between hospital outpatient departments and office-based 
infusion centers, where the same services are delivered at lower cost to Medicare and beneficiaries 
without compromising quality. 
 
Off-campus PBDs are often indistinguishable from physician offices aside from the hospital signage; 
nothing about the site of care has meaningfully changed to justify higher payment rates. They are not 
providing true hospital-based care and do not require additional payment for 24/7 capacity or 
emergency standby services.

 
As we have repeatedly noted, the office setting is the most cost-effective and patient-centered site of 
service for drug administration. Delivering drug therapies in the office setting not only saves the health 
care system money, but also avoids unnecessary risks such as hospital-acquired infections—risks that are 
particularly concerning for immune-compromised patients. While this proposal is limited to off-campus 
settings, we encourage CMS to consider extending site-neutral payment to on-campus PBDs in the 
future. Patients requiring additional services beyond drug administration can still be treated in an 
on-campus setting, where hospitals may bill for those added services when warranted for higher-acuity 
patients. 
 
In the meantime, this proposal is an important step toward eliminating unwarranted payment 
differentials, promoting fair competition, and preserving patient access to cost-effective, high-quality 
office-based infusion care. We also urge CMS to pair this policy with reforms to improve transparency 
and accountability in the 340B program to prevent hospitals from offsetting site-neutral reductions by 
shifting drug administration volume to on-campus settings. 
 
Sincerely,

Dear National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS):
My name is Natalie Pemberton, I am a current sophomore at the University of Miami studying 
marine affairs. I am please to be able to share my thoughts with you today regarding the 
rebuilding plan of bottomfish in the American Samoa region. I have always had a passion for the 
environment and have known that I want to devote my life to trying to preserve it. As a result of 
my coursework, I am becoming more familiar with the proceeds necessary to actually implement 
proposed rules. This rebuilding plan addresses key concerns in the the bottomfhish fisheries in 
the American Samoa region. In this letter I plan to highlight both the strengths on this rule as 
well as potential modifications.
The tragedy of the commons is one of the first things I remember learning about in my AP 
Environmental Science class my junior year of high school. It is when a common resource is 
overused by humans and the resource diminishes as a result. The intersection between human 
behavior and the natural world was always my favorite thing to learn about. Fish populations 
depend on human activity and it's up to policy makers to control that behavior. The bottomfish 
stock complex in the American Samoa region was subjected to overfishing and the populations 
are declining at alarming rates. The NMFS first alarmed the Council on February 10, 2020. An 
effort was then put in place to construct a rebuilding plan to replenish the bottomfish 
populations. This plan consists of an annual catch limit (ACL) and two accountability measures. 
The ACL will be set at 5,000 lbs beginning in 2022. This would include fish caught in both 
territorial and Federal waters. Once this ACL is reached, the fishery will then be closed for the 
remainder of the year. This would pose potential complications as it would be incredibly hard to

 
enforce these closures. There are numerous rules and regulations in place that are regularly 
overlooked by citizens. This is also especially hard as at this time, the American Samoan 
Government is not able to enforce closures in territorial waters while the Federal waters close. 
Fishing can be expected to take place in these areas that will go unreported to the ACL. Of 
course any efforts taken in the step of conservation are worth while, however this rule could be 
made stronger if supplemented by one that allows for the territorial water closures. 
This rebuilding plan addresses a lot of key concerns in the American Samoan bottomfish 
fisheries. Catch rates must decrease to allow the fish population to replenish as to not completely 
wipe out the fish species. These policies must be paired with human cooperation and motivation 
to a common goal. Whether it's through motivation or regulation, it is up to policy makers to 
shape human behavior to the needs of the environment. A compromise must be met between the 
human world and our needs and the needs of the environment. 
Sincerely,
Natalie Pemberton

Airlines began to charge baggage fees around the recession years of 2007 and 2008 when oil reached close to $150/barrel and airlines were suffering due to extremely high fuel costs. At the time, I think many passengers were unhappy, but understood why these and other fees were being added. Since then, many of these fees have increased and almost doubled in some cases. All major airlines with the exception of Southwest, now charge baggage fees. In 2016 oil dropped to around $50/barrel. I don't think anyone is real surprised to learn that airlines did not eliminate or even reduce the baggage fees being charged. According to data from DOTs Bureau of Transportation Statistics, the top 13 U.S. airlines generated over $3.8 Billion in revenue in 2015 from baggage fees (DOT 2016). 
The 12/15 hour rules are too lengthy in my opinion. Many passengers are traveling for short vacations or business meetings and 12 or 15 hours, many times would result in the bags arriving the next day. This can ruin a short vacation or cause someone not to have their clothing or other items in time for business the following morning. I would recommend a 6/10 hour rule before refunds are issued.
The time when the clock would stop should be when the passenger has the bags in their possession. The airlines will argue that they consider bags delivered when they are in the luggage claim area at the airport. Passengers should not be responsible for making a trip back to the airport, hours after arrival to retrieve their bags and therefore should receive a refund if the bags are not in their possession by those times. 
Passengers should expect the refund from whichever airline they paid the fees to regardless of which airline they finished their last flight on or which airline is responsible for the delayed bags. Airlines can work those issues out among themselves and collect form one another if needed, but it should not be the responsibility of passengers to determine who is at fault.
Refunds should be made automatically back to the passenger's credit card with an email confirmation. If a credit card was not used, passengers will most likely need to see an Agent or work with the airline over email or phone to receive the refund. Although I think the computer systems currently in use should allow these refunds to be made almost immediately, a seven day allowance to receive the refund would be reasonable. 
I think everyone understands that mistakes are made. Checked baggage, especially during connecting flights when time can be minimal is a complicated process. There is no doubt it will never be a perfect process and passengers will always deal with lost or delayed bags. But when you are paying for a service, sometimes as much as $35 for each checked bag, there is an expectation that these bags will be delivered with the passenger. The financial impact to the airlines of required refunds should be motivation to improve their service to the highest standard possible. It is obvious these fees were implemented during hard times and were not removed when airline profits increased. I applaud DOT for implementing the rule and feel the airlines should be held responsible for providing the service passengers are paying for.

I support the petition requesting that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) ban use of FD&C Red No. 3 in foods, drugs, and dietary supplements. I strongly agree with the decision Congress made in 1960 that cancer-causing color additives have no place in our foods, drugs, supplements, or cosmetics. I am appalled that FDA has known for more than thirty years that Red 3 can cause cancer, but still approves the dye to be used in foods, drugs, and supplements. 

In 1990, FDA concluded that Red 3 causes cancer when ingested by animals after reviewing studies it received in the early 1980s. From this conclusion, FDA revoked the provisionally allowed uses for Red 3, which at the time included use in cosmetics and externally applied drugs, claiming it would separately take steps to revoke the permanently approved uses, namely drugs and foods, including supplements. Three decades have elapsed, and yet Red 3 remains approved for use in foods, drugs, and supplements and is, in fact, still widely used. FDA estimated in 2016 that 84 percent of the U.S. population two years of age and older is exposed to Red 3. Red 3 is found in thousands of food and drug products currently on the market, including many marketed to children. 

A full ban on Red 3 is long past due. I ask that FDA act quickly and decisively to prohibit all uses of Red 3 to protect consumers, especially children, from this cancer-causing chemical.

Sincerely,
David Miller
Jamaica Plain, MA

Summary: I am enthusiastically in favor of planting the majestic American Chestnut tree with the needed genetic modification to be blight resistant (Darling 58).

Who am I? I am an unaffiliated outdoorsman and wildlife enthusiast. I have had an interest in chestnut trees, from times in the 1960s when I would hike in the Shenadoah National Park, searching for and finding small sprouting chestnut trees. Over the years, the density of the chestnut finds in forests has seriously declined. I have not found any mature trees.
 
The issue? My concern is that we would lose the niche of tall overstory trees in eastern US forests. Other avenues to re-populate the ecological community all have more precautionary risk.
 
The hybridization project with Chinese chestnut trees, I believe, will not result in trees with the height and grandeur of the American variety, because there are so many different genes controlling the resistance. Now is also a time when ash trees are dying off, leaving a hole in the eastern forest diversity.
I believe that the evidence is sufficient to prove the safety of the genetic manipulation. I DO NOT believe that this should lower the bar for other genetic manipulations: each should be evaluated on its own merits and risks. For instance, I continue to be against the regulatory approval of the AquAdvantage salmon (which will spread to wild salmon).

I see no evolutionary impact to the added gene, other than tree survival. Testing has not found any negative impact on wildlife. There is, however, a positive impact for the wildlife consumers of their nuts.

There is no selective advantage for the modified chestnut trees other than blight resistance. The transgene is derived from wheat, which is widely consumed by man, and wildlife. This solution to the chestnut blight is narrowly tailored. 
I would purchase and plant these Darling 58 trees if they became available.

The Arizona State Board of Pharmacy protects the health, safety and welfare 

of the citizens of Arizona by regulating the practice of pharmacy and the 

manufacturing, distribution, sale and storage of prescription medications and 

devices and non-prescription medications. The Board accomplishes its mission, in 

part, by: issuing permits to pharmacies, manufacturers, wholesalers, distributors, 

non-prescription retailers and third party logistics providers (3PLs), conducting 

compliance inspections of permitted facilities, and investigating complaints and 

adjudicating violations of applicable state and federal laws and rules. The Board 

currently oversees 10,236 permitted facilities, including 2503 Pharmacies, 648 

Manufacturers and 503B Outsourcing Facilities and 1083 Wholesalers. At present, 

the Board employs 5 Pharmacy Inspectors/Investigators, each of whom conducts on 

average 250 inspections and 80 investigations per year. These Inspectors account 

for 25% of the Board’s workforce and 33% of its payroll allocation. Accordingly, we 

appreciate the opportunity to submit comments regarding the MOU and hope that 

FDA will take these comments into consideration when finalizing the MOU for 

submission to the States. As set forth below, the MOU as currently proposed will 

have a profoundly negative impact on individual State Boards of Pharmacy as well 

as pharmacies, physicians, and patients across the country. We strongly recommend 

FDA withdraw the proposed MOU and work with representatives of the State 

Boards of Pharmacy as well as the major Pharmacy Associations to formulate a 

version that works best for patients, physicians, and pharmacies. 

FDA continues to define “distribution” in the MOU to include dispensing. The 

plain language of Section 503A, definitions of distribution in similar statutes, and 

the Arizona Pharmacy Practice Act, demonstrate that the terms “distribution” and 

“dispensing” mean separate and mutually exclusive things. Congress did not give 

FDA the authority to regulate patient-specific dispensing through the MOU. 

Moreover, construing “distribution” to cover patient-specific dispensing is 

inconsistent with the structure of Section 503A, which applies the term distribution 

to compounding for office use, i.e., compounding pursuant to a non-patient-specific

 
order by a physician who needs compounded drugs in his or her office to administer 

directly to patients. Section (3)(B) of Section 503A establishes two categories of 

permissible activity for Section 503A pharmacies: dispensing and distribution. 

21 U.S.C. § 353a(b)(3)(B)(ii). Section (3)(B) then limits the interstate “distribution” 

of compounded medications to 5% of total prescription orders dispensed or 

distributed, and permits FDA to develop an MOU to further address the interstate 

“distribution” of compounded medications above and beyond 5%. Limiting FDA’s 

authority over “distribution” to office use—and even then only where such 

distribution is either “inordinate” or in a State that has not adopted the 

MOU—would best serve the clear statutory dichotomy between “dispensing” and 

“distribution.” 

Even assuming that FDA’s interpretation of “distribution of inordinate 

amounts of compounded drugs interstate” withstands scrutiny, FDA has failed to 

provide any sort of guidance as to the penalties that may result once compounding 

pharmacies are deemed to have distributed in inordinate amounts. Accordingly, 

FDA has given itself unfettered discretion to enforce its interpretation in a 

subjective and discriminatory fashion.

HEALTHY VS. HEALTHFUL

While the FDA is re-considering the definition of the word healthy, I want to point out a semantic error that is common in the English language as spoken in the US. We use the word healthy when we should be using the word healthful instead. Let me explain.
Definitions
Healthy: having good health, well, sound; the absence of disease in a living entity; showing or resulting from good health 
Healthful: helping to produce, promote or maintain health; salutary, wholesome.

For example, when people say "eat this apple, it's healthy", that is an erroneous use of the word. Instead, we should say "eat this apple, it's healthful", meaning it will be good for one's health. To say that the apple is healthy doesn't make sense. The apple is not alive. Whether or not the apple is in good health is not the point of the suggestion. Saying that the apple is healthful means that, if eaten by someone, the apple will promote health. That is what is intended by the suggestion from one person to another.

This mistake is commonly made by most people in the US. Common usage doesn't make it correct. By re-visiting the definition of healthy the FDA could bring attention to the correct use of the English language in the context of an official regulatory document.

If manufacturers want to mention in a label the idea that the product will promote health, I suggest two approaches for setting a standard for all products regarding healthfulness. Products could be classified as follows:
1. No evidence that this product is healthful (no studies to document healthful benefits).
2. Minimally healthful (evidence is weak or inconsistent).
3. Healthful: (evidence is adequate to support a claim of healthfulness).
4. Very healthful: (evidence is adequate and clearly shows a degree of healthfulness higher than other products in its class).

A less complex way to label products would be to permit a comment on the label that 'there is evidence that this product is healthful' only when such data are available. Labels of products that don't meet this standard are silent about any possible healthful effects.

This clarification of terminology relating to health is within the purview of the FDA. It is an error that has been ignored by the FDA for many decades. I hope this is a good opportunity to correct this erroneous use of an important word in our vocabulary.

Public Comment: Protect the Tongass National Forest, Federal Register Number: 2021-25467 Dear Forest Service FRN: 2021-25467, Federal Register Number: 2021-25467 CFR: 36 CFR Part 294 US Secretary of Agriculture Vilsack, I am a physicist and transdisciplinary scholar of climate change. I teach young people. Inevitably they ask me why our leaders don't do what the science says we need to do to solve our inter-related social-environmental crises. You may have come across the Planetary Boundaries framework, which tells us that climate change and species extinction are inextricably connected, as are land system changes and various other natural cycles and processes. It should be blindingly clear that we need to protect our forests, with the leadership of Indigenous peoples who have lived with them for millenia, if we care about future generations. Our young people are judging you, as will History. Therefore I urge you to fully reinstate the Roadless Rule protections to the Tongass National Forest with robust involvement and direction from Southeast Alaskan Tribal communities. The Tongass includes the last, best wildlands in our National Forests. But it is far from an empty wilderness. Indigenous Haida, Tlingit, and Tsimshian peoples have unbroken cultural, spiritual and economic ties to its lands and waters. Their voices and involvement in the conservation of roadless wildlands is key to protecting their rights and their ways of life. Roadless forests in the Tongass should also be protected for the sake of our climate. The Tongass holds more than 40% of all ecosystem carbon in the entire National Forest system. As we witness droughts, extreme weather and a near year-round fire season threaten other National Forests, conserving the wild forests of the Tongass can actually help us fight climate change by continuing to absorb and safely store carbon. In addition to the climate crisis, we are experiencing an extinction epidemic. Roadless forests in the Tongass, and the life-sustaining waters that flow from them, should be a refuge for wildlife. From world-class wild salmon runs to wolves, bears and birds, we need to protect roadless forests to safeguard the last best habitat for many species. The last roadless forests in the Tongass should not be sacrificed for short-sighted, taxpayer-subsidized logging and mining. Industrial boom-and-bust logging in the Tongass has cost Americans $1.7 billion over the last four decades, and remote, expensive roadless forest logging would make this even worse. Instead, the government should support building the resilient, thriving economy of the future. The priceless value of the wildlife, lands and water in the Tongass, if properly stewarded, will be of much greater value to Tribal Nations, Southeast Alaskans and the American people. We are watching. Please be on the good side of history and make an ethical and courageous decision to favor the future of our children and of the biosphere. I hope to give my students good news about Tongass and your decision. Sincerely, Vandana Singh Professor of Physics and Environment Framingham State University Framingham MA Sincerely, Vandana Singh -PII-

The Department of Homeland Securitys (DHS) proposed rule, Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, DHS Docket No. 2021-0006, does not go far enough to preserve and fortify the Deferred Action and Childhood Arrival (DACA) policy-- the stated goal of the proposed rule. As an undocumented individual living in the U.S., I strongly encourage DHS to ensure that both deferred action and work authorization for DACA recipients are protected, regardless of which Administration is in office, so that we can at least feel temporary security in being able to feed ourselves and our family. 

If finalized, this rule would directly impact me and my community, because depending on what Congress does, it could determine my near and long-term future in this country, impacting if I will have access to work authorization in the only country Ive known as home or whether I can live with the dignity undocumented people deserve by protecting me from deportation.

The legal uncertainty Ive experienced has been cruel no one should have to live with the legal threat of being torn away from their family and community. It has been very cruel that I was not able to say goodbye to my grandmother when she was sick. Even worst that I was not able to attend to her funeral and have not been able to visit her burial site. The temporary reprieve through DACA has been vital but like all undocumented immigrants, we want permanent protections and the ability to thrive to our fullest potential. DACA has made it possible to legally work in this country. By working legally I'm able to provide for myself, my daughter and help out my family and community as needed. DACA has allowed me to obtain higher education and graduate from San Jose State University. However, I can't fully complete my education path since my major is in international business management and I can't travel without fear to various countries where I can help my company grow. If I were assured that I could rely on DACA and work authorization, I would hope to pursue my MBA and expand my career to be able to help my American employer grow and be able to provide more employment opportunities for other Americans. I would also go see my maternal grandparents and spend more time with them before they pass. 

But as this proposed rule makes clearer than ever before, the DACA policy is not stable enough to ensure that I can fulfill such personal life goals, and that DACA recipients will be able to continue to make all of the contributions that the proposed rule acknowledges we have made since the policys inception. The time is now for Congress to create a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants so that we can continue to contribute in the place we call home. Reconciliation is the perfect opportunity and Congress must deliver.

Unfortunately, the revision proposal to reduce restrictions on manufacturers of vending machine food, also reduces the visibility of necessary nutrition information. Adjusting the label size in proportion to the small "net weight" label is not sufficient for consumers to have easy access to calorie content in a vending machine. The font size will be too small, and be less effective in helping the consumer make educated food choices. With child obesity concerns in the U.S. and the obesity related health risks (such as diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease), it is our responsibility to provide clear and visible labels on the products. While it may be challenging for manufacturers to adjust their product packaging designs, it is not impossible. In fact, product packages are changed all of the time for new flavors, new seasonal options, new promotions. Some candy manufacturers have already started adding calorie labels to the front of their package and I support these efforts. The revision of this rule, to allow for a smaller font size, is irresponsible. Vending machines are available on many school properties, giving even more reason to provide bold, clear, calorie information. We owe more to the youth and their future health. Please consider allowing time for the original rule to be implemented, but do not reduce the size and visibility of the labeling requirement. Thank you.

To fulfill the requirements of Section 231 of the Clean Air Act and the guiding objective 

of the Act to “prevent” pollution, EPA is required to set standards that reduce harmful emissions 

from aircraft.1 Yet the Biden administration continues to embrace weak, industry-developed 
standards that do not improve air quality at all.2 Like the 2021 greenhouse gas emissions 
standards that the Biden administration is defending in court,3 EPA’s Proposal here does not 

reduce emissions. EPA has rubberstamped international standards that intentionally lag behind 

current pollution control technologies, making no effort to study alternatives that would decrease 

emissions. As described below, the Proposal violates the Clean Air Act and is arbitrary and 

capricious. EPA should replace the Proposal with strong, technology-forcing standards to 

advance environmental justice and demonstrate international leadership. 

I. Aircraft Contribute to Particulate Matter Emissions that Harm Human Health and 

Welfare 

Particulate matter (“PM”) pollution from burning fossil fuels, including aviation fuels, is

RE: Examinations of Working Places in Metal and Nonmetal Mines: Proposed 

Rule; delay of effective date (RIN 1219-AB87) 

The National Lime Association (NLA) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on 

MSHA’s notice referenced above. The notice proposes an extension to the effective date of 

MSHA’s January 23 final rule on examinations of working places in metal and nonmetal mines. 

NLA is the trade association for manufacturers of high calcium quicklime, dolomitic quicklime, 

and hydrated lime, collectively referred to as “lime.” Lime is a chemical without substitute, 

providing cost-effective solutions to many of society’s environmental problems. Lime is 

produced by calcining limestone, and thus most lime manufacturers also quarry limestone, with 

mining operations under the jurisdiction of MSHA. 

MSHA has proposed extending the effective date of the January 23 final rule from May 23, 2017 

to July 24, 2017. While NLA agrees that a delay of the effective date is essential, it does not 

believe that the proposed delay is sufficient. For the reasons detailed below, MSHA should 

suspend the final rule without an effective date until uncertainties over the rule or resolved, or at 

a minimum should create a longer extension of at least six months (i.e., until November 27, 2017 

or later). 

1. The Status of the Final Rule Is Uncertain 

The status of the rule is currently unclear as a legal and procedural matter. The rule was 

promulgated after the issuance of an executive order “freezing” most new regulations, and the 

question of whether that order applied to the final rule here has not yet been definitively 

answered. MSHA has announced that it has “paused” the rule while it considers its future 

actions, and as part of that pause, the agency has not, as far as NLA is aware, carried out any of 

its planned efforts to provide guidance and training to the regulated community on how to 

comply with the rule.

Furthermore, NLA is aware that several mining organizations have challenged the validity of the 

rule in federal court. This creates additional uncertainty as to the status of the rule. In particular, 

it is not yet clear what position the Justice Department will take with respect to the issue of 

whether the rule was properly promulgated in view of the executive order freezing new 

regulations. 

NLA believes that if the rule is not withdrawn, the rule’s effective date should be suspended, and 

a new date should only be set if and when the question of the rule’s procedural validity is 

definitely determined. At that point, the effective date should be set no less than six months after 

such a decision is made, given the challenges many mines will face in complying with the rule in 

its current form. 

2. Preparation to Comply with the Final Rule Will Be Burdensome 

As NLA pointed out in comments on the proposed examination rule (attached), if implemented, 

the final rule will impose substantial burdens on all mining operators, including those that 

already have a robust system for identifying and correcting hazardous conditions at the mine. 

This is because the rule requires corrective actions to be included as part of the workplace 

examination record. This is a major departure from the prior rule, under which the workplace 

examination record is intended to serve as documentation that the examination was performed. 

Most, if not all, mine operators currently use a different system to track corrective actions, and 

consolidation and linkage of these systems will be costly

I am the current president of the Southeastern Minnesota Saddle Club Association (SEMSCA). This is a group of 13 local saddle clubs. We host 11-13 horse shows each summer.

I personally manage 2 local horse shows including the county fair open show as a volunteer and I volunteer for 4H at the county and state level. This law will be the death of local shows as folks will not be willing to have their name listed as the manager. This would be the straw that breaks the camel's back for the amount of additional planning and record-keeping which would be required. 

The cost of hiring an inspector is too much to bear. Our association emphasizes keeping costs as low as possible to encourage local folks to show. Many exhibitors only participate in one or 2 of the local shows as practice for 4H. Our clubs just barely make any profit on our shows and adding the price of an inspector may cause clubs to give up having performance classes at their shows. Everyone is a volunteer except the WSCA judge (and sometimes they are volunteers as well). 

The facility requirements of the law are designed for major shows with indoor facilities. They expect an indoor area that can safely be used to examine a horse and a holding area for the horses that have been inspected. This is not something that can be met at a lot of horse shows since the arena is in the middle of a pasture with a small entry/announcer stand next to the arena fence. The exhibitors use that pasture as a parking lot and there is no designated warm up area. If a show is at a fairgrounds, you would have to rent a building if the show is not held during the fair. If the show is held during the fair, there are no buildings to use.

Everyone involved is a volunteer except the WSCA judge (and sometimes they are volunteers as well). Our clubs just barely make any profit on our shows and adding the price of an inspector may cause clubs to give up having performance classes at their shows so they will not need to allow for the inspection process. One club did already switch to a games-only day due to the threat of this law for the 2025 season.

At this time, APHIS doesn't have the training available for the inspectors and does not have a method for a horse show manager to reserve time with an individual. I am doubting that there will be enough individuals available to do the inspections for the number of shows that happen in a year. In 2024, the list of shows inspected was approximately 50 nationwide. For Minnesota alone, with 87 counties, and shows generally all happening in late April through September due to the weather. Each county typically has a county fair, a 4H show and most have a local independent saddle club. Multiply that by 50 states and the number of inspectors needed becomes astronomical.

I request that the updates to the Horse Protection act be cancelled completely. If that is not possible, the updates should be restricted to multiple day shows where more than 200 horses are present, the horses are required to be stalled at the show and where there is a suitable inspection facility available. If the rule is kept, the effective date should not be set until the inspector training is finalized and the USDA has enough inspectors trained to be able to schedule them for the shows required to have inspection.

I can't believe that we are even considering putting radioactive waste in our roadways. This is NOT a solution to the problems with phosphogypsum. We should be avoiding more phosphate mining, as it is destroying the local environment, polluting our waters and putting us at risk of sinkholes in Florida.

For the rest, I will quote Glenn Compton of Manasota88, a local environmental watchdog:

Phosphogypsum is the radioactive waste product left over from fertilizer production, and Florida has a lot of phosphogypsum. 
 
High radionuclide levels, increased health risks, increased groundwater contamination and lack of state regulatory oversight are some of the many reasons why phosphogypsum should not be used in road construction.

The Environmental Protection Agency and other studies have previously determined that the use of radioactive phosphate gypsum wastes as building materials is unsafe and should not be done. This decision reflects the EPA's past concern that the radium-bearing waste, if spread throughout Florida, would present a public health threat that would continue for generations, given radium's 1,630-year radioactive decay half-life. 
 
The lifetime cancer risk for adults resulting from exposure to this waste is one excess fatal cancer per 10,000 people. The risk for children is significantly higher.
 
Some elected officials are aiding the phosphate industry in their efforts to convince people that phosphogypsum will soon become an important asset in the form of material used for construction.
 
More stringent environmental regulation is needed to control the adverse impacts of phosphogypsum. Allowing the widespread distribution of phosphogypsum for road construction will lead to less oversight of a dangerous waste product. The EPA and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection lack adequate regulations needed to protect the public and the environment from hazards associated with gypsum stacks and the dispersal of phosphogypsum. 
 
The distribution of phosphogypsum in road construction will unnecessarily expose workers, the environment, and the public to otherwise avoidable radiation exposure.
 
To allow the use of phosphogypsum as a construction material is the height of irresponsibility. Allowing phosphogypsum to be used for road construction will open the regulatory door for the use of phosphogypsum in construction or agricultural applications. The radioactive decay of this material will emit particles that can cause increased cancer risks and unacceptable radiation levels in areas that normally do not have such problems.
 
To date, no published scientific studies have confirmed that there is a "safe" industrial process to convert phosphogypsum for use in roads. All uses of phosphogypsum can cause significant health risks. 
 
In addition to high radium 226 levels, central Florida phosphogypsum also contains significant amounts of sulfur and various heavy metals such as arsenic, barium, cadmium, and lead. Contaminated water and dissolved materials containing these toxins have the potential to seep from phosphogypsum used for construction purposes and pollute the underlying aquifer.
 
Phosphate companies have had more than 70 years to figure out a way to dispose of their radioactive gypsum wastes in an environmentally acceptable manner but have yet to do so. Instead, the industry produces tens of millions of tons of waste annually and continues expanding its dumping operations.
 
ManaSota-88 does not believe the phosphate industry should be permitted to externalize the costs of its phosphogypsum waste disposal problem at the public’s expense. The cost is too high. More stringent regulation is needed to control the adverse impacts of alternative uses of phosphogypsum, not only in the United States but worldwide.

Glenn Compton is the Chairman of ManaSota 88, a non-profit organization that has spent over 30 years fighting to protect the environment of Manatee and Sarasota counties.

The modifications required to accommodate a transponder installation are invasive, and will require structural modification to the aircraft and penetrations of the skin to accommodate external antennas. Air Traffic Control transponders need a large amount of power, so heavy batteries need to be installed. These modifications will impact airworthiness in the areas of weight and balance and drag, and will impact glider performance. The costs are high for equipment, installation and re-certification of the glider, and for those that own several gliders, like a glider school, it could drive them out of business.

The addition of a transponder to a glider will also be ineffective because gliders usually operate well away from air traffic radars. Many gliders don't have radios, and couldn't hear or respond to air traffic messages. The combination of remote operation and fiberglass construction means that there will be little radar return from the glider and it could easily be lost in ground clutter or filtered out by the air traffic radar.

There are other, larger issues with the proposed ruling such as the use of primary and secondary radar is on the way out, in favor of the NextGen air traffic control system utilizing Automated Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) devices. These devices need much less power than transponders, and can be made small and portable, even carried on to gliders without installation. The FAA already has a mandate in place to equip all general aviation aircraft flying above 10,000 feet and in Class A, B, C and E airspace to have ADS-B out capability by 1 January 2020 and this includes a waiver for gliders and balloons below 10,000 in uncontrolled airspace.

The FAA has made a recommendation for use of Traffic Awareness Beacon System (TABS) devices that utilize a Universal Access Transceiver (UAT) radio for gliders and balloons. This technology shows promise, as the non-profit company Mitre has produced a UAT Beacon Radio (UBR) that is very small, and can run off of AA batteries for several hours of flight time (http://www.mitre.org/research/technology-transfer/technology-licensing/universal-access-transceiver-beacon-radio-ubr). This technology is licensed by MITRE for commercial use. 

Europe has the right idea, with the FLARM system (FLARM.com). This system is carried onto gliders and installed on the glare shield with Velcro. It receives GPS and broadcasts position once a second. HIV care & medication access is the lifeblood of people with HIV. We must maintain full control over decision making of which & what regimen & when to begin therapy for HIV. we MUST MAINTAIN the current situation. HIV antiretrovirals MUST continue to be a protected class for all insurers including Medicare Part D. Antiretrovirals are one of the six protected classes or classes of clinical concern in Medicare Part D. Allowing more restrictive formularies for HIV is not recommended by medical professionals nor policymakers, nor is it widely practiced in the private sector.

In 2004, I lost my daughter Roya to a side underride crash. After obtaining the FARS report I discovered that her death was not counted as an underride fatality. In the FARS report, it states no underride/no override. The report was inaccurate. 

Training law enforcement to identify underride and accurately describe and code underride deaths will improve the accuracy of underride fatalities. 

Not all underride crashes look the same. Some cars are lodged under the trailer when police arrive, others enter on one side of the trailer and exit out the other side, shearing off the roof of the vehicle. Some underride crashes are not under the trailer when law enforcement arrives. This was true in my daughter Roya’s crash. 

Her car was trapped under the rear tire of the trailer. Because of the momentum of the moving tractor trailer, my daughter's vehicle was released and ended up next to a guardrail.

There was PCI - Roya’s hair was found on the rear wheel of the trailer. Roya’s crash and death was NOT coded as an underride in the FARS data. It’s important to ensure that ALL underride crashes are captured on any/all accident reports.

According to a recent GAO report on underride fatalities, underride is underreported. There are two GAO recommendations relating to data collection that have yet to be implemented. These recommendations will have a positive impact on capturing underride fatalities in the FARS databank. 
1. The Administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration should recommend to the expert panel of the Model Minimum Uniform Crash Criteria to update the Criteria to provide a standardized definition of underride crashes and to include underride as a recommended data field.

2. The Administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration should provide information to state and local police departments on how to identify and record underride crashes. 

Underride is a decades old problem. There is significant research that front, side and rear underride protection around tractor trailers will save countless lives. Accurate FARS data is important to developing standards that will prevent underride fatalities. 

Lois Durso 
STOP UNDERRIDES- 
In Loving Memory of Roya

the line between federal and state authority over water resources and addressing water 
pollution is not—and has never been—a solely scientific inquiry. The Connectivity 
Report prepared for the 2015 Rule demonstrates that even the scientific community 
recognized, as it had to, that it is up to the policymakers to draw that line, which would

I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and

Dear Secretary Mnuchin, Director Mulvaney, Administrator McAleenan, and Administrator Rao: 

On behalf of the undersigned organizations, we write in opposition to the proposed rule restricting the 

use of duty drawback for federal excise taxes including alcohol, tobacco, and fuel taxes. This rule is being 

proposed as part of regulatory implementation of the Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015 

(TFTEA) through the Modernized Drawback Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (USCBP–2018–0029). 

We have concerns that the drawback NPRM lacks clear policy justification, undermines American competitiveness 

by restricting exports, goes against the legislative intent of Congress, and sets a precedent of using tax and trade 

export programs to discriminate against industries. 

The Trump administration has championed pro-growth policies focused on tax reform and regulatory reform. 

These policies have promoted American competitiveness and investment in order to create jobs and grow the 

economy. Unfortunately, the proposed duty drawback rule undermines these gains. 

Duty drawback allows the refund of duties, taxes, and fees paid on imported product when a similar product is 

exported or destroyed. Today, drawback is used across the world and is available to any industry. The program has 

a long history stretching back more than 200 years, and has proven successful in incentivizing U.S. manufacturing 

and reducing the trade deficit. 

Congress passed TFTEA with the goal of updating and modernizing the duty drawback proposal in order to 

promote U.S. exports and reduce compliance burdens for business and the government. For example, Congress 

made the program easier to administer and comply with by tying drawback eligibility from the vague and subjective 

standard of “commercially interchangeable goods” to goods that are classified under the same eight-digit 

Harmonized Trade System (HTS) number.

 
In fact, lawmakers actively chose to retain drawback for excise taxes, a position which has a long record of support

The purpose of this comment is to encourage the USFWS to list Whitebark Pines under the Endangered Species Act.

Whitebark pines are swiftly dying out due to blister rust fungus, an exotic disease that has killed up to 90% of whitebarks in many areas. Climate change is another big threat. Its heating up the pines mountain habitat, and triggering extreme droughts and wildfires. Overall, there are now more dead than living whitebarks left in the U.S.

If whitebarks go extinct and they will, without help forests in the West will be in big trouble. Whitebark pines grow on windswept mountain slopes, creating shelter that acts as a nursery for less-hardy trees, such as subalpine firs. Their fat-rich seeds feed animals as big as grizzly bears and as small as the Clarkes nutcracker. 

Whitebarks are even important for regional water supplies. They shade snow from the sun and act as natural snow fences, ensuring a steady release of water in the spring. 

American Forests have a science-based strategy to bring whitebark pines back. Weve played a key role in crafting the National Whitebark Pine Restoration Plan, which will help form the basis for the USFWSs restoration work. American Forests also help to identify, grow and plant whitebark pines with natural resistance to blister rust fungus. 

Whitebark Pines must get the legal protection they need to survive, and as such must be listed under the Endangered Species Act.

I look forward to hearing that Whitebark Pines have been added to the Endangered Species list, and thank you in advance for keeping me advised on the progress of this critical species.

I am writing this message in commenting upon the NPRM by the Office of the Secretary within the U.S. Department of Transportation entitled “Procedures for Transportation Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Programs: Addition of Oral Fluid Specimen Testing for Drugs” (RIN 2105–AE94). I support the requirement of drug testing for federal DOT safety-sensitive employees, as well as expanding this testing to include the addition of oral fluid specimen testing.
 Oral fluid testing benefits both employers and employees by allowing the employer to directly observe the sample while refraining from violating the employee’s right to privacy. The time needed to acquire the sample is also reduced in comparison to urine sample testing, resulting in monetary savings. I would predict that oral testing could be used as the preliminary form of federal employee drug testing with urine sample testing being required only if there is suspicion of drug use. The use of oral fluid testing in lieu of observed urine tests would directly eliminate the possibility of cheating or adulterating the results. However, it is important to remember that oral fluid testing does have a much smaller average window of detection for each category of drug. I do not believe that a certain kind of testing should be mandated or prohibited based upon these windows of detection. Mandating or prohibiting one form of testing over another would reverse the purpose of this proposed rule by reducing the flexibility in testing. 
 Given that HHS can scientifically determine that oral fluid testing is an appropriate alternative testing method, the type of test required should be at the discretion of the employer. I sustain this opinion in situations where a second drug test is required due to either an inconclusive or failed drug test resulting from the first sample. In response to seeking public comment as to whether the collection devices (tubes) for oral fluid collection should be transparent, I believe the tubes should be transparent. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the mandatory periodic COVID testing provided by my university use the oral fluid type of test. The specimen was taken in a clear tube, and it was required of us to show it to the administers of the test for confirmation that it was done correctly (or that there was enough saliva in the tube to provide and accurate result). I would imagine that these procedures would also be beneficial for the purposes of oral fluid drug testing. 
 I believe that the benefits of offering oral fluid testing for federal employees and employers far outweighs the costs of implementing such testing. While the statistics provided in this NPRM estimate that that only 7% of drug tests each year would be oral fluid tests, I predict that this statistic will be much larger than anticipated in the first several years. I believe that the lower cost, greater speed, and lower risk for cheating will make oral fluid drug testing the preferred option by both employers and employees.

It is incredibly important to protect the Tongass National Forest for its value as wildlife habitat and as a lace to store carbon in the fight against climate change. Loss of biodiversity and climate change both threaten our existence on the planet. We can't afford to lose any of it.

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

I strongly oppose the proposal to remove Endangered Species Act protections from gray wolves in the contiguous United States. As with past delisting attempts, this action is premature and would undo the gradual, fragile gains that wolf populations have made while under federal protection.

I was a founding member of the Wolf Sanctuary in St. Louis, Missouri in 1970. Wolves were endangered in the Lower 48 at that time -- and they still are endangered. Data exist to prove the status of the gray wolf qualifies as an endangered species. The possibility of removing ESA protection is abhorrent.

The 5,000-6,000 gray wolves that occupy the contiguous 48 states are a small fraction of the hundreds of thousands of wolves who once roamed this area. Currently, wolves occupy only about 10 percent of their historic range. To establish a reasonable, scientifically valid level of recovery for gray wolves, they must be given the opportunity to repopulate their remaining suitable habitat.

This proposed rule would cede management of the species to state agencies, and many states (such as Idaho, Wyoming, and Montana, where wolves previously were stripped of ESA protections) have already instituted wolf hunting seasons that permit cruel killing methods. These state seasons intentionally reduce wolf populations to low numbers, which is antithetical to scientifically sound wildlife management and wastes decades of efforts and massive amounts of taxpayer funds that have been used to protect wolves. Wolves who are not protected under the ESA have legally been snared and caught in barbaric steel-jaw leghold traps, and Wyoming has gone even further by allowing wolves to be run over by snowmobiles and ATVs, poisoned, incinerated in their dens with gas or dynamite, and gunned down from aircraft.

Lethal control is not the only threat gray wolves face. Due to expanding human populations, gray wolves now struggle to survive in fragmented habitats that are in close proximity to human settlements. This fragmentation threatens the genetic health of gray wolf populations due to inbreeding and increases human-wolf conflicts. Furthermore, climate change will likely exacerbate habitat degradation, prey shortages, and other survival challenges.

Many studies and polls show that a majority of Americans want wolves protected and humanely treated. In addition, wolf-watching tourism brings immense benefits to local communities. 

For these reasons, I urge the USFWS to reconsider its proposal to delist gray wolves.

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

Animals have no hope when cruel and heartless humans are in control of them! Those who abuse, torture and neglect animals , make them live in cages, and filth,y crowded , no open range ,light and fresh air, in unhealthy conditions should be forced to live in the very exact same conditions they do to animals in zoos, farming mass production buildings, dog houses, chains, so on. I quit eating meat ( dead flesh ) because the USDA allows horse flesh , and because of the cruelty allowed in slaughterhouses. I am healthier now. No dead flesh for me! The USDA can not be trusted!

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

Louisiana Pine Snake Listing Comments
After reviewing the data for the potential listing of the Louisiana Pine Snake (LPS), I believe that listing of the species as either Threatened or Endangered may be premature and based on faulty, unverified historical assumptions. From the Species Assessment: 
Historical Range/Distribution:
"The Louisiana pine snake historically occurred in portions of northwest and west-central Louisiana and extreme east-central Texas (Conant 1956, p. 19). This area coincides with an isolated, and the most westerly, occurrence of the longleaf pine ecosystem and is situated west of the Mississippi River. Most of the sandy longleaf pine-dominated savannas believed to be the preferred habitat of the Louisiana pine snake had been lost by the mid-1930's (Bridges and Orzell 1989, p. 246; Frost 1993, p. 30). Therefore, it is extremely likely that undocumented populations of this species historically occurred but were lost before the 1930s, since virtually all virgin timber in the south was cut during intensive logging from 1870 to 1920 (Frost 1993, p. 38)." (Emphasis mine). 
Because of the extreme reclusive nature of the snake, too much emphasis has been placed on unverifiable sightings and anecdotal data. While the snake has inhabited Longleaf Pine habitat in the past, there has not been sufficient study of other habitats to determine that only savannas are used by the snake. That also leads to questions about placing such emphasis on longleaf in its recovery. There doesn't appear to have been any definitive studies indicating that the LPS needs a forest overstory of any density to base those assumptions upon.
The recommendation to list may also have included other questionable assumptions from LPS literature:
"However, most populations appear to show either a decline or no conclusive change in trap success through time, indicating that numbers of individuals are likely decreasing (Rudolph et al. 2015, page 8)." How can no conclusive change indicate that numbers of individuals are likely decreasing? Wouldn't that be more evidence that population numbers are stable in those areas instead?
There has also been inadequate data to estimate the historical population and densities, and therefore to compare those figures with current numbers, or to understand what would constitute a recovered population. The trapping that has been done in the past has not been unbiased in its design or practice, and records are largely based on sightings of a species identifiable to too small a percentage of the public for reliable estimates. 
The data used to recommend listing also assigns a high correlation to Baird's Pocket Gopher (BPG), but there are a number of issues associated with assuming such interdependence:
1. There are no population estimates of the BPG within LPS range
2. There has been no apparent study of the correlation with other species or subspecies of pocket gophers
3. There has been inadequate study of the relationship of the LPS and pocket gophers on pasture and agriculture lands, pipelines, powerlines and other man-made and natural openings on sandy soils. In the past major efforts have been made in many of those areas, (mostly unsuccessfully), to reduce or eradicate gopher populations.
4. There has been inadequate or no sampling of agriculture lands occupied by BPG or other pocket gophers, resulting in no viable LPS population estimates on grazing or other agriculture lands.
4. There has been no outreach to the Agriculture sector for input about past or current snake populations, or potential effects of listing on pasturing and agriculture practices.
I feel it would also be beneficial to include private experts in the review process. There are a number of experts who have worked with the snake on private lands for decades, and I can provide names upon request by the US Fish & Wildlife Service.
For the reasons listed above, the listing of the Louisiana Pine Snake should be delayed and its Candidate status co

The Drug Recognition Expert program has been a boon to traffic safety since its adoption. DRE officers have successfully removed many thousands of impaired drivers and have no doubt saved countless lives in the process. While state-to-state variability in the DRE evaluation process causes some challenges, many of these are a result of state law and will be very difficult to standardize. However, the ability for the DRE protocol to capture evidentiary data is currently extremely limited and the evaluation process is exposed to opportunities for human error, bias, and other inaccuracies. This represents the greatest opportunity for improving the DRE program at a national level. Deep reliance on human-conducted and interpreted tests with no corroborating evidence (like video and other data) captured during the investigations are the causes of most of these inaccuracies. 

There are several easy ways that additional objectivity and accuracy can be added to DRE evaluations. At minimum, officers should be instructed to record their evaluations so that video evidence is available to both prosecutors and defense attorneys. The current manually filled form and testimony from DRE officers is deeply inadequate when the rights and freedom of an individual are at stake. 

To complement a video record of the DRE investigation, eye movement video and data would be an extremely valuable addition. Since eye movements related to impairment are extremely subtle and may only be seen from near distance to the eye, a simple video record of the interaction is insufficient to allow a court to observe them. Rather, a device like Gaize with records eye movement from close proximity should be utilized. 

As a way to drive further objectivity into the process and eliminate human error, methods of automating and standardizing the DRE tests should be explored. These can include standardized instructions, automating the tests with technology and other tools, and improving data capture throughout the tests to generate a meaningful body of evidence.

I am writing in support of the proposed Organic Livestock and Poultry Standards rule that would finally establish much-needed and long-overdue animal welfare standards under the National Organic Program. This rule has been decades in the making and has received overwhelming support from a wide array of stakeholders, including organic farmers, businesses, consumers, and advocacy organizations.

The USDA has a clear mandate under the Organic Foods Production Act to regulate the care and welfare of livestock and poultry raised organically. The OLPS rule will finally help fulfill this mandate by ensuring all animals raised organically live more natural lives and have real access to the outdoors. Allowing some producers to display the organic label while failing to provide this is detrimental to organic producers who commit to standards that benefit the animals and meet the expectations of organic consumers.

I support key elements of the rule that will ban gestation crates and require group housing of sows, prohibit certain painful physical alterations, and require environmental enrichment that allows birds to engage in natural behaviors, among other noteworthy improvements. Without animal welfare updates, production practices will continue to vary widely and perpetuate consumer confusion. This regulation is vital to my continued trust in the organic label.
 
I support swift implementation of the OLPS rulemaking. The suggested 15-year implementation timeframe for organic egg operations is far too long and will lead to more market failure. The rule should be implemented in three years.

I will pay more for eggs and poultry products if they legitimately meet a high standard for animal welfare (especially knowing that animal welfare correlates to more nutritious products).

I urge the USDA to quickly finalize the OLPS rule and require swift compliance with all provisions, especially outdoor access requirements for poultry. Doing so will bolster the integrity of the organic label and ensure that the conditions under which organic animals are raised more closely align with consumer expectations.

Thank you for your consideration.

As a retired State Veterinarian from Georgia, Brucella species have always been a concern. My state eradicated Brucellosis in our domestic livestock herds back in the 1980's. However, brucellosis continues to be a concern in feral swine and thus any domestic species that comes in contact with feral swine. This includes livestock as well as human and pet interaction. With the trend to organic and free-range farming, feral swine are increasingly interacting with domestic animals and humans. 

Feral swine are an invasive species that is rapidly increasing in population. They can serve as reservoirs for Brucella and many other diseases that can not only infect our domestic animals, but many are zoonotic.

We do not have adequate tests available to quickly and economically identify the disease. Due to cross reactions and reliance on culture of the organism, often disease-free animals are sacrificed or animals escape awaiting on a culture result. 

I approve of removing Brucella abortus, Brucella suis, and Brucella melitensis from the Select Agents and Toxins List. This will hopefully allow increased research and development of better tests and vaccines.
