RE: Draft Environmental Assessment on General Swan Hunting Seasons 

Dear Mr. Bortner: 

The National Audubon Society seeks practical solutions to the challenging issues that 

confront birds and people. In that regard, we have reviewed the draft environmental 

assessment on the “Proposal to Establish a Framework for General Swan Hunting 

Seasons in the Atlantic, Mississippi, and Central Flyways” and offer the following 

comments. 

The proposed framework is intended to address the issue of “misidentification and 

accidental take of trumpeter swans that may arise with existing tundra swan hunting 

seasons.” However, several of the proposed alternatives suggest the establishment of a 

limited take of trumpeter swans, accidental or intentional. While we recognize the issue 

of accidental take, the proposed alternatives, including the preferred alternative (#2) of 

taking an adaptive management approach, do not sufficiently protect trumpeter swan 

populations that have been rebounding through a concerted and intense reintroduction 

effort. The trumpeter swan interior population recovery is a conservation success story, 

yet they continue to face additional population-level threats. Without a thorough 

understanding of the potential population impacts of annual permitted harvest of this 

species, it is premature to consider any alternatives besides “no change” in the draft 

framework. 

We respectfully propose an alternative that would address the misidentification issue 

that this framework seeks to address: If a tundra swan hunter mistakenly harvests a 

trumpeter swan, the harvested swan should be confiscated with no fine or punishment 

to the hunter. This alternative provides protection to hunters, while serving as a 

disincentive to harvest of a species of conservation concern. This approach allows for 

greater transparency in regard to accidental take and creates an opportunity to improve

 
enforcement and monitoring. Indeed, any change to the current framework and 

regulations must be accompanied by increased commitments to and funding for 

monitoring and enforcement to ensure there is a sufficient basis for evaluation and 

adaptive management in the future.

fees and limitations, including the merchandise processing fee, established by the Consolidated 
Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) will be adjusted for inflation in accordance with 
the Fixing America’s Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act). 
 
EAA members are DHL, Federal Express, and UPS, the three largest express delivery service 
providers in the world, providing fast and reliable service to the U.S. and more than 220 other 
countries and territories. These EAA member companies have estimated annual revenues in 
excess of $200 billion, employ more than 1.1 million people, utilize more than 1700 aircraft, and 
deliver more than 30 million packages each day. 
 
Comments: 
 
A. In paragraph 24.23(b)(4)(i) CBP proposes that each carrier or operator using an express 
consignment carrier facility or a centralized hub facility must pay to CBP a fee in the 
amount of $1.00, as adjusted in accordance with the terms of paragraph (k) of Sec. 24.22 
of this chapter, per individual air waybill or individual bill of lading for the processing of 
airway bills for shipments arriving in the United States. In addition, if merchandise is 
formally entered and valued at $2,500 or less, the importer of record must pay to CBP the 
ad valorem fee specified in paragraph (b)(1) of this section, if applicable. 
 
a. EAA understands this language has only been revised to reflect the addition of the 
reference to paragraph (k) and the remainder is identical to the current 
language. We believe this is the opportunity to correct the double assessment of 
processing fees in certain circumstances.

assessment of the merchandise processing fee. If a formal entry is presented to

84 (CPI-U). EAA suggests using the index "All items less food and energy" as food and 
energy prices are relatively volatile. This index is perceived to be the "core" or 
"underlying" rate of inflation and better reflects the costs of business administration 
activities.

information or to answer any questions, please contact Michael Mullen at 703 759-0369 or

Dear Dr. Tucker,

I am writing to urge the USDA National Organic Program to move swiftly to finalize the Origin of 

Livestock rules in a manner that closes existing loopholes and restores fairness for organic dairy 

producers. 

I am a small market farmer in mid-Michigan specializing in organic production of mixed 

vegetable crops for sale through Community Supported Agriculture (CSA). I market my product 

to customers who eat organic food (including organic dairy products). When they see the 

“organic” label on food, they need to trust that it protects their health, the health of the planet, 

and the health of the animals associated with it.

Loopholes in the National Organic Program, such as the ones to be closed by this proposed rule, 

harm public perception of organic food as a legitimate enterprise. Ultimately these loopholes 

dilute and harm my brand. They also harm the viability of organic operations in general by 

giving the advantage to large producers who use their size to challenge the limits of the 

National Organic Program. My customers want to buy from small organic farms like mine. 

Finalizing the Origin of Livestock rules to close loopholes for large producers ensures that small 

producers will compete on a level playing with large ones.

The delay in issuing a final rule has resulted in a great deal of economic harm for organic dairy 

farmers and puts at risk the integrity of the organic seal. The organic dairy farmers who have 

been managing their cows as organic from the last third of gestation are suffering economic 

harm compared to operations that are taking advantage of loopholes to continuously convert 

conventional cows and heifers or those who have been cycling calves in and out of organic

 
management. Oversupply conditions in the organic dairy sector, and therefore the low pay 

prices to organic dairy farmers, have been greatly exacerbated by the continued existence of 

these loopholes. 

To close these loopholes, USDA needs to take the following steps in the final rule:

I.

Movement of Transitioned Cows

The final rule should prohibit organic dairy operations from acquiring transitioned animals to 

expand or replace animals in the organic dairy herd. USDA should prohibit the sales of 

transitioned animals as certified organic. Not being able to sell transitioned animals is a small 

price to pay for closing this destructive loophole.

Transitioned organic dairy animals should only be classified as organic dairy animals on the 

operation on which they were transitioned from conventional to organic. The transitioned 

animals should lose their organic dairy status if they are: sold, transferred, gifted, moved to 

another operation, or they are included as part of a merger.

Allowing transitioned animals to be sold, transferred, gifted, or moved to another operation 

while maintaining their status as certified organic dairy animals creates a loophole that will 

be exploited. Some operations are continually sourcing off-farm transitioned animals, which is 

less expensive than raising animals as organic from the last third of gestation. This creates an 

unfair economic advantage for operations making use of the loophole. 

Limiting the movement of transitioned animals has economic benefits. Start-up operations 

should buy organically certified cows. Increased demand for animals raised as organic will 

create a thriving market for organic replacement animals. This will allow small-to-mid-size 

organic dairy operations to diversify into breeding replacements whose price will reflect the 

true cost of organic dairy at their scale of production.

Before finalizing the rule, APHIS should substantially revise its proposals to revise and update the standards governing the humane care and handling of captive marine mammals. The current proposal ignores a wealth of scientific evidence obtained over the past three decades and essentially maintains a long-outdated status quo for the captive marine mammal industry.

While the agency has proposed several improvements to the standards, such as requiring shade for all outdoor marine mammal enclosures and ramps for older or injured seals, sea lions, polar bears, and sea otters to exit pools more easily, these are minor compared to the significant failures in the proposed rule.

The agency proposes no changes to the space requirements, claiming it is unaware of any science on which to base such changes. In fact, there is a tremendous body of recent research using increasingly sophisticated tagging technology to monitor fine-scale movement patterns of individual marine mammals, especially cetaceans and polar bears. These species travel tremendous distances and dive very deep, making the current minimum space requirements totally inhumane. The best available science for seals, sea lions, and sea otters--even for the slow, plant-eating manatee--also supports major space increases.

The current space standards were set over 30 years ago and have no basis in science or even best practices within the captive display industry. As an example, for up to two orcas, a facility need only provide a circular tank with a diameter twice as wide and a depth half as deep as an average adult orca is long. This standard does not even allow the animal to position itself fully in the vertical plane (its tail would touch and drag on the bottom before the animal reaches full upright orientation). This cannot be considered adequate!

While the rule refers to peer-reviewed papers for proposed changes to some standards (e.g., lighting requirements), it claims the agency is unaware of such papers for other standards (e.g., temperature requirements) and therefore proposes no major changes. Yet a considerable amount of research has been conducted within the past 15 years related to most if not all of the affected standards. 

The proposed rule would still allow pinnipeds to be housed in enclosures with tanks filled with fresh water. Allowing the maintenance of a marine mammal in fresh water is clearly an inappropriate welfare standard.

Several standards have been weakened, particularly regarding interactive programs such as swim-with-dolphin encounters. For example, the standard for the interaction time for each cetacean per day has been increased from two hours to three hours, not based on science or even industry best practices, but simply "on information provided by licensees ... which suggested that the marine mammals would not be harmed by a modest increase in interactive time per day." Facility "suggestions" represent a clear conflict of interest and should never be the sole basis for changes to standards.

The agency asked in previous notices if noise standards should be established. In several instances, noise levels, particularly in air, are extremely high (in theme parks, virtually every night there is a fireworks display directly over the marine mammal enclosures). Noise standards must be established for marine mammal facilities.

In sum, the proposed rule is grossly inadequate and fails to take into account current scientific understanding of the needs of marine mammals. APHIS must substantially strengthen the requirements for keeping cetaceans in captivity before the rule is finalized.

I am writing to share my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and Department of Justice (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) (the Departments) Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Security Bars and Processing; RIN 1125-AB08 / 1615-AC57 / Docket No: USCIS 2020-0013/ A.G. Order No. 4747-2020.

I object to this proposed rule, because it is wholly unnecessary and could result in barring people with well-founded fear of persecution from exercising their legal right to seek asylum. It would, among other things:

Bar asylum-seekers if they come from a country where COVID-19 is present.

Bar doctors, nurses, aides, and other essential personnel who work in medical settings from asylum if they have come into contact with COVID-19 while they have served American communities during the pandemic response.

Bar asylum seekers from protection if they contracted COVID-19 while waiting for their asylum hearing, including asylum seekers who contract COVID-19 while in immigration detention centers.

Allow the administration to possibly expand the ban to bar asylum seekers with other diseases.

The United States already has the tools that it needs to screen immigrants for potential health risks. Additionally, U.S. borders have been shut down to asylum seekers since March, making this proposed rule redundant. 

Turning back asylum seekers to countries where they might face serious harm upon return, without allowing them meaningful opportunities to seek protection, violates the United States international treaty obligations under the 1951 Convention Related to the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol to which the United States is a signatory. The U.S. is obligated to comply with the principle of non-refoulement-an asylum seeker cannot be sent to another territory or state where they fear threats to their life or freedom on protected grounds. The tenants of these international treaties are also codified in our domestic law, the Refugee Act of 1980 (Pub. L. No. 96-212).

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), recently issued a guidance that underscores that states have the authority to take necessary measures to attempt to thwart the rapid spread of a public health threat, but they cannot do so in violation of long standing legal standards. If implemented, this rule would allow DHS to quickly deport people it determines pose a danger to the security of the United States based on public health grounds, without any due process. 

To deny asylum to someone because they could possibly transmit an infectious disease is criminal. We can easily identify those who are potentially capable of spreading infection and isolate them until the threat is over. Thus, no harm is done. However, denial of asylum and deporting people to their home country is knowingly subjecting them to abuse, assault and death.

For these reasons, the Departments should immediately withdraw this proposed regulation. Instead, the administration should ensure that any public health efforts designed to combat the spread of COVID-19 do not violate individuals right to seek asylum, even during a public health emergency.

We the undersigned 32,880 residents of the United States support the proposed rule to prohibit

backbone of a healthy ocean ecosystem. 
Forage species, via their role as prey for other fish and wildlife, contribute to jobs and revenue on 
the West Coast. These small fish indirectly support ocean-based tourism and recreation sectors 
that provide 400,000 jobs and $18 billion in revenue to California, Oregon and Washington, 
according to the National Ocean Economics Program. When forage fish decline, so do the 
predators dependent on them, including fish like salmon, tuna and halibut, and wildlife like 
seabirds and seals. 
Demand for forage fish is increasing as aquaculture and agriculture industries expand worldwide. 
Most forage fish catch is not consumed directly as human food, but is sold in global markets as 
ground meal for farmed fish, chickens and pigs. With the global expansion of aquaculture and 
agriculture comes concern that the demand for fish meal will increase pressures on wild forage 
fish stocks, and forage fish that are not currently desirable may soon become commercially 
targeted. 
Rather than wait for new fisheries to start up on these ecologically important forage species, and 
then have to rush in afterward with conservation and management measures, the Pacific Fishery 
Management Council is being proactive by first protecting these important forage species. 
We applaud the Pacific Fishery Management Council and National Marine Fisheries Service for 
this forward-thinking, ecosystem-based fishery management approach. Protecting these forage 
species from the development of new fisheries, unless and until it can be proven they can be fished 
sustainably and without impacting the health and biodiversity of the ecosystem, or existing 
fisheries, will ensure dependent wildlife has enough to eat.

CALIFORNIA ANCHOVY POPULATION REMAINS LOW, 2012–16
ABSTRACT
Updated abundance estimates of the central subpopu-
lation of northern anchovy (Engraulis mordax) are devel-
oped from California Cooperative Oceanic Fisheries 
Investigations (CalCOFI) data on egg and larval den-
sities for 1951–2011, with new estimates for 2012–15. 
We followed the approach of MacCall et al. (2016; Fish. 
Res.) which corrected for a hyperstability bias due to 
nearshore concentration of CalCOFI stations and the 
tendency of the anchovy population to contract into 
this area when abundances are low. We corrected pre-
vious estimates based on calibration using an erroneous 
absolute biomass value from the 1980s, and extended 
estimates up through 2015. Anchovy spawning biomass 
remains below 100,000 metric tons, at an average of 
20,700 metric tons over the past 7 years. Although the 
most recent 2016 CalCOFI data are not yet available, 
recent results from the continuous underway fish egg 
sampler (CUFES) do not indicate any substantial recov-
ery of the anchovy population to date.
INTRODUCTION 
Northern anchovy is an important component of the 
forage fish community of the California Current eco-
system (CCE). Anchovy are schooling coastal pelagic 
fish that have undergone large oscillations in abun-
dance for thousands of years, with periodicity of ~60 
y (­Baumgartner et al. 1992; MacCall 1996; Field et al. 
2009) which have been linked to climate influences 
(Lehodey et al. 2006; Lindegren et al. 2013). Anchovy are 
a relatively small and short-lived species (most <16 cm in 
length; most fishes <5 y in age; Schwartzlose et al. 1999), 
with high fecundity and mortality, and are thought to 
do well in colder waters associated with high coastal 
upwelling (Rykaczewski and Checkley 2008; Linde-
gren et al. 2013). There are historically three oceanic 
population centers for anchovy along the Pacific coast 
of North America: a northern stock near the Colum-
bia River mouth, a central stock concentrated in the 
Southern ­California Bight (SCB) and Monterey Bay, and 
a southern stock off of Baja California (Huppert 1980; 
Schwartzlose et al. 1999; Zwolinski et al. 2012). 
Anchovy is an important prey resource for many 
upper trophic level predators in the CCE (Szloboszlai 
et al. 2015), and supported historically significant fish-
eries in California and Mexico (CDFG 2001). Anchovy 
stock assessments were conducted until 1995 (Jacobson 
et al.1995); since then, only spawning biomass estimates 
exist (MacCall et al. 2016). After a spike in estimated 
spawning biomass briefly exceeding a million metric 
tons (MT) in 2005–06, the population subsequently 
collapsed by 2009 (MacCall et al. 2016). The systemic 
causes of the recent decline in abundance are not clear, 
although one of the proximal causes of the decline has 
been hypothesized to be the decrease in egg and larval 
survivorship during the 2000s (Fissel et al. 2011; ­MacCall 
et al. 2016). The cause of that mortality is not presently 
known, but intensified filter feeding cannibalism by the 
parents is a likely possibility (i.e., high density of adults 
can occur from the range contraction at low popula-
tion sizes; MacCall 1990). The consequence was a severe 
reduction in the production of recruitment-age fish. 
Given the short timing and the magnitude of the decline 
in abundance, it happened faster than could be explained 
by poor recruitment alone, indicating that the natural 
mortality rate of adults also probably increased. The esti-

Based on actual inspection results, FedEx observes that the inspection intervals in 
777-57A0125RB original issue dated July 25, 2023 (Ref /B/) and the added

cracking was found.

inspected regions or approximately thirty-five percent (35%). Based on the low rate

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speedup the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

ALL ANIMALS MATTER!

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

Public Funds Public Schools (PFPS) is a collaboration of Education Law Center, the Southern 
Poverty Law Center, SPLC Action Fund, and Munger, Tolles & Olson LLP that strives to ensure all 
public funds for education are used to maintain and support public schools. PFPS writes to 
comment on a specific aspect of Regulation 107431-19 related to the potential for businesses 
to profit from contributions to private school voucher programs. 
 
We appreciate the steps this Department has taken to curtail taxpayers’ ability to profit on 
contributions to state tax credit programs that fund private school vouchers. Diverting tax 
dollars to pay private education expenses hinders the ability of public schools to provide the 
programs and resources necessary to meet the needs of all their students. There should be no 
opportunity to profit from contributions to such programs, which only increases the cost to the 
public. 
 
Specifically, there is one aspect of the proposed regulation that could open the door to 
inappropriate tax avoidance opportunities for taxpayers who donate to certain school voucher 
programs. PFPS is concerned by the possibility that some owners of passthrough businesses 
may be able to circumvent the $10,000 State and Local Tax (SALT) deduction cap by 
recharacterizing the nondeductible portion of their state and local income tax payments as 
deductible business expenses. 
 
Example 2 provided in 1.162-15(a)(2)(ii) states that a business partnership (P) may deduct a 
$1,000 payment to a charity as a business expense even if it “expects to receive a $1,000 
income tax credit on account of P’s payment, and … the credit can be passed through to P’s 
partners.” 
 
Putting aside the question of money spent on advertising, this example affords the business a 
$1,000 increase in their business expense deductions even though their “expense” was entirely 
offset by a state income tax credit. This outcome may not be problematic if the business’s 
partners also see an offsetting decrease of $1,000 in their SALT deductions. But the example 
seems to leave open the possibility that these partners can increase their business expense

 
deductions even in situations where their SALT deductions will remain unchanged because, both 
before and after the payment to the school voucher program, they will continue deducting the 
maximum allowable amount of state income tax ($10,000). 
 
By redirecting a mandatory $1,000 payment away from their state government and toward a 
school voucher program instead, they have avoided the SALT cap limitation and have engaged 
in behavior that could prove profitable for the business based on the federal income tax 
consequences alone. 
 
In other words, the language in this proposed regulation may embolden some businesses to 
attempt to circumvent the SALT deduction cap by donating to private school voucher programs 
because the regulation fails to adequately delineate between using a state income tax credit to 
offset taxes that would have been deducted for federal purposes, or using that credit to offset 
taxes that would have been nondeductible. 
 
We ask that the IRS clarify that the SALT deduction cap cannot be circumvented for businesses 
that donate to private school voucher programs in this manner and defer to the comments 
submitted by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy for additional explanation of how 
this could be avoided.

service members, privacy advocates, and national security experts, will be essential to
refine and improve the rule over time.

Department’s consideration of these suggestions to enhance the balance between national

I'm writing as an outdoorsman and small businessman. I think it's imperative to safeguard wolves and not remove any existing protections for these fantastic animals.

Wolves fill vital roles in ecosystems, and are essential to maintaining processes and functions in the natural systems in which they evolved. For example, wolves help to protect our streams and rivers from overgrazing by ungulates. This, in turn, helps to support native populations of fish, birds, and riparian vegetation. The presence of wolves contributes to healthier soils, helps to sustain robust populations of birds of prey, and may buffer the negative effects of climate change on ecosystems.

Killing wolves harms wolf pack structure, which may cause young, inexperienced, or immigrating wolves to be more likely to prey on livestock. Killing wolves will, in most situations, make livestock-wolf conflicts worse.

Non-lethal control is effective. Working ranches that fully implement non-lethal measures have been successful at keeping depredations very low, even in areas of high wolf activity. Resources are in place for compensation, as well as for grants to help ranchers implement non-lethal control measures. Co-existence with wolves is possible and necessary.
The public supports wolf recovery, and strong legal protections for wolves.

Dear Ms. McArdle: 

Student Debt Crisis is writing to you in response to Federal Register notice ED-2018-OPE-0041. The Departments proposal would delay the 2016 rule regarding state authorization of distance education programs. We urge the Department to reconsider the delay and modification of these rules as it has created confusion for students, institutions, and states. The regulation was developed during two prior negotiated rulemaking sessions and has received proper review and scrutiny. We encourage the Department to immediately implement the 2016 rule.

Delaying regulations would have a major impact on current and future student loan borrowers:

- Students leave distance-education-only, for-profit education programs with significantly higher student debt loads than the average for students in programs not entirely online.

- Borrowers enrolled in distance-education-only programs carry higher loan debt on average at for-profits than their counterparts at brick-and-mortar for-profit programs.

- The average cumulative federal student loan debt for graduating borrowers at distance-education-only programs is highest at for-profit institutions; and is higher than those not enrolled in entirely-online programs.

Students enrolled in distance education programs are older, poorer, and more likely to be an underrepresented minority than those enroll in non-distance-education-programs. These students are more likely to be exposed to fraud and abuse by low-quality, costly education programs. Further, nearly 1 in 5 veterans are enrolled at riskier online-only, for-profit schools.

Delaying the 2016 rule removes consumer protections that are vital for vulnerable students to make informed financial and education decisions. The state authorization rule is essential to ensuring program quality and integrity for consumers. Additionally, the regulation provides additional protections that include a way to file consumer complaints and creating a way for states and institutions to address them.

For nearly a third of students enrolled in distance education programs, delaying rules that protect students could mean life-long student loan debt. Students should be offered the piece of mind that their education program will actually provide credentials that meet industry standards and are valuable to the current job market.

Finally, the Department has an obligation to provide students with disclosures and information that help people make informed decisions about their education financing. Reviewing regulatory rules for the third time is an unnecessary delay that puts many students and borrowers at risk of falling victim to expensive, low-quality education programs.

Again, we urge the Department to immediately implement the 2016 state authorization regulations.

I respectfully submit this comment to strongly oppose USCIS's NPRM, USCIS-2020-0019; RIN 1615-AC61. This misguided rule, which dramatically alters the way in which H-1B registrations are selected for the annual H-1B statutory cap, is inconsistent with Congressional intent, is in violation of the statute, and will undermine our nation's pipeline of global talent we need to drive innovation and foster economic growth.

I am an immigration professional and I have seen the terrible effects this is having in American businesses.

This Proposed Rule is a Clear Violation of the Statute and Congressional Intent:

The H-1B program was established by Congress to provide an avenue for employers to hire a foreign worker in a specialty occupation. This proposed rule is a clear violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which prioritizes the selection of H-1B cap-subject petitions in the "order in which they are filed" and does not limit who is selected for the H-1B cap to those employers who pay the most. USCIS lacks the statutory authority to make such a change and cannot use the statute's silence as an invitation to adopt criteria, such as wage level or skill level, to prioritize the selection of H-1B cap subject visas. 

This Proposed Rule is Based on a False Premise That Salary Alone Equates with Value: 

This proposal, which is based on the false premise that individuals who earn more in their profession contribute more to the economy or society, is yet another misguided and illegal attempt by the Trump administration to weaken our legal immigration and promote falsities about the workers who, contrary to what this rule implies, strengthen our economy.

If implemented, this rule will have a direct and negative impact on U.S. employers and college-educated foreign-born professionals by dramatically reducing access to the H-1B visa program for early-career professionals, including those completing Master's or Doctoral degrees at U.S. colleges and universities. Indeed, USCIS has acknowledged that if this new regulation is implemented, no individuals who are paid a Level 1 wage would be selected to submit a H-1B cap-subject petition for the annual H-1B cap. These proposed changes would effectively eliminate the H-1B program as an available visa option for new graduates seeking employment in an entry-level position.

USCIS Should Refrain From Implementing this Rule For the FY2022 H-1B Cap Filing Season:

Many U.S. employers and immigration attorneys start preparing for the H-1B cap filing season months in advance, in some cases as early as August depending on the industry. Any changes by USCIS to the H-1B cap filing process this late in the year would have an adverse impact on U.S. employers, immigration attorneys and individuals, as hiring decisions and filing processes and procedures have already been put in place by many employers and immigration law firms. Thus, if USCIS finalizes this illegal and misguided rule, USCIS must refrain from implementing it for the upcoming FY2022 H-1B cap filings season in order to allow U.S. businesses, immigration attorneys and individuals sufficient time to adapt to the new wage-based selection process.

I oppose the proposed rule change to NEPA that would effectively expand the number and type of projects that would count as Categorical Exclusions under current law. 

Categorical Exclusions are necessary for ensuring the federal government accurately assesses projects that may cause undue harm to the health and safety of the public as well as maintain effective long term stewardship of public lands. 

In the White and Green Mountain National Forest where I regularly visit for both work and play, weakening the threshold under which projects are defined as categorical exclusions would negatively impact the White and Green Mountain National Forests in their ability to provide recreation for hunting, trapping, fishing, whitewater rafting and kayaking, bird watching, hiking and a myriad of other popular uses. 

Furthermore, the proposed changes would negatively impact critical wildlife habitat and the ongoing important research into endangered species such as Bicknell's Thrush, Spotted Turtle, Wood Turtle, Black Racer, Lynx, Pine Marten, Snowshoe Hare and many other species native to the Green and White Mountain National Forest. 

The main reason the administration cites for the proposed rule change is to speed up the backlog of forest service projects under environmental review. However, the backlog has been worsening as the Forest Service's budget has been repeatedly cut. Removing outright a stakeholder's participation in the review process, in this case the American Public, is neither an effective or ethical means for reaching consensus on important decisions involving our precious public lands. The obvious solution is to restore adequate funding for the important work of the US Forest Service. 

Sincerely, 
Michael Lunter

Dear Secretary Purdue:

I write to urge you to promptly withdraw the proposed rule to 'modernize' swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes your responsibility to ensure food safety for all Americans.

This proposed rule puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. In place of these requirements, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide.

The rule also proposes a New Swine Inspection System that hands over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter establishment employees. The proposal also removes caps on line speeds, increasing the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination, and other food safety issues. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have decreased.

In any modernization of inspections, both the goal and the outcome should be making our food safer, not making things more convenient for industry at the expense of consumers. This proposal is the latter by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards essential to verifying that industry is performing those duties effectively.

In short, this is an absurd proposal that represents abdication of your agency's responsibility. 

Please immediately withdraw the proposed rule and design a new one that prioritizes food safety through better microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly lower contamination rates and foodborne illness.

Sincerely,

Wallace Elton
Saratoga Springs, NY

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

As an advocate for my son who is impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make bathrooms more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make bathrooms more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when traveling, including around issues with inaccessible bathrooms. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible bathroom on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

Blood lancets for multiple patients present a potential unreasonable risk of illness that cannot be adequately addressed either through the 510(k) review or PMA process. The National Center for Health Research appreciates the opportunity to comment on the FDA’s proposed 

administrative order to reclassify blood lancet devices from class I to class II special controls and class III 

(PMA requirements). Our senior fellow, Dr. Jennifer Yttri, previously commented on blood lancet

through the 510(k) review. Unfortunately, even the PMA process cannot ensure the safety of these 

devices. Therefore, such products should be removed from the market until and unless the risk of 

contamination has been eliminated. 

One of the main uses of blood lancet devices is to check the blood glucose levels of diabetes patients. The 

number of people suffering from diabetes in the US has dramatically increased since the 1990s and “along 

with the increased incidence of diabetes has come a progressive increase in the reports of blood borne 

infection transmission (primarily HBV), resulting from the shared use of fingerstick and POC blood 

testing devices.”2 

The Proposed Order 

We support the part of the proposed order that would reclassify single use only blood lancets with an 

integral sharps injury prevention feature and single use only blood lancets without an integral sharps 

injury prevention feature, from class I to class II special controls. Because of the likelihood of off label 

use, we urge the reclassification of multiple use blood lancets for single patient use only from Class I to 

Class III.

multiple patient use from class I (general controls) exempt from premarket notification into class III 

(premarket approval) is not sufficient to protect patients from serious infections. We strongly 

recommend that these devices be removed entirely from the market. The risk of spreading 

bloodborne infections through them is too high to justify the use of the devices. If the FDA is not 

willing to remove them from the market, then blood lancets for multiple patients should be Class 

III and be reviewed through the PMA process with very stringent safety criteria.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

Save Earth and animals

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

As a neurosurgeon from Annapolis, MD, Iam writing to comment on what I believe to be the inadequate service valuation for minimally invasive surgical sacroiliac joint fusion (CPT code 27279).

Sacroiliac (SI) joint pain is a common cause of low back pain that is easily identified and often misdiagnosed. Every month I consult on dozens of patients with chronic low back pain seeking surgical solutions because conservative treatment has failed. After careful evaluation and a thorough clinical workup, many of the them are diagnosed with sacroiliac joint instability. These patients are often surprised at the diagnosis because their other treating physicians had never considered it. The majority have endured years of inadequate pain management and some have had to endure unnecessary lumbar spine or hip surgeries (and, in some unfortunate cases, both)

I have been an early adopter of lateral transiliac placement of titanium implants across the SI joint and witnessed for myself the life altering effect that this innovative out-patient operation has had on a great many patients. The clinical evidence supporting the procedure is now very strong (two randomized trials(1,2)and one large prospective multicenter single-arm study(3)). Trial data are consistent with my experience of excellent responses in carefully selected patients.

Unfortunately, Medicare reimbursement for minimally invasive SI joint fusion is insufficient. 3 studies have compared the overall work associated with SI joint fusion (9 units in 2016) to that of lumbar microdiscectomy (13 units). I participated in a multicenter study wherein surgeons reviewed charts for the last 20 cases of each procedure and rated the level of preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative work associated with each case(4). Although intraoperative times were slightly lower in SI joint fusion compared to lumbar microdiscectomy, mean preservice and post-service total labor times were substantially longer and the mean number of postoperative physician visits was higher. Total service time (preoperative + intraoperative +postoperative time) was approximately 50 minutes longer in SI joint fusion. Two other studies showed similar findings(5,6). Taken together, these studies provide strong direct evidence that the RVU for SI joint fusion is currently undervalued.

If an effective procedure is undervalued, surgeons will not take the time from their practices to learn it and, thus, not offer it to their patients. The negative outcomes are then two-fold. Firstly, patients fail to receive the care that they need. Secondly, surgeons remain uninformed regarding the benefits of the operation and continue to offer other unnecessary surgeries or pain management procedures, thereby exposing patients to additional risks and complications

I encourage CMS to adjust the RVU for SI joint fusion commensurate with its work value.

On behalf of the over 600 member companies of the American Petroleum Institute (“API”) I write in response to 
the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (REG-117589-18) concerning statutory limitations pertaining to like-kind 
exchanges. Natural gas and oil companies make frequent use of the section 1031 rules as the industry’s investments 
are heavily intertwined with real property assets. As such, we encourage the Department of the Treasury and the 
Internal Revenue Service (“Treasury and the IRS”) to consider natural gas and oil specific concerns detailed in this 
letter as well as provide additional examples pertaining to large fixtures such as refineries, petrochemical plants, 
manufacturing plants, offshore platforms, and storage tanks. 
Characterization of Offshore Platforms 
Offshore platforms can be constructed to support drilling, production operations or both drilling and production 
operations. An offshore drilling platform includes a drilling rig, which is the machinery used to drill an offshore well. 
An offshore production platform on the other hand treats and separates production from offshore wells on the 
deck of the platform. All offshore platforms are structurally similar, regardless of whether they include drilling rigs 
(with the main differences arising in the type and purpose of the equipment contained on the platform). 
Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.1031(a)-3(a)(2)(ii)(C) identifies offshore drilling platforms as inherently permanent structures. 
As an offshore production platform is structurally similar to an offshore drilling platform, there should be no 
distinction for purposes of Treas. Reg. § 1.1031(a)-3(a)(2)(ii)(C) between offshore platforms used for drilling as 
compared to offshore platforms that are used for production. As such, API recommends that Treasury and the IRS 
replace the term “offshore drilling platform” with the more inclusive term “offshore platform” on the list of 
inherently permanent structures in Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.1031(a)-3(a)(2)(ii)(C).

I am writing to oppose EPA's proposed revisions to the "Effluent Limitations Guidelines and Standards for the Steam Electric Power Generating Point Source Category" ("ELG rule"). This proposed rule weakens standards and delays compliance deadlines for some types of coal ash wastewater and weakens or eliminates pollutant reduction requirements for broad categories of coal-fired power plants. This would lead to hundreds of millions of additional pounds of pollutants, including toxic arsenic, lead, mercury, and selenium being released into our waterways.

These revisions are being proposed nearly five years after the original rule was finalized, which means that there have been over five years of technological advancement since EPA last considered these standards. EPA's ELG revisions should reflect these advances and require more stringent pollution discharge limits, not weaker ones.

For too long, the coal industry's business model included profits built on the backs of poisoned communities and waterways. With the revision, EPA is perpetuating this injustice, trading away the health of our waterways in another desperate attempt to prop up the failing coal industry. Please do not finalize this rulemaking.

SUBJECT: Comment on Food Labeling: Nutrient Content Claims; Definition of Term ‘‘Healthy’’ 

DATE: November 10, 2022 

Executive Summary 

The FDA faces one major challenge with this new proposal: there is no accurate way in which we 

can label a food or beverage as ‘healthy,’ either with the old definition or the new, and have it be an 

accurate representation of a healthy choice for an individual. An individual requires unique nutrition 

that is specific to their age, sex, and race (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2005)

Back in the early 2000s, elementary and middle school students would be taught about the food

2020). In 2022, the food pyramid has transformed into ‘MyPlate,’ a new guide to healthy eating 

supported by new research in nutritional sciences (What Is MyPlate? | MyPlate, 2022). The FDA’s 

purpose is to improve dietary patterns in the United States to help reduce the burden of nutrition-

related chronic diseases and advance health equity as nutrition-related chronic diseases are 

experienced disproportionately by certain racial and ethnic minority groups and those with lower 

socioeconomic status (Food and Drug Administration, 2022). In order to do this, the FDA should 

focus on the fact that nutrition does differ from different groups of people. According to several 

sources it is highly recommended that individuals should form eating habits with attention to their 

sex, age, and race (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2005)(U.S. Department of 

Health and Human Services and U.S. Department of Agriculture, 2015). The biggest problem in the 

United States from a public health standpoint is the alarmingly high rates of diabetes and obesity 

(Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee, 2020). We must change the way that our current labeling 

system if we want to attempt to reduce these rates; our current labeling system is not doing the job. 

Reject the Status Quo 

Just as the food pyramid became an outdated method, it is important to constantly be improving 

everything that we do. It is time that we review how outdated the United States’ food and beverage 

labeling methodology has become. At the moment, we present a nutrition chart that includes 

quantities and ingredients and bases all calculations off of a base 2000 calories per day metric (U.S. 

Food and Drug Administration, 2018). With this method, we cannot assume that the average U.S. 

citizen knows what the information and quantities on the nutritional label indicate. We should look 

towards more efficient systems, such as the Traffic Light Food Labeling system (Food Standards 

Agency, n.d.). This system utilizes a green, yellow, and red color coordinated labeling system that 

places the focus on unhealthy quantities of certain ingredients. This can allow the consumer to have

 
more knowledge at their disposal and an at-a-glance view of what the FDA deems to be unhealthy 

from their conducted research and yearly nutritional reports.

Dear Tom Vilsack,

The Tongass is a national treasure that helps fight climate change. I am writing in support of your agency’s proposal to fully reinstate the Roadless Rule on the Tongass National Forest in Alaska. The Roadless Rule was implemented with unprecedented public support to protect some of our nation’s most pristine public lands, including large parts of the Tongass National Forest. It retains wide bipartisan support, including from 96 percent of people who commented on the recent rollback of the rule in Alaska. 

In the middle of multiple national crises, the Trump administration focused on finalizing its plan to remove crucial protections for Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, serving industry interests aiming to open the forests to clear-cutting. Anything other than a full reinstatement of the Roadless Rule will have far-reaching impacts on indigenous communities, climate, and wildlife, and ignores overwhelming public support for the safeguard, including from Alaska Natives, Alaskans, and taxpayers across the nation. 

President-elect Biden promised bold climate action — and full protection of the Tongass is an integral part of that. It’s already stored over 3 billion tons of carbon — about 15% of what the United States produces in a year — and continues to store more and more each passing year. 

I urge you to fully reinstate the Roadless Rule protection to the Tongass National Forest and put the public interest, environmental justice, our public lands, and taxpayers above corporate profits. 

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Brandon Breen
Saint Paul, MN 55105

Dear Secretary Purdue,

I DON'T TRUST THE SLAUGHTERHOUSE, PERIOD! I am urging you to withdraw the proposed rule to 'modernize' swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety.

The proposed rule puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. In place of these requirements, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide.

The rule also proposes a New Swine Inspection System that hands over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter establishment employees. The proposal also removes caps on line speeds, increasing the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination, and other food safety issues. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer, and this proposal will not achieve that. Instead, it has the potential to make food less safe by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

We urge you to withdraw the proposed rule and design a new rule that prioritizes food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness.

Sincerely,

Diane Stanley
Georgetown, IN

Chronic pain is a prominent cause of disability with significant 

socioeconomic impact (1,2). The prevalence is variably reported but can range from 

11% to 43% amongst adults in the United States (3,4). We appreciate the CDC’s 

efforts in creating guidelines to assist healthcare providers in treating patients with 

chronic pain. In 1986 the World Health Organization created a stepwise approach to 

the treatment of cancer pain known as the “WHO analgesic ladder” (5). This 

treatment model emphasized the use of oral pain medication and with time, was 

expanded to a multitude of non-cancer pain conditions (6). The current opioid 

epidemic has placed a spotlight on chronic pain management and has lead to 

emphasizing a multi-modal approach to pain management. This modern model is 

analogous to a toolbox with various tools that can be used by patients and clinicians 

to help address chronic pain including interventional pain procedures, exercise 

therapy, psychological treatments, and pharmacologic treatments (7,8). 

As the CDC contemplates updating the 2016 Guideline for Prescribing 

Opioids for Chronic Pain we ask that more consideration be given to FDA approved 

and evidence based interventional pain procedures available to help manage a 

multitude of chronic pain conditions. While the 2016 guidelines gave consideration 

to non-pharmacologic treatments such as exercise therapy and cognitive behavioral 

therapy, we believe that interventional pain techniques also serve as an effective 

non-pharmacologic tool in our patients’ toolbox. Interventional Pain Physicians 

have robust clinical practices where they use their advanced training to deliver safe 

and effective interventional options to appropriate patients for a variety of chronic 

pain conditions such as chronic neck and low back pain, cancer pain, various 

neuropathic pain conditions, chronic post-surgical pain, etc. 

Below is a short list of FDA approved minimally invasive interventional pain 

techniques that have demonstrated reduction in oral opioid consumption: 

1. Interspinous process decompression. This device is indicated for lumbar 

spinal stenosis with symptoms of neurogenic claudication and has been shown to be 

effective in oral opioid reduction (9). 

2. Lumbar facet joint thermal radiofrequency neurotomy (RF neurotomy). 

Studies suggest that approximately 20-40% of axial low back pain is caused by facet 

joint arthropathy (10). RF neurotomy is a minimally invasive procedure that can 

reduce oral opioid consumption by using thermal lesions that ablate the sensory 

innervation of facet joints (11). 

3. Spinal cord stimulation therapy (SCS). SCS is a neuromodulation technique 

with various FDA indications such as post-laminectomy syndrome and has been 

shown to reduce oral opioid use (12). 

4. Intrathecal pump therapy. This intervention has FDA approval for chronic 

cancer pain. While oral opioids are considered to be a main component of cancer 

pain management, intrathecal drug delivery allows for overall dose reduction which 

can not only reduce adverse side effects, but also lead to improved pain control 

compared to oral administration (13).

 
5. Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS). PNS is a reversible neuromodulation 

technique that stimulates specific peripheral nerves for a variety of chronic 

pain conditions such as chronic low back, chronic post-amputation stump and 

phantom limb pain, as well as acute post operative pain following total knee 

arthroplasty (14–17). PNS has also been shown to reduce opiate consumption 

in chronic low back pain (LBP) (16,17). LBP is the leading cause of disability 

in adults in the United States and has a global prevalence of approximately 

12% (18–20).

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. The proposed regulations would result in a gratuitously cruel situation for children and families, all of whom deserve respect and compassion.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Is there no end to the flagrant abuse of animals in the USA, Canada and elsewhere. Withdrawing this long-awaited rule, and ignoring its overwhelming support from organic producers and consumers alike, is a failure of public policymaking. Never in the last 27 years has the USDA been confused over its authority to issue organic rules improving the welfare of animals. Scrapping this important rule threatens the integrity of the organic label and the many family farmers who rely on their customers' faith in it. This is a poor decision and will affect the marketing of organic foods in USA and Canada and will endanger people's and animals lives.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

Stop The Madness 
Help The Voiceless

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Dear Members of the Tax Legislative Committee: 
Proposed Regulation §1.861-19 (“Prop. Reg. §1.861-19”) and the proposed modifications to Regulation 
§1.861-18 (“Reg. §1.861-18”) that were published in the Federal Register on August 14, 2019, do not 
adequately identify the following issues: 
1) Cloud computing transactions that are classified as leases of property 
2) Income sourcing for “cloud computing” transactions 
The committee has specifically requested comments from the public on administering rules for sourcing 
income from cloud transactions in a manner consistent with Internal Revenue Code Sections 861 
through 865 and for classifying cloud computing transactions as leases. The comments and suggestions 
I’ve made in this letter reflect solely my own personal and professional views and not the views or 
opinions of my employer or any person, entity or organization associated with my employer. Below, I’ve 
provided a general overview of my recommendations followed by a more detailed discussion which 
explains the rationale for my viewpoints. 
Recommendations 
1) Cloud computing transactions that are classified as leases of property 
The factors identified under Prop. Reg. §1.861-19(c)(2) are not adequate to distinguish between 
a lease and a provision of service. I believe most of the factors listed under this section would 
be satisfied in cloud computing transactions qualifying either as a lease or a provision of 
services. I recommend that the factors originally published under IRC §7701(e)(1) not be 
applied to cloud computing transactions because the factors are not adaptable to transactions 
of this nature. Taxpayers need a set of factors that clearly delineate a service from a lease 
transaction for cloud computing transactions. If the committee were to proceed with the 
existing factors listed under Prop. Reg. §1.861-19(c)(2), then I recommend that the committee 
provide more examples that cover a wider breadth of fact patterns because the current 
examples are too similar and allow for too much subjectivity in determining when factors have 
been met and which factors take precedence which will result in varying interpretations and 
applications of these rules among taxpayers.

 
2) Income sourcing for “cloud computing” transactions 
I am requesting that the committee provide more concrete guidance on sourcing income earned 
from cloud computing transactions especially when on-demand access to intangible assets is 
accessible from anywhere in the world via an internet connection. In addition, more guidance is 
needed to conclude when the use of a computer server constitutes a physical presence versus 
when the use of a computer server is deemed inconsequential or de mininis when sourcing 
income from cloud transactions pursuant to Internal Revenue Code Sections 861 through 865.

and the millions of patients they serve, we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Centers for 

Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule Medicaid and CHIP Managed Care Access, Finance

California’s 21 public health care systems (PHS) play a central role in the state’s safety net and health 

care landscape, delivering care to all who need it - 3.7 million Californians each year - regardless of 

ability to pay or circumstance. On average, 60% of our patients are on Medicaid (called Medi-Cal in 

California) or uninsured and in some of our systems, nearly 80% of patients. Patients served by PHS 

often have multiple, complex medical and social needs. Considering PHS’ significant and multiple roles, 

PHS and the care they provide have a profound impact on the health care and health of millions of 

Californians. 

Medicaid managed care is the predominant means through which beneficiaries of California’s Medi-Cal 

program access services, and we are pleased to submit these comments to help CMS strike the right 

balances in updating its Medicaid managed care regulations. 

1. 

 CAPH Appreciates CMS’ Continued Acknowledgement of the Role of State Directed Payments 

Our health systems depend on Medicaid managed care payments to continue to be able to have 

sufficient funding to support the provision of care to the complex patient populations we serve. As a 

result, State Directed Payments (SDPs) have become an important means of financial support and have 

provided our PHS with the opportunity to improve quality of care and address disparities for their 

patient populations. Preserving the ability of states to pursue their respective programmatic goals by 

directing payments to defined classes of providers is critical to the ability of our members to continue to 

provide high quality care to Medi-Cal patients. 

a. CMS should not impose a limit on total SDP expenditures in a state. 

P a g e | 1

 
In the proposed rule, CMS invites comments on “potentially imposing a limit” on the amount of 

expenditures for SDPs. (Proposed Rule at 28127). We appreciate CMS’ acknowledgement that imposing 

such a limit could have negative impacts, including potentially limiting access to care. Because of the 

potential to disrupt important financial streams in ways that could harm beneficiaries, we believe that 

taking steps to finalize such a limit would not benefit the Medicaid program. 

In California, the base payment rates from managed care plans are well below cost, and the additional 

funding provided through SDPs are critical to ensuring an actuarially sound rate, as CMS itself 

acknowledges in the preamble. Unless CMS is willing to impose a firm payment adequacy standard on 

base provider payment rates, which historically it has not been willing to do, an arbitrary SDP 

expenditure limit could result in total payment rates that are inadequate to meet the full needs of the 

managed care population, especially beneficiaries with complex health and social needs. As full systems 

of care and core safety net providers, PHS provide the full array of services for these complex 

populations, which we wouldn’t be able to do without these targeted SDPs. An arbitrary SDP limit would 

force California to decide which of its competing policy objectives it must sacrifice and would pit 

different classes of critical providers against each other in seeking SDP funding.

As a health care worker and advanced practice nursing student, I'm in firm opposition to the proposed Modernization of Swine Slaughter Inspection rule. It is a rights violation to the animals and the workers of these plants and it is unsafe for the consumer. Under this rule, the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System (NSIS) would place key food safety inspection duties into the hands of slaughter plants themselves. These plants are only concerned with their bottom line. Allowing them perform their own inspections is extremely dangerous to consumers and will promote increased cruelty practices to these animals and unsafe working conditions for their employees. Compassion Over Killing's investigation of a plant under the pilot high-speed slaughter program, HIMP, revealed pigs covered in feces and pus-filled abscesses being processed for human consumption with a USDA seal of approval. The investigation also showed pigs being dragged, kicked, excessively shocked, and improperly stunned as workers struggled to keep up with the facility's high line speeds. There is widespread opposition to the high-speed slaughter program within the federal government, including by USDA whistleblowers and members of Congress. The USDA's own Office of the Inspector General stated that the "HIMP program has shown no measurable improvement to the inspection process." I urge you to protect workers, consumers, and animals and end, rather than expand, this program.

I join all those asking you for a Final Rule on the origin of organic livestock. We need this rule desperately, and we need it now.

However, much of the growth in the industry has been usurped by industrial scale operations gaming the system. If it wasn't for the factory farms there could have been thousands of additional dairies saved and converted to organic. The resulting psychological damage to families in rural communities is almost incalculable.

In order to protect the integrity of USDA organic certification and establish a level playing field for a thriving organic dairy market, the Final Rule must:

Prohibit organic dairy operations from acquiring transitioned animals to expand or replace animals in the organic dairy herd. USDA should prohibit the sales of transitioned animals as certified organic.
Limit the movement of transitioned animals has economic benefits. Start-up operations should buy organically certified cows. I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

43
Heather Place

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.
