Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Consumers deserve to know the truth about what's in the meat they are buying and how it was sourced with the attendant care.

Thank you for considering my request.

I am submitting comments on the Select Agent status of Brucella abortus. I support the removal of B.abortus from the select agent list. My background and connection to this issue is that I am a strong advocate for wild, free-roaming bison (buffalo).

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country — the last continuously wild herds — continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

It is time to put the responsibility back onto those who want to blame every wild being except their own property. Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

operations. Especially in the case of hospital continuum of care, of which SNFs 

are an important part, the health care system continues to reel from the effects of 

the pandemic and the extraordinary inflationary environment. Challenges facing 

the field include skyrocketing labor-costs, critical staffing shortages, and 

unprecedented rises in supply and drug costs. These have been felt by all 

providers, including hospital based and freestanding SNFs. 

The AHA would like to stress to CMS the importance of SNFs’ role in the 

continuum of care, including on hospitals’ ability to properly care for and safely

discharge patients in a timely manner. As SNFs and other post-acute providers 

have been strained by the pandemic, the ripple effects have been felt throughout 

the continuum of care. For example, a December 2022 report from AHA showed 

that the average length of stay (ALOS) for patients awaiting discharge to a SNF 
rose by more than 20% from 2019 to 2022.1 This increase is driven in large part 

by the difficulties SNFs and other post-acute providers have had in staffing and 

operating at full capacity. This, in turn, has limited hospitals’ capacity as hospital 

beds and resources remain dedicated to patients awaiting post-acute placement. 

Therefore, its vital to the entire health care continuum that CMS provide 

adequate reimbursement and resources to SNFs to help ensure all patients 

receive timely, appropriate care. 

The AHA also would like to call out the unique experience and role played by 

hospital based SNFs during the PHE, which in some ways was notably different 

than their freestanding counterparts. Hospital-based SNFs’ connection to their 

host hospitals facilitated more robust infection control, improved access to 

personal protective equipment and other factors that affected their overall PHE 

response. That said, hospital based SNFs also faced immense challenges with 

each surge of the pandemic and its after-effects, including skyrocketing labor and 

supply costs, as well as acute labor shortages. Therefore, as CMS considers how 

to ensure SNFs are adequately resourced to care for Medicare beneficiaries, we

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

2015 and extremely high bluefin discards prior to 2015 is no longer necessary for

bluefin tuna discards:
●
The fishing effort has decreased (see HMS 2022 SAFE Report (Table 6.9)
and 2017 SAFE Report (Table 5.8): 56 vessels fishing with pelagic
longline gear in 2021, while there were 104 vessels fishing with pelagic
longline gear in 2017)(respectively); Similarly, the number of sets have
declined: from 7,769 in 2015 to 4,822 in 2021
●
The IBQ program was successful at changing fishing behavior (National
Academy of Sciences: The Use Of Limited Access Privilege Programs in
Mixed Use Fisheries, 2021);
●
The observer program will continue to monitor discards and be able to
detect meaningful changes in the rate of bluefin discards. NOAA Fisheries
relies principally on observer data to meet its international reporting
obligations regarding bluefin discards (to the International Commission for
the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT)).(eg. TAble 2.5; 2019 US
Annual Report to ICCAT).
2) National Standard 8: Not-withstanding the importance of the conservation
aspects of the Magnuson-Stevens Act (NS Guidelines (50 CFR Section
600.345(b)(1)), the requirement providing for the sustained participation of fishing

 
communities must be considered, and not minimized based upon a NOAA
Fisheries Policy (Cost Allocation Policy Procedure 04-115-02; 2019). Consistent
with paragraph (b)(1) of the NS 8 guidelines, two of the alternatives in
Amendment 15 would achieve similar conservation goals, and the alternative that
provides the greater potential for sustained participation of the community and
minimizes the impacts on the community (i.e., Alternative F3 - removal of the EM
requirement) should be viewed as the proposed alternative.
●
Amendment 15 notes the potential for large reductions in trip profit (up to
19%)
●
SAFE Report 2022: Table 8.7: Median unit costs for fuel, bait and light
sticks have increased over time. The median labor inputs have increased
in cost over time (Table 8.9)
●
Pelagic longline communities are among those listed as high or medium
high commercial engagement (Table 4.1) Amendment 15 DEIS); and high
or medium high social vulnerability (Table 4.2 Amendment 15 DEIS).
How is a requirement for the pelagic longline fishery to pay for the costs of electronic
monitoring justified or consistent with NS 8, in light of the shrinking PLL fishery, the
potential economic impacts, and lack of a counterbalancing ecological benefit? How is
NOAA Fisheries sustaining the PLL fishery and the associated benefits to the fishery
participants, and the seafood eating American public by proposing this EM measure?

The Checkerspot Butterfly has been on the cusp of the endangered species list for many years,

Sacramento Mountains of New Mexico and are known to thrive in high elevation mountain-

meadows with cool/wet temperatures. The butterfly is also considered a keystone species 

because they are pollinators. Pollinators help hold ecosystems together by supporting plant 

reproduction and plant diversity. The average life span of an adult butterfly is about a month, but 

the Checkerspot butterfly’s adult lifespan is only 14 days. This small span does not give them 

much time to pollinate, which emphasizes the need to protect not only the species but their 

habitat as well. Although there is no precise count for how many Checkerspot butterflies we have 

left, surveys completed between 1996 and 1997 showed that the butterfly occupied roughly 85 

square kilometers within the vicinity of the village of Cloudcroft. Yet, recent surveys show that 

butterfly's suitable habitat is likely less than 2 square miles within the range. As anyone could

plants and the development of these plants are constantly affected by climate changes. If the 

plant shifts its range due to changing temperatures/weather patterns, hosts and guests may miss 

each other. The Checkerspot butterfly is considered an endemic species with low dispersal 

capabilities and small geographic ranges. They can only survive in specific elevations and 

temperatures in the meadows, but with constant changes in temperatures, their habitat is 

extremely affected. It is also very hard for the checkerspot butterfly to reproduce quickly given 

their short life span and the dying population of their host plant.

The second major threat to the Checkerspot Butterfly is that their habitat and plants they feed on 

continue to be destroyed by livestock grazing, fire suppression, offroad vehicle use, inadequate 

state and federal regulations, and pesticides. Although these are many different examples, they 

all play a role in loss of habitat for the butterfly. Unlike climate change, this threat is specifically 

something that can be worked on because they all involve human activities. The butterfly’s 

reliance on meadows makes it particularly sensitive to habitat loss because meadows are easily 

accessed, clear of obstacles and inviting for human activities. This loss of habitat lowers the 

quality for the remaining habitat, creating less plant diversity. Loss of habitat from these 

activities ultimately results in habitat fragmentation, producing separated isolated locations of the 

butterfly. It seems that there is a cause and effect with these many threats to the Checkerspot

Jobs for the Future (JFF), a national nonprofit organization that works to ensure that all

Priorities, Requirements, Definitions, and Selection Criteria-Perkins Innovation and

We appreciate the named proposed priorities in this notice and agree that these priorities 
should be elevated in the Perkins Innovation and Modernization Grant Program. 
 
Regarding Proposed Priority 1 – Career-Connected High Schools 
 
JFF played a key role in launching the college and career pathways movement over a decade 
ago and currently leads several national initiatives closely aligned to the Career-Connected High 
Schools initiative. We support the prioritization of Career-Connected High Schools in grant 
applications, as well as the named four pillars for career-connected learning. 
 
We agree that all four of the pillars are critically important, however are concerned that only 
one of the four pillars is required to be implemented, without additional requirements for a 
design strategy that is cohesive outside of that one element. For example, as the notice is 
currently written, an applicant could suggest only increasing an existing concurrent or dual 
enrollment offering, as opposed to taking advantage of this opportunity to push forward new 
innovations and a more comprehensive education to career approach. While we understand 
that grantees are likely to be in different stages in the implementation of the four pillars, and 
that it may therefore be reasonable to focus on a subset of them during a particular grant 
period, this should be done in the context of a vision for career-connected learning that brings 
together all four pillars as part of a cohesive vision and system for career-connected learning. 
We suggest that the language at minimum provide a coherent vision of how the four pillars 
intersect and that the proposed priority require applicants to submit a coherent design that 
includes all four pillars, though proposed grant activities may focus on implementation of a 
subset of them. 
 
Additional factors for consideration regarding the four pillars: 
• Work-based learning: Applicants should build on current work-based learning efforts 
and incorporate innovative models that leverage shared facilities and staffing for 
integrated programming and curricula. One way to do this is through work-based

 
courses that: 1) allow students to take college-level technical courses that maximize on-
the-job training and in-classroom instruction; 2) leverage existing dual enrollment 
courses; 3) are co-taught by faculty and employer supervisors, using the workplace as a 
learning lab (at least 20% of the course should be taught at the workplace by an 
employer instructor); and 4) combine hands-on skill building with academic instruction 
to meet the training needs of employers and the skills and educational needs of workers 
and students. 
• Dual enrollment and guided pathways that reach back to 11th grade: Applicants should 
build on current pathways efforts, such as starting pathways as early as 11th grade and 
clearly defining recommended course sequences across high school and college to save 
time and money toward attaining one or more postsecondary credentials of value. The 
pathways should be endorsed across systems; discoverable and transparent to guide 
decisions for all students and their families; and permeable, durable, and stackable to 
avoid pathways that limit options and create dead ends. D

I am currently using sUAS for Search & Rescue in Backcountry areas and would like the FAA to consider a category of Flight over people that takes into account the probability of an incident. Use of sUAS is often blocked by 2 issues, Visual Line of Sight, and incidental flight over people. We are searching for a lost or injured hiker on or off trail, the trail and area surrounding it may have only a few unrelated hikers over several square miles but we cannot be 100% certain that none of them will not be momentarily overflown. The sUAS we use are reliable commercially available craft with well established reliability measures so the chance of an immediate, crash inducing failure, exactly when over one of the few unrelated hikers unprotected by intervening vegetation is exceedingly small.

A category allowing incidental overflight by reliable aircraft in low population areas would allow agency administrators to be comfortable that we are flying within FAA rules and allow potentially lifesaving flights to take place. There may be categories of agency flight that would allow this but we are volunteer members of an organization providing search & rescue resources flying under Part 107 rules not under a COA.

The Visual Line of Site issues that also impede our ability to operate while not under direct review in this rulemaking deserve some comment as well. A small sUAS operating in backcountry areas are quickly lost against a variable background of vegetation. This would limit use to a few hundred feet even in a discreet canyon bounded area of airspace that can be viewed by our observers to detect unaided any manned incursion. Why must we see a 10" long sUAS against wilderness background when obvious manned aircraft is what we seek to see and avoid.

I appreciate the opportunity to provide input on the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) for side underride guards on large trucks, as this issue holds significant importance for the safety of vulnerable road users.

Ensuring the safety of everyone on our roads necessitates the implementation of measures to enhance the protection of all users. Among the most fatal roadway crashes, those involving large trucks and vulnerable road users (VRUs) remain a significant concern, with a staggering fatality rate of 152.8 deaths per 1,000 crashes.

By requiring side underride guards, we have the potential to save numerous lives. Each year, approximately 500 vulnerable road users lose their lives in collisions with large trucks. A study conducted by the National Transportation Safety Board highlights that a majority of bicyclist and pedestrian fatalities involving large trucks occur in side impact crashes. Furthermore, the US DOT Volpe Center's research reveals that side guards can reduce fatalities from bicycle-large truck crashes by 55-75 percent and pedestrian-large truck crashes by 20-29 percent.

Regrettably, the current approach by NHTSA overlooks the lives of non-motorized users, disregarding the most vulnerable road users who face the highest risk of fatality in crashes involving large trucks.

Therefore, I wholeheartedly support the League of American Bicyclists' request for NHTSA to reassess the cost-benefit analysis by incorporating the fatalities and serious injuries of vulnerable road users and motorcyclists into the rulemaking process for side underride guards. Taking these critical steps will not only protect the lives of vulnerable road users but also contribute to achieving the goals outlined in the National Roadway Safety Strategy.

Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter. I trust that you will consider the invaluable impact that side underride guards can have on road safety for all users.

I submit this comment today to oppose USCIS-2019-0007-0001 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), which would cause dangerous privacy issues for children seeking safety in the United States.

The proposed rule expands the criteria under which children are required to provide biometric and DNA samples for immigration and asylum proceedings. As it stands, only children 14 and older were required to provide biometric data. The proposed rule would remove that age restriction, leading to the collection of sensitive data from much younger children who do not understand the implications and removing the protections provided by parental consent.

Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, coercing children to submit biometric data without explicit understanding and consent violates their rights and causes indefensible mental stress.

DHS estimates an additional 2.17 million new biometrics submissions will be collected annually. Many of these additional submissions will be of children under the age of 14.

The proposed rule also uses very vague language to explain how it will store biometric data and the instances in which it might share this biometric data with other government agencies. This raises many questions about data privacy and the ways that this data might be used against migrants. 

Children are particularly vulnerable to invasions of privacy that can result in long-lasting negative consequences. While it may be inconvenient to change your password when your identity is stolen, it is impossible to change your fingerprint or your DNA. A breach of a child's biometric data can result in lifelong and potentially life-threatening consequences.

That is why in most cases, parental consent is required before data like these are collected from children. Children in asylum or immigration proceedings, however, often are traveling alone or with parents who may not fully understand the consequences of agreeing to provide this information to U.S. border authorities. Refusal could result in expulsion from the country.

Please take into consideration this comment and the impact that the proposed rule would have on the right to privacy that should be extended to children fleeing violence who are seeking safety in the U.S.

I acknowledge that present Forest Service policy is to continue protecting state listed and forest sensitive species, however, this policy could be changed at any time to eliminate this protection. As I understand it, these policy changes could be made without further public comment. Without some safeguards in place to maintain this current level of protection, I have to question the potential consequences of adopting the proposed changes. 

More specifically, I have severe concerns regarding the proposed new Categorical Exclusions d12 and e 20 which would allow activities on existing roads or trails and allow the restoration of land occupied by roads or trail to a more natural condition. While both of these activities are beneficial in most cases, they still need to undergo scrutiny before being implemented. It is shortsighted to assume that only common weedy and non-native plants occur in disturbed areas and that very rare plants would be absent.

Placing limits on the amount of interaction that an animal receives per day ignores the inherent differences between animals, which are best judged by their keepers and trainers who work with them every day and know each individual best. Interaction is accepted to be enriching to animals' lives throughout the animal training community. It is offered to each animal through its own choice, one of the pillars of animal welfare. No animal is forced to interact when it does not want to. However, many animals choose to participate in interactions, and making laws to prevent them from doing so would be deleterious to their welfare. Our training and enrichment programs are exemplary, leave the judgement of administering them to people who know what they're doing.

If you regulate that there must be one trainer to each animal, most of the animals will be denied the opportunity to participate in their training/interactive session, because it is too difficult to obtain enough qualified staff for that. Animal trainers with appropriate experience can easily work with more than one appropriately trained animal at a time. Again, this should be left to the judgement of those administering their programs. They know what they can and can't do, and I wish to emphasize that human and animal safety is a top priority for everyone involved.

As a trainer, I have some concerns with the language used to describe "unsatisfactory" or "undesirable" behaviors. Using broad examples followed by "not limited to" could create confusion for trainers leading these programs. A performance-based approach focusing on unsafe behaviors specific to an individual, the circumstances at hand and the location in which they reside is a preferable way to ensure safety-based decision making. Trainers are in the best position to best determine if an animal exhibits unsafe behavior and facilitate behavioral redirection or the termination of its participation in a session due to such behavior.

Thank you, APHIS, for your concern. I am sure you will hear from a lot of people who think that we are treating animals wrong. This could not be further from the truth. We are absolutely dedicated to their welfare, and these additional regulations will not benefit the animals. They are merely meant to mollify those who are uneducated about the exemplary care we provide, including the extremely important facet of enriching animals through training sessions and interactive programs. They ignore the peer-revied, scientific evidence available, and should not be enacted without such evidence supporting them.

I urge the USDA to adopt the strongest possible standards of care for birds used in commercial enterprises and for wild-caught birds used for research. It is unconscionable that for the past 50 years these animals have been denied coverage under the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) and that--even after a court ruled against this exclusion--the department dragged its feet for 20 years. The number of investigations by animal welfare organizations for cruel treatment by bird breeders and others during this time is only the tip of the iceberg of the suffering that could have been avoided had the USDA acted sooner. Now the USDA is finally initiating efforts to promulgate regulations to protect birds under the AWA.

Please act! birds deserve protection without them the forests would be silent and we would live in a world devoid of the natural beauty of bird song. Birds are amazing please protect them and their habitats.
Thank you
Maryann T. Spanski

There should be no double standard when it comes to protecting birds; they should receive the same level of oversight as other animals covered by the AWA, regardless of other laws that may apply to birds. Regulations regarding their welfare should include the following basic elements: 

1. No sale of unweaned or prematurely weaned baby birds. These young, fragile birds are at great risk of succumbing to disease, mishandling, and the extreme hazards of transport. 

2. Environmental enrichment for all birds. Achieving the AWA's goal of ensuring "humane care and treatment" requires that species-specific physical and psychological needs of birds be met. 

3. Health certificates and record keeping for all birds. Records (including but not limited to acquisition and disposition of the birds) and disease testing are essential to prevent disease transmission and illegal trade in wild-caught birds. 

4. Enclosures that enable the birds to express normal behavior, including flight. Confinement in cages causes poor welfare in birds and can lead to destructive habits, including feather plucking. Birds need to be able to fly and express other natural behaviors. The USDA should adopt enforceable standards that don't rely solely on subjective assessments. 

5. No painful physical mutilations. Pinioning (severing of wing muscles or amputation of wings), toe clipping, devoicing, and beak alterations are examples of painful procedures that are typically done for the convenience of keepers and are extremely detrimental to the welfare of the birds. 

6. Coverage of all bird species. There is no justification for exempting certain species because they are addressed in other laws such as the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Many animals covered by the AWA are regulated under state or other federal laws, and such laws do not nullify their protections under the AWA. The same should be true for birds. The ESA does not ensure humane care and treatment.

I was pleased to read the guidance for industry for the regulation of intentionally altered DNA in animals and to see a common sense, case by case approach. I do not see genetic alterations as inherently dangerous especially in organisms that do not infect other organisms, but each one should be looked at separately. Approaching each genetic alteration as a new drug seems to be a good course of action. 
Section 514.1(b)(4) says the NADA will require a statement of composition of the drug product and that this will enable the FDA to determine if the new product "contains any potentially mobilizable DNA sequences, and whether sequences are present that encode pathogens, toxicants, allergens, or substances likely to dysregulate the growth control of cells, tissues, or organs, except by explicit design". This covers many of the concerns that will be applicable to any genetic variation and is reassuring, but how will the FDA be able to tell all this from a composition report? Will the composition include the genetic sequence and the proteomics of the new genes? Even if the gene and primary protein sequence are the same as a one found elsewhere the folding of a protein in a different organism may change its function and toxicity.

We are writing to (1) oppose the proposed expansion of the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS) in its current form; (2) urge NOAA to expand the boundaries and protections of the FGBNMS to a greater extent than considered in the proposed expansion; and (3) urge NOAA to apply existing restrictions to the FGBNMS expansion with no exemptions for spearfishing, longline fishing, or any other destructive fishing practice within sanctuary boundaries.

Please consider implementing Alternative 5 from the DEIS, which would provide greater protections to the FGBNMS than the final alternative chosen in the EIS. Alternative 5 would increase the sanctuary boundaries to include 57 national significant natural features and eight nationally significant cultural and historic resource sites. Even Alternative 3, which was identified as the preferred alternative in the DEIS, would be preferable to the final alternative chosen. Alternative 3 would have expanded the existing sanctuary from 56 square miles to 383 square miles and includes a total of 18 nationally significant natural features within 11 discrete proposed boundary areas.

The FGBNMS mission is to identify, protect, conserve, and enhance the natural and cultural resources, values, and qualities of FGBNMS and its regional environment for this and future generations. The FGBNMS provides a wide range of habitat conditions that support several distinct biological communities, including the northernmost coral reefs in the continental United States. Sanctuary formations provide the foundation for essential habitat for a variety of species, including sea turtles, sharks and other important marine wildlife.

In order to realize the FGBNMS mission, NOAA must restrict fishing in the sanctuary boundaries. Allowing spear fishing or longlines in FGBNMS boundaries would otherwise undermine the proposed expansions prohibition from taking any marine mammal or sea turtles.

Thank you for considering our opinions.

Sincerely,

Doug & Karen Lenier

I am an undergraduate student at Purdue University studying agriculture business with a concentration in management. I am currently taking an agriculture law class where we were encouraged to share our views on a proposed federal environmental regulation that directly impacts agriculture. 

Being from the Midwest and not being a seafood lover myself, I think I have a unique perspective. After reading through the proposed Amendment 18, I have a couple major concerns I would like to address. First, while it appears the red snapper population has begun to improve to the point of even considering this amendment, how can we be sure history will not repeat itself? If this amendment were to be put into place what will ensure that once again small red snapper will continue to get caught in the bycatch will be returned to the water in an efficient manner so when they are returned, they are still well. Not only does the shrimping industry effect the red snapper population but other finfish as well that could get caught in the shrimp trawls. This reduction in overall finfish could affect the Gulf of Mexicos, Caribbeans, and South Atlantics ecosystem. As Mark Twain once said, Those who do not learn history are doomed to repeat it. I believe there should be different ways investigated to reduce bycatch and also allow for the shrimping industry to pick back up. 

The demand for shrimp in the United States is continuing to grow and is arguably the most consumed seafood item we have. Unlike in the past where imported shrimp ruled the locally grown market due to the low costs we saw. More recently, Vietnam and Thailands shrimping industry has been hit with serious disease, increasing costs to import. This has expanded the fish farming industry here in the US over the past couple years. 

A short-term solution I see to a much more long-term problem would be to find a way to implement some sort of seasonality to the shrimp fishing. While I will not claim to be any sort of expert and am fairly nave to the issues at hand, I could see how this could be a solution for both of the parties at stake. After some quick research it appears that shrimping season doesnt open until late summer to early fall. So maybe creating a period within the already stated shrimping season to allow for more regulation. Another solution I could see working would be to put some sort of quota on the amount of shrimp able to be harvested. This would still in some ways hurt the red snapper population as well as some of the other finfishs, but it would also help drive shrimp prices down for American shrimp consumers. The amendment mentioned gas prices being a factor for some shrimp fisherman. Possibly opening up waters closer to shore as a starting point could be another small solution to the issue at hand. 

After further investigation, this amendment which I had no prior knowledge about seems to for lack of better words like ripping a bandage off a wound that is still healing. While the red snapper population is improving, we cannot just revert to our old ways and expect no change.

To Whom It May Concern, 
 
The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) greatly appreciates the Proposed Framework 
to Assess the Risk to the Effectiveness of Human and Animal Drugs Posed by Certain 
Antibacterial or Antifungal Pesticides and the continued opportunity for comments. Public 
health and health care experts have long held that a One Health approach is critical for 
addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR). As such, a multipronged strategy to address 
inappropriate antimicrobial use in human health, animal health, agriculture and the 
environment is essential, and the proposed framework is an important step forward. IDSA 
strongly supports this collaborative interagency effort, and we would welcome further 
opportunities to inform and support your work. 
 
IDSA represents over 13,000 infectious diseases (ID) physicians, scientists and other clinical and 
public health professionals dedicated to the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infectious 
diseases. Our members see firsthand the devastating impacts of AMR on medical care and 
patient outcomes, as more infections become difficult or even impossible to treat. Because the 
availability of safe and effective antimicrobials enables so much of modern medicine, increasing 
resistance jeopardizes our ability to safely provide cancer chemotherapy, organ transplantation 
and other complex surgeries, and the use of many new biologic agents that suppress the 
immune system. In addition, the pipeline of novel antimicrobials in development is extremely 
slim. These realities underscore the urgent need to combat AMR and promote appropriate 
antimicrobial use in all settings.

implementation of the proposed framework:

 
Antifungal resistance: IDSA is especially pleased to see the attention to antifungal resistance 
throughout the Framework because of its importance to public health and the unique 
challenges in preventing emerging antifungal resistance. In addition to the items already 
included in the Framework, the Interagency Drug and Pesticide Resistance and Efficacy 
Workgroup (IDPREW) should prioritize addressing other aspects of antifungal resistance 
because of pesticide use. Areas for prioritization include: the limited routine susceptibility 
testing in human and veterinary medicine, lack of surveillance for antifungal resistance 
emergence, less established breakpoints and clinical data to interpret fungal resistance testing, 
and the need for greater awareness of the increased risk of resistant fungal infections in 
immunocompromised patients.

Today learned that the 2017 summer flounder recreational fishery will face a reduction of up to 40 percent due to estimated declines in the stock and because of the recreational sector having been estimated to go over the quota in 2016. I am opposed to these changes for the following reasons.

As an avid flounder fisherman, I fully support conservation. However, I am concerned about the significant negative impacts this reduction will have on fishing participation and coastal communities. Over 10,000 jobs depend on the recreational fishery for summer flounder, which generates over $1 billion in sales.

New science from Cornell University will help form a more accurate stock assessment for summer flounder, which is desperately needed. A new benchmark stock assessment is expected in early 2017 which would replace the out-of-date assessment from 2013 that is currently be used. Given that this new information will provide a more accurate indication of the true health of the fishery, NOAA Fisheries should delay such a drastic and potentially catastrophic reduction until the new stock assessment that incorporates the science from Cornell is complete.

Knowing the history of this fishery and how important it is to the fishermen of the mid-Atlantic region, a 29 percent ABC reduction going into 2017 is unnecessary and reactionary. I recommend that NOAA approve a 16.26 million pound ABC for 2017 and 2018 and assume that the recreational sector met but did not exceed its recreational harvest of 5.42 million pounds in 2016.

The following comments were compiled by a team of staff experts from the Shedd Aquarium, 
and represent veterinary care, animal husbandry, water quality, animal behavior and facility 
maintenance, especially life support systems. We thank the Agency for this opportunity to 
comment on the proposed rule as pertains to marine mammals in the Animal Welfare Act. 
 
Compliance and Variance Requests 
 
At those times when an application for a variance request is received relative to the space 
requirements (§ 3.104) it is proposed that “…APHIS may require the submission in writing of a 
report by two recognized experts selected by the Deputy Administrator…”. We understand the 
need to minimize potential bias as evidenced by the removal of the language referring to 
“…two experts recommended by the American Association of Zoological Parks and Aquariums” 
from the existing rule. We would appreciate clarification, however, on how the experts are 
chosen, with the right of refusal should there be a perceived conflict of interest. 
 
Indoor Facilities 
While the newly created standard for ventilation is not problematic (Shedd Aquarium far 
exceeds the proposed minimum standard), the expected cost for lighting could be significant 
should specialized lamps be required (Table I. Summary of expected benefits and costs of the 
proposed rule). We feel confident our combination of natural lighting (skylights and a large 
window wall) and artificial illumination meet the intent of the proposed rule. In the 25 years 
we have maintained marine mammals in our Oceanarium we have seen no evidence of animal 
health issues related to inadequate lighting. We would appreciate clarification, however, on 
what is meant by the “full spectrum lighting” language as specified for artificial lighting. 
 
Additionally, we are concerned with how rigidly an inspector might interpret “…should 
approximate the lighting conditions encountered by the animal in its natural environment.” 
Certain marine mammals found in high latitudes, for instance, could experience prolonged 
daylight (seasonally), and even be in conflict with the proposed 6 hours of uninterrupted 
darkness each day. We do provide at least 6 hours of uninterrupted darkness for our marine 
mammals with no deleterious effects with the animals’ exposure to our local photoperiods. 
 
We believe the statement “Artificial light levels measured 1 meter above pools or decks should 
not exceed 500 lux” to be in error. 500 lux is fairly dim light. We believe the statement should 
read that artificial light levels should not be less than 500 lux. We feel comfortable that our 
lighting meets the intent of not causing “…overexposure, discomfort, or trauma to the marine 
mammals.” 
 
 
 
 
 
Outdoor facilities 
Even though Shedd Aquarium’s marine mammal pools are completely indoors we do transfer 
animals to facilities with outdoor pools. While we appreciate the intent of this proposed 
statement: “A marine mammal must not be introduced to an outdoor housing facility until it is 
acclimated to the air and water temperature ranges that it will encounter there.”, we question 
the practicality of achieving these parameters and even more, the need to do so. Even if an

 
animal were fully acclimated to the air and water temperatures of the receiving facility prior to 
its move, it is likely to experience a variety of temperature changes during the transport itself. 
We work to minimize temperature fluctuations during transport, and have trained staff who are 
in constant attendance to monitor the animal’s wellbeing during a move. We have over 25 
years of institutional experience in moving marine mammals with no temperature acclimation 
challenges. Additionally, our staff has experience working in a variety of facilities, both indoors 
and outdoors, and ranging from aquarium and marine parks to stranding centers and the Navy.

I am writing to express my disappointment with the US Department of Agriculture's decision to withdraw the 2017 final Horse Protection Act rule, which was intended to curb the rampant abuses associated with "soring" (Docket No. APHIS-2011-0009 "Horse Protection; Licensing of Designated Qualified Persons and Other Amendments"). An upgrade to the HPA is desperately needed as horses continue to suffer under a status quo that allows that industry to police itself despite the obvious conflict of interest.

According to the USDA's own review of data in recent years, there remains a persistent and vast discrepancy between violations found by industry appointed inspectors vs. those found by USDA inspectors (despite the latter attending only a small proportion of shows). Unfortunately, it is clear that the industry continues to turn a blind eye to evidence of soring.

Rather than withdraw the rule, the USDA should reissue the rulemaking until the department is prepared to move forward with a new HPA rule containing, at a minimum, all the key components of the 2017 rule. Importantly, the 2017 rule included prohibitions on ankle chains and other "action devices" associated with soring and eliminated the failed industry-run self-enforcement system.

Over 100,000 public comments were submitted in support of the 2017 rule; hundreds of members of Congress voiced their support as well. The 2017 HPA rule would achieve many of the recommendations outlined in the USDA Office of Inspector General audit and the recent National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report, both of which called for an end to the industry self-policing scheme.

In 2021, the USDA announced that the "development of a new and improved HPA proposal [was] a top regulatory priority," but the decision to withdraw the 2017 rule, coupled with the lack of progress on a new rule, suggests satisfaction with the status quo and that the USDA is not serious about fulfilling its legal duty to end soring.

You have got to be kidding! There has been no meaningful protection for these horses at all ever, and you want to withdraw the rule? Something is definitely not right here. Horses suffer every day from nails in their hooves, intentional chemical burns, chains on their ankles. You are not doing your job; you are abdicating your responsibility. Shame on you! Do the right thing; do what it takes to get a proper rule protecting these horses in place and ENFORCE IT!!! Because right now it looks like you seriously lack any will to do what needs to be done.

The wide range of abusive practices associated with soring have plagued the Tennessee walking horse industry for decades. The USDA must expeditiously issue a new HPA rule in order to protect horses from abuse.

 Mining continues to be one of the most hazardous occupations in the United States. Miners are extremely important to our country because they retrieve and allocate natural resources that we need, as a nation, to function. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 521occupational mining fatalities from the years 2003-2013 (2013). Although the number of fatalities drastically decreased from 2010-2012, the numbers are beginning to trend upwards (Centers for Disease Control, 2013). Miners go to work everyday chancing death. Under the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act, miners are promised to be alerted of unsafe or unhealthy conditions in the mine (United States Department of Labor, 1977). Because there are not tight standards on examination and reporting regarding working conditions in mines, miners are essentially not protected under this act. 
 The proposed rule to amend the current standards is crucial in regard to decreasing mining fatalities and accidents. As of 2013 there were over 13,000 active mines in the united states(CDC, 2013). The new rule standards state that the mine be checked once at the beginning of every shift, to ensure safety and identify hazards (United States Department of Labor, 2016). In addition to examination standards, the MSHA also sets forth reporting standards. The MSHA proposes that all hazards be reported and documented along with the health risks associated and corrective action taken (United States Department of Labor, 2016). By adding these two aspects to the examination standards, many hazards, accidents, and fatalities can be avoided. Therefore, healthcare costs in the mining community may decrease. The reporting aspect is where the most public health benefit will derive from. The more aware the miners are of the hazards and the health risks associated with them, the more cautious and willing they may be to report a hazard. Occupational health is a strong component of public health, and if occupational health is significantly changed, then the public health of that community is significantly changed.
 With implementation of a new rule, there will always be resistance and a degree of non-compliance in the early stages. However, I do not see any negative impacts that would arise due to the implementation of this new rule. The rule is designed to improve health and safety through simple measures and minor changes. The implementation and compliance with the new standards will only bring about positive change regarding health and safety of the miners. However, a measure included in the new standards may offer a degree of inaccuracy secondary to the quality and accuracy of the reporting. Some days they may forget to document a hazard, or be document the hazard inaccurately or not in enough detail. The point of the documentation is to have the miners be aware of their risks. If someone is not documenting properly, the post implementation evaluation of the new standards might be skewed. 
 The mining community are the largest stakeholders that are going to be affected by the proposed new standards. The miners deserve environmental justice. They deserve to be protected when they go to work and to be aware of all the risks associated with their chosen career. If we do not protect our miners and place standards on how to evaluate working conditions, we could see a decrease in the amount of employees in mines. As mentioned earlier, we need these miners to gather these natural resources from the earth to sustain life on our planet. 
 In summary, health should not be compromised due to your choice of occupation. All miners need to be aware of hazards and safe working practices. I strongly advise the implementation of these new standards to ensure we are doing everything we can to protect our miners, as we had promised them initially under the Mine Safety and Health Act. I think what the United States Space Force (USSF) is doing is setting a bad precedent for the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS). The USSF has requested permission for incidental takings for a five-year period, however the end of this period does not mean the end of their research using rocket and missile launching. Takings of pinnipeds will continue past the five-year request, in such that it will need to be requested again, and maybe again after that. There must be a clear mitigation plan with an end goal of eliminating any potential takings to the pinniped species. USSF gave a short adaptive management plan and has extensive research, however it is more of a hopeful outlook, rather than a concrete plan. The consequence of continuous requests such as this is that it normalizes them and takes away from the reason these regulations were put into place. Getting special permission is always a dangerous game, especially regarding the environment. 

 According to the NOAA Fisheries Office of Protected Resources, “Activities with the greatest potential to harass by noise include: seismic airguns, ship and aircraft noise, high energy sonars, and explosive detonations” (page 2, Incidental Take Authorizations). This means that it is not unusual for the USSF to request an incidental taking of this nature, however, a five-year request is redundant if it will continue to be requested. It is imperative for the USSF to find a way that either absorbs or reflects the sound of sonic booms away from seals. Despite not doing substantial harm to them, it should be of importance to minimize or potentially eliminate any take to the pinnipeds. If these pinnipeds were humans, they would contact officials to complain, but they do not have a voice for themselves. We must treat these marine mammals as we would treat ourselves as they do not have the voice we were given. 

Overall, a factor that is often overlooked are factors we cannot see. A study of physical response from the pinniped species is not enough to prove minimal harm. I admire the amount of research and attention the USSF gave to including biological effects in their research, and I see that they acknowledge there is harm in these disturbances. However, “high noise can result in stress and contribute to cardiovascular, circulatory problems and digestive problems; psychological disturbances and symptoms such as nervousness, sleeplessness, reduced performance and changes in social behavior in the infected” (ILO 2006). These are factors that over time will result in adaptations within individuals. It causes a response from the endocrine system and repetitive tests will cause the release of stress hormones in the body.

possible applying the definition of “public charge” in the law and limiting it to only those 

likely to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence.

right. Therefore, AWHONN strongly supports policy initiatives that guarantee access to such 

health care services for all people including immigrants. Individuals who fear being

treatment.

populations.

unwanted outcome is to exclude all Medicaid benefits from the public charge determination. 

Public assistance does not lead to dependence on government aid. People’s situations change, 

often suddenly, and public assistance may help them to get back onto their feet. In addition, 

pregnant parents, whose pregnancies may not have been planned, need prenatal and

Action by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to support industry-wide sodium reduction is crucial for Americans’ health, and I support the agency’s efforts with its recommendations draft guidance on Phase II voluntary sodium reduction targets for commercially processed, packaged, and prepared foods. 

We also need to drastically reduce sugar. 

However, the FDA must be more aggressive with its sodium reduction efforts. Given the life-saving potential of sodium reduction, the FDA should set more aggressive Phase II targets to more quickly reduce consumption to recommended levels. 

The FDA should also do more to hold food companies accountable for meeting these targets. Specifically, the agency’s monitoring and evaluation of Phase I and II targets must be timely, transparent, and methodologically rigorous. The FDA should also secure public commitments from industry to meet these targets and publicize companies’ progress to highlight those that are leading and those that are falling behind. Finally, if the agency’s evaluations find that industry is failing to meet the voluntary targets, the FDA should consider setting mandatory targets. 
 
The FDA has an obligation to protect Americans’ health by ensuring that industry reduces sodium. I urge the FDA to act quickly on these recommendations to ensure a safer U.S. food supply.

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

I respectfully submit this comment to strongly oppose USCIS's NPRM, USCIS-2020-0019; RIN 1615-AC61. This misguided rule, which dramatically alters the way in which H-1B registrations are selected for the annual H-1B statutory cap, is inconsistent with Congressional intent, is in violation of the statute, and will undermine our nation's pipeline of global talent we need to drive innovation and foster economic growth.

I am an immigration attorney who represents small businesses and hospitals in H-1B visa petitions to bring in the foreign staff they need to provide world class care and service.

This Proposed Rule is a Clear Violation of the Statute and Congressional Intent:

The H-1B program was established by Congress to provide an avenue for employers to hire a foreign worker in a specialty occupation. This proposed rule is a clear violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which prioritizes the selection of H-1B cap-subject petitions in the "order in which they are filed" and does not limit who is selected for the H-1B cap to those employers who pay the most. USCIS lacks the statutory authority to make such a change and cannot use the statute's silence as an invitation to adopt criteria, such as wage level or skill level, to prioritize the selection of H-1B cap subject visas. 

This Proposed Rule is Based on a False Premise That Salary Alone Equates with Value: 

This proposal, which is based on the false premise that individuals who earn more in their profession contribute more to the economy or society, is yet another misguided and illegal attempt by the Trump administration to weaken our legal immigration and promote falsities about the workers who, contrary to what this rule implies, strengthen our economy.

If implemented, this rule will have a direct and negative impact on U.S. employers and college-educated foreign-born professionals by dramatically reducing access to the H-1B visa program for early-career professionals, including those completing Master's or Doctoral degrees at U.S. colleges and universities. Indeed, USCIS has acknowledged that if this new regulation is implemented, no individuals who are paid a Level 1 wage would be selected to submit a H-1B cap-subject petition for the annual H-1B cap. These proposed changes would effectively eliminate the H-1B program as an available visa option for new graduates seeking employment in an entry-level position.

Wages alone are not a true measure of someone's value. There are many highly skilled workers who work in professions that historically pay less. For example, medical researchers and scientists often have master's or even PhD degrees. Despite this advanced education and the important research they undertake, depending on where they're located, they may only make $40k to $60k per year, particularly for those researchers and scientists who are recent graduates.

USCIS Should Refrain From Implementing this Rule For the FY2022 H-1B Cap Filing Season:

Many U.S. employers and immigration attorneys start preparing for the H-1B cap filing season months in advance, in some cases as early as August depending on the industry. Any changes by USCIS to the H-1B cap filing process this late in the year would have an adverse impact on U.S. employers, immigration attorneys and individuals, as hiring decisions and filing processes and procedures have already been put in place by many employers and immigration law firms. Thus, if USCIS finalizes this illegal and misguided rule, USCIS must refrain from implementing it for the upcoming FY2022 H-1B cap filings season in order to allow U.S. businesses, immigration attorneys and individuals sufficient time to adapt to the new wage-based selection process.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

EPA is taking comment on establishing a separate subcategory and acid gas standard for existing EGUs that fire eastern bituminous coal refuse. Ebensburg Power Company supports the creation of this subcategory and alternate acid gas hazardous air pollutant (HAP) standard as proposed by the Agency. Ebensburg Power Company utilizes fluidized bed combustion (FBC) boiler technology to convert coal refuse to electricity. Ebensburg Power Company agrees with the Agencys MACT Floor Analysis and Beyond the MACT Floor Analysis for Subcategory of Existing Eastern Bituminous Coal Refuse-Fired EGUs Under Consideration, and specifically requests an acid gas HAP standard with SO2 as a surrogate at a limit of 0.6 lb/mmBTU averaged over a rolling 30-day period. 
Ebensburg Power Company (EPC) has historically been a plant that has predominantly fired greater than 98% refuse coal with exception being natural gas used for boiler starts and load stabilization during upset conditions. Reducing stack emissions to meet a 0.2 lb/mmbtu limit would require two simplistic approaches to either capture more sulfur in the combustion process and/or alternatively to input less sulfur in the combustion process. 
 The first approach of capturing more sulfur would require either increasing limestone feed rates or secondly installing a post-combustion polishing system. The design of the plant was for a 90% capture rate to achieve 0.60 to 1.0 lb/mmbtu SO2 using pulverized limestone while firing coal refuse. Trying to over capture to reach a 0.2 lb/mmbtu SO2 emission rate with a fuel made up of locally available refuse coal sources would first max out the sorbent feed rate equipment capability; the plant would then need to reduce fuel firing rates to meet the 0.2 lb/mmbtu limit. The combination of increased limestone and reduced generation would result in production costs higher than power sales revenues and assure plant closure. 
Alternatively, adding on back-end control equipment such as a dry sorbent injection system would boost the sulfur capture, but the capex and operating costs increases would not be supported by power sales revenues and the plant could not operate with a profit.
The second approach of inputting less sulfur in the process would require either reducing plant output or fuel switching to fire a lower sulfur content fuel blend with something less than 100% coal waste. That could be a combination of a small amount of natural gas but to a greater extent a higher percentage of higher-grade bituminous coal. If low sulfur coal were added to the typical EPC refuse fuel blend with the goal of reducing the inlet sulfur and maintaining a minimum 75% refuse heat input portion, the fuel sulfur is only lowered to 2.65lb/mmbtu based on current fuel sources. Even with significant load reduction with the cost per megawatt with 25% high grade coal would be $48.17. This cost increase would result in station closure. 
EPC and similar facilities were constructed and continue to operate for the purpose of combusting coal refuse. Fuel Switching is not a viable compliance option for EPC relative to the MATS standard from both design impact and financial perspective.

Comment for Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OLEM-2020-0107

In the docket, there is a request for comment regarding what Coal Combustion Residual (CCR) requirement may not be necessary to comply to legacy CCR impoundments given the legacy CCR surface impoundments are no longer receiving waste. Since a legacy impoundment is defined as an impoundment that is no longer in operation and has not received waste since October 19, 2015, according to the exclusion provided in the Hazardous and Solid Waste Management System; Disposal of Coal Combustion Residuals from Electric Utilities (40 CFR, Part 257, Subpart D), the location requirements presented in § 257.60 should be waived for legacy CCR impoundments. This waiver is appropriate as the location restrictions were enacted to ensure that new or actively operating CCR impoundments facilities are not constructed in locations that increase the likelihood that a release of CCR from the impoundment into the environment occurs due to a foreseeable incident and/or geological process. By providing this waiver, there will be a mechanism for current property owners who may not have operated or contributed to the legacy CCR impoundment to avoid a prohibitively expensive removal action. However, as the CCR had already been deposited into the ground at a potentially risky location, the risk for a release of CCR must be assessed to evaluate if the CCR can be managed as a closed impoundment when it is located within a prohibited location identified in § 257.60. 

In order to be able to manage the legacy CCR impoundment in place, the owner should be required to perform an investigation to evaluate if the legacy CCR impoundment could be left in place and that their placement within a prohibited location does not increase the risk of a release when compared to legacy CCR impoundments constructed in non-prohibited location. In order to utilize this option, the data collected during the investigation should demonstrate the conditions listed in § 257.100 (b)(1) have been met by the existing legacy CCR impoundment construction, that the CCR within the legacy CCR impoundment comply with the free liquids requirement presented in § 257.100 (2)(i), and if detection monitoring completed in accordance with § 257.94 can demonstrate the CCR within the legacy impoundment has not leached or is not actively contributing the constituents listed in appendix III to the groundwater and/or surface waters in excess of the regulatory limits provided. If these conditions are met, the owner of the CCR should be allowed to proceed with the post closure requirements presented in § 257.104 and be allowed to maintain the landfill without further modification of the legacy CCR impoundments. If any of the aforementioned criteria are not met, then the owner of the legacy CCR compound should proceed with closure in accordance with § 257.102 or § 257.103.

The impact of Brucellosis on the import of dogs from countries with a high prevalence is a crucial concern that demands our attention. Brucellosis is a highly contagious bacterial infection that can spread among dogs and humans, posing a significant public health risk. To mitigate this risk, it becomes imperative to implement strict measures to prevent the spread of this disease by importing dogs.

One effective strategy is to focus on importing dogs at a young age, ideally under six months. This approach is rooted in sound reasoning. Dogs under six months of age are less likely to have engaged in sexual activity, reducing the chances of them being carriers of sexually transmitted infections like Brucellosis. This preventive measure addresses a key factor in the transmission of the disease, thereby safeguarding both the imported dogs and the local dog population.

Importing dogs over six months of age, especially those that have not been spayed or neutered, creates a potential challenge. Unaltered street dogs, prevalent in some regions, tend to become sexually active around this age. This increases the risk of Brucellosis transmission through sexual activity. By focusing on importing younger dogs, we minimize this risk and create a healthier foundation for them to adapt to their new homes while reducing the potential for disease transmission.

With the potential ruling of import restrictions from countries like Mexico to dogs over the age of 6 months, we may be increasing the chance of importing Brucellosis into the US. I therefore ask that we strike this ruling from the proposed rule.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I am commenting on the Proposed Rule "Clarification of When Products Made or Derived From Tobacco Are Regulated as Drugs, Devices, or Combination Products; Amendments to Regulations Regarding 'Intended Uses'"(Docket No. FDA-2015-N-2002)

The FDA is requesting comments on a proposed rule about "Clarification of When Products Made or Derived From Tobacco Are Regulated as Drugs, Devices, or Combination Products; Amendments to Regulations Regarding 'Intended Uses.'"

By way of background, FDA considers nicotine-containing products to either be pharmaceuticals (regulated as a drug, device, or combination product) or tobacco products. Pharmaceuticals are subject to a lengthy and expensive approvals process, and any e-cigarette products treated as pharmaceuticals would be immediately removed from the market as unapproved drugs/devices. Regulation as a tobacco product is problematic as well1, but regardless, it is imperative that if e-cigarettes are to be marketed as tobacco products, manufacturers2 be permitted to make reasonable claims in their marketing and not be hamstrung by FDA's over-zealous regulation. Prohibiting manufacturers from providing honest and helpful information is bad for consumers and bad for public health.

Ostensibly, FDA is doing this to help avoid consumer confusion. We believe that this will actually increase confusion and will dramatically limit the ability of consumers to make informed decisions about the products they use.

To help you understand the effects of this proposed rule ("Intended Use Regulation"), manufacturers would be prevented from making any substantive claims about the value of e-cigarettes for smoking cessation or suggesting that they are less harmful than smoking.3 Urging consumers to make the switch from smoking to vaping is potentially problematic if FDA determines that it suggests an intended use of smoking cessation. FDA is even going so far as to invite comments on whether manufacturers should be able to make claims such as "satisfying smoking alternative," "provides all the pleasure of smoking, "get your nicotine fix," or "provides smokers the same delight, physical and emotional feelings" as smoking."4 

The Intended Use Regulation would not be limited to statements contained on labels, packaging, and traditional advertisements. The FDA is casting a wide net. For example, even posting a consumer testimonial on a company's website would be potentially problematic since FDA could use that as "evidence" of intended use.

I suggest water workers should honor the intent of the 2011/2015 HHS recommendation to lower the optimal fluoride levels from a range to 0.7 - 1.2 ppm to a single limit of 0.7 ppm for the purpose of reducing the incidence of dental fluorosis among our population by setting their operational target below 0.7 ppm in order not to exceed 0.7 ppm. 

FACT: Dental fluorosis is a lagging indicator of fluoride exposure during early childhood and a leading indicator of increased dental and other health expenses in adulthood. 

When about one third of the American population was fluoridated circa 1970, we saw a dental fluorosis rate in American teens of 22% in 1986-87. When close to three quarters of the population was fluoridated circa 2000, we see a dental fluorosis rate in American teens of 60%. Worse, one in five of todays teens have the brown stains of moderate to severe dental fluorosis on at least two brittle fluorosed teeth which not only causes social distress in many, but will also result in costly veneers and crowns. Beyond this, we know that dental fluorosis is associated with increased learning disabilities, bone fractures and kidney disease - all of which have dramatically increased over the last 20 years and which are also known ill effects of fluoride ingestion. 

The maximum legal limit for fluoride in drinking water in communities that have opted for fluoridation should be 0.7 ppm. Period. Honor the intent of the recommendation to eliminate the range that included 1 ppm and respect the consumers by setting operational targets of 0.5 or 0.6 ppm in an effort not to exceed 0.7 ppm. 

I further suggest that Water Workers should openly advise their communities of the overall risks of fluoridation policy which not only include other health effects denied by fluoridationist organizations, but also to contaminants in fluoridation products not regulated by NSF and environmental impact on their communities.

The water supply system of this city is not a gigantic medicine bottle into which one may combine ingredients and shake well before using. We control the concentration of fluoride going into the water at the beginning. But no one knows what concentration will reach the households, except that it will be different all over the city. - Arthur C. Ford, Water Commissioner of the City of New York (1957)

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Consumers deserve to know the truth about how animals that they and their families might consume, are raised and treated. I myself am a vegan because I cannot in good conscience support such a cruel industry.

Thank you for considering my request.
