The New York City Brownfield Partnership (the Partnership) is submitting this comment to EPA's 
proposed rule (87 FR 14224-14227, March 14, 2022) and direct final rule amending 40 CFR Section 
312.11 (87 FR 14174- 14177, March 14, 2022) proposing to and amending its All Appropriate Inquiries 
Rule (AAI) to reference the ASTM El527- 21 "Standard Practice for Environmental Site Assessments: 
Phase I Environmental Site Assessment Process" (El527-21) and allowing it use to satisfy the 
requirements of AAI. 1 
The Partnership is a NYS incorporated nonprofit organization whose members include environmental 
consulting firms, environmental lawyers, environmental remediation contracting organizations, 
brownfield redevelopment organizations, and community-based organizations in New York City. Its 
mission includes advancing public awareness and understanding of benefits, opportunities, and best 
practices of brownfield redevelopment, promoting excellence in brownfield redevelopment by honoring 
successful brownfield projects as well as fostering collaborative relationships among brownfield 
developers, property owners, government agencies, and community groups. 
The Partnership recommends that the proposed rule and direct final rule remove the reference to the 
superseded ASTM E 1527-13 standard and explicitly disallow the continued use of El 527-13 to satisfy 
AAI. 
Allowing ASTM E 1527-13 to remain as an acceptable alternative for complying with AAI will create 
chaos and confusion in the marketplace. El527-21 represents what the industry now considers to be 
"good commercial and customary practice". 
One of the important clarifications ofE1527-21 is the clarification on the scope of historical research that 
should be conducted for a phase 1. Comprehensive historical research is critical for brownfield 
development so that developers understand their potential risks. Allowing El527-13 to continue to 
satisfy AAI may lead to reports that provide inadequate historical research that E1527-2 l says no longer 
complies with current good commercial and customary practice. 
1 The New York City Brownfield Partnership respectfully requests that the comment previously submitted to EPA 
on March 22, 2022 be deleted from the record and replaced in its entirety by the instant comment.

 
Another important feature of E 1527-21 is the clarification about Controlled Recognized Environmental 
Conditions (CREC). Retaining E1527-13 will cause sites to be erroneously identified as having 
Recognized Environmental Conditions (REC) instead of CRECs which will cause many brownfield sites 
to be unduly stigmatized since many developers and lenders are wary of sites with RECs. 
Moreover, allowing two standards with differing requirements to satisfy AAI will cause property owners 
to become confused over how to comply with AAI and could unnecessarily inject further uncertainty 
about liability concerns over brownfield sites, which already have a host of challenges. 
When EPA recognized E1527-13, the agency removed the reference to the superseded El527-05 (see 79 
FR 60087- 60090, October 6, 2014). Accordingly, the Partnership respectfully requests EPA follow the 
process it previously used by withdrawing the direct final rule and issuing a new proposed rule 
recognizing that that El527-21 may be used to satisfy AAI and removing the reference to El527-13 for 
commercial real estate transactions after the effective date of the amended rule. 
Sincerely,

address the lack of equitable access to Vocational Rehabilitation (VR). Historically, there has

Indigenous and Native American persons, Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, and other

research on best practices to bring more equity to VR accessibility for all backgrounds.

Problem Summary

in our workforce, but also supporting all voices. “According to the study, 83 percent of all
survey participants preferred race concordance and believed it was important for providers to
be of the same race or ethnicity as their patients” (Department of Education). This statement
is a clear indication that we need to address race and ethnicity in the workforce to improve
the quality of support for underrepresented patients and workers. This leads to lack of race
concordance between provider and patient which can lessen the customer satisfaction. There
has been a clear indication reading this proposed policy by the Department of Education that
commonality of race leads to improved quality for underserved communities. Additionally as
technology advances, if we don’t begin to address this issue now it could lead to a greater
disparity and negative quality of experience for underserved populations.

Problem Analysis
In analyzing the problems summary an important question brought to attention, which is what
lead to “Improving the Delivery of Vocational Rehabilitation Services to, and the
Employment Outcomes of, Individuals with Disabilities from Underserved Populations”
(Department of Education). Several things that come to mind are historical racism and
discrimination within the US that has stunt the development of workplace diversity. Before
we can address the equity for others, we must address the inequity within ourselves. I have
black friends who have been discriminated against because of their appearance, specifically
their hair. In that particular case, if you want more representation for race concordance you
have to be accepting and understanding of workers who don’t look like you. Additionally,
certain communities are not provided the same quality of care as other areas. It goes to ask
the question to those in power perhaps not what, but who is their priority. We see this even in

rapid transport for underserved communities. Even during COVID-19, it was communities
that already had resources that would have access to getting vaccinated quickly. Vocational
rehabilitation would be distributed within well resourced communities before it reached
underserved communities.

only recommendation is that the short and long term implication should be clearly defined.

more flexibility because addressing historical disparities faced by underserved communities
takes time. I propose that instead of a five-year period there should be an interval of checking
in to see the effectiveness of providing training and technical assistance to the minimum of

I am a Professor in the Department of Zoology at the University of Otago, an elected Fellow of the 

Royal Society of New Zealand, and a member of the IUCN (World Conservation Union) Conservation 

Translocation Specialist Group (CTSG), in which capacity I was head of the CTSG Bird Section for 10 

years. I am a co-author of the IUCN’s 2013 Reintroduction Guidelines, and have participated in and 

advised on species reintroduction projects in New Zealand, Australia, Europe, North America, and the 

Middle East, over the last 30 years. 

I have reviewed the Proposed rule to establish an experimental population of sihek on Palmyra Atoll as 

part of ongoing efforts for the conservation of this critically endangered species, and in the following I 

offer my comments, and my strong support, for this important project. 

The sihek (Guam kingfisher, Todiramphus cinnamominus) is as endangered as a bird species can get, 

officially designated as “Extinct in the Wild” following its extirpation, largely as a result of predation 

by invasive brown tree snake, from Guam some 30 years ago. Sihek are island endemics, once found 

nowhere else apart from the island of Guam, but now reduced to some 150 individuals across fewer 

than 30 AZA institutions. Captive populations cannot be maintained indefinitely without inadvertent 

selection for undesirable traits, so while the sihek studbook management has worked to sustain genetic 

and demographic health of the captive populations, there is a slow decline in total population size and 

increasing risk of inbreeding depression that could compromise future restoration efforts. There is 

some urgency therefore, to enhance population size and diversity. 

At present sihek habitat on Guam is compromised by the continued presence of brown tree snakes. 

Under the IUCN CTSG Guidelines, reintroductions should not take place until the original cause of 

extirpation has been addressed, therefore release of sihek back onto Guam is not currently possible. 

Nevertheless, good progress is being made towards the eventual eradication of brown tree snake so the 

future restoration of sihek to Guam remains a goal. However, any reintroduction is a complex process 

carrying a risk of failure. The development of the science of reintroduction biology over the last 20 

years has indicated that reintroduction success can be markedly improved through the development of 

species-specific translocation procedures that refine the stages of transport, release, and post-release 

monitoring and care. The very best way to develop and refine translocation procedures is through 

experimental releases to create trial populations where management options to enhance survival rates, 

productivity, and population persistence can be tested and compared. The current proposal aims to do 

just that through the creation of an experimental population of sihek. 

 Sihek is endemic to Guam and with Guam unsuitable currently for sihek reintroduction it is necessary 

to consider creation of an experimental population through translocation outside the indigenous range. 

The IUCN recognises such conservation introductions as legitimate species management actions. The 

proposal is to introduce an experimental population of sihek to Palmyra Atoll, an extra-limital site that 

has been deemed to hold suitable areas of habitat through a robust site assessment process.

My comment highlights the importance of accessibility, and how it plays a necessary role in effectively protecting consumers. 

1. Mobile Websites and Mobile Applications 
Ancillary fee disclosures should be required on both mobile websites and mobile apps. In particular, there should not be any difference in disclosure of ancillary fees between mobile websites and mobile apps. Mobile apps, especially when compared to mobile versions of websites on mobile phones, are a significantly more accessible interface. Text is properly formatted onto screens, and app layout allows for easier use and navigation. Mobile versions tend to minimize text, and almost nothing is adapted for screen size, which creates a difficult navigation experience. Accessibility is a crucial part of consumer protection and ensuring everyone receives necessary information in wholly accessible formats is critical to well-regulated and protective systems. 
2. In-person or Telephone Disclosures of Airline Ancillary Service Rees 
Similar to my previous discussion of mobile website versus mobile app disclosure differences, telephone or in-person disclosure is another accessibility issue. Consumers should not be given differing disclosures (i.e., some receiving a full disclosure of ancillary fees while others do not receive any disclosures). In other words, I do not believe the described alternative option (of merely explaining that there are disclosures that can be accessed online) should be implemented. While I acknowledge the Department would only allow for this option if the website’s disclosure is fully accessible, just vaguely stating that there could be ancillary fees that one would have to search for themselves not only seems unnecessary (i.e., putting burden on consumers when it should be on sellers), but it also goes against the very general purpose of this proposed rule—to be transparent about ancillary airline fees. 
3. Seat Assignment Policies and Fees for Families Traveling with Young Children 
Airline carriers and ticket agents should disclose whether there are adjacent seats for parents/guardians to sit with their children, and whether there are ancillary fees for adjacent seating. If there are no adjacent seats, that deficiency should be noted and reported to consumers, so they are not misled. Further, the Department should be more prescriptive in their required disclosures for ancillary family seating fees. As seen earlier in the proposed rule, the Department proposed a requirement for airline carriers to disclose baggage and carry-on fees at an early or first point of search for a flight. This proposed requirement should apply to family seating. Again, there is no reason for one group of individuals to fill out more information about themselves, then receive necessary information about ancillary fees, when other groups will likely receive all relevant (to themselves) information for their travel without inputting any detail.

I' support the USDA's proposed Organic Livestock & Poultry Standards rule, which would improve the welfare of the more than 186 million animals raised under the USDA Organic label. Animals deserve adequate space, meaningful access to the outdoors, and the ability to engage in natural behaviors. By requiring a higher standard of care, USDA can improve the health and well-being of animals, the environment and consumers. 
I believe USDA's organic label should signify higher welfare standards than conventional animal production, and in fact, consumers have expected higher-welfare conditions under the organic label for over 15 years. Yet contrary to these perceptions, the organic program does not currently provide clear requirements for space, outdoor access and many other benchmarks of welfare. 

Consumers pay premium prices for organic products from animals raised in conditions nearly indistinguishable from factory farms. The lack of clear standards undermines consumer confidence in the organic label and undercuts organic farmers who already raise animals more humanely. As a mother who is deeply concerned about the effects of trauma on children and as an American who believes that our country must hold ourselves to a high bar on treatment of all children, I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I am an A&P/IA who has specialized in the maintenance, repair and restoration of tube and fabric Piper aircraft for almost 30 years. Having worked with the FAA, ACO and the Small Aircraft Directorate on issues effecting Aging Aircraft in the past I have to say that I have been very disappointed in the communication with the type clubs on this rudder issue. When you eat, sleep and breath these aircraft and spend lots of time insuring that they are flown, maintained and restored in the safest possible condition you hope you would be contacted when these type of issues come up as I personally have in the past. Some of these previous correspondences have resulted in SAIB, AD revisions and others were just general knowledge. It proved to me personally that this was not “us against them”. Nothing to do with this issue has made me feel that way.

Piper built in excess of 50k airplanes with this rudder. I have read the ACS dated 9-4-2020, NTSB AIR-22-02 and the NTSB Aviation Investigation Final Reports for the aircraft listed in the preceding documents. Having maintained, repaired and rebuilt fabric covered aircraft for almost 30 years I have discovered there are lots of causes of failures. I am curious as to the history of the aircraft involved, modifications, history of repairs, etc. Way more questions than answers in the data provided.

Since this issue came up almost 4 years ago I have investigated several ways to both verify the integrity of the rudder and to reinforce it. A simple fixture can be fabricated to fit over the top of the rudder to attach a fish scale to or even a torque wrench to allow a pull test to a minimum standard. Also I have installed a 3/4”x.035” wall 4130 steel tube into several rudders to verify that it is both doable and to check the tightness of fit. It is doable and tight. Could even be held to the outside tube via Cherry rivets. 

I would be curious to know the load on the rudder on any given model. Is a J3 with a 65 hp engine even close to the load put on the rudder of a PA12 with 180 hp, on floats with no ventral fin? Again, more questions than answers. 

This proposed AD will take years to comply with given the availability of rudders and experienced personnel to do the cover work. I would hope that the FAA takes all things into account and realizes that 2 or 3 incidence in a fleet of at least 30,000 aircraft is a probability of .0001 to .000066.

Please do not allow use of mobile wireless devices for voice calls on aircraft. Passengers do NOT deserve to be subjected to another's endless prattle during a flight, since the passengers not using the device are a captive audience with no means of escaping the unwelcome public conversation. While I am generally supportive of the proposed rule, I am concerned that it does not go far enough to meet the Department of Transportation’s goals, and I hope some revisions are considered to make the rule stronger.

 For example, one of the requirements of the proposed rule is that airlines would have to disclose “change fees” to customers at the time of ticket purchase. While I am supportive of transparency when it comes to pricing, I think that airlines may have the ability to easily circumvent this rule. For example, Southwest Airlines (the airline I fly most frequently) advertises four different fare types when selecting a ticket. To find out what each fare offers, the customer needs to click on the fare, which then provides a table of “Fare Benefits.” Each fare advertises “No fees to change or cancel.” But there are small superscript numbers around that statement, meaning the customer needs to go locate what they mean. After closing the “Fare Benefits” table and scrolling down to the bottom of the page, the customer can find the small print. There, the customer is informed that “If you need to change an upcoming flight itinerary, you’ll only pay the cost in fare difference.”

 While Southwest may not be charging a “change fee” customers are still left guessing how much they will need to pay if they have some type of change in their schedule. Last-minute flights are often expensive, and there is no transparency in the pricing. As a result, customers can end up paying high prices to change flights, although there is technically not a separate “change fee.” This is something I experienced earlier this year. I needed to fly home two days earlier than originally planned on Southwest. I ended up paying $250 to change my flight, more than the original round trip cost. Although there may not have been a “change fee” I still felt the price was unreasonable, but I had no choice other than to pay it.

 Requiring clear disclosure of baggage fees is a great consumer friendly requirement. Although I regularly fly Southwest, which does not charge for checked bags, I have flown on other airlines, and have been frustrated by the lack of transparency when it comes to the cost of checking a bag. When booking a flight on Alaska Airlines, there is at least a link at the bottom of the page which says “Baggage fees may apply.” Clicking that link opens a dialog box, which contains another link for customers to click on, which then informs customers about the price to check a bag. Delta Airlines, however, just has small text at the bottom of the page informing customers that “Final baggage fees will be assessed and charged at time of check in.” The proposed rule will instead require airlines to provide this important information to customers prior to purchasing a ticket, which I think is a great change. More transparency always benefits consumers.

 Finally, I want to note that over the course of the pandemic the federal government has given the airline industry more than $50,000,000,000.00 in relief money. At the height of the pandemic air travel fell by more than 90%. Now that Americans are starting to fly again, they are starting to wonder what their $50 billion bought them. So far, from what I have personally experienced, there has been subpar customer service compared to the flying experience before 2020. Airlines have cut thousands of flights from their schedules, leaving customers with fewer options to choose from. Providing transparency when it comes to pricing will at least help consumers make informed decisions when booking a flight, even if they currently have fewer options to choose from.

 Other than my concerns about the ability to get around the change fee, I am supportive of this rule. I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. The regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law.
Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children
The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The federal government has repeatedly demonstrated that it lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I strongly oppose the alterations to the process of designating critical habitat that are proposed in this rule. These changes expand the USFWS's ability to exclude areas essential to the conservation of threatened and endangered species from designation as critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act. Among other problematic provisions, it states that the USFWS must exclude such areas if the economic benefits of using the land for development, such as for oil and gas extraction, grazing, and logging, are greater than those of protecting the area for wildlife (except in cases where extinction will result). These changes would grant economic considerations outsized weight in decisions about habitat, which is inconsistent with the ESA's intent that species' recovery needs should be prioritized and should be determined using the best available science.

Designation of critical habitat is a vital tool available under the Endangered Species Act to help conserve species. Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors. 

The exclusion of areas that do not meet the new standards for the designation of critical habitat could significantly decrease the amount of habitat that can be protected. This would represent a severe setback to conservation, because critical habitat is vital for stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species that have protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species without it. Designation of critical habitat is more important than ever as species face increasing habitat loss due to conversion, pollution, and climate change.

I am an attorney in Washington State. I am a former chairperson of the Washington State Bar Association's Animal Law Section. My comments are my own and do not represent the views of either the Bar Association or the Animal Law Section. It is clear that the USFWS is not working for the American people or for animals, but for private interests. Apparently, the goal is to eviscerate the Endangered Species Act. 

Agencies such as USFWS are commonly referred to as "The Fourth Branch of Government" because they are totally unaccountable to anyone. Sadly, USFWS uses its power and authority in ways that diminish protections for endangered species.

Americans recognize the ESA's vital role in conserving beloved wildlife species, and a 2018 survey found that four out of five Americans support the law. At a time of unprecedented wildlife extinction and habitat destruction, we should be working to strengthen--not weaken--the ESA. For these reasons, I urge the USFWS to withdraw this proposed rule.

committed to assuring the safety of chemicals used in our homes, workplaces and the many products to which 

our families and children are exposed each day. We took a leadership role during the TSCA legislative process,

Our comments provide cross-cutting recommendations to improve the scoping documents and upcoming risk

 Recommendations to Improve Scoping Documents and Risk Evaluations 

The seven chemicals are among a group of 20 substances that EPA designated as high priority under TSCA on 

December 20, 2019. High-priority designation triggers EPA’s obligation under TSCA to conduct a risk evaluation 

under TSCA. Scoping documents are the first step in that process. Under TSCA section 6(b)(4)(D), their role is 

to provide stakeholders and the public with a clear roadmap to the risk evaluation by describing the “hazards, 

exposures, conditions of use, and the potentially exposed or susceptible subpopulations the Administrator 

expects to consider.” Section 702.41(c) of EPA’s 2017 risk evaluation framework rule elaborates on the 

elements scoping documents must contain. If draft scopes do not contain these elements, the public will have 

limited ability to comment on the data and analytic approach EPA will use to conduct its risk evaluations. 

Measured against TSCA and EPA regulations, the 20 draft scoping documents are woefully inadequate. As we 

underscored in our May 13, 2020 comments, they lack many required elements, including a description of 

human health hazards from acute and chronic exposures to the high priority chemicals, the results of EPA’s 

systematic reviews of available data, and the Potentially Exposed or Susceptible Subpopulations (PESS) that 

EPA intends to address. Moreover, the scopes fail to explain how EPA will analyze exposure and hazard data 

and integrate different lines of evidence for the chemical at hand. Instead, they consist mainly of boilerplate

As an immigration attorney and a US citizen, I strongly oppose this proposed rule.

1) Data storage for such massive amounts of data is expensive, as too is security for such data. For frequent travelers, this data would be reduplicated an unnecessary number of times.

2) Such data is extremely personal and vulnerable to hacker or ransomware attack. Collecting and storing this data runs the risk of such data being stolen and used by bad actors or sold to private corporations. Were such data collected for healthcare purposes, accidental disclosure of such data would be a severe HIPAA violation; in this context, aliens would have no recourse in the event that their extremely private data were compromised. This is even more severe for the collection of DNA data.

3) Collection of such data would lengthen travel times for all travelers, hurting the economy of the United States and causing delays for not only all aliens but all persons traveling with aliens.

4) The proposed collection of DNA data constitutes a massive invasion of privacy, and will have a disproportionate impact on the following communities in the following ways:
- Citizens and LPRs will face barriers to sponsoring fully qualified aliens due to fears about the collection of their data.
- Citizens and LPRs with sensitive medical conditions such as HIV that can be detected through DNA testing will feel unsafe sponsoring their family members due to concerns about their private medical conditions being outed, whether to their family members whom they are sponsoring or to the immigration officers who will have access to the data. This will lead to discriminatory impact on persons with disabilities in access to the immigration system.
- Aliens with sensitive medical conditions that can be detected through DNA testing such as HIV will similarly feel unsafe accessing immigration services for which they are completely qualified due to valid concerns about their private and sensitive medical history being disclosed.
- Officers collecting data may be subject to additional risks when collecting DNA information, such as accidental exposure to HIV or herpes
- Persons with medical conditions that prevent easy collection of DNA information will be chilled from applying and potentially face adverse health effects. For example, if DNA is collected via blood samples, a hemophiliac petitioner or applicant will be frightened to apply because they will fear a medical emergency.
- Those with latex allergies will be chilled from applying and face danger to exposure that would not otherwise be present in the course of their immigration application process.

5) USCIS offices are already heavily overburdened with appointments, and will struggle to accommodate the many additional appointments. Applicants and petitioners will have to repeatedly miss work and other important obligations to attend these appointments.

6) The purpose of this rule, purportedly to catch fraud or criminals, does not concord with data showing that the additional collection of biometric data in airports and many other contexts has not led to successfully detecting significant amounts of fraud or criminals with outstanding warrants.

7) There is a risk of litigation based on the possibility that the true motivation behind this rule is not what is stated, but rather is part of a policy designed to make the immigration process more difficult and burdensome.

8) This proposed rule, which would increase paperwork, would be in violation of the Paperwork Reduction Act.

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Children do not belong behind bars. The intergenerational trauma that the US is creating through this practice is going to increase our instability, decrease our peace, and negate our humanity. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Upon reviewing the ANPRM, I see great potential for consumer gain within the industry. Quite frankly, this lack of accountability in regards to delayed baggage stains air carriers reputations. One of the greatest issues that could possibly form from this legislation is the shifting of fees from baggage to other fees associated with air carriers. As stated within the ANPRM, 13 of the largest air carriers received 2 million mishandled baggage reports in 2015. Instead of working to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of baggage handling, I see air carriers choosing a much more cost effective solution: eliminating baggage fees and displacing that revenue elsewhere, such as Wi-Fi/entertainment packages or more expensive flights altogether. With this in mind, air carriers are still expected to follow the industry standard; however, there is no direct financial effect associated with compliance to delayed baggage regulations. 

To protect the consumer from such a loophole, I would suggest a small percentage should be used as a means of financial compensation for delayed baggage. This will guarantee a monetary motive by the air carrier to deliver baggage on time as well as rectify consumer issues. 
 
As for determining how a late bag is defined, the current 12 and 15-hour rule is a good starting point. This will benefit consumers in the industry through set deadlines; however, air carriers may need to have more room for error. A basic algorithm that takes certain aspects of each individual flight, such as size of flight, type of company, and distance flown, should be taken into consideration when determining late baggage from an air carriers point of view. Truthfully, it will be difficult to define late baggage in an appeasing matter for both air carriers and consumers.

I support the FAAs effort to expand Part 107 operations in a safe manner. The changes should be based upon sound and relevant science that is appropriate for the operations being considered. I support the FAAs proposal of creating Category 1 for small drones to operate over people; however, the weight limit is too low and restrictive, and should be increased. Larger drones can be safely operated over people assuming the appropriate precautions are taken. 

I disagree with the FAAs proposal to further restrict flight over vehicles. People operating vehicles are protected from injury by the vehicles roof. Much like operating over a building containing people, the risk of injury to the people underneath the protective layer (roof in the case of a building) is minimal, and additional restrictions only serve to unnecessarily burden our industry. Also, vehicles are typically moving on roadways, and a damaged/malfunctioning drone falling from the sky would not be over the vehicle by the time it fell from the sky. Also, risk of distracting drivers on the roadway are very minimal as there are a number of other distractions to motorists that they must notice and handle safely through the course of normal operations (birds, other motorists, pedestrians, larger airplanes/helicopters, other wildlife, weather, etc).

I agree with the FAAs proposal to expand night operations for drones. While the operating conditions are different, it is not excessively difficult to operate safely at night; in fact, it can be quite easy to do so. With proper lighting and precautions, night operations can be safe and are a huge opportunity for the drone industry to provide useful services to the public. Since night operations have been allowed over the last few years, there have been minimal displayed risk to the public due to accidents or unsafe conditions. 

The lighting requirements proposed by the FAA are adequate; anti-collision lighting that is visible for 3 statute miles is sufficient to ensure safe flights and operations, and mitigates the risk of collision. Colors and type of lighting should not be dictated, as long as the end goals for safety and visibility are achieved. 
The FAA should not move to restrict drone manufacturers, and should instead focusing on allowing market-driven innovation. Setting goals for safety, operational performance, etc, and allowing manufacturers to be free to design drones that meet these goals would be a less restrictive, more effective, more efficient, and less burdensome method of meeting the same goals. 

I support the requirement of Part 107 pilots to be required to pass a pilot knowledge test. However, the required knowledge and testing should be narrowed to better reflect the actual challenges, conditions, and operations of a drone pilot rather than the much more expansive knowledge required for a pilot operating a larger manned aircraft. The tests required to expand operations should be individually designed and administered so that additional operations, such as night operations, can be tested and approved via a night operations-specific test instead of requiring the pilot to return to a test center, pay, and take the test again in its entirety.

I agree with the Food and Drug Administration's decision to lower nicotine levels in tobacco products. Regulating nicotine content is essential to reducing the addictiveness of these products. However, the FDA does not address potential challenges that could arise from implementing this policy.
One major concern is that if legal cigarettes contain lower nicotine levels, individuals addicted to high-nicotine cigarettes may turn to unregulated alternatives through illegal markets. To prevent this, the best approach would be to gradually reduce nicotine levels rather than implementing a sudden decrease, which could lead to consumer resistance.
Another issue is that reducing nicotine content may cause people to smoke more cigarettes to compensate for the lower nicotine levels. This could result in increased exposure to carcinogens and harmful chemicals, ultimately worsening health outcomes. Additionally, consumers may turn to alternative nicotine products such as e-cigarettes, nicotine patches, or gums, whose long-term effects remain largely unknown.
A well-planned, phased approach that includes comprehensive public health strategies is necessary to ensure the success of this policy while minimizing unintended consequences.

Dear Dr. Wester: 

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the draft CDC recommendations for hepatitis B 

screening and testing. We appreciate and commend CDC’s leadership in this undertaking to update and 

expand hepatitis B screening and testing recommendations. 

Virginia Hepatitis Coalition 

Contact Information: vhc-organizing-committee@googlegroups.com; 

virginiahepatitiscoalition@gmail.com

Overall, we are pleased to see the expansion of hepatitis B screening to a universal recommendation for 

adults 18 and older. Additionally, we strongly support the recommendation to provide hepatitis B 

screening with the 3-part panel for all adults including pregnant persons, providing a more complete 

picture of potential infection and clear steps for clinical management. The addition of risk factors to 

include persons currently or formerly incarcerated, with current or past STIs or multiple sex partners, 

with current or past HCV infection and anyone who requests a hepatitis B test, regardless of disclosure of 

risk, are reflective of the current trajectory of hepatitis B epidemiology in the United States and will be 

supportive of the work of hepatitis B service providers to reach all highly impacted populations. We 

believe these new recommendations will greatly increase access to hepatitis B screening and testing, 

removing barriers such as individual and community stigma and anxiety related to hepatitis B risk factors, 

and improve testing rates. 

Additionally, we appreciate the timeliness of the expanded screening recommendations to align with the 

recent decision by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to recommend all adults 

aged 19-59 years be vaccinated against hepatitis B infection. We believe it is critical to coordinate clinical 

guidance for screening and vaccination. We believe screening for hepatitis B infection, with the 3-part 

panel, is primary and essential to finding susceptible persons and preventing new infections and agree 

that offering a first dose of the vaccine at the same time as screening to the hardest to reach populations 

is beneficial.

According to data from the Virginia Department of Health, since 2012, there have been two hepatitis B 

outbreaks in Virginia. One of the two hepatitis B outbreaks was in a rural community in Southwest 

Virginia among IDU, while the other was in an assisted living facility in Central Virginia associated with an 

infection control breech involving shared blood glucose monitoring (BGM) devices. VDH assists with 

detection and mediation of infection control breeches at healthcare facilities and, from 2012-2015, seven 

infection control breeches involving BGM were identified in Virginia and warranted testing of exposed 

individuals. We believe the expansion can help to prevent outbreaks. 

We also believe the expansion of the recommendations for hepatitis B screening and testing is an 

opportunity to promote awareness and screening for hepatitis delta infection. There are very low levels 

of awareness and knowledge about hepatitis delta in the U.S. among the persons at risk for infection and 

health care providers. Given the promising treatments currently in clinical trial and anticipated 

dissemination of research related to hepatitis delta prevalence, we encourage the CDC to take the 

opportunity to include a statement on hepatitis delta. 

Thank you again for this opportunity to comment on the draft recommendations. We are excited to see 

the expansion of hepatitis B screening in the U.S. These updates will improve access to and increase

 
screening and testing rates, bringing the United States closer to achieving global viral hepatitis 

elimination goals.

We the undersigned fuel marketers and retailers, who representing nearly 160 c-stores and gas stations, urge the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to use the mid-term evaluation of the 2022-2025 model year vehicle emissions and efficiency standards to level the playing field for alternative fuel technologies. Specifically, we encourage EPA to restore incentives to automakers for the production of flexible fuel vehicles (FFVs) because they are an imperative tool in reducing petroleum use and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

This issue is critical to us because we have made significant investments in site upgrades and fueling equipment to offer our customers E85 and other flex fuels. In recent years, EPA has pointed out the ethanol capabilities of FFVs were underutilized due to insufficient E85 infrastructure, and we took action to remedy that situation by making flex fuels more widely available. Our investments are beginning to pay off as motorists fill up with cost-effective E85 at the highest volumes our stations have ever seen. However, if FFV incentives are allowed to die on the vine, flex fuel volumes will dwindle, and our investments will be stranded along with over $200 million in new flex fuel infrastructure investment made at other petroleum marketers businesses over just the past two years. 

It seems counterintuitive for EPA to take the FFV credit away from auto makers when flex fuel availability and use is finally expanding the way EPA had envisioned. The federal government provides generous incentives for EVs, PHEVs and CNGs, allowing them to count as more than one vehicle in the manufacturers compliance calculation and assuming high levels of alternative fuel use for CAFE and GHG purposes. Meanwhile, the rapid decline in FFV credits has already caused the automakers to begin phasing out production of FFVs at the same time E85 use is increasing and E85 stations are expanding. Alternative fuel vehicle technologies should receive fair and equal treatment by the federal government, and the government needs to be patient and maintain consistent policies that support long-term investment in fuels and infrastructure.

Restoring FFV credits would not only help reduce GHG emissions, it would do so at no cost to the federal government, while also reducing fuel cost for American drivers. With more than 20 million FFVs on the road nationwide and with E85 currently priced between 50 to 60 cents less than regular gasoline at 4000 fueling locations nationwide, restoring credits for FFVs would help millions of Americans save at the pump. 

We encourage EPA to create a level playing field by restoring a meaningful credit or multiplier for future FFV production.

To Whom it May Concern,

This comment is in response to the proposed 2018 rule to rescind the leak repair requirements from substitute refrigerants and the proposed withdrawal of the full set of Subpart F requirements from substitutes. The ruling stated that a change in the interpretation of the EPAs authority as granted by section 608 of the Clean Air Act is the reason for this action. It seems hypocritical for EPA to change its stance on specific interpretations of statutes as its administration changes. The regulated community, and the environment, cannot afford this frequent change in interpretations that can occur when the EPA changes its administrators. We deserve a consistent regulatory framework, as it relates to refrigerants and the environment, that has been developed with industry participation and that is line with the EPAs core mission of protecting the environment and its inhabitants. The 2016 Final Ruling fits this description and should be supported, and defended, by the Environmental Protection Agency, regardless of administration changes. 

There are plenty of legal statutes and Supreme court cases that can be sited to establish the authority conveyed in the 2016 Final Ruling. It is disappointing to see that EPA would adopt a position that would allow systems containing substitute refrigerants to legally dump these refrigerants into the atmosphere through system leaks. There are many millions of pounds of refrigerants in systems across the country. As more and more systems are switched to substitute refrigerants, as HCFCs are phased out, this rescission will directly result in millions of pounds of refrigerant legally seeping into the atmosphere. This is an assault on our environment by the very organization tasked with protecting it. 

The petitioners asking EPA to adopt this position do not represent a majority of the regulated community, nor is their position in line with the industry at large. The 2016 Final Rule was supported by a large majority of the industry and was done with stakeholder involvement and participation. The interpretation that Congress specifically left the word substitute out of 608(a) and (b) so as not to convey authority to regulate is shortsighted and close-minded. Furthermore, if it was indeed Congress intention in 1993, it should not prevent EPA from performing its duties in 2018 as technology advances the industry. The Clean Air Act should not be picked apart section by section to determine authorities. It should be taken as a whole, (a), (b), and (c), and used to enforce regulations that are in line with the spirit of the entire document and EPAs core mission of protecting the environment and its inhabitants. 

The rescission of the full set of Subpart F requirements from substitute refrigerants would be a disaster for both the environment and the industry. It will result in significantly increased refrigerant emissions (both ODS and substitute), the loss of thousands of American jobs, and countless injuries and/or deaths as untrained or unlicensed persons would have access to these refrigerants. It would create a scenario that would make venting a substitute illegal yet have no legal mandate that it be recovered and would allow the charge to legally leak into the atmosphere. Extremely redundant. 

Please support the 2016 Final Rule and drop this proposal to roll back 2018 regulations to 1993 regulations. Lets move forward together, not backward. Thank you.

Respectfully Submitted,
Jason Obrzut

I am writing to express my dismay at certain glaring deficiencies in the present proposed regulations concerning the cultivation of Domestic Hemp (Federal registration number 2019-23749.)

I see 5 really major problems in the new regulations:

1)
 The pre-harvest hemp sampling procedures to test for total THC content (<0.3%) currently defined by the USDA interim rule restrict pre-harvest sampling to only be conducted by DEA registered labs, of which there is currently only a handful. The process for DEA lab certification currently takes 6-9 months, which will surely result in pre-harvest sampling bottlenecks for the thousands of American hemp farmers (17,000 in 2019, and expected to double for 2020). 
 This is really important! There's no way I can get my hemp tested in the 15 day window with time left for me to harvest my crop. Shoot! I won't even be able to get my test results back before my 15 day window closes. The USDA really has to fix this discrepancy so that we can comply with the law.

Also:
 Rather than utilizing full-plant pre-harvest sampling, the USDA interim rule restricts the plant sample to be composed of clippings from only the top two inches of the hemp flower, which contain higher concentrations of THC than the rest of the plant harvested for hemp biomass. This is not an accurate representation of the total THC level, but rather the highest THC level
 I think that USDA change the pre-harvest plant sampling to include full-plant representative samples. After all, CBD oil is made from the whole plant, not just the top 2 inches.

3. The 15-Day Harvest Rule
The current USDA rule limits farmers to 15 days from the time the pre-harvest sample was taken to await the results and then harvest their entire crop. It cannot be overstated that part of the 15-day window is waiting for the results of the test, which currently takes up to a week, and considering the potential bottleneck of relying on DEA registered labs could easily take two weeks. (If the pre-harvest sample is not under the legal total THC limit of 0.3%, the farmer has to destroy the crop.) 
If the pre-harvest sample tests under the legal limit, the farmer then has only a short time to harvest the plant before the 15-day window is up. Harvesting an entire hemp field, even with mechanized harvesters, often takes over a month. As the new USDA rule currently stands, if the farmer doesn't make the 15-day deadline, the crop has to be tested again and the farmer will again have to wait for the second round of pre-harvest results before they can continue harvesting. This 15-Day Rule was clearly not well thought out and it puts farmers at risk of losing their crop due to logistical nonsense.
 I oppose the new USDA 15-day limit and recommend the deadline be changed to 30 days.

4. 0.3% vs 1.0% Total THC Testing
Let's be honest. Nobody is getting high off of hemp. The USDA's regulation of THC in hemp should be intended to prevent hemp farmers from growing high-THC cannabis in their hemp fields. The USDA's adherence to a strict 0.3% total THC limit for hemp is not based on sound science or any non-psychedelic metric. Rather it is based on an arcane Canadian hemp standard implemented for the hemp grain market in the 1990s. Because the natural range of CBD:THC in hemp is 20:1 to maximum 40:1, limiting the total THC to 0.3% limits the maximum CBD percentage in hemp to (0.340) = 12%, which is less profitable to the farmer than growing current varieties that are 20% -25% CBD with only 0.5% total THC.
 I think that the USDA should adopt a more reasonable 1% total THC limit for hemp flower and biomass. 

5. If we accidentally go over our 0.3% THC-A limit (or total 1% Total THC limit), because of hang ups with the lab testing, we should be allowed to plow our crop under, improving our soils.

 
Make Hemp Production viable by giving us:

 A 1% total THC limit for hemp. 
 If the 0.3% total THC remains, then establish a 1% total THC threshold before the farmer faces any strikes

Dear Secretary Purdue:

I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule to "modernize" swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety.

The proposed rule would put consumers at risk of food-borne illness by removing important microbiological-testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. 

In place of those requirements, slaughterhouses would be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide.

The rule also proposes a New Swine Inspection System that would hand over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter-establishment employees. The proposal would also remove caps on line speeds, increasing the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination and other food-safety issues. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with those additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer. The current proposal would not achieve that. Instead it has the potential to make food less safe by deregulating swine inspection, transferring important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

I ask you to withdraw the proposed rule and design one that will prioritize food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements, which will significantly reduce contamination and food-borne illness.

Very sincerely yours,

Jane Rigney
Newton, NJ

An open letter to: 
 President Trump and Commerce Secretary Ross 
One of your Administrations signature campaign promises was cutting onerous 
regulations that promote economic inefficiencies and stymie a business’s growth 
with no clear public benefit. 
The Ventura County Commercial Fishermen’s Association would like to bring to 
the Administration’s attention an example of a proposed regulation looking for a 
nonexistent problem. 
The ‘Proposed Rule for Vessel Monitoring for the Pacific Coast Groundfish Fishery’ 
(Docket NO. NOAA-NMFS-2019-0093) is a regulation that is entirely unnecessary 
and would be an additional financial encumbrance on the many small and 
medium size commercial fishing businesses on the West Coast. Currently, vessels 
participating in the Pacific Groundfish Fishery are required to have a Vessel 
Monitoring System (VMS) on board that reports a position once per hour (a ping). 
This is so vessels that are transiting a ‘closed area’ can be monitored to determine 
if they are fishing or traveling through it. This VMS ping rate has worked 
effectively since its inception over 15 years ago. 
In 2013 the NOAA Office of Law Enforcement (OLE) prosecuted a case (NOAA Case 
No. SW1002974) and lost. The case was weak from the get-go and bad blood 
between the OLE and the defendants were a contributing factor for the case 
going forward. An Administrative Judge assigned to the case ruled in the 
defendant’s favor. 
Due to that ruling, NOAA wants to increase the ‘ping rate’ from once per hour to 
four times per hour for Pacific Coast Groundfish Fisheries. This increase will cost 
fishermen 3 to 4 times more per month than the already exorbitant fee they are 
presently paying. There will be no benefit to the groundfish resources on the 
Pacific Coast with this proposed rule. In actuality, the only beneficiaries will be the 
service providers for VMS units from the increased revenue they will receive.

 
The VMS ping rate at once per hour has worked as originally designed since 2003 
when VMS became mandatory. The current once per hour ping rate has proved to 
be an effective deterrent to illegal fishing in Essential Fish Habitat Areas, Rockfish 
Conservation Areas, Marine Protected Areas and the multitude of other Reserves 
and Conservation Areas up and down the Pacific West Coast. 
Groundfish fisheries on the East Coast use VMS with the one-hour ping rate 
unless the vessel has a scallop permit attached [to the vessel] where it would then 
be twice per hour. The once per hour reporting rate there has been working 
effectively and the OLE isn’t complaining about enforcement issues on the East 
Coast. 
It’s been 6 years since NOAA lost case No. SW1002974. One must wonder, if 
monitoring transiting vessels in a closed area was such a problem, why has the 
NOAA OLE dragged its feet for this long and not gotten this proposed regulation 
enacted? Answer; it’s a regulation that is not necessary. 
While we help feed this nation, fishermen are continually faced with a bloated 
regulatory onslaught. The Ventura County Commercial Fishermen’s Association 
needs the help of your Administration. Free us from this unnecessary regulatory 
prison sentence. 
Sincerely, 
The Ventura County Commercial Fishermen’s Association

I write this public comment to voice my strong support of banning the use of cellular devices for voice calls on an aircraft. The rule is needed on a legislative level to solidify its importance and to maintain its enforcement.Traveling by plane is an intense experience in itself, piling on the possibility of falling out of the sky because someone wants to answer or start an inconsequential call distresses the circumstance further.
All in-flight voice communication should be prohibited. While there are cases of emergencies (death, birth, accidents), where one would need to be able to have such calls, the phone on the aircraft should be sufficient enough to handle that contact. Exceptions should be made for Federal law enforcement officers, the Federal Air Marshal, and FAA Aviation Safety Inspectors as their conducting official work/business is essential in securing the safety of all those on board. Once the aircraft's door shut all passenger's communications on mobile wireless devices should cease and once the aircraft lands and doors open they can proceed. This gives passenger's a decent amount of time to end their conversations and sets clear guidelines on what is acceptable and what will not be tolerated. In addition, mobile wireless device should be confined to cell phones, computers, tablets, and any other device that uses radio links to establish a voice call with any other party or parties, essentially the House bill, Prohibiting In-Flight Voice Communications on Mobile Device Act of 2013 definition of "mobile wireless device" will do. If a charter flight, in-flight voice communications could be allowed due to the flight being yours only and you're disturbing only your party and/or endangering them. This would be another acceptable exception along with foreign air carriers. Due to them not being under American jurisdiction, it wouldn't exactly be the government's place to mandate that they enforce the ban on their aircrafts. 
On an airplane overhearing someone's personal conversations puts passengers in an awkward and unnecessary position. For some, it also brings a sense of anxiety as some regard using electronics on planes at all as dangerous and risky, many know that such use has an ability to interfere with ground networks. Barring such use eliminates said disruptive, potentially harmful and injurious scenarios from manifesting, making the environment as a whole a safer space which is optimal for all those involved. Text messaging, emailing, and/or surfing the web should be still allowed as total isolation from the outside world could have negative effects for the passengers and crew members alike. This day and age cutting someone off from the electronic word is devastating (often used as a punishing tactic by parents on misbehaving children) and it wouldn't be within the rights or obligatory for the government to demand as such. Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing in response to the ANPR related to the labeling of cultivated (cell-based) meat and poultry products published on Sept 3, 2021 (FR86.169).  I appreciate the opportunity to provide feedback – I believe that the introduction of cultivated meat and poultry products is of huge import as we collectively work to fight the climate crisis.

In a time of both population growth and GDP growth, we know that the trend of rising demand for meat will only continue. I believe that cultivated meat and poultry products will be an important supplement to traditional meat products, making it possible to expand access to high-protein foods without additional climate impacts.  This should be a priority for the USDA and I'm hopeful that the Federal Government will take a leadership role in developing new regulations to control the marketing of these products.

Regarding how these meats should be labeled, I support using the term ‘cultivated’ for these new products as it is sufficient to describe and to convey meaningful information to consumers like myself.  For example, ‘cultivated beef’ or ‘cultivated chicken’ is a good word to distinguish these new products from conventional slaughtered meat products.

I feel it would be inappropriate and cast a negative light over this new industry if terms like ‘fake meat’, ‘synthetic meat’ or other obviously demeaning terms were approved by the FSIS.

Finally, the USDA should make it easy to use  these new meat and poultry products in traditional foods.  If regulations and standards need to be modified to facilitate these new ingredients the USDA should put enough resources into these needs to prevent unnecessary delays in getting these products to consumers.

Again, thank you for your leadership on this important topic. I am optimistic about the future we are working to create.

Best,
Dakota

appreciate its effectiveness in providing for efficient processing of re-entry to the United States at 

various airports. The purpose of my comment is to request temporary delay and further study prior to 

implementing this rule change. In light of COVID-19 and its effects upon the travel activities of our 

citizens, this change would potentially cause an undue financial burden upon many citizens. 

There is no doubt that these three trusted traveler programs ease the time and stress involved with 

crossing borders. However, is it necessary to have three separate programs that are so similar? Under 

the “Background” section, it is stated that “the programs have a nearly identical application process and 

participants in any one of the programs can enjoy nearly all the benefits of the other two trusted 

traveler programs.” My suggestion is not to simply harmonize the fees, but to seek to further 

consolidate the programs, themselves, into one program. By allowing the Global Entry program to 

absorb NEXUS and SENTRI, unnecessary operating costs associated with duplicate programs could 

potentially be decreased. This suggestion appears more consistent with Executive Orders 13563, which 

directs agencies to reduce costs, rather than simply passing the costs off to the American people in the 

form of increased fees. 

Furthermore, I suggest the discussion of this rule change be paused until further notice, due to the 

economic impact of COVID-19. According to the footnotes, the data collected regarding operating costs 

spans from 2010 to 2019. However, due to the COVID-19 crisis, this data is outdated and does not 

reflect the impact of COVID-19 on the U.S. workforce or travel industry. According to the U.S. Bureau of 

Labor Statistics, COVID-19 has resulted in historically high numbers of job loss and unemployment 

claims.i According to the economic impact analysis conducted by Oxford Economics in March 2020,ii a 

31% decline in the travel industry was predicted, with losses of over $355 billion. This study was based 

on a 12-16 month recovery time for a disease-related crisis. A similar assessment by the World Tourism 

Organization in May 2020 projected a decline of 58% to 78% in international tourist arrivals.iii This 

reflects an enormous decline is discretionary spending by consumers. However, with so many travel 

restrictions ongoing worldwide, it is difficult to see in the near future a rebound to the statistics upon 

which this proposed rule change was based. 

In conclusion, I do not see the present time as the correct time for fee increases through the proposed 

harmonization of fees to the three trusted traveler programs of the CBP. An increase may cause an

 
unnecessary financial burden. More so, uncertainty about the future is currently dominating the average 

American household and has resulted in shock and decline in consumption. Basu and Bundick argue that 

increased uncertainty about the future worsened the Great Recession.iv If accurate, then present 

American uncertainty nullifies the statistical forecasts this upon which this proposed rule change is 

based. 

Thank you for your kind attention to this comment,

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Currently, I avoid all animal products because one cannot be sure of the labeling claims. Since the USDA apparently cannot make consistent rules for humane animal welfare and ensure they are followed, I do not trust any of the labeling.

Thank you for considering my request.

The economic prosperity of fishermen depends on the ability of a species population to continue to replenish at a consistent rate. As the red grouper stock is decreasing, limits must be placed on catch totals in order to preserve the fish for others to continue fishing. Stock decreases could also affect tourism in the areas where the red grouper is present. As someone who goes to Florida every year, the draw of the ocean is huge. I strongly oppose the definition of "habitat" that is proposed in this rule. Designation of critical habitat is a vital tool available under the Endangered Species Act to help conserve species. Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors.

This change would result in the exclusion of areas that do not meet the new, narrower definition of habitat, thereby decreasing the amount of habitat that can be protected. This would represent a severe setback to conservation, because critical habitat is vital for stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species that have protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species without it.

The loss of any species diminishes the whole world. Please let us use what we have already to save species around the world.

Americans recognize the ESA's vital role in conserving beloved wildlife species, and a 2018 survey found that four out of five people support the law. At a time of unprecedented wildlife extinction and habitat destruction, we should be working to strengthen--not weaken--the ESA. For these reasons, I urge the USFWS and NOAA to withdraw this proposed rule.

As a Canadian CTO of a high-tech startup that has had to wrestle with TN, F1, F1-OPT, and probably H1B visas in the future, I am a big fan of the idea of an entrepreneur visa.

One minor suggestion is to lower the financing and revenue criteria. Most highly innovative high-tech startups (like mine) are "pre-revenue", and $500,000 is a large number to a lot of people. I do understand that there need to be black and white guidelines that regulators can use, but I believe that the current proposal will exclude many small-scale startups that are the ones most in need of these types of visas. The larger a company gets, the more likely it will be able to afford lawyers for H1B visas, etc. Therefore, I believe that this proposal should cater to small innovative businesses, rather than explicitly exclude them by imposing minimum funding targets.

In the current proposal, I could not deduce what entity is adjudicating the process (ie who is saying "yes, visa approved" or "no, visa denied"?). From what I could tell, it seems to be up to the sole discretion of the DHS. My suggestion is to integrate an independent peer-review process to adjudicate a business ranking to give independent metrics for entrepreneurial impact. I would want to see my scores from 3 different independent sources to yield a total score, to be sure that I wasn't excluded due to cronyism. Allowing businesses to see their scores would increase transparency and reduce the potential for corruption. I suppose this is more of a general comment on the visa system: it is not very transparent and could be improved by a scoring system.

I believe that lowering minimum financing and revenue numbers, and integrating independent peer review, would solve many of the minor issues in the current proposal, and help give the DHS some black-and-white independent numbers on which to base yes/no decisions.

If the DOT's proposed rule, 14 CFR Part 382, is enacted and challenged in court, it will most likely survive judicial review under the arbitrary and capricious standard set forth in 706(2)(A) of the APA. 

First, a court will confirm the DOT is authorized to promulgate this rule. The enabling statutes applicable to this proceeding include the ACCA and the FAA Act. The ACCA grants the DOT broad discretion to prescribe regulations that further the statute's purpose to prohibit discrimination in airline service on the basis of disability. Accommodations must factor in the overall safety of the traveling public and be reasonable in light of the realities and limitations of air service and the onboard environment of commercial airplanes. 

The FAA Act requires the DOT to conduct a rulemaking proceeding on the definition of the term, "service animal," and to develop minimum standard requirements for service and emotional support animals. In addition, the agency must (1) consider several measures to ensure that pets are not claimed as service animals; factor in necessary health and safety measures onboard aircraft; and (3) decide whether the DOT should align its definition of a service animal with the service animal definition established by the DOJ under the ADA. (Generally, the DOJ defines a service animal as a dog but, under certain conditions, the agency makes exceptions for miniature horses.) Since the FAA Act does not require the rule to be "made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing," the DOT is permitted to conduct an informal notice-and-comment rulemaking proceeding. See 553(c). 

The following rule, 14 CFR Part 382, is the product of the DOT's informal rulemaking efforts: a service animal is "a dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a qualified individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability." Airlines are allowed "to require all passengers with a disability traveling with a service animal to complete and submit to the airline forms developed by DOT attesting to the animal's training and good behavior [and] certifying the animal's good health...." 

A reviewing court will "consider whether the [DOT's rule] was based on a consideration of the relevant factors and whether there was a clear error in judgment" and most likely find 14 CFR Part 382 survives the arbitrary and capricious standard. See Overton Park. After reviewing the "concise general statement" of the rule's "basis and purpose," a court should conclude the DOT took a "hard look" at the material issues, explained the evidence in the record, and offered a "rational connection between the facts found and the choice made." See 553(c) of the APA; see also State Farm. 

For instance, the DOT carefully reviewed the 4,500 comments submitted by disability advocacy organizations, airlines, human and animal health organizations, consumer groups, and individual members of the public. The agency found (1) the majority of commenters all supported dogs as service animals; (2) a smaller majority advocated for both dogs and miniature horses; (3) some disability organizations argued against miniature horses, because they are not commonly used as service animals and excluding them from the rule would not impact many individuals with disabilities; (4) airlines receive very few requests about miniature horses; (5) some commenters advocated for capuchin monkeys, but acknowledged they must be kept in containers; (6) and other advocates expressed concerns about capuchin monkeys, e.g., they are prone to aggressive behavior and can transmit diseases. 

In addition, the DOT conducted a cost-benefit analysis and found the new rule could increase total air carrier revenue by $70M per year, because it would be more difficult for passengers to defraud the system and travel with pets in the cabin.
