I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable. CHILDREN DO NOT BELONG IN DETENTION.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. Given the barrage of recent reports on conditions and abuse at currently contracted detention facilities for adults, along with the debacle created in the effort to separate children from their parents at the border as a deterrent, leaving many orphaned or abandoned due to a dismal failure of appropriate oversight, the government cannot be entrusted to provide the specialized care these traumatized children need. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I find it amazing that the FAA managed to take action on this in a span of days, yet myself and at least one other person reported a safety of flight issue with another ADS-B transponder over a month ago and have heard nothing in response. The text of my report is below... my confirmation email receipt shows 9/20/16 at 3:56 PM CST

I have identified a safety of flight issue with the Garmin GTX345 transponder, STC #SA01714WI.

The transponder receives heading input over multiple serial data sources, and per the STC holder's installation manual (190-00734-10) a discrete heading input wired by the installer to the transponder is an optional connection (page 1-30, section 1.5.6).

My installer and I have determined that the heading input is not optional, it is sent over all compatible input interfaces. Furthermore, the required RS232 interface that carries GPS position data from a compatible GPS reveals a bug in the transponder's heading data implementation that causes the transponder to crash and reboot repeatedly on a heading of 360.
When notified of the bug by multiple installers in differing aircraft with differing interfacing equipment, despite a preponderance of evidence suggesting that the fault lies in the software of the transponder, Garmin field service representatives have over the span of the last three months repeatedly refused to accept responsibility for this fault, but rather blamed various other instruments in the aircraft of those who have reproduced this issue, even in cases where those instruments were not connected to the transponder.

The issue may be reproduced by the following...

1) Interface a Garmin GTX345 transponder to any compatible Garmin GPS (400W, 500W, GTN 650, GTN 750, GNS 480) over the RS232 data interface, per the GTX series installation manual, part number 190-00734-10.

2) Supply ARINC429 heading input to the GPS supplying position data to the transponder that indicates magnetic heading of 0 to 359 degrees. In my case, a Garmin GNS480 GPS was supplied with ARINC429 heading data from an Aspen EFD1000 primary flight display.

3) With all avionics turned on, align the aircraft on a 360 magnetic heading.

The above will cause the GTX345 transponder to persistently reboot in two to three second intervals. All transponder output transmission will obviously be lost when flying a magnetic heading of 360, due to the reboot loop condition.

Garmin field service representatives have told those of us who have reproduced this issue that the problem is a heading of zero, and insisted that other avionics that are connected upstream of our GPS units are to blame. That is obviously not an accurate assessment of the issue, since the ARINC429 specification defines a circle as 0 to 359 degrees per "ARINC Specification 429 Part 1-17: Mark 33 - Digital Information Transfer System," page 13.

I was a chemical engineering faculty member for 47 years at the Universities of Florida and Virginia. I am a Fellow and former member of the Board of Directors of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers.

As a result of my experience, I am appalled that the EPA is currently attempting to reverse, rather than strengthen, the Risk Management Program (RMP) standards for chemical facilities. Such action flies in the face protecting life and property from the destruction caused by inevitable chemical disasters. The 2017 Arkema disaster is an example of what happens without proper regulations in place. 

As an instructor, consultant, and professional society member, I have always focused on safety first, but I am a realistic engineer who knows that accidents happen from human error, especially when corporations attempt to limit costs by reducing vigilance. It is up to the federal government, especially EPA, to provide information, to initiate and enforce regulations, and to lead our country in protection the middle word in the agencys name! 

Specifically, I wish to comment that:

1. The most dangerous facilities must be required to continually seek safer alternatives by periodic assessment of their situation and determine what better practices can be used. Not requiring assessments will mean they will not be done, and dangers will continue until disaster strikes.
2. The airline industry has become amazingly safe because it instituted mandatory reporting of incidents and near-misses. This model can work well in the chemical industries, so incident analysis should be maintained.
3. It is well-known that individuals and companies cannot be relied on to objectively determine the causes and effects of incidents they create. Third-party audits are essential to prevent coverups and repeats of incidents.
4. Like most organizations, chemical facilities, run by nonresident managers, naturally focus only on their property. Incidents with chemicals can kill and injure people and significantly damage property outside the fence, especially if located in metropolitan areas. Local emergency officials and first-responders must be given advance information about the possibilities of incidents and what the facility plans are to handle them. Further, such information should be made available to the public that could be affected. It is unthinkable that EPA would not insist that such information be promulgated.
5. Maintaining and upgrading the RMP will be vital for the many workers at chemical facilities. These highly skilled technical employees and contractors are the first to be affected by incidents. They deserve the greatest of protection, which would be eliminated by the proposed policy. 

Thus, I urge that the proposed policy, EPA-HQ-OEM-2015-0725-0890, not be instituted. The result of its passage would unnecessarily take us back many decades to the suffering and damages of the early days of the chemical industries.

J.P. OConnell, PhD, FAIChE

+ Nuremberg Code - The ten points are from the United States National Institute of Health.

1. The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. This means that the person involved should have legal capacity to give consent; should be so situated as to be able to exercise free power of choice, without the intervention of any element of force, fraud, deceit, duress, over-reaching, or other ulterior form of constraint or coercion; and should have sufficient knowledge and comprehension of the elements of the subject matter involved as to enable him/her to make an understanding and enlightened decision. This latter element requires that before the acceptance of an affirmative decision by the experimental subject there should be made known to him the nature, duration, and purpose of the experiment; the method and means by which it is to be conducted; all inconveniences and hazards reasonable to be expected; and the effects upon his health or person which may possibly come from his participation in the experiment.

The duty and responsibility for ascertaining the quality of the consent rests upon each individual who initiates, directs or engages in the experiment. It is a personal duty and responsibility which may not be delegated to another with impunity.

2. The experiment should be such as to yield fruitful results for the good of society, unprocurable by other methods or means of study, and not random and unnecessary in nature.

3. The experiment should be so designed and based on the results of animal experimentation and a knowledge of the natural history of the disease or other problem under study that the anticipated results will justify the performance of the experiment.

4. The experiment should be so conducted as to avoid all unnecessary physical and mental suffering and injury.

5. No experiment should be conducted where there is a prior reason to believe that death or disabling injury will occur; except, perhaps, in those experiments where the experimental physicians also serve as subjects.

6. The degree of risk to be taken should never exceed that determined by the humanitarian importance of the problem to be solved by the experiment.

7. Proper preparations should be made and adequate facilities provided to protect the experimental subject against even remote possibilities of injury, disability, or death.

8. The experiment should be conducted only by scientifically qualified persons. The highest degree of skill and care should be required through all stages of the experiment of those who conduct or engage in the experiment.

9. During the course of the experiment the human subject should be at liberty to bring the experiment to an end if he has reached the physical or mental state where continuation of the experiment seems to him to be impossible.

10. During the course of the experiment the scientist in charge must be prepared to terminate the experiment at any stage, if he has probable cause to believe, in the exercise of the good faith, superior skill and careful judgment required of him that a continuation of the experiment is likely to result in injury, disability, or death to the experimental subject.

In the GOA trawl fishery as a whole, there is concern that the value of bycatch is exceeding the value of target species catch. 

For example:

If an out-of-state sport fisherman flies to Alaska to fish for halibut for a day, he would, on average(at minimum), spend; $500 on airfare, $100 per night for a Hotel, $30 per day on a rental car, $30 per day on food and drink, $300 for a halibut Charter, $25 for a sport fishing license, and $50 to have his fish vacuum packed, frozen, and shipped. 

So.... if that individual flies to Anchorage, rents a car, drives to Homer, spends the night, fishes for a single day, drives back to Anchorage that night, and flies out the next morning, he would be looking at three days worth of rental car and food, plus two nights in a hotel. Assuming that guy caught his 3A limit of a couple 11.5 lb halibut, he would spend $54 for each 1 lb of halibut removed from the biomass. Sidenote: I believe the average success rate is closer to 1.6 fish per day.

Obviously, someone who traveled in this way would be an anomaly. Most would bring a spouse or children, stay for a week, buy souvenirs, spend money on other fishing or recreational activities, etc etc.

The above example could be applied to King Salmon as well, though the success rate would likely be much lower, and thus the average investment in economy per pound of fish harvested would be much greater.

Further, if one accounts for the potential for under-reporting aboard unobserved trips, a strong case could be made that over 1 billion pounds of halibut have been discarded by the Alaskan trawl Fleet over the last 60 years.

student pharmacists, and pharmacy technicians. For more than 75 years, ASHP has been at the forefront of 

efforts to improve medication use and enhance patient safety. 

ASHP advocates for a strong compounding framework. We believe that a robust 503B outsourcing facility 

program is essential to realizing the goals of the Drug Quality and Security Act (DQSA). For many of our 

members, 503Bs are a vital link in their compounding supply chain. ASHP appreciates FDA’s efforts to guarantee 

the quality and safety of products prepared in 503B outsourcing facilities. 

ASHP also shares FDA’s goal to increase the number of 503B outsourcing facilities, especially those owned by or 

partnered with health systems. We believe that regulations and guidance, including this current good 

manufacturing practices (cGMP) draft, should include the specific designs and needs of health-system 503B 

outsourcing facilities. 

Beyond-Use Dates 

ASHP supports the use of default beyond-use dates in the guidance in place of a full stability program in specific 

cases. This allowance will increase the likelihood of hospitals and health systems developing 503B programs, 

since they are far more likely to use a product within the default beyond-use date (BUD). 

ASHP asks that FDA consider aligning the use of BUDs with existing standards set by USP General Chapter <797> 

to reduce confusion on the definition of the term. USP allows a product to be used as long as administration 

begins before the BUD. In lines 1161-1162, FDA states “administration to the patient should be completed 

before reaching the BUD.” The guidance also sets the conditions in Appendix B (line 1617) that the BUD is used 

as the expiration date. This should be the case only if an expiration date is the limiting factor in establishing a 

BUD. Having two definitions for the term BUD will make an already confusing principle even more unclear.

reached very quickly by repackaging products in short supply into unit-of-use package sizes. It’s highly unlikely

Children do not belong behind bars. I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations related to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-002.

Not only is indefinite detention of families and children unconscionable, it is unnecessary and wasteful. The Family Case Management Program had a nearly perfect record of ensuring participants appeared ICE check ins and court dates -- at a fraction of the cost of family detention.

The proposed regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

On behalf of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), representing more than 60,000 physicians and partners dedicated to advancing women’s health and the health of all those seeking obstetric and gynecologic care, thank you for the opportunity to submit written public comments on the draft Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommendations for hepatitis C testing among perinatally exposed infants and children. Obstetrician‐gynecologists, as trusted women’s health physicians, are dedicated to ending hepatitis C infections in the United States. 

ACOG recommends hepatitis screening for all pregnant individuals during each pregnancy. Hepatitis C screening during the first prenatal blood assessment obtained in every pregnancy is recommended to identify pregnant individuals with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and infants who should receive testing at a pediatric visit. Hepatitis C screening during pregnancy should be an opportunity to promote a dialogue between pregnant individuals and their clinician about hepatitis C transmission and risk factors. Part of management of hepatitis C and pregnancy should include plans for pediatric follow-up and linkage to care. 

The CDC document is comprehensive, but there are some aspects of research and care that are excluded. This CDC document would be strengthened by including a section on “gaps in knowledge”. Potential items for inclusion: 
I. Include a discussion of the spectrum of illness of hepatitis C. The hepatic sequelae of hepatitis C are well known but there are also extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis C virus infection. Extrahepatic manifestations may be relevant when considering the risks involved with mother-to-child transmission. Hepatitis C virus infection is a multifaceted systemic disease with both hepatic and extrahepatic complications. Rheumatologic, cardiovascular, metabolic, renal, neurologic, lymphoproliferative, and psychiatric diseases have all been causally linked to hepatitis C and likely mediated by HCV’s effects on the immune system. 
II. There is an assumption that the spectrum of illness associated with congenitally acquired HCV infection is the same as an adult acquired HCV infection. That may not be the case. For example, serious long-term neurocognitive sequelae are often seen with congenitally acquired infections and are not seen when the same infection is acquired in adulthood (e.g., cytomegalovirus, Zika). 
III. Timing of transmission is unknown. It is unclear if transmission occurs in-utero, intrapartum, or both. Timing of transmission would likely modulate the spectrum of pediatric illness. 
IV. There is an assumption that “transient infection” of newborns is benign without any long-term sequelae. It may not be, especially given what we know about extrahepatic manifestation of HCV. 
V. There is an assumption that there is no benefit in preventing either a “transient” or “chronic” pediatric infection. This may not be true. For those exposed in-utero to HCV, maternal treatment may be the better strategy than pediatric follow-up/treatment of babies with established/chronic infections. 

ACOG Reviewers indicated confusion with this statement:
“A pregnant person is considered to have confirmed HCV infection if HCV RNA is detected during pregnancy. If HCV RNA results are not available, a pregnant person is considered to have probable HCV infection during pregnancy if anti-HCV testing is reactive.” 

If an obstetrician-gynecologist identifies a positive HCV antibody test result, they would be encouraged to evaluate a patient for chronic HCV by ordering an HCV RNA test. Are the CDC authors suggesting that some persons will present at delivery without a complete evaluation for chronic HCV? In that case, an HCV RNA test could be ordered on admission for delivery or before discharge in order to determine the potential risk of perinatal transmission to the neonate. Introduction: The Rule
On October 20, 2022 the Department of Transportation (DOT) proposed a rule named
Enhancing Transparency of Airline Ancillary Service Fees. This rule is an initiative of the Biden
Administration to create transparency in airline pricing in the wake of displeasure with and
increases in prices of the airline industry. The proposed rule requires U.S. airlines, foreign
airlines, and ticket agencies to clearly disclose all additional fees with base airfare rates including
baggage fees, change fees, and cancellation fees to consumers when fare and schedule
information is displayed. Among the main rule directives, the Department of Transportation also
proposed multiple supplementary measures to the rule to further promote clarity in airfare
pricing. These accessory regulations require airlines and agencies to divulge fees for adjacent
seating to consumers traveling with their families and make these fees transactable. An
additional portion of the rule further proposes that airlines must also provide any and all ancillary
fee information to ticket agents that sell or display the airline carrier's fare and schedule
information. Such information provided to the travel agents from airlines must be a current,
functional, and accurate representation of baggage, change, cancellation, and adjacent seating
fees. The Enhancing Transparency of Airline Ancillary Service Fees Proposed Rule is one of the
implementation directives from the Biden Administration's Executive Order (EO) on Promoting
Competition in the American Economy. This EO directs the DOT among other departments and
agencies to take coordinated action to promote the interests of American workers, businesses,
and consumers. This initiative is one the most directly impactful and therefore newsworthy
proposed rule as it aims to ensure that consumers have ancillary fee information at the time of
ticket purchase when comparing various airlines and fare options against each other.

 
3
Background and Context
At a White House Competition Council meeting, President Joe Biden contextualized his
intent behind the rule, claiming that Americans “should know the full cost of your ticket right
when you're comparison-shopping to begin with what airline you're going to fly with, so you can
pick the ticket that actually is the best deal for you” (CBS Interactive). Although President Biden
is pushing his administration to make this rule as part of his larger economic plan, the history of
this regulation dates prior to his administration taking office. In 2014, the DOT released a notice
for a new rule proposal titled Transparency of Airline Ancillary Service Fees and Other
Consumer Protection Issues. The goal of this notice was to gauge public opinion and collect
commentary from potential stakeholders in this rule. In reaction to the abundance of comments
specifically related to the airline ancillary fees, the DOT released a supplemental notice of
rulemaking in 2017 labeled Transparency of Airline Ancillary Service Fees which included some
of the provisions of the latest version of the rule but lacked specificity regarding transactability
to travel agents and other additional fees. This 2017 rule never left the rulemaking stages and
was withdrawn until 2021 when President Biden released his aforementioned Executive Order
which then prompted multiple departments and agencies like the DOT to push
competition-promoting policies like this rule. The rationale of this rule in these economically
related terms holds that greater transparency upfront in airline and travel agency ticket fares
including all the many “hidden” fees will result in better competitive practices by the merchants
and the consumers when comparing options.

To Whom it May Concern,
As a media scholar and historian, I am very, very opposed to the proposed federal rules 
that will undoubtedly continue to hinder the free and vital journalism that Stars and 
Stripes’ journalists have been providing continuously since the early years of World War 
II. Without the ability to do their jobs free from federal government rules to which NO 
other journalists are compelled, the reporters, editors and photographers at Stars and 
Stripes become no different than the immense and already existing public relations 
staffs of the Department of Defense and military services. Already in the U.S., the ratio 
of public relations professionals to journalists stands at more than six to one.1 Is this 
really what we want? Those in one of those groups owe their allegiance to their 
employing organizations. The other – journalists – owe their allegiance to the public at 
large.
We need real journalism – no more so than for the men and women of the armed forces 
who are deployed or living overseas with their families. What are they fighting for, if not 
for our full First Amendment rights and norms in this country? Yet, we also know that 
tens of thousands of journalists have lost their jobs over the past 20 years, interestingly 
in tandem with the growth in public relations and “spin.” The military family stationed in 
Germany or Okinawa or Bahrain doesn’t need more “spin.” They need unfettered and 
real journalism. 
What I hope to see are the changes suggested by Stars and Stripes Ombudsman 
Jacqueline Smith, as explained in her May 30, 2024, column in the Stars and Stripes
(see: https://www.stripes.com/opinion/2024-05-30/limiting-stripes-reporters-harms-
stripes-readers-14030502.html).2 She calls for rules changes that will permit the 
journalists at Stars and Stripes to file Freedom of Information Act requests – just as 
other journalists are able to. She calls for rules changes that will no longer prevent Stars 
and Stripes from republishing classified or uncontrolled information that has already 
been published in other media. Why would we want to hide from military servicemen 
and women the same information being publicly reported by respected journalists

 
elsewhere? Lastly, she calls for rules changes that will ensure that Stars and Stripes
journalists are always permitted to cover events on installations to which they already 
have access and to interview personnel there. As Smith writes, Stripes journalists have 
already been vetted for security clearances by the federal government. Why vet them 
and then tie their hands? Why have journalists and not let them do real journalism?
As a former Stars and Stripes reporter myself, I regularly come across military veterans 
who ALWAYS tell me that they loved the newspaper when they were stationed 
overseas. Believe me, they don’t share those same sentiments or compliments about 
their military installation newspapers put out by the PR staff. Stripes’ unique and robust 
reporting has even been noticed and praised by international journalists, including one 
writing in The Times of London during the peacekeeping mission in the Balkans in 
1996.3
While describing the Stars and Stripes, Times reporter Roger Boyes praised the bravery 
of an “army newspaper” willing to “risk arguments with senior officers in writing about 
the daily realities of a battlefield unit.” That’s what real journalists have to do sometimes 
to tell the truth. Write rules that allow the reporters of this legendary news outlet to fulfill 
their historic mission just as other American journalists can do. 
Sincerely,
Cindy Elmore, Ph.D

We support FDA's goal of addressing education among tobacco retailers about compliance and enforcement of The Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act (Tobacco Control Act). 

We recommend that: 

1) As planned, encourage all tobacco retailers have a basic program that meets FDA proposed educational standards. Currently no requirement exists for retailers to implement education among their employees about compliance or enforcement of the Tobacco Control Act. An incentive to do so exists only if retailers have a documented violation of the Tobacco Control Act and want to avoid resulting fines. 

2) FDA could consider additional methods to provide an in-person educational training to tobacco retailers that receive citations for violating provisions of the Tobacco Control Act. We believe that if the FDA developed and implemented an in-person retailer education training program for those that have received citations, it may increase retailer compliance with provisions of the Tobacco Control Act. This is particularly true for retailers who may not allocate sufficient resources to their own retailer educational programs. Also, rather than relying on retailers to learn about the details of the Tobacco Control Act themselves, FDA may be ideally positioned to provide education to retailers. This is particularly true for lesser-known provisions of the Tobacco Control Act. For instance, while most retailers may be aware of the minimum age of sale, other provisions of the Tobacco Control Act (e.g., existence of self-service displays and vending machines) may be less obvious and therefore less likely to have compliance at the retail level. Evidence of this is found in publicly available warning letters, where the majority of warning letters from advertising and labeling inspections are for self-service displays [1]. In-person education to tobacco retailers that receive citations could help retailers better understand the role that the FDA plays regulating the marketing, advertising and sale of tobacco products, the rules of the Tobacco Control Act, and repercussions of violating the rules. FDA could consider ways of leveraging the already-existing FDA retailer inspections program, which sends adult FDA inspectors into tobacco retailers, for such in-person retailer training.

3) FDA could consider convening an in-person meeting of state and national experts and stakeholders on educational programs that may increase tobacco retailer compliance with the Tobacco Control Act. Evidence from a 2000 systematic review by Stead and colleagues [2] shows that retailer education alone may not be sufficient to maximize retailer compliance with federal tobacco sale regulations. Interventions which only supplied retailer education (often via a mailed informational packet) did not produce statistically significant decreases in sales of tobacco products to minors [3-5]. However, more intensive interventions that included in-person visits to retailers, community education and engagement, and media coverage had greater effects in terms of compliance with tobacco sale laws [6, 7]. An in-person meeting on educational programs to increase retailer compliance with the Tobacco Control Act may provide the opportunity for state and national experts and stakeholders to discuss innovative ways to complement retailer education with more intensive interventions and engagement. 

We believe these efforts to increase education of retailers could allow greater compliance with the Tobacco Control Act and one of its goals of improving rates of compliance with tobacco regulations among retailers.

Dear Mr. Lulli:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Rehabilitation Short-Term Training: Client Assistance Program (CAP) Proposed Priority from the U.S. Department of Education. The Minnesota Disability Law Center (MDLC), a division of Mid Minnesota Legal Aid and serving as Minnesota’s Protection and Advocacy (P&A) System, writes in support of some provisions and in opposition to other provisions of the proposed priority.

MDLC includes the federally funded Client Assistance Program (CAP). We provide civil legal representation and related advocacy services and investigates abuse and neglect of individuals with disabilities in a variety of settings. MDLC is proud to be part of the nationwide P&A and CAP Network that comprises the nation’s largest provider of legally-based advocacy services for persons with disabilities including advocacy on employment services to ensure people with disabilities who want to become employed can do so.
MDLC is dedicated to preserving the rights of people with disabilities. A particular focus of our work is the employment of individuals with disabilities. It is essential to have effective CAP programs in order to ensure that Vocational Rehabilitation (VR) clients receive the services they need and deserve.
Thank you for the significant revisions regarding the focus and requirements of this CAP training grant. We appreciate the renewed focus on the importance of legal advocacy and ongoing technical assistance involving both our cases and our clients. This approach will more effectively meet the needs of our CAP staff.
However, this proposed priority has a new emphasis about helping CAP staff to consider and understand the challenges that VR agencies face in trying to implement the expanded requirements of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act. While we think that it is always a good idea to learn about and understand all perspectives, we believe that the challenges of the VR agencies should not be used as a “shield” for not providing the quality services that all VR clients deserve. Moreover, CAPs face similar difficulties, so, at the very least, this approach should encompass both perspectives. 
A portion of this training requires that CAPs be prepared to provide assessments about the needs of the VR agencies using a variety of tools. It is unclear whether the National Disability Rights Network (NDRN) would have easy access to some of the suggested tools including the RSA 227 forms (e.g., the CAP Program Performance Reports) as well as the monitoring reports and feedback from VR clients in order to perform and/or provide training about the requested “targeted reviews”. 
There is also a greater emphasis on the strategic and fiscal needs of the CAPs throughout this proposed priority, relative to previous CAP short-term training grant iterations. NDRN has the knowledge and expertise to meet these needs, but additional funding would be needed to ensure adequacy of resources.

I am strongly opposed to USCIS-2020-0019; RIN 1615-AC61. This misguided rule, which dramatically and improperly alters the way in which H-1B registrations are selected for the annual H-1B statutory cap. This rule will stifle economic growth which is counterintuitive during this economic downturn. Further, this rule is wholly inconsistent with Congressional intent and in violation of the statute.

I have been a practicing business immigration attorney for 18 years. Many small and mid-size clients in the IT and biotech industries that I represent are gravely concerned about how this rule will significantly stunt their economic growth.

This Proposed Rule is a Clear Violation of the Statute and Congressional Intent:

The H-1B program was established by Congress to provide an avenue for employers to hire a foreign worker in a specialty occupation. This proposed rule is a clear violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which prioritizes the selection of H-1B cap-subject petitions in the "order in which they are filed" and does not limit who is selected for the H-1B cap to those employers who pay the most. USCIS lacks the statutory authority to make such a change and cannot use the statute's silence as an invitation to adopt criteria, such as wage level or skill level, to prioritize the selection of H-1B cap subject visas. 

This Proposed Rule is Based on a False Premise That Salary Alone Equates with Value: 

This proposal, which is based on the false premise that individuals who earn more in their profession contribute more to the economy or society, is yet another misguided and illegal attempt by the Trump administration to weaken our legal immigration and promote falsities about the workers who, contrary to what this rule implies, strengthen our economy.

If implemented, this rule will have a direct and negative impact on U.S. employers and college-educated foreign-born professionals by dramatically reducing access to the H-1B visa program for early-career professionals, including those completing Master's or Doctoral degrees at U.S. colleges and universities. Indeed, USCIS has acknowledged that if this new regulation is implemented, no individuals who are paid a Level 1 wage would be selected to submit a H-1B cap-subject petition for the annual H-1B cap. These proposed changes would effectively eliminate the H-1B program as an available visa option for new graduates seeking employment in an entry-level position.

USCIS Should Refrain From Implementing this Rule For the FY2022 H-1B Cap Filing Season:

Many U.S. employers and immigration attorneys start preparing for the H-1B cap filing season months in advance, in some cases as early as August depending on the industry. Any changes by USCIS to the H-1B cap filing process this late in the year would have an adverse impact on U.S. employers, immigration attorneys and individuals, as hiring decisions and filing processes and procedures have already been put in place by many employers and immigration law firms. Thus, if USCIS finalizes this illegal and misguided rule, USCIS must refrain from implementing it for the upcoming FY2022 H-1B cap filings season in order to allow U.S. businesses, immigration attorneys and individuals sufficient time to adapt to the new wage-based selection process.

I oppose The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) and Food Safety and Inspection Services (FSIS) proposed regulation for allow increases in slaughterhouse line speeds and in-house inspections by employees (United States Department of Agriculture, 2018). I support the aspect of the proposal that requires more pathogen sampling. 

The USDA and FSISs slaughterhouse testing through the HACCP-based Inspection Model Project (HIMP) did not conclusively prove that these increased line speeds and employee reporting mechanisms provide increased food safety. Specifically, there have been ten slaughtering plants operating under this more flexible rule since 1997. An audit in 2013 found many issues with these programs, including lack of oversight by the USDA, higher risks for food safety issues, and one slaughterhouse with more citations than any other slaughterhouse(Office of Inspector General, 2013). For example 73% of the non-compliance reports were due to carcass contamination, which this rule claims to help eliminate(Food & Water Watch, 2018). 

Despite the USDAs claim that there will be a continued 100% FSIS inspection, the number of inspectors at each swine slaughterhouse will likely decrease, as they move inspectors to offline, rather than online tasks. With less inspectors online and the allowance for increased line speeds, the task of identifying unsafe meat will naturally be more difficult. FSIS inspectors will individually have more hogs to look at and employees will now continue their same tasks, while having the added task of looking for bad hogs. This has critical implications for a more unsafe work environment for those employees in the slaughterhouses, as noted by the Government Accountability Project and Food & Water Watch (Whitworth, 2018). 

Food security is a very important issue, as every person consumes food every day, much of which is processed and grown by other people or companies. It is important that the mass production of food is done safely. This acknowledgement of need change is a step in the right direction, however some of the proposed changes may make this issue worse, rather than better.

The proposed rule to improve American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter training is essential for the future advancement of vocational and rehabilitation services for deaf, hard of hearing, and DeafBlind individuals. Interpreters will be instructed through redefined mentoring and coaching programs on how to cater to growing and diverse deaf communities. Great emphasis will be placed on enhancing the overall quality of remote-learning for individuals with hearing and sight impairment. The Department of Education also stated that it will make a conscious effort to take certain ethical considerations into account when dealing with complicated mental or behavioral health problems.
There has been an overwhelming amount of positive feedback regarding this issue due to the fact that if deaf, hard of hearing, and DeafBlind children and adults are taught with and to use innovative techniques and strategies, they will be able to lead independent lives without reliance on family members or caretakers. I am writing to comment on the Public Lands Rule and its goal of elevating conservation to equal footing with other uses of our BLM lands, consistent with the Federal Land Policy and Management Act [FLPMA] of 1976. This is a vital and overdue correction. I urge you to strengthen the rule in a number of ways before finalization. 

America's public lands offer some of the most readily available solutions for addressing the increase in drought conditions, storm impacts, catastrophic fires, and biodiversity loss across the West. For more than 40 years the BLM has prioritized resource extraction over other land uses to the detriment of wildlife, healthy ecosystems, cultural preservation, and climate resiliency.

It's time to balance the BLM's approach and elevate conservation to its proper standing in order to help sustain the nation's last wild landscapes and the plants, animals, and human communities that rely on them. The future of Utah's redrock country, where mining, off-road vehicle use, fossil fuel development, and other high-impact activities threaten sensitive ecosystems and cultural sites is critical. 

The draft rule is an important step forward, it must be strengthen in the following ways:

- Prioritize the inventory of intact natural landscapes, including lands with wilderness characteristics, at both the land use planning and project development stages. Ensure that any proposed development will not degrade such landscapes.

- As directed by FLPMA, prioritize the identification and designation of all eligible areas as Areas of Critical Environmental Concern and manage these areas appropriately.

- Require the BLM to consult with Tribes to ensure that it fully advances opportunities for incorporation of Indigenous Knowledge, respect for Tribal sovereignty and treaty rights, and protection of Tribal cultural sites.

- Conserve old and mature forests from logging, vegetation removal projects, wildfire, and climate change, informed by the best available science and Indigenous knowledge.

This administration has made a commitment to conserving and restoring America's public lands. Strengthen the Public Lands Rule and work to bring balance to BLM-managed landscapes.

To whom it may concern:
Terrebonne Parish has enjoyed a long partnership with FEMA in our joint effort to reduce flood and other risks. In that spirit, we have outlined our response to the proposed Agency Information Collection Activities, Proposed Collection: Comment Request; Property Acquisition and Relocation for Open Space Notice and Request for Comments on the Docket FEMA-2018-0006; OMB No. 1660-0103. We are encouraged by the flexibility of the land ownership options for buyouts, and concerned about the reduction in autonomy and increase in unfunded mandates for monitoring. A full comment is attached due to size constraints. 
FEMA is legitimately concerned about claims by severe repetitive loss properties, and the Parish participates regularly in the elevation programs for these and repetitive loss properties and appreciates the opportunity for this assistance. The Parish has less interest in buyouts for these or other properties due to the continuing obligations and real costs borne by the community. 
Severe Risk Property Acquisition (SRPA)
It is our understanding from the Federal Register Notice that FEMA intends to offer buyouts to SRL properties regardless of the state or local government decision not to provide buyouts in a particular area. This is helpful for those areas that do not, for whatever reason, have the capacity to run a buyout program, or those that have not competed well for funding. Other local governments have made a conscious decision not to buy more properties with FEMA funding due to legitimate factors such as the cost and loss of revenue.
Setting aside for a moment the loss of autonomy in deciding land use issues at the local government level, the details of the process are unclear. Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on NPRM, 85 Fed. Reg. 23266. The 
Disability Law Center (DLC) is Utah’s Protection and Advocacy (P&A) system and Client 
Assistance Program (CAP) under federal law for people with disabilities. Through the DLC’s 
CAP, we advise people with disabilities of the services available to them under the 
Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and advocate for the rights of people with disabilities in their 
relationships with these programs. The DLC reviewed the Department of Education’s NPRM, 85 
Fed. Reg. 23266, April 27, 2020, entitled “Proposed Priorities—Innovative Rehabilitation 
Training Program.” We submit the following comment, specific to Proposed Priority 1, 
“Innovative Rehabilitation Training Project, Client Assistance Program.” 
 
The proposed approach in Priority 1, which is similar to that described in Priorities 2 and 3 
governing the vocational rehabilitation training program, will not adequately meet the needs of 
CAP programs. The training needs of CAP staff are distinct from the beneficiaries of the other 
proposed priorities. CAP programs provide advocacy to clients of VR who may be experiencing 
disagreements with the services the VR program has provided, making the proposed approach in 
Priority 1 ineffective. The DLC does not see a need to merge the CAP training program with an 
academic program for VR professionals. The roles played by VR and CAP staff are distinct, one 
of counselor and one of legal advocate, and require very different training and skillsets. The CAP 
program, as the advocate for VR clients, may even have conflicting purposes and goals with the 
VR program. For example, the DLC’s CAP program has advocated for a broader interpretation 
of state VR policies when not in alignment with federal regulations. Although there is a need for 
some cross-training on VR services for CAP staff, joining these distinct entities for training 
purposes could damage the integrity of the programs. 
 
The proposed approach focuses on setting up an initial training within an academic setting. 
Although we agree that initial training is important, this framework does not adequately meet the 
needs of CAP staff. In addition to initial training, there is a great need for ongoing technical 
assistance and guidance that is responsive to the ever-changing needs of CAP programs. As a 
legally based advocacy program, we must remain up to date on changes in legislation, regulation 
and court decisions that may impact our work. The DLC’s CAP relies on the ability to consult 
with the National Disability Rights Network’s (NDRN) advocates and attorneys about fact-
specific cases in order to effectively serve our clients. NDRN assisted our CAP program to better 
understand the requirement of VR to provide higher education assistance where necessary and 
appropriate after having received a number of cases specific to this issue. This past year we have 
benefited from NDRN’s expertise both in individual cases, and in interpreting federal law. Our 
training and technical assistance needs are different from year to year and we are concerned that 
the framework described in Priority 1 too narrowly restricts the range of topics and type of 
assistance available to CAP staff. 
 
Additionally, this proposal fails to recognize the legally based advocacy requirements of CAP. 
CAP staff need to be trained on the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Rehabilitation 
Act. In addition to advocating for the rights of clients in the VR program, we must be able to 
inform VR eligible individuals of their rights and protections available under these laws. Utah’s

 
CAP regularly presents information to the public on the rights of individuals with disabilities 
under these acts in our public outreach on CAP and VR services.

higher incidence that minority populations suffer from various chronic diseases, and you end up

disincentive for providers to make these state-of-the-art drugs available to their patients. It is

pay separately for diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals.

missing habitat after almost one hundred years of absence, one does need to concede

harm is conjecture at this point, and the amount that we as a species have altered our 

woodlands and forests far outstrips any harm that the reintroduction of this native 

member could do. 

We can consider the possible harm that this action can bring on our forests, 

especially the Appalachian Temperate Forests. First and foremost is the sheer shock of 

reintroduction. As a species disappears from an environment, its absence shocks the 

community. Consumers, predators, apex predators and decomposers all have to adjust. 

It is well documented that in North America, various species of megafauna used to roam 

the eastern reaches. One such inhabitant we would be beside ourselves to learn about 

is the Jaguar, or the "Carolina Tyger" as one early explorer called it in the late 1600s. 

As shifting populations changed ecological relationships - the Jaguar started to 

disappear from the Gulf Coast. Buffalo and Elk became less common in the East - and 

plants such as Buffalo clover therefore were reduced to only a few locations. Later, in 

these areas, domesticated oxen replaced native Bison, which by then was making its 

famous retreat to the American West. It can be argued a return of the Bison to the 

American East would be environmentally traumatizing, and a return of the Jaguar would 

be not only environmentally, but socially so. However as humans, we fundamentally 

changed this environment when we arrived. Therefore, would returning the Bison be 

good or bad for the environment? Is it our obligation, or burden, or should it be avoided

caliber. This much could be said about many birds, such as the Ivory-Billed 

Woodpecker; or the Passenger Pigeon and the Carolina Parakeet. How about entire

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable. It is absolutely against American values to detain anyone indefinitely, but it is even more sickening that our nation would do this to children.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. This would be a souless mive against the welfare of children, and cannot be allowed to occur. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that

Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI), submits this comment urging you to withdraw the proposed rule on the Modernization of Swine Slaughter Inspection.

The Centers for Disease Control has estimated that over 500,000 people become ill and 82 die each year from foodborne illness attributable to pork. The goal of modernizing swine slaughter inspection should be to reduce these numbers by enhancing food safety and making pork safer. 

This proposal will not accomplish that goal. Instead, it puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by privatizing and deregulating aspects of swine slaughter inspection, lifting line speed caps and handing important government duties to industry while also removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

When the USDA finalized a similar rule for poultry in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed cap and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, the food-safety impact of poultry modernization has been uncertain.

While we support minor elements of the Proposed Swine Rule, the overall proposal will not substantially enhance food safety, and may even increase contamination and foodborne illness. We therefore urge you to withdraw the proposed rule. Any new modernization proposal offered in its place should aim to significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements.

Both Class 1 and 2 e-bikes with a maximum speed of 20 mph, and class 3 e-bikes with a maximum speed of 28 mph travel much faster than hikers, horseback riders, and traditional mountain bike riders. When on trails, e-bikes have a greatly increased risk of severe accidents and injuries with other people due to their speed.

The motorized mechanisms in e-bikes are prone to wheel slippage, and combined with their increased range and speed, would significantly increase wear and environmental degradation of trails. This would cause increased monetary cost for maintenance of trails, decrease the usability of trails and land, and overall is contrary to the Fish and Wildlife Service's purpose of protecting public land for the conservation and protection of wildlife, plants, and their habitats.

Finally, the speed, land wear, and noise due to e-bikes pose a severe threat to wild animals and livestock. These disruptions will harm animal populations, including those of endangered species, reducing their numbers and health on National Wildlife Refuge land, harming hunters, birders, and all people who enjoy the presence of wild animals and nature.

Reiterating, I strongly oppose all classes of e-bikes on all National Wildlife Refuge System land, and I urge the FWS to take my opinion and the factors I stated into consideration.

I am deeply concerned by the proposed, severe cuts to Medicare home health services in the Home Health Prospective Payment System Proposed Rule for CY 2023.

The law requires that Medicare expenditures for home health be budget neutral as CMS implements PDGM, but the new methodology results in significant reductions. In addition to a -7.69 percent permanent payment adjustment starting in 2023, the Proposed Rule forecasts additional cuts of more than $2 billion in 2024 for services provided to Medicare beneficiaries during the pandemic. Over the next decade, these proposed cuts total $18 billion. 

Cuts of this magnitude would be devastating to patients and providers. At a time when both demand for home health and the costs of delivering care are rising significantly, this proposal will significantly limit access to patient-preferred home health, especially among America's rural and medically underserved seniors. 

Further, the proposed methodology in the rule is technically flawed and counter to the intent of budget neutrality of the new payment system. The methodology for annually determining the impact of differences between assumed behavior changes and actual behavior changes on estimated aggregate expenditures and the related proposed permanent and temporary adjustments do not align with the requirements of the statute or its intent to ensure budget neutral rates. The agency also makes no attempt to compare the behaviors assumed by CMS in establishing the initial payment amounts for CY 2020 and the actual behavior observed on aggregate expenditures. Rather, CMS' proposal retroactively re-prices 2020 and 2021 claims payments to establish an artificial target amount and reduces the 30-day payment amounts under PDGM to meet that target. In effect, rather than ensuring the payment amounts are budget neutral, it constitutes an unauthorized rebasing of the 30-day payment amount. 

I hope you will reconsider the methodology to more accurately ensure budget neutrality while avoiding an unauthorized rebasing of the payment system. For the sake of the millions of seniors who rely upon the Medicare Home Health Benefit, please reconsider these cuts before finalizing the Proposed Rule.

to require that a project proponent request in writing a pre-filing meeting with EPA as the certifying authority at least 30 days before submitting a certification request

following notice of a section 401 certification, the EPA Administrator shall within 30 days notify neighboring jurisdictions in writing (dated) and state that the affected jurisdiction has 60 days to notify the EPA and the federal agency, in writing, whether or not the discharge will violate any of its water quality requirements and whether the jurisdiction will object to the issuance of the federal license or permit and request a public hearing from the federal agency. Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I'm sick of the government siding with producers instead of consumers. Your job is to work for citizens--not business.

Thank you for considering my request.

ARTICLE 6 - CONSENT 
1. Any preventive, diagnostic and therapeutic medical intervention is only to be carried out with the prior, free and informed consent of the person concerned, based on adequate information. The consent should, where appropriate, be express and may be withdrawn by the person concerned at any time and for any reason without disadvantage or prejudice.

The Department of Transportation should allow voice calls via passenger mobile wireless devices (Wi-Fi) on U.S. flights at the federal policy level, while letting each airline to freely formulate its own policies, under the condition that airlines must provide explicit notification and disclosure on their in-flight voice call policy to customers. While many would contend that this "deregulating" of the rules, would lead to more disturbances and safety risks to the passengers, and be a giveaway to large airline corporations at the expense of consumer protections, this could not be further from the truth. Implementing the new proposal by the Department of Transportation ensures that passengers are not unwillingly, and without their consent, exposed to bothersome voice calls; this only emboldens aviation consumer protections under the "unfair" and "deceptive" air transportation practice clauses of 49 U.S.C. 41712, while offering more freedoms to consumers who want to make voice calls.
Opponents of this new proposal contend that permitting voice calls could jeopardize the safety of those on the aircraft. They argue that a pro-voice calling policy leads to increased incidents of "air rage" between agitated passengers and put additional strains on the flight attendants (Association of Flight Attendants). Similar organizations also cite security concerns from the possibility of terrorists to exploit this new voice calling capability (Air Line Pilots Association). 
But both industry experts and foreign airlines who have already implemented voice-call-positive policies prove that claims of such calls jeopardizing safety to be completely baseless and untrue. Airlines such as Emirates, permitted voice calls since 2008, and maintain that "phone calls do not cause problems on our airplanes". Emirates passengers have "placed more than 1 million voice calls" and "the response of passengers to the service has been overwhelming positive" (Emirates). On the issue of "air rage", experts cite instead that "voice calls are rarely placed", and tend to be of short duration (Technology Industry Council). These experts also note that even in the extreme case of a "terrorist exploitation" (which is debunked by the International Institute for Counter-Terrorism), the pilots can simply disable voice calling capabilities at any time during the flight. 
But even if all these security threats were true, the Department of Transportation in this proposal should only be concerned (and only has authority) over aviation consumer protection. The Department is "not based on considerations of safety or security" (Department of Transportation). The FCC has authority over other technical issues and the FAA has authority over safety issues (Federal Register).
 Opponents also argue that voice calls are disturbing, especially so in a confined space such as an airplane cabin, and thus voice calls should be prohibited. Voice calls cause "annoyance", says Professor Whitbourne, "significant discomfort, invasion of privacy, lack of sleep, and other harmful effects" (University of Massachusetts) (Department of Transportation). 
Even if all the opposing arguments on the harmful disturbances of voice calls mentioned earlier were valid (which they are), they do not give sufficient merit for a full prohibition on the federal scale. Take for instance, train rides. The Department of Transportation does not have a federal voice calling ban policy of phones on cross-country trains (Federal Register), despite it also having confined spaces in a public setting. People are also trying to sleep, and crewmembers could potentially be strained from "railroad rage" between two agitated passengers, but there is no federal ban on voice calling imposed on the entire train industry. The Department of Transportation allows voice calling on cross-country trains on a broad federal scale, but also allows individual train companies to make their own policies to ban voice calling. The documentation supporting the revised proposed critical habitat is impressive; kudos to the

Thamnophis rufipunctatus and T. eques megalops, and do not reflect the opinion or positions of 

my employers. 

i. My overall assessment of the current revisions to the proposed critical habitat first released on 

July 10, 2013, is that the current significant reduction in critical habitat will jeopardize species 

recovery due to the limited delineation of critical habitat, which now apparently only includes 

“currently occupied habitat in areas that may require special management considerations or 

protection” (e.g. p. 23625). If the goal of the US Fish and Wildlife Service is to recover the 

species, this extremely narrow definition of “critical habitat” is not sufficient. Restricting 

designation of critical habitat to that which is currently occupied may contribute to the extinction 

of both species, due to currently highly fragmented populations (Woods et al. 2018), especially 

given that within the proposed critical habitat definitions, lateral extent may not include suitable 

hibernation (“brumation”) habitat, and that significant populations of the species have been 

proposed for exclusion. 

a. Such a narrow definition, which excludes “specific areas outside the geographical area 

occupied by the species at the time [of listing], upon a determination that such areas are 

essential for the conservation of the species.” (p. 23608, p. 23610), does not allow for natural 

range expansion into formerly occupied suitable habitat, nor expansion or repatriation into newly 

created suitable habitat, e.g., as a result of habitat restoration. 

b. This narrow definition also does not take into account future discovery of new populations, 

nor rediscovery of populations currently thought to be extirpated that may be (or have been) 

discovered since the initial proposed critical habitat designation. New populations of both 

species are still being discovered, e.g., a new population of T. rufipunctatus on Reservation 

Creek (Apache County, Arizona) in 2016 by Bergamini et al. (2017), and a population of T.

This letter is in response to the proposed rule change by the Federal Aviation Administration concerning The Medical Certification Standards for Commercial Balloon Operations. I am writing this response to proposed rule change, in hopes that the FAA will consider all testimonies being made about the proposed rule change, and will not put the Rule Change in to effect as written.
Commercial Hot Air Balloon operations take in so many different facets that need to be considered. Commercial Hot Air Balloon Pilots have the Commercial rating for many different reasons. There are pilots, that fly Corporate balloons, perform tethered operations for events, fly special shapes, fly corporate banners and advertising, train new pilots, preform biannual flight check rides for other pilots, attend organized events around the country and fly passengers for the event organizers, operate small businesses providing occasional Hot Air Balloon Flights, for 3-6 passengers. and then you have the pilots that fly large balloons that can carry more than six passengers up to 20 passengers.
​History shows that the majority of Hot Air Balloon incidents and accidents, occur from the large ride balloon (8 or more passengers), and not so much from the smaller activities that require a commercial license.
If the proposed Standards for Rule Change is actually imposed as written, it will have far over reaching consequences, for other industries that are part of the aviation industry. This proposed change will not only effect more than 3000 pilots that currently hold a commercial pilot license for Hot Air Balloons, but it will also have an effect, on, Flight Training schools, repair stations, insurance companies, and even affect the decision of future people thinking about becoming a licensed Hot Air Balloon Pilot.
This proposed change in the Standards requiring a Second Class Medical Statement across the board of all pilots that hold commercial licenses, it will also create a logistics night mare for the FAA itself. The tracking and oversight of such a regulation will further overburden the FAA system. 
At the present time there is a very small amount of Doctors that are certified to do a 2nd class medical. With the passage of tis new standard, even the doctors that are approved by the FAA to preform these medical exams will be over burdened, The time frame of 180 days for compliance to obtain the 2nd class medical is not enough time. This time frame if implemented should be atleast one year, to allow all persons involved, time to comply. 
With the limited amount of Pilots that carry a commercial Hot Air Balloon License, that are currently training new pilots, the growth in the industry will come to a near standstill, if commercial pilots are forced to obtain a 2nd class medical exam. Most new pilots come from being part of a Hot Air Balloon team, and decide to work with their pilots to obtain their own pilots license. If the commercial pilot is unable to teach or continue their small business, because of a mandatory rule change, the Hot Air Balloon Aviation industry will slowly become a thing of the past.
In final thoughts, I urge the committee to table this proposal in order to consider all the ramifications of the change. I further urge the committee that if they do go forward, to do it in three phases. First only Balloon Pilots that fly large balloons that can carry 8 or more passengers be required to obtain the 2nd class medical exam. The second phase would be to add more FAA personnel that are trained in the operations of Hot Air Balloons, including adding more DPE Flight examiners. The third phase would be after one year to put together a realistic 3-5 year program, and then revisit the proposed rule change, and look at the historic data, to see if the change is actually necessary. 
Please Please listen to the leaders in our industry concerning Hot Air Balloons, especially the Balloon Federation of America (BFA), before any changes are made.

Respectfull

And while most of my experience is in low-income urban communities, I know a majority of Americans face similar challenges. So many of our citizens experience our food system as desserts of healthy produce, and swamps of highly processed, high sodium foods. 

Given the current state of our food system, and the lack of progress in reducing sodium in the American diet, federal regulation of some kind becomes essential to modulate the food companies practice of adding sodium to foods in efforts to protect the health and wellness of our citizens.

This is a crucial opportunity for the FDA to not only encourage sodium reductions, but also to encourage the reduction of processed foods in general. I firmly oppose the Department of Transportation's proposed rule to "[allow] passengers to make voice calls using mobile wireless devices." Permitting the airlines to set their own policies on this issue would create large-scale market failure. Specifically, this measure would increase the risk of "air rage," traumatizing passengers while making cabin crews' duties substantially more onerous. Analyzing this rule makes clear that, from the perspective of consumer protection, costs to passengers far outweigh the benefits. 

First, "air rage" is a problem that passengers and flight crews already face at alarming rates. In September 2016, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) reported that aircraft incidents involving unruly passengers had increased by 16%. Most incidents involved what the IATA described as "anti-social" behavior, which includes verbal abuse and disobeying cabin crew members. In 11% of cases, aircraft employees reported physical aggression, and/or damage to the plane. According to IATA data, one in every 1,205 flights will involve an incident of air rage. Given that passengers and flight crew cannot leave an airplane in flight, any cases of abuse would create significant costs for their safety and mental health. 

Logic dictates that voice calls could create tension in an already fraught environment, increasing rates of air rage. For example, if a passenger discussed adult topics over the phone, parents might become upset over their children's exposure to such language. Passengers might also become irritated at someone for speaking too loudly. These conflicts would be exacerbated by the annoyed passengers' inability to exit until the plane landed. Further, many passengers might be belligerent, due to interruptions in their sleep cycles caused by late or early flights. Hence, allowing voice calls on planes could significantly increase incidents of air rage, creating market failure. 

Empirical evidence also indicates that voice calls would increase air rage. In 2012, researchers explored causes of air rage through a peer-reviewed report, entitled: "Physical and situational inequality on airplanes predicts air rage." The authors noted that "situational inequality" had a significant, positive correlation with air rage incidents in economy class. Situational inequality involves an unequal distribution "in physical space or amenities" that has particular "salience" to the individual. Allowing voice calls on a plane would likely increase situational inequality. Similar to in-air wifi, these calls would almost certainly be a paid service - an amenity only wealthier customers could afford. Further, the noisy nature of voice calls would draw passengers' attention to the inequity, increasing its salience. Given the above research, allowing voice calls through mobile wireless devices would thereby increase rates of air rage. 

Certain commentators might argue that voice calls could benefit passengers by increasing their in-flight productivity. However, this assertion conflicts with travelers' overwhelming support of an in-air ban on voice calls. For example, a 2013 poll from Quinnipiac University found that 60% of Americans oppose allowing phone calls during flights. Further, an Associated Press-GfK survey from the same year reported that only 19% of respondents supported voice calls on planes. As such, there exists no consensus among travelers that their in-flight productivity would be increased through voice calls. Additionally, passengers already have numerous opportunities to work via digital devices; many airlines currently allow customers to access wifi through wireless mobile devices.
