Comment: Although the Minnesota Department of Transportation, Office of Transit and Active Transportation, is not a transit employer, our onsite drug and alcohol program compliance reviews have found that many of our subrecipients that provide rural transit service continue to experience difficulties with the limited availability of DOT testing service providers during all hours of the day and days of the week that safety-sensitive functions are performed, specifically outside of normal collection site business hours and weekends. Mobile collectors, if available, are increasingly unwilling to provide their testing services that comply with the requirement for random testing to be unpredictable and spread throughout all days of the calendar year and times of day that safety-sensitive functions are performed. Some mobile collectors won’t provide a DOT testing service without a minimum number of employees to test on the same day within a limited timeframe. In addition to saliva alcohol testing, oral fluid drug testing will provide rural transit employers with a quick and efficient testing option under direct observation conditions. Oral fluid drug testing will provide an opportunity for employers to train a non-supervisory employee to provide onsite DOT drug testing.

Section IV. Principal Policy Considerations, Page 11160. We also seek comment on whether remote virtual evaluations and assessments should be limited to certain circumstances, e.g., natural disasters, pandemic situations, and where there are few or no SAPs available.

We support the option for the employer or employee to choose either in-person or remote virtual evaluations and assessments with a SAP.

As someone who’s concerned with the welfare of horses, I’m disappointed to learn the U.S. Department of Agriculture has proposed withdrawing its 2017 rule to protect horses from the cruel practice of soring under the Horse Protection Act (HPA). I sincerely hope that a timeline will be announced for a new one, or that the rulemaking be reissued until further action can be taken. 
 
While the HPA ought to be sufficient to protect horses, decades later they are still being subjected to soring. The 2017 rule included provisions that would disallow the industry from continuing to self-police with the use of DQPs, and ban the use of chains and other action devices used to sore horses. 
 
Over 100,000 public comments were submitted on the proposed rule, while hundreds of members of Congress also wrote in support.
 
The USDA must act expediently to end this cruelty, which continues to plague the Tennessee walking horse industry and affect other gaited breeds. 

I do not support withdrawing this rule without the introduction of new regulations to ban soring, and I hope a rule will be quickly introduced that incorporates new information, including recommendations found in the 2021 National Academies of Science report, “Review of Methods for Detecting Soreness in Horses.”

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Neal Marchuk

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

No deceptive labeling please. Consumers should not be mislead to buying humanely raised chicken when it isn't true. This is wrong for both the farm animals as well as for consumers.

Subject: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002 - Public Comment Opposing Proposed Rule
 

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

As a former legal advocate for survivors of domestic and sexual violence, and a current advocate for victims of crime, I know that detaining children away from the comfort and stability of their families creates lifelong trauma with negative, collateral impacts on communities. I strongly oppose the detention of children and families, and urge lawmakers to say "No" to regulations that would compromise children's safety, and undermine the Flores Settlement Agreement.
 

Sincerely,
 
Kimberly Jordan
Burlington, Vermont

Dear Administrator Andrew Wheeler,

I strongly oppose the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) proposal to restrict the science that is used in its decision-making processes.

contrary to the title of the bill, it makes science LESS transparent. This is suspicious timing, to say the least, when most of America is otherwise occupied with corona virus, and it seems like you are trying to pull a fast one.

Science needs to be available for policy making, otherwise, what is the point? And why would we not want to use science to it's full advantage?

In issuing this proposed rule, the EPA claims that it would be making science more transparent. But it instead would put researchers in the difficult position of choosing between protecting privacy and security versus allowing their work to be used in EPA decision-making. It would excessively burden EPA staff with reanalyzing data from each study used to support a rule-making which is not only pointless as peer review already is a check on the work of researchers, but it would be resource intensive and time consuming.
 
The EPA's proposed rule has three fundamental flaws that render it unfeasible. 

First, the agency provides insufficient justification and analyses to support the rule. The proposal includes no analyses of the rule's effect on the EPA's mission-related work, the costs or benefits of such a move, and the problem that such a rule is addressing.

Second, the proposal would restrict the agency's ability to implement and enforce mission-critical laws by blocking the EPA from using many kinds of scientific studies vital to its decisionmaking, including studies that rely on personal health data, confidential business information, intellectual property, or older studies for which the authors or data sources may not be accessible. 

Finally, the rule would grant the EPA administrator broad authority to exclude individual studies or entire decisions from being subject to its provisions on a case-by-case basis, giving the administrator unprecedented power to decide what the best available science is. 

The rule does nothing to advance the cause of transparency in the broader scientific community. This issue is best addressed with the full involvement of scientists, science advisors, and scientific institutions, not designed solely by political appointees.

The EPA must not move forward with this rulemaking as it would undermine science-based decisionmaking at the agency, and limit its ability to protect public health and the environment.

Sincerely,
Mary Ferm

As I read this proposal for the refunding of baggage fees, I feel that I am uniquely qualified to comment as I have been on both sides of the baggage delay issue. In a previous career, I worked for Delta Airlines at the Baggage Service Center as a Customer Service Manager and now as a Government contractor, I have had to travel quite a bit and so I have both been a victim of a delayed bag as well as having to listen to angry customers about their bags. With that being said, I read six questions that need to be addressed in this proposal. 

Question 1 deals with the appropriate length of time to trigger the refund of the baggage fee. This is probably the toughest question to answer in this proposal. From the airline perspective, a 12-hour window is probably enough time for an airline to be able to deliver a bag without having to refund the baggage fee. Because airlines deal with hundreds of thousands of bags daily and trying to locate one of those bags is similar to finding a needle in a haystack and does require time. Also, if a bag gets put on the wrong flight it obviously takes time for the bag to get back onto a flight that gets to where the passenger is located. Anyone who is traveling would argue that their bag needs to land with them because they paid for that exact service. If the airlines are going to charge a baggage fee, then they need to deliver as charged. I am a law student currently residing in Oregon. I have been interested in immigration law at a personal level since I was 8 years old, and I have had the opportunity of learning about and working in immigration law for the past two years. 

There's absolutely no doubt in my mind that, taken as a whole, DACA is a net-positive program. Since its inception, DACA has faced many challenges from those who wish to deprive and marginalize immigrant communities. The benefits of DACA are all-encompassing. DACA helps provide stability to this nation at local, statewide, and national levels. 

I don't know a single person who's plans from March 2020 onward were not derailed. For many of us, we felt short and long term instability for the first time. We learned how difficult it can be to make plans and goals that are months or even just week away. 

For DACA recipients, this uncertainty is nothing new. DACA recipients know they have a limited, pre-determined time they can plan ahead for. Their future plans depend on the legal limbo that has been surrounding DACA for nearly 10 years now. It is worth remembering that DACA recipients are not immune to the effects of the pandemic - for them, the levels of uncertainty are tenfold. 

DACA does a lot to provide at least some stability to undocumented youth. DACA allows these undocumented youth to work and study, becoming integral pieces to their community. This in turn fortifies the country's workforce and allows these individuals to stimulate the U.S. economy. But more importantly, DACA allows these individuals to feel like they have a home. 

I thoroughly support DACA for both the micro and macro positive impacts it has on this country. However, I think the program can be strengthen even further, and doing so would multiply such positive impacts. 

First, I am worried that the proposal to separate work authorization from the DACA
application will mean that many DACA recipients will not receive their work
authorization in a timely manner or at all. I believe deferred action and work authorization should remain connected within the program. This is the most efficient route. 

Second, I support Advance Parole for DACA recipients “for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit.” USCIS should interpret this expansively to not restrict DACA recipients’ travel abroad to employment, educational, or humanitarian purposes only. This broader definition allows undocumented youth to fulfill goals and experiences they have, just like we all do. As integral members to society, they should have the opportunity for these experiences. 

Lastly, and perhaps most importantly, I strongly support expanding DACA eligibility. DACA is currently only available to those who can demonstrate that they have “continuously resided in the United States from June 15, 2007, to the time of filing of the request.” 86 C.F.R. §§ 53766-67. I do not support this limitation. The June 15, 2007 continuous presence start date was five years before President Obama created DACA by Executive Action and it has not been changed since then. I strongly encourage that USCIS creates a new continuous presence start date that is five years before the publication of this proposed rule. Additionally, DACA is currently only available to those who were born on or after June 16, 1981 and entered the U.S. before they turned 16. 86 C.F.R. § 53766. I do not support this limitation. It excludes undocumented immigrants who came to the U.S. as children, but were born before June 16, 1981. These undocumented immigrants likely have longer residency in the U.S. than many of the current DACA recipients. The current cutoff date seems far too arbitrary. Thank you.

BLM’s proposed rule to require public land use planning to consider “conservation” as well as the implementation of conservation leases is a step in the right direction. To make the rule as effective as possible, the BLM should clarify and strengthen language around listing “conservation” as a primary use of a public land. The BLM’s proposed rule has potential to fall victim to the outcome of many American environmental regulations in that its language is theoretically beneficial but lacks the teeth of enforcement to make any difference. The agency’s own summary states that “the proposed rule does not prohibit land uses that impair ecosystem resilience; it simply requires avoidance and an explanation if such impairment cannot be avoided.” The language was understandably chosen to appease grazers, miners, and silviculture who fear their extraction rights may be in jeopardy. Indeed, the rule, like many, exposes the struggle between enforcing economic versus environmental rights. However, there is a big difference between “considering” a conservation use and “requiring” a conservation use. 

The legislative history of environmental regulations like CERCLA and the Clean Water Act has proven that industry is eager to exploit loopholes and weak statutory language. In just one case out of many, the Hanford Downwinders Coalition brought a citizen suit against the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) citing compelling evidence that radioactive emissions from the government’s Plutonium reactors near Hanford, Washington between 1940 and 1949 had been responsible for a spate of thyroid diseases and cancers in the area. The Coalition argued that the government’s own assessments had implicated Hanford in exposing the public to huge doses of radiation and that the ATSDR was therefore obligated to perform further health-related activities as mandated by the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA), especially as Hanford had been elevated to the National Priorities List. However, the weak language allowing citizen suits to challenge agency activities also allowed federal judge after federal judge to dismiss citizen suits under CERCLA’s “timing of review” statues, including the Hanford Downwinders’ suit. Moreover, the government spent millions of dollars litigating these suits which is money that could have been spent on expanded health-related activities or clean-up. Interestingly, the judicial decision in the Hanford Downwinders case cited an era of “fiscal austerity” as an argument for dismissing the Downwinders’ claims.

Item 1: Thank You for Allowing Hospitals to Bill on the UB-04

The UB-04 claim is the appropriate claim form for reporting institutional services. CMS has clarified in the Interim Final Rule that non-excepted PBD services are institutional services and therefore billable on the UB-04. As hospital-owned and operated departments, CMS confirmed that non-excepted departments will be reported as full-fledged cost centers on the hospital cost report. Because both excepted and non-excepted locations are provider-based departments, their services should always be billable on an institutional claim form. Therefore, I hope CMS will maintain the requirement to bill on the UB-04 claim form and not ever require the use of a 1500 claim form for institutional billing as this would result in significant administrative burden for hospitals. 

Item 2: Please Ensure that Sub-Regulatory Guidance on Cost Reporting is Consistent with Current Practices

I've received a number of questions about how the agency will direct hospitals to account for the services provided in non-excepted off-campus PBD in their cost reports and in the associated PS&R reports. At a high level-- I would assume that services provided in non-excepted off-campus PBDs would be treated just as the services reported by clinical laboratory departments on the cost report and PS&R. CLFS is a separate payment system from OPPS, but generates payments that must be tracked by both CMS and the hospital, and that's the same situation here with the "applicable payment system" (MPFS) under Section 603. In practice, the clinical lab department or departments show up individually in the hospital's general ledger and aggregate to a unique cost center on the cost report. The PS&R shows the revenue paid under the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) on a separate PS&R type (xx5) from that paid (i.e., packaged) under the OPPS (xxP). Likewise, for non-excepted PBDs, Medicare patient care revenue will be provider revenue, but the PS&R will show the portion paid under the "applicable payment system," currently the MPFS. I assume that the non-excepted PBDs' charges/payments are on a separate PS&R which is not included on the cost report (similar to CLFS claims), meaning: 

 For excepted PBDs, the charges should remain on the OPPS PS&R types (xxP), because they continue to be paid at the OPPS rates and reported on the cost report.

 Hospitals will bill excepted PBDs for on-campus services without any PBD modifiers and excepted off-campus services with PO modifier. Both of these services should remain on the OPPS PS&R types (xxP) for proper inclusion on the cost report.

 Hospitals will bill non-excepted off-campus PBD services with PN modifier. These services would be reported on a separate, non-PPS PS&R, similar to the Clinical Lab Fee Schedule (xx5) to ensure these claims are not included as OPPS services in the cost report.

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. I am a Registered Dietitian Nutritionist (RDN), and I do not support labeling human food products as "healthy." Foods may be healthful, nutritious, or health-promoting, but the types of foods can vary depending on each individual's health status. For example, someone with kidney disease may need to limit foods high in phosphorous, which include foods like whole grains, beans, peas, lentils and nuts. These foods are typically considered "healthy" to many people, but may not be health-promoting for certain individuals. While this may help to reduce decision fatigue for consumers when comparing products, I believe that people should have the ability to decide which foods are "healthy" for them, rather than rely on a label that is based on general standards that do not consider individual health needs. "Healthy" should not be used essentially as a marketing tool, as this invites businesses to take advantage of the term for promotion of profits rather than health. By allowing companies to utilize this term to brand food products, I am concerned that this will negatively influence public knowledge of what is considered "healthy" for them by encouraging consumers to rely on businesses, rather than credentialed health professionals for individualized nutritional information.

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Officials, 

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on portions of your existing Mitigation Policy and Endangered 

Species Act Compensatory Mitigation Policy (ESA-CMP). From my perspective, as a wildlife 

professional for 35 years, I believe the policies' overall mitigation planning goals must retain “net 

conservation gain” consistent with the former Memorandum on Mitigating Impacts on Natural Resources 

From Development and Encouraging Related Private Investment (November 3, 2015). Effective 

mitigation is a powerful tool for furthering the Service’s essential mission to conserve, protect, and 

enhance fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats to the continuing benefit of the American people for 

current and (especially) future generations. 

“Mitigation,” as broadly defined in current policy, “measures to avoid, minimize, and compensate for 

impacts” is an essential means of achieving the overarching purpose of the ESA (to conserve listed 

species and the ecosystems upon which they depend), and the current mitigation policies provide 

guidance for doing so most effectively. The changes made to these mitigation policies in 2016 were 

based on numerous growing conservation challenges and practices, including accelerating loss, 

degradation, and fragmentation of habitats; effects of climate change, human population growth and other 

new threats; and advances in fish and wildlife conservation science. These challenges and practices 

remain today and are expected to increase in future years in the USA and worldwide. Designing 

mitigation that ensures a ‘‘net conservation gain’’ in the status of affected resources is imperative to 

address the additive impacts that lead to significant deterioration of resources over time, to foster recovery 

of listed species, and perhaps most significant, to avoid listing of additional species. This is an obligation 

of the Service as an administrator of the ESA. 

As of the end of 2016, more than 1,500 species listed have been listed under the ESA since its 

inception. While the challenges of protecting biodiversity are great, the ESA is working, and mitigation 

policy is a key to its continued success. Without a commitment to responsible and implementable 

standards and polices for accomplishing effective, sustainable mitigation that more than fully offsets the 

adverse impacts of actions to listed species and other resources of concern, these species and resources 

are unlikely to recover and persist. Mitigation with a “net conservation gain” is necessary because an 

accurate accounting of the functions and services lost at impact sites and gained at mitigation sites is 

rarely possible due to the variability and uncertainty inherent in biological systems and ecological 

processes. Programs and projects should be designed to achieve mitigation beyond no net loss in order to 

effectively buffer risk, reduce uncertainty, and ensure sufficient conservation benefits for species to 

promote their recovery. 

Since its inception in 1940, USFWS has been strongly science-based and consistently has taken a 

precautionary approach to protecting our biological resources. Please do not succumb to short-term 

political objectives. The American people are counting on your integrity. Please retain all the 

fundamental principles for guiding mitigation as defined in the 2016 policies (a -h) across all Service 

programs, especially maintain the the goal of “net conservation gain.” Finally, rescinding this important 

mitigation policy goal of net conservation gain is not necessary to achieve the economic goals of the 

Secretary of the Interior's Order 3349 on American Energy Independence (March 29, 2017). 

Sincerely, 

Fred W. Koontz, Ph.D. 

Duvall, WA

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

Webster Street

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

As the owner of a 1946 Piper J3 Cub airplane, I am writing to comment on the Proposed Airworthiness Directive that will mandate the replacement of rudders on certain Piper aircraft, including the Piper J3 aircraft, that are constructed of type 1025 Carbon Steel. Because I frequently fly with my family members and friends, safety of flight is always foremost on my mind. As an aircraft owner, I’m also keenly aware of the costs associated to maintain our aircraft in airworthy condition. As such, I believe that all AD’s for our aircraft must be carefully considered, scientifically justified, and must have a demonstrable effect on overall safety of flight.

After careful consideration, I believe that the proposed Airworthiness Directive is overly broad by including the Piper J3 airframe in the draft document. It is my understanding that the rudder failures that prompted the proposed AD occurred in PA-12 and PA-14 model aircraft equipped with 150 HP engines, and rudder mounted anti-collision lights. The higher horsepower engines and the presence of the rudder mounted lights surely put more aerodynamic and bending loads on these aircraft rudders that would not be present in the J3 airplane. Moreover, the Piper J3 airframe utilizes a completely different rudder (P/N 41313) than the accident aircraft (P/N 40622) – being different in both overall shape and area.

Further, I don’t believe that there is any evidence to suggest that airframes such as the Piper J3, which are limited to 90 HP, should be included in the proposed AD. These aircraft, by virtue of their slower operating speeds, place significantly lower loads on the rudder. These aircraft also lack the rudder mounted anti-collision light of the accident airplanes. Piper J3 aircraft have operated for 86 (!) years without a single documented case of rudder failure. This fact alone seems to outweigh the small number of failures occurring on dissimilar aircraft, which prompted this action.

In summary, I believe the proposed AD will place a significant financial burden on Piper J3 owners like myself without a commensurate increase in the safety of these slower, and lower horsepower airframes. I therefore respectfully request that Pipe J3, and other similar Piper models, that might be subject to this proposed AD be excluded from the AD process. 

 
John Morley

Dear FWS Staff:
Please do not weaken protections for the Greater Sage Grouse, a bird already in steep decline!
 
Thank you for considering this comment on the proposed Threatened listing of and critical habitat designation for the Bi-State Greater Sage-Grouse. Protection under the Endangered Species Act is urgently needed for the Bi-State population and its remaining habitat. Due to its small size and severely degraded habitat condition, I believe that Endangered status is warranted rather than the proposed Threatened listing.

The range of the Bi-State Sage-Grouse distinct population segment (DPS) has been reduced by nearly 50 percent, and the remaining habitat is poor. In addition to habitat loss, the estimated population of Bi-State Sage-Grouse has declined by over 90 percent from historic levels, while the number of leks staging areas for breeding birds has declined by close to two-thirds. Experts believe the effective population size for the entire Bi-State Sage-Grouse DPS could be as low as 230 and only as high as 770 birds.

The federal Bi-State Sage-Grouse Conservation Action Plan 2017 Progress Report reveals that the number of grouse at lek sites is in decline in most areas. In California, the count declined 21% from 2016 to 2017 in Mono County and was down 31% in the Bodie Hills. In Nevada, the population was down 2% at lek sites overall and fell 19% at Mount Grant. Only Nevadas Desert Creek population showed an uptick (5.5%). 

These declines are particularly worrisome considering the cyclical nature of grouse populations. Based on historical population trends, the Bi-State population was due for a significant uptick. Instead, it appears the overall downward trend continues. Given the grouses low population, along with the risks of drought and habitat degradation, I believe the strongest level of protection is warranted.
I
m also concerned about the proposed 4d rule that would accompany the Bi-State populations listing as Threatened. The Bi-State area is already heavily impacted by roads, power lines, and fences in addition to cell towers and waste dumps. The proposed 4d rule is very broad, and its acceptance of grazing in areas occupied by sage-grouse may result in nest destruction or abandonment. Grazing is inappropriate in areas where this dwindling grouse population hangs on to survival. 

For all of these reasons, I ask that you list the Bi-State Greater Sage-Grouse as Endangered. Thank you for time and consideration of this matter.

Sincerely,

Adirondack Medical Center strongly supports the proposed improvements to the VDA calculation, however we urge CMS to go further and extend its proposal to apply to VDA determinations both prospectively and retrospectively. 

Under the proposal, substantial repayments demanded from VDA hospitals would continue unchanged even though use of the newly proposed VDA calculation standards retrospectively would greatly mitigate the recoupment amounts. In addition, other adverse VDA determinations would remain in place when use of the new calculation would result in favorable VDA determinations and access to the payment adjustment.

If CMS does not extend its proposal, VDA determinations would severely lack in consistency and hospitals would be inequitably denied an adjustment or be required to repay funds based on use of a superseded calculation. Simply put, critical hospital funding should not be at risk due to admitted lack of clarity in rules and lack of standardization across CMS and MAC decisions.
 
To align past VDA determinations with CMS' proposal, we request that CMS:
 
 Instruct NGS to recalculate the previously issued recoupment demands to align with its newly proposed calculation standard.
 
 Instruct NGS to re-review and reissue past VDA determinations for open cost reports based on the retroactive application of the newly proposed calculation standardregardless of whether the hospital appealed the VDA determination.
 
 Allow hospitals with open cost reports that have been unable to apply for VDA requests under the current methodology to submit VDA requests under the newly proposed calculation standard. 
 
Additionally, given that many VDA determinations are under appeal for various reasons, we urge CMS to apply its proposals retroactively while maintaining all appropriate appeal rights.
 
Adirondack Medical Center appreciates CMS' consideration of these alignment requests. Standardized VDA decisions both prospectively and retrospectively are critical to maintain fairness with Medicare funding decisions.

However, in the latest HPA updates the USDA plans to add inspections at stock horse events without evidence of wrongdoing.

The USDA is not staffed to handle the thousands of shows that would be added to the list of events subject to inspection. AQHA alone held 1,923 events in 2023 compared to the Tennessee Walking Horse (TWH) breed which held approximately 80 in 2023 and 59 in 2024. The largest 5 AQHA shows in 2023 had entries totaling between 31,822 and 8,608. By comparison in 2021 there were 209 Tennessee Walking Horse events with a total of 49,002 entries. This would be an average of 234 entries per show. There are single classes and divisions at large AQHA shows that have more entries than the average Tennessee Walking Horse Show.

As of March 21, 2025, the USDA had 67 potential contract inspectors identified and of this number 17 had receive training. The list of “Designated Qualified Persons” (DQPs) eligible to conduct inspection under the current rules totals 68. So as of the start of this comment period the USDA had just enough potential inspectors to replace the DQPs. USDA/APHIS is just barely staffed to cover the Tennessee Walking Horse Events. APHIS is ill prepared to take on the entire equine industry.

AQHA has a proven stewardship program in place. All shows are accessed a fee for drug testing which is unannounced and random. The AQHA Stewards program places certified individuals at shows in the capacity to oversee the stalls, warm up areas and show pens. Stewards monitor for inhumane treatment of horses, illegal equipment, unsportsmanlike conduct, and unsafe conditions such as poor footing. Stewards not only patrol the riding areas but also stalls. Also, all carded judges have commitment to AQHA to remove any horse from the show pen that exhibits unsoundness. AQHA also has a Professional Horseman Association. Members adhere to the highest standards of personal and professional integrity. Their job is to set the bar high in demonstrating quality horsemanship and training methods. This group educates youth and amateur riders in best practices and has been a positive asset to the association. Members of AQHA’s Professional Horseman’s Association have also committed to intercede at shows where and when needed.

In all my years of being a vet tech, a breeder of AQHA horses and exhibitor at AQHA approved shows I have never witnessed any acts of intentional soring therefore I see no need for APHIS to expand inspection coverage outside that of the Tennessee Walking Horse Industry. I feel that APHIS needs to concentrate efforts to where the problem is not where it is not.

My name is Elizabeth Rush Mueller. I am an Affiliated Fellow at the Institute at Brown University for the Environment and Society. As someone who has studied and written about buyouts in coastal communities around the United States over the past half a decade, I strongly recommend that when FEMA proceeds to purchase and demolish a flood-prone property they must keep the land associated with the property as open space in perpetuity. Over the past half a decade I have carried out hundreds of interviews in coastal communities where buyouts are an option. Time and time again residents would tell me that they were only interested in participating in a buyout if the property would become open space in perpetuity. They were often adamantly opposed to participating in a buyout if the land were going to be redeveloped. That is because many of the coastal communities where buyouts make the most immediate financial sense are low-middle-income communities. And as I found, those who have the least are often more reluctant to give up their small share, especially if others will turn a profit. Or a Joe Tirone, the leader of the grassroots buyout campaign that swept across Staten Island in the wake of Hurricane Sandy told me, "One of the biggest concerns [residents had when deciding whether or not to participate in the buyout] was that the land was going to be redeveloped. It was a lower-middle-class neighborhood, and everyone was pretty much at the same level of wealth or lack of wealth. If their homes were going to be given to a rich person, or if they were going to be knocked down so some developer could build a mansion or a luxury condo, they were not leaving. They'd stay there, they'd rot there, they'd drown there, but they were not leaving." 

If FEMA wishes to acquire a building, in accordance with the law, it must acquire the property. Investing a large amount of taxpayer funds to pay for the pre-flood market value of a home should result in the public benefit of the deed-restricted land so that no future disaster assistance is provided on it, so that there is no flood insurance available on it (another potential taxpayer exposure).

I think you will find that it was, amongst many other things, a desire for justice and bettering the common good. Were you to allow purchased properties to be redeveloped you would be jeopardizing these aims and would likely lead future buyouts to fail while also costing taxpayers money. Indeed, it is likely as difficult or more so to complement inactivating mutation(s) or loss of plasmid in B. anthracis conferring attenuation than in other bacterial select agents. The retention of Pasteur type strains on the select agent list has hindered work on the anthrax capsule.

Comments on section 111.23 Retention of Records
Section 111.23 sets forth the location in which a broker may retain its records relating to customs transactions. Currently, paragraph (a) provides that a customs broker may retain customs records at any location within the U.S. customs territory. (19 CFR 111.23(a)). CBP proposes to amend paragraph (a) to require that a customs broker must maintain customs records, including any electronic records, within the U.S. customs territory. 

CBP should allow electronic records relating to customs transactions to be store securely in other areas of the world and not be limited within the US Customs territory. In this age of global companies and cloud computing, data can be stored securely on servers located in other countries. Brokerage Companies can be global and have offices in many countries. Software has been created that can assist the company with filing entries/declarations for multiple countries using the same software program. Dear Acting Administrator Carlson: 

The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) welcomes the opportunity to comment on the National 

Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s (NHTSA’s) proposed upgrade to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety 

Standard 208. Seat belt reminders meeting the existing standard do not motivate unbuckled occupants to 

use a seat belt (Robertson & Haddon, 1974), but persistent reminders meeting the requirements proposed 

by NHTSA will increase seat belt use and save lives. Our research has shown that seat belt reminders with 

persistent auditory signals lasting 100 seconds or longer increase the belt use of drivers who do not always 

buckle up by up to 34% (Kidd & Singer, 2019a). Increasing seat belt use of unbuckled occupants 

throughout the vehicle by this amount would save about 1,600 lives each year (Kidd & O’Malley, 2023) and 

underscores why the proposed requirements must be implemented immediately. 

IIHS first published ratings of seat belt reminder systems in 2022 to encourage automakers to strengthen 

reminders for unbuckled front-row occupants and add reminders for unbuckled second-row occupants. 

NHTSA’s proposed requirements for front and rear reminders are consistent with many of the criteria IIHS 

requires for a good-rated seat belt reminder system. To earn a good rating, a seat belt reminder system 

must have an auditory alert for front-seating positions that lasts at least 90 seconds; is at least 6 dB(A) 

above ambient background noise; and has at least one dominant frequency between 500 and 2,250 Hz. 

The system must provide a 30-second auditory alert when a second-row occupant unbuckles while the 

vehicle is in motion and inform the driver about second-row belt use for at least 60 seconds after the 

vehicle starts. We also have criteria for when the reminders must begin. Manufacturers have responded 

quickly to our requirements and are well positioned to meet NHTSA’s proposed requirements. 

As detailed in our comments on the following pages, NHTSA can strengthen the proposed seat belt 

reminder requirements by (1) ensuring auditory reminders are easy to hear above other noise in the 

vehicle, (2) limiting periods of silence between auditory signals, (3) making the requirements for auditory 

reminder characteristics the same in front and rear seats, and (4) implementing the requirements 

immediately. Critically, NHTSA’s proposed requirements should emulate those from other organizations that 

are already pushing manufacturers to develop acceptable and effective seat belt reminder systems that are 

saving lives today. 

We appreciate the opportunity to share information and our suggestions with NHTSA.

I submit this comment in response to the U.S. Department of Educations interim final rule Eligibility of Students at Institutions of Higher Education for Funds Under the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act (Docket ID ED-2020-OPE-0078), published June 17, 2020. I write to express my opposition to the exclusion of those who do not qualify for Title IV assistance from receiving emergency financial aid under the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act. I particularly oppose the rules exclusion of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) and undocumented students enrolled in institutions of higher education.

The Department estimates that its Title-IV-eligibility requirement would exclu[de] more than 1.12 million noncitizens from receiving emergency financial aid, to say nothing of the many other students who are ineligible for Title IV assistance on different grounds. Separately, the Department has acknowledged the urgent economic challenges facing many students as a result of the crisis. Many students who are not eligible for Title IV benefits are experiencing those challenges particularly acutely. But the Department does not consider the economic and non-economic costs of excluding more than 1.12 million students from access to emergency financial aid during this national emergency. 

All students are facing unprecedented economic and non-economic challenges as a result of COVID-19. The United States has had millions of cases of COVID-19. Meanwhile, unemployment has skyrocketed, leaving many students in dire economic circumstances. Many students face unique economic challenges: Many students lost their on-campus jobs due to COVID-19, lost their summer internships or jobs, or were ineligible for a Recovery Rebate check under the CARES Act.

The Department previously encourage[d] institutions of higher education to prioritize students with the greatest need in awarding emergency financial aid. We agree. And we note that many students who are not eligible for Title IV assistance are among those with the greatest need.

Many immigrant students ineligible for Title IV assistance face unique challenges. For one, many ineligible students (and their families) do not have health insurance. Those same populations of students are suffering disproportionate health effects as a result of this pandemic.

It is unsound policy to prevent those ineligible students at both two- and four-year institutions from accessing emergency financial aid to meet their most fundamental needs.

Contrary to industry representations, wireless technology is neither a sustainable nor environmentally-friendly technology because wireless connectivity uses far more energy than wired connectivity. According to Energy Consumption in Wired and Wireless Access Networks, "Wireless technologies will continue to consume at least 10 times more power than wired technologies when providing comparable access rates and traffic volumes. PON [passive optical networks] will continue to be the most energy-efficient access technology."

"Our energy calculations show that by 2015, wireless cloud will consume up to 43 TWh, compared to only 9.2 TWh in 2012, an increase of 460%. This is an increase in carbon footprint from 6 megatonnes of CO2 in 2012 to up to 30 megatonnes of CO2 in 2015, the equivalent of adding 4.9 million cars to the roads. Up to 90% of this consumption is attributable to wireless access network technologies, data centres account for only 9%."

Wireless devices use radiofrequency (RF) radiation sent indiscriminately through the air to communicate. The ambient levels of RF radiation have increased rapidly with the proliferation of wireless technology. Unfortunately, regulators around the globe have had their heads in the sand, refusing to believe that RF radiation emitted by common wireless devices can have biological effects, unless they cook you. Regulations in the U.S., Canada and many other parts of the world are based on the avoidance of thermal harm, not protection from non-thermal detrimental biological effects, despite numerous studies documenting their existence.

The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) states:

"Different groups in a population may have differences in their ability to tolerate a particular NIR (non-ionizing radiation) exposure. For example, children, the elderly, and some chronically ill people might have a lower tolerance for one or more forms of NIR exposure than the rest of the population. Under such circumstances, it may be useful or necessary to develop separate guideline levels for different groups within the general population, but it may be more effective to adjust the guidelines for the general population to include such groups. Some guidelines may still not provide adequate protection for certain sensitive individuals nor for normal individuals exposed concomitantly to other agents, which may exacerbate the effect of the NIR exposure, an example being individuals with photosensitivity."

Radiofrequency sickness is a functional impairment caused by overexposure to radiofrequencies, which includes the pulsed modulated microwave frequencies used in wireless communication, as well as "Incidental" and "Unintentional" radiators (Mahra et al 1971)(Cherry 2000)(Grant)(Johnson Liakouris 1998). Once one has radiofrequency sickness, exposure to radiofrequencies causes functional impairments which can range from frustrating to life-threatening. EHS or electrohypersensitivity, which often encompasses radiofrequency sickness, affected 3% of the population twelve years ago, according to the California State Department of Health. More recent independent studies show the numbers may be higher now.

The proliferation of wireless technology is increasing the number of people with radiofrequency sickness and also restricting the daily activities of people with radiofrequency sickness. Past rules changes by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration have made it more difficult for people with radiofrequency sickness to get vehicles that do not cause functional impairment for them - one example of an access-limiting requirement is the requirement for wireless tire pressure gauges. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. 

***Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

These are families who deserve a thoughtful response. We are all related to each other. The incarceration and separation of refugee and migrant families is inexcusable. We can do better.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

The food we choose to feed our families is a cornerstone of American life. I would like access to the information that allows me to make those choices according to my values.

Thank you for considering my request.

Dear Administrator Rosekind: 
 
The National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL), the bi-partisan organization representing the 
legislatures of our nation’s states, territories, and commonwealths, appreciates the opportunity to 
provide public comment on the Interim Final Rule (IFR) for implementing the federal grant 
program to states for behavioral highway safety programs authorized by the Fixing America’s 
Surface Transportation (FAST) Act. 
 
The passage of the FAST Act in December 2015 ensured program and funding stability for states 
that will help to save lives. While this stability is always important, the recent rise in traffic fatalities 
brings an ever greater need. The FAST Act made relatively few changes to the state grant programs 
that are administered by NHTSA. The changes that were made focused primarily on increasing the 
overall flexibility of the program for states. The funding increases for section 402 grants and 
flexibility for the Section 405 programs and Highway Safety Plan (HSP) were a priority for NCSL 
and we were very pleased that the final bill addressed the challenges states had previously faced. 
 
However, in reviewing the IFR, NCSL was disappointed to find a number of administrative 
requirements included that were not called for by Congress. In the preamble of the rule, NHTSA 
states that the “FAST Act did not significantly change the structure of the grant programs” and that 
it “made limited administrative changes to the Section 402 grant program.” NCSL agrees with these 
statements, but unfortunately, in our view, they do not line up with the changes included in the IFR. 
Specifically, the regulations put forward to restructure the format of Highway Safety Plans (HSP) 
increase the administrative burden on states, and create structural changes that are not required by 
the FAST Act. Additionally, the proposed changes to the state performance reports (1300.11), seat 
belt enforcement grants (1300.21(e)(3)), traffic safety information system improvement grants 
(1300.22), impaired driving countermeasures grants (1300.23) and motor cycle safety grants

While I understand your reasoning that standards under the New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) can restrict the 

emissions of volatile organic carbons (VOCs) and methane simultaneously, you neglect a very important provision in 

the NSPS. Section 111Dstates that if a material is regulated under NSPS but has no specific guidelines under the 

Hazardous Air Pollutants or National Ambient Air Quality Acts, a regulation standard must be created for it. These 

created standards apply to not only New Sources, but to existing companies and structures. Now, admittedly, most new

Department of Transportation -- DOT-OST-2016-0208: 

(1) With respect to interline itineraries, informational asymmetries between consumers and carriers demand that all entities responsible for carrying a passenger and her baggage be held jointly and severally responsible under the rule for delayed-baggage-fee refunds. The ANPRM observes that where "multiple entities [are] involved in the transactions of bag fees," there is a substantial risk that passengers may be "sent back and forth between two entities to determine which entity is responsible" for the delayed bag for refunding their bag fees. The same risk exists where, as in a standard interline arrangement, multiple carriers are responsible for transporting the passenger and her bags. With multiple carriers involved in her itinerary, there is a substantial risk that a passenger may be bounced around between carriers to determine which one caused the baggage delay and which is ultimately responsible for the delayed-baggage refund. 

To remedy this problem, the final rule should state that all carriers involved in a standard interline itinerary are jointly and severally liable for delayed-baggage refunds and that the first carrier the passenger contacts - most likely the last one she travelled upon - must promptly refund the baggage fees she paid. This will induce carriers to contractually determine amongst themselves (for example, in a codeshare agreement) how best to resolve baggage-fee refunds on interline itineraries while also alleviating a great deal of stress and anxiety for travelers - an outcome no doubt consistent with the Congress's intent in enacting Section 2305 of 2016's FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act. (No such rule should apply to non-interline itineraries involving multiple carriers. Since the passenger in such a case is responsible for transferring his baggage airline-to-airline mid-itinerary, any informational asymmetry as to which carrier is responsible for a baggage delay is largely nonexistent.)

(2) While not statutorily required, it is imperative that the final rule amend 14 CFR 254.5 to require conspicuous notice of 254.4 carrier liability not only in a carrier's carriage contract but also before a passenger finalizes a baggage-fee transaction. Such notice could take the form of "clickwrap," for example, before a consumer agrees to pay a baggage fee, whether online or at an airport check-in kiosk. This would create a better informed flying public; thereby induce greater care by carriers in preventing and promptly resolving baggage delays; and be consistent with Congress's serious concern, reflected in Section 2305, with these issues.

 It is my thought that a non-native migratory bird that either flies the Mississippi Flyways or the Eastern Neotropical migration or the Atlantics Americas does so because of their survival instinct thanks to hormones and because they follow the earths magnetic field. Sadly, our wetlands and grasslands are disappearing at an alarming rate due to urban defragmentation, agriculture and now solar farms. It is because of these circumstances that food and nesting grounds are becoming scarce; thus causing a bird colony to migrate elsewhere for a better nest site, for more prey or possibly wildflower seeds among the meadows. The result is an Increase in competition for limited resources and range of territory. An example of this is the rapidly declining Snowy Owl of Canada that is now seen in Rhode Island. There is also the fact that the USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map is changing. Migrating microbes, vegetation and animals are on the move to different climates in part because of Climate Change. This in itself will likely shift the migration patterns of many bird species forcing them to adapt to another environment. To not adapt to change means to perish. On another note Rachel Carson once said, it is the birds and insects of the forest that keep it healthy. Trees are the life and soul of Mother Earth and they are very much under attack from warmer soil temperatures, diseases such Fire Blight, insect infestation such as the Asian Long- horned Beetle and the lack of stewardship i.e. prescribed burning of overcrowded forests that are now a fire hazard. Birds are said to eat tons of insects each year, where a hummingbird alone can eat 2,000. As you can see one cannot undervalue the importance of birds with regards to keeping the greatest oxygen producers of our planet healthy. 
 Now I like to mention a mutual relationship of two birds that being the Yellow-bellied Sapsucker and the Ruby throat hummingbird. Though the Sapsucker lives among different areas of North America, it can migrate as far as the West Indies. Come spring the woodpecker needs to be there for the Ruby- throat Hummingbird as its tapping of tree sap becomes a vital food source for the hummingbird in the early, cold months of spring. If the woodpecker were to become an endangered species, it would also bring a similar fate to the hummingbird. It is this bit of knowledge that makes me want to raise a caution flag to the draft listing of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. It is my feeling that we do not fully understand the intricate relationships of multiple bird species sharing a common habitat such as the Rowe Sanctuary or Magee Marsh. Every animal on Mother Earth has a role to play in the Food Chain, however it cannot be dismissed that certain bird species i.e. Starlings are displacing native species. Yesteryear, we use to eat pigeon and goose. Just saying. 

P.S. On another note, I have read that invasive species of vegetation can toxify the soil; thus making the area inhospitable for native plants to grow.

A key concern is that this regulation is still ambiguous in the definition of adversely affects and that MSHA will expand this beyond its intent. Imprecise wording has caused inspectors to gradually expand jurisdiction, until a standard is applied to miscellaneous things for which it was never intended. 

The standard still requires that all hazards that "adversely affect" a miner's safety need to be documented. Is a pile of material that could be walked around an adverse effect? What about a small puddle of oil, or a smear of grease? If an examiner comes across something that adversely affects safety, this regulation requires certain actions. In the interest of training our examiners, it would be beneficial if MSHA would define this, so that laymen could utilize it. Otherwise, we are at the mercy of every inspector and the ever changing definitions of "adversely affects" that they bring with them each inspection. 

The rule to require recordkeeping of these conditions and documentation of their fix is still difficult to understand and implement. How would MSHA best proposed mine operators do Recordkeeping of hazards abated? Use an example that will be commonplace in many operations: A hazard is noted by an examiner (examiner 1), and documented on the inspection. A second examiner is also in the area, later, and also notes the hazard on his inspection sheet. Workers, who come to prepare the area for hazard abatement, also do an exam for their safety, and all three note the hazard (even if the hazard has been cordoned off, barricaded, etc., it is still a hazard, and a hard working examiner may still note it on their documents). If the hazard needs another shift, or a part that may not be available for a day, or a specialized operation (say, aluminum welding), it may exist for days, or weeks, and be noted on examiner's records. Regardless of WHY, it is very likely that a given hazard might be noted on multiple exams, by multiple examiners, in a mine.
When the hazard is abated, each of those exam records must be found, and the corrective action date placed on it. If ten exam records are made noting the hazard (by, for example, a crew of laborers each doing a workplace exam prior to entry), they all ten must be "finalized". If one of the exams gets turned in late, or is missed by the "abatement documenter", that exam is now citable. This creates a situation where the more pro-active a miner/examination program is, the more likely MSHA can (and will) find an error, and cite the company for it. The mine does everything right, goes over and beyond by having every employee looking for and documenting hazards, and earns a citation because MORE people are looking for hazards, rather than less. 

Rather than dismiss this as "it can't happen, or would be rare", think about how many miners cross a parking lot on a snowy, winter day. If each of them noted in their workplace exams that "walkways are icy/slippery", then each of those exams would have to have a documented termination date. If you had 100 miners turn in an exam, and you managed to get the date properly on 99, but one stuck to the back of another inspection form and you missed it... you are just as liable for a citation as a company that did nothing at all. All it would take is the inspector looking through the workplace exams, and finding every one without a termination date. 

Conflict/Duplication of efforts
MSHA states that this information is needed as part of the workplace exam record. Many operators already have systems in place to track work orders, repairs, etc., including completion. When such systems are in place, requiring this same detail on the workplace exam itself is duplicative and provides no benefit; moreover it would increase administration time without making the workplace safer. In fact, duplicative efforts would take time that could be spent in making the workplace safer, and eliminating hazards. We hope MSHA can consider how this new requirement should

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

It seems like a no-brainer - putting children in jail is wrong. I don't want my tax money going toward keeping children in jail longer, whether they're immigrants or not.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I strongly disagree with this proposal because all remaining spotted owl habitat is essential for the survival of the species. Instead of excluding 200,000 acres of Critical Habitat, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service should protect what remains of the older forests where the owl lives. 

The lands (200,000 acres( in question are key to the recovery of the owl because they provide habitat connections between the coast range and the Cascades. Much of the habitat proposed for removal is in SW Oregon on lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management. This is an area known regionally to provide for forest habitat connectivity. 

Barred owls are not native, but threaten spotted owls through competition. They have been able to move into spotted owl areas, likely due to fragmentation brought on by past logging. This makes it even more important to protect the habitat that remains for the spotted owl. The added stress that barred owls place on remaining spotted owls makes every acre of spotted owl critical habitat necessary for the survival and recovery of the owl 

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is changed with recovering threatened and endangered species. How will the removal of this habitat enable the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service from carrying out its duties? Please explain why the Service is neglecting its primary duty to recovery at-risk species. 

This is not a scientific decision, rather it is political. The Service knows that the lands in question are the public lands where the last best owl habitat is located. All the private industrial land and much of the federal land in this area has been logged. What remains is absolutely critical to the recovery of the owl. Protection of spotted owl habitat is the highest and best use for this land and it is what benefits America the most, by far. Thank you.

As a clinician, I urge CMS to ensure the final Physician Fee Schedule for 2023 strengthens access to psychological services and gives behavioral health professionals the tools they need to meet the mental health needs of diverse communities. Many of the issues raised in this year’s Physician Fee Schedule have serious implications for equity in access to behavioral health care. Through my comments, I urge CMS to adopt policies with the overall goal of facilitating access to mental and behavioral health treatment in underserved communities to the maximum extent possible. 

Strengthen the Practice of Psychology
• BHI Codes 
I support CMS’ proposed coding and payment for General Behavioral Health Integration (BHI) to recognize psychologists’ role in integrated care. I appreciate CMS’ support for multiple evidence-based models of integrated care, as it allows psychologists the flexibility required to support the behavioral health needs of the broader community.
• Medicare Potentially Underutilized Services
I appreciate CMS’ request for comments on potentially underutilized services, as several of the services CMS identified are performed by psychologists. I recommend CMS create additional Cognitive Assessment & Care codes without the medication reconciliation service because medication management is outside the scope of a psychologist’s license in many states. Additionally, I recommend CMS allow reimbursement for Intensive Behavioral Therapy for Obesity services provided by psychologists. 
• Chronic Pain Management and Treatment (CPM) Bundles
I ask CMS to create additional bundled pain management codes that do not include medication management. I am concerned that psychologists would be excluded from this new bundled service because in most states medication management is outside the scope of a psychologist’s license. Psychologists play a critical role in implementing non-pharmacological approaches to treatment, which may be safer or more effective for some patients, as well as team-based comprehensive pain management.
• Telehealth
Many patients in rural and underserved areas are now able to access mental health services, often for the first time. Many of my patients have chronic illness that makes unpredictable their capacity to travel on any given day. We use Telehealth to provide a responsive treatment plan. Reverting to the non-facility rate for telehealth services after the end of the COVID public health emergency will lead practitioners to offer telehealth less frequently or to restrict the number of Medicare beneficiaries they treat using telehealth. 

Expand Psychology Training and Workforce Development
• Supervision by Psychologists 
I applaud CMS’ Proposed Revisions to the “Incident to” Physicians’ Services Regulation for Behavioral Health Services to allow for reimbursement for Physicians and Non-Physician Providers (NPPs), which include psychologists, who supervise these practitioners in their everyday practice. This will help expand access to and coordination of mental health services in rural and underserved areas where masters’-level practitioners represent a substantial segment of the mental health providers in the area.
• Advanced Psychology Trainee Services 
I urge CMS to allow for Medicare reimbursement of services provided by advanced psychology trainees under the supervision of a licensed psychologist. Although psychology interns receive extensive clinical experience prior to their internship, services provided by trainees under the supervision of a licensed psychologist are not reimbursable under Medicare. Without Medicare reimbursement of services provided by trainees, training programs lack a steady source of funding.

My name is James Alexander. I respectfully ask that the Department of Education keep the current regulation protecting religious student organizations without any changes to its language. I am concerned that the proposal to strike the language in CFR Sections 75.500 and 75.600 eliminates language that ensures religious student organizations will be treated fairly and will be allowed to flourish at public college and universities. I believe that religious student organizations add greatly to university communities and should be protected.

The language in these sections is necessary because it enables religious organizations to apply policies that are inherent to, and wholly consistent with, their religious practices. The idea that "applying neutral, generally-applicable nondiscrimination policies that would otherwise be compliant with the First Amendment" is not reasonable. It implies that the religious organizations could be forced to accept policies, such as which leaders they must allow, that are in direct conflict with their religious beliefs. This, by definition, reduces their religious freedom. It is critically important that faith communities be led by student leaders who embrace and represent each faith tradition.

Religious expression still needs additional protection. When students can form authentic faith communities and express their faith, it adds to the diversity of college campuses and improves our communities. By changing the current regulation, the federal government would send the wrong message to religious student groups that they are not a valued presence on college campuses.

Respectfully,
James Alexander
