Dear USDA Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack,

My Grandfather owned tacking horses a long time ago. I'm now 61. None of this lunacy was done then. And it needs to stop NOW!! As someone who’s concerned with equine welfare, I’m disappointed to learn the U.S. Department of Agriculture has proposed withdrawing its 2017 rule to protect horses from the cruel practice of soring under the Horse Protection Act (HPA) and I sincerely hope that a timeline will be announced for a new one, or that the rulemaking be reissued until further action can be taken. 
 
While the HPA should protect horses, decades later they are still being subjected to soring. The 2017 rule included provisions that would disallow the industry to continue to self-police with the use of DQPs, and ban the use of chains and other action devices used to sore horses. 
 
Over 100,000 public comments were submitted on the proposed rule, while hundreds of members of Congress also wrote in support.
 
The USDA must act expediently to end this cruelty, which continues to plague the Tennessee walking horse industry and affect other gaited breeds. 

I do not support withdrawing this rule without the introduction of new regulations to ban soring and hope a rule will be quickly introduced that incorporates new information, including recommendations found in the 2021 National Academies of Science report, “Review of Methods for Detecting Soreness in Horses.”

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Ms Linda Lam

I submit this comment letter in response to the United States Department of Homeland Security's (Department or DHS) proposed rule, Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DHS Docket No. USCIS-2021-0006), published September 28, 2021. I write in support of codifying DACA into regulation.

When pursuing a higher education, DACA recipients or DREAMers cannot access federal Pell Grants, student loans, or federal work-study. Additionally, many states refuse to offer in-state tuition to DACA-recipient state residents. DACA recipients and DREAMers contribute substantially to the American economy and work in many front-line or essential capacities. The employment authorization that comes with DACA status is incredibly important to DACA recipients.

Unfortunately, DACA still remains out of reach to many DREAMers because they can no longer apply for it and, even if they could, they would not meet the requirement that they have arrived in the country before June 15, 2007.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit public comment on the proposed rule.

going through similar challenges. This sense of community and peer support can be highly motivating and can reduce feelings of isolation,

therapists. This ensures a seamless continuum of care, with regular communication and coordination among healthcare professionals to 

address all aspects of an individual's well-being.

manage cravings and high-risk situations. This proactive approach can significantly reduce the likelihood of relapse.

issues such as trauma, co-occurring mental health disorders, family dynamics, and lifestyle factors. This comprehensive approach increases 

the chances of long-term success in recovery.

range of individuals who may not have the financial resources for more intensive forms of treatment.

Dear Mr. Molton, 
I am quite concerned about the impact of the new proposed regulations for Atlantic Cod, Framework 
Adjustment 63, now being considered for passage. I am a 72 year old recreational fisherman from Pt. 
Judith and I have always endeavored to act responsibly with regard to the local fisheries. My fishing 
partners and I have elected to stop fishing for striped bass to help alleviate some of the pressure on this 
treasured species. Recently the RI fluke fishery has become challenging and is no longer a viable source 
of food for the dinner table. It is thus with delight that we have channeled some of our fishing efforts on 
the RI Atlantic Cod, traveling to the area just east and south of Block Island, some 35 miles from our 
home port. Admittedly, we never catch our limit of these fine fish, and it would be quite unusual for us 
to catch a “trophy”. Nevertheless, we catch sufficient numbers of “keeper” fish along with black seabass 
to make the trip worthwhile and enjoyable during the summer season. 
I believe that it is scientifically incorrect to lump the RI cod fishery with that of the rest of New England. 
There is little to suggest that it is overfished and there is evidence that these fish spawn as a separate 
group in Narragansett Bay. Addressing Atlantic cod fishing with such a broadly restrictive brush stroke is 
just plain wrong. 
The proposal to close the season from May 1 to August 1 would effectively shut down most of this 
recreational fishing opportunity, which will already be challenged by high fuel prices this summer. The 
Rhode Island recreational boating and fishing industry is extremely important to the State, and this 
heavy handed restriction by NOAA will further damage the sustainability of this economic sector. Once 
again, we recreational fisherman feel that we are being unfairly targeted for conditions created by the 
commercial fishing industry. 
I strongly urge you to reject these new proposals. If you must impose some new restrictions, please 
consider a small reduction in the bag limit and perhaps allowing one “trophy” to be kept per trip, which 
would allow for the preservation of breeder fish. 
Sincerely 
Mark Jacobs MD

However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

Look, we really need to know the truth about our food. We need to know how in what conditions it was made. It's a simple health issue. We need to know everything about our food to make the best choices for our health. I'm positive if we knew more about our food, our diets would be much different and we would be much healthier.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

Re: 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule Dear USDA Forest Service, I am writing to request that you fully restore 2001 Roadless Rule protections on the Tongass National Forest and end large-scale old growth timber sales on the entirety of the forest. The Tongass is a key weapon for fighting climate change, with its old-growth trees effectively trapping and sequestering climate-warming greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Scientists have estimated that the forest accounts for about 8 percent of the carbon sequestered by all national forests. Protecting the Tongass from old-growth logging will not only preserve that capacity, but avoid releasing carbon currently sequestered in its trees. The Tongass is also the ancestral and contemporary homeland of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples, and they have been the driving force of the effort to protect the forest. Their way of life is inextricably linked with these lands and waters. They hunt, gather, fish and harvest medicines in the Tongass that their ancestors have stewarded for more than 10,000 years. Restoring full protections will allow their traditional use of the land to continue. As part of planning for a future beyond old-growth timber, please also make a sustained investment in the Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy. Operating in full consultation with Tribal governments and local communities, this program will help the region stoke the already robust fishing and recreation industries that are driving the economy. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Melissa Beaudet - PII -

The National Lime Association (NLA) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on 
MSHA’s notice referenced above. The notice proposes changes to MSHA’s rules governing 
workplace examinations in metal and non-metal mines, found in 30 CFR Sections 56.18002 and 
57.19002. 
 
NLA is the trade association for manufacturers of high calcium quicklime, dolomitic quicklime, 
and hydrated lime, collectively referred to as “lime.” Lime is a chemical without substitute, 
providing cost-effective solutions to many of society’s environmental problems. Lime is 
produced by calcining limestone, and thus most lime manufacturers also quarry lime, with 
mining operations under the jurisdiction of MSHA. 
 
NLA believes there are a number of serious ambiguities and unanswered questions with regard to 
the proposed rule, and that the rule should not be finalized until these questions are answered and 
the regulated community has an opportunity to comment on them. While NLA commends 
MSHA for providing clarification of some points in its Federal Register notice published on 
August 25, 2016, this clarification did not go far enough, and several important points were 
unanswered, most notably the intended connection of the rule with enforcement policies and 
actions. NLA’s concerns are set out in detail below. 
 
1. MSHA Should Define Interaction of the Rule with Enforcement Policy and Actions 
 
Multiple commenters at public hearings have pointed out that the proposed rule preamble is 
silent on how the workplace examination records under the revised rule would be used by 
MSHA inspectors in an enforcement context. This is a question that must be answered before a 
final rule can be crafted. At present, the regulated community is obligated to speculate on this 
vital topic.

 
Page 2 
The proposed rule calls for the record of a workplace examination to identify “conditions that 
may adversely affect safety or health.” It also calls for the record to be later modified to indicate 
what corrective actions were performed, and when. 
 
MSHA should clearly state the following policy in conjunction with this rule: 
 
No citation will be issued for a condition that was identified pursuant to a workplace 
examination if: 
 
(1) The appropriate miners were notified of the condition and appropriate steps were taken to 
protect miners from the risk pending corrective action; and 
 
(2) Appropriate corrective action was performed in a timely manner. 
 
This policy would be consistent with MSHA’s policy as expressed in its Enforcement Manual 
that citations should not be issued for defects in equipment if the equipment has been tagged and 
removed from service as a result of a preoperational inspection. 
 
As the rule currently stands, there is no clear guidance to inspectors on whether they are 
permitted to write citations for violations identified on workplace examination records after they

that promote safety and reduce incidents. 
 
MSHA should state its position on this issue and allow for public comment before a final rule is 
published.

There is no practical way to coordinate V2V communications without a truly massive monitoring system, with strict controls over the transmitters of each and every signal.
This means the identity of every transmitter has to be established, it's just folly to believe this information could not (and would not) be used to identify individual drivers and vehicles. 

The proposals dealing with 'misbehavior' fail to take into account that code will change over time, the service life of vehicles is generally greater than the life of a computer code or program. Witness the millions of General Motors vehicles now on the road with outdated, non-functioning "OnStar" communications systems. Assume that some systems will fail incrementally, send out signals intermittently or send the wrong signal out consistently due to a bad sensor inside the vehicle. 
The potential exists for a vehicle with a faulty ABS sensor to indicate abrupt braking every 150 feet, or at every left turn. These signals will poison the data for the vehicles nearby and render the messages useless. Drivers can and will be in greater danger than they might have been without the inaccurate information to begin with.

Forcing citizens to spend hundreds of dollars on a communication system that will be deemed to enhance public safety exposes citizens to countless legal dangers. What if his or her transmitter malfunctions, sends the wrong data and someone crashes? Attorneys will soon find a way to identify the data and go after the owner of the vehicle. NHTSA will then tell us it's in the public interest to have the systems inspected, they'll mandate it and make the citizens responsible for the cost. When a software update is needed, who will pay? 
The proposal to flood the radio spectrum with more messages to attempt to compensate for a failed driver-training system, an inadequate driver licensing and recertification system and the general trend towards permitting and encouraging massive audio/video systems inside vehicles makes this proposed rule a solution to the wrong problem. Train the drivers, get them off their phones, dim those massive in-dash displays that show music videos to young, poorly-trained drivers and you won't need to use up the spectrum to send all of our data to the adjacent cars (and Washington, D.C.) every nanosecond. This rule needs to be rejected.

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more.

More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

The government, intending this to act as a deterrent for others who are considering crossing the border, thereby acknowledge the harmful consequences of these proposed regulations. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. I believe that the Flores Settlement Agreement should remain in place and should not be dismantled.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Could you please clarify in the final regulations whether a cafeteria plan can provide for both a health flex contribution and an eligible opt-out payment and, if so, how?

Notice 2015-87 provides that the amount of an employer contribution reduces the employee's required contribution for affordability purposes if the amount constitutes a "health flex contribution" under Treasury regulations sections 1.5000A-3(e)(3)(ii)(E) and 1.36B-2(c)(v)(A)(6). An amount is a health flex contribution if (i) the employee may not opt to receive the amount as a taxable benefit, (ii) the employee may use the amount to pay for minimum essential coverage, and (iii) the employee may use the amount exclusively to pay for medical care, within the meaning of Code section 213. Notice 2015-87 also addresses "opt-out payments" (the subject of proposed Treasury regulations sections 1.5000A-3(e)(3)(ii)(G) and 1.36B-2(c)(v)(A)(7)) that are payments that are available only if an employee declines coverage and that are not permitted to be used to pay for coverage under the eligible employer-sponsored plan.

Proposed Treasury regulations sections 1.5000A-3(e)(3)(ii)(G) and 1.36B-2(c)(v)(A)(7)) refer to Treasury regulations sections 1.5000A-3(e)(3)(ii)(E) and 1.36B-2(c)(v)(A)(6) "for the treatment of employer contributions to a cafeteria plan." Notice 2015-87, Q&A-8 provides, "See Q&A-9, however, concerning treatment of amounts that are not available to pay for coverage under an eligible employer-sponsored health plan and are available only if the employee declines that coverage." However, neither Notice 2015-87 nor the proposed Treasury regulations address whether a cafeteria plan can provide for both a health flex contribution and an eligible opt-out payment and, if so, how.

Suppose the employer's cafeteria plan provides both (i) an employer contribution of $200 per month that can be used towards the purchase of minimum essential coverage, dental coverage or vision coverage and (ii) a cash payment of $200 per month if the employee declines coverage but that cannot be used towards the purchase of minimum essential coverage. Do they qualify as a health flex contribution and an opt-out payment respectively? Or will the Service treat the situation as if there is a single arrangement that provides $200 per month that can be either (i) used towards the purchase of minimum essential coverage, dental coverage or vision coverage or (ii) received in cash, with the result that the arrangement fails as both a health flex contribution (i.e., because the amount can be received in cash) and an opt-out payment (i.e., because the amount can be used to purchase minimum essential coverage)? If that is how the Service would treat such a cafeteria plan, does the answer change if the amounts involved under the two aspects of the plan are not the same and, if so, does it matter which one is larger or smaller?

The National Council of State Boards of Examiners for Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology (NCSB) is a non-profit membership organization of boards that license and regulate the practice of speech-language pathology and audiology. Consumer protection is core to our mission. 

Labeling Outside the Package and Condition for Sale
NCSB requests the FDA expand its proposed outside the package warning to prohibit not only sale of the device to someone under the age of 18 but also sale for the use by anyone younger than 18. Similarly, at the time of sale, NCSB recommends affirmation the purchase is not for use by anyone younger than 18. Children with hearing loss provided with OTC devices are at risk for complications due to untreated ear disease, inadequate/inappropriate amplification or the failure to identify other conditions that require specialized treatment.
NCSB recommends the FDA consider using the following clarifying warning statement:
WARNING! This device shall not be sold to or purchased for use by anyone younger than 18 years old. 

Labeling Inside the Package
NCSB recommends inside packaging include information about preventing damage to hearing. Information should provide consumers with warning signs the amplified sound from their OTC aid might be too loud and damage their hearing, e.g. the consumer is having difficulty talking or hearing others talk over the sound, the sound makes the consumer’s ears hurt or ring, or other sounds seem muffled after the consumer leaves an area where there is loud sound. NCSB recommends inside product labeling include information about conditions that contribute to or cause hearing loss, e.g. ear wax, other ear growths, ear infections, or perforation of the eardrum. Additionally, NCSB recommends inside product labeling include information advising a consumer to seek help from a hearing care professional if they have any of the FDA’s listed warning signs or are concerned about their hearing after use of the device. NCSB recommends the following important notice be included as part of inside labeling:
IMPORTANT NOTICE: Be careful when using this device. Do not use your hearing device more than 12 hours a day. Do not use if the device exceeds your comfort level due to loudness or physical fit of the device. If set to the maximum output level and worn for longer than recommended, you may damage your hearing.

Output Limits
The FDA is proposing 115 dB as maximum acoustic output for an OTC hearing aid and 120 dB SPL for one that implements input-controlled compression and user-adjustable device volume control. NCSB believes the proposed output limits, even with user-adjustable volume control, are potentially unsafe and can further impair hearing. NCSB recommends a maximum acoustic output limit of 110 dB, particularly for those with hearing loss levels in the mild to moderate hearing loss range. Limits of 120 dB are not consistent with formula fitting ranges for consumers with mild to moderate hearing loss. In fact, these higher dB levels are utilized in fitting for severe to profound hearing loss ranges. According to the CDC, exposure at 120 dB can cause pain and ear injury, and exposure to noise at levels between 105-110 dB can cause hearing loss in less than 5 minutes.
https://www.cdc.gov/nceh/hearing_loss/what_noises_cause_hearing_loss.html

NCSB recommends user-adjustable device volume control with maximum acoustic output limit of 110 dB output be required as a design feature for OTC hearing aids to minimize harmful high output levels. 

NCSB recommends output levels include examples of the type of noise a consumer would be experiencing, e.g. noise at 110 dB would be equivalent to the maximum volume level for personal listening devices, a very loud radio or television, and loud entertainment venues. NCSB recommends the information indicate that as loudness increases, the amount of time you can hear the sound before damage occurs decreases.

outcomes versus inactive control therapies” is problematic. In these trials, patients in the control group 

received usual care, specialist medical care or were put on a waiting list. The term ‘control therapies’ is 

inappropriate because in many of these trials patients in the control group did not receive an intervention. 

It is, for example, misleading to speak of ‘control therapy’ if patients are put on a waiting list for several 

weeks to get the treatment the other group received. More accurate would be to name these comparisons 

CBT or exercise therapy versus ‘no intervention’. 

Because patients in the control group in these trials received no intervention, any improvement in

nature of the intervention itself. Despite this limitation, the review has not downgraded the strength of 

evidence of these trials for failing to use an active control intervention. Therefore, the control condition 

and its limitations need to be explicitly described in the text. It is important, for example, to avoid 

formulations that imply that CBT and exercise therapy lead to improved fatigue as it remains uncertain if 

improvements are due to the intervention itself or other factors such as expectancy effects or inequal 

attention of healthcare professionals. 

Recommendation: A more cautious formulation is advised when discussing comparisons to control 

groups where no intervention was given, for example: “Patients who received CBT and exercise therapy

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable. 

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.
I myself work with immigrant children, and they are young people who want to better their lives and their families lives as well. They are enthusiastic about their future in this country and reunifying with their families. Many of them have plans to get an education and learn the English language, allowing them to have broader opportunities for a successful future that they envision, these young people are resilient and courageous, at such a young age they have taken the course of their lives into their own hands and with limited resources, they fight to get to where they want to be. 
Sincerely,
Belinda Contreras

On behalf of the National Viral Hepatitis Roundtable (NVHR), I am pleased at the opportunity to submit 

the following comments on the draft HBV (hepatitis B virus) screening and testing recommendations. As 

an organization committed to viral hepatitis elimination and health equity, NVHR strongly supports the 

recommendations for universal screening of adults using a 3-test panel, use of the 3-test panel for 

screening during pregnancy, and inclusion in risk-based testing recommendations of persons currently 

or formerly incarcerated, persons with current or past sexually transmitted infections, and persons with 

current or past hepatitis C virus infection. 

The persistence and burden of undiagnosed HBV infection, coupled with incidence of acute infection 

indicative of ongoing community transmission, provides stark and compelling testimony to the gaps in 

our current and complex risk-based approach to screening and testing. Screening challenges are 

compounded by recognition of disparate prevalence among communities and groups with limited or 

fragmented access to health care and greater susceptibility to stigma and discrimination, including 

foreign-born populations, people with histories of substance use and incarceration, and men who have 

sex with men. Risk-based screening algorithms are inherently reliant on clinician judgment and patient 

disclosure, factors that are especially fraught for conditions such as HBV with sexual and parenteral 

transmission modes that may evoke bias or shame, and for diseases that disproportionately affect 

people of color and other marginalized communities. The recommendation for universal adult 

screening, supplemented by risk-based testing, therefore provides an epidemiologically sound and 

evidence-based response to the stigma-inflected social determinants of health that have fueled an 

unacceptably low rate of diagnosis under the current risk-based testing guidelines. 

The prospect of universal adult screening recommendations for HBV warrants attention and innovation 

to a range of implementation considerations. NVHR offers the following comments in support of 

planning for robust implementation of the draft guidelines:

ACIP (Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices) recommendations on universal HBV vaccination

Ideally, scientists will be capable of discovering new technology and techniques that will allow us to one day successfully and consistently breed Nautilus in captivity. However, without such knowledge being currently available following a 25 year absence of progress in the captive reproduction of nautilus, and without governmental/financial support or interest available to implement such advancements, the idealistic concept of humanity being able to successfully restock unprotected wild populations of nautilus is unfortunately a far cry from what published primary literature (already cited within the petition) shows to be possible today.
Successful listing of the family Nautilidae under the ESA (along with CITES) will effectively outlaw the shell trade for the species, the main purpose of the fishery. While black market trade will undoubtedly continue, as long as enforcement of fishery laws is upheld then the overall take of wild nautilus should decrease. The resultant reduction in fishing pressure may give these disparate populations of nautilus a chance to reestablish themselves in at least some of the ranges in which they were historically found to be thriving. Simultaneously, unfished populations will be given the chance to escape the "boom and bust" fishery fate which has been seen in previously and currently fished populations.
Admittedly, more stringent permitting will undoubtedly be required for educational, research based, and conservation oriented uses of nautilus, but we cannot allow global demand for an iconic curio to drive the oldest, most unique family of cephalopods towards extinction unhindered.

Protection of old growth forests are not only important to the communities in Southeast Alaska and Native communities, they are important to all the animals and aquatic live living there. I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

The Bureau of Land Management's (BLM) proposed rule for managing the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska (NPR-A) is a commendable step towards balancing resource extraction with environmental and cultural preservation. This proposal aligns with BLM's obligations under the Naval Petroleum Reserves Production Act (NPRPA) and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), ensuring that the management of surface resources and Special Areas in NPR-A adheres to legal and ethical standards.

Firstly, the emphasis on revising the framework for designating and ensuring maximum protection of Special Areas' significant resource values is crucial. This approach acknowledges the intrinsic value of Alaska's unique ecosystems and the need for their preservation. By focusing on safeguarding these areas, BLM demonstrates a commitment to environmental stewardship, ensuring that the ecological integrity of these regions is maintained for future generations.

Secondly, the proposal's intent to protect and enhance access for subsistence activities throughout the NPR-A is a significant aspect. This approach respects the rights and traditions of indigenous and local communities, recognizing their dependence on these lands for their livelihoods and cultural practices. It ensures that while the area is utilized for national energy needs, the traditional ways of life and the rights of these communities are not overlooked.

Moreover, the incorporation of aspects of the NPR-A Integrated Activity Plan (IAP) approved in April 2022 into the proposed rule is a positive move. This integration indicates a thoughtful, comprehensive approach to land management, considering various factors and stakeholder inputs. It shows BLM's willingness to adapt and update its strategies in response to changing circumstances and emerging insights.

Furthermore, the assurance that the proposed rule would have no effect on currently authorized oil and gas operations in the NPR-A is a pragmatic aspect of the proposal. It balances the need for ongoing energy production with the new regulations aimed at protecting the environment and supporting subsistence activities. This balance is crucial for ensuring a smooth transition to more sustainable practices without disrupting current economic activities.

Lastly, the BLM's solicitation of comments on all aspects of the proposed action is a commendable approach, promoting transparency and inclusivity. It allows for a diverse range of perspectives to be considered, ensuring that the final rule is well-rounded and takes into account the concerns and suggestions of various stakeholders.

In conclusion, the BLM's proposed rule is a forward-thinking initiative that promises to manage the NPR-A in a manner that is environmentally responsible, culturally respectful, and economically pragmatic. It represents a significant step towards sustainable management of natural resources, demonstrating a commitment to conservation, indigenous rights, and responsible land use.

As a PA and member of the Oregon Society of Physician Assistants and American Academy of Physician Assistants, we are writing in support of language in the proposed 2020 Physician Fee Schedule that increases the utilization of PAs by aligning federal Medicare PA policy regarding supervision with state law. Sincerely,

There are many reasons to reject the application to plant Darling 58 Chestnut trees. 
1. Efforts to genetically engineer pathogen resistance, even in agricultural crops, have been unsuccessful because pathogens evolve to overcome plant defenses. These genetically modified trees could live for up to 200 years, providing a free education to pathogens for all that time, which they may use to overcome plant defenses both in the Darling 58 and other plants. 
2. There is no way of assessing the impact on native species, or on wildlife, from eating the nuts, inhaling pollen, pollinators, other plants, soils and waterways. 
3. All tree roots depend on the fungal network, also called the “Wood Wide Web.” We don't know if other trees could survive a fungal resistant forest created by fungal-resistant chestnut trees. 
Biotech has a history of causing unintended consequences, ostensibly to "help" the world, but really, to create valuable intellectual property for these companies. Please reject this application.

As a double board certified Interventional Pain Physician I treat chronic pain and degenerative spinal conditions on a daily basis. With the current opioid issues gripping our patients across the nation, it is imperative, that we employ interventional techniques to improve pain and function long term without the use of these dangerous substances. Spinal stenosis is a degenerative pathology of the spine that may cause significant pain in the back and legs as well as significant functional limitations in walking and standing that can have deleterious effects on a person's quality of life. Spinal stenosis has been difficult to treat in the past by conservative measures including medications, physical therapy, spinal injections. Surgical intervention may not improve the patient's symptoms, and may not be in option in this setting due to comorbidities. I have employed the Superion spinal spacer for indirect decompression of the spinal column for hundreds of patients over the past 2 years. This is a treatment option with robust Level 1 evidence that supports its effectiveness. Due the minimally invasive nature of the procedure, the patients are able to undergo this procedure on an outpatient basis without any hospitalization or prolonged recovery following the procedure. The patient outcomes that I have experienced in both pain improvement and functional restoration has been remarkable. These patients have not had the need for further surgical intervention following the placement of the spinal spacer and consistently comment on the improved quality of life following the procedure. The patients that presented to my practice taking opioids for the symptoms of spinal stenosis were able to discontinue their opioid medications within 4 weeks of the procedure. 
The proposed payment reduction for 2020 for this procedure will be detrimental for a large amount of people suffering with the symptoms of spinal stenosis. The majority of Ambulatory Surgery Centers review facility reimbursements regularly, and if no longer financially viable, they may no longer allow this procedure in their facility. In cases where such patients are no longer able to undergo the Superion spinal spacer procedure, the alternatives may be opioids or major spine surgery, which are both potentially high risk options that are not cost effective.

I'm especially worried about the future of Utah's redrock country, where mining, off-road vehicle use, fossil fuel development, and other high-impact activities continually threaten sensitive ecosystems and cultural sites. 

While the draft rule is an important step forward, I urge you to strengthen it in the following ways:

- Prioritize the inventory of all intact natural landscapes and ensure that any proposed development will not degrade such landscapes.

- As directed by FLPMA, prioritize the identification and designation of all eligible areas as Areas of Critical Environmental Concern and manage these areas appropriately.

- Require the BLM to consult with Tribes to ensure the incorporation of Indigenous Knowledge, respect for Tribal sovereignty and treaty rights, and protection of Tribal cultural sites.

- Protect old and mature forests from logging, vegetation removal projects, wildfire, and the effects of climate change, informed by the best available science and Indigenous knowledge.

I'm grateful for this administration's commitment to conserving and restoring America's public lands. Please strengthen the Public Lands Rule and work swiftly to bring balance to BLM-managed landscapes.

This letter is in response to the solicitation from AMS for comments from stakeholders 
regarding the methodology for determining maturity groupings for USDA Quality 
Grades. I am a seedstock and cow calf producer from Fauquier County, Virginia, and I 
strongly oppose the requested changes to the current standards. 
 
I oppose the suggested change for the following reasons: 
 
(1) Not enough research. 
 
---The research referenced in the solicitation looks promising for the merits of dentition 
as a method of maturity segregation for beef cattle. However, two trials from one 
university do not constitute the scope of information needed to justify universal changes 
to the grading standards. The White Paper referenced in the provided information states 
that “differences in dental age do not appear to consistently reflect differences in beef 
tenderness”, and “whether or not such differences in carcass maturity are related to beef 
tenderness differences among cattle whose dental age is less than 30 months is an 
important question that has not been addressed in the scientific literature”. Clearly, more 
research and more information on dentition are needed. For example, are cattle with zero 
permanent incisors more tender than cattle with two permanent incisors? Should zero 
permanent incisors become the new “A” Maturity and one or two permanent incisors the 
new “B” Maturity? 
 
(2) The proposed change complicates and compromises the grading process. 
 
---Having two methods of maturity identification can only complicate what has been a 
simple process. USDA should only use one method of maturity identification. If 
additional research confirms the merits of dentition are superior to ossification, then the 
system should be changed to dentition. 
---The grading system is compromised under the new proposal because AMS does not 
control all aspects of Quality Grade determination. Under the new proposal, an employee 
of the packer determines maturity via dentition. AMS is ultimately responsible for the 
final Quality Grade, therefore AMS employees must control all aspects of the grading 
process (maturity and marbling).

 
Page 2 
 
 
 
 
(3) Proposed change does nothing to improve Quality Grade standards. 
 
---If those individuals requesting change were interested in improving Quality Grades, 
then their request should have been to replace ossification with dentition. Instead they 
want to add dentition and allow dentition to override ossification whenever possible. 
 
(4) Concerns over biased statements in the solicitation. 
 
---I felt like the solicitation for changing the standards was written by a used car 
salesman. For example, there is constant encouragement to “modernize” the grading 
standards, as if “modernize” had some meaning. In this instance, the proposed change is 
not “modern” at all, it is only different. Neither counting teeth nor studying skeletal 
ossification is modern. (If the solicitors wanted to modernize grading, then they should 
support the development of hyperspectral imaging.) 
 
---Statements which reference an increase in revenue of between $55 and $59.5 million to 
producers are misleading. All of the increase in revenue will go to the packers. None 
will go to producers. 
 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment. It should be clear that now is not the time to 
change the methodology for maturity determination.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on FDA's proposed rule for establishing over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids. The FDA is required by Congress to ensure that these regulations are safe and effective. To that end, I recommend that the FDA adopt the recommendations established by the national associations representing hearing care professionals, which call for a maximum output limit of 110 dB SPL and a gain limit of 25 dB. Implementing these limits will not have any impact affordability or accessibility of new OTC hearing aids, but it will go a long way in preventing consumer harm. 

It is my understanding that the consumer technology industry urged FDA to implement output limits of 115/120 dB and no gain limit. However, in real life, when it comes to developing devices for individuals with mild-to-moderate hearing loss, it acknowledged that lower output and gain limits are appropriate for those with mild-to-moderate hearing loss. For example, Bose's 510(k) for its own self-fitting hearing aid for mild-to-moderate hearing loss states that 106 dB output and 30 dB gain is "adequate for fitting moderate hearing loss."

Additionally, given that this technology already exists, and these devices are already on the market, setting safe and effective limits proposed by the audiologists and hearing instrument specialists does not stifle innovation or limit affordability. 

I urge the FDA to prioritize the safety of consumers who will begin self-diagnosing and treating their hearing loss after this new category of hearing aids is created. They deserve nothing less from the FDA.

From my perspective as a physician advocating community water fluoridation for nearly two decades I strongly endorse the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and Prevention's recommendation that the national non-regulatory technical and administrative guideline for operational control of fluoride concentration in fluoridating water systems be 0.6 - 1.0 ppm.

The rationale, objective scientific justification for the asymmetric operational control range of -.1ppm and +.5 ppm is well described in the CDC proposed guideline and the supporting background document

https://www.regulations.gov/contentStreamer?documentId=CDC-2018-0064-0001&contentType=pdf
 
 and
 
https://www.regulations.gov/document?D=CDC-2018-0064-0002

Over 70 years of large population fluoridation causes us to be very confident that the upper operational limit of 0.1 ppm is associated with no health harms. 

I am particularly in agreement that the asymmetrical standard have 0.6 ppm as the low allowable fluoride concentration. 

It is likely that fluoride ion concentration falling below 0.6 ppm, especially if prolonged, will cause increased caries disease (cavities). This reality coupled with a national experience of water operators more commonly undershooting rather than exceeding the target underscore the CDC operational recommendation as correct and important.

The American Fluoridation Society is aware of many instances of misinformed and misguided operators purposefully subverting fluoridation programs. The CDC's operational guideline recommendation is an important part of ensuring proper consistency for community water fluoridation nation-wide.

CORRECTION TO MY EARLIER COMMENT: Lost ROI income to investor is $790,099.31, not "over $1.5M". Corrected comment appears below.

My firm, EB-5 Analytics, reviewed the self-reported net worth of over 150 of our prior clients to determine the distribution of investors across various income levels. The data showed that 26% of investors have a net worth under the $1.35M investment level proposed by USCIS. Another 8% have net worth above $1.35M but below the $1.8M non-TEA investment level proposed. Obviously, these persons are highly unlikely to pursue an EB-5 visa if the investment levels are raised as USCIS proposes. At the next level, we see 35% of investors who have net worth between $2M and $5M. These persons may consider an EB-5 visa under the new price regime, but they are likely to be price sensitive, and may well consider another country for investment (or, just stay home).

The "cost" of the visa will rise not just in terms of the minimum investment. It will also rise in terms of the lost return on investment. Most foreign nationals can earn 10% to 20% on their savings if invested in their home country. Even if we assume a conservative opportunity cost of capital of 10%, the typical EB-5 investor receiving 0.5% from the EB-5 project already sacrifices $ $292,629.37 in lost investment income over the five-year life of the $500,000 investment. If the investor participates at $1.35M, he or she sacrifices $790,099.31.

One might argue that lost income due to fewer investors may be compensated by the higher minimum investment, but jobs are almost certain to be lost unless the Service requires a higher number of new jobs per investment.

These trees had died from the blight over 50 years before I saw them. I later learned how integral the American Chestnut was to early Americans as well as to the numerous wildlife species that depended on it. As a woodworker, I also know that American Chestnut wood was used for almost anything from fencing, railroad ties, interior millwork to furniture. 
In my view, loss of our native biodiversity is a larger issue and more individually actionable than climate change. Each of our native trees, shrubs, and native plants support a wide variety of native insects, pollinators, and other wildlife in our food web. These native insects have adapted to specific host trees or plants and often cannot survive without them. The insects generally will not feed or live on non-native plants or cultivars even of the same family. Native oak trees, for example, support several hundred native insects and pollinators. Restoring the American Chestnut is important as a biodiversity component of our food-web. The non-native grass, plant, and tree cultivars that we typically plant through-out our country and homes do not support these native insects and pollinators and endanger our food web. Not all green space has the same value to the ecosystem. By offering an all-encompassing framework that covers the several facets of resource management and preservation inside the reserve, the BLM's proposed rule seeks to achieve this balance.

The protection and improvement of access for subsistence activities inside the NPR-A are also highlighted in the proposed regulation. I, like many consumers, rely on on-package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised" I assume that there is value and meaning behind that claim and that is backed by a regulatory agency.

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. Companies will still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit. 

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Time and time again industry has shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating/policing itself. Companies are taking advantage of consumers, and grossly overcharging them, by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels to bring in more profits all the while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare.

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers.

FSIS owes it to the American public to set a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," take steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensure that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

Specifically, the FDA must amend the Draft Guidance so that the requirements related to allergenic extract preparation in an ISO Class 5 environment do not apply to preparation of allergenic extract prepared in a physician's office.

 Allergists have over 100 years of experience preparing allergenic extract in their offices without a single report of a sterility issue.

 Allergists currently comply with USP Chapter 797 guidelines.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

I buy meat, eggs and dairy products from local Midwestern farmers because I know the 'truth in labeling' law is not respected nor conformed to by the USDA. A third party overseer may help correct this irresponsible method.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

This proposed rule is important to the citrus industry in the region of Florida. While only 14 handlers will be impacted it is still important to do some due diligence and verify that this new rule would not vastly impact the economy, the welfare of people, or the integrity of those who work for the Citrus Administrative Committee. 
Florida is one of the largest producers of citrus in the world. While these fruits originated in Asia, the colonization of the US by the Spanish transported seeds here, where they were sold to Native Americans in the Florida area and cultivated. Citrus was incredibly important to these Native peoples who continued to cultivate citrus even as the US conquered their lands in 1821. Native Americans traded these citrus fruits with people North of Florida (n.d., The citrus industry in Florida). Thus, it is important to note the history of citrus in the US is closely tied with the history of the Native American tribes in the Florida area. However, the relationship between Native people and citrus is not just history, but also the future of the region. It is important to note that the Seminole Tribe acquired Blue Lake Citrus in 2014 before it was subsequently closed forever (n.d., Seminole tribe acquires Blue Lake citrus products). This was not the only Seminole contribution to citrus as the Seminole tribe is actively partnered with the Roe family in producing citrus at Nobel Citrus (n.d., Seminole PrideTM Noble). 
The majority of citrus farmers in this region are white and native peoples like the Seminoles no longer cultivate citrus at the capacity they used to in the 1800s. Increasing regulations and adding costs like these are potentially limiting factors that may be preventing native peoples from returning to citrus cultivation, which was incredibly important to these native tribes after the introduction of citrus over 200 years ago. I urge the committee to look more closely into the demographics of the 14 organizations that will be impacted by this new rule. I also urge the committee to understand that the increased variable costs may deter newer, smaller Native citrus producers from returning to the industry. 
I also think it is important to acknowledge a legal case that was just taken to the Supreme Court over a similar issue. Fishermen have been required to take federal observers out with them to sea to make sure they are not overfishing and following regulations. The costs of these observers are likely much greater than the proposed costs of increased assessments of the citrus crates, however, it still makes an interesting point on the pressures placed on producers (2024, Dwyer & Herndon). If the government is interested in more assessments being done, then they should fund the cost of doing so rather than pressuring small American producers to raise their prices. While the price increase is minimal on a small scale (only a few cents increase per 4/5-bushels of citrus), this will have sent a shock on the regional and federal economies for things like juices, candies, and raw citrus. 
While increased assessments are likely valuable to protecting consumers and the quality of products for producers, it is important to very closely monitor the economic and ethical impacts on the future, not just in the short term.

COMMENTS OF THE INTERNATIONAL AIR TRANSPORT ASSOCIATION 
 
The International Air Transport Association (IATA) appreciates the opportunity to provide 
comments in response to the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT)’s Notice of Proposed 
Rulemaking (NPRM), Refunding Fees for Delayed Checked Bags and Ancillary Services That Are 
Not Provided.1 
 
IATA is the trade association for the world’s airlines, representing some 290 carriers based in 
120 countries. Our airline members are committed to providing the best customer service 
possible, including ensuring that their customers receive their checked luggage and ancillary 
service purchases in a timely and efficient manner. 
 
We support the goals of this congressionally-mandated rulemaking to ensure that customers 
receive timely refunds for delayed checked baggage and ancillary services that are not 
provided. However, DOT must provide airlines with the necessary flexibility to provide service 
and service recovery within the operational constraints of the airline. In addition, the final rule 
should not act as a disincentive for airlines to improve their services as this will ultimately end 
up harming consumers. 
 
Length of Delay Triggering Refund Requirement 
 
As noted in our comments on the ANPRM, IATA believes that carriers should be afforded the 
maximum amount of time allowed under Section 2305 of the FAA Extension Act of 2016 (P.L. 
114-190) to return a passenger’s delayed checked baggage for both domestic and international 
flights. We appreciate DOT’s acknowledgement that many international flights are scheduled 
once a day and that it would be extremely challenging, if not impossible in many instances, for a 
carrier to deliver a delayed checked bag within the minimum length delay of 15 hours 
prescribed in the statute for international flights. Further, as noted in the NPRM, a 15-hour

deadline could be a disincentive for carriers to deliver the bag on the next available flight, 
potentially negatively impacting consumers further. However, we are concerned that the 
proposed 12- and 25-hour delay timeframes for domestic and international flights, respectively, 
fail to take into account the myriad factors that are outside of the airline’s control that could 
have a significant impact on the time it takes for an airline to return delayed baggage to a 
customer, including: 
 
• passenger travel that originates on the last flight of the day out of a particular airport; 
• the next available flight to transport a delayed bag might not have space available; 
• aircraft weight/balance limitations; 
• passenger negligence (e.g., failure to pick up bags, traveling on two separate tickets, 
baggage contains dangerous goods); 
• passenger inadmissibility or deportation; 
• another passenger inadvertently claims the wrong checked bag; 
• labor strikes and work slowdowns; 
• severe weather conditions; 
• airport congestion; 
• airport procedures; and 
• customs/security inspection. 
 
Domestic Segments of International Itineraries 
 
We support applying the international standard to the domestic segments of international 
flights. Applying different standards to different flight segments may cause passenger 
confusion as to the expectations regarding baggage delivery. Also, air carriers may not be able 
to determine to which segment the delay should be attributed. Applying a single standard will 
help to ensure that airlines and passengers have a common understanding of when refunds are 
due.

Colleges and universities should inform students of the specific debt levels and expected earnings for their majors in a clearer and more standardized manner before enrollment.This will not only enable students to understand and plan ahead, but also help them prepare for their future development.
At the same time, annual and lifetime limits should be established for both Graduate PLUS and Parent PLUS loans.If such limits are established,loan amounts should be determined based on parents’ actual income and repayment capacity, and the approval process should be more rigorous.
For high-tuition majors, although loans can provide students with fairer access to higher education, it is essential to ensure that graduates' post-graduation incomes can afford the high debt. If students' loan money is not spent on "value-for-money" higher education, or if graduates are forced to abandon low-paying careers that interest them or have high social value in favor of high-paying jobs that may not suit them, this constitutes deception. Therefore, a strict "debt-to-income ratio" accountability mechanism should be established, and federal loan eligibility should be suspended for those "low-quality" programs with high graduate debt, low earnings, and high default rates.
In addition, combining the existing 4 to 5 repayment plans into a single Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) can help students understand the relevant policies more easily. Furthermore, since some students are unaware of the need to apply, do not know the application process, or even forget to apply, students should be automatically enrolled in an Income-Driven Repayment (IDR) plan without needing to submit an application proactively.

Abstract
Public lands of the USA can play an important role in addressing the climate crisis. About 85% of public lands in the western
USA are grazed by domestic livestock, and they inﬂuence climate change in three profound ways: (1) they are signiﬁcant
sources of greenhouse gases through enteric fermentation and manure deposition; (2) they defoliate native plants, trample
vegetation and soils, and accelerate the spread of exotic species resulting in a shift in landscape function from carbon sinks to
sources of greenhouse gases; and (3) they exacerbate the effects of climate change on ecosystems by creating warmer and
drier conditions. On public lands one cow-calf pair grazing for one month (an “animal unit month” or “AUM”) produces
875 kg CO2e through enteric fermentation and manure deposition with a social carbon cost of nearly $36 per AUM. Over 14
million AUMs of cattle graze public lands of the western USA each year resulting in greenhouse gas emissions of 12.4 Tg
CO2e year−1. The social costs of carbon are > $500 million year−1 or approximately 26 times greater than annual grazing
fees collected by managing federal agencies. These emissions and social costs do not include the likely greater ecosystems
costs from grazing impacts and associated livestock management activities that reduce biodiversity, carbon stocks and rates
of carbon sequestration. Cessation of grazing would decrease greenhouse gas emissions, improve soil and water resources,
and would enhance/sustain native species biodiversity thus representing an important and cost-effective adaptive approach to
climate change.

To Whom It May Concern:

On November 2, 2018 in its 2019 Final HOPPS/ASC Rule, CMS inexplicably and without comment moved CPT 50590 (SWL) from APC 5375 into APC 5374. In disregard of its mandate to create clinically homogeneous groupings, CMSs change creates potential perverse consequences for patients, providers, and itself. The following points speak to the reasons your decision seems unwise, unfair, and possibly dangerous for Medicare beneficiaries. 

 Clinical Homogeneity: For many kidney stone patients, both SWL (CPT 50590) and ureteroscopy with lithotripsy (URS) (CPT 52356 and CPT 52353) are appropriate options. In other words, they are poster children for clinical homogeneity.
 APC Groupings: By separating SWL (Lithotripsy) and URS (Ureteroscopy with lithotripsy, stone manipulation and stent) into separate groupings, CMS creates a nearly $1100 incentive for both hospitals and ASCs to perform URS. Conversely, it creates a disincentive to provide SWL. 
 Patients May Suffer: Many patients prefer SWL. It is non-invasive, can be done without general anesthesia, and returns them to normal activities quickly. Unlike URS patients, most do not have stents put in after the procedure and thus they avoid the pain and suffering stents cause. URS (ureteroscopy) requires stent placement. This stent must be removed several days to weeks after the procedure, many times at additional cost to Medicare as a separate procedure. 100% of my patients who have needed a stent in the past, never want one again in the future.
 Unintended Consequences: Recent studies have shown that unplanned admissions post-URS (ureteroscopy) are significantly higher than those after SWL (lithotripsy). The complication rates are also higher after URS, compared to SWL. In other words, Medicare will pay significantly more because its payment model penalizes the use of SWL. Perhaps tens of millions more.
 Unfair and Deceptive: Whether intended or not, CMSs process in making this change looks terribly flawed. In its 2019 Proposed HOPPS/ASC Rule, CMS included SWL in APC 5375, alongside URS. There was no suggestion of the coming change. Thus we were all blindsided by the Final Rule move of SWL to APC 5374. Anyone interested in the issue would have had no reason to comment on a move of CPT 50590. It was not proposed.
 Costs and Charges: What we know is that extracorporeal shock wave lithotripters cost around $500,000, have significant annual maintenance fees, and have expensive component parts like shock wave generators. These lithotripters can only be used for one CPT code and that is 50590. Ureteroscopes, on the other hand, cost less than $10,000 and can be used for dozens of CPT codes. Perhaps hospital charges do not reflect the costs of SWL because the facilities do not own the equipment. They cannot afford to do so. Consequently, the true cost of providing SWL is underestimated by hospital charges.
 CMSs Inexplicable Inconsistency: In all of its previous groupings based upon clinical homogeneity and mean costs, CMS has found SWL to be appropriately placed in APC 5375. On July 25, 2018 CMSs data justified including CPT 50590 in APC 5375 in its Proposed Rule. Yet only three (3) months later in its Final Rule, CMS places SWL in APC 5374. What changed and why did it not trigger public comment? Again, on multiple levels, CMSs decision regarding SWL makes little sense. 
 
For all of these reasons, I ask you to reconsider your move of CPT 50590 out of APC 5375. 

Sincerely,
