Dear Fish and Wildlife Service,

I'm disturbed to learn that you're entertaining the idea of killing more Double-crested Cormorants. Past actions killing a large number of these birds has not increased the survival rate of salmon in Pacific Northwest Rivers - it has only resulted in the near colony collapse of the birds. The Cormorant killings are not based in science. All scientific studies show that the removal of dams is what is needed to restore plummeting salmon populations. Stop scapegoating these birds for simply eating and existing. Turn your efforts towards policy change centered on dam removal in order to save salmonids. I oppose the proposed rule and recommend the No Action Alternative for the following reasons:

 Allowing the killing of as many as 123,157 Double-crested Cormorants nation-wide each year perpetuates a long-term pattern of persecution of this species by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and is in direct conflict with the agencies mission and mandate to conserve, protect and enhance fish, wildlife and plants and their habitats for the continuing benefit of the American people protect native bird species. 
 Allowing the killing of as many as 123,157 Double-crested Cormorants annually violates the Migratory Bird Treaty Act which mandates that the agency only allow killing if it can ensure the continued viability of the species.
 Allowing the take of nearly 9,000 Double-crested Cormorant annually west of the Rocky Mountains (representing >14% of the western population) where populations are already as risk, in part due to prior actions by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, would put the western population at extreme risk and could result in the need for a future listing under the Endangered Species Act. 
 The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to consider any strategies other than lethal control of Double-crested Cormorants in any of the action alternatives.
 The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to include adequate monitoring in the proposal alternative to ensure that it would be able to modify killing levels if significant declines occur.
 The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to adequately address risks to non-target species.
 The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to address humane and animal welfare issues.
 The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to adequately address illegal take of cormorants and disruption of colonies in their modelling.
 The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has failed to demonstrate that killing Double-crested Cormorants would benefit imperiled fish species.
 Delegation of permitting authority to states is an abdication of a core responsibility of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and would put management of cormorants in the hands of state agencies that lack both resources and expertise and which in many cases have explicitly expressed a desire to see even more aggressive control of cormorants than has been allowed to date by USFWS.

I am deeply disappointed that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is continuing to pursue the unwarranted persecution of Double-crested Cormorants. Prior actions by the Service have put cormorant populations at risk, resulted in the deaths of tens of thousands of cormorants, wasted millions of taxpayer dollars and failed to achieve stated goals. It is time for the killing to stop. I respectfully urge you to adopt the No Action Alternative. 

Sincerely,

Dawn Smallman

the production area, the fruit must undergo cold treatment as outlined in the appropriate

concluded that they would provide sufficient control. However, FDACS-DPI notes this

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. Children do NOT belong behind bars. The number one priority of the Flores Settlement Agreement is that children not be incarcerated.

The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay". This proposed regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. There is a lot of evidence showing the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Our government must do better than these proposed regulations.

I thought that we, the public and the Fish and Wildlife Services, were committed to preserving habitat for the Northern Spotted Owl and all of the many creatures and plants that live and multiply in this same old growth landscape. But now, the Trump Administration is proposing to remove over 200,000 acres of the Northern Spotted Owl's Critical Habitat. This is horrifying and short-sited. Therefore, I am responding to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed rule, Docket No. FWS-R1-ES-2020-0050. We must save this 200,000 acres of the Northern Spotted Owl critical habitat in Oregon. And, there are many reasons why:
*Please note that all remaining spotted owl habitat is essential for the survival of the species. Instead of excluding 200,000 acres of Critical Habitat, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service should protect what remains of the older forests where the owl lives. 

*The lands (200,000 acres( in question are key to the recovery of the owl because they provide habitat connections between the coast range and the Cascades. Much of the habitat proposed for removal is in SW Oregon on lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management. This is an area known regionally to provide for forest habitat connectivity. 

*Barred owls are not native, but threaten spotted owls through competition. They have been able to move into spotted owl areas, likely due to fragmentation brought on by past logging. This makes it even more important to protect the habitat that remains for the spotted owl. The added stress that barred owls place on remaining spotted owls makes every acre of spotted owl critical habitat necessary for the survival and recovery of the owl 

*The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is changed with recovering threatened and endangered species. How will the removal of this habitat enable the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service from carrying out its duties? Please explain why the Service is neglecting its primary duty to recovery at-risk species. 

*This is not a scientific decision, rather it is political. The Service knows that the lands in question are the public lands where the last best owl habitat is located. All the private industrial land and much of the federal land in this area has been logged. What remains is absolutely critical to the recovery of the owl. 

Thank you for considering my words and for stopping this heinous act of decimating over 200,000 acres of the Northern Spotted Owl's Critical Habitat. - Nadine Lefkowitz, Ashland, Oregon

I oppose the delisting of Grizzly Bears in the Greater Yellowstone Area (GYA). Their population has recovered to what appears to be a stable point at which it's able to sustain itself. Many would like to see it expand further, for reasons of population health and viability. 

With food supplies limited and natural migration and reproductive imperatives and behaviors what they have always been (and hopefully what they always will be), they need room to roam outside the borders of Yellowstone National Park. And we need to continue to conserve their habitats in that broad range.

Grizzlies and other large predators are essential to their ecosystems. This is how nature was created, and this is how it should be conserved and restored under our stewardship.

Recreational hunting in the GYA is not needed as an additional source of mortality to control their numbers. Furthermore, recreational hunting is not well suited to use as a wildlife-management technique targeted at the attainment of ecosystem-based management objectives; to the contrary, it tends to be directed at the taking of "trophy" animals rather than problem animals, or the young, old or otherwise weakened individuals that tend to suffer the highest mortalities in nature.

Hikers, campers, and visitors to the off-trail areas of GYA are generally well aware of the need to be alert and avoid encounters with wildlife. Those that are not need to improve; we should not enable their ignorance or stubbornness by imposing it on their natural surroundings.

Although there is something to be said for providing recreational opportunities to the sporting community, there is more to be said for moving more toward the ecosystem-based management that a growing number of U.S. environmentalists, students, tourists, etc. are learning to understand, appreciate, and enjoy. 

Human society's way into the future will be less about making the outdoors our drop-off points for human-centered recreational activities; and more about supporting and enjoying our wild ecosystems for what they are in their own right. As a strong step forward into that future, let us continue our protections of GYA Grizzlies under the U.S. Endangered Species Act.

Sharks risk being driven to extinction due to overfishing, with almost 100 million killed each year, scientists have warned.

Many species of shark need better protection to prevent their extinction within coming decades, researchers warned in advance of a global conference on the trade in threatened species.

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (Cites) will consider greater protection of vulnerable sharks, including porbeagles, oceanic whitetip and three types of hammerhead to preserve their populations.

Sharks are caught for their fins for use in shark fin soup, a delicacy in Asia. The fins are cut off with the dead carcass being thrown back into the sea. Sharks grow slowly and take years to reproduce, which makes them vulnerable to overfishing.

The researchers estimated that global reported catches, unreported landings, discards and sharks caught and thrown back after their fins were cut off - a process known as finning - added up to 97 million fish caught in 2010.

The figure is only slightly less than the estimated 100 million caught in 2000, and could be anywhere between 63 million sharks and 273 million a year, according to research by North American scientists published in the journal Marine Policy.

It is estimated that between 6.4% and 7.9% of all sharks are killed each year, leading to decline in the number of some species.

Boris Worm, one of the report's authors, from Dalhousie University in Halifax, said: "Biologically, sharks simply can't keep up with the current rate of exploitation and demand. Protective measures must be scaled up significantly in order to avoid further depletion and the possible extinction of many shark species in our lifetime."

Although some regions, including the European Union, have banned shark finning, commercial fisheries for fins, meat, liver oil, cartilage and other body parts are largely unregulated in much of the world.

The DPCNA opposes – in part - the proposed rulemaking as it would introduce an unduly restrictive importation process, detrimental for our breed, that fails to serve a demonstrated public health purpose. Drents are imported from European countries that have eradicated rabies: Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark and Sweden. The CDC neither requires nor proposes a rabies vaccination requirement for dogs coming from these countries. Nonetheless, the proposed rule-making would needlessly apply an age restriction, expressly tied to the need to verify rabies vaccination, to the importation of puppies from countries without a rabies vaccination requirement.

The DPCNA proposes that the exception to the age requirement provided to arrivals from Canada and Mexico should be extended on equal terms to other low-risk or DMRVV-free countries, which would also necessitate striking the land crossing requirement. This modest solution fully addresses the public health concerns outlined in the notice of proposed rulemaking. The solution has the added benefit of making the proposed rule internally consistent.
There is no commercial importation of Drents: United States citizens import individual Drent puppies based on a personal relationship with a European breeder. Drent puppies mostly come from the Netherlands, but also Belgium, Denmark and Sweden. Each of these countries is not only free of canine rabies, but – unlike the United States – completely rabies free.1 Documentation accompanying puppies establishes their age and vaccination status as well as ownership by the citizen returning home with the puppy. Traveling at eight weeks of age, consistent with USDA requirements, a puppy travels in the passenger cabin with its owner and not as unattended cargo.

Unless modified, the proposed rule would create insurmountable and unnecessary barriers to the success of the Drent in the United States. The Drent is a rare breed. The North American population is small and largely comprised of dogs imported as puppies and the immediate offspring of these dogs. Genetic diversity is limited in the current population. The breed in North America will not thrive and may not survive without the infusion of diverse genetics through the further importation of Drent puppies from rabies-free countries.

There is no public health justification for applying the proposed six-month age requirement to puppies coming from rabies-free countries. The age requirement is an overbroad, inconsistently applied, and misguided animal welfare provision, at least where older dogs may enter the United States without proof of rabies vaccination. The age provision may have merit for dogs coming from high-risk countries where CDC requires vaccination for rabies that is not possible in young puppies. But it has no applicability where no vaccination requirement currently exists or is proposed.

Proposed Solution: The exception to the age requirement provided to arrivals from Canada and Mexico should be extended on equal terms to other low-risk or DMRVV-free countries, which would also necessitate striking the land crossing requirement.

Thank you for providing the opportunity to provide comments on the establishment of an 
IDEA Data Management Center, as published by the Department of Education (ED) on 
November 13, 2019, and in particular, the Department's directed question to establish two 
centers (i.e., one Center addressing the needs of Developed Capacity States, and another 
Center addressing the needs of Developing Capacity States). This comment speaks to that 
question and provides feedback regarding whether or not the establishment of such 
centers would be an efficient and effective approach to meeting the diverse needs of 
States in integrating, reporting, analyzing, and using high-quality IDEA Part B data. 
 
At WestEd we have had the opportunity to work as a subcontractor on the IDEA Data 
Management Center for the past five years. Based on this and other experience in 
providing technical assistance (TA) to states on IDEA data collection, management, and 
reporting, we strongly support the establishment of one center – not two – in order to 
address the Department’s priority “to address the diverse needs of states in integrating, 
reporting, analyzing, and using high-quality IDEA Part B data.” 
 
Our consistent experience is that States’ capacity does not often fall cleanly in the 
Developed or Developing category. A State’s capacity to collect, manage, and report data 
exists on a continuum, and in our experience, fluctuates, given changes in federal and state 
policy as well as turnover in SEA leadership and staff, which can quickly shift state agency 
priorities and directions. Successful TA under this context must be designed to meet states 
at their current levels of need and priority, and guide them through the challenges of 
increasing capacity for effectiveness. At times, that may mean the TA engagement takes 
longer because initially the focus is on getting them ready. 
 
A long-term TA relationship is best configured to support states through the developing 
stages to those of continuous improvement, whether those stages are short, long, or 
constant. If this priority resulted in two centers, we believe that there is a risk of the TA 
being less effective – not more. Additionally, we also know that a Center, as it matures, can

Thank you for proposing to expand critical habitat for the Southern Resident killer whales (SRKW) to include marine waters from Monterey Bay in California through Cape Flattery in Washington State. I fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

These are God's creations, we need to take better care of them, and their environment. 

Protecting this full range as critical habitat reflects new and best available science as new sightings and data show that SRKW regularly forage in the coastal waters off Washington, Oregon, and California and is essential to help get the southern resident orcas off the path to extinction and on the way to recovery.

The final rule designating critical habitat identified three essential habitat features essential to the conservation of the SRKW: (1) Water quality to support SRKW growth and development; (2) prey species of sufficient quantity, quality, and availability to support individual growth, reproduction, and development, as well as overall population growth; and (3) passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

However, the proposed rule exempts the Navy's Quinault Range Site off the coast of Washington from being designated as critical habitat due to national security. The Quinault Range Site includes part of two high-use foraging areas, as recognized by NMFS in the Biological Report, and completely bisects the proposed expanded critical habitat area. From the tagging data, about half the time that K and L pods spend in coastal habitat is in Area 1 (Washington and Northern Oregon inshore habitat). This exemption could impact their foraging ability in an area and season when nutritional stress is a significant concern and impact their ability to migrate up and down the coast. Therefore the exempted area is in conflict with the third essential habitat feature: passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

The proposed rule should include a narrow area sufficient in width between the shoreline and the eastern border of the Quinault Range Site to ensure orca migration along the coast and for foraging for limited prey. 

The science also shows that sound from vessels and other sources undermines orcas ability to echolocate to forage for salmon as well as to communicate and navigate. The Washington Governors Orca Recovery Task Force and the ESA Recovery Plan have noted that noise and disturbance are key threats hindering orca recovery and have recommended decreasing, not increasing, military noise. To sufficiently protect SRKW, NMFS must include sound as a fourth essential feature. Urge them to ensure that it is at least retained as an explicit factor in the prey and passage essential features. 

I am grateful that NMFS has engaged and consulted with Tribes to ensure that this rule does not impact Tribal Treaty rights and usual and accustomed fishing areas.

Again, fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

I strongly oppose the definition of "habitat" that is proposed in this rule. Designation of critical habitat is a vital tool available under the Endangered Species Act to help conserve species. Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors.

This change would result in the exclusion of areas that do not meet the new, narrower definition of habitat, thereby decreasing the amount of habitat that can be protected. This would represent a severe setback to conservation, because critical habitat is vital for stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species that have protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species without it.

Biodiversity is key to the health of the planet that sustains us. Every time a species goes extinct, our environment becomes less viable. Most citizens believe that funding agencies such as the USFWS protects our wilderness areas and the animals that inhabit them. This should be a priority for the USFWS and NOAA. Spend our money responsibly.

Americans recognize the ESA's vital role in conserving beloved wildlife species, and a 2018 survey found that four out of five people support the law. At a time of unprecedented wildlife extinction and habitat destruction, we should be working to strengthen--not weaken--the ESA. For these reasons, I urge the USFWS and NOAA to withdraw this proposed rule.

“Why? What will they look at? How will they use that information?1” This social experiment 

serves to illustrate that people want to be informed, and they want to give their consent. It would 

come as a surprise if one found out their cells, which contain all of the genetic sequencing that 

makes them entirely unique, are being passed around by researchers without one’s consent. 

U.S. informed consent law takes its roots in the Nuremburg Code2, explicitly spelling out 

the need to proactively secure voluntary consent of any human research subject, but one of the

which eventually became a “cell line” that was patented and sold for commercial use, without 

Moore’s knowledge of the physician’s research interest. Although rejecting the theory of 

conversion allegation, The Court noted, “that the breach of fiduciary duty and the lack of 

informed consent theory were better suited to protect the rights of patients3.” I argue that the 

devolution of informed consent into a nationalized “broad consent” standard would be a 

detriment to public trust in the study of human subjects because deference given towards 

researchers prioritizes the advancement of medical discovery over the protection of patients’ 

rights. The authorization requirements set forth by the regulations should bolster public trust by

I respectfully submit this comment OPPOSING the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family member. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

The United States has a moral obligation to welcome and to help these immigrants, whose lives have been ruined in large part due to US foreign policies.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed rule, Affordability of

“family glitch” that was created by a 2013 misreading of the Affordable Care Act (ACA).
That misreading erected a barrier to affordable coverage for millions of Americans barring them
from eligibility for premium tax credits despite having an offer of unaffordable employer
coverage.
The interpretation applied in this proposed rule is the best reading of the statute and consistent
with the goals of the ACA to expand access to affordable coverage. As noted in the preamble to
this proposed rule, the current interpretation was originally proposed in a broader rule on
premium tax credits (76 FR 50931), but not finalized in 2012 (77 FR 30377). Instead, the final
policy (78 FR 7264) adopted in 2013 used an interpretation inconsistent with the text and intent
of the ACA, thereby creating the “family glitch.”
The current interpretation affects as many as 5.1 million Americans, including at least 40,000
Oregonians who are barred from obtaining premium tax credits because “affordable” coverage
is based only on the cost to cover the employee.1 Most of the people impacted are children, and
nearly half a million people go uninsured when faced with unaffordable coverage under a family
member’s employer plan.2 In Oregon, employee premiums were approximately 8.1 percent
of family income in 2019; adding in the average deductible for a family health insurance
plan increases household spending on health insurance to 13.5 percent of income.3
The family glitch has a greater impact on low-income families, but it is also a problem for
middle-income families. Almost half (46%) of the people in the family glitch have incomes under
250% of the federal policy level (FPL) and another third (33%) have income between

Dear Assistant Director, Office of Policy Debbie Seguin,

I write in opposition to this Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) proposed rule that would allow this administration to undermine the current protections outlined by the 1997 Flores settlement. The Flores decision sets clear guidelines that direct the government to reunite children with a parent or relative without delay and provides standards and protections for children while in government custody. The proposed rule seeks to weaken or remove those protections and allow children to be jailed indefinitely.

Among many other concerning changes, this rule would:
- Give the administration the power to self-license and implement standards at detention centers at a time when reports that show that DHS is not capable of maintaining clean, humane and safe detention centers currently.
- Weaken protections for children as they undergo processing in detention facilities and make release from detention and reunification with family members a more difficult process. DHS would have increased authority to change the rules regarding when and how children can be reunified and with whom. DHS and HHS are also given the authority to declare an emergency and completely suspend protections for children.
- Reverses a child’s right to a bond hearing and instead creates an agency-run administrative process that poses threats to due process.

This rule outlines a system where an openly anti-immigrant administration, responsible for deliberately separating over 2,000 children from their parents, is able to create and change the rules of immigrant enforcement, due process, and the already horrific detention conditions for children as they see fit. These changes are unconscionable, inhumane and would directly harm children and families who have come to the United States to seek a better life.

Imprisonment of children and families seeking a better life and often fleeing life-threatening violence is adding trauma to trauma, and these policies that criminalize immigrant communities threaten all of us. The government should focus instead on policies that keep families together, outside of detention, and that guarantee full due process under the law.

I am writing in opposition to the proposed amendments regarding the Risk Management Programs. These common-sense amendments are essential in reducing the impacts and frequencies of dangerous chemical spills or other disasters that can occur at major chemical plants and other facilities. 

Suggesting that these amendments are needed to reduce costs to such businesses shows complete disregard for the effects of such disasters and the impacts they have on surrounding communities and the environment. It also ignores the fact that cleaning up after such disasters comes with tremendous costs. We need regulations in place that require independent audits regarding the safety practices of such facilities, so that assessments are done with accuracy, by appropriately trained professionals, and so that they are unbiased. 

In addition, the general public deserves the right to know what risks may be related to those chemicals at such facilities. It is also imperative that emergency response personnel and those involved in cleaning up after a disaster be informed about those things necessary in facilitating the clean-up and keeping both workers and nearby communities as safe as possible during and after such an event. 

Staff at these chemical facilities should be required to carefully evaluate past disasters at such facilities and to take appropriate steps to learn from the events. Whenever possible, advancements in technology should be applied to better control or manage risks in order to reduce the chances that such disasters should occur again. The safety of workers and those in surrounding communities should be a priority for all facilities. 

Relaxing or even eliminating these important components of these programs is irresponsible, since it is the responsibility of the EPA to protect both the natural environment and people from the devastating and often fatal consequences of chemical-related disasters. 

Thank you for considering my comments on this important issue.

I urge the EPA to take concrete steps to strengthen public health protections, address existing lead contamination as well as legacy lead contamination for communities experiencing the highest exposure levels. The proposed EPA plan addresses legacy contamination sites, but lead is still emitted at alarming levels from steel mills, incinerators, battery recyclers, and other industrial sources. There is no safe level of lead exposure, yet lead is still being actively released into the environment around us. 

The EPA recognizes how dangerous lead poisoning is to children and communities but the proposed EPA plan falls short on specifics beyond describing the serious lead problem that communities face. The EPA must commit to change its regulations for lead paint hazards (which includes lead in paint, soil, and dust) and lead in water to effectively protect public health.

I urge the EPA to adopt regulations that tackle lead contamination that can be found in homes and schools from hazards such as peeling paint, contaminated dust, toxic soil, and contaminated water. As many as 22 million people in the United States drink water that passed through lead pipes. In many places, lead leaches into the water as it did in Flint, Michigan. And there are about 3.6 million residences nationwide where young children live with lead hazards such as peeling paint, contaminated dust, or toxic soil. 

While this draft lead strategy has admirable goals, it does not commit to establishing lower acceptable lead levels for lead-based paint nor does it commit to requiring the speedy replacement of all lead pipes delivering drinking water.

I urge EPA to adopt a plan with immediate concrete steps to address these sources of lead exposure and protect communities with the highest lead exposure.

Re: Proposed Priority and Requirements - Docket ID_ED-2021-OSERS-0003; CFDA #84.160D
Project CLIMB: Cultivating Legal Interpreters from Minority Backgrounds is grateful for the
opportunity to submit comments regarding the Proposed Priority and Requirements for Training
of Interpreters for Individuals who are Deaf or Hard of Hearing and Individuals who are
DeafBlind.
Project CLIMB has conceived, developed, and implemented a 84.160D funded grant project over
the last grant cycle (2017-2021). Our project has increased the number and quality of interpreters
of color and/or interpreters from heritage signing backgrounds (Deaf & Coda) in the legal
interpreting specialty. Along the way, we have learned a few things and take this opportunity to
share what we have learned with the hope that future projects are prepared and effective in
supporting diverse populations.
Critical mass in cohorted learning
Project CLIMB invested in carefully creating learning groups with balance; incorporating
numerous factors such as lived experience, native languages, geography, working experience,

 
2
and gender identity within a context of the skills and strengths of the facilitator. The participant
composition of the Communities of Learning developed and supported in Project CLIMB’s
training program applied an overt and deliberate approach to creating cohorts of participants who
represented homogeneous language &/or racial backgrounds within a larger context of diverse
participants. In short, all learning groups were developed with the aim that an individual
(participant or facilitator) would not be the ‘only’ person with their background in the group.
Based on feedback from participants and the high retention rate, 81% for a 10 month online,
remotely delivered program, we believe that this approach, along with other supports addressed
later in this comment, has been successful in ensuring participants’ successful program
completion. A race-neutral, all things are equal approach to cohorted learning, does not create
the safe environments that ensure successful learning.
We recommend that in the section: Application Requirements, c) “Quality of Project Services”,
1) that the requirement be more explicit in asking applicants to “demonstrate how the project
will ensure equitable access, treatment, and supports that takes into consideration lack of access
to educational opportunities and lack of critical mass in those opportunities for members of
groups who have traditionally been underrepresented within the field of ASL/English interpreting
based on race, color, national origin, gender, age, disability, or heritage language background”.
Training tailored for heritage users of signed language (Coda & Deaf)
Almost 50% of the participants in Project CLIMB trainings are working interpreters who are
heritage users of ASL, either Coda or Deaf. Almost all of these interpreters entered the
profession of interpreting without completing a formal, structured interpreter education program.
They often started interpreting based solely on their language and cultural competency. The
shortage of interpreters led to opportunities that they may not have been ready for. In focus
groups conducted by Project CLIMB, Coda and Deaf interpreters reported seeking interpreter
education that would meet their needs as native, and for deaf participants- primary, users of ASL;
however, found this very difficult and frustrating.
Interpreter Education Programs’ curricula are designed for the non-native user of ASL who is
doing translation for the first time. Coda and Deaf circumstantial bilinguals do not learn ASL in
a structured classroom format and have lifelong experiences translating as language brokers
between signers and non-signers in their personal life.

Dear Secretary Betsy DeVos,

Docket ID ED-2020-OPE-0078

I urge the Department of Education to withdraw its interim final rule imposing student eligibility limitations on federal emergency funds for college students. 

College students across the country are in need of relief to overcome the financial devastation brought on by the coronavirus pandemic. That is why Congress passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act, to provide wide scale relief as quickly as possible directly to students. The more than $6 billion in emergency student grant aid was meant to be widely available to support the academic futures of college students. Requiring students to demonstrate that they are eligible for federal financial aid dollars will exclude large numbers of students, many of whom are historically marginalized. 

Students are already experiencing delays in receiving emergency aid because the Department of Education gave colleges mixed messages about who is eligible to receive the funds. Students deserve the emergency aid Congress intended them to receive; and many are in desperate need of it to continue their education.

Most concerningly, large numbers of students will be excluded, including many historically marginalized students. For instance, undocumented students, borrowers who have defaulted on their loans and are currently enrolled in school, and students with poor grades will be excluded from this funding. These are students who arguably need more help, not less, to complete their college education.

This interim final rule will only harm students and create more confusion for colleges. And implementing it will disproportionately harm the nations most vulnerable students who are simply trying to improve their futures. I urge the Department to withdraw its interim final rule.

Sincerely,
Julie Carlisle
Gainesville, GA 30506

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on CDC’s proposed rule updating federal dog importation requirements.

I am writing in support of CDC’s proposed rule which would add much needed safeguards to protect animals and the public from the introduction of rabies via imported dogs.
 
In particular, the proposed requirement for permanent identification, a six-month age minimum for imported puppies, incorporating greater veterinary oversight, and requiring verification of documentation prior to transport are essential provisions in the proposed rule that will reduce the risks associated with dog importation.

Large shipments of dogs without the individual requirements listed above is a health risk to the US.
 
Absent these proposed updates to CDC regulations, the risk of reintroduction of dog-maintained rabies virus variant will persist, as we saw with the increased numbers of dogs imported with rabies leading up to CDC’s 2021 import suspension.

 
The public health risks are too high to continue without these significant changes, and I urge the CDC to move forward with this rulemaking.

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

We need more locally raised food so we don't have to deal with this bs.
BUT there needs to be regulation so that the unconscious grocery store consumer can get accurate information that will provide healthier product and humanely raised product

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

I strongly oppose the alterations to the process of designating critical habitat that are proposed in this rule. These changes expand the USFWS's ability to exclude areas essential to the conservation of threatened and endangered species from designation as critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act. Among other problematic provisions, it states that the USFWS must exclude such areas if the economic benefits of using the land for development, such as for oil and gas extraction, grazing, and logging, are greater than those of protecting the area for wildlife (except in cases where extinction will result). These changes would grant economic considerations outsized weight in decisions about habitat, which is inconsistent with the ESA's intent that species' recovery needs should be prioritized and should be determined using the best available science.

Designation of critical habitat is a vital tool available under the Endangered Species Act to help conserve species. Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors. 

The exclusion of areas that do not meet the new standards for the designation of critical habitat could significantly decrease the amount of habitat that can be protected. This would represent a severe setback to conservation, because critical habitat is vital for stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species that have protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species without it. Designation of critical habitat is more important than ever as species face increasing habitat loss due to conversion, pollution, and climate change.

It is a matter of national pride to protect our unique species.

Americans recognize the ESA's vital role in conserving beloved wildlife species, and a 2018 survey found that four out of five Americans support the law. At a time of unprecedented wildlife extinction and habitat destruction, we should be working to strengthen--not weaken--the ESA. For these reasons, I urge the USFWS to withdraw this proposed rule.

As a long time UAS operator and a 107 certified pilot, I do not believe stand-off distances should be implemented. Many operations are done withing the vicinity of the public and are completely safe. The rules already prohibit flight over people not involved in the operation. Stand-off distances would be an added burden to operators as they would likely need to hire more people to handle crowd control, road closures, more crews on the ground enforcing the stand-off distance. It would make the majority of my operations too costly for the client. It could easily increase the cost of a half day operation by $1,000. If roads need to be closed or crowds controlled, the costs will easily increase by $5,000 and no client will pay for that and I will not have a business.

I do not believe any changes to the current limitations on speed/performance need to be made. There is no category over another which should be more limited. There is very little risk reduced by further restricting because most small UAS cannot travel faster than 87 knots and the ones can and will be built without the ability to govern their speed anyway. If someone wanted to use a small UAS for ill intent, they could easily build a home-made model for very little money and skill that could carry a heavy payload, go very fast and not utilize an app or other navigational devices which allow for stopping drones from flying into NFZ or other sensitive airspaces. The professional drone is not the one who should bare the burden.

I am in favor of UTM research but right now a lot of work needs to be done to see what the expense will be for operators and how it can be integrated. 

Hazardous materials and weapons should not be part of a small UAS payload but there should be a path for waivers.

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

I have been in the animal training field for 5 years, and during that time have dedicated my life to the animals in my care. Facilities caring for these animals meet and exceed the regulations set forth by APHIS, because animal care professionals strive to take the best possible care of the animals. And as their caregivers, these marine mammal experts should be in charge of making decisions regarding the animals' lives and wellbeing. I currently work with a variety of marine mammal species, including several rescued and rehabilitated animals, and am honored to see them inspire thousands of guests each year to care more about our planet, and to do things in their every day lives to help our animals' counterparts in the ocean. I have reviewed the proposed edits, and would like to offer these comments.

I strongly believe, based on the animals' own behavior, that interacting with the public, whether through encounter programs or in presentations, is a very enriching part of their lives, and a great way to add variability to their days. Putting limitations to these activites has not been shown to improve the animals' lives in any way. These programs have a proven track record of safety, and are one of the main ways that facilities can instill the values of conservation to countless guests. By allowing guests to interact closely with these animals, they begin to think more about how their actions influence our environment. I have had the pleasure of having hundreds of guests leave my encounter programs enlightened about perils marine mammals face in their natural habitat, and vowing to make changes in their daily lives to help be a solution to these issues. Defining an interactive program as "any human-marine mammal interactive program where a member of the public enters a primary enclosure for a marine mammal with the intent of interacting with the marine mammal(s)" is very broad. Restrictions on trainer to dolphin ratio and daily time contraints are also something that should be decided on an individual level to fit each animal and facility's needs. These limitations would not benefit the animals in any way, and would limit trainers in their goals to make the animals' lives variable and to be effective at inspiring guests to conserve. 

I am also concerned about the language to describe "undesireable" or "unsafe" behavior. Trainers are in the best position to best determine if an animal exhibits unsafe behavior and facilitate behavioral redirection or the termination of its participation in a session due to such behavior. They know the animals individually through countless hours of interaction and observation. Each animal is different, and we cannot create blanket statements about their behavior.

I would like to thank APHIS for its diligent commitment to animal welfare. I appreciate that you also recognize that U.S. marine mammal parks are dedicated to providing top quality care and public education and that you did not feel compelled to unnecessarily change regulations. Thank you!

I, like many consumers, rely on on-package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised" I assume that there is value and meaning behind that claim and that is backed by a regulatory agency. 

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. Companies will still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit. 

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Time and time again industry has shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating/policing itself. Companies are taking advantage of consumers, and grossly overcharging them, by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels to bring in more profits all the while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare. 

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers. 

FSIS owes it to the American public to set a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," take steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensure that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment in response to the Department of Transportation Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. My comments are limited to the areas of collector training and collection devices, and are based on my 16 years of experience as a Collector/BAT, and Trainer.

§ 40.35 What training requirements must a collector meet for oral fluid collection?
Regarding who is authorized to monitor the mock collections exercise for oral fluid collectors, I firmly believe it is not sufficient to have oral fluid collectors monitored/trained by collectors who simply have one year’s experience in Non-DOT oral fluid collections. It is imperative to have collectors trained/monitored only by collectors who have been properly trained in DOT Collections, having completed a Train the Trainer course and proper instruction on training collectors in the use of the specific oral fluid collection devices that will be used.

§ 40.49 What materials are used to collect oral fluid? states “Each collection must include a split that is subdivided from the original specimen collection,” and “All the devices meeting the requirements in appendix B will allow a single specimen to be subdivided in the presence of the donor.” Currently, the only oral fluid collection device that meets these requirements is the newly patented OraSecure collection device. 

In addition, a device such as the OraSecure collection device offers solutions to the following problems presented by Oral Fluid Collection Paddles/Swabs, such as: inadequate specimen for multiple drug confirmations; sample-adequacy indicators are not reliable indicator of specimen volume as donors attempting to “beat” the test often suck on the device to draw saliva out of the paddle or swab; absorbent material in paddles/swabs have no consistency in sample volume collected; there is no standardization of oral fluid collection devices that a offers a reproducible, sufficient (1 mL) sample, and is not a true neat split when using multiple devices; and screening for a wide variety of drugs/metabolites in oral fluid collected with paddles/swabs may present a problem as paddles/swabs have been known to retain the drug/metabolite.

I'm writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed Modernization of Swine Slaughter Inspection rule, which would roll back progress for animals, consumers, and workers. Allowing companies to police themselves has proven over and over again not to work. Motivation is to cover or hide or ignore problems. The New Swine Slaughter Inspection System (NSIS) would place key food safety inspection duties into the hands of slaughter plants themselves, while these facilities operate at dangerously high line speeds, and many problems will likely go unnoticed. Compassion Over Killing's investigation of a plant under the pilot high-speed slaughter program, HIMP, revealed pigs covered in feces and pus-filled abscesses being processed for human consumption with a USDA seal of approval. The investigation also showed pigs being dragged, kicked, excessively shocked, and improperly stunned as workers struggled to keep up with the facility's high line speeds. There is widespread opposition to the high-speed slaughter program within the federal government, including by USDA whistleblowers and members of Congress. The USDA's own Office of the Inspector General stated that the "HIMP program has shown no measurable improvement to the inspection process." 

Please stop this irrational rule. It is your role to to protect workers, consumers, and animals. Knowing the dangers to all, please end this program.

AAJ, with members in the United States, Canada, and abroad, is the world’s largest trial bar. It 

was established in 1946 to safeguard victims’ rights and strengthen the civil justice system. AAJ 

members represent victims sickened by asbestos exposure and asbestos-related diseases and their 

families. We now provide our input for the EPA’s review of the significant new use rule for 

asbestos. 

AAJ believes the evidence of asbestos’ deadly health effects justifies a complete ban on new 

uses of asbestos and anything short of that puts consumers, workers and their families at risk. As 

a result, EPA should revise its proposal to prohibit all new uses of asbestos. As proposed, the 

rule provides too little protection against deadly asbestos exposure because it allows for workers 

and others to continue to be exposed. 

In 1989, EPA published a ban on all uses of asbestos. Significant portions of that ban were 

invalidated by the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals.2 EPA’s ban on asbestos remains in effect for 
new uses of asbestos initiated for the first time after August 25, 1989.3 Currently, manufacturers 

and importers face no limits on reviving uses of asbestos that were in effect on August 25, 1989, 

but which have since been discontinued. Under the proposed rule, manufacturers and importers 

seeking to revive such a use must notify EPA of their intent to do so. 

This proposal is an improvement over current law, but it is woefully inadequate to protect the 

public from the unreasonable risks posed by any exposure to asbestos. AAJ supports EPA’s 

effort to require manufacturers and importers to notify the agency if they intend to resume 

currently discontinued uses of asbestos. Nonetheless, AAJ is concerned that the proposed rule

In reading the proposal, for the reclassification of Stephens' Kangaroo Rat, I find a contradiction which needs to be addressed, before a decision can be made. The proposal summary, clearly states, "This proposed action is based on a thorough review of the best scientific and commercial data available, which indicates that the Stephens' kangaroo rat no longer meets the definition of endangered under the Act.". This statement suggests that all scientific and commercial data available is complete and accurate. Furthermore, it is stated under the section labeled Species Report for Stephens' Kangaroo Rat that, "a species report, which includes a thorough review of the species' taxonomy, natural history, habitats, ecology, population, range and threats facing the species or its habitat to assist us in determining the status of the species.", was used to determine whether a reclassification from endangered to threatened was warranted. The proposal goes on to say under the Population Trend and Demographic Information section that, "Exact population trends and density estimates for the Stephens' kangaroo rat are not determinable at this time given the incomplete surveys of all potentially occupied areas and variable information collected during those surveys.". These statements, in my opinion contradict each other. The population data is incomplete, as stated previously in the proposal. One cannot base this proposed action on contradicting information. I believe that this proposal needs to be reviewed before any other action is taken. The population data/survey results need to be completed before a decision can be reached on reclassifying the Stephens' kangaroo rat from endangered to threatened. Once the completed population data/surveys are reviewed, if at that time, the data suggested the population has increased to an adequate level, then reclassification would be warranted. For the above-mentioned contradiction, I am opposed to this rule. If a reclassification from endangered to threaten is warranted, I am pleased to know that the habitat areas will continue to be protected for the foreseeable future, to ensure the population levels remain well above the threshold for endangered species status.

I am writing to you today to urge the US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) not to implement the policies proposed under docket FWS-HQ-ES-2020-0047.
The new definition of "habitat" proposed by FWS will allow the agency to block setting aside any area that isn't currently habitat but that might be needed in the future, which is of particular importance as our climate changes. The purpose of the Endangered Species Act is to help endangered species flourish and expand back into their former range (including habitat in need of restoration). This rule would accomplish the polar opposite, and would likely hasten the extinction crisis. I strongly oppose this CHANGE TO THE DEFINITION OF HABITAT.
This change would result in the exclusion of areas that do not meet the new, narrower definition of habitat, thereby decreasing the amount of habitat that can be protected. The move would serve as a grave setback to conservationthis reduction in available "habitat" would make difficult, or completely prevent, stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species allowed ample protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species denied it.
Limiting critical habitat designations will hamper recovery efforts and tie the hands of government agencies when designating habitat. Rather than providing the space an endangered species needs to recover, expand, and thrive, the proposed new definition risks providing species just barely enough habitat to eke out a meager existence, and, shamefully, comes at a time when the world is currently undergoing an unprecedented biodiversity crisis (https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-53008292).
Nothing about this new definition helps animals and plants facing extinction. Habitat should not only "include areas with existing attributes that have the capacity to support individuals of the species," but should and must include areas that are restorable to such a condition.
Again, we should be working to strengthen, not weaken, the Endangered Species Act. I urge the USFWS and NOAA to withdraw the proposed rule listed under docket FWS-HQ-ES-2020-0047, issuing a new definition of "critical habitat" under the Endangered Species Act.
Sincerely.

Dear Administrator Carlson, 

The American Motorcyclist Association appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 

proposed changes to the New Car Assessment Program in Docket No. NHTSA-2023-0021. 

Founded in 1924, the American Motorcyclist Association is the premier advocate of the 

motorcycling community. We represent the interests of millions of on- and off-highway 

motorcyclists. Our mission is to promote the motorcycling lifestyle and protect the future 

of motorcycling. 

The AMA has long advocated for including motorcycles in all stages of research and 

development of new vehicle technology. Changes to the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety 

Standard, including advancements in vehicle and infrastructure technologies, must provide 

potential safety benefits for all road users. 

The AMA agrees with NHTSA that Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), including 

Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) and the ability to detect motorcycles, will improve 

safety. We are encouraged that NTHSA is actively researching to characterize the 

performance of AEB systems in response to motorcycles. 

Since publishing AEB Request for Comments, NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting Systems 

(FARS) data from 2015-2021 shows motorcyclist fatalities have increased by 1,058, 21% 

over six years. According to FARS data, there were 6,084 fatal motorcycle crashes in 2021, 

the highest number recorded since NHTSA began tracking this information. Most of these 

crashes result from right-of-way violations wherein another vehicle turns in front of a 

motorcyclist or lane departures, striking a motorcyclist. Proposed ADAS technologies, 

including AEB, could prevent these crashes if they can detect motorcycles reliably. 

Continuing to include motorcycles in the future AEB testing is crucial to ensure 

motorcyclists can safely use the nation’s roads. 

In this rulemaking NHTSA, notes it “does not have data on how AEB systems would 

respond to other vehicle types such as heavy vehicles or motorcycles.” Without sufficient

 
data, NHTSA should observe and adapt the European New Car Assessment Programme 

(Euro NCAP) testing procedures for vulnerable motorists. Further, NHTSA should use the 

Euro NCAP tests as a model for creating a US standard to include scenarios for detecting 

stationary, braking, turn across the path, oncoming, and overtaking collisions with 

motorcycles. 

The AMA has engaged on this issue with NHTSA and congressional committees for nearly a 

decade. In 2015, the AMA submitted comments to NHTSA Docket No. 2015-0006 regarding 

implementing automatic emergency braking into its New Car Assessment Program (NCAP). 

These comments outlined concerns for NHTSA, including tests with motorcycles, size and 

weight calculations, and acceptable standards for AEB systems registering motorcycles. In 

2022, the AMA again engaged with NHTSA on the NCAP AEB issue Docket No. 2022-0002 to 

outline motorcycle fatality data and urge NTSHA to include motorcycles in testing these 

systems. We again encourage NTSHA to continue making progress on these issues. 

Thank you again for the opportunity to submit these comments, and the AMA looks 

forward to working with NTHSA to improve motorcyclist safety.

teachers, principals, or school leaders.

for purposes of the SEED grant, an entity must serve “3 or more” states.

NIET supports the proposed requirement that a national nonprofit meet the requirements of 34

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. The FSA was reached after negotiation and was approved by the court to address clearly unlawful practices by the government concerning the detention of children. The proposed regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." The proposed regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children. These children would suffer considerable and lasting harm with significant adverse effect on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. This is unacceptable. The government lacks the impartiality and most importantly, the expertise, to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Changing the post-harvest requirement from 0.3% delta-9 THC to 0.3% total THC would have a devastating effect on the hemp industry. What good will it do to legalize growing hemp if no one can meet an unattainable standard?

We have a very short growing season in northeast Nevada: June 15-September 15 -due to the possibility of freezing at any time. The maturation of our plants is therefore already at a huge disadvantage. We need to be able to capitalize on all of the time nature gives us in order for our plants to develop and produce a marketable level of CBD. Imposing the restriction of allowing only a maximum of total 0.3% THC only exacerbates the hurdles that we already face. 

We are small hemp farmers in Nevada. We grew our second crop last year. Our first crop was grown on 100 acres and we lost $25,000 due to mismanagement by the company that leased our land for the grow. We lost $25,000 on our second crop as well, which was raised on 60 acres.

It is difficult enough to cover costs for seed, fertilizer, monumental power bills ($1,000 - $1500/month) without having to worry about the State shutting us down because our THC ratio is more than .3%. Think about it: .3%? That is three tenths of a percent!

We are meticulous and responsible farmers. Even with constant surveillance, monitoring, and testing, we had borderline results. If you impose this new regulation, it will be impossible to achieve sufficient levels of CBD to make the overwhelming investment worthwhile. We will have to start growing corn instead.

 Extend the harvest time to 30 days to help with unforeseen delays and allow CBD to still be profitable for farmers
 Require accreditation of a testing facility, and not through the DEA. This would be 17,025 standardization through a third party. This would ensure the integrity of the hemp market, as well as options for farmers to test in a timely manner.
 Increase the negligent threshold from 0.5% to 1% total THC in order to provide a safe environment for first-time and veteran farmers who would otherwise face criminal sanctions.
 Require state sampling to be 8-10 inches from the top, middle and bottom of the plant to be a representative sample of the plant.
Allow for remediation processes of hemp testing under 1% total THC to go to processors that will ensure the product is compliant and can then flow into normal commerce channels regulated by the state.

There is no doubt that our United States Forest Service is under-staffed and underfunded and that NEPA compliance takes both time and money, especially in an era of increasing extreme weather events and fire danger. However, an important part of NEPA-related decision-making is the requirement for public review of -- and comment on -- proposed actions. An increase in categorical exclusions would substantially decrease the public's chance to weigh in on proposed FS actions. Demands on FS lands from special interests (whose end goal often is corporate profit) need to be balanced with a careful review of the potential impacts of FS projects. The NEPA review process includes public participation and input as essential elements in FS planning and decision-making. More logging (especially in old-growth forests), additional road-building, and new pipeline construction are examples of cases in which public (as well as scientific) input is crucial. In sum, please do not alter the current NEPA regulations, do not change the limits governing categorical exclusions, and please retain all public review procedures in place.

"DHS also requests public comments on the initial evidence applicants should provide regarding each of the statutory minimum factors. DHS is particularly interested in what specific questions should be included on the Form I-485, Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status, to document information and evidence relevant to the statutory minimum factors without placing an unreasonable evidentiary burden on the public or significantly delaying adjustment of status adjudications by USCIS."

I think considerable evidentiary burden can be avoided if the information collected before filing Form I-485 can be utilized. In other words, there is no need to provide the same evidence/document repetitively across different phases of immigrant application. For example, if an applicant has previously filed H-1B or Form I-140, then there is probably no need for him/her to provide any additional evidence on the 'financial status' factor, because he/she has probably already shown his/her wage/income information in the previous H-1B or I-140 application. Similarly, in this case there should be no need for this applicant to provide any additional evidence on the 'education and skills' factor, because his/her education information must have been already well-documented in his/her previous H-1B or I-140 application. 

Also, considerable evidentiary burden can be avoided if applicants are required to provide evidence only on a 'most-recent' basis. For example, salary/income information of the most recent 1-2 years should be enough for making a decision on the 'financial status' factor; showing only the highest education degree attained should be enough for making a decision on the 'education and skills' factor; similarly, showing the asset attained most recently (or during the past 1-2 years) should be enough for making a decision regarding the 'asset' factor.

The EPA should preserve the benefits to public and worker health and safety provided by the 2017 RMP rule, rather than eliminate them via the proposed rule. The proposed rule makes unwise and irresponsible changes as outlined below:

 1) Eliminates a requirement that the most dangerous facilities undertake a safer technology alternatives assessment.
 This change is unwise because it is important that industries seek out solutions that pose less risk and danger to their employees and surrounding communities.

 2) Removes a requirement that an incident analysis include determining the root cause of accidents and near-misses; that the team investigating an incident include at least one person knowledgeable in the process; and the requirement to include incident investigation reports in hazard reviews.
 This change is unreasonable because root cause analyses, knowledgeable investigative teams, and documentation of investigations are critical to accountability.

 3) No longer requires qualified, independent, third-party audits to be conducted when a facility has an incident to ensure the cause of the incident is addressed.
 This change is insufficient because only qualified, independent, third-party audits can produce accurate and effective results.

 4) Strikes a provision that requires facilities to provide the public with information critical to understanding the potential risks from these facilities, including how communities can protect themselves and what potential health risks they might face from an incident.
 This change is irresponsible because public access to sources like emergency plans and contact information for coordinating officials in local governments and agencies is helpful to personal and family plans should a chemical disaster occur.

 5) Deletes the requirement that facilities provide emergency planners and first responders with essential information needed for responding to a chemical release, allowing companies to claim confidential business information, and thus either provide limited or no information.
 This change is irresponsible because first responders and emergency personnel need information and better coordination between emergency responders and facilities with the potential for catastrophic damages.
