I am writing to express my strong support for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) proposed rule aimed at enhancing safeguards to protect both animals and the public from the introduction of rabies through imported dogs.

The proposed rule, with its comprehensive provisions, is a critical step forward in mitigating the risks associated with the importation of dogs. Specifically, I applaud the following aspects of the proposed rule:

Permanent Identification: The requirement for permanent identification of imported dogs is crucial for traceability and accountability, ensuring that imported animals can be properly tracked throughout their lives.

Minimum Age Requirement: The establishment of a minimum age of six months for imported puppies is a prudent measure to prevent the importation of younger and more susceptible animals, which can be at higher risk of carrying and transmitting rabies.

Enhanced Veterinary Oversight: The incorporation of greater veterinary oversight is a necessary step to ensure that imported dogs are in good health, free from communicable diseases, and properly vaccinated against rabies.

Documentation Verification: Requiring verification of documentation prior to transport is a sensible approach that will help verify the accuracy and authenticity of health records, ensuring that dogs entering the country are compliant with rabies vaccination requirements.

It is evident that these proposed updates to CDC regulations are essential to reduce the risk of reintroduction of the dog-maintained rabies virus variant into the United States. The increased numbers of dogs imported with rabies leading up to CDC's 2021 import suspension underscore the pressing need for these protective measures.

The potential public health risks associated with rabies are too significant to ignore, and these proposed changes are a responsible and necessary response to safeguard our communities. I wholeheartedly urge the CDC to move forward with this rulemaking to protect both the welfare of animals and the health and safety of the public.

Thank you for your dedication to public health and for considering my support for this vital initiative. I look forward to seeing these important safeguards put into place.

Sincerely,

Jeff San SOuci

services when ordered by other Allied Health Professionals who are TRICARE-authorized

We are commenting on the Select Agent status of Brucella abortus. We support the removal of B.abortus from the select agent list so that scientists can develop a safe and effective vaccine for the cattle industry to protect against brucellosis in their herds and allow for the unique, genetically pure wild bison of Yellowstone National Park (YNP) to then roam on appropriate public and tribal lands around YNP and in the West. We value our precious native wildlife such as our national mammal, the bison (buffalo). We met working in YNP in 1978 and shared the ecology, geology and history of the area from visitors from around the world. But YNP bison have been treated badly over past decades and we want that treatment to end. The cattle industry deserves an effective and safe vaccine but has been unable to get one because of B. abortus being on the select agent list.

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing battle waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

Thank you for considering our comments.

Sincerely,

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

If it is important to the USDA to support American farmers, it needs to insure that consumers can trust labels to be accurate and informative. I cannot buy eggs unless I know that the chickens are living a good life. As it stands, labeling a carton "free-range" does nothing to assuage my concerns. 

Please rectify this so I can start buying eggs again

Thank you for considering my request.

I am deeply concerned by the proposed, severe cuts to Medicare home health services in the Home Health Prospective Payment System Proposed Rule for CY 2023.

The law requires that Medicare expenditures for home health be budget neutral as CMS implements PDGM, but the new methodology results in significant reductions. In addition to a -7.69 percent permanent payment adjustment starting in 2023, the Proposed Rule forecasts additional cuts of more than $2 billion in 2024 for services provided to Medicare beneficiaries during the pandemic. Over the next decade, these proposed cuts total $18 billion. 

Cuts of this magnitude would be devastating to patients and providers. At a time when both demand for home health and the costs of delivering care are rising significantly, this proposal will significantly limit access to patient-preferred home health, especially among America's rural and medically underserved seniors. 

Further, the proposed methodology in the rule is technically flawed and counter to the intent of budget neutrality of the new payment system. The methodology for annually determining the impact of differences between assumed behavior changes and actual behavior changes on estimated aggregate expenditures and the related proposed permanent and temporary adjustments do not align with the requirements of the statute or its intent to ensure budget neutral rates. The agency also makes no attempt to compare the behaviors assumed by CMS in establishing the initial payment amounts for CY 2020 and the actual behavior observed on aggregate expenditures. Rather, CMS' proposal retroactively re-prices 2020 and 2021 claims payments to establish an artificial target amount and reduces the 30-day payment amounts under PDGM to meet that target. In effect, rather than ensuring the payment amounts are budget neutral, it constitutes an unauthorized rebasing of the 30-day payment amount. 

I hope you will reconsider the methodology to more accurately ensure budget neutrality while avoiding an unauthorized rebasing of the payment system. For the sake of the millions of seniors who rely upon the Medicare Home Health Benefit, please reconsider these cuts before finalizing the Proposed Rule.

Eventual development of substantial populations of blight-tolerant chestnuts in our eastern hardwoods would be a boon for wildlife species, in particular black bear, white-tailed deer, turkey, and squirrel. Restoration of the American chestnut would provide a bulwark against such potential losses in the future.

In conclusion, I believe that the benefits associated with use of the Darling 58 to rescue the American Chestnut far outweigh any hypothetical risks resulting from its incorporation of the oxalate oxidase gene from wheat and believe that the Petitioners have adequately addressed these issues; thus, Nonregulated Status for Darling 58 is justified.

In addition to current NASA and commercial research on sonic boom reduction through changes in aircraft geometry, our company is currently developing high speed commercial aircraft that would reduce boom overpressure by gliding at extremely high altitudes. At some point in the development of our technology, we foresee the need to apply for the § 91.818(b)​ operating allowance in order to conduct extended testing. ​For that reason, removal of this rule could have a serious impact on the development of our technology and the commercial prospects of our company. We respectfully request that the language in section § 91.818(b) remain “as is”. Concern #2 - ​throughout the existing and proposed rule, the adjective "measurable" is used to describe sonic boom intensity on the ground and to make judgments with respect to the permissibility of supersonic flight. I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. The regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The federal government has repeatedly demonstrated that it lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I have been a PTA for 28 years, working mainly in skilled nursing facilities as a treating clinician and as manager at various levels. Throughout this time, I have experienced many changes in our reimbursement model. 

As a health care professional providing rehabilitation services to Medicare beneficiaries, I am very concerned about the parity adjustment proposal that would be implemented under the FY 2023 Skilled Nursing Facility Prospective Payment System Proposed Rule. While I understand the expectation that PDPM was to be a budget neutral payment method, I urge you to not apply the parity adjustment in a single year reducing repayments to nursing facilities by $320 million. With the implementation of PDPM, we can capture a complete picture of a patient's health more accurately and should not be penalized for this improvement over the previous payment model. Myself, and my company's, primary focus is providing quality care to all of our patients, including Medicare beneficiaries.

We have endured continuous reimbursement reductions, significant changes in regulations and overwhelming staffing shortages which combined makes it difficult for us to overcome current obstacles. If CMS were to move forward with this implementation of this parity adjustment, I request a phase-in period of two or three years after the PHE has ended. The profile of patients we are treating tend to have more acute conditions, experience lengthy isolation, suffer from the effects of "long COVID" or are without the community support needed to immediately return home. These types of patients cost the system more to care for and we should not be penalized for providing appropriate care for all types of patients admitted to our facilities. It will take several years for us to recover from the shear impact of the COVID crisis which may result in an access to care issue as we prepare for the coming "silver tsunami" of the Baby Boomer generation.

In my current position as Director of Quality Assurance, I have directly experienced, on more than one occasion in the past 2 years, reduction in force cuts to not only my department, but our Clinical Services department and Appeals/Denials department which has directly affected our ability to provide support services to our therapists, patients, and clients in the field. 

I would also recommend that CMS review in depth current practices and requirements of Medicare Advantage Organizations (MAO) to ensure Medicare beneficiaries are receiving timely care. As a provider, I share the concerns from the recent OIG report on MAOs denying and/or delaying services for beneficiaries found that MAOs did in fact delay or deny Medicare Advantage beneficiaries' access to services, even when the services met Medicare coverage and billing rules. 

Our company has experienced more and more additional medical review requests from these MAOs as well as billing denials with no basis. These take a considerable amount of time to address and appeal in order to get the reimbursement for medically necessary services that we have already provided to patients. 

The skilled services provided to our patients are greatly needed and I greatly enjoy the work I do; however, I am concerned because skilled nursing facilities are still struggling from the impact of the pandemic. I strongly urge CMS to not implement yet another reduction to payment that will impact patient access to care and only worsen the struggles being felt in long term care. We thank you for the opportunity to provide comments related to this proposed rule.

Dear Acting Administrator Wheeler:

New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services (NHDES) opposes the EPA’s proposed

Significant New Use Rule (SNUR) for asbestos. Under the SNUR, the EPA proposes adopting a rule
setting out a regulatory path for federal approval of the re-introduction of several uses of asbestos that
are not currently in production, including: adhesives, sealants, roof and non-roof coatings, arc chutes,
beater-add gaskets, extruded sealant tape and other tape, filler for acetylene cylinders, high-grade
electrical paper, millboard, missile liner, pipeline wrap, reinforced plastics, roofing felt, separators in
fuel cells and batteries, vinyl-asbestos floor tile, and non-cement building materials. This would open
the door to more widespread applications of asbestos in the United States, and increase the serious
public health risk posed by this well-documented carcinogen.

Given that the domestic market has already adapted and has developed alternatives to asbestos

in nearly all the products listed, NHDES sees this rule as unnecessary. Instead, NHDES urges the EPA to
promulgate a ban on the import and manufacture of these asbestos-containing products. New
Hampshire’s asbestos-related mortality rate is higher than the national average, and more than 1,200
state residents died from asbestos-related diseases between 1993 and 2013.1 Asbestos in our homes,
schools, and other buildings and products continues to endanger the health of New Hampshire

residents.

It is well-settled that there is no “safe” level of exposure to any kind of asbestos fiber.2

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 
I have worked with immigrant families and have seen first-hand the great harm done to children threatened with detention, and whose family members have been detained.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

the reference to primary source of calories or required macronutrient from the manual to align with the full NDAA-17 
definition of medically necessary foods.

Dear NOP,

 I am informing you of my opposition to your latest proposed rule to change the use restrictions on substances and to add new substances as allowable for organic production and handling. When the concept of organic agriculture first arose, people were attempting to remedy problems created by farming: erosion, soil depletion, declining crop varieties. The idea that the health of the nation correlated with the long-term well-being of the soil prompted a soil management practice that became known as organic or sustainable agriculture. Farmers adopting organic agriculture avoided the use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides, as they were cutting corners to improving soil quality and resulted in negative environmental side effects. 
 While there is still limited evidence that organic food is nutritionally healthier than conventionally grown food, the notion of healthy food is also largely tied to its production. Since the 1960s, consumers have been concerned with the use of synthetic and chemical substances in food production. The restricted use of pesticides in organic agriculture has been a selling point for consumers, as research shows organic fruits and vegetables has lower pesticide residues. Studies suggest that consumers are fearful of the effect of agrochemicals, hormones, and medicines in animal products and fruits and vegetables on their health. This fact has often influenced them to buy organic, as they are under the impression that little to no agrochemicals are used in organic food production. 
 Even though I am aware that the new substances supposedly "would not be harmful to human health or the environment; [are] necessary to the production or handling of the agricultural product because of the unavailability of wholly natural substitute products; and [are] consistent with organic farming and handling," amending the National List of Allowed and Prohibited Substances will cause the word "organic" to further digress from its original foundation. The average consumer will most likely be unable to identify the seventeen new substances and some of them, such as parasiticides, are closely linked to pesticides. People pay a higher price for organic foods, under the impression that this ensures their and the environment's long-term health. To keep in line with the basic understanding and ideals consumers have, it is best to limit the number of allowable substances in organic agriculture, keeping closer in line with the start of the organic movement. 
 As an aside, I agree with prohibiting the botanical pesticide rotenone and removing ivermectin as an allowable pesticide. 

Sincerely,

 Stephanie McCulloch

DEPARTMENT OF BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES 

June 15, 2017 

I am writing to request that APHIS should consider deregulating genome-edited (GE) 

plants whose natural counterparts have been deemed safe to the environment, as a food, or other 

material source. 

Genetically modified transgenic plants have been cultivated since 1987 (and since 1983 

in the laboratory). These plants contain genes (transgenes) that impart novel characteristics upon 

the plant, such as herbicide tolerance, pathogen resistance, improved nutritional quality, or 

environmental stress tolerance. After extensive testing, these plants have been approved for 

growth and use in the US and many other countries without any known adverse health 

consequences. The initial guidelines for release, transport, and consumption of these plants were 

based on the scientifically well-documented safety of these organisms, even though they 

contained novel genes introduced by means other than natural crossing. 

The more modern GE plants contain mutations in native genes; these mutations were 

obtained without stable integration of foreign genetic elements into the plant genomes. As such, 

they are the equivalent to non-regulated plants generated by, e.g., crossing, natural selection, or 

mutation breeding. Genome editing is just another technology, such as those listed above, that 

results in alterations to the natural plant genome. These plants contain no “foreign” DNA. Thus, 

GE merely accelerates a natural process that has been used in agriculture for thousands of years. 

APHIS should consider regulating the final product, not the process by which this product was 

derived. 

Although particle bombardment (“gene gun”) has in the past been used to generate 

transgenic plants, most frequently Agrobacterium-mediated transformation is the method of 

choice for this process. Agrobacterium strains used to generate transgenic plants are “disarmed”, 

i.e., the oncogenes within the T-DNA have been deleted so that when T-DNA is transferred to 

the plant, tumors cannot form. Thus, these Agrobacterium strains are no longer pathogenic. 

APHIS should consider deregulating the use of disarmed Agrobacterium strains for use in 

generating genetically modified plants because there is no potential for these strains to cause 

disease in plants. 

Sincerely,

Interim Final Rule for the U.S. Domestic Hemp Program (the “IFR”) on behalf of the West 

Virginia Hemp Industries Association (“WVHIA”). These comments will identify each section 

of the rule for which we have concerns. We will make reasonable recommendations that we feel 

will protect and benefit farmers across the country that produce hemp according to state and 

tribal plans. 

II. State and Tribal Plans 

A. Land Used for Production 

● We recommend that AOSCA seed certification guidelines be adopted for 

domestic hemp seed certification. Many states, including West Virginia, have 

already adopted such protocols for the production of certified hemp seed for 

commercial sale to farmers. Strong certification programs are needed to prevent 

the commercial sale of unreliable hemp seeds, which has already become

 
prevalent in the industry. These standards, at a minimum, will ensure that seeds 

will have good germination and sanitation for the production of healthy plants. 

B. Sampling and Testing for Delta-9 Tetrahydrocannabinol 

● The 15-day post-sample harvest window does not allow enough flexibility for 

farmers to account for variables such as weather, equipment delays, and arranging 

transportation for harvested materials. We recommend a 30-day post-sample 

harvest window. 

● We recommend that the acceptable hemp THC level set a measurement of 

uncertainty be defined at +/- 0.09 to account for uncertainty and variability in test 

results. 

C. Disposal of Non-Compliant Plants 

● We recommend that farmers with non-compliant crops be permitted to develop a 

corrective action plan that permits homogenization of hemp crops to bring them 

into compliance with the acceptable hemp THC level or, in the event that cannot 

be achieved, to allow the farmer to produce commercially viable products that are 

not intended for human consumption (i.e. compost, biological feedstocks, fuel, 

etc.). This will allow the farmer to recover at least a nominal value for their crops 

in the event of an adverse THC test while ensuring that non-compliant plant 

materials are not consumed by the public. 

D. Compliance With Enforcement Procedures Including Annual Inspection of Hemp 

Producers 

● We strongly disagree with setting an arbitrary standard of 0.5 percent to 

determine whether or not a negligent violation has occurred. It is apparent that the 

USDA realizes that a hemp producer can act prudently in selecting seed and 

raising hemp and still violate the acceptable hemp THC level due to factors 

outside of their control. We recommend that the 0.5 percent standard be removed 

entirely as negligence is a state of mind rather than a predetermined number. 

● The corrective action plan should be the first step taken in the event of an adverse 

THC test result. The USDA should do everything possible to avoid a complete 

economic loss by the farmer. Corrective action plans could include:

 
○ Post-harvest homogenization of the entire crop and re-testing to bring the 

crop into compliance with the acceptable hemp THC level. 

○ Processing the crop for other commercial uses that do not include human 

consumption (i.e. compost, biological feedstocks, fuel, etc.).

make comments and hope that the USDA will consider our recommendations in implementing 

the final rules for the domestic hemp program.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. It also exponentially compounds the ill effects resulting due to lack of competent legal representation and inability to adequately prepare lawful defenses to removal while in a detained setting. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

employing staff to the 15-member National Pork Board. 7 U.S.C. §4808(b)(l)(G) ("The

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

As a taxpayer, I strongly support the Open Licensing Requirement for the Department of Education's grant programs. This is an opportunity to ensure that government is acting in the interests of the public--rather than using taxpayer money to enrich private organizations--who will then turn around and leech even more money from taxpayers, by licensing their grant-funded intellectual property to schools, students, and parents. The public should not have to pay again for something we've already paid for. 
Additionally, this licensing rule does not limit the ability of private organizations to develop and monetize intellectual property--it would only apply to those organizations and individuals seeking free funding from the U.S. government. The market is full of mechanisms for funding commercial ideas and innovation--venture capital, angel capital, crowdfunding, private investors, philanthropic organizations--so if someone wants to create and sell intellectual property, they have many paths to funding. 

Professionally, as an academic librarian, I strongly support the Open Licensing Requirement because it aligns the outcomes of ED grant programs with the highest values of education: sharing knowledge with others, creating a foundation for future discovery and innovation, giving future generations the tools they need to exceed. Every discovery, invention, work of art, and innovation is built upon the ideas and information that came before--as Isaac Newton wrote, describing the source of his genius: "if I have seen further than others, it is because I was standing on the shoulders of giants." Openly licensing ED-funded intellectual property makes that intellectual property available as the "shoulders" for the next generation of Newtons, in America and around the world.

Dear Secretary Purdue,

I am urging you to withdraw the shortsighted proposed rule to 'modernize' swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety.

The proposed rule puts consumers at higher risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. In place of these requirements, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide; not a good idea.

The rule also proposes a New Swine Inspection System that hands over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter establishment employees: i.e. the fox is guarding the henhouse. The proposal also removes caps on line speeds, ensuring the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination, and other food safety issues. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place commonsense updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down. Speeds should be slower and inspections take a bit longer.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer, not less safe, and this proposal will not achieve that. Instead, it has the potential to make food less safe by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

We urge you to withdraw the proposed rule and design a new rule that prioritizes food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness.

Sincerely,

Jon Krueger
Jackson, MI

I am a pediatrician and have been actively involved in the care of children for over 40 years. I am deeply concerned about the response of the US government to the care of the refugee children presently in custody after entering our country. I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. The regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

The entire proposed regulation should not be finalized as it is to the detriment of these refugee children.

Overall, I agree with the main recommendations of earlier screening among infants born to mothers who are VL+ and HCV Ab+/VL unknown and guidelines overall. However, I would like the guidelines to clarify some situations that occur clinically and will be important for guiding clinicians in real-world settings: 1) Many women are screened for HCV during the 1st trimester and it is recommended that they are rescreened closer to delivery if they have on-going risk factors -- this does not happen often, or results are not available prior to discharge and link to maternal records is then lost. This guideline only vaguely addresses how this should impact infant screening - suggesting that infants exposed to mothers with risk factors should be screened at 18 months with Ab testing. First, it would be helpful if the guideline can specifically define what it considers to be on-going maternal risk factors are (IVDU, sex work, etc). Second, I would argue that kids exposed to on-going IVDU during pregnancy are at high enough risk of HCV exposure and are at the highest risk of loss to follow-up as they are often in foster care etc, that there should be a clear recommendation that they are still screened at 2-6 months of age with RNA testing, particularly since the guidelines are saying infants born to moms who are VL negative should not be screened at all. While there is not clear objective evidence to guide my suggestion, I think based on clinical experience working with these populations (these mothers often don't receive reliable prenatal care and many don't have HCV testing at all or it's not available quickly enough prior to discharge from the hospital if done on admission) and the evidence from other perinatal viruses (we know from other viruses that perinatal transmission risk is higher during maternal acute infection phase when there is typically high viral load and low maternal antibodies – I’m not sure if this has been looked at yet with HCV for a variety of reasons) that it is a reasonable recommendation in a very high risk patient population. At our institution, we have seen perinatal transmission occur among HCV Ab+/VL- mothers tested during pregnancy with on-going risk factors. If a child is in foster care and there is NO known maternal risk factors, then that screening could still be on a case-to-case basis at either 2-6 months of age or 18 months of age. 2) Specifically addressing how maternal treatment for HCV should be incorporated -- in this case, I don’t think it changes any recommendations but I think the situation of treatment in the context of a positive Ab, regardless of VL should be explicitly addressed; 3) specifically addressing what defines a positive viral load -- any viral load? or above a certain threshold (I think it should be any maternal VL but I've seen maternal counts in the 20s and think this should be made explicit in the guidelines; 4) specifically addressing if a mother has repeat VL testing during pregnancy and 1 is positive and 1 is negative then infant screening should still occur (I've seen this happen many times).

If it wasn't for the factory farms there could have been thousands of additional dairies saved and converted to organic. The Queen Conch should not only be listed a threatened, but protective regulations should be put in place. 

Given the fact that female conch does not reach sexual maturity for several years, the continual removal of large fecund females for human consumption results in a population that cannot easily bounce back after depletion. Even though conch produce hundreds of thousands of eggs, this is not indicative of a resilient population, as most of the eggs are expected to fall prey to predation and other environmental factors. In addition to the threats faced from slow maturation, the conch reproductive process is not a quick endeavor. Female conch will be vulnerable in the days it takes to physically lay eggs as well as incubate them. This in-depth reproductive process is dependent on the survival of the mother, rather than simply partaking in broadcast spawning.

The conch population is also likely to suffer as climate change progresses due to the juvenile’s dependence on seagrass. Seagrass beds are facing threats from nutrient loading, overfishing, and mechanical damage from boating and the fishing industry. With the continual loss of seagrass beds, there is less available food for the juvenile conch. 

Without proper regulatory measures the conch population will continue to fall. By setting catch standards the largest and most fecund females can remain in the population. Protecting seagrass beds by creating “no-boating” zones would also be beneficial in aiding the survivorship of the juvenile conch.

I am a scientist working for a contract laboratory, but over my career have worked in a variety of roles in the development and manufacturing of foods. Having some basis to the standards that foods are regulated to is necessary to establish specifications and resolve disputes between supplier and customers, as well as issues related to direct government enforcements. Continuing to reference AOAC OMA, is quite adequate for the roughly 80% of regulatory inquiries, and we can dig deeper into the 20% that are not well covered. Removing the reference to AOAC methods, takes a step back to a point where each interested party can argue that their particular method is the correct one, versus comparison to an industry concensus standard to be compared first. I live in New York’s Hudson Valley, in a farmhouse dating to 1780. My home and a sturdy barn from the 

same period are built using traditional post-and-beam style, with hand-hewn timbers from American 

Chestnuts. Today the 11 acres that I call home are fundamentally different from the forests that helped to 

erect my house and barn; those forests were robbed of a keystone species by an introduced fungal pathogen, 

Cryphonectria parasitica, that fundamentally changed our American landscape, our buildings, our culture. 

That harm need not be irreparable. With judicious use of gene editing, researchers have produced the 

Darling 58 trees with capabilities to detoxify oxalic acid produced by the fungus and survive the blight. As 

a member of the American Chestnut Foundation, I have planted three orchards of wild-type American 

Chestnuts on my property, in hopes that some of those trees might survive to maturity, such that they may 

be crossed with the Darling 58 trees, and that their offspring can be the first in a homecoming of the 

American Chestnuts to American forests. 

My hopes for a restored American Chestnut population are not just romantic. The forests of the U.S. east 

coast and my own woods are being ravaged by Emerald Ash Borer, Hemlock Wooly Adelgid, thousand 

Canker disease of the Black Walnuts, the expanding range of the voracious invasive Spotted Lantern Fly, 

and heat stress on the Maples induced by a rapidly warming climate. I fear for what lies ahead for our 

forests, with fields invaded by the Ailanthus Altissima (Tree of Heaven) which poisons the soil. I see hope 

in the potential to bring back a keystone species to the forest to store carbon and stabilize the climate, shade 

our communities, feed wildlife, and once again provide valuable timber.

I completely disagree with removing the requirement for an instructor to be present to observe the time a pilot is using the simulator to meet the instrument recency of experience. While the pilot can meet the recency of experience in actual instrument conditions or solicit a safety pilot in simulated conditions, the pilot is still flying a real airplane, in the real world, with real dynamics not found in a simulator. The simulator is a sterile environment. To allow a pilot to use the simulator without the presence of an instructor to sign off on the time, what is to stop any pilot from going into a simulator room, turn on the simulator, go out to Starbucks for a coffee for 2 hours, turn off the simulator, and log what ever s/he wants? This is akin to falsification of a logbook entry, except the FAA has given the pilot the loop hole to do it legally.

"Yes sir, Mr. Inspector, the simulator was in fact running for 2 hours on this date and time you are investigating. No, the simulator does not provide a log of the pilot's actions. No, the simulator did not print out the pilot's flight track and activities while the simulator is running."

Gaining recency of experience in actual conditions has an element of threat to life if the pilot does not conduct instrument procedures correctly. Where is this element of threat in the simulator? It does not exist. A pilot using the simulator can crash many times in the simulator, intentionally or not, without ever having to feel any threat to life or the expectation of performance by ATC, or the threat of enforcement action. The pilot in the real world has many incentives to conduct the flight correctly. In the simulator, the pilot can do anything they want, including violating any and all rules, without any repercussion.

One could argue that a pilot with a safety pilot could do the same. However, under investigation, the safety pilot will have to corroborate with the pilot on the lie. A pilot using an simulator after-hours when everyone has gone home for the day, sitting alone in the simulator, can say and log anything.

It is important that we consider the reasoning for recency of experience. Is it to enhance safety? How does allowing an unsupervised pilot using a simulator by him or herself with the open ended possibility of logging anything they want without any supervision enhance safety?

The statement in the NPRM:

"It can be expensive to hire an instructor to observe a pilot performing the instrument experience requirements solely to verify that the instrument recency experience was performed."

It can be even more expensive when said pilot crashes an airplane because of lies on the pilot's logbook pertaining to instrument recency of experience gained through the use of the simulator in an unsupervised manner.

In my experience, when a pilot expires on recency of experience, especially toward the end of their 6-month grace period, their performance is marginal at best, and often requires additional flight training from an authorized instructor to regain their proficiency. How is proficiency addressed through the unsupervised use of a simulator? Humans are excellent at seeing what they want to see and believe what they want to believe. This is why we need a second pair of experienced eyes to observe and provide critique and recommended actions via an authorized instructor. I know of many pilots who believe they are highly skilled but can't perform under real world, dynamic conditions. A sterile simulator environment will never emulate the real world of flying, and it will never have the element of threat to life or enforcement action due to incorrect pilot actions.

The removal of the instructor lowers the bar for safety and has the potential to create the illusion of pilot proficiency while satisfying the legal requirements for instrument recency of experience. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. critical infrastructure, has been declining for more than a decade, increasing the risk that it 
will fall below the required amount necessary to continue operating and supplying oil to West 
Coast refineries. The estimated production rate from Willow will increase the current TAPS 
throughput by 20% and ensure its long-term viability. 
 
Additionally, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has highlighted the importance of energy 
security for the U.S. and its allies. Europe and Asia are again preparing for a winter heating 
season with very little Russian energy imports, driving up prices and threatening physical 
supplies of energy commodities. Increased and reliable production of oil and natural gas from 
the United States has blunted Russia’s ability to use its energy exports to undermine global 
support for Ukraine. As one of the largest exporters of petroleum in the world, the United

 
States’ ability to facilitate global diversification from Russian energy can only be enhanced by 
future NPR-A development. 
 
Analysis from the U.S. Geological Survey estimates there are 8.7 billion barrels of 
undiscovered oil in the NPR-A, an important reserve created specifically by Congress for 
energy production. By denying development in the region, BLM is denying the state of Alaska, 
and the U.S., billions of dollars in revenue. BLM’s proposed plan will also deny American 
consumers affordable and reliable energy at a time of persistently high fuel prices. This 
proposed plan undermines the reality that oil produced from the NPR-A can displace imports 
and will increase the likelihood of imports from less environmentally regulated regions of the 
world. 
Economic & Environmental Benefits 
The proposed plan relies on flawed economic analysis, which does not accurately 
account for the significant economic benefits delivered to local Alaska communities 
(including Alaska Native organizations) from NPR-A development. Federal law mandates that 
50% of lease revenue from NPR-A projects go towards a unique grant program that prioritizes 
improvement projects to deliver social and environmental justice benefits to impacted 
communities, many of which are Alaska Native communities. The economic analysis fails to 
consider the impact to local communities of losing these future revenues. Additionally, the 
economic analysis does not consider the social implications of eliminating or dramatically 
restricting future development in the NP

We have read the proposed Airworthiness Directive No. FAA-2025-1102.
We do NOT concur with your proposed requirement to systematically remove the paint every 
60 flight hours, on all six arms of the swashplate assembly.
This would create a real danger of new corrosion areas. 
While we believe that repainting will be performed without error 99% of the time, we cannot rule 
out painting errors. There are 3 layers of protection coats (Alodine, Chromate primer, Paint), all 
must be applied correctly. 
The benefit vs risk must be considered. Here, the risk of creating new corrosion largely exceeds 
the benefit.
The root cause of the cracks has been ascertained to be stress corrosion cracking (SCC). This 
happens when we have the simultaneous presence of :
1.
A corrosive atmosphere 
2.
Residual stress inside the metal
3.
A material sensitive to SCC
A paramount information regarding the Cabri G2 swashplate design is this:
On every clevis, the bore inside the Right-Hand arm is protected by a steel ring which is 
interference-fit inside the bore. Therefore, RH arm has permanent residual stress.
The bore inside the Left-Hand arm is protected by a steel ring which is free to slide inside the 
bore. Therefore, LH arm has no residual stress.

 
All the cracks found in service were on the RH arm.
No cracks were ever found on the LH arm.
Our stress calculations were reviewed by EASA structures Expert (panel 03) Mr Aiko DUEHNE.
Mr Aiko DUEHNE also reviewed results of a static test to the ultimate load of the swashplate 
with a cracked RH arm, showing that the swashplate bears more than twice the ultimate load 
even though the RH arm is fully cracked.
Stripping paint to inspect was also discussed with EASA. Considering all of the above facts, 
systematic stripping of paint was ruled out. In the final version of EASA AD (and our SB), 
removing the paint is only required “In case of doubt”. 
EASA airworthiness directive was written following this technical work we made in close 
collaboration with the EASA expert, the EASA PCM, the EASA AD section.
Publishing this FAA AD as it is would be hazardous in the long term, with corrosion 
consequences happening years after repaintings, only in the USA.

On behalf of the NYC Health + Hospitals WTC Environmental Health Center, the current contractor for the Survivor WTC Health Program, to follow are comments on items of concern in the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, listed with the section referenced:

88.11 Initial health evaluation for screening-eligible survivors.
 (1) "A CCE or NPN will provide" 
COMMENT: This appears to officially open up access to any CCE for Survivors to obtain an initial health evaluation and treatment, a circumstance of concern to the current CCE for Survivors. The complexities of benefit differences between the populations merit specific and distinct attention that a mixed population (including a Survivor and Responder sitting side-by-side in the waiting room) may make all the more, and unnecessarily, complicated in a co-located CCE. 

88.13 Disenrollment
COMMENT: There is no concrete language addressing whether grandfathered members, whose circumstances may differ from the geographic boundaries and exposure time frames articulated in current policy, are immune from disenrollment on these grounds. 

88.17 Decertification
COMMENT: There is no concrete language addressing whether grandfathered members who were certified via a the WTC-2 process, whose exposure history and symptom onset dates may differ from the geographic boundaries, exposure time frames and symptom onset intervals articulated in current policy, are immune from decertification on these grounds. 

88.20 Authorization of treatment
(b) Standard for determining medical necessity
 "All treatment provided under the WTC Health Program will adhere to a standard...which has been included in the medical treatment protocols developed by the Data Centers, with input from the CCEs, and approved by the Administrator of the WTC Health Program."
COMMENT: Although this language has not changed from the previous rule, there is an increasing number of situations involving treatment of cancer, organ transplant sequelae and similar cases in which have not been and cannot be included in the protocols developed by the Data Centers. There should be flexibility in the rulemaking language to accommodate complex care situations. Medical necessity can be differentially interpreted by experts with similar qualifications and should not be a hard and fast determination.

( c ) Treatment pending certification
"While certification is pending, ...authorization shall be obtained from the WTC Program Administrator before treatment is provided, except for the provision of treatment for a medical emergency."
COMMENT: Although this language has not changed from the previous rule, the ability to cover treatment while certification is pending is an extremely important element, particularly for members who present with cancer that is in the midst of treatment. This language appears to indicate that without the highest level of approval (the Administrator him/herself) only emergency care could be covered until a certification decision is received. Given the growing length of time between submission of certification requests and the receipt of decisions, a strict interpretation of this language would be detrimental to member wellbeing. Unless there is flexibility of interpretation to allow delegation of authorization for treatment pending certification, this language is unacceptably restrictive.

CITATION 190.26 — Recordkeeping (d) Purchase of manufactured or produced articles for exportation: 
190.26(b), as written, requires that the claimant maintain not only records to support the transfer, but also the 
manufacture of the articles received from the manufacturer or producer. Through the normal course of business 
and even beyond the normal course of business, manufacturers and producers, in most cases, will not so 
willingly share manufacturing records with their customers. 
Throughout 190, CBP regulates liability amongst the various parties involved in the flow of merchandise from 
import, to manufacture, through ultimate exportation. Each of those movements necessitate various compliance 
actions, agreements, and material movements between parties who may be completely unrelated and, as seen on 
occasion, in competition with each other in the market. For the regulations to require that a claimant/customer 
possess production records from their producer/operator/vendor puts claimants in a position where they may not 
be able to claim on those articles. 
Alternatively, for a manufacturer or producer to be required to provide production records to their customer can 
be seen as a risk for their business. If a producer or operator is required to share this information, it could harm 
small businesses and innovative and proprietary operations, as well as put manufacturers in a compromised 
position. Manufacturing and production records are often business sensitive and unique and should be 
maintained by that party, not the claimant. This section should read as follows: 
Where the claimant purchases articles from the manufacturer or producer either directly or 
indirectly, the manufacturer or producer must maintain records, kept in the normal course of 
business, to document the manufacture or production of the articles, and the claimant must 
maintain records kept in the normal course of business to document the transfer of those

Background 
 
FEMA published a proposed rule on November 12, 2015, to amend 44 C.F.R. 
206.48(b) (Factors considered when evaluating a Governor's request for a major 
disaster declaration) to revise the factors that FEMA considers when evaluating a 
Governor’s request for a major disaster declaration authorizing Individual 
Assistance. 
 
FEMA proposes to revise its regulations in an effort to meet requirements in section 
1109 of the Sandy Recovery Improvement Act of 2013, which requires FEMA, in 
cooperation with state, local, and tribal emergency management agencies, to 
review, update, and revise through rulemaking the Individual Assistance factors 
FEMA uses to measure the severity, magnitude, and impact of a disaster. 
 
The intent of the proposed rule is to provide more objective criteria, clarify the 
threshold for eligibility and speed the declaration process. 
 
Proposed Factors 
 
FEMA is proposing to revise 44 CFR 206.48 to include the following factors: 
(1) State Fiscal Capacity and Resource Availability 
(2) Uninsured Home and Personal Property Losses 
(3) Disaster Impacted Population Profile 
(4) Impact to Community Infrastructure 
(5) Casualties 
(6) Disaster Related Unemployment

 
Factor 1 - State Fiscal Capacity and Resource Availability 
 
Recommend FEMA does not use State Fiscal Capacity as an Individual Assistance 
(IA) Declaration Factor. 
• 
The Stafford Act Sec. 320 Limitation on Use of Sliding Scales (42 U.S.C. 5163) 
states that no geographic area shall be precluded from receiving assistance 
solely by virtue of an arithmetic formula or sliding scale based on income or 
population. 
• 
A state fiscal factor biases declarations towards states with fewer resources, and 
not taking into account personal resources, local government resources or other 
resources. 
• 
Using Total Taxable Resources (TTR) as a measurement of fiscal capacity does 
not truly represent the ability to recover from a disaster without federal 
assistance. This is the potential to tax, not actual amount taxed and has a two 
year data lag. Also, this includes many assumptions by FEMA. 
• 
It is difficult to ascertain a direct connection to the state’s fiscal capacity versus 
individual and household need. If this is indeed a requirement, then FEMA 
should provide a framework under which the states must operate in order to 
make the states, tribes, and territories eligible. 
• 
FEMA should also take into consideration that rural areas of a state might not 
have the same resources and funding opportunities available as metropolitan 
areas of the state. In smaller, rural communities with diverse population the per 
capita personal income factor might be skewed by a few exceedingly wealthy 
residents. FEMA criteria should be flexible enough to carefully consider and 
evaluate local circumstances. 
• 
FEMA is requiring the state to explain or justify why the state does not have its 
own IA program. The information provided under the Fiscal Capacity category 
will allow FEMA to disclaim or approve any argument under this section for a 
request of declaration. State IA programs are not required by the Stafford Act.

are protective of water quality and aquatic habitat for important uses such as drinking water, fish, wildlife, and outdoor

The issue is not with the proven design, but rather specific aircraft that had beacons on the rudder. Having an AD that would affect 30,000+ aircraft that are not similar enough in application would be harmful to the aviation community and not reduce the risk to the public. The AD should be further narrowed down to specific models affected. Additionally, instead of a full rudder replacement, there should be specific time intervals (TIS or calendar year) for inspection. Replacing the rudder with one of a different material does not resolve the issue that caused these failures in the first place. 

In conclusion, I believe the AD should:
1 - Incorporate only specific models affected (those with beacons)
2 - Incorporate specific inspection criteria instead of a blanket one time replacement

HPSA scores do not fairly prioritize potential slots for rural teaching hospitals. Any rural 

community possessing the where-with-all to accomplish the development, implementation, 

and sustainability of a rural residency program is unlikely to have a high enough HPSA score 

to outcompete urban hospitals and communities. The irony of it all is that high-scoring urban 

HPSAs can be blocks away from well served tertiary care or academic medical centers.

The highest scoring geographic HPSA for primary care in Ohio, 21, is in the city of 

Cleveland and includes census tracts within a mile of tracts well served by primary care. The 

highest scoring rural county in Ohio is Champaign County, a micropolitan area with a HPSA 

score of 12. In North Dakota, a state with major rural primary care needs, the highest scoring 

rural geographic HPSA for primary care is 16.

Our research has shown that although rural residencies do develop in HPSA’s, they tend to 

develop in communities with at least enough physicians for core faculty. What we see is a u-

curve, with sustainable sites in the HPSA score mid-range. And yet rural residencies

contribute 5 times as many physician years to practice in rural communities than urban

as rural, should not be included in this carve-out, or, as in past efforts at redistribution, the 

proportion of residents training in rural places will continue to decrease. And I firmly believe 

that does not represent legislative intent.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed rule, Affordability of Employer 
Coverage for Family Members of Employees, issued by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). We are writing 
in strong support of the proposed rule, which would correct the “family glitch” that was created by a 
2013 misreading of the Affordable Care Act (ACA). That misreading erected a barrier to affordable 
coverage for millions of Americans barring them from eligibility for premium tax credits despite having 
an offer of unaffordable employer coverage. 
 
We have long supported the interpretation applied in this proposed rule as the best reading of the 
statute and consistent with the goals of the ACA to expand access to affordable coverage. As noted in 
the preamble to this proposed rule, the current interpretation was originally proposed in a broader rule 
on premium tax credits (76 FR 50931), but not finalized in 2012 (77 FR 30377). In that final rule, IRS 
noted that commenters opposed the proposed interpretation, calling instead for the IRS to adopt an 
affordability test for family members based on the cost of family coverage. Despite these objections, IRS 
finalized the policy in 2013 (78 FR 7264), with an interpretation inconsistent with the text and intent of 
the ACA, thereby creating the “family glitch.” 
 
The current interpretation affects as many as 5.1 million people who are barred from obtaining 
premium tax credits because “affordable” coverage is based only on the cost to cover the employee.1 
Most of the people impacted are children, and nearly half a million people go uninsured when faced 
with unaffordable coverage under a family member’s employer plan.2 Workers in small businesses are 
also impacted as they are more likely to face higher premiums for family coverage. Five percent of 
covered workers in large businesses face a premium of at least $10,000 to enroll family members in 
their employer plan. That number grows to 29 percent of covered workers in small businesses who must 
pay $10,000 to obtain family coverage.3

animals to be sold, transferred, gifted, or moved to another operation while maintaining

 
their status as certified organic dairy animals creates a loophole that will be exploited. 

Some operations are continually sourcing off-farm transitioned animals, which is less 

expensive than raising animals as organic from the last third of gestation. This creates 

an unfair economic advantage for operations making use of the loophole.

destructive loophole. In addition, limiting the movement of transitioned animals has

We are writing to you regarding a specific aspect of the temporary regulations issued on

partnership debt allocation for federal income tax purposes. The New BDPO Regulations

to such debt. A partner generally bears the EROL for a partnership liability to the extent 
the partner, or a related person, would be obligated to make a payment if the

implemented using discretionary provisions in the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and

deep-sea corals, to designate areas closed to fishing, and to conserve target or non-target species

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law.

I have worked with asylum applicants for over 30 years including many families. I know the difficulty of presenting all the evidence necessary in an asylum case before the Asylum Office or an Immigration Judge. Indefinite detention of children would necessarily be detrimental to not only the health of the children, but their family's opportunity to fully invoke all the protections offered by the Refugee Act of 1980. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Sincerely,

Rev. Craig B. Mousin

Before finalizing the rule, APHIS should substantially revise its proposals to revise and update the standards governing the humane care and handling of captive marine mammals. The current proposal ignores a wealth of scientific evidence obtained over the past three decades and essentially maintains a long-outdated status quo for the captive marine mammal industry.

Marine mammals are highly intelligent animals with great sensitivity to unnatural stressors in their environment. Instead of helping them, humans all too often further damage their well being, often with torturous and deadly results. This need to stop NOW!

While the agency has proposed several improvements to the standards, such as requiring shade for all outdoor marine mammal enclosures and ramps for older or injured seals, sea lions, polar bears, and sea otters to exit pools more easily, these are minor compared to the significant failures in the proposed rule.

The agency proposes no changes to the space requirements, claiming it is unaware of any science on which to base such changes. In fact, there is a tremendous body of recent research using increasingly sophisticated tagging technology to monitor fine-scale movement patterns of individual marine mammals, especially cetaceans and polar bears. These species travel tremendous distances and dive very deep, making the current minimum space requirements totally inhumane. The best available science for seals, sea lions, and sea otters--even for the slow, plant-eating manatee--also supports major space increases.

The current space standards were set over 30 years ago and have no basis in science or even best practices within the captive display industry. As an example, for up to two orcas, a facility need only provide a circular tank with a diameter twice as wide and a depth half as deep as an average adult orca is long. This standard does not even allow the animal to position itself fully in the vertical plane (its tail would touch and drag on the bottom before the animal reaches full upright orientation). This cannot be considered adequate!

While the rule refers to peer-reviewed papers for proposed changes to some standards (e.g., lighting requirements), it claims the agency is unaware of such papers for other standards (e.g., temperature requirements) and therefore proposes no major changes. Yet a considerable amount of research has been conducted within the past 15 years related to most if not all of the affected standards. 

The proposed rule would still allow pinnipeds to be housed in enclosures with tanks filled with fresh water. Allowing the maintenance of a marine mammal in fresh water is clearly an inappropriate welfare standard.

Several standards have been weakened, particularly regarding interactive programs such as swim-with-dolphin encounters. For example, the standard for the interaction time for each cetacean per day has been increased from two hours to three hours, not based on science or even industry best practices, but simply "on information provided by licensees ... which suggested that the marine mammals would not be harmed by a modest increase in interactive time per day." Facility "suggestions" represent a clear conflict of interest and should never be the sole basis for changes to standards.

The agency asked in previous notices if noise standards should be established. In several instances, noise levels, particularly in air, are extremely high (in theme parks, virtually every night there is a fireworks display directly over the marine mammal enclosures). Noise standards must be established for marine mammal facilities.

In sum, the proposed rule is grossly inadequate and fails to take into account current scientific understanding of the needs of marine mammals. APHIS must substantially strengthen the requirements for keeping cetaceans in captivity before the rule is finalized.

Lockheed Martin proposes an alternate compliance time for the reference AD. The proposed compliance 
time would be, "At the next engine shop visit or within the remaining service life of the Low Pressure (LP) 
turbine stage 2 blades." 
Rationale: The root cause of the failure was release of the Low Pressure (LP) turbine stage 2 blade. The 
failure of the LP turbine support bearing cage was a secondary event cause by the blade failure. 
Discussion: The NPRM's compliance timeframe does not take into account that the only remaining active 
L-1 011 TriStar operator does not operate as a regular airline. This operator flies limited flights for training 
and customer missions. Due to this limited operational schedule, the engines will not be removed from the 
aircraft within the proposed 24 month timeframe. The result will be unscheduled engine removals and 
unscheduled engine shop visits to comply with the proposed AD. The NPRM cost estimate does not 
account for this situation. The cost of compliance in this case would likely be orders of magnitude greater 
than the NPRM's cost estimate. Additionally, the NPRM also does not factor in the lack of approved repair 
stations for the RB211 engine in the United States. 
It is important to note that the root cause failure that initiated this NPRM was not a failure of a LPT support 
bearing. The root cause was fracture failure of an LPT blade, causing secondary damage and imbalance in 
the engine which then overloaded the support bearing. If the LPT blade(s) do not fail, the LPT support 
bearing is not an issue. It is recommended that the compliance period be based on the remaining life of the 
LPT blade sets in each engine versus an arbitrary calendar limit. This approach would maintain safe 
operation of the aircraft while preventing the operators from having costly unplanned engine removals and 
shop visits.
