The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

People choose these products because they are distressed by the brutality of facory farming.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

fact, the importer’s adherence to the audit requirements and production of the audit report to the

I am the General Manager of Lahaina Divers on Maui. While we do not operate dolphin tours, many times a pod of spinner dolphins will approach our boats while underway to ride the bow wake or in the wake behind the boat, clearly making the choice to come to us as we do nothing to attract them other than just being underway. Other times a pod will happen by while we are on a dive allowing us to watch them as they pass. 
Even the exception to the regulations of "Persons who inadvertently come within 50 yards of a spinner dolphin, or who are approached by a spinner dolphin, provided they make no effort to engage or pursue the animals and take immediate steps to move away from the animals", from the point of view of the dive operator, puts us and our guests in the position of being in violation of these rules whenever a pod is within 50 yards of our bubbles, even though, at that distance, we wouldn't even know that they are there as visibility of 150 feet is rare at most dive sites.
Unauthorized take of marine mammals, including harassment of spinner dolphins, already is and continues to be prohibited under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. However, the near total lack of enforcement in Hawaii (with the exception of humpback whales) since its passing Congress in 1972 has brought us to this point. Even as studies were being done 10-20 years ago, no increased enforcement of the existing protections was done. We do not need additional regulations and protections nor additional monies wasted on more studies until NOAA and DLNR enforce the regulations already in place (see MMPA regulations, CFR 216.3). 
I believe that effective enforcement of the current regulations rather new regulations will be sufficient protection for the spinner dolphins and recommend alternative #1, NO ACTION.

My name is Corey Gammill and I own both a tackle shop and a charter fishing service that operates out of Nantucket, MA. Just like the commercial fishermen, I make my living off the water. In the last 6 months I have logged 150 days on the water, 50+ of which were spent in the waters that are being discussed. I regularly fish the exemption areas being discussed at McBlair's and Old South Rips. I fish these areas because they are rich with fish and bird life. I am not a biologist, nor am I in fisheries management, in short, I am a fishermen who has the privilege to showcase to my clients the amazing fisheries that exist East of Nantucket. From what I understand, the design of fisheries management is to think about the greater good of the population as a whole and not just focus on just one user group. As is commonly known, the recreational fishing impact on an economy is much larger than that of the commercial fishermen. Recreational fishermen should certainly share the burden when it comes to "overfishing" and regulations, but on the flip side, we should also be able to enjoy the benefit of decisions to protect our eco-system. 

Some of the greatest triumphs in rebuilding fisheries over the last 30 years have come when recreational and commercial fishermen have worked together for the common good of protecting fish, habitat, forage and fauna. Think to swordfish, striped bass, Maine lobsters, just to name a few. From my understanding the original intent of declaring this entire area Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) was an intent to help both commercial and recreational fishermen in the long term. By protecting the habitat, we are creating an area where Fluke, Striped Bass, Bluefish, Baby Cod, and other migratory species can feed and forage can develop. This closure helps all fishermen: commercial, recreational as well as charter captains. Yes, it helps recreational fishermen in the short term, but any protected area gives fish a chance to spawn, recover and grow, which ultimately helps commercial fishermen as well. 

With this said, and all the research and energy done, why open up these exemption areas to disruptive and destructive fishing gear? From my understanding, the hydraulic sea clammers and mussel dredges have plenty of other locations to fish, why open up an area to them that both data and the eye test see as great fish habitat. 

I am not naive enough to think we should be all catch and release, but I firmly believe in sustainability and managing fisheries as a whole and not specie by specie. Understanding and managing all aspects of the food chain is paramount to preserving a fishery that we hope will be better when our kids are able to fish it, both commercially and recreationally. The designation of this area as EFH was a thoughtful and collaborative approach by many people, agencies, and user groups to take care of our fishery looking forward. Let's not adjust the hard work of many to protect an incredible habitat for the benefit of a few.

Capt. Corey Gammill

KLM appreciates the opportunity to comment on Ref. /A/ FAA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. The proposed Airworthiness Directive affects the KLM 747-400 and 747-400F fleet. 

The NPRM proposes accomplishment of the actions described in Ref. /B/ Service Bulletin. This would require repetitive high frequency eddy current (HFEC) inspections for cracking in the strut side skin; an open-hole HFEC inspection for cracking, applicable related investigative and corrective actions; and a fastener installation modification. Accomplishment of the modification requires removal of the engine, the pylon and both spring beams from pylons 1 and 4. The cost to perform the modification of one airplane is 490 man hours plus a $56,414.00 top kit. The NPRM requires a compliance time within 60 months after the effective date the AD, meanwhile the structure is to be inspected at 500 flight cycle interval for aircraft with 9.000 total flight cycles or more. 

The proposed rulemaking will have a tremendous impact on the KLM 747-400 and 747-400F fleet. KLM will be obliged to start the inspections this year and schedule them in A-checks. The follow-on inspections will need to be planned in A-checks, due to the relatively short 500 cycle repeat interval. In case of findings, modification is required before further flight resulting in substantial additional downtime during A-check and even C-check. Unplanned removal of struts and engines introduces a lot of extra work and requires extra airplane system testing. 

Between 1996 and 2001, KLM accomplished the strut modification per Ref. /F/ SB on its CF6-80C2 powered 747-400 fleet. The strut modification enhanced the fail-safe capability of the struts, improved the durability, and reduced non-routine inspections, as is noted in the description of Ref. /F/ SB. During the 747 Structure Task Group meetings that were organized by Boeing in 1993 to support the strut modification, Boeing informed that "The new pylon structure design goal is to tolerate one major load path failure and meet all regulatory requirements for a period longer then the inspection interval of 2C"; see Ref./G/ STG meeting summary 1993. And regarding fatigue and damage tolerance: "the fatigue lives exceed the 747 economic design life goals and crack growth intervals support visual inspections at "C" checks"; see Ref/H/ STG meeting summary 1993.

Based on these statements from the TC holder, KLM believes that the proposed inspection compliance time and inspection interval can be 1C or 1250 flight cycles, and still provide an acceptable level of safety.

NOAA Proposed Rule concerning Hector's Dolphin and Maui's Dolphin Subspecies/New Zealand

Earth Island Institute's International Marine Mammal Project supports the United States National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Agency's (NOAA) initiative to list New Zealand's Hector's Dolphin Subspecies (C. hectori hectori) as Threatened and the Maui's Dolphin Subspecies (Cephalorhynchus hectori maui) as Endangered under the Endangered Species Act. 

We agree that New Zealand needs to substantially improve its marine mammal protection and fisheries management systems in order to secure a future for both these species.

Clearly, urgent action is needed. 

Hector's dolphin is considered to be one of the world's rarest dolphin species. The North Island Maui's dolphin, is estimated to have a population of around 111 individuals and is ranked as nationally critical by the Department of Commerce and critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

Both dolphin subspecies have a lifespan of only about 20 years, have low reproduction rate (calving every 2-3 years) and have late onset of sexual maturity (7-9 years). These factors result in a low maximum population growth rate, which put Hector's and Maui's dolphin at threat from even low levels of human-induced mortality. 

Threats to both these species include:

 Mortality from entanglements in commercial and sport fisheries, as well as inshore trawl fisheries.

 Disease from anthropogenic and human sources.

 Disturbance from permitted and non-permitted tourist vessels.

 Pollution discharge into the coastal marine area.

 Plastic debris generated from dumping of both urban and marine based waste.

 Injuries and mortality by boat traffic.

Action by NOAA to propose listing the species on the Endangered Species List would help spur New Zealand to take further action to secure a future for these species.
It is important that New Zealand increase the size and number of sanctuaries in the species range, increased levels of fisheries monitoring (via observer coverage and electronic monitoring) and put in place stricter regulations that are rigorously enforced. 

Sincerely,

Katherine Hanly
Earth Island Institute's
International Marine Mammal Project

Earth Island Institute’s International Marine Mammal Project supports the United 
States National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Agency’s (NOAA) initiative to list 
New Zealand’s Hector’s Dolphin Subspecies (C. hectori hectori) as Threatened and 
the Maui's Dolphin Subspecies (Cephalorhynchus hectori maui) as Endangered under 
the Endangered Species Act. 
 
We agree that New Zealand needs to substantially improve its marine mammal 
protection and fisheries management systems in order to secure a future for both 
these species. 
 
Clearly, urgent action is needed. 
Hector’s dolphin is considered to be one of the world’s rarest dolphin species. The 
North Island Maui’s dolphin, is estimated to have a population of around 111 
individuals and is ranked as nationally critical by the Department of Commerce and 
critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). 
Both dolphin subspecies have a lifespan of only about 20 years, have low 
reproduction rate (calving every 2-3 years) and have late onset of sexual maturity 
(7-9 years). These factors result in a low maximum population growth rate, which 
put Hector’s and Maui’s dolphin at threat from even low levels of human-induced 
mortality. 
Threats to both these species include: 
• Mortality from entanglements in commercial and sport fisheries, as well as 
inshore trawl fisheries. 
 
• Disease from anthropogenic and human sources. 
 
• Disturbance from permitted and non-permitted tourist vessels. 
 
• Pollution discharge into the coastal marine area.

To the Food Safety and Inspection Service,

I fully support FSIS’s proposed updates to its guidelines on documentation for animal-raising and environment-related claims on meat and poultry products. As consumers, we’re often far removed from the farming process, yet we make choices daily about the food we put on our tables. For this reason, I believe it’s essential that product labels are transparent and trustworthy. The updated guideline’s focus on documentation and third-party verification for claims like “Raised Without Antibiotics” and “Grass Fed” is a positive step towards ensuring consumers have accurate information about how their food was produced.

I strongly believe that clear definitions for labeling terms are necessary to bridge the gap between consumers and farming practices. For example, terms like “free-range” or “environmentally responsible” should be well-defined to ensure they accurately reflect what consumers believe they signify. Without clear definitions, labels can easily be misunderstood or even misleading, eroding consumer trust. FSIS’s proposed encouragement of third-party certification will further support truth in labeling, allowing consumers to confidently support farming practices they value.

Ultimately, these changes empower consumers to make informed decisions, aligning their purchases with their values. With access to transparent labeling and reliable standards, consumers can actively support farmers and industries that prioritize sustainable, humane, and environmentally responsible practices. I commend FSIS for this commitment to clarity and truth in labeling, as it’s a critical component of maintaining consumer trust and promoting informed, values-based choices in the marketplace. My only concern with this proposed rule would be around a potential price increase on the consumer for the truth in labeling. I do not think that the consumer should have to bear the burden of requiring truth about an industry’s products. 

Thank you,

Thank you for proposing to expand critical habitat for the Southern Resident killer whales (SRKW) to include marine waters from Monterey Bay in California through Cape Flattery in Washington State. I fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

Protecting this full range as critical habitat reflects new and best available science as new sightings and data show that SRKW regularly forage in the coastal waters off Washington, Oregon, and California and is essential to help get the southern resident orcas off the path to extinction and on the way to recovery.

The final rule designating critical habitat identified three essential habitat features essential to the conservation of the SRKW: (1) Water quality to support SRKW growth and development; (2) prey species of sufficient quantity, quality, and availability to support individual growth, reproduction, and development, as well as overall population growth; and (3) passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

However, the proposed rule exempts the Navy's Quinault Range Site off the coast of Washington from being designated as critical habitat due to national security. The Quinault Range Site includes part of two high-use foraging areas, as recognized by NMFS in the Biological Report, and completely bisects the proposed expanded critical habitat area. From the tagging data, about half the time that K and L pods spend in coastal habitat is in Area 1 (Washington and Northern Oregon inshore habitat). This exemption could impact their foraging ability in an area and season when nutritional stress is a significant concern and impact their ability to migrate up and down the coast. Therefore the exempted area is in conflict with the third essential habitat feature: passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

The proposed rule should include a narrow area sufficient in width between the shoreline and the eastern border of the Quinault Range Site to ensure orca migration along the coast and for foraging for limited prey. 

The science also shows that sound from vessels and other sources undermines orcas ability to echolocate to forage for salmon as well as to communicate and navigate. The Washington Governors Orca Recovery Task Force and the ESA Recovery Plan have noted that noise and disturbance are key threats hindering orca recovery and have recommended decreasing, not increasing, military noise. To sufficiently protect SRKW, NMFS must include sound as a fourth essential feature. Urge them to ensure that it is at least retained as an explicit factor in the prey and passage essential features. 

I am grateful that NMFS has engaged and consulted with Tribes to ensure that this rule does not impact Tribal Treaty rights and usual and accustomed fishing areas.

Again, fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

Thank you for this opportunity to comment on rule changes specific to CMS-1718-P. I am a social work

mental health and transitions of care from skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) to the community. 

A brief set of comments follow that are of greatest interest/ relevance to my work and expertise: 

1) I endorse the collection of information pertaining to Veteran status as part of Standardized Patient 

Assessment Data Elements (Table 13, p. 17643). Many Veterans are provided care outside the VA 

system. Adding this as a SNF QRP measure may encourage more patient-centered care practices and 

system-wide focus on older Veterans’ post-acute healthcare needs. This may also encourage more 

research/ analysis of Veteran status as a health determinant in PAC settings, particularly for 

investigators outside of VA for whom this information may be more difficult to access. 

2) I heartily endorse the inclusion of an item related to social isolation. As the proposed rule notes, it is 

associated with negative clinical outcomes (physical/ mental illness and mortality) in this population, 

though it is rarely measured/ reported. As others have noted, it is also an important predictor of suicide 

in this population (See Van Orden et al. 2010; doi: 10.1037/a0018697). Thus, inclusion of this item 

represents an innovation toward routine data collection and reporting of social isolation – a far too 

common condition among older adults in PAC settings. 

3) I am more qualified in my thoughts on introduction of a new depression screening process. While I 

value the benefit of reducing patient burden, a paper by McCarthy et al. (2013) identified elevated rates 

of suicide among older Veterans within three weeks of discharge from VA nursing homes (doi: 

10.2105/AJPH.2013.301292). Likewise, experts in geriatric psychiatric have identified care transitions as 

a prime period for intervening in suicide risk among older adults (Szanto et al., 2013, doi: 

10.1176/appi.ps.003582012). Studies of older adults and older Veterans transitioning from community-

based, CMS regulated nursing homes have not been published; therefore, we do not know whether 

suicide risk is elevated after discharge from these SNFs. Implementation of PHQ-2/ 9 suggests that there 

will be no universal screening for suicide risk in this population (using item 9), unless the patient reports 

depressive symptoms first that meet the required threshold on the PHQ-2 assessment and completes 

the full 9 item measure. VA has handled this by including both the PHQ-2 and item 9 (suicide ideation) as 

part of a combined approach to depression/ suicide risk screening across care settings. CMS may 

consider adding the PHQ item 9 at points of transition (e.g. discharge and transition to the community or 

between settings), as a step toward universal screening of suicide risk in combination with PHQ-2/9. See 

also Louzon et al., 2016 (doi: 10.1176/appi.ps.201500149) and Uebelacker et al. 2011 (doi: 

10.4088/PCC.10m01027).

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

I am writing to urge you to reject the proposed rul-e to downlist West Indian manatees to threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Please keep this species listed as endangered.

There simply aren't enough West Indian manatees to warrant delisting them. Way too many continue to be killed by boats as the drivers refuse to slow down and they also are extremely vulnerable to the affects of climate change that can kill them. I have to assume that special interest groups are the driving force behind this proposal? The USFWS's job is protect endangered animals like the manatees, not protect special interest groups' selfish agendas. You are basing your delisting proposal on flawed science that hasn't taken into account the recent massive die-offs and you haven't conducted a required five- year revie-w since 2007. Please stop defying science and shirking your responsibilities and take this extinction proposal off the table.

Manatees were originally listed as endangered in 1967 due to the threats they faced from boat strikes, habitat loss, and pollution. These threats have not decreased, in fact, they have increased. Within the last two years, at least 1,200 Florida manatees have died from boat strikes, the effects of algal blooms, and other threats. In the first three months of 2016 alone, the number of watercraft mortalities was double the previous five-year average. Compliance with existing speed zone restrictions averages only 54 percent.

I am also concerned about the 'evidence' that USFWS is relying on for the proposed downlisting. The USFWS is proposing to undertake a reclassification of the species without first conducting the required five-year status revie-w under the Endangered Species Act. The last status revie-w for West Indian manatees took place in 2007. This revie-w has been questioned by numerous scientists, as it appears to be ba-sed on one computer model 'the Core Biological Model' which failed to take into account recent massive die-offs of hundreds of manatees from prolonged cold snaps and toxic red tide blooms between 2010 and 2013. It also did not take into account habitat loss due to waterfront development and the anticipated loss of artificial warm water. Without incorporating the full data set, it is impossible to assess the long-term viability of the Florida manatee population. 

In sum, the USFWS is proposing to undertake a downlisting without basing it on concrete scientific studies that demonstrate that the manatee population has recovered sufficiently. Before such a move is even considered, the USFWS needs to put together a viable plan to reduce mortality and establish achievable recovery benchmarks. Specifically, the agency should account for the increase in boating hours, algal blooms, loss of artificial warm water, Lake Okeechobee discharges, and state speed zones. 

After losing over 3,000 manatees in Florida waters alone between 2010 and 2015, there is no evidence that they are ready for downlisting. Please keep them listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act.

down the cost of health care for all Americans. CAHC promotes policies that lower health costs through 
increased competition, informed consumers and more choices. Our members include medical providers, 
patient groups, insurers, pharmaceutical manufacturers, pharmacy benefit managers, and employers. 
HRA’s have long been used by employers as a way to provide flexibility in the design of their benefits and to 
provide employees with choices. With the passage of the 21st Century Cures Act, Congress certified the use of 
HRA’s in the small employer market and provided the option to allow an HRA to be used to fund an 
individual’s health insurance expenses. This rule builds off of that approach by providing an expansion of 
HRA’s to cover a variety of consumer health needs while clarifying how an HRA interacts with the Affordable 
Care Act’s employer mandate.

insurer may have a limited presence in the employee’s area, and the employee may have to rely on rented 
networks that may not be as robust as the primary location’s employee network. In other cases, employees 
have more limited plan options and may face higher cost sharing requirements. In short, the new rules solve 
a fundamental problem for employers by giving both the employer and employee new options.

offer better options to their remote workers. Listed below are a number of important modifications.

To Whomever It May Concern, 

I am writing to comment on docket no. FDA-2013-N-1619. Overall, I am in support of the 

document. However, there are a few concerns that I would like to address. 

These concerns include: 

-Whether the processes being used to assess the contents of supplements are genuine and 

 accurate/how this is regulated 

-Records regarding labeling and what is actually contained in the supplement 

-Whether these records will be available to the public or not 

How and When Will it be Determined Whether a Company is Using Accurate and Genuine 

Methods in Order to Produce Their Supplements? 

It is to my understanding that records will be kept on the process of production for supplements. 

However, the document is not clear about what measures will be taken for reviewing the records 

kept. It is also unclear whether there is a line drawn for safe and unsafe production. There have 

been cases in the past where processes have been proven hazardous, and keeping records does 

not mean any of this is bound to change. The FDA does not regulate supplements until they have 

been out on the market and something has proven to be wrong with them (Dietary Supplements). 

The FDA will only investigate a certain supplement if there are multiple complaints, and/or 

deaths from the drug (Lattman). Record keeping may make it easier to track down the source of 

damage and get a supplement taken off the market. However, I would like to see regulation 

implemented before supplements go on the market in order to prevent harm to the consumer. 

How Will the Records Change Labeling Regulation? 

Many consumers are not aware of the detriment that overdosing on certain nutrients can do. The 

even more twisted reality is that many supplements do not actually contain what is stated on the 

label, meaning that there could be an improper portion, or unknown contents to the consumer 

(Dangers of Vitamins and Supplements). In relation to my first concern, records may provide 

insight into where the error in production and/or labeling is, but it is my presumption that the

 
2 

records will not be looked at until the supplement is already on the market and issues with it have 

arisen. To ensure safety, practices should be proven to be accurate with depiction of contents and 

should be proven so before the supplements hit the market. 

Will the Records Be Released to the Public, or Stay Private? 

Though these records will be helpful to the FDA for regulating supplements, they could also be 

helpful to those in the public who are interested in what they are taking. At the moment, if one 

wants to obtain more information about a certain supplement, the only option they have is to 

contact the manufacturer or distributor (Dietary Supplements). This process can often times be 

time consuming, but if the records were available to the public, it would increase ease of finding 

information on the supplements. A consumer has a right to know what they are putting in their 

body. It is unclear in the document whether records will be publicly released or not, but it would 

be beneficial for the general public. 

I would like to thank you for the opportunity to express my views on this document and taking 

the time to consider my thoughts and concerns shared in this response.

An upgrade to the HPA is desperately needed as horses continue to suffer under a status quo that allows that industry to police itself despite the obvious conflict of interest.

According to the USDA's own review of data in recent years, there remains a persistent and vast discrepancy between violations found by industry appointed inspectors vs. those found by USDA inspectors (despite the latter attending only a small proportion of shows). Unfortunately, it is clear that the industry continues to turn a blind eye to evidence of soring.

Rather than withdraw the rule, the USDA should reissue the rulemaking until the department is prepared to move forward with a new HPA rule containing, at a minimum, all the key components of the 2017 rule. Importantly, the 2017 rule included prohibitions on ankle chains and other "action devices" associated with soring and eliminated the failed industry-run self-enforcement system.

Over 100,000 public comments were submitted in support of the 2017 rule; hundreds of members of Congress voiced their support as well. The 2017 HPA rule would achieve many of the recommendations outlined in the USDA Office of Inspector General audit and the recent National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report, both of which called for an end to the industry self-policing scheme.

In 2021, the USDA announced that the "development of a new and improved HPA proposal [was] a top regulatory priority," but the decision to withdraw the 2017 rule, coupled with the lack of progress on a new rule, suggests satisfaction with the status quo and that the USDA is not serious about fulfilling its legal duty to end soring.

DOT solicited comments on the length of delay that would warrant a baggage refund. Specifically, the DOT ANPRM questioned whether or not the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act's double standard for domestic and international flights is the best guideline. Pub. L. No. 114-190, 2305(a) (2016). As a consumer, I believe that the DOT should create a more comprehensive scheduled guideline to determine delay time based on a variety of factors. This would allow for more accurate accounting of passenger hassle without inefficiently raising costs on airlines that might pass these costs down to the consumer. 

Congress explicitly considered a bipartite requirement for determining delay time in which domestic flights had a 12-18 hour window and international flights had a 15-30 hour window to deliver baggage. Although this signals some congressional intent to treat international and domestic flights differently, there is still significant ambiguity for the DOT to regulate outside of this framework. The statutory language includes an exception that gives the DOT latitude to "modify one or both of the deadlines specified" if the "Secretary makes a determination on the record that a requirement under subsection (a) is not feasible and would adversely affect consumers in certain cases." Allowing the DOT to modify one or both of the deadlines means that Congress explicitly considered the fact that the agency could align the two schemes by just extending/limiting one of the proposed deadlines. The Secretary would be authorized to make this change if there were evidence on the record of consumer harm. Assuming that airlines will present evidence of how this regulation as a whole burdens them and would lead them to raise prices for flights or baggage fees, the Secretary should have enough evidence to change the deadlines. 

Instead of going forward with the domestic/international dichotomy, the Secretary should solicit commentary from the airline industry about a possible scheduled guideline that creates deadlines based on length of flight, frequency of route travel, etc. For example, airlines would then have more time to deliver a bag for a flight from New York to Los Angeles (6 hours, very frequent route) than from Los Angeles to Mexico City (4 hours, frequent route) but would also have more time to deliver from New York to Santa Ana, CA (6 hours, once a day) than New York to Los Angeles. While this timetable would be more difficult for airlines to navigate, they likely would find it preferable because it tailors the deadlines to the realities of their practices. This would complicate the refund process for consumers as well, but if the refunds are automatic, as proposed in this regulation, then this should not actually have an effect on consumers accessing compensation. 

I believe that this would go a long way in helping frequent fliers like myself feel compensated when we do experience delays, without scaring airlines into raising their already exorbitant baggage fees.

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposal to allow the annual killing of upwards of 124,157 federally protected Double-crested Cormorants nationwide of which nearly 9,000 would occur in the Western United States where populations are already at risk due to previous mismanagement by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. I also strongly oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s related proposal to delegate responsibility for overseeing the killing of Double-crested Cormorants to States. The proposal being put forth by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service amounts to wanton slaughter. I urge you to abandon this proposal and adopt the No Action Alternative. 

Double-crested Cormorants are one of the most persecuted wild birds in the United States. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has a long history of failing to meet its statutory responsibility to protect this species. This proposal unfortunately perpetuates that pattern.

I oppose the proposed rule and recommend the No Action Alternative for the following reasons:

Allowing the killing of Double-crested Cormorants nationwide each year perpetuates a long-term pattern of persecution of this species by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and is in direct conflict with the agencies mission and mandate to conserve, protect and enhance fish, wildlife and plants and their habitats for the continuing benefit of the American people protect native bird species. 
Allowing the killing of Double-crested Cormorants annually violates the Migratory Bird Treaty Act which mandates that the agency only allow killing if it can ensure the continued viability of the species.
Allowing the take of nearly 9,000 Double-crested Cormorant annually west of the Rocky Mountains (representing >14% of the western population) where populations are already as risk, in part due to prior actions by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, would put the western population at extreme risk and could result in the need for a future listing under the Endangered Species Act. 
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to consider any strategies other than lethal control of Double-crested Cormorants in any of the action alternatives.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to include adequate monitoring in the proposal alternative to ensure that it would be able to modify killing levels if significant declines occur.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to adequately address risks to non-target species.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to address humane and animal welfare issues.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service failed to adequately address illegal take of cormorants and disruption of colonies in their modelling.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has failed to demonstrate that killing Double-crested Cormorants would benefit imperiled fish species.

Delegation of permitting authority to states is an abdication of a core responsibility of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and would put management of cormorants in the hands of state agencies that lack both resources and expertise and which in many cases have explicitly expressed a desire to see even more aggressive control of cormorants than has been allowed to date by USFWS.

I am deeply disappointed that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is continuing to pursue the unwarranted persecution of Double-crested Cormorants. Prior actions by the Service have put cormorant populations at risk, resulted in the deaths of tens of thousands of cormorants, wasted millions of taxpayer dollars Rachel M. Rogge

Dear Chief, Division of Environmental Review Craig Aubrey, 

The Endangered Species Act is one of our nation’s greatest environmental success stories. I’m alarmed by the proposed

modifications that would undermine it. 

1. Economic Analysis: Economic impacts are not a part of the criteria for a listing under the ESA. Adding the

information to the process raises the possibility that the information will improperly influence the Fish and Wildlife Service

and National Marine Fisheries Service (the Services) when making their decisions about the impact of protecting a

species. It will also add to the burden and cost of the agencies. 

2. Critical Habitat: By ignoring climate change threats such as melting glaciers, sea level rise, or reduced snowpack,

this proposed rule encourages death by 1,000 cuts. The Services are not going to prevent climate change from occurring,

but they can take actions to prevent habitat from being destroyed. Designation as critical habitat will ensure actions are

taken to minimize the effects of climate change. The proposed change would force Services to wait to act well into the

late-game of a species’ peril (if at all). This would be more costly in the long run and the delay in acting on the problem

may mean the species is harmed to an even greater degree while Services try to find a suitable habitat for the species. 

3. Threatened Species: It is easier and cheaper to save a threatened/endangered species sooner rather than later.

The Endangered Species Act is far more effective if the Services acts proactively, before population levels are critically

low. The proposed rule would permit, not require, the Services to do anything. This will hasten the march from

“threatened” to “endangered.” 

These proposed rules put rare animals, birds, and plants at risk unnecessarily, and undermine protections for important

habitat areas like Plum Island, which is home to the endangered roseate tern and piping plover, along with endangered

marine species like the hawksbill sea turtle, green sea turtle, and loggerhead sea turtle, and endangered plant species

like spring ladies-tresses. 

I ask that you abandon these rule changes and protect what we have left.

Agricultural Marketing Service’s (AMS) July 22 proposed rule to update the List of

sweeteners in manufacturing their products, as well as trade associations representing those 

companies. The segments of the U.S. food industry that use sugar in their business operations 

employ some 600,000 Americans. 

SUA believes it is inappropriate to add sugarcane to the List of Bioengineered Foods. Our 

understanding is that the single variety of insect-resistant sugarcane approved by Brazil is only 

being raised in test trials and in only one region of the country, and not the region from which 

Brazilian sugar imported under tariff-rate quotas is typically sourced. Brazil is one of 40 

different countries from which the United States imports sugar, in addition to our domestic cane 

supply, which is not bioengineered. Thus, the chance that BE sugarcane was used to produce

List would be reasonable. However, this is not the case today. Therefore, SUA respectfully 

requests that AMS refrain from finalizing the proposed rule for at least one to two years in order 

to better determine the extent, if any, of actual commercial adoption of BE technology in the

I am writing to (1) oppose the proposed expansion of the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS) in its current form; (2) urge NOAA to expand the boundaries and protections of the FGBNMS to a greater extent than considered in the proposed expansion; and (3) urge NOAA to apply existing restrictions to the FGBNMS expansion with no exemptions for spearfishing, longline fishing, or any other destructive fishing practice within sanctuary boundaries.

Please consider implementing Alternative 5 from the DEIS, which would provide greater protections to the FGBNMS than the final alternative chosen in the EIS. Alternative 5 would increase the sanctuary boundaries to include 57 national significant natural features and eight nationally significant cultural and historic resource sites. Even Alternative 3, which was identified as the preferred alternative in the DEIS, would be preferable to the final alternative chosen. Alternative 3 would have expanded the existing sanctuary from 56 square miles to 383 square miles and includes a total of 18 nationally significant natural features within 11 discrete proposed boundary areas.

The FGBNMS mission is to identify, protect, conserve, and enhance the natural and cultural resources, values, and qualities of FGBNMS and its regional environment for this and future generations. The FGBNMS provides a wide range of habitat conditions that support several distinct biological communities, including the northernmost coral reefs in the continental United States. Sanctuary formations provide the foundation for essential habitat for a variety of species, including sea turtles, sharks and other important marine wildlife.

In order to realize the FGBNMS mission, NOAA must restrict fishing in the sanctuary boundaries. Allowing spear fishing or longlines in FGBNMS boundaries would otherwise undermine the proposed expansions prohibition from taking any marine mammal or sea turtles.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

Jessica

Restore Conservation Safeguards in the Tongass National Forest Dear Decision Makers, Please reinstate the 2001 Roadless Rule on the Tongass National Forest! I have been aware of how quickly roads can bring development into a pristine natural area since I saw a striking exhibit at the Museum of Natural History many years ago that explained how logging roads brought development into rainforests in South America. Since then, I have seen many other examples of how one road -- such as a logging road -- can be the first step toward bringing development to an area. In addition, roads can cause fragmentation of wild lands and harm populations of species that are already facing many challenges. We have too few large, roadless areas in our country, and with the challenges our earth is facing, we need to maintain those few roadless areas we have -- especially in a rare and valuable natural resource such as the Tongass National Forest. Therefore, I strongly support reinstating the 2001 Roadless Rule on the Tongass National Forest as part of the USDA's Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy. The Tongass is one of North America's premier destinations for hunting, fishing, and outdoor recreation. The remaining stands of mature, undeveloped forests play a critical role in Southeast Alaska's productive fish and wildlife habitats, which support more than 400 species, including popular game animals like Sitka black-tailed deer, mountain goats, and brown bears. The watersheds of "America's salmon forest," as the Tongass is commonly known, contribute approximately 50 million fish annually to Alaska's multi-billion-dollar commercial salmon industry. More than one-quarter of all jobs in the region-in fisheries, recreation, and tourism-directly rely on the balanced management of the Tongass National Forest. Simply put, Southeast Alaska's economy, culture, and storied fish and wildlife resources are all tied to the health of the Tongass. That's why I support the Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy, which directs the Forest Service to transition away from large-scale old-growth logging and invest in more sustainable activities such as young-growth forest and watershed restoration that improve habitat for salmon, deer, and other game species. I also support investments in recreational access and infrastructure, which support Alaska's outdoor recreation and visitor industries, as well as local workforce development. While the Forest Service and community partners ramp up capacity to perform more restoration and recreation-based work, a swift reinstatement of the 2001 Roadless Rule is in order. By safeguarding undeveloped landscapes and watersheds in the Tongass, the Roadless Rule supports industries that depend on intact forests and high-quality habitat, such as commercial fishing, tourism, and the wide range of businesses that serve hunters, anglers, and other outdoor recreators. The rule also has built-in flexibility and allows for community development projects to serve the public interest. This is a critical time for Southeast Alaskans who rely on the Tongass to support their families and sustain their outdoor traditions, as well as for the future generations of Americans who have yet to experience the vast wetlands, lush rainforests, vibrant streams, and high alpine meadows of our nation's largest national forest. Thank you for your time and attention to this important matter. Sincerely, Suzanne Didier -PII-

I submit this comment to oppose USCIS-2019-0007-0001 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), which would cause dangerous privacy issues for children seeking safety in the United States.

If you dont collect citizens DNA dont collect foreigners DNA either!!

The proposed rule expands the criteria under which children are required to provide biometric and DNA samples for immigration and asylum proceedings. Currently, only children 14 and older were required to provide biometric data. The proposed rule would remove that age restriction, leading to the collection of sensitive data from much younger children who do not understand the implications and removing the protections provided by parental consent.

Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, coercing children to submit biometric data without explicit understanding and consent violates their rights and causes indefensible mental stress.

DHS estimates an additional 2.17 million new biometrics submissions will be collected annually. Many of these additional submissions will be of children under the age of 14.

The proposed rule also uses very vague language to explain how it will store biometric data and the instances in which it might share this biometric data with other government agencies. This raises many questions about data privacy and the ways that this data might be used against migrants. 

Children are particularly vulnerable to invasions of privacy that can result in long-lasting negative consequences. While it may be inconvenient to change your password when your identity is stolen, it is impossible to change your fingerprint or your DNA. A breach of a child's biometric data can result in lifelong and potentially life-threatening consequences.

That is why in most cases, parental consent is required before data like these are collected from children. Children in asylum or immigration proceedings, however, often are traveling alone or with parents who may not fully understand the consequences of agreeing to provide this information to U.S. border authorities. Refusal could result in expulsion from the country.

Please take into consideration this comment and the impact that the proposed rule would have on the right to privacy that should be extended to children fleeing violence who are seeking safety in the U.S.

As a well-established education nonprofit, the Institute for the Study of Knowledge Management

higher education organizations, including library consortia, system, and coordinating boards. 
Our work has ranged from research studies assessing statewide readiness for a shift to OER, 
development of state-specific OER digital libraries, OER curation and metadata initiatives, and 
both in-person and hybrid training engagements with state-level stakeholders, OER grantees, 
and librarians. With a foundation of that experience, we offer the following comments on this 
proposal. 
 
Program Structure 
 
Topic 1, Award Size:​ We believe this program will best accomplish its stated purpose if it 
(1) invests in a wide variety of potential concepts and models, and (2) is accessible to a 
diverse set of institutions and consortia. 
 
In the past, the Department has chosen to invest in larger-scale, infrastructure-building 
projects - which are a core element of sparking sustainable change in the market - but 
we note that many existing, successful OER projects on college campuses to date have 
accomplished worthwhile progress with significantly fewer resources. 
 
Therefore, we recommend an award range of $250,000 to $1 million.

 
By awarding different amounts to multiple projects, the Department can ensure that this 
opportunity is available not only to well-entrenched, long-standing institutions with 
capacity to handle multi-million dollar projects in a short timeframe, but also smaller 
institutions and community colleges with innovative ideas and outsized impact on 
traditionally underserved populations. 
 
Topic 2, Matching Contributions:​ We strongly recommend that the Department should 
not require matching contributions. While we understand the appeal of having institutions 
contribute some of their own resources to a project as a way to deepen their 
organizational commitment, we raise two concerns about it in relation to this program. 
First, similar to the impact a large award size might have on the applicant pool, a 
matching requirement would preclude many institutions with less unrestricted funding but

resulting savings from open education projects are only experienced by the institution

Brucellosis, caused by B. abortus, is enzootic in elk (Cervus elaphus) and wild bison (Bison bison) 

of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem (GYE) in Wyoming. The disease causes pregnant females to 

abort following initial ingestion of the bacteria through contact with aborted materials. In the GYE 

of Wyoming, elk are considered the primary host and potential vector of transmission to livestock 

(primarily cattle, Bos Taurus). This is based on the species’ life history and identification of genetic 

isolates of B. abortus from elk and reactor cattle. Although brucellosis has been known to infect elk 

on supplemental winter feedgrounds and the National Elk Refuge since the 1930s, and feedgrounds 

concentrate elk during a portion of the abortion period (February-June) thereby promoting 

transmission, free-ranging populations with limited interchange of elk attending feedgrounds appear 

to maintain the disease and have seen prevalence increase since the 1990s. 

The impacts of brucellosis on the relative health of populations of elk and bison are limited. Despite 

prevalence estimates that average from 25% in elk to 66% in wild bison, these have translated to 

slight reductions in pregnancy rates, but have not resulted in reduction of elk productivity as 

population trend counts, hunting seasons, and harvest permits have been stable or increasing. 

Regardless, the disease is not native to North American wildlife, and spillover events to cattle have

I respectfully submit this comment to strongly oppose USCIS's NPRM, USCIS-2020-0019; RIN 1615-AC61. This misguided rule, which dramatically alters the way in which H-1B registrations are selected for the annual H-1B statutory cap, is inconsistent with Congressional intent, is in violation of the statute, and will undermine our nation's pipeline of global talent we need to drive innovation and foster economic growth.

This rule would undermine the country's capability to retain talent. Lot of budding H1Bs come up with start ups and generate jobs for American citizens.

This Proposed Rule is a Clear Violation of the Statute and Congressional Intent:

The H-1B program was established by Congress to provide an avenue for employers to hire a foreign worker in a specialty occupation. This proposed rule is a clear violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which prioritizes the selection of H-1B cap-subject petitions in the "order in which they are filed" and does not limit who is selected for the H-1B cap to those employers who pay the most. USCIS lacks the statutory authority to make such a change and cannot use the statute's silence as an invitation to adopt criteria, such as wage level or skill level, to prioritize the selection of H-1B cap subject visas. 

This Proposed Rule is Based on a False Premise That Salary Alone Equates with Value: 

This proposal, which is based on the false premise that individuals who earn more in their profession contribute more to the economy or society, is yet another misguided and illegal attempt by the Trump administration to weaken our legal immigration and promote falsities about the workers who, contrary to what this rule implies, strengthen our economy.

If implemented, this rule will have a direct and negative impact on U.S. employers and college-educated foreign-born professionals by dramatically reducing access to the H-1B visa program for early-career professionals, including those completing Master's or Doctoral degrees at U.S. colleges and universities. Indeed, USCIS has acknowledged that if this new regulation is implemented, no individuals who are paid a Level 1 wage would be selected to submit a H-1B cap-subject petition for the annual H-1B cap. These proposed changes would effectively eliminate the H-1B program as an available visa option for new graduates seeking employment in an entry-level position.

If the talent is not available, the job could get outsourced. The opportunity follows talent so this rule will weaken the country's capacity on innovation and technology.

USCIS Should Refrain From Implementing this Rule For the FY2022 H-1B Cap Filing Season:

Many U.S. employers and immigration attorneys start preparing for the H-1B cap filing season months in advance, in some cases as early as August depending on the industry. Any changes by USCIS to the H-1B cap filing process this late in the year would have an adverse impact on U.S. employers, immigration attorneys and individuals, as hiring decisions and filing processes and procedures have already been put in place by many employers and immigration law firms. Thus, if USCIS finalizes this illegal and misguided rule, USCIS must refrain from implementing it for the upcoming FY2022 H-1B cap filings season in order to allow U.S. businesses, immigration attorneys and individuals sufficient time to adapt to the new wage-based selection process.

The Pacific Coast Federation of Fishermen’s Associations (PCFFA) is providing these public comments to 
NOAA Fisheries regarding proposed management measures for the California Coastal Chinook salmon 
(CCC). For decades PCFFA has been at the forefront of advocating for sustainable fisheries and 
advancing ocean conservation and habitat protection. We are dedicated to ensuring that California 
commercial fisheries remain the important economic and cultural pillars of our coastal communities that 
they have been for generations, and that consumers in California and beyond continue to enjoy access 
to healthy, wild, locally harvested seafood. 
 
Our commercial fishing members and their communities depend on a vital California commercial troll 
fishery, and while we acknowledge the importance of ensuring the conservation of California Coastal 
Chinook, we have significant concerns about the potential economic and ecological impacts of these 
proposed measures. 
 
The reliance on the Klamath River fall-run Chinook Salmon (KRFC) as a surrogate stock for evaluating 
impacts on CCC is deeply flawed. While this surrogate may have been appropriate in the past when 
ocean abundance of KRFC was high and relatively stable, we have no confidence in the use of KRFC as 
the sole method to manage potential harvest of CCC. Declining returns of KRFC and the rapidly 
changing Klamath River spawning habitat necessitate a reevaluation of this management strategy. There 
is little evidence that the KRFC proxy accurately reflects the dynamics of the current CCC population, 
spawning success, or ocean contact rates. These shortcomings are especially problematic considering 
the current removal of the Klamath dams and the uncertainty surrounding the impact of dam removal on 
fish stocks and river habitat. 
 
California Coastal Chinook comprise an evolutionarily significant unit (ESU) of salmon that return to rivers 
and streams south of the Klamath River up to and including the Russian River. Counts or estimates of 
adult returns to these rivers are sorely lacking. Current management does not incorporate estimates of 
adult returns, redd counts, spawning success, or juvenile outmigration. We recognize that monitoring the 
life stages of CCC is a massive undertaking, but efforts must begin to understand the population 
dynamics of CCC themselves, rather than relying on the unreliable KRFC surrogate. 
 
Higher than expected catch rates in the California commercial troll fishery is evidence that harvest 
models have been unreliable over the past decade, particularly under lower abundance conditions.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on the National Marine Fisheries 
Service’s (“NMFS”) proposal to designate the Sakhalin Bay-Nikolaya Bay-Amur River stock of 
beluga whales as a depleted under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (“MMPA”). 81 Fed. Reg. 
19542 (Apr. 5, 2016). These comments are submitted on behalf of the Center for Biological 
Diversity (“the Center”). The Center works to secure a future for all imperiled species and their 
habitats around the globe through science, law, and creative media with more than 1 million 
members and online activists in the United States and abroad. 
 
We urge NMFS to designate the Sakhalin Bay-Nikolaya Bay-Amur River stock of beluga 
whales (“Sakhalin beluga”) as “depleted,” and we are grateful for the work NMFS, its staff, and 
the status review team have committed to this issue. As NMFS is aware, in April 2014, the 
Animal Welfare Institute, Whale and Dolphin Conservation, Cetacean Society International, and 
Earth Island Institute submitted a petition to list the Sakhalin Bay-Amur River stock of beluga 
whales (Delphinapterus leucas) as “depleted” under the MMPA. In June 2014, the Center 
submitted detailed comments strongly supporting the petition and a depleted listing for this 
stock.1
 
 We incorporate those comments by reference here. 
Under the MMPA, a stock is “depleted” under the MMPA if the “stock is below its 
optimum sustainable population,” or OSP. 16 U.S.C. § 1362(1). The statute defines “OSP” to 
mean “the number of animals which will result in the maximum productivity of the population or 
the species.” Id. § 1362(9). NMFS’s regulations further define OSP to mean “a population size 
which falls within a range from the population level of a given . . . stock which is the largest 
 
1 See Center for Biological Diversity. Support for Petition to List the Sakhalin Belugas as “Depleted.” (June 19, 
2014).

 
2 
 
supportable within the ecosystem to the population level that results in maximum net 
productivity [“MNPL”]. Maximum net productivity is the greatest net annual increment in 
population numbers or biomass resulting from additions to the population due to reproduction 
and/or growth less losses due to natural mortality.” 50 C.F.R. § 261.3. The Sakhalin stock of 
beluga clearly meets these MMPA standards and thus we urge NMFS to promptly finalize its 
proposal to designate the stock as “depleted.” 
 
Specifically, we first acknowledge and thank the agency for recognizing that it has the 
authority to designate stocks as depleted, even if the stocks occur outside of U.S. jurisdictional 
waters. 81 Fed. Reg. at 19,542. As detailed in our 2014 comments, the MMPA’s plain language, 
the purpose of the depleted provisions, and the agency’s previous practice of listing foreign 
stocks all clearly demonstrate that NMFS must list foreign stocks as depleted when warranted. 
 
Second, Sakhalin belugas clearly qualify as a distinct “stock.” As described in NMFS’s 
proposed rule and the Marine Mammal Commission’s comments, genetic evidence, including 
mtDNA differences, and movement data support recognizing Sakhalin Bay-Nikolaya Bay-Amur 
River belugas as a distinct stock.2 Additionally, the best available scientific information 
demonstrates that the Sakhalin stock is below OSP. The most recent population estimate from 
2010 is low – approximately 3,960 belugas in the Sakhalin Bay stock and an unknown but likely 
very low number in the Nikolaya Bay region,3
 
 and NMFS estimates the stock’s carrying capacity 
at 17,700. 81 Fed. Reg. at 19,546

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

The Florida Skin Divers Association is a network of several hundred divers and spearfishers around the state of Florida. We are writing to provide comment on the Direct Enhancement of Snapper Conservation and the Economy through Novel Devices Act of 2020 (Descend Act) section 321, titled “Required possession of descending devices,” which requires vessels to possess a descending device when fishing for reef fish in the Gulf of Mexico.

We admire the rule for its reduction of barotrauma and discard mortality in the hook-and-line fishery. However, spearing gear is used to visually select and harvest target species and therefore does not result in the barotrauma or discard mortality issues that are inherent when using hook-and-line gear. Many spearfishers across the state of Florida and beyond make many trips to target reef fish solely using spearing gear without carrying a single rod and reel on the vessel, therefore, it would not be practical for these vessels to be required to carry a descending device during these spearing trips.

We respectfully request NMFS to consider amending the section 321 language to include an exemption to the required possession of descending devices for spearing gear only vessels.

We greatly appreciate your consideration of this suggestion and are happy discuss this in more detail.

Thank you,

The Florida Skin Divers Association

Assistance Declarations Factors Guidance. I urge you to make adjustments to the both the 
proposed rule and proposed guidance document that make individual assistance factors 
fairer for California. 
I am most concerned with the agency's proposal to rely heavily on a cost-to-capacity 
ratio that is calculated wholly based on a state's total taxable resources. According to 2016 
data from the Department of the Treasury, California has the largest total taxable resources 
of any state at $2.777 trillion. The difference between this statistic for California and the 
second largest state, Texas, is greater than each of the total taxable revenues of 45 other 
states and the District of Columbia. I have serious concerns that relying on this equation 
would make it significantly more difficult for Californians to access individual disaster 
assistance. 
Your staff indicated that the agency believes total taxable resources is an appropriate 
way to determine whether a disaster is, according to the Stafford Act, "beyond the 
capabilities of the State and the affected local governments." It is my view that total taxable 
resources is too broad of a factor to provide a useful assessment of this statutory 
requirement for a state's capacity - let alone a local government's capacity - to manage a 
disaster. While I support having a more transparent calculation of when a disaster exceeds a 
state's capacity such as a cost-to-capacity ratio, I urge the agency to find a factor other than 
total taxable resources that is better representative of both state and local resources available 
to each specific disaster. I understand that the guidance does take into account other diverse 
factors, but these factors are not weighted and it is unclear to what extent they will relate to 
the agency's proposed cost-to-capacity ratio.

Please move forward with the implementation of the new and improved welfare standards for certified organic farm animals--Organic Livestock and Poultry Practices (OLPP) Rule. (AMS-NOP-15-0012, RIN 0581-AD75)

Our family is a consumer of organic products and I am writing to explain why, as a consumer, it is important for the USDA to implement stronger regulations for organically produced livestock products. We should be able to make informed purchases with respect to how the animals are raised. We choose organic foods for several reasons, with humane treatment of animals, avoidance of antibiotics, and avoidance of pesticides being the most important ones.
Farmers who currently meet very high standards on their organic farms have pride and integrity in what they have done for years to produce organic products. However, due to the growing demand for organic foods, some industrial-style operations have taken advantage of loopholes in the organic rule, thereby allowing them to expand into the organic marketplace. This is not fair to farmers who are committed to preserving the integrity of organic agriculture. These small farmers are at a competitive disadvantage because they do not take shortcuts when it comes to the care they take with their animals. The new proposed welfare standards should level the marketplace and create more uniform animal welfare expectations. Having clear rules allows for proper enforcement and fair competition amongst certified organic livestock producers.

Now, however, the USDA has announced it intends to withdraw this rule, claiming it lacks authority to regulate animal welfare. But, the department has a history of regulating animal welfare under the National Organic Program (NOP), including setting standards for animal care and living conditions.

In summary, stronger welfare standards would improve the lives of millions of farm animals each year. The clarified standards would also help level the playing field for farmers who already meet a very high standard of welfare for their animals. In addition, the new standards would reduce confusion and inspire consumer confidence that the meat, milk, and eggs purchased bearing the USDA Certified Organic seal do come from animals that were raised humanely. The OLPP Rule should be implemented soon.

Thank you for considering the views of my family.

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

This is terrible that we as consumers whom are wanting to only purchase meats, daily etc. That we know have truly been humanly raised...free , experiencing daylight, etc. Can't rely on our Government to be honest about how these beautiful animals of God are treated. I implore you to change these policies. Please hear our voices because we are their only voice.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

As a director of a training clinic who has witnessed the tremendous impact that trainees can have on their clients, I urge CMS to evaluate how the Physician Fee Schedule can improve access to mental and behavioral health services by supporting recruitment and retention of psychologists. Recruiting more psychologists is an essential strategy to meet patient needs wherever they are, particularly in underserved communities. In that spirit, I also urge CMS to work with the American Psychological Association (APA) Services to develop new rate-setting methodologies to improve access to behavioral health services.

Strengthen the Practice of Psychology
BHI Codes 
I support CMS' proposed coding and payment for General Behavioral Health Integration (BHI) to recognize psychologists' role in integrated care. I appreciate CMS' support for multiple evidence-based models of integrated care, as it allows psychologists the flexibility required to support the behavioral health needs of the broader community.

Medicare Potentially Underutilized Services
I appreciate CMS' request for comments on potentially underutilized services, as several of the services CMS identified are performed by psychologists. I recommend CMS create additional Cognitive Assessment & Care codes without the medication reconciliation service because medication management is outside the scope of a psychologist's license in many states. Additionally, I recommend CMS allow reimbursement for Intensive Behavioral Therapy for Obesity services provided by psychologists. 

Chronic Pain Management and Treatment (CPM) Bundles
I ask CMS to create additional bundled pain management codes that do not include medication management. I am concerned that psychologists would be excluded from this new bundled service because in most states medication management is outside the scope of a psychologist's license. Psychologists play a critical role in implementing non-pharmacological approaches to treatment, which may be safer or more effective for some patients, as well as team-based comprehensive pain management.

Telehealth
Many patients in rural and underserved areas are now able to access mental health services, often for the first time. Additionally, many patients prefer utilizing telehealth for a variety of reasons. Reverting to the non-facility rate for telehealth services after the end of the COVID public health emergency will lead practitioners to offer telehealth less frequently or to restrict the number of Medicare beneficiaries they treat using telehealth.

Expand Psychology Training and Workforce Development
Supervision by Psychologists 
I applaud CMS' Proposed Revisions to the "Incident to" Physicians' Services Regulation for Behavioral Health Services to allow for reimbursement for Physicians and Non-Physician Providers (NPPs), which include psychologists, who supervise these practitioners in their everyday practice. This will help expand access to and coordination of mental health services in rural and underserved areas where masters'-level practitioners represent a substantial segment of the mental health providers in the area.

Advanced Psychology Trainee Services 
I urge CMS to allow for Medicare reimbursement of services provided by advanced psychology trainees under the supervision of a licensed psychologist. Although psychology interns receive extensive clinical experience prior to their internship, services provided by trainees under the supervision of a licensed psychologist are not reimbursable under Medicare. Without Medicare reimbursement of services provided by trainees, training programs lack a steady source of funding. 

Support the Psychological Research-to-Practice Pipeline
Caregiving Behavior Management Training
I ask CMS to reconsider its position on the caregiver behavior management training codes. There is extensive empirical support for caregiver behavior management training and it is the gold standard treatment approach for several health behavior issues.
