FDAs decision to refrain from assigning suffixes to products already approved and marketed without a distinct suffix is a practical means of achieving the best possible safety framework for biologics. Over time, the vast majority of biological products will have a suffix. Ideally, the suffix policy would have been in place before the first biologic was approved and every product would have a suffix. FDAs policy of assigning suffixes for new products but not products already on the market makes the best of a difficult situation. In practice, relatively few biologics will have multiple versions by different manufacturers on the market. Attention must be paid to those products to ensure accurate prescribing, dispensing and adverse event reporting. For pharmacists, it will improve the important role in pharmacovigilence by enabling accurate identification of the drug prescribed and administered to patients if and when a treatment outcome changes or and adverse drug event is suspected. This is becoming an increasingly important role for pharmacists as the abbreviated pathway for biosimilars places more reliance on analytics and much less on clinical trials. This places increased importance on clinical observations (real world evidence), which pharmacists are best positioned to make as we encounter and monitor patients more frequently than other practitioners. One of the reasons for slow update in the use of biosimilars might be a lack of confidence in their use and the perception that quality is being sacrificed for cost. While some may argue that distinguishable non-proproprietary names underscores the differences in these products, or even inferiority of biosimilars, it is far more likely that strong pharmacovigilence programs strengthened by the ability to accurately gather real world evidence will actually improve confidence, increase update, and ultimately reduce the cost of care without jeopardizing effectiveness and safety.

While some have argued that state substitution laws with communication requirements make unreasonable time demands on pharmacists and delays in patient care, in reality it saves time and improves efficiency by empowering the pharmacist to make changes without having prior authorization from the prescriber. It also fosters inter professional collaboration and pharmacovigilence we should be willingly engaging in to help improve patient care and safety. Having a suffix to a non-proprietary name simply improves the accuracy of this communication among prescribers, pharmacists and patients, and strengthens pharmacovigilence programs essential to improving confidence in biosimilars.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

We need to know the truth to make intelligent purchases.

Thank you for considering my request.

Dear Director Stone-Manning,
As a livestock producer and a steward of the land, I am gravely concerned by the Bureau of Land 
Management’s (BLM) new proposed rule “Conservation and Landscape Health.” The mission of BLM is to 
balance the multiple uses of our nation’s public lands including recreation, energy, and livestock grazing. This 
proposed rule violates the multiple use mandate and gives “conservation” the ability to override and exclude 
other uses that the agency or a third party consider “incompatible.” There is no other use of public lands that 
has this much power. 
Conservation has always been tied to the land. Now, BLM is proposing that conservation be its own category.
Adding conservation as a new use on federally administered lands is a significant change. As a steward of the 
land I work tirelessly to make sure that I leave the land in better shape than what I found it. If I don’t take care 
of the land, it can’t take care of us. Creating a level where a lessee must work with a “Conservation lease 
holder” is creating a situation that can be bad for land health. Public lands grazing is an important tool for 
managing these landscapes and grazing improves soil, plant, and wildlife health. Grazing also helps reduce the 
buildup of grasses and other fuels that contribute to catastrophic wildfire, as New Mexico saw in 2022. 
I am also concerned that the proposed rule opens BLM to the risk of exploitation and more litigation in the 
future. BLM is already falling behind on agency responsibilities. Adding an additional component, individual 
approvals of conservation leases will only put the agency further behind on other permit approvals, including 
grazing permits. This proposed rule changes BLM’s entire management objectives with no analysis under the 
National Environmental Policy Act and no analysis on how this rule would cripple small businesses and rural 
communities. 
When a land management agency proposes new rules and regulations or amendments to current rules and 
regulations, there is a process of revisions, meetings, amendments, and coordination with many local, state, 
and federal entities. Affected entities need time to study and understand how the change will affect them. 
There are over twenty new and revised definitions. There needs to be additional time to evaluate how these 
new activities will affect me as a producer and my community. 
I urge you to withdraw this rule and engage with the local communities, producers and permittees who will be 
directly impacted by it. We, the farmers and ranchers, are original conservationists of these lands and I hope 
you will listen to our insights before crafting sweeping regulations that impact our public lands.
Sincerely,
Michele W McKissack
Luna County, New Mexico

I am an aquatic ecologist and Oak Ridge Institute of Science and Education (ORISE) fellow 

working at the US Environmental Protection Agency Region 4 office in Atlanta, GA and I oppose 

the proposed WOTUS rule. I believe that the proposed rule is not based on sound science and 

will not protect a large percentage of water resources that contribute to downstream physical, 

chemical, and biological health, especially in southwestern regions of the US. By limiting 

protections, this rule will make it impossible for the Clean Water Act to achieve its goals. 

The proposed departure from the 2015 definition of “Waters of the United States” (80 FR 37054) 

moves towards an interpretation in line with the Scalia opinion from the Rapanos v. United 

States (547 U.S. 715) 2006 case, which considers “Waters of the US” as “relatively permanent, 

standing or continuously flowing bodies of water . . .,” that are connected to traditional navigable 

waters, as well as wetlands with a “continuous surface connection . . .” to such water bodies. 

This definition would jeopardize protections of intermittent and ephemeral streams across the 

US, and thus I do not support the proposed rule. 

Ephemeral streams may comprise 96% of stream systems (Meyer et al. 2003), with the many 

of these streams located in the western US. Although these streams may not often appear as a 

traditional stream with surface water, they are critical to maintaining downstream water quality 

and human health. 

Extensive research in Arizona streams shows that even when there is no surface water present, 

there are active ecological processes occurring below the streambed surface (i.e., in what is 

known as the hyporheic zone). These processes affect the physical, chemical, and biological 

integrity of the groundwater below, as well as downstream surface waters in relatively 

permanent streams that are used for drinking water and recreation. For example, in Sycamore 

Creek, an intermittent stream with seasonal flow, the biological community is highly retentive of 

the nutrients nitrogen and phosphorus. This capacity to retain nutrients prevents excessive 

export of these nutrients to Verde and Salt Rivers, which combined supply up to one-half of 

municipal water to the greater Phoenix metropolitan area. Sycamore Creek continues to provide 

subsurface habitat for invertebrates even when surface water is not present. If activities such as 

land filling or pollutant discharge were to be permitted in these intermittent and ephemeral 

streams, they would inevitably have negative impacts on the quality of the water resources and 

food webs on which we all rely. 

The proposed rule indicates that only waters which are perennial or intermittent in a ‘typical 

year’ will be protected; however, the term ‘typical year’ is arbitrary, has no scientific basis, and 

will limit the number of important protected resources, making it impossible for the Clean Water

year’ ignores the incredible variability in seasonal rainfall and streamflow, especially in the

 
southwestern U.S. The term ‘typical year’ does not encompass the natural variability in flows 

and water presence that still have important impacts on downstream water quality and human

On 11 March 2024, NMFS published a proposed rule that would revise regulations 
governing the confidentiality of information submitted in compliance with Magnuson-Stevens 
Conservation and Management Act (MSA) regulations. The Marine Mammal Commission (the 
Commission), in consultation with its Committee of Scientific Advisors on Marine Mammals, has 
reviewed the proposed rule and offers comments and recommendations herein. 
The MSA specifies requirements for the confidentiality of fisheries information, including 
that collected by fisheries observers.1 NMFS may disclose confidential fisheries information if it is 
aggregated or summarized in a form that does not disclose the identity or business of the submitter. 
NMFS is proposing to implement new control procedures that would apply to the collection, 
maintenance, accessibility and release of confidential fisheries information. Among other changes, 
‘confidential information’, as defined in the proposed rule, would exclude information collected by 
fisheries observers that is related to interactions with species protected under the Marine Mammal 
Protection Act (MMPA). 
The Commission notes that an observer may collect information under the authority of both 
the MMPA and the MSA. Therefore, the Commission recommends that NMFS clarify in the final 
rule (1) the relationships between the two Acts, (2) the authorities governing deployment of 
observers and the collection of information under each statute, and (3) whether the confidentiality 
rules differ depending on the type of information and purpose for which they will be used. 
The information provided by observers regarding marine mammal interactions with fisheries 
is essential to understanding the factors contributing to those interactions and to mitigating marine 
mammal bycatch. Further, access to such information by Take Reduction Teams (TRTs) is essential 
if they are to fulfill their mandate under the MMPA to develop Take Reduction Plans that will 
reduce bycatch of marine mammals to acceptable levels. Because of these imperatives, and because 
the aggregation or summarization of marine mammal bycatch information can compromise its

I am writing in support of the proposed rule [DOD-2016-OS-0116-0001] regarding the establishment of requirements and benefits for the Transitional Compensation for Abused Dependents program. While the 2010 National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey found that there were no statistically significant differences between rates of domestic abuse in the military and civilian populations, the issue is substantial for both groups [1]. Additionally, military families face unique difficulties involving their dependence on the military for both work and private life, issues surrounding geographic relocation, as well as psychological impacts from combat exposure and PTSD [2]. All these elements make this program timely and necessary.

Formalizing the Transitional Compensation program would take an important role in destigmatizing victim-hood of affected spouses and dependent children and can provide the crucial resources necessary to create new personal avenues of recovery and stability. It will be of the upmost importance that the program be sufficiently advertised and easily accessible to ensure that there are few, if any, boundaries to application for benefits. Most victims of domestic abuse suffer in silence, a status that is only intensified by military service culture. I would also like to comment on the provision regarding medical and dental care to eligible dependents (as defined and limited under 10 U.S.C. 1077) to emphasize the importance of accessible psychological and mental healthcare access in addition to primary and physical care. Intimate partner violence and domestic abuse results in psychological trauma that is just as prevalent as the physical.

Dear Bureau of Land Management,

I am vehemently opposed to any future oil and gas development in the Western Arctic. Such development would be incompatible with meeting urgently needed commitments by your administration to address the climate crisis that it has promised the American people it would. To demonstrate climate leadership and meet our commitments, the nation needs to move rapidly away from burning fossil fuels. There is no room for expansion, particularly in the Arctic, where oil would not come to market for years. The huge infrastructure build-out required would lock us into reliance on fossil fuels, while bringing further stress to a region feeling climate effects even more acutely than lower latitudes. I urge the administration to take measures to bring its management of the Western Arctic in line with its commitment to address the climate crisis. 

The proposed regulations are a step in the right direction but do not go far enough to prevent future development. They offer important incremental protections for some areas of the Western Arctic’s most ecologically and culturally important areas, such as Teshekpuk Lake, an internationally vital wetland critical for birds from around the globe and for caribou herds that are integral to Alaska Native communities in the region. However, they do not do enough to address the most imminent threat to the region and the planet—the over two million acres of existing oil leases in the Western Arctic that this administration inherited. Development on these existing leases—like Willow—threatens the sensitive habitat of the Western Arctic and the nation’s ability to meet its climate goals. 

The current environmental analysis of the Western Arctic, written in the previous administration, fails to study the impact oil development in the region would have on the climate and the nation’s ability to rapidly reduce its reliance on fossil fuels to meet climate goals. We urge the administration to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the climate impacts of Western Arctic oil development, and to bring its management of the region in line with climate policy by expanding its proposed regulations to require limits on drilling on the millions of acres already leased to oil companies to protect the climate and the fragile resources of the region already under severe strain from climate change.

If it is decided that the ban is to be lifted on inflight phone calls - whether to allow such 
phone calls should be left to the discretion of the airlines, so long as adequate notice is provided 
to the consumer, because it provides airlines opportunity for a competitive advantage in the 
market and, furthermore, the consumer a choice in his/her transportation. While, the overall 
findings of the research provide that the ban on inflight phone calls should be upheld due to, 
among other things, the potential invasion of privacy, uncomfortable conditions it could impose, 
or the potential cost the consumer could incur, are all logical and valid points. I agree with the 
department that such hardships encountered without adequate notice are not outweighed by the 
benefits to the consumer. However, if adequate notice is provided to the consumer he/she could 
take necessary precautions to avoid such hardships. 
Allowing the airlines, the discretion to adopt an inflight phone-call policy so long as it 
provides adequate notice to the consumer allows the consumer, who is likely aware of the new 
policy due to the notice, to take appropriate steps to avoid any hardship caused by this new 
policy. This notice could simply be added to the page, that most airlines have when consumers 
purchase a ticket, that informs consumers on what they can and cannot bring aboard the aircraft, 
or, the notice could be a page that pops up alerting consumers to the new policy and requiring 
them to indicate that they have read the new policy before entering the actual airline’s website. 
Putting the notice in mandatory pages the consumer required to fill out or come across ensures 
that the diligent consumer has had the opportunity to read the new policy. Informing the 
consumer will allow him/her to decide whether to purchase a ticket from this airline, cause them 
to take precautions for the new policy, such as, getting earplugs, bringing headphones, charging 
up their cellphones to make phone calls etc. 
What the notice should include would depend on the policy the airline adopts. For 
example, an airline that allows phone calls for “emergencies only” should disclose this to the 
consumer because the consumer may purchase under the pretenses that casual inflight phone 
calls were permitted. Or, if phone calls are permitted only at certain times this should be 
disclosed to the consumer so one doesn’t purchase the ticket under the pretense they may make a 
call at any-time day or night. The notice should inform the consumer of the airline’s policy and 
the airline is in the best position to create and enforce its policies, thus, whether to allow inflight 
phone calls should be left to the discretion of the airline.

Comment 1: Prohibit Unauthorized Surveillance and Directed Energy Use by UAS
The FAA must explicitly prohibit the use of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) for unauthorized surveillance, directed energy emissions, and acoustic harassment in residential and public spaces. These activities pose serious risks to public health, civil liberties, and constitutional protections.
Recommendations:
- Require onboard logging of all sensor activations (infrared, RF, acoustic, electromagnetic) with audit access for FAA and independent oversight bodies.
- Mandate geofencing and strict altitude restrictions near residential areas, unless a documented and publicly disclosed public-safety exemption is granted.
- Coordinate with the FCC and EPA to establish enforceable exposure limits for RF, microwave, and infrasound emissions from UAS platforms.
- Prohibit the integration or use of directed energy, microwave, or acoustic disruption technologies in UAS platforms without explicit federal authorization and oversight.
These safeguards are essential to prevent abuse, protect public health, and uphold the constitutional rights of individuals and communities.

Comment 2: Enforce Transparency and Accountability in Government and Contractor Drone Operations
The FAA must require full transparency and accountability for all UAS operations conducted by government agencies and private contractors, particularly those involving surveillance, crowd monitoring, or electromagnetic technologies.
Recommendations:
- Require public disclosure of drone use policies, flight logs, and sensor payload configurations.
- Mandate reporting of all surveillance deployments, including purpose, duration, and geographic scope.
- Integrate Remote ID data with publicly accessible platforms to enable real-time awareness and community oversight.
- Coordinate with the FCC to detect and investigate unauthorized RF transmissions, jamming, or interference.
These measures are critical to ensure that drones are not used to suppress lawful expression, target vulnerable communities, or operate without public knowledge and consent.

Comment 3: Require Identification and Oversight of Military Drone Subcontractors
The FAA must require the identification and oversight of all military and defense subcontractors operating UAS platforms, particularly those capable of surveillance and electromagnetic or directed energy emissions.
Recommendations:
- Mandate full disclosure of subcontractor identities, including operators from companies such as MAG Aerospace and RPS Defense, when conducting UAS operations in domestic airspace.
- Require comprehensive background checks, training certifications, and operational logs for all subcontractor personnel involved in drone operations.
- Establish a federal oversight mechanism to monitor and audit subcontractor activities, especially when involving surveillance, RF emissions, or directed energy technologies.
- Prohibit the use of such technologies in domestic airspace without explicit legal authorization, public notice, and independent review.

Comments regarding: Medicare Program: Revisions to Payment Policies Under Physician Fee Schedule and Other Revisions to Part B for CY 2018; Medicare Shared Savings Program Requirements; and Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program
(34) ULTRASOUND OF EXTREMITY (CPT CODES 76881 AND 76882)
The current CY 2018 proposal reference above would decrease the technical component (TC) of 76881 by 91% and increase the TC of 76882 by approximately 500% WITHOUT an actual change in the definition of these codes. This change will lbe effected by moving the practice expense (PE) of the respective technical components from 76881 to 76882.
It is entirely unclear to us why the PE of each code should be different. Each code is performed in the same clinical settings and use the same technology and staff. Indeed, their PE should be exactly the same. The only differentiation between these codes is the time and skill involvement in performing each with 76881 requiring more time and skill than 76882. While the definition of 76881 is defined as a complete joint, in reality, multiple joints of the same limb are typically examined under this code.
This change would create a perverse situation in which a tissue focused and "limited" examination would be reimbursed at nearly 10 times the rate for a "complete" examination. For example, a targeted evaluation of the supraspinatus tendon would reimburse much higher, than a complete examination of all four rotator cuff tendons with dynamic imaging. This change, aside from being absurd, will not likely decrease overall Medicare expenditures on diagnostic limb ultrasound. With the time and skill restrictions on the higher reimbursing code now significantly relaxed (that is to say, with 76882 being more highly remunerated), potentially dozens of targeted examinations could occur in a single day by a single biller without concomitant increase in overhead or investment.
We feel it also may be pertinent for CMS to know, that none of the four members of the AMA RUC who signed off on their recommendation, actually bill for these codes which are being so dramatically altered. Hence making recommendations with no practical expertise or experience in the utilization of US. 
We ask that you strongly consider postponing this change until a more reasonable approach to cost containment may be proposed after collaboration with actual stakeholders such as rheumatologists who actually use US in clinical practice.
 
Sincerely,
 
 Gwenesta B. Melton,MD
VP, Association of Women in Rheumatology

I am a concerned citizen writing in opposition to USCIS' proposed rule that will raise the

The proposed increase would raise the naturalization application fee from $725 to 

$1,170, putting access to citizenship out of reach for a significant portion of individuals 

with lower-wage jobs. Similarly, the curtailing of fee waivers would almost certainly 

mean that significant numbers of people with limited means, including people with 

disabilities, those with larger families to support and others, would be unable to apply for 

citizenship. 

A 2018 Stanford research study on naturalization1 concluded that the current much lower 

application fee of $725 already has prevented a “considerable share” of low-income 

immigrants from applying for citizenship. It’s logical to assume that raising the fee so 

steeply and curtailing fee waivers will preclude citizenship for an even greater share of 

low-income people, as well as disproportionately impact non-white applicants, who make 

up a disproportionate share of the low-income population. This attempt to limit 

immigration to wealthier applicants is unfair and out of keeping with our long-held 

tradition of offering the American Dream to all.

associated with increased rates of naturalization. For example, studies have consistently 

shown that naturalization has a positive impact on wages,2 as well as on the economy as a

promotion of wild red wolf recovery in North Carolina, and to express our opposition to the U.S. 

Fish and Wildlife Service's (“FWS”) proposed changes to the Red Wolf Recovery Program

North Carolina project, despite decades of demonstrated success (Beeland 2013; Hinton et al. 

2013, Gese et al. 2015, Hinton et al. 2015, 2017a). Below, we provide the FWS with alternative 

actions that will enhance the North Carolina Nonessential Experimental Population’s (NC NEP) 

future. 

The FWS’s Draft Environmental Assessment for Proposed Replacement of the Regulations for 

the Nonessential Experimental Population of Red Wolves in Northeastern North Carolina (“Draft 

EA”) examines four alternative management actions, of which only one alternative (“Alternative 

2”) promotes wild red wolf recovery in North Carolina. In contrast, the implementation of the 

FWS preferred alternative (“Alternative 3”) would mark the end of federal efforts to recover red 

wolves in the wild in North Carolina. For these reasons and those described below, the 

undersigned write in support of the adoption of Alternative 2, with possible modification as 

indicated below, and in opposition to the adoption of Alternative 3. 

The FWS is legally responsible for preventing the decline of the only wild population of red 

wolves in the world. With perhaps fewer than 30 wild red wolves left, and only three known 

breeding pairs, the species could be soon extirpated from the wild unless the FWS pursues (at a 

minimum): 

1. Maintaining an area of sufficient size to allow concentration of resources for securing 

a viable wolf population against both human hostility and hybridization; 

2. Increasing the current wild population in North Carolina; 

3. Increasing the recovery area: Technically, FWS could increase the RWEPA while 

fencing a small area (i.e., Zone 1) to limit threats to several core packs; 

4. Re-implementing the Red Wolf Adaptive Management Plan (RWAMP) to curtail 

hybridization with coyotes; 

5. Improving law enforcement efforts to disincentivize the poaching of red wolves; 

6. Monitoring all “take” of red wolves; 

7. Improving outreach to residents in the recovery area; and 

8. Establishing additional reintroduction sites across the red wolf’s historic range.

We offer the following comments to further inform NHTSA’s deliberations. 

1. Denial of petition regarding a floor 

We remain disappointed that the petition to provide a floor was denied as this limits the ability 

of child restraint systems (CRS) to include a support leg in their design. While NHTSA did not 

rule out the use of a support leg, the need to have the CRS be certified without the support leg 

compromises and makes more complex their design. Given that the goal of FMVSS 213 is to 

“replicate the real world vehicle features” that “bear on a child restraint’s performance”, it 

seems appropriate that the regulation incorporate a floor as a vehicle floor is a real-world 

vehicle feature that can enhance the performance of CRS. Specifically, a floor and the use of a 

support leg for rear-facing CRS can enable accommodation of larger children rear-facing safely 

and more comfortably by ensuring robust load transfer and providing more space for leg room.

The proposed rule expands the criteria under which children are required to provide biometric and DNA samples for immigration and asylum proceedings. Currently, only children 14 and older were required to provide biometric data. The proposed rule would remove that age restriction, leading to the collection of sensitive data from much younger children who do not understand the implications and removing the protections provided by parental consent.The proposed rule also uses very vague language to explain how it will store biometric data and the instances in which it might share this biometric data with other government agencies. This raises many questions about data privacy and the ways that this data might be used against migrants. Please take into consideration this comment and the impact that the proposed rule would have on the right to privacy that should be extended to children.

Dear Administrator Verma: 

Iowa Legal Aid is a non-profit organization that provides free civil legal services to low-income 

and elderly Iowans. We serve eligible clients in all of Iowa’s 99 counties from our ten regional 

offices. Iowa Legal Aid helps the legal system to work for those who cannot afford an attorney, 

as do the roughly 1,600 volunteer attorneys signed up as participants in our Volunteer Lawyers 

Program. Typical cases we handle involve problems with access to basic necessities, 

fundamental rights, or safety. Our priorities include protecting victims of domestic violence, 

preventing illegal evictions and unsafe housing, securing income support such as SSI, Medicaid 

and disability benefits, and preventing consumer fraud and abusive debt collection practices. In 

2018, we closed approximately 15,072 cases in which legal assistance was provided to low-

income and older Iowans. 

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the federal nursing 

facility regulations. Our interest in this matter stems from the frequent requests we receive from 

long-term care facility residents for help with the appeal of involuntary discharges from nursing 

facilities. While all of our clients come from marginalized and vulnerable groups, in our 

experience those clients residing in long-term care facilities are among the most vulnerable and 

least able to advocate for themselves. Often, these residents are only connected to our services 

through the long-term care ombudsman’s office. The proposal to alter the notification 

requirements to the long-term care ombudsman’s office on the transfer or discharge of residents 

will have the greatest impact on the most vulnerable population of an already vulnerable group. 

Those residents with no family, no friends, no one to advocate on their behalf rely solely on the 

long-term care ombudsman’s office for advocacy.

 
Page 2 

Iowa Legal Aid’s experience in representing residents of long-term care facilities has shown that 

residents need the protections in the current regulations more than ever before. Over the years, 

residents have become frailer and more dependent. Increased physical and cognitive impairments 

mean residents need more care and are more vulnerable to abuse and neglect. In the last few 

years, Iowa Legal Aid has seen an increase in referrals for residents who were brought to a 

hospital by their long-term care facility, who then refused to allow their return. Any revisions to 

the regulations should only be made if they improve resident protections, not reduce them. 

ADMISSION, TRANSFER, AND DISCHARGE RIGHTS (Section 483.15) 

Iowa Legal Aid supports continued notification to Ombudsman programs in situations 

where a resident is not being allowed to return from a hospitalization and objects to any 

inclusion of the terms “involuntary” or “facility-initiated” in the regulations. 

We agree with CMS that notice to Ombudsman programs of transfer or discharge related to 

hospitalization (or other temporary absence) should be focused on situations where the facility is 

not allowing a resident to return, rather than on all instances when a resident is hospitalized. The 

scenario where a resident is sent to the hospital, treated, and then not permitted to return to their 

nursing facility continues to be a widespread problem and deserving of as many protections as 

we can provide.

I strongly oppose EPA's effort to exempt concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) from the reporting requirements under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act (EPCRA). This exemption only serves to benefit CAFOs at the expense of the general public and will prevent local communities from accessing information that is critical to protecting public health.

Contrary to industry claims, air emissions from concentrated farming operations are not "normal" farm odors. It is irresponsible for the EPA to exempt those responsible for such emissions from reporting them to state and local emergency responders.

I urge the EPA to withdraw its proposed rule that would exempt CAFOs from EPCRA's reporting requirements. 

Regards, 
Nathan Kropp

National forests have been important to me since I first stepped foot in one. Their beauty and what they offer to humanity is untouched. Please do not destroy our planet even more. She does not need us, we need her.

I am commenting to oppose the new proposed Title IX rules because the new rules would make it harder to sexual assault 
survivors and victims of sexual harassment from coming forward. As a result, it would exacerbate the problem of underreporting
further. In addition, the new rules will not give due process because they further stack the system against survivors. I am
concerned because as a queer disabled women of color in my first year of college, the new rules would ensure that students 
like me won't get a fair hearing if the rules get put in place.

The new rules would discourage students from reporting sexual assault and sexual harassment by allowing schools to not 
investigate reports of sexual assault that occur off-campus, letting them raise the standard of proof from preponderance of the
evidence to clear and convincing standard, and allow an accused student's representative to grill sexual assault survivors and
victim blame them. 

These new rules are problematic because they would further discourage students from coming forward about sexual assault 
and sexual harassment since they know that nothing will be done to give them justice. There is already much underreporting 
of incidents of sexual harassment and assault in college. In fact, currently, 88% of women don't report sexual assault and 
because of underreporting, 45% of schools report zero sexual assaults. There can't possibly by zero sexual assaults in 45% 
of schools because while an average of 1 in 4 women are raped on campus, the rate of assault is higher for women of color,
the LGBTQIA+ community, and the disabled. Allowing the accused student's representative to directly question survivors is
also troubling because of would further traumatize survivors when they are already distressed from their rape.

The new rules will not give due process because the system is already stacked against sexual assault survivors and victims of
sexual harassment. In fall 2018, Ms. Magazine reported the case of Amelia W. She was raped and even though a school
investigation determined that her rapist was guilty, nothing was done because the Title IX laws were too weak. Indeed, she
was the one who had her freedom restricted through a no-contact order rather than her rapist. In addition, the documentary 
"The Hunting Ground" reported that at worst, rapists are suspended, have to pay a small fine, are given a warning, have to write
a poster on how to approach a woman they like, or volunteer for 50 hours at a rape crisis center.

The new rules clearly will not give due process to all parties and will just further stack the system against students who 
experienced sexual assault and sexual harassment. To truly give due process to all parties, please restore the original "Dear 
Colleague" letter and the Obama-administration guidelines on Title IX.

To Whom it May Concern,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Sex in Education Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance. I am a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner, with experience in caring for university students who have been sexually assaulted. 

In particular I am concerned about the purpose of this rule change. It appears to allow universities/colleges to subjectively and inappropriately handle allegations of sexual assault on or off campus. It is not intended to improve the academic experience for students, but to reduce the liability of said schools. It looks like the government is, again, placing dollar values over people. And it looks like another form of violence against women. 

The related research and data summarized below show that the regulation will harm students and student survivors. 34.1% of students who have experienced sexual assault dropout of college , higher than theoverall dropout rate for college students (Mengo & Black, 2015). An estimated 40% of rape victims suffer from severe emotional distress (requiring mental health treatment) ( Miller, Cohen, & Rossman, 1993 ). More than 40% of college students who were sexually victimized also reported experiences of institutional betrayal ( Freyd, 2018 )). Survivors rarely report cases of sexual violence to their schools largely because they dont know how to report or who to report to on their campus. Survivors often dont report their sexual assaults because of fear of being disbelieved or their assault not taken seriously (Holland & Cortina, 2017). Only 2%-10% of reported cases of sexual assault are false (Lisak et al., 2010); the proposed rule changes demonstrate a lack of evidence-based decision making on the part of the Department of Education. 

For the foregoing reasons, these sections of the rule should be struck.

Sincerely,
Andrew J Mahoney RN SANE
New Orleans Family Justice Center

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

Threatened and endangered species must continue to be treated the same. "Threatened" means on the way to "endangered". It means serious population problems which should not be allowed to worsen with relaxed regulations.
The changes on "takings" would make threatened species situations worse.

The "habitat as a whole" concept allow nibbling away at species habitats slowly over time, which in effect is taking them away and further threatening the animals.

How can one put a price on a bald eagle population or even one bald eagle? These are not mere aesthetic considerations. Animals play a role in maintaining overall environmental stability necessary for human life. How do you measure that in monetary terms? It cannot be done.

As a consumer, I want truthful package labels. "Humanely raised" labels should mean exactly that! No room for deception with food labels. Achieving a higher price for inferior quality is deception and should be punished by fines and imprisonment if necessary.

Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare.

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers.

FSIS owes it to the American public to set a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," take steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensure that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

I believe the Black Warrior Waterdog (Necturus alabamensis) meets several criteria for meeting the need fro listing the species as endangered, including: the present or threatened destruction, modification, or curtailment of its habitat or range; potential for

We would like to thank the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) for their efforts to recognize 

the impact that Health-Related Social Needs (HRSNs) have on health outcomes, quality of care, and cost of 

care. Incorporating new payment codes for conducting assessments to identify HRSNs and for providing 

services to aptly integrate coordination of community services into the delivery of care are critical to 

advancing health equity and breaking down barriers to care faced by many vulnerable populations. 

These HCPCS codes for community health integration (CHI), social determinants of health (SDOH) risk 

assessment, and principal illness navigation (PIN) services are the most progressive approach, proposed by 

CMS to date, for creating a pathway for providers to sustain the essential contribution that community health 

workers (CHWs) can play in addressing HRSNs and supporting a whole person model of care. 

While we recognize the establishment of these codes is a critical advancement, the Collaborative expects 

challenges in implementation including encouraging clinical providers to adjust workflows to adopt and 

integrate CHI into their practices. We encourage CMS to develop technical assistance opportunities to 

encourage providers to integrate SDOH screenings and CHI services into their workflows. 

Furthermore, community-based organizations (CBOs) are unlikely to broadly benefit from CHI as a sustainable 

revenue stream. CBOs are a critical employer of CHWs. When CHWs work in the communities they serve, they 

have the greatest impact on addressing HRSNs including connecting individuals with primary care. CBOs in our 

region face challenges encouraging clinical providers to partner and contract with them to conduct HRSN

 
screenings and to develop and implement plans to address identified HRSNs. Often, agreements between 

CBOs and clinical providers for CHI-type services do not include payment to the CBOs. Requiring 

documentation in the electronic medical record (EMR) is an additional barrier for clinical providers to

As a mother of two young children and as a lawyer who believes in justice and the rule of law, I am compelled to write. I would like to respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. What is going on is an embarrassment as far as how the rest of the world views the United States, and it is just plain wrong.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

PDF p. 330 of the Draft Technical Support Document states "DOT’s guidance assigns a lower hourly valuation to personal travel time than to business travel time and specifies separate distributions between personal and business travel in urban and rural areas". The statement about different values of time in urban and rural areas is not correct. Trips are differentiated based on whether they are trips over 50 miles (see the cited value of time guidance at https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/docs/2016%20Revised%20Value%20of%20Travel%20Time%20Guidance.pdf). Thus, while a personal trip through a rural area between cities that are 100 miles apart would qualify as long-distance personal travel, a personal trip through a rural area to reach a town 4 miles away, then return home would not qualify as long-distance personal travel. NHTS data indicates that 31.6% of personal light-duty vehicle travel is long-distance trips.

Methodology for estimating long-distance personal travel share:
1. Download NHTS data from https://nhts.ornl.gov/media/2022/download/csv.zip
2. Download the NHTS codebook from https://nhts.ornl.gov/media/2022/doc/codebook.pdf
3. Open the tripv2pub.csv file from the downloaded NHTS data
4. Remove on-the-clock travel from the data set: According to the documentation, WHYTO = 4 or 5 corresponds to on-the-clock travel. Delete all rows with WHYTO = 4 or 5
5. Reduce the dataset to light-duty vehicle travel: According to the documentation, TRPTRANS contains the trip mode. I include TRPTRANS = 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6. I include vans (TRIPTRANS = 2) since the VEHTYPE documentation in the NHTS indicates that minivans are considered a type of van (the appropriateness of this inclusion is less certain given that the van category includes full-sized passenger and cargo vans, which might not be light-duty vehicles). Eliminate all rows except those with TRPTRANS = 1, 2, 3, 4, or 6.
6. Remove trips of unknown length: According to the documentation, TRPMILES is the trip length in miles is known and trips of unknown length have TRPMILES = -9. Remove all trips with unknown length by deleting each trip with TRPMILES = -9.
Use weights to calculate the number of miles represented by each trip: The documentation states WTPERFIN is the 7 day National person weight. After these steps, TRPMILES represents the trip length in miles. Create a column called "Weighted miles". Fill this column with the product of TRPMILES and WTPERFIN. 
7. Use weights to calculate the number of long-distance trip miles represented by each trip. Create a column named "Weighted long-distance trip miles". Set it equal to "Weighted miles" if TRPMILES > 50 and equal to 0 otherwise. 
8. Divide the sum of the entries in "Weighted long-distance trip miles" by the sum of the entries in "Weighted miles".

Dear Dr. Howard, 

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on the 2020 NIOSH List of Hazardous Drugs 

in Healthcare Settings and the related documents. The Oncology Nursing Society (ONS) is a 

professional association of over 37,000 oncology nurses and their colleagues, dedicated to 

improving the safety of the delivery of cancer treatment for nurses and other healthcare 

providers, patients, and families across the healthcare spectrum. In addition to the content in this 

letter, we have encouraged our members to provide individual feedback on the proposed 

documents relevant to their practice settings. 

ONS is opposed to a change in the definition of hazardous drugs at this time. The definition 

in the 2020 draft document is a change from the definition in the 2004 through 2016 NIOSH 

Lists. The current definition is accepted globally by more than 50 agencies. The proposed 

changes in the 2020 draft document have been made in isolation, without consensus of all 

stakeholders that may be impacted by the change. 

In the 2020 draft document, it is proposed that a hazardous drug is one “Approved for use in 

humans by the FDA-CDER [Center for Drug Evaluation and Research].” This is a change from 

the previous definition. It would be helpful to understand the rationale for this decision, and the 

detail future impact of this change. 

The second, and more concerning change in the definition is the statement, “unless the drug also 

exhibits a molecular property that may limit the potential for adverse health effects in healthcare 

workers from exposure to the drug.” With this change to the definition, agents that have 

hazardous drug characteristics may be automatically eliminated from the evaluation process due 

to physical properties, such as molecular weight, which result in decreased biologic uptake. The 

“Procedures” document provides an example of a drug, “potentially toxic when injected, being

Given the crowding on airplanes, I think letting people use mobile wireless devices for voice calls would be a very bad idea. There would likely be isolated incidents of Air Rage, and certainly many passengers would have their travel experience degraded.

And since it is already possible on many airliners to exchange text or email messages from airliners using inflight WiFi, I believe those who actually need to communicate with others from onboard airliners already have the means of doing so.

That this new grant cycle does not allow for the continuation of the Deaf Self-Advocacy Training (DSAT) nor the training for Deaf interpreters (DIs) seems to be in contradiction to the goals of the new priorities. 

The DSAT directly impacts consumers, and those who have gone through the training have the ability to advocate not only for themselves but for other Deaf consumers including those who have dysfluent language. Consequently, they can do so from a more informed viewpoint as they have the lived experience to accompany their academic knowledge. Likewise, training interpreters to work with Deaf individuals with dysfluent language will require collaboration with highly trained Deaf interpreters. For both of these reasons, the DSAT and DI training should remain a priority and this new grant cycle should take advantage of expanding upon the initiatives from the previous grant cycle.

DSAT prepares Deaf individuals to take jobs as trainers and educators. Again, this means that the individuals most qualified to work with Deaf individuals with dysfluent language are being given the tools to take on positions where they may have a significant impact. When hearing professionals or interpreters work in these settings, best practice would be to do so with DIs. This is another reason why the DSAT and DI training should remain another priority. DSAT should be recognized as a specialization that enables interpreters (Deaf and hearing) to work in more collaborative ways towards communication equity.

I strongly support the DoDs proposal to add licensed or certified physical therapist assistants (PTAs) and certified occupational therapist assistants (COTAs) as TRICARE-authorized providers, operating under the same qualifications established by Medicare (42 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 484.4). 

I support DoDs proposal to tie the qualifications of PTAs and COTAs under the TRICARE program to Medicares requirements as codified at 42 CFR 484.4. 

I disagree with DoDs proposal to require direct supervision of PTAs and COTAs. Direct supervision requires a supervising PT/OT to be in the room when the PTA/COTA is treating. DoD is proposing to require direct supervision in the private practice setting but will allow general supervision in every other setting. General supervision does not require the therapist to be present when the PTA/COTA is treating but does require the therapist to be available and responsible for the course of treatment. 

The vast majority of payers only require general supervision of PTAs and COTAs. Likewise, most state laws only require general supervision of PTAs and COTAs in the private practice setting and every other setting. In addition, the DoD is proposing to allow general supervision in all setting other than in private practice. 

The DoD proposal to require direct supervision in the private practice setting will make it more difficult to provide physical and occupational therapy to veterans and other Tricare beneficiaries who live in rural areas because a physical therapist will need to be physically present whenever a PTA/COTA is treating a Tricare patient. In many of these rural communities, PTs and OTs are not readily available to be onsite whenever a PTA/COTA is treating. DoDs direct supervision requirement will undoubtedly limit access of veterans to much needed physical and occupational therapy. I therefore recommend that the final regulations allow for general supervision of PTAs/COTAs in all settings.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Addition of Physical Therapy Assistants and Occupational Therapy Assistants as TRICARE-Authorized Providers proposed rule.

Shark fishing is incredibly inhumane. The practice has been extensively carried out for too long, as the small enjoyment that comes to one from eating a bowl of soup can never compare to the death and suffering of millions of sharks every year. These are highly intelligent creatures who feel feelings like us, think thoughts like us, and enjoy life like us. In fact, the only difference we maintain between them is our capability to sleep at night knowing all the mass murders we commit to sharks and other animals every day. Limitations must be set, if not to ban the practice at all. Not only is this morally absolutely awful, but sharks are one of the most important creatures in their ecosystems, and destroying them only furthermore destroys the oceans. A bowl of soup and a couple of bucks are not worth it.

Sharks of all kinds are vital to the health of oceans. Shark populations have been so drastically depleted by over fishing and finning that alarming numbers of species are endangered and closing in on ultimate extinction. 

Sharks do not even begin to bear young until they are 10 years old. It is critical that their populations are not only healthy and vibrant, but mature and productive if they are to recover, globally, from the toll taken on their numbers when, world wide, between 17 to 200 million (depending on who you talk to) individual sharks are killed every year. 

Please take this small step to protect these impressive, ancient, beautiful animals and by extension, the health and longevity of our Oceans and Planet. Thank You.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Open Textbook Pilot program. My comments represent my own personal views, not those of my employer or any other organization, and they are informed by my experience as a librarian who has been supporting faculty in adopting and creating open educational resources for several years, including involvement with both institutional and state-level grant programs. From this experience, I understand the difficulty of balancing the desire to fund multiple projects and the need to fund projects at a high enough level to ensure their success and impact. The Open Textbook Pilot program has already provided and is positioned to further provide some of the highest-level funding available for open textbook projects (at the multi-million dollar level). However, any steps taken to increase the total number of funded grants and to fund a broader range of award amounts would be very welcome. 

Award Size: I recommend an award range of $100,000 to $1.5 million. The maximum award size would ensure that at least four projects can be funded. The minimum award size would open this program to much greater diversity of projects that would spread the programs impact across more disciplines and institution types. This range would provide funding for a wide array of projects whose budgets are beyond what an institutional or state-level program can typically fund but whose size and scope are appropriate for funding across a wider spectrum. Given that a large number of institutions and states do not currently offer funding for open textbook projects, this range would also encourage funding and more immediate impact across the nation.

Matching Requirement: Again because of the number of institutions and states that do not currently offer funding for open textbook projects, I recommend not including a matching contribution requirement as this would further disadvantage otherwise highly qualified projects that do not have institutional or state funding available.

Eligible Applicants: More flexibility around the 3-institution requirement for eligibility would also increase the diversity of projects funded through this program. Examples could include large-scale single institution projects to create a degree program that uses only open educational resources, or a partnership between 4-year and 2-year institutions to co-develop open educational resources that will improve transfer pathways.

Proposed Priority 4: The requirement for projects to incorporate the principles of universal design is a good step to increase accessibility. However, I have concerns about other aspects of this priority. While the creation of open source technologies that support student learning and affordability is a worthwhile endeavor, Proposed Priority 4 should be considered as an Invitational Priority. Any technologies or technology-based strategies proposed as part of a project should be chosen for the specific context of that project. However, this requirement prioritizes adaptive learning technology and personalized learning strategies, which will not be the most appropriate choices for projects where other options better meets the goals of improving student learning and increasing affordability. Additionally, development of new technology tools requires considerable expense and expertise. Therefore it is both reasonable and strategic for some project proposals to exclude use or development of these tools when they will not produce the greatest benefit to students or when their development would not yield a strong return on investment. This priority, if it remains as a Competitive Preference Priority, would present a disadvantage to these projects.

As a trailblazing biotechnology firm based in San Diego, California, Avidity Biosciences is 
committed to developing oligonucleotide-based (RNA) therapeutics for people living with rare 
diseases including Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 (DM1), Facioscapulohumeral Muscular 
Dystrophy (FSHD), and Exon 44 Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD44). Avidity's three 
neuromuscular programs are in clinical development at the Food and Drug Administration’s 
Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER). All three programs target the underlying 
genetic drivers of disease, and Avidity is the first company to deliver RNA therapies outside the 
liver. 
As the effects and understanding of prescription drug promotion evolve, so does the biological 
understanding of rare diseases and the innovative biotechnology treating those conditions. 
Changes to promotional guidance from the FDA’s Office of Prescription Drug Promotion (OPDP) 
will influence all players equally, including the rare disease industry, as more groundbreaking 
products come to market. The insights from the current market research study will not fully 
capture the perspectives of rare disease patients or physician specialties, many of whom deeply 
understand the disease states and treatment options available. 
Rare disease communities are often small and geographically dispersed, leaving many patients 
without the opportunity to meet others who share their condition. Understanding patient 
preferences becomes essential in providing meaningful support, as this insight can empower 
patients with shared decision-making frameworks, helping them navigate treatment choices 
that align with their unique needs and values. It is important to ensure the research outcomes 
represent not only consumers (as described in the research plan) but specifically, patients with 
rare and often serious or life-threatening conditions (or their care partners or advocates) to 
inform a broadly applicable policy. 
Given the intricacies of rare disease communities, we recommend broadening the research 
scope to include rare disease patient populations, their caregivers, and their physicians, 
accounting for the fact that many conditions have no treatments or only one treatment 
available.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Rehabilitation Short-Term Training: Client Assistance Program (CAP) Proposed Priority from the U.S. Department of Education. Disability Rights Michigan (DRM) writes in support of some provisions and in opposition to other provisions of the proposed priority.

DRM is a private, nonprofit, nonpartisan organization mandated to advocate for people with disabilities in Michigan. DRM is the designated protection and advocacy (P&A) agency for Michigan and houses the state’s Client Assistance Program (CAP).
 
P&A agencies and CAPs are authorized under various federal statutes to provide legal representation and related advocacy services, and to investigate abuse and neglect of individuals with disabilities in a variety of settings. The P&A and CAP Network comprises the nation’s largest provider of legally-based advocacy services for persons with disabilities including advocacy on employment to ensure people with disabilities who want to become employed can do so.
DRM’s work includes advocacy to secure competitive integrated employment rights and supports for people with disabilities. As part of this work, it is essential to have effective CAP programs in order to ensure that Vocational Rehabilitation (VR) clients receive the services they need and deserve.

DRM supports the focus on Rehabilitation Act knowledge and discrete skills in support of individual and systems advocacy. Comment:
I am a retired U.S.F.S employee. I was a timber cruiser/timber marker for 25+ years. I do believe in timber production. Done correctly & considering all aspects of proper forest management. Conservation, recreation and wildlife are as important as logging & fuels. 
My friend wrote this below. She is much better with words than myself. 

 I agree with her. We, the public, own National Forests, National Parks, National Monuments etc.

The mission statement of the US Forest Service is "Caring for the Land, and Serving the People". As a thirty year career employee of this agency, I and my colleagues worked with passion and dedication to support this mission. I learned, on a daily basis, how deeply Americans care about their National Forests. 

National Forests, like National Parks and Monuments, are the crown jewels of our nation. All of these are public lands, owned and managed for the benefit of ALL CITIZENS OF THE UNITED STATES, not a handful of extractive industries driven by corporate profits. The mandate of National Forests is to manage for multiple uses such as camping, hiking, birdwatching, fishing, boating, picnicking, snowplay, driving for pleasure, hunting and fuelwood gathering, as well as logging, grazing and mining, as well as the preservation of species' diversity and forest ecological health, as well as clean air and water, in a way that none precludes the others. 

That is why the NEPA process, including the weight of public comment, was developed. It has functioned for nearly fifty years to balance these diverse needs, and so that the public has a say in the outcome of the lands that are our legacy.

To exempt areas of 42,000 acres (over 6.5 square miles) from public scrutiny and buy-in is a flagrant violation of the law. The extent of irreversible environmental destruction that can occur on this scale has the potential to turn our forests into corporate tree farms and fossil fuel tracts, drastically affecting the sustainability of all resources and public opportunities. Natural ecosystems are interdependent, and once vast areas of forest are significantly altered, the plant and animal life dependent on these habitats cannot survive. 

I am now retired, and already looking hard to find areas that were unspoiled in the early 1970's, where I used to recreate. Yes, there are still wilderness areas, but many of these have become overused, and some of us are no longer able to backpack 20 or 30 miles to get to our special place. 

From my perspective, neutering the NEPA process through the inappropriate application of Categorical Exclusions, and eliminating the public voice from the process, should be regarded as a crime against nature and humanity. "Caring for the Land and Serving the People" is not "Carving up the Land and Screwing the People", although that does appear to be the vision of current management. 

I only learned about this proposed action and the imminent close of public comment today. How many others who truly care will be denied the opportunity to comment on management of the lands they own? I ask you to publicize this action and extend the public comment period. Then, to listen to the citizens who own and treasure their National Forests, one of the last few options for low cost, inclusive experiences. The proposal steals not only from them, but generations far into the future who may never experience the natural world as God made it

Organizations such as ours with a central, corporate HR function but multiple work locations spread across the U.S. are significantly challenged to inspect documents for each new hire within the required time frame. This requires us to rely on others who are on site at these locations who are so unfamiliar with how to complete the form (even with training), more often than not completing them incorrectly. Additionally, confidential employee data (PII) is exposed to employees outside of HR who should really not have access to it. In the case of fully remote workers and having to rely on an “authorized agent,” security of employee confidential information becomes an even greater concern. Continuing the remote confirmation of documents process permitted during the COVID-19 pandemic will help insure the documentation is completed both correctly and timely by well-trained HR individuals with significant knowledge of required documents. The remote document review process implemented during the pandemic was successful and gave many companies such as ours the ability to support our businesses/customers while maintaining the very important goal of employing only those authorized to work in the US.

The added protections provided by participation in E-Verify coupled with advances in technology, remote verification poses a lower risk than in the past. Given that E-Verify is the “gold standard” for U.S. work authorization, for companies participating in E-Verify, there should be less concern about the physical review I-9 documents. I would take this a step further and perhaps define a different standard for companies enrolled in and using E-Verify; perhaps only companies using E-Verify should have this remote review flexibility. This could encourage more employers to participate in E-Verify.

The new proposed rule by DHS will impose severe infringement on personal privacies for people living in the US including US citizens while doing little to better "verify the identity of an individual" than the existing regulation. The new rule will also significantly slow down or even shutting down the immigration system due to the lack of proper assessment for implementing the new biometric collection.

 1. DHS does not specifically prove the existing biometric definition and its collection method failed to identify a person. Fingerprints, facial images and signatures have been used for years and there is no report that a person can fake them to obtain immigration benefits. These existing modalities are very difficult, if not impossible, to fake and when they are, the proposed new modalities cannot prevent this possibility either. By requesting additional modalities, such as palm print, voice print and iris image, DHS has imposed unreasonable burdens to immigrants while doing little help identifying a person.

 2. DHS is asking for very broad authorities to collect personal information about immigrants and US citizens, which is far beyond the original scope set by INA. INA only authorizes DHS to collect necessary information from immigration applicants for the purpose of processing their applications, in which the existing biometrics can already fulfill the requirements. The new rule greatly expands the information collected by DHS and is not envisioned or authorized by INA or other laws in any specific ways. It tried to request biometric information from all "applicant, petitioner, sponsor, beneficiary, or individual filing or associated with an immigration benefit or request, including United States citizens" which is not only unreasonable but dangerous. With this broad authority but no check on its power, DHS are threatening not only the privacy rights of immigrants but also US citizens, potentially violating the 4th Amendment. Due to the lack of corresponding statutes concerning handling and storing the personal information collected by DHS, the more it is asking for the more likely the information will be misused and causing irreparable harms to immigrants and US citizens. When such broad collection of personal information is requested, new laws must be discussed and passed with proper restrictions and limitations instead of in the form of a regulation, which offers no protection to any party involved.

 3. The new proposed rule can significantly delay the processing of immigration petitions. DHS has not established a way to collect the information without greatly delaying the processing time. Currently the whole immigration system is already running slow with backlogs lasts for years. Together with the covid-19 situation, the processing time for a typical i-539 form can be more than 19 months which can exceeds the extension period requested by the form itself. Adding more biometric information collection will simply further delay the whole system, making it virtually stop functioning. Moreover, not only does DHS not know the new rule's impact on the processing time, it does not have a plan to do so either, which makes it more worrying since it seems DHS are intentionally jamming the immigration system and abolishing its key functionality on enforcing immigration laws.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

All animals should receive proper care. And consumers should be able to rely on labeling yo be factual.

Thank you for considering my request.

As a frequent air traveler, I am opposed to allowing voice calls in flight.

Airplanes provide significantly less space than other forms of mass transportation, while simultaneously entailing significantly longer trips. There's a world of difference between being stuck on the subway for an hour, vs stuck in a plane for a 6 hour flight across the country.

Further, many air travelers already show a complete disregard for common rules of courtesy in the air-- arguing with attendants about bags being on their laps during takeoff, removing their shoes and placing their feet on the back of their seat, or trying to carry on a bag that the baggage handlers would be challenged to load into the plane.

It is these travelers that will ruin it for the rest of us.

If you get stuck on a train or a bus next to someone who insists on talking on their phone the whole time, you have the option of moving, and in the worst case, you're only stuck there for an hour.

In a plane, you don't have that recourse.

Every individual within 10 feet of the rude talker will have to listen to their conversation until they hang up. And heaven help those who are seated right next to them.

And I fully expect that the majority of these calls will not be urgent, or even business-related- they will be someone killing time, ignorant or indifferent to how they are inconveniencing those around them. 

With the majority of airlines providing in-flight Internet, it is simply not necessary to allow voice calling-- if you really do have an urgent need to communicate with someone while in flight, you have the option of getting online and sending an email or instant message. It would only be the rarest of situations where a live conversation was required.

With over 100,000 flights a day, we're looking at a handful of people for whom this would be a benefit, while millions of others would suffer a gross inconvenience.

I also don't see airlines offering "quiet flights" or similar services-- if for no other reason, once people get used to using their phone in flight, they will assume it's always available. Airlines will ditch quiet flights simply so the flight attendants don't have to argue with the passenger about how they bought the wrong ticket. 

Remember, if these people were considerate in the first place, this wouldn't be an issue-- the person who is going to fight on speaker phone with their significant other from LAX to EWR is the one most likely to fight with the flight attendant when they're told they can't.

Air travel continues to get worse and worse as airlines move to maximize profits. But you have the opportunity here to at least partly hold the line-- maintain the ban on voice calls during flight. Allow us to hold onto one small shred of sanity amidst the chaos of air travel.
