For background that may lend weight to the rest of this letter, Summit Helicopters, Inc. is one of the most experienced operators and maintainers of Hiller UH-12E helicopters in the United States still active today. Since 1982, we have accumulated an estimated 80,000 flight hours on our Hillers. In the last ten years our Hiller fleet, currently down to five aircraft, has averaged over 1300 hours per year. We regularly perform 1200-hour transmission overhauls, which include a magnetic particle inspection of the rotor drive shaft. While we have scrapped masts for wear or corrosion, we have never had one with a crack.

To make our situation clear, all of our M/R drive shafts are more than four years old and they all have more than 1200 hours since new. As the AD is currently written, this means our fleet would be grounded as soon as this AD is issued. Our Hiller fleet operates between 100 to 900 miles away from our maintenance facility between the months of March till October. Bringing the aircraft back to our maintenance facility may harm our ability to perform time sensitive operations so most maintenance needs are addressed by sending our mechanics to the aircraft rather than the other way round.

These Hillers continue to provide our company with a substantial percentage of our income. Grounding this fleet at the beginning or during the season would disrupt our operations and have a severe economic impact on our company that goes beyond the cost of the inspection itself.

Considering our substantial experience maintaining these aircraft and the impact of immediate compliance, we request that an additional time margin be added to the Required Action. We need to be able to delay this inspection until November of 2025.

We have a question regarding paragraph (g)(1). Paint stripper specifications TT-R-248B and TT-R-2918A have been difficult to find during an initial search. We ask that the FAA provide additional specifications that meet the need for non-embrittling paint stripper. For example, would Boeing DPM-5549-1 be acceptable as well?

We have two comments regarding the Cost of Compliance in the prelude. First, the cost of baking is not accounted for. The Hiller M/R drive shaft is 46 ½ inches long by 4 inches in diameter. We do not have an oven capable of baking a shaft this length and I’m sure neither does any other average repair station. We were able to locate a nearby metal treatment facility that quoted us to bake up to four shafts at a time for $1850. That cost does not go down if we only had one shaft. We will need more than four done so we are looking at $3700 in baking costs alone. We have been able to find a facility close enough to hand deliver our parts to them. Other Hiller owners may not be so lucky and incur shipping and handling costs.

Second, we believe the labor to inspect the mast is too low. Our rotor drive shafts are not sitting in stock, they are installed in aircraft ready to begin a new season of operations. A complete view of the situation should include time to remove the main rotor blades, collective ballast assembly, main rotor hub assembly, wobble plate assembly, and transmission. The drive shaft would then need to be removed from the transmission. We estimate this removal and reinstallation process would take at least an additional 11.5 hours. We also believe the strip, bake, inspect, prime, & paint process will take 6 ½ hours instead of five based on our experience.

Thank you for taking the time to consider our comments and questions.

The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) is seeking information and data on 

engineering controls that could reduce the risk of accidents and improve miner safety. MSHA is 

also seeking suggestions from stakeholders on: Best practices, training materials, policies and 

procedures, innovative technologies, and any other information they may have to improve safety 

in and around mobile equipment, and working near and around belt conveyors. 

Mining safety could be substantially improved by preventing accidents that involve 

mobile equipment at surface coal mines and metal and nonmetal mines and belt conveyors at 

surface and underground mines. The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) is taking a 

number of actions related to mobile equipment and belt conveyors to improve miners' safety, 

including providing technical assistance, conducting awareness campaigns, and developing best 

practices and training materials. MSHA is also considering the role of engineering controls that 

would increase the use of seatbelts, enhance equipment operators' ability to see all areas near the 

machine, warn equipment operators of potential collision hazards, prevent equipment operators 

from driving over a highwall or dump point, and help prevent entanglement hazards related to 

working near moving or re-energized belt conveyors. 

Mobile equipment used at surface coal mines, surface metal and nonmetal mines, and the 

surface areas of underground mines is a broad category that includes bulldozers, front end 

loaders, service trucks, skid steers, haul trucks, and many other types of vehicles and equipment. 

Accidents involving mobile equipment have historically accounted for a large number of the 

fatalities in mining, especially in metal and nonmetal mines. In 2017, for example, nearly 40 

percent of the 28 mining fatalities and more than 30 percent of injuries involved mobile 

equipment. 

Since 2007, 61 miners have been killed in accidents involving mobile equipment. MSHA 

conducted an investigation of all of these accidents. MSHA determined that contributing factors 

in many of these accidents included: (1) No seatbelt, seatbelt not used, or inadequate seatbelts; 

(2) larger vehicles striking smaller vehicles; and (3) equipment operators' difficulty in detecting 

the edges of highwalls or dump points, causing equipment to fall from substantial heights.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

I'd like to hear terms like: These animals were fed an organic vegetarian diet free range with no harmful antibiotics, or something.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

Farmers should be able to participate in producer organizations and associations. Farmers have expressed concern that associations, organizations and the farmers who join them have repeatedly been targets of retaliatory behavior by meat companies. When farmers participate in these organizations it helps fill in the information gap for their business. When they are retaliated against for participating in these groups, we lose the potential of receiving better quality products and that hurts economic market competition.

Farmers and Ranchers should be able safely participate as witnesses in any proceeding relating to violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act. Unfortunately, there are recent examples of cattle rancher witnesses who were threatened and intimidated so much that they decided not to testify before Congress on a hearing about cattle markets. The ability to testify without fear of retaliation is essential to promoting fair and competitive markets in the livestock and poultry industries.

Discrimination and retaliation mean big profits for companies at the farmer’s expense. While meat-packers rake in record profits during the pandemic, farmers make less, and eaters are left paying more at the grocery store. Farmers who complain about their pay or the fairness of their contracts run the risk of losing their contracts, putting their homes and livelihoods at risk.

Fear of retaliation keeps people from knowing the truth about their food. 77% of consumers said they are concerned about the welfare of animals raised for food according to a study by the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. You deserve to know how farmed animals are treated: Farmers have told us that companies have changed very little about how animals are treated. If you care about animal welfare, then you want farmers to be able to speak the truth.

Meat industry consolidation threatens the global supply chain. Ninety percent of all meat consumed comes from industrial farm operations. Farmers should be able to speak up about the overuse of antibiotics and other routine practices that put all of us at risk of disease spread that could morph into the next pandemic flu and exposure to “super bugs.” Even when farmers know that the company is doing wrong, they are afraid to speak out because doing so only puts the farmer at risk of retaliation.

Farmers and Ranchers provide us with the foods we eat and they should not have to face retaliation or fear for their lives. This must stop now.

I urge you to approve the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Councils Coral Amendment 9.

Please approve the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council's Coral Amendment 9. Deep-sea ecosystems are vital to a healthy environment.

Healthy fisheries and oceans drive the success of the Gulfs coastal economies. This proposal would safeguard coral ecosystems that provide food, shelter, and breeding grounds for fish and other ocean wildlife.

Coral Amendment 9 would allow fishing for valuable commercial species to continue while protecting these deep-sea gems as Habitat Areas of Particular Concern and, in some cases, restricting bottom-contact fishing gear. After the plan received more public support than any previous proposal, the Council selected these 21 sites totaling 484 square miles as priorities for protection. 

Some deep-sea corals live thousands of years and can take centuries to recover from damage, if they survive at all. Coral ecosystems also contain natural disease fighters that can produce treatments for human medical conditions, including cancer, strengthening the case for protection.

The Gulf Council has shown its commitment to conserving vital habitat for an array of marine life. The proposed measures would help future generations reap benefits from a healthy ocean. Please approve Coral Amendment 9 so that the Councils plan can take effect.

Gilead Sciences, Inc., (Gilead) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) proposed updated recommendations for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection screening and testing (Proposed Updated Recommendations). 

The Proposed Updated Recommendations are aligned with Gilead’s belief that public health policies should be grounded in the most current scientific evidence and guided by epidemiological data and implementation science. Below we offer our comments on the Proposed Updated Recommendations to help ensure that they are responsive to the populations most impacted by HBV.

Gilead supports the CDC’s proposed recommendation to augment the existing risk-based hepatitis B screening recommendations with a universal screening recommendation, specifically adding hepatitis B screening at least once in a lifetime for persons 18 years of age and older. We believe the inclusion of a universal HBV screening recommendation will improve hepatitis B screening rates, result in earlier diagnosis, and facilitate timely interventions that prevent disease progression, improve quality of life and reduce avoidable mortality. 

Gilead believes the Proposed Updated Recommendations provide a unique opportunity to build upon the CDC’s 2008 guidelines, which recommend screening for HDV coinfection as part of initial evaluation of patients with chronic HBV infection. We therefore request that the CDC consider expanding the Proposed Updated Recommendations to include: (1) HDV screening at least once in a lifetime among all patients with HBV infection (universal HDV screening); and (2) annual HDV testing in HBsAg+ patients with ongoing risk for exposure, including active intravenous drug users (IVDU), men who have sex with men (MSM), and sex workers (periodic HDV testing). Expanded screening and testing recommendations for HDV will help address underdiagnosis and increase the chances of intervention at an earlier disease stage.

As a charter operator, I am not opposed to the idea of the Proposed Rule to collect halibut stamp fees/taxes with the intent of using said fees to purchase un-used quotas from the commercial fishing industry to make them available to recreational quotas. However, to support the proposal, there would need to be a few key changes to the current proposal: It would need be to be administered by, and through, ADFG like King Stamps so the individual anglers would be purchasing the stamps directly from ADFG, along with their regular AK fishing license. ADFG could easily collect these fees and then make them available to NMFS vs the proposed multi-step process of the CHP owners purchasing them, the guides assigning them, ADFG policing them, and the business tracking them. This is exactly the opposite of striving for government efficiency. More importantly, any new taxes/fees targeting the AK small business charter companies, should be paired with equitable changes on “Self-Guided” Lodges and Boat Rental operators in terms taxes/fees and harvest limits. This could be addressed with ADFG charging the fee to all anglers as noted above. As written, it feels punitive to small charter operators and pushes the burden of halibut management on the charter companies, while at the same time encouraging more Out-of-State Alaska visitors to choose "self-guided" operators. With the current proposal, not only will a portion of recreational anglers be exempt from the Charter Stamp Tax/Fee of $20 per person, per day, by opting for “Self-Guiding”, they will also then be further rewarded by being allowed to harvest at least 2x the total halibut that a chartered angler (2 large halibut of any size, every day, vs 1 smaller size restricted halibut with possible additional day closures. – Area 2C). The timing is too close to the start of the 2025 season creating a financial hardship for small business operators. As operators we often sell the majority of trips 1-2 years in advance. Implementing this change, and the new fees, with such short notice puts small business operators in a difficult position. Because the fees are not going to be collected by ADFG as part of regular 2025 fishing licenses, and as many operators have pre-sold and pre-collected trip fees for 2025, these operators will need to either pressure their existing reservations for additional money to cover the new fees/tax, or they will need to personally absorb these new costs in the 2025 season. Because the fee is to be levied per person, per day, the impact will be tens of thousands of dollars for many small businesses. KLM has great concerns regarding the proposed NPRM on the 747-400 FQIS as:

 NPRM 2015-NM-056-AD does not clarify the rational/necessity of additional actions beyond currently applicable SFAR-88, AWL, CDCCL requirements. To KLM's understanding, Boeing also is not able to explain or substantiate the rationale behind this NPRM.
 KLM has been informed by Boeing that currently the sole method of compliance for paragraph (g) of NPRM 2015-NM-056-AD will be the implementation of a Flammability Reduction Means (FRM) which means accomplishment of SB 747-47-2006 (INERT GAS SYSTEM - Nitrogen Generation System - Installation). This will add a huge financial burden to KLM. 
Based on Boeing SB 777-47-2006:
a. The material cost is USD 427,000 per airplane.
b. The modification requires about 400 man hours per airplane. The elapsed time requires about 270 hours per airplane. This will require a considerable extension of existing C-check ground time to accommodate this modification. This will consequently reduce the airplane availability which substantially increases the financial impact even more.
c. The weight increase of the proposed modification is 129 kg per a/c, increasing the a/c fuel usage cost and reducing the payload capability.
d. The installation of the NGS system will increase maintenance cost.
e. The additional weight and consequential increase of fuel usage will have an environmental impact due to the additional carbon dioxide emissions of all affected airplanes.
 
With the above in mind, KLM urges the FAA to encourage Boeing to provide an alternative solution to comply with this requirement which has less impact on the operators and cancel any plans that require retro-active modification to install FRS on in-service airplanes. 
KLM proposes to also review if the "Alternative Actions for Cargo Airplanes" as described in paragraph (h) of NPRM 2015-NM-056-AD is a possible acceptable means of compliance for passenger airplanes. 

Paragraph (h) of NPRM 2015-NM-056-AD "Alternative Actions for Cargo Airplanes" prescribes a BITE check of the FQIS per Boeing Service Bulletin 747-28-2340 at an interval not to exceed 650 flight hours. To avoid delays during operation KLM strongly prefers this test at A-check interval (at KLM this is 1000 flight hours).

1. With reference to EASA SIB No. 2010-10, the EASA did not adopt the FAA Operational Requirement, but did adopt the requirement that newly delivered aircraft should be equipped with a FRM. After extensive and careful consideration EASA decided in 2014 not to amend Part-26 nor CS-26 (ref EASA ED 2014/024/R). This was also based on the fact that various other requirements were implemented which increase the fuel tank safety level.
2. Since 2008 the level of fuel tank safety has been improved by the implementation of several costly SFAR-88 Service Bulletins, implementation of AWL's into the Scheduled Maintenance Program and implementation of CDCCL's into Maintenance Documents. All these additional actions are considered mandatory.

Majority of my summer flounder fishing this year was land based from the back bay sod banks. Commercial fishing is the issue, they are the ones who are allowed to keep 14" flounder. They are allowed to keep all of the ones i have to throw back. Funnier part is i caught more keeper sized Weakfish this year than summer flounder, and i didn't catch one of them for 9 years before that. Out of maybe the 10 or 12 that i caught, there were 6 between 14" and 23" and i released every one of them. In all honesty i would like to see a smaller size limit with a less amount of fish per person a day. 3-4 fish at 17" would satisfy me more than 5 fish at 18" that nobody can catch around here. I also think there would be more honest recreational fisherman with a 17" size limit.

The proposed rule does not explain how the categorize contingent restitution orders. For example, a settlement agreement orders restitution to a group of harmed consumers based on improper fees collected by the defendant from the harmed consumers. The total fees collected equal $500,000 and the settlement orders $500,000 in restitution for the harmed consumers. The settlement agreement specified that if there is residual restitution due to inability to locate the harmed consumers and refund their fees, that residual amounts will be disgorged to the U.S. Treasury.

In such an event, how are the amounts to be reported under 6050X? $500,000 was "ordered to be paid" in restitution, but that order was contingent on successfully locating and refunding harmed consumers. I would ask IRS to clarify that phrase "ordered to be paid" and whether it means what has been ordered at the time of the settlement agreement regardless of the actual disposition of payments OR if it means the actual disposition of the payments, which might not occur for several months or years after the settlement agreement has been entered into by the parties.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Please make every effort for HONEST labeling and to distinguish pastured from free-range, etc. Please put an end to deceptive practices. Whenever possible, enable humane measures be adopted and put into practice routinely!!!!!!!!!!!!!

Thank you for considering my request.

It could also affect regional weather patterns as warmer areas affect the formation of cloud and even wind speeds Satellite data over a large area in Texas, that is now covered by four of the world's largest wind farms, found that over a decade the local temperature went up by almost 1C as more turbines are built.. Taking the ground temperatures measured by satellites, they detected a warming of 0.5C at night in the region directly under the farm. New report was also first attempted by David Keith and colleagues back in 2004 but was ignored by leaders. 

When they compared the climate in their model with and without extremely large wind farms (large enough to generate about twice the world's total present electrical demand), they found that in addition to climate effects in the immediate vicinity of the wind farms, there were changes in climate all around the world. Vautard's study agrees with this earlier work, in finding that the climate impacts of wind farms extend beyond the farms themselves and are caused by changes in the flow of the atmosphere that bring warming and cooling to different regions around the wind farms. 

Note Farmers have been using wind fans to heat the air over crops in times of frost for years

Re: 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule Dear USDA Forest Service, I am writing to request that you fully restore 2001 Roadless Rule protections on the Tongass National Forest and end large-scale old growth timber sales on the entirety of the forest. The Tongass is a key weapon for fighting climate change, with its old-growth trees effectively trapping and sequestering climate-warming greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Scientists have estimated that the forest accounts for about 8 percent of the carbon sequestered by all national forests. Protecting the Tongass from old-growth logging will not only preserve that capacity, but avoid releasing carbon currently sequestered in its trees. The Tongass is also the ancestral and contemporary homeland of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples, and they have been the driving force of the effort to protect the forest. Their way of life is inextricably linked with these lands and waters. They hunt, gather, fish and harvest medicines in the Tongass that their ancestors have stewarded for more than 10,000 years. Restoring full protections will allow their traditional use of the land to continue. As part of planning for a future beyond old-growth timber, please also make a sustained investment in the Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy. Operating in full consultation with Tribal governments and local communities, this program will help the region stoke the already robust fishing and recreation industries that are driving the economy. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Jerrilynne Titsworth -PII-

Clinical social workers are an integral part of a treatment team and providing many services via Medicaid that could support the health and wellness of the millions of people with Medicaid.

As a clinical social worker, I am writing to provide my feedback on the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule regarding CY 2024 Medicare payments under the Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) and other Part B Payment Policies (CMS-1784–P).

I want to thank you for many of the provisions in this proposed rule that will expand access to mental health care and to social care, including:
• Recognizing clinical social workers as providers of Health and Behavior Assessment and Intervention services. 
• Increasing the valuation of psychotherapy services through a similar process as primary care payments will help address provider concerns with Medicare – this is especially critical for clinical social workers, who only receive 75% of the amount psychologists receive for providing equivalent services and billing the exact same codes. I urge CMS to increase the reimbursement rates for CSWs to at least 85 percent of the Physician Fee Schedule. Such an increase will remove a significant barrier to CSW participation in the Medicare program as well as improve access to beneficiaries.

I applaud CMS for recognizing the importance of several services on beneficiary treatment and health – including screenings for health-related social needs, community health integration services, principal illness navigation services, and caregiver training services. Social workers provide services aligned with these proposed codes day in and day out across the country, yet they are not identified among lists of providers recognized for offering these proposed services. 
• I urge CMS to deepen its understanding of how social work’s disciplinary competencies apply to health care and how social workers already collaborate with interprofessional team members, including community health workers, to address these issues. 
• I urge CMS to recognize clinical social workers as qualified health providers of screenings for health-related social needs, community health integration services, principal illness management services, and caregiver training services. Non-clinical social workers, including bachelors-level, also regularly carry out these services. 

The proposed provision to require that an in-person, non-telehealth service be furnished by a provider at least once within 6 months before each telehealth service furnished for the diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment of a mental health disorder is problematic. There is no clinical evidence to support, or show benefit of, this proposed requirement. Indeed, such a requirement will pose substantial barriers to service for a broad range of clients, especially people with disabilities and others for whom going to an in-person appointment is exceedingly difficult. Millions of Americans have received mental health services for the first time due to the telehealth flexibilities instituted during the pandemic, which has prevented acute exacerbation of mental illness and saved lives. I urge CMS to maintain the current policy under the Public Health Emergency which does not require an in-person visit. If CMS is forced to establish an interval for subsequent in-person visits, the interval should be at least 12 months. 

Thank you for your consideration of my input, and for taking steps to ensure that the social work profession can continue to enhance the mental, physical, and social health of Medicare beneficiaries.

conjecture. I encourage the FDA to remain focused on this goal. To do this, the FDA must 
ensure that they properly consider the risk of counterfactuals. If the status of regulated tobacco 
products changes, it may incentivize users to seek out less regulated alternatives. People may 
smoke more cigarettes or figure out new techniques for smoking that result in more nicotine 
being ingested, similar to what happened with “light” cigarettes in decades past. (1) Therefore, 
the risk of combustible and non-combustible tobacco products must be compared not only to 
abstinence from tobacco use, but to the real-world use of other nicotine sources or other 
stimulants.
Summary of the Proposed Rule: 
Smoking-related illnesses result in 480,000 premature deaths per year. According to the 
agency, the primary attribution of these deaths is nicotine addiction. The most common cause of 
deaths were cancer, but cardiovascular and metabolic diseases were common as well. (2)) The 
latter are significant as nicotine consumption, not just smoking, is associated with this outcome. 
(3)
The FDA has proposed to limit the concentration of nicotine in cigarettes and other heated 
tobacco products to 0.70 mg per gram of tobacco. The limit would include cigarettes, cigarette 
tobacco, roll-your-own tobacco, cigars, and pipe tobacco. However, this action would exclude 
non-combusted cigarettes and waterpipe tobacco, as well as premium cigars. According to the 
FDA, the regulation is intended to “reduce the addictiveness of tobacco products, thus giving 
people who are addicted and wish to quit the ability to do so more easily.” (4)

We are proposing to cover the following products under this proposed product standard:

tobacco, cigars (including little cigars, cigarillos, and large cigars but excluding premium 
cigars), and pipe tobacco (other than waterpipe tobacco). FDA requests comments, 
data, and research regarding this proposed scope.
It is well established that the FDA has the authority to regulate all forms of tobacco and nicotine-
containing products. (5) As recognized above, nicotine consumption, not just smoking, is 
associated with cardiovascular disease. Joel et al. found that reducing the nicotine content of

 
cigarettes not only lowered nicotine dependence but also reduced cardiovascular toxicity, 
suggesting significant public health benefits from nicotine reduction across all product types. (6) 
The public generally perceives e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products to be less harmful 
compared to combusted tobacco. (7) While e-cigarettes may be safer than traditional cigarettes 
for some health outcomes, the long-term evidence is inconclusive. (8) These products still

I have driven trucks with automatic transmissions, elogs,speed limiters and lots of sensors - and manual transmission trucks that you actually have to shift. I currently use paper logs, drive a 2000 Kenworth, and my most important sensors are my eyes and ears, along with watching gauges instead of waiting on buzzers or beeps to tell me somethings wrong or in my way.

The ATA and FMCSA have, against logic, achieved progress in passing speed limiters in ALL trucks - this is bad! The inability for a truck to accelerate to passing lane speed has (formerly) put me and many drivers in dangerous situations MANY times. When a pickup truck is loaded down pulling a trailer with precariously loaded furniture and flopping mattresses with hazard lights, driving 40 - 45 mph in the right lane, it is imperative that a truck can maneuver - sometimes that means we have to accelerate to transition into the left lane where cars are driving 70 - 80 mph. It was not long ago that I avoided an accident because after I got around the curve in the road and saw this slow pick up truck in my lane, I ACCELERATED from my typical cruising speed of 65 mph to safely move into the left lane. Slamming on the brakes is a much more dangerous move in many cases - both because of distance it takes to stop a truck and for traffic behind me. I am a much safer driver in an unlimited truck than I was driving a limited truck for Averitt.

If safer roadways are the priority, I emplore you to fight this regulation. The studies and facts show that the roadways will become LESS SAFE by limiting all trucks. The large trucking companies of the ATA are the most guilty of turning out poorly trained drivers, expecting technology to replace training and experience. Only in the trucking industry can a new driver with ONLY 6 MONTHS EXPERIENCE be considered a "professional" in SOME ATA MEMBER COMPANIES and train new drivers. Making trucks a bigger hazard, elogs, automatic breaking systems and automatic transmissions will not make our roads safer - TRAINING WILL!

This new proposed regulation will not affect my truck since it's proposed for all new trucks produced, but it will affect road safety when a large percent of trucks can not thin out after metro areas and construction zones, where trucks typically bunch up. For myself and everyone around me, increasing my speed to posted speed limit to get away from bunched up trucks, then slowing down to a reduced speed for fuel economy has proven to be safer than being stuck with other limited trucks - cars whizzing past in the left. Having a dozen trucks with slightly different limits and drastically different weights in their trailers, add a few small hills and cars driving 10 - 20 mph faster than the truck can go, it's a fatal mistake to let this regulation pass.

I appreciate your time and consideration. Please help our roadways became safer, NOT MORE DANGEROUS! My kids and grandkids and loved ones are on the roads, and your loved ones, too!

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule Docket No: USCIS 2020-0013, A.G. Order No. 4747-2020, which is a devastating and unjust attack on asylum seekers that lacks any real public health rationale.
I believe that the United States should welcome asylum seekers and immigrants because both the domestic laws, international laws and human rights norms require it to do so. Asylum seekers are not a threat to public safety. Rather, they are people who have made the incredibly difficult yet brave decision to leave behind their homes in search of safety.

This rule would roll back due process rights and cause undue harm to individuals who need protection. Hundreds of public health experts around the country have made it clear that turning away asylum seekers in a public health emergency would not mitigate the spread of disease. Instead of implementing a policy based on false rationales and xenophobic tropes of immigrants as carriers of disease, the United States should follow policy guided by public health experts and rooted in compassion. I urge the government to immediately withdraw its current proposal and instead focus on implementing procedures that would actually protect both the health of those seeking refuge in the United States and those already residing within. 
First, when the proposal states that the rule would make these same bars applicable to the initial credible fear screening stage, it provides no fair mechanism to demonstrate how the immigration officers determine whether an applicant would bring potential public health threat nor does it ensure dual process in this screening process. With the rule implementing, applications with fair grounds of reasonings can be easily rejected on arbitrary grounds, which is extremely unfair and unjust. Unless DHS provides a feasible and fair mechanism, this proposal appears to be nothing but a pure anti-asylum political tool. The bottom line is that the safety and right to life of people should not politicalized and should not be used as a mean to a certain end.
Second, this is especially concerning that none of the implementing agencies of this rule is an expert on public health. Both DHS and DOJ, the critical decision makers evaluating asylum cases, are not authorized to determine based on public health grounds. There has been best practices and recommendations suggested by legitimate public health experts, but the rule simply ignores those. If anything, the authorized agencies should be the ones to make guideline rather than unqualified ones. This should especially be the case when the decision is going to have a huge impact on others' lives. 
Moreover, according to a policy brief on the impact of COVID-19 on Refugees, IDPS and Migrants written by Antonio Guterres, an inclusive public health response is preferable to an exclusive one. Second, Human dignity is important and can be protected by implementing proper travel regulations. If the U.S. claims itself to the frontline flag holder of human rights in the world, it should also sets an example for other countries in this issue.
Asylum seekers are seeking protection because of persecution; it is not their fault that their country or the countries they transit through fail to contain prevalent illnesses. Labeling asylum seekers a "danger to the security" of the U.S. does not just trample our legal obligations; it also dehumanizes and vilifies those seeking refugees.
Therefore, I urge that the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice should immediately withdraw their current proposal, and instead dedicate their efforts to ensuring that individuals fleeing violence are granted full and fair access to asylum protections in the United States.

Re: Food Labeling: Calorie Labeling of Articles of Food Sold From Certain Vending Machines; Front of Package Type Size

Docket No. FDA-2011-F0171

To Whom it May Concern: 

The proposed rule to revise the type size requirement for calories labeled on the front of vended food packages is a powerful way to enable the general public to make healthier decisions on a day to day basis. The rules original purpose to encourage many vending machine owners to stock food items with visible nutritional information positively affects the general welfare of society. Even when necessity forces individuals to make quick and convenient food decisions, it is important that people are aware of the contents of the food they purchase. 
 This rule is important because healthy eating choices start at a young age. Many vending machines are strategically placed in schools and often become a large attraction for children. Placing the caloric content on the front of packaging can teach children two things: The importance of paying attention to what goes into their bodies and the nutritional value that food can offer them. 
Additionally, vending machines provide a low-cost option for those who cannot afford an alternative. By implementing this rule, the FDA is giving individuals the ability to choose healthier options. By displaying nutritional information before purchase, even those who can not afford alternatives are still able to retain some control over the food they eat. By increasing flexibility on the required caloric formatting regulations, food manufacturers will have room on the packaging to include additional nutrition information, such as fiber content, on the front of the packaging. Food manufacturers are incentivized to add additional health information to give them a competitive edge when people make a quick decision at a vending machine. This additional information provides yet another benefit to the consumer. 
Lastly, while relieving the vending machine operators of some burden, the regulation also inadvertently places pressure on them to foster honesty in the foods they distribute through their machines. Promoting this type of transparency is a powerful practice to continue to encourage in the food industry as a whole. The modification to the original rule will lessen the burden on vending machine owners because the standard is more flexible. This flexibility will make it easier to abide by the regulation and thus increase overall compliance.

agriculture, energy, and mineral industries. The Committee respectfully requests the BLM withdraw 
its proposed rule. 
 
1. Congress did not intend conservation to be included as a multiple use under FLPMA 
 
The Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) requires the BLM to "manage the 
public lands under principles of multiple use and sustained yield."1 The United States Supreme Court 
has stated that "'multiple use management' is a deceptively simple term that describes the enormously 
complicated task of striking a balance among the many competing uses to which land can be put[.]"2 
These competing uses are outlined in the definition of multiple use under the FLPMA as "including, 
but not limited to, recreation, range, timber, minerals, watershed, wildlife and fish, and [uses serving] 
natural scenic, scientific and historical values[.]"3 The definition requires managing these uses 
"without permanent impairment of the productivity of the land and the quality of the environment 
with consideration being given to the relative values of the resources."4 Conservation is not expressly 
included in the definition of multiple use. However, the proposed rule would allow the BLM to 
authorize a conservation use, which would place conservation on par with other uses of public lands.5

At the beginning of the organic dairy movement, one of the big drivers was economic justice for farmers. We have lost thousands of farmers since then. Organic production was intended as an alternative for family-scale producers and it has worked. However, much of the growth in the industry has been usurped by industrial scale operations gaming the system. If it wasn't for the factory farms there could have been thousands of additional dairies saved and converted to organic. The resulting psychological damage to families in rural communities is almost incalculable.

In order to protect the integrity of USDA organic certification and establish a level playing field for a thriving organic dairy market, the Final Rule must:

- Prohibit organic dairy operations from acquiring transitioned animals to expand or 
 replace animals in the organic dairy herd. USDA should prohibit the sales of 
 transitioned animals as certified organic.
- Limit the movement of transitioned animals has economic benefits. Start-up 
 operations should buy organically certified cows. Increased demand for animals 
 raised as organic will create a thriving market for organic replacement animals. 
 This will allow small-to-mid-size organic dairy operations to diversify into 
 breeding replacements whose price will reflect the true cost of organic dairy at 
 their scale of production. 
- Clarify that a "responsibly connected" person who transitions a herd is bound by the 
 same limit as the operation they are connected to. The intent of the rule can be 
 most effectively accomplished by tying the transition to the responsibly connected 
 person(s).
- Be implemented as soon as it is finalized with transitions already in process 
 completed within 12 months. All requirements of the rule should be implemented 
 immediately upon publication of the Final Rule, with the only exception being those 
 dairies that have already started their transition and were already approved by a 
 certifying agent.

 person, with no exceptions. This will prevent the rule from being abused.

Thank you for your consideration.

from outside of Central America faced journeys of several months and even over a year on the road. 

Those who entered the U.S. through the official ports of entry waited weeks or even months in Mexico 

for their turn to be processed, exhausting the meager savings that they possessed to make the trip to 

the U.S. and settle in to a new life. Those that entered the U.S. without inspection were often robbed or

These comments are being submitted by the Working Group for Competitive International Taxation (the Working 
Group), a group of 23 U.S.-headquartered companies that include industrial companies, manufacturers, financial 
services companies, and service providers.1 While from a mix of industries, the companies in the Working Group 
share a number of characteristics: they are all subject to the new global intangible low-taxed income (GILTI) 
provisions created by the Tax Cut and Jobs Act (TCJA), and much of their income subject to GILTI derives from 
operations in higher taxed jurisdictions. 
As noted in the preamble to the Proposed Regulations, “the legislative history evidences an intent to exclude high-
taxed income from gross tested income,” in determining GILTI.2 Therefore, the Working Group very much 
appreciates and supports the efforts of the Department of Treasury (Treasury) and the Internal Revenue Service 
(IRS) to provide rules that acknowledge this intent and thus exempt from additional U.S. tax GILTI that is subject to 
high tax in local jurisdictions – the GILTI high-tax election (HTE). 
Summary of recommendations 
In the context of the Proposed Regulations, our comments focus on achieving a design for the GILTI HTE that best 
achieves Congressional intent – to exempt high tax foreign income in a manner that allows taxpayers to blend tax 
attributes of CFCs for section 951A3 purposes – while creating the least amount of administrative friction for both 
taxpayers and the government. Therefore, we recommend the final regulations: 
• 
Make the GILTI HTE an annual election; 
• 
Apply the effective rate test at the controlled foreign corporation (CFC) level; 
• 
Replace the all-or-nothing election with a CFC-by-CFC election; 
• 
Conform the meaning of high-taxed GILTI to Congressional intent by applying a 13.125% tax rate to define 
“high tax;” 
• 
Apply the GILTI HTE to match the effective date of section 951A;

This is incorrect. One of the three hallmarks of the disease, according to the CDC itself, is 

PEM. And, unlike the other symptoms which may overlap with other diseases, the NIH website 

notes that PEM is the “distinctive characteristic” of ME/CFS - i.e., the one used to distinguish the 

disease from other diseases.

A recent study using diffusion tensor imaging showed microstructural abnormalities in the brains

investigation of the pathophysiology of ME/CFS.” 

The only relevant question for the purposes of the Report should be “Do any of the proposed 

therapies help ME/CFS patients?” The only logical way to answer that is to consider only those 

studies that require subjects to actually have the disease and hence the abnormalities that go 

with it. That wasn’t done.

Instead, the Report considers studies on people who have PEM “or” persistent fatigue. Adding 

the word ‘or’ opens the door to irrelevant studies on people who didn’t have PEM, and thus 

didn’t have ME/CFS. 

Many research studies have been done using overly broad, outdated criteria that didn’t include 

PEM. The Report laments that these multiple case definitions present an “ongoing challenge” in

the CDC’s own criteria, thus torpedoing the CDC’s (and NIH’s) disease definition.

If the Report were appropriately limited to only those research studies requiring PEM, it would 

be clear that there is insufficient support for the two “therapies” highlighted in the report -

“treatments” help a few, miscellaneous test subjects fatigued by different conditions. That’s like 

treating cancer patients with only antibiotics simply because those antibiotics helped ‘strep 

throat’ patients recover. It’s illogical and deeply unethical.

this thought is ludicrous on its face.

Regulations, as well as our thoughts on some changes that could be made to make the hemp

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has proposed a rule that would ban the sale of almost 
all cigarettes available on the U.S. market. The agency’s proposed nicotine cap of 0.5 mg per 
cigarette is 95% lower than what is found in most conventional cigarettes sold today, and only 
one cigarette—with 0.001% market share—currently meets this standard. 
 
Enacting an effective prohibition on almost every cigarette currently used by the approximately 
30 million U.S. smokers would inevitably give rise to yet another robust illicit market. And with 
cigarettes currently accounting for billions of dollars in retail sales each year, this rule would 
divert massive profits toward organized crime and other criminal enterprises. The problems that 
follow would have disastrous consequences for public health and safety, directly undercutting 
the FDA’s stated justification for imposing a nicotine cap. 
 
As executive director of the Law Enforcement Action Partnership (LEAP), I speak on behalf of 
more than 5,000 current and retired members of law enforcement across the country. Many of 
our members have worked for decades attempting to enforce drug prohibition measures such 
as the one FDA is proposing. We have seen firsthand how these policies routinely fail to deter 
drug use, while driving criminalization regimes that bog down the criminal justice system and 
make policing more difficult by straining relationships with the communities we serve. The most 
reliable beneficiaries in the War on Drugs have been organized crime syndicates, which fight 
violently against law enforcement and each other to corner the market on newly banned 
products. 
 
The FDA’s proposed nicotine cap is now seeking to repeat mistakes of the past, with the agency 
showing little indication that it understands the complexity of this problem. If this rule were to go 
into effect, state and local law enforcement would be strapped with the added responsibilities of 
combatting the market for products that had previously been fully legal and used regularly by 
tens of millions of Americans. And unlike the current market, this emergent underground trade 
would feature no product or safety standards, age controls, or taxable revenue. 
 
Prohibiting—and consequently criminalizing—cigarettes and other tobacco products will 
necessarily drive further bloating in our criminal justice system. All 50 states consider the sale of 
illicit cigarettes to be a serious crime, with 44 of them classifying it as a felony and 37 of them

 
carrying mandatory minimum sentences. The severity of these charges means that a person 
caught selling or distributing cigarettes would not only be stuck with a criminal record, but in 
some cases enhanced prison terms, parole revocation, and disenfranchisement. 
 
As enforcement commences, the resulting wave of investigations, arrest, prosecution, and 
incarceration would drain policing and justice system resources at a time when police are 
already struggling to solve major crimes and many courts are facing a crushing backlog of 
cases. These impacts would likely fall most heavily on lower-income and often Black and brown 
communities, where residents would have the greatest financial incentive to engage in illegal 
cigarette sales, and where existing racial disparities in policing and the justice system have 
already eroded both public safety and law enforcement’s ability to uphold it.

This comment addresses two questions posed by the Department of Transportation regarding Section 2305 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016. The first is whether the length of delay should be modified using a second set of criteria. And the second is when the clock measuring the delay should stop.

In assuming the language "in certain cases" from the Act provides for some modification of the length of delay, I would propose one additional secondary criteria that may be appropriate. That additional criterion would be severe weather. This is because severe weather can cause substantial problems with entire airline industry and significantly disrupt baggage handling systems. Additionally, this criterion would be a reasonable interpretation of the "in certain cases" language. The language of the Act itself appears to imply that modification should occur only rarely. Some other factors, such as the number of connections or airlines involved, are more common occurrences and are likely outside the reasonable interpretation of the statute's language. Severe weather is a much less likely scenario for delayed baggage, but is a more legitimate reason to increase the length of delay.

Although the Act provides specific language for stopping the delay clock when the carrier "delivers the checked baggage to the passenger," requiring actual physical delivery for the carrier would likely create an undue burden on carriers and create practical enforcement problems. Taking the Act's language literally would likely result in some absurd results where the delay time may depend on how long it takes for the airport delivery driver to arrive at the passenger's hotel. The fact that the carrier has possession of the bag and it is en route to the passenger should be sufficient to satisfy the intent of the Act to cut down on excessive baggage delays. 

A good stopping point for measuring delay is when the passenger is notified that the baggage has been found and is either available for pickup or is on its way to the passenger's location. To include the time in between pick-up of the luggage or its ultimate delivery to the passenger would not necessarily address the problem of avoiding delayed baggage. Additionally, literal adherence to the Act's language may lead to increased cost and waste by the carriers because of the incentive to deliver all delayed baggage as quickly, and perhaps as inefficiently as possible.

Dear Sirs:

I'm a psychiatrist who has administered ECT to selected patients for 25 years. I support reclassification of ECT devices from Class III to the less restrictive Class II. I ask that this classification apply to all the indications for ECT, including younger patients, bipolar patients, and others--and not just to adults with depression. That is, I ask that ECT devices be reclassified without any further specification. Even though the FDA specification does not prevent justified use in other than specified areas, I fear that specification will be used by insurance companies and regulators to block use of ECT in other areas. There is more than sufficient evidence that ECT is useful in treating patients younger than 18 and for conditions other than depression.

My first experience with ECT was during my first year of psychiatric residency. My patient was a 22-year-old college student. When I first met her she was standing in the middle of the day room of a psychiatric ward in a state-funded psychiatric hospital. She stared blankly ahead, did not make eye contact, and shifted from foot to foot drooling, defecating, and urinating, creating a puddle of waste beneath her. She emitted soft hoarse sounds but no coherent words. She had a history of bipolar illness. Under the direction my training supervisors, I diagnosed her with bipolar illness and agitated catatonia and referred her for ECT. Two weeks later she was to all appearances normal. She came into my office appropriately dressed. She talked about her history of bipolar illness. She talked about the recent breakup of a romance. She suffered no problems with memory or cognition beyond the immediate post-ictal effect. I treated her for four more years with medications and psychotherapy but she did not again need ECT. This case demonstrates the life restoring and life saving benefit of ECT for cases of bipolar illness and cases of catatonia.

Not all ECT cases I've seen have been as remarkable. I've known patients who did not respond at all to ECT. I have known patients who had memory problems, and cases of patients who alleged that they were disabled by memory problems. My general experience is that, like all medical procedures, ECT has risks as well as benefits, but the extraordinary benefits outweigh the occasional risks, and in the hands of skilled practitioners, benefits can be maximized and risks minimized.

I'm not an expert on autism. I received a referral from a psychiatric program that specializes in autism to administer maintenance ECT to an autistic child with relentless aggression and self injury. With ECT her symptoms improved to a manageable degree. She has since turned 18, but at the time ECT was initiated she was under the age of 18. I've seen other cases of self injury in mentally retarded and autistic children that resulted in significant organ damage, including eye gouging, severing fingers by biting, and headbanging. These behaviors often do not respond to other interventions. Use of ECT to remediate self injury is in the investigational stage. This case demonstrates the importance of not prematurely restricting the range of indications for ECT in terms of either diagnosis or age.

Sincerely,

Richard Owings, M.D., PhD

care settings, including hospitals, ambulatory clinics, and health-system community pharmacies. 
ASHP has been at the forefront of hazardous drug safety for over 40 years. A practice spotlight article 
published in 1983 first outlined recommendations for cytotoxic drug handling in hospitals.1 A follow-up 
bulletin published in 1990 established characteristics of drugs that can represent occupational exposure 
hazards: genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, teratogenicity, fertility impairment, and organ or other toxicity at 
low doses.2 The initial 2004 NIOSH Alert about preventing occupational exposure to hazardous drugs 
included those original characteristics in its definition of a hazardous drug and included an additional 
characteristic: drugs with structure and toxicity that mimic a drug already determined to be hazardous.3 
The NIOSH list has become the standard in hazard identification for drugs used in healthcare settings.

ASHP expresses concern that the methods used to reevaluate liraglutide and pertuzumab for inclusion in 
the list of hazardous drugs represent risk assessment, not hazard identification. The physical properties 
of a drug molecule are not among the six characteristics considered for hazard determination. The 
purpose of the NIOSH list should be to identify hazards so that healthcare settings can assess and 
mitigate risk. If NIOSH removes these drugs based on risk assessment, healthcare settings may 
incorrectly think that a hazard does not exist. 
While ASHP agrees that a drug’s physical properties may reduce the risk of absorption through common 
methods of occupational exposure, NIOSH should not assume that all healthcare staff and healthcare 
environments are the same. Exposure through mucous membranes or other routes of exposure may be 
rare, but they are still important considerations that healthcare settings should evaluate when 
performing a risk assessment specific to their environment and to their employees.

available dosage forms of a drug. NIOSH should not base hazard identification on a specific route of

Dear Madam/Sir: 

Canada writes further to the United States’ notification to the WTO TBT Committee, 

G/TBT/N/USA/424/Add.5, regarding implementation of revised Lacey Act provisions. We 

want to bring to your attention serious concerns regarding the proposed new provisions, 

including concerns raised by Canada’s Wood Pallet and Container Association (letter from 

the association attached for your review). 

Proposed Phase VI expansion of the Lacey Act enforcement schedule: HS Code 4415 

As explained in detail in the association’s letter, the inclusion of wood pallets and related 

products (HS Code 4415) in the amendment to the Lacey Act will have significant 

negative effects on bilateral trade between Canada and the United States. While pallets 

“under load” are exempt from the new provisions, we note that almost 40 million empty 

pallets were exported last year from Canada to the Unites States. In Canada’s view, 

subjecting these pallets to the provisions of the Lacey Act plant import declaration 

requirement will create a substantial burden not just for Canadian and United States 

companies that trade in pallets, but also for the wide range of United States exporters that 

make use of these pallets to ship their goods to Canada and other markets. 

The issue stems from the nature of the manufacturing and maintenance process for pallets 

and related products, as well as the high volume and unique nature of cross-border 

movement within the industry. As noted in the association’s letter it is very difficult if not 

impossible to provide required information on species and origin given the nature of how 

pallets are manufactured and maintained. Pallets are largely constructed out of wood that 

is unsuitable for the manufacture of other products. In many cases, pallets are constructed 

from “mixed hardwoods” from a sawmill; they may also be made of recycled wood. As a 

result, a single pallet could be made of many species of wood, both new and reclaimed, 

making it difficult to identify genus, species and origin. In addition, pallets used in bilateral 

Canada-United States trade are frequently recycled and repaired in both Canada and the 

United States. For example, a Canadian pallet recycling company may collect a number of 

used pallets and repair them for re-use, in which case neither the recycling company nor 

the pallet purchaser (in the United States or Canada) is able to identify the origin of the 

wood used in the pallets.

professional membership association of more than 2,200 physicians, scientists and other 

healthcare professionals promoting blood and marrow transplantation and cellular therapy 

research, education, scholarly publication and clinical standards. ASBMT is dedicated to 

improving the application and success of blood and marrow transplantation, and ensuring access 

to all patients who need hematopoietic cell transplants. 

Blood and marrow transplantation has several pseudonyms, including bone marrow 

transplantation, stem cell transplantation, cord blood transplantation, peripheral blood stem cell 

transplantation and hematopoietic cell transplantation. For purposes of simplification and 

scientific comprehensiveness, we will utilize hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) for the 

remainder of this document. 

Hematopoietic cell transplantation is a medical sub-specialty comprised of physicians with 

Board Certifications in Internal Medicine, Medical Oncology, Pediatrics, Hematology and/or 

Immunology. Despite common misconceptions, HCT physicians are not surgeons and the 

introduction of hematopoietic cells into patients is performed via infusion, not open incision or 

other surgical procedures. HCT is a procedure that involves the infusion of either autologous 

(self) or allogeneic (donor) hematopoietic stem (progenitor) cells into a patient to reconstitute the 

patient’s immune system as part of a larger treatment course for three primary clinical purposes: 

1) treatment of malignancy, 2) replacement or modulation of an absent or poorly functioning 

hematopoietic immune system, 3) treatment of certain genetic diseases.1 CMS recognized the

Dear Secretary Purdue,

I too am urging you to withdraw the proposed rule to 'modernize' (essentially deregulate) swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety.

The proposed rule puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. In place of these requirements, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide.

The rule also proposes a New Swine Inspection System that hands over important duties currently fulfilled by USDA?s Food Safety Inspection Service inspectors to slaughter establishment employees. The proposal also removes caps on line speeds, increasing the risk that carcasses will fly by too quickly for inspectors to detect animal disease, fecal contamination, and other food safety issues. 

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer, and this proposal will not achieve that. Instead, it has the potential to make food less safe by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

I too urge you to withdraw the proposed rule and design a new rule that prioritizes food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness.

Sincerely,

Ross Lockridge
Cerrillos, NM

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. Who benefits from keeping them so long, under under conditions no decent person would wish for their own children?

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable. Again, it is worth figuring out who benefits from this policy.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children. It's very important to figure out who benefits from policies like this, and to refuse to allow them to influence what this nation does in the name of all its citizens.

Thank you for considering this comment on the proposed Threatened listing of and critical habitat designation for the Bi-State Greater Sage-Grouse. Protection under the Endangered Species Act is urgently needed for the Bi-State population and its remaining habitat. Due to its small size and severely degraded habitat condition, I believe that Endangered status is warranted rather than the proposed Threatened listing.

The range of the Bi-State Sage-Grouse distinct population segment (DPS) has been reduced by nearly 50 percent, and the remaining habitat is poor. In addition to habitat loss, the estimated population of Bi-State Sage-Grouse has declined by over 90 percent from historic levels, while the number of leks staging areas for breeding birds has declined by close to two-thirds. Experts believe the effective population size for the entire Bi-State Sage-Grouse DPS could be as low as 230 and only as high as 770 birds.

The federal Bi-State Sage-Grouse Conservation Action Plan 2017 Progress Report reveals that the number of grouse at lek sites is in decline in most areas. In California, the count declined 21% from 2016 to 2017 in Mono County and was down 31% in the Bodie Hills. In Nevada, the population was down 2% at lek sites overall and fell 19% at Mount Grant. Only Nevadas Desert Creek population showed an uptick (5.5%). 

These declines are particularly worrisome considering the cyclical nature of grouse populations. Based on historical population trends, the Bi-State population was due for a significant uptick. Instead, it appears the overall downward trend continues. Given the grouses low population, along with the risks of drought and habitat degradation, I believe the strongest level of protection is warranted.
I
m also concerned about the proposed 4d rule that would accompany the Bi-State populations listing as Threatened. The Bi-State area is already heavily impacted by roads, power lines, and fences in addition to cell towers and waste dumps. The proposed 4d rule is very broad, and its acceptance of grazing in areas occupied by sage-grouse may result in nest destruction or abandonment. Grazing is inappropriate in areas where this dwindling grouse population hangs on to survival. 

For all of these reasons, I ask that you list the Bi-State Greater Sage-Grouse as Endangered. Thank you for time and consideration of this matter.

Sincerely,

ASHP is pleased to submit comments to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regarding the draft 

guidance about what constitutes a copy of a commercially available drug under Section 503B of the 

Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. ASHP represents pharmacists who serve as patient care providers in 

acute and ambulatory settings. The organization’s more than 43,000 members include pharmacists, 

student pharmacists, and pharmacy technicians. For over 70 years, ASHP has been at the forefront of 

efforts to improve medication use and enhance patient safety. 

ASHP advocates for a strong compounding framework. We believe that a robust 503B outsourcing 

facility program is essential to realizing the goals of the Drug Quality and Security Act (DQSA). For many 

of our members, 503Bs are a vital link in their compounding supply chain. ASHP appreciates FDA’s 

efforts to clarify the types of products 503B outsourcing facilities can permissibly compound under 

503B. Greater clarity around certain terms used in Section 503B may reduce confusion and assist with 

compliance. Although ASHP is supportive of FDA’s work, our review of the draft guidance, as well as 

discussions with our members, indicate potential issues with interpretation and application of some 

guidance provisions. Specifically, the scope of the drug shortages provision, the definition of bulk drug 

substances to include approved drugs, and the documentation requirements raise concerns. To assist 

FDA in refining the guidance document, ASHP offers the following recommendations. 

I. 

Definition of Bulk Drug Substances 

ASHP urges FDA to further clarify its definition of the term “bulk drug substance” as used in the draft 

guidance. In the guidance, FDA states “if a component of the compounded drug is a bulk drug substance 

that is also a component of an approved drug, the compounded drug product is essentially a copy of an 

approved drug and cannot be compounded under section 503B, unless there is a prescriber 

determination of clinical difference...”.1 The guidance further notes that “[t]his provision applies to a 

compounded drug whether it was compounded from bulk drug substances or from drugs in finished 

form.”2 The application of the bulk substances prohibition to “drugs in finished form,” which we 

understand to mean approved drugs, is confusing and contrary to statutory differentiation between bulk

Designated List of Analytes

analyte or test for which it is certified under CLIA. The current list of analytes for which a

Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors.

I am a final year veterinary medical student at the Royal Veterinary College in the United Kingdom and have been an active member of the animal training community since 2007. I hold memberships with the AVMA (American Veterinary Medical Association), AZA (Association of Zoos and Aquariums), IMATA (International Marine Animal Trainers Association), IAAAM (International Association of Aquatic Animal Medicine), BVA (British Veterinary Association), and WAVMA (World Aquatic Veterinary Medical Association). In addition, I will become a member of the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons following my graduation in July of this year. I have had the opportunity to review the proposed changes to the regulations and would like to submit the below comments for consideration.

I am in firm agreement with the proposed regulations regarding ventilation, as marine mammals can be particularly prone to respiratory illnesses. The threat of viral, fungal, and bacterial infections is far more pertinent than objectionable odours. 

I am also in agreement regarding proposed regulations for shade in outdoor enclosures. Marine mammals are prone to certain ophthalmic diseases and specific neoplasias which are more likely following lengthy exposure to UV-light.

After performing a thorough literature search, I am unable to find peer-reviewed scientific data that demonstrates a need for time constraints on interactive programming, or how such regulation would benefit marine mammals. I do support an increase in the amount of interactive programming (i.e. from 2 to 3 hours per day), however I struggle to support the overall notion that interactive sessions must not exceed 'x' hours per day per animal. It is my opinion that interactive programming itself is of benefit to the animals, as it provides a multitude of sensory and cognitive enrichment. Programming should be limited, however, if an individual animal demonstrates a specific need (e.g. neonates, pregnant or lactating females, ill animals, etc). This specific need should be assessed and determined by a qualified veterinarian.

Limiting interaction could decrease the amount of cognitive stimuli available for the animals. Many, if not all, of marine mammal interactive programs in the United States utilize classical and operant conditioning techniques based on positive reinforcement. A critical component of this is that the animals are provided with the opportunity to voluntarily participate in training sessions and interactive programming, and likewise are provided with the opportunity to refuse participation, if they so choose. The animals, therefore, regulate the amount of time they spend in interactive programs themselves; training staff simply provide them with multiple opportunities to participate throughout the day. (The inclusion of the 'buffer' areas could potentially benefit this concept further.)

I am in support of regulations that enhance the enclosure environments, or increase the amount of environmental enrichment available to the animals throughout the day. For example, regulations about the amount of shade provided to animals in enclosures, or that animals should have a minimum mandatory amount of time available to explore novel food items, toys, or conspecifics, would be of benefit, in my opinion. 

With respect to the proposed changes in attendant/animal ratios, creating a requirement that there must be at least one attendant per marine mammal in each session and at least one attendant positioned to monitor the session is not necessary, and removes the opportunity for an animal to experience novel scenarios interacting with conspecifics. I am, however, in support of the proposal for at least one attendant being available to monitor each session, much the same way a lifeguard monitors a public pool. 

I would like to thank APHIS for its diligent commitment to animal welfare, and for providing the opportunity for the public to share its opinion on the proposed regulations.
