To Whom it May Concern at the FDA:
Re: Proposed OTC law

The audiologists at the University of Colorado Health Hearing and Balance Clinic do hearby support the issues raised by the American Academy of Audiology regarding the proposed rules/law for Over-the-Counter Hearing Aids. 
• The FDARA specified that the FDA would create a new category of hearing aids specific to OTC; however, the FDA instead has proposed to retain the existing classifications and offer only the distinction of “non-prescription” for OTC devices. 
• The inclusion of an effective and safe gain range (lower and upper limit) requirement is essential for the purposes of patient protection and to ensure that OTC hearing aids are appropriately targeted to individuals with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.
• We encourage the FDA to stipulate that only instant-fit eartips, or custom/semi-custom eartips that were fabricated based on non-invasive scans of the patient’s ears, be used as the forms of coupling between the OTC device and the wearer’s ear canal. In the case where a custom earmold or ear shell would be required, based on current and future techniques that require inserting impression materials or scanners inside the ear canal, the service of a licensed hearing healthcare professional should be required.
• The Hearing and Balance Center encourages the FDA to specify that all OTC hearing aid devices will need 510(k) clearance prior to marketing and sales.
• The Hearing and Balance Center requests that the FDA: 1) define self-fitting in a manner such that it is clear OTC hearing aids must be manipulatable by the general public; and 2) add some requirement that OTC hearing aids be self-fitting.
• For consistency and for maximal consumer protection, the federal regulations should establish the guidance that manufacturers accept returns for OTC hearing aids.
• The Hearing and Balance Center recommends that the labeling for OTC hearing aids include guidance that, for optimal hearing health, the consumer is best served by obtaining a hearing test to confirm the presence and degree of hearing loss. A hearing screening obtained online or through an app or online does not capture the complexities of hearing loss.
• Unclear guidance can open the pathway for a market for OTC devices that are locked by proprietors (i.e., can't be adjusted by the public without special software) and that use rigid fitting patterns. This is a potential predatory company issue and is contradictory to legislative intent for OTC hearing devices. Currently, direct to consumer products often market themselves as programmable yet turn out to be not programmable by the consumer.
• Defaulting to the CTA 2051-2017 (ANSI) Personal Sound Amplification Performance Criteria is not appropriate for a hearing aid. This standard is specifically designed for a consumer product that is for situational use - not full-time use - and is not intended for individuals with hearing loss. Application of this standard jeopardizes patient safety and efficacy.
• The section of the proposed rule pertaining to state pre-emption needs extensive review to ensure that the effort to increase consumer access to OTC hearing aids does not have any adverse impact. The language to pre-empt state regulations would remove layers of state-level protections for consumers, and it is important to make sure that comparable protections are in place, particularly to respond to potential unethical business practices that could spring up around the devices. The FDA could consider new state exemption proposals from federal pre-emption that aim to respond to issues states are observing with respect to consumer and financial protection, and patient safety, as OTC devices enter the market.

Dear Mr. Green, 
I am writing this out of of concern regarding the NOAA proposal to create a Marine Sanctuary in 
Lake Michigan east of Manitowoc, Sheboygan, and Ozaukee Counties. 
 
One provision of the proposal will do irreparable harm to riparian property owners. 
 
The proposed Marine Sanctuary’s shoreline boundary is the Ordinary High Water Mark, thus 
potentially giving public access to the beach. 
 
The Wisconsin State Supreme Court ruled that riparian property owners have exclusive privilege 
from the OHWM to the water’s edge (Doemel v. Jantz, 1923). This overlapping jurisdiction is a 
serious concern to shoreline property owners. At the least it creates confusion of jurisdiction and 
law and a colorable argument for trespassers on our property. I am a shoreline property owner on 
Lake Michigan, in Wisconsin. The amount I paid for my property and the value of my property 
was based upon the settled law in Wisconsin of Doemel v. Jantz. For the Federal Government to 
change this by rule-making would be a taking of my property without compensation nor due 
process. I have no objection to the Sanctuary, but the definition of the border needs to be 
changed to be consistent with established Wisconsin law. 
 
Please note : The shores of Lake Michigan are fragile. Plants and rocks on the beaches are 
essential for the Lake’s stability. The Great Lakes differ from smaller inland lakes in that storms 
widen the beaches, and lake levels change, beyond any recognizable mark. Trespassers, and 
often their dogs, come close to my home. This reduces properties and values. 
 
Given that resources (monies) are scarce, I personally think that money should be allocated to 
cleaning up the water and the shoreline and the invasive species rather than to this. But if you do 
decide to proceed, do not destroy value of all the property owners in so doing. 
 
Sincerely,

I am submitting comments on the Select Agent status of Brucella abortus. I support the removal of B.abortus from the select agent list. My background and connection to this issue is that I am a strong advocate for wild, free-roaming bison (buffalo).

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

Thank you for this opportunity and your consideration of my comments.

As a general comment, it would appear that the Kirtlands Warbler population has been brought above the identified target of 1000 pairs identified in the Kirtlands Warbler Recovery Plan, and that the processes of management planning and action, and silviculture by a consortium of federal and state agencies, and regional NGOs have been brought to bear for controlling brood parasitism by brown-headed cowbirds, and in creating and maintaining an area of jack-pine forest suitable in size and condition for the target population-addressing the threats identified as significant in the Warbler Recovery Plan. 

There are basically two dimensions to population viability; the number of young produced and survival. Survival for Warblers is at highest apparent risk during migration. Production of young occurs in breeding areas. The recovery of this species has focused almost entirely on the enhanced production of young, creating appropriate amounts of the Warblers specialized habitat and controlling the negative effects of brood parasitism by brown-headed cowbirds. While investigations for increasing survival were not explored in this process, they might remain an alternative consideration or option for maintaining population viability, should other circumstances warrant.

There is still limited information about the Warbler on the wintering grounds in the Bahamas where it is difficult to study. However, the increasing population size over the decades on the breeding grounds would suggest that any threats or issues on the wintering grounds or during migration are not significant to population viability, and/or are ameliorated by recovery actions on the breeding grounds. 

On page 15760, under the subheading from previous page Distribution middle column, the concept is projected that the Warbler is spread over a wide-enough area that it is unlikely to experience range-wide catastrophic events. While no imminent threats have (yet) surfaced, I might take issue with this broadly in consideration of the potential for insect and fungal infestations as have been experienced in the Mountain West and Boreal forests (e.g. pine beetle epidemic) in recent decades (Safranyik et al. 2012; The Canadian Entomologist 142:415-442), or the species-specific declines in tree species such as the American Elm (Ulmus americana) and American chestnut (Castanea dentata) in the Northeast, or, most recently, with the hemlocks (Tsuga spp.; Lovett et al 2006; Bioscience 56:395-405), or the potential deterioration of forests that might occur with changing levels of acid rain (Menz and Seip 2004; Environ. Sci. and Policy 7:253-265). That said, the identified insect or fungal threats to jack-pine or red pine are possible to manage, and forests in this region are under the oversight of forest-management agencies. Acid-rain has been a more long-standing issue that has undergone various levels of regulation to control, and with no to limited apparent impact here at this time. While these pose no imminent threat at this time, the Warblers limited range and its concentration in part of this range do not necessarily negate the potential to experience a range-wide catastrophic event. At the same time, the Warbler population is probably at a level at or above historical levels, so may be at a less vulnerable point than historically to these or avian disease outbreaks. 

The expectation of decline with decreased management effort is incorporated into the reasoning to delist. Such is estimated through multiple population modelling exercises; expectations are to be about or less than 1 %/year, still leaving the warbler population above the recovery target after 50 years. Dear Division Director Wester, 

The National Coalition for Infant Health (NCfIH) is a coalition of more than 200 professional, 

clinical, community health, and family support organizations across America focused on 

improving the lives of infants and their families. We are committed to advocating for patient-

centered care for all infants to ensure they are safe, healthy and their families can access the 

information, care and treatment their babies need. 

We at NCfIH write today in full support of swift approval and dissemination of the Center 

for Disease Control and Prevention’s recent draft recommendations: 

• 

• 

for all infants and children born to pregnant women with confirmed or probable hepatitis 

C virus (HCV) infection to receive HCV testing; and 

for referral of certain infants and children to a health care provider with pediatric hepatitis 

C management expertise. 

These new recommendations address the goal of hepatitis C eradication and a pressing public 

health matter for infants in the United States by fostering an earlier linkage to care, evaluation, 

and possible treatment. 

Hepatitis C virus 

According to the CDC, “Hepatitis C is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV). 

Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood from an infected person. Today, most people 

become infected with the hepatitis C virus by sharing needles or other equipment used to prepare 

and inject drugs.” The primary risk factors for young children and infants involve perinatal 

transmission during pregnancy and delivery. HCV causes liver inflammation which may lead to 

other long-term health problems, such as long-term cirrhosis and cancer. 

Rates of HCV infections have increased among adults in the past decade. As CDC mentions in 

the draft, this increase corresponds with the ongoing opioid crisis.

 
Screening to protect infants and children 

Knowledge of perinatal infection of HCV in the United States continues to evolve, as 

demonstrated by the literature referenced throughout the draft recommendations. According to 

the draft for public comment, rates of HCV infections have quadrupled among adults from 2010 

to 2020. It is now understood that approximately 7% of perinatally exposed infants develop an 

HCV infection. 

If perinatally exposed infants are not tested for HCV infection, they are likely not to be referred 

for curative anti-viral therapy which is approved to be administered as early as the age of 3. This 

creates a scenario where some infants are tested and referred for care, while many other infants 

that ought to be tested and referred for care or future follow-up, are not. As such, many infants 

and children with HCV, or those at risk of developing future complications, do not receive 

treatment or referral for a treatable disease. 

Swift approval of guidelines 

The CDC took a significant step in 2020 to address the increase in HCV infections across the 

United States by releasing universal screening guidelines for all adults including pregnant 

women. NCfIH thanks the CDC for those guidelines, which promote access to care and early 

intervention. 

NCfIH supports the swift approval and dissemination of these additional guidelines specific to 

perinatally exposed infants and children. Thank you for your work protecting our public’s health 

and thank you for the opportunity to share our comments. Please do not hesitate to contact us so 

we may answer any questions or provide further information: susan@infanthealth.org.

government and general staff of the Army who wanted the paper, basically, to lie. My 
grandfather fought all those fights successfully to make The Stars and Stripes a paper the 
soldiers trusted. 
Since The Stars and Stripes reemerged in WWII, the paper has continued to fight forces that 
were curtailing its freedom of speech. And now it has to do it again. 
The proposals as published in the Federal Register (Vol. 89, No. 79) will curtail The Stars and 
Stripes' ability to do its intended job: Giving our Armed Services personnel accurate and 
unbiased news. 
1

 
1.) As proposed, reporters may ask questions of DOD officials and may cover events open to 
those with installation access. However, the word "may" denotes permission. It is not 
absolute. As you may know, Stripes' staff are Department of Defense employees and MUST go 
through federal background checks to receive their Common Access Card -- the same card used 
by the military for unclassified areas. By right of that Card, they should have the same rights as 
any other military personnel with the card to the same areas. 
A better word than "may" would be "authorized". 
2)The language regarding FOIA should be changed to allow Stripes' reporters to access 
documents under the FOIA. Stripes journalists, because they are DOD employees, already 
adhere to many policies not required of commercial media and that's fine. However, the 
language regarding FOIA is confusing. 
I suggest the following wording: "DOD shall not use the U.S. government employee status of 
Stripes' reporters to block the release of, or access to, information through the FOIA statute 
provisions of otherwise releasable FOIA information." 
3) Stripes adheres to guidelines that would neither harm national security nor put the lives of 
U.S. military personal at risk. I agree with this statement and I know that it was my 
grandfather's intention NOT to release any information that would help the enemy. The 
decision whether to republish classified or controlled unclassified information that has already 
appeared in other news media must reside with Stripes' editors and publisher, as called for in 
the news organization's independence ordered by Congress. When the rules of federal 
employment conflict with the First Amendment in the U. S. Constitution, the First Amendment 
must prevail. 
Preferred wording would be: "Stars and Stipes can republish, in whole or in part, reports 
already available to or known by the public based on classified or controlled unclassified 
information." 
American citizens' rights need to be protected! 
Very truly yours,

Thanks to FDA for keeping patients safe from hospital acquired infection.

Section VII "Summary of Data Upon Which the Reclassification Is Based," details cases of infection transmission. These involve hundreds of patients around the world over three decades. In many situations, human error facilitated infection transmission.

As well as the cases cited in this FDA guidance, other evidence points to additional cases of disease transmission. In diabetes, notably glucose meters and other materials can used to transmit infection. FDA has rasied concern over clinical use meters. CDC has detailed that test strip containers are one such other means of passing infection from one patient to another. FDA should consider the total risk, not piecemeal responses.

ALL of the evidence presented in the docket is of transmission in professional care facilities. It is clear that healthcare facilities are where FDA should address the problem of lancets infection transmission. Don't fix what isn't broken. The draft presents no evidence to support the proposed up-regulation of personal lancet devices.

I appreciate FDA efforts to protect people in the clinical setting. That is a setting where we, as patients, have no way of knowing if we are getting fresh blades and disinfected devices. In some cases, we may not even be conscious to ask.

FDA's 2013 draft meter guidance is instructive to this docket. While the final guidance is not yet out, the draft made a clear distinction between the setting of professional use and individual over the counter home use. Separating devices based on these environments is a logical precedent to follow with lancets.

FDA should be addressing documented problems. All of the evidence FDA presents is in clinical settings. Therefore, FDA should be using guidance and labeling to address the clinical setting where we need protection and device design that can minimize human factors that contribute to risk.

Section VII shows that multiple patient devices in-clinic use are a particular risk. The proposed up-regulation to class III of such devices is an indication of FDA's appreciation of that risk. FDA should be clear how unique device identifiers will usefully implement with replaceable blade devices and how both components will be tracked.

I support FDA taking reasonable regulatory precautions and labeling steps to guide health care providers to use single patient, one-time use, disposable devices. Specifically, those that have blade protection as outlined in section V part B. Multi-patient devices should discourage through regulatory and labeling measures. FDA should address the real risk of transmission and create a clear delineation that safe, single-use, disposable lancets are the best practice.

Labeling is a tool FDA can use to differentiate between use devices intended for home use and professional settings.

Devices for a single patient, over the counter, with replaceable blades, should carry a black box label NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. One time use disposable lancets, with blade protection as outlined in section V part B, should be labeled APPROVED FOR CLINICAL USE.

Price is a driver of purchasing behavior. Third party purchasers, other than the caregiver and patient, may assume that any FDA-approved device is safe in all settings. Clear labeling, as suggested above, will create an economic liability for clinical purchasing agents and insurance payers who require anything for clinical use but lancet devices explicitly approved for clinical use.

Price driven purchasing is a documented source of safety disruption related to blood testing. The Journal Diabetes Care recently detailed the disruption of testing supplies as a source of increased hospitalization and mortality in diabetes patients served by Medicare. I fear a similar economic driven disruption will occur with lancet access driving use of less expensive devices not intended for clinical settings. FDA labels can protect patients with labels.

The EPAs proposed interpretive statement (EPA-HQ-OW-2019-0166) is not consistent with the language of the Clean Water Act, which forbids polluters from discharging pollutants to navigable waters without a permit. 

The purpose of the Clean Water Act is to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nations waters. This proposed interpretation thwarts that purpose by unlawfully exempting pollution that passes through groundwater. 

The water my family and neighbors drink, play in, and live near must not be polluted with sewage or heavy metals. The effects of pollutants that reach our rivers, lakes and oceans through groundwater are serious and long-lasting: Aquatic life dies, ecosystems fall apart, and our communities get sick.

Clean water is a fundamental right, and its the job of EPA to protect it. Abandon the proposed interpretive statement (EPA-HQ-OW-2019-0166) and continue to regulate discharges that pollute our nations rivers, lakes and oceans through groundwater.

We are writing in regards to your request for comments concerning the decision to cease funding for the Deaf Self-Advocacy Training (DSAT) initiative and deaf interpreting at the end of the current cycle. New RSA priorities describe three new specializations areas for four grant awards: 1) training interpreters to work with deaf individuals with dysfluent language, 2) interpreters to work in trilingual, and 3) field-initiated training specializations. The last grant cycle requires deaf consumer training, but is silent on the subject. We are expressing our support for identifying DSAT as the forth specialization.

As a national service provider to secondary and postsecondary institutions, pepnet 2 (pn2) is acutely aware of the critical role self-advocacy skills play in the success of deaf, hard of hearing and deaf-blind (DHH) youth as they move through educational and employment settings. PN2's mission is to collect and disseminate promising and evidence-based practices to agencies and institutions to increase the educational, career and lifetime choices available to their DHH students. The evidence is clear: students who demonstrate strong self-advocacy skills have enhanced educational and personal outcomes .

It is essential that postsecondary institutions are capable of providing effective self-advocacy training to their DHH students. Unfortunately, many hearing providers are still not aware of the unique self-advocacy challenges facing DHH students as they transition to and from postsecondary settings. It is critical that a person who is culturally and linguistically competent is available to provide specialized trainings to DHH individuals - particularly for those who lack fluency in English or have idiosyncratic language skills. 

As DHH students transition to postsecondary settings, self-advocacy is an indispensable skill, according to pn2's Needs Assessment. Yet a study in the Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education found that one of the major deficits in mainstream secondary schools was related to inadequate preparation for transition ). Post-high school, the onus to determine educational access needs falls on the student because s/he is no longer eligible for IEP services under IDEA. After years of being provided with access services in primary and secondary schools, postsecondary students are expected to be able to identify their preferred accommodations, make appropriate requests, and advocate for themselves. Yet, few are taught to do so.
Self-advocacy is equally important for DHH individuals transitioning to employment or other postsecondary settings. PN2's research and experience shows specific discussions about accommodations in the workplace are needed and may have a positive effect on employment outcomes. Yet, very few students receive instruction on these self-advocacy skills. Most have only a rudimentary knowledge of their basic legal rights and many have been sheltered without the opportunity or confidence to develop these skills. DSAT is one of the few projects funded by RSA that has a direct tie to enhanced employment outcomes. DSAT also creates jobs for deaf individuals as trainers in secondary and post-secondary education, in community-based agencies and in private practice. The project strengthens the capabilities of deaf interpreters and their ability to secure employment in the interpreting field.
PN2 research shows DHH students need direct instruction to build a strong self-advocacy foundation - incidental learning is not enough. They profit from learning negotiation and assertiveness strategies, and the ability to compromise, particularly with people in positions of power. Students need a targeted, practical focus on how legal rights both change and are applicable to a variety of postsecondary settings. They also need practice with a range of accommodations so they know exactly what their needs are. Training on these skills are almost non-existent at the primary and secondary levels.

I am writing to provide my input on the proposed management and protection of the National Petroleum Reserve: Alaska (NPR-A). As a concerned citizen, I strongly urge the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to prioritize robust measures that not only consider the preservation of the reserve but also take into account the well-being of indigenous populations, the local and global impact on ecosystems, and the significant implications for greenhouse gas emissions.

As a global citizen, I recognize the interconnectedness of our planet's ecosystems and the far-reaching implications of actions taken in one region. The proposed drilling for oil in Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve has repercussions that extend beyond local boundaries. The environmental consequences, such as increased greenhouse gas emissions and potential ecological disturbances, contribute to the broader challenges of climate change. These impacts, though originating in Alaska, have cascading effects on weather patterns, sea levels, and overall environmental stability that can affect communities worldwide. Furthermore, the continued reliance on fossil fuels perpetuates a cycle of environmental degradation, impacting the air we breathe and the climate we share. Therefore, I believe it is essential for the Bureau of Land Management to consider the global implications of drilling in the NPR-A and prioritize sustainable, environmentally responsible practices for the benefit of our interconnected world.

Indigenous Populations
The NPR-A is home to diverse indigenous communities, including the Inupiaq people, whose traditional practices and ways of life are deeply intertwined with the land. It is crucial that any management plan acknowledges and respects the rights and needs of these communities. The BLM should engage in meaningful consultation with indigenous stakeholders to ensure their voices are heard, and their cultural and subsistence practices are adequately protected.

Local and Global Ecosystem Impact
Drilling for oil in the NPR-A has the potential to cause irreparable damage to local ecosystems, disrupting wildlife habitats and threatening biodiversity. The delicate balance of the Arctic environment, already vulnerable to climate change, requires careful consideration to prevent long-lasting harm. Additionally, the global impact of continued reliance on petroleum extracted from such reserves should be acknowledged. The BLM should prioritize sustainable management practices that minimize the ecological footprint of oil extraction and explore alternative energy sources to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels.

Greenhouse Gas Emissions
The commodification of petroleum from the NPR-A contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions, exacerbating the global climate crisis. It is imperative that the BLM takes into account the full lifecycle emissions associated with oil extraction, processing, and consumption. Incorporating renewable energy solutions and transitioning to cleaner energy alternatives should be central to any management plan to mitigate the environmental impact and address the urgent need for climate action.

Statistics and Scientific Evidence
I urge the BLM to base its decisions on the latest scientific evidence and reliable statistics regarding the environmental, social, and economic impacts of oil drilling in the NPR-A. Transparent and accessible information will enable informed decision-making and foster public trust in the management process.

In conclusion, I request that the BLM adopts a comprehensive and sustainable management plan for the NPR-A that prioritizes the protection of indigenous rights, preserves local and global ecosystems, and addresses the pressing issue of greenhouse gas emissions. Thank you for considering my comments, and I trust that the BLM will act responsibly in safeguarding the NPR-A for future generations.

Currently, technical assistance on disproportionality, including significant disproportionality, is available to states through at least three OSEP funded technical assistance centers – IDEA Data Center (IDC), National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), and Center for IDEA Fiscal Reporting (CIFR). While additional technical assistance around disproportionality may be needed, it would be best to keep the technical assistance under the existing centers rather than add another center. Adding an additional center is not a good use of taxpayer funds in that it is not effective or efficient - creating a new TA center requires funds for start-up and overhead; many of the existing centers already share personnel; and states will have to manage additional center contacts and webinars that overlap in both content and timing. As an example of the content overlap, it is impossible to separate the calculations for disproportionality from the data itself. IDC provides technical assistance to states on the collection, reporting, and use of child count, educational environments, and discipline data that are then used in the calculations for disproportionality. It would be a far better use of taxpayer dollars to expand the technical assistance on disproportionality currently offered by IDC, NCSI, and CIFR than to add on an additional center. 
 
If an additional center is deemed necessary, their scope of work should include all areas of disproportionality, including SPP/APR indicators 4, 9, and 10. Confusion between the required methodologies would only be exacerbated by having one center focused exclusively on significant disproportionality.
 
The Directed Questions request information about common challenges or barriers experienced by SEAs and LEAs regarding significant disproportionality, and how the investment in a new center could address them. The basic challenge at both the SEA and LEA levels is the differences in requirements for SPP/APR Indicators 4, 9, and 10, compared to significant disproportionality. Existing centers have developed and disseminated technical assistance in this area. Again, more assistance would be helpful, but not to the extent of needed an additional center. 
 
The second and third directed questions ask about supports for conducting the review of policies, procedures, and practices in LEAs as well as the root cause analysis. Here again, existing centers have created toolkits and provided technical assistance to both SEAs and LEAs in these areas.
 
The fourth directed question asks about the supports needed by SEAs to conduct the analysis of significant disproportionality. Technical assistance has been available to states in many forms through the existing centers. 
 
Finally, the fifth directed question asks about supports needed regarding CCEIS. Again, technical assistance is currently available in this area through CIFR and other TA centers.
 
In summary, technical assistance is readily available through several existing centers, several of which already share personnel and/or collaborate on the creation and provision of assistance to states. The creation of a new technical assistance center would, in theory, consolidate the resources, but at the cost of the additional overhead of a new center, and additional contacts and possibly redundant offerings to states that can become burdensome to manage and coordinate.

The concern is not with considerate users, but the exception - the inconsiderate user.

There are already too many instances where passenger misbehavior contributes to an unpleasant, tense atmosphere in a tight, no-exit environment. A loud and/or long conversation is one of the most invasive breaches of social etiquette there is and would certainly, and regularly, exacerbate an already uncomfortable situation. Passengers already make ready use of texting and email for 'critical' communications during flights with minimum disruption to other passengers.

Please listen to the concerns of flight attendants and other professionals who feel similarly. They already have enough trouble maintaining a civil, safe cabin environment without attempting to be heard over cell phone conversations, or getting callers' attention.

I am strongly in favor of letting the markets decide most commercial matters. However, this is a matter of basic safety, like the frequency of maintenance schedules, and cannot be the subject of a product strategy. 

Thank you for your consideration.
Mark Lohr

Comments on Proposed Changes to Individual Assistance Declaration Factors

 Clarification is needed on exactly how fiscal capacity will be formulated. Especially how TTR, GDP and per capita personal income by local area will be weighted in determining a disaster declaration.
o The two year lag in TTR data causes the current fiscal capacity of the state to be inaccurate. 
 Greater clarity is needed concerning how VOAD capabilities will be weighted.
o FEMA must define how the capacity of the volunteer agencies are determined. 
From year to year Volunteer Organizations Active in Disaster resources can change dramatically. Depending upon the number of active disasters at the time, there may be grant funding available and plentiful volunteers. However, this year in particular, we have experienced a shortage of volunteers mainly due to large disasters occurring in other parts of the nation. Donations are being made to high profile disaster areas leaving VOADs locally with little financial resources to provide for unmet needs. A state's capacity to recover should not be based on past VOAD/NGO data when availability of these resources are unpredictable. 

FEMA will consider private resources that could potentially be available. 
o In 2008 & 2012, Indiana received a Lilly Foundation grant due to the magnitude of the disaster events. Grants are usually made for specific purposes. A grant should have no bearing on the fiscal capacity of a state. Nor should it be considered a part of the resources available to assist in recovery. Generally, such grants are rarely made available. A state has no authority to direct NGOs to provide funding.
FEMA will consider state and local resiliency efforts.
The state and local governments have ongoing mitigation projects. FEMA must define how resiliency will be measured and weighted in the declaration determination process.

FEMA must define "technically qualified" individuals who will conduct damage assessments.
o Individuals performing damage assessments require proper training and an in-depth understanding of the specific damage they will assess. The individuals should be certified to perform their assessment role. 

FEMA will use the post-disaster unemployment as a measure.
o Post-disaster unemployment is certainly an impact, however pre-disaster unemployment is equally important. Above average unemployment exists in certain areas of every state. When disaster strikes these areas it has greater impact on the communities. FEMA must continue to include pre-disaster unemployment as a consideration in the overall demographics and impact data.

Thank you for the opportunity to offer comments on Proposed Priorities, Requirements, Definitions, and Selection Criteria-Comprehensive Centers Program. We’d like to focus our comments on section 4, Strengthening and Supporting the Educator Workforce. 

We’re glad to see this area of focus included, as it is such an urgent need in the field. We also appreciate that the proposed guidelines acknowledge that States and LEAs need to create new systems of support for educators and technical support in both designing and scaling those systems. 

As the Department of Education works to achieve academic excellence and improve learning conditions as part of the “Raise the Bar” initiative, it’s imperative to recognize how much of US students’ instructional time is currently spent with substitute teachers. The need to create new systems to address the current reality of school staffing is especially evident for substitute teachers as chronic under-investment in the preparation, integration, and ongoing development of subs has resulted in inconsistent (and insufficient) learning experiences for students. This has become particularly evident as the need for substitute teachers has increased. We recommend including language that clarifies that the focus on strengthening and supporting the educator workforce includes all educators responsible for instruction, including substitute teachers and other uncertificated teachers. 

Here’s why:

- For many students, these are the only teachers that they will have. 
Substitute teachers are essential educators, responsible for a growing share of instruction. Pre-pandemic, the average student spent about 10% of their time with substitute teachers. Limited research is available to demonstrate the post-pandemic increase, but evidence suggests that subs are now needed 20-25% of the time. Put another way, on any given day, one in five of the educators in America’s classrooms are subs (or teachers/admins/coaches filling in because schools couldn’t get a sub). Of course, that number varies significantly by district. We’ve spoken to communities where teachers on substitute licenses are serving in most (or all) of their classrooms. And, there’s a disproportionate impact on our most vulnerable students – Title 1 schools are more likely to need substitute teachers because of both vacancy patterns and teacher absence patterns. They are also less likely to get substitute teachers because of how interim staffing is designed – substitutes typically have choice in where and when they work, and while many factors go into those individual choices, the result is that Title 1 schools have less reliable sub coverage. 

- Substitutes typically don’t receive any training. 
Subs have historically received almost no training or ongoing professional learning. A recent survey found that 89% of school districts did not provide substitute teachers with training in the skills they need in the classroom, such as classroom management or instructional skills. Just 6% of school districts offer ongoing professional learning for subs. It’s especially urgent to create robust - and highly practical - systems of training and support for substitute teachers in long-term assignments. Many of these subs are covering vacancies, fully stepping into the role of a teacher to provide instruction for students, but they lack the preparation and ongoing support of their credentialed (or on-track-to-credential) counterparts. They are disconnected from all of our systems for teacher preparation, induction, and ongoing professional learning.

-Substitutes support teacher well-being. 
Seventy-seven percent of school districts report that it’s more difficult than before the pandemic to find a substitute teacher, and 59% report very frequently not having enough subs. Dear Secretary Vilsack,

roadside zoos, and research facilities throughout the country. At this time, USDA does not require that

disaster – placing both animals and staff at risk.

animal will be left behind when disaster strikes.

Dear Mr. Michel: 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary’s 
(MBNMS) General Management Plan Update and Proposed Rule-making. The National Park 
Service (NPS) suggests for your consideration some minor changes to the proposed regulatory 
language that will allow more flexibility for using suitable sediment for beach nourishment, near-
shore placement, and other restoration projects. 
 
The NPS supports the placement of clean, suitable sediment for beneficial use in properly 
designed beach nourishment projects. These projects can restore beach habitat that have been lost 
as imbalances of the natural sediment supply to the coast, historical shoreline development, and 
use of hard coastal armoring structures that change how sediment moves. The MBNMS General 
Management Plan and Environmental Assessment (GMP/EA) assess the clear benefits of using 
suitable sediments for habitat restoration within the MBNMS. However, the proposed rule-
making language limits the dredged material source to just four harbors in the MBNMS when 
there are likely many other suitable sources available in the north-central California coastal 
region. Further, the proposed language restricts beneficial use to beach restorations. There are 
other potential uses such as near-shore placement and wave attenuation projects. Placement of 
suitable sediments within the MBNMS promotes nature-based solutions to coastal erosion that 
protect and restore habitat, protect structures, reduce the proliferation of coastal armoring, and 
directly benefit the MBNMS and its neighbors. As coastal erosion increases with a changing 
climate from increased storm intensity to sea level rise, it is likely that suitable sediment will be 
in greater demand along the coasts, so maintaining flexibility in sourcing is key to a ready 
supply.

 
The beneficial use of suitable sediment is not a controversial regulatory action and is supported 
by pertinent state and federal regulatory and resource management agencies, as well as the 
general public. The current proposed language is too restrictive to meet current and future project 
needs that would otherwise be appropriate for implementation under NEPA and other statues and 
regulations within the MBNMS.

I support the U.S. Food and Drug Administrations (FDAs) efforts to strengthen the stewardship of antibiotics in animal agriculture by bringing all medically important antibiotics used in food animals under veterinary oversight. Veterinarians have unique training to determine when an antibiotic is needed to address an illness and which drug, dosage, and duration is likely best. Veterinarians must oversee any use of antibiotics important for human health because such use can contribute to the emergence of resistant bacteria. Ensuring veterinarians have appropriate oversight is a logical, important and easy-to-implement step that should not take years to carry out. 

Given the urgency of the threat of antibiotic resistance, it is simply unacceptable to delay appropriate veterinary oversight any further. Nobody should be allowed to use these lifesaving drugs without adequate involvement of a veterinarian. Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed NEPA rule changes presented in Federal Register Number 2019- 12195. These comments are submitted on behalf of the Sierra Club, Missouri Chapter. Our chapter has over 10,000 members in Missouri, all of whom value public lands in our state and across the country. 

The Mark Twain National Forest, located in Missouri, is fragmented, interspersed with private lands, other public ownerships and impacts from past mining. Thus, the interface with these areas is an added potential impact when evaluating USFS projects. 

The Proposed Rule document would exclude the public from heretofore required notice and offer of input to many activities which could significantly impact forest users, adjacent landowners and the ecological integrity of the forest. Projects such as mining operations with land disturbance of less than 640 acres, projects converting unauthorized off-road vehicle trails to FS roads, and commercial timber projects harvesting up to 4200 acres could all be imposed on the forest with no request for public input (scoping) and limited decision documentation. (see changes at Section 220.7, 220.5 (e), 220.5 (23)).

While it is commendable for an agency to propose rule changes which will enable it to complete its mission with increased efficiency, many of the changes proposed would not achieve that. 
In fact, the agency argues that the proposed rule is needed because the USFS is spending too much time and money on fire fighting and the agency overall has not enough funds or staff. Thus, in response the agency plans to cut the public out of up to 90% of its work. This is hardly a recipe to engender public support for what it really needs, more dollars and staff. The agency is clearly admitting it is proposing this rule out of what it claims is desperate necessity, not as a way to fulfill its NEPA requirements. 

Many USFS projects are complex and may impact multiple known stakeholders as well as the general public. Yet the agency seems to want no help in making decisions. Does the agency think that excluding the public from notice and input regarding potentially controversial projects will make things easier? NEPA should not operate in a vacuum that excludes the public. NEPA process is designed to invite input so as to address impacts, options and alternatives which are not readily apparent. NEPA is a process, not just a stamp used to rationalize actions. 

The proposed rule removes scoping requirement from all but EIS projects. Just posting an action on the Schedule of Projects (SOPA) website page and then reserving the right to consider, or not, any feedback is a poor way to manage public lands. 

 Why, for example, are state listed endangered species not included in extraordinary circumstances to apply when considering using a categorical exclusion? (220.5 (b) 

The rule does preserve the full EIS process, including scoping, for the Forest Plan process. Public participation in the Forest Planning process is valuable and essential for a good plan. But as the agency knows, it is when management prescription-based site-specific projects are proposed that many people have valuable input. Forest users may have particular experience and history via hiking, hunting, floating etc. in a project area. They may have valuable input and concerns to share, and the agency should not shut them out. But the proposed rule will. 

The Sierra Club Missouri Chapter has, over the years, commented on many projects in the MTNF including timber sales, ORV trails, prescribed burnings and more. We participate in MTNFs Collaborative Gathering workshops and one member has applied to the MTNF Resource Advisory Committee. We welcome many ways to be involved. But we fear that the USFS is backing out of its NEPA responsibilities. It will become more difficult to assume the good faith of any agency process if it does not fulfill its responsibilities through this landmark legislation.

Our organizations have repeatedly urged the Department of the Treasury to use its administrative authority

called for Treasury to revise the proposed definition to make clear that at least children and family members 
would be eligible for subsidized exchange coverage if the cost of family-based insurance – not just individual 
coverage – exceeds 9.5 percent of household income.2 Despite these objections, IRS finalized the policy in 2013 
(78 FR 7264), with an interpretation inconsistent with the text and intent of the ACA, thereby creating the 
“family glitch.” 
 
Children are disproportionately impacted by the family glitch—more than half of the 5 million people who are 
locked out of subsidized coverage are children. 3 Through no fault of their own, children have suffered the 
consequences of this incorrect regulatory interpretation of the ACA, which considers whether family coverage 
is “affordable” based only on the cost to cover the employee. While most employers offer family-based

workers and their families. Data from the Kaiser Family Foundation’s Employer Health Benefits Survey shows 
that in 2021, the average annual employee contribution for employee-only coverage was $1,299, while the 
average contribution for family coverage was $5,969.4 Consequently, nearly half a million people go uninsured 
when faced with unaffordable coverage under a family member’s employer plan.5 Workers in small businesses 
are also impacted as they are more likely to face higher premiums for family coverage. Five percent of covered

Re: Requirements for Additional Traceability Records for Certain Foods; Compliance Date Extension – FDA-2014-N-0053-1330

To whom it may concern:

On behalf of the Global Cold Chain Alliance (GCCA) and our members, we appreciate the opportunity to comment on FDA’s proposal to extend the compliance date for the Food Traceability Rule under Section 204 of the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA). 

GCCA represents more than 1,500 member companies in 92 countries who provide third-party, temperature-controlled logistics and supply chain services. Our members are critical to ensuring safe, high-quality, and reliable access to food worldwide, and the majority operate FDA-registered facilities. 

We reiterate our longstanding position that traceability requirements must be clear, achievable, and sufficiently flexible to adapt to evolving supply chain practices and technology innovation. This rule adds significant complexity to transport and warehousing operations. The requirement for multiple actors to capture Critical Tracking Events (CTEs) and differing Key Data Elements (KDEs) for similar products risks imposing unnecessary burdens that go further than necessary in ensuring incident identification and fast product recalls. 

We strongly support FDA’s proposal to extend the compliance date, because it provides a significant opportunity to refine how the rule will work in practice, especially through development of guidance to ensure data standards are workable for all parties. 

We urge FDA to use this extended period to lead structured, collaborative pilot projects. These pilots are essential to test real-world scenarios across every part of the supply chain, including the cold chain and third-party logistics (3PL) providers, so that practical challenges are fully represented. Without such pilots, there is a risk that compliance efforts will not actually enhance traceability. 

The flow of products through temperature-controlled facilities is inherently complex. Our members often receive and ship multiple food products on the Food Traceability List daily, with ownership and responsibility for records changing hands frequently. These complexities underscore the need for FDA to coordinate closely with industry rather than leaving the burden on a complex web of companies to organize workable systems. 

The additional time provided by the compliance date extension must be used effectively to ensure covered entities thoroughly assess the operational impact of the rule, address irregularities in data capture and exchange, and implement workable software solutions. Third-party logistics providers rely on proprietary Warehouse Management Systems (WMS) and Transport Management Systems (TMS), which must interface with varied customer systems, usually using different data formats. 

We urge FDA to produce prescriptive guidance that covers verification of Key Data Elements (KDEs), ensuring that systems can capture and validate data consistently with clear expectations for verification will be key to addressing this challenge. In addition, FDA must support the standardization of data elements by promoting the use of identifiers such as Global Location Numbers (GLN) or Food Facility Registration (FFR) numbers, and by implementing a standardized lot code nomenclature to ensure consistency across the supply chain from beginning to end. 

GCCA and our members remain committed to advancing food safety and stand ready to participate in pilots, share operational realities, and collaborate with FDA to ensure the success of the Food Traceability Rule. 

Thank you for your consideration of these comments. We would be pleased to address any questions you may have.

Sincerely,

appropriate for all situations. It is our opinion that the decision regarding where to draw the line between providing off label 
information to medical practitioners and withholding it depends critically upon: 1) the severity and prognosis of the illness; 
2) the risk-benefit profile of the treatment; and 3) the availability and risk profile of other treatments.

We recognize the complexity of the real world situation, the potential conflicts of interest involving commercial interests, and 
the value of having a single approach and set of guidelines. However, there are also clearly some patient populations which 
would benefit from off label communication between their physicians and medical product manufacturers, and in which the 
cost and complexity of doing an RCT to achieve approval is not feasible for ethical and/or financial reasons.

Revenue Service (“IRS”) for comments regarding the provisions contained in the proposed Update 
to Minimum Present Value Requirements for Defined Benefit Plan Distributions (the “proposed 
regulations”)1 and to request the opportunity to testify at the March 7, 2017 hearing on this subject. 
Our testimony will address the points made in this comment letter. 
ERIC’s Interest in the Minimum Present Value Requirements 
ERIC is the only national association that advocates exclusively for large employers on health, 
retirement, and compensation public policies at the federal, state, and local levels. ERIC’s 
members provide comprehensive retirement benefits to tens of millions of active and retired 
workers and their families. ERIC has a strong interest in proposals, such as the proposed rule, that 
would affect its members’ ability to provide predictable and secure pension benefits in an efficient 
and tax-compliant manner. 
Predictability and stability are cornerstones of the voluntary pension system for both plan sponsors 
and participants. This is particularly true when it comes to defined benefit plans, most of which are 
either closed to new participants or frozen for all participants. Regulatory guidance that creates 
uncertainty or introduces new risk can drive plan sponsors further away from offering important

Comments: To make changes in the Quality Systems Verification Program 7 CFR Part 62 that would allow 

approved service providers to conduct USDA PVP verifications. 

Proposal: That USDA AMS Livestock and Poultry Program (L&P) provide accreditation to private entities 

(Approved USDA PVP Service Providers, here referred to as “Certification Bodies CB”) to certify companies to 

the USDA QAD 1001 USDA Process Verified Program using the current USDA ISO/IEC Guide 65/17065 

Program listed on the USDA AMS website at: https://www.ams.usda.gov/services/auditing/iso-guide65. 

The QAD 1012 Procedure outlines the general requirements of the USDA ISO/IEC Program and indicates that 

this program is available to U.S. and international certification bodies (CB) that perform certification for 

livestock, meat, seed, and other agricultural products and services. 

As required by QAD 1012 the certification body (CB) would identify the QAD 1001 Process Verified Program 

as the standard/scope they are seeking accreditation for. Upon accreditation of the CB, USDA AMS would 

allow the CB to issue a USDA Process Verified Program approval as outlined in the QAD 1000 and 1001 

procedures or allow product certified to the USDA PVP by the CB to enter the USDA PVP as certified with no 

further requirements. It should be noted that this would be the same process the USDA National Organic 

Program uses for their Accredited Certifying Agents under 7 CFR Part 205:501 General requirements for 

accreditation. 

Background: Currently AMS LP QAD conducts verification audits of approved service providers using the 

QAD 1001 and ISO 19011 as an auditing guideline to conduct the audits. AMS L&P QAD uses the 

International Organization for Standardization's (ISO) 9000 series standards for documented quality 

management systems as a format for evaluating USDA Process Verified Program documentation to ensure 

consistent auditing practices and promote international recognition of audit results. These audits are 

conducted yearly and include several field audits. The more appropriate ISO standard to use for CB’s 

accreditation would be the ISO 17065 since that includes requirements that focus on making certification 

decisions as well as management of impartiality along with a number of other certification specific 

requirements. 

Several international bodies, including ANSI use the ISO 17065 as the minimum standard when they are 

conducting accreditation activities. GlobalGap, BRC, GFSI are just a few that make this a requirement. The 

underlying standard for the NOP 7 CFR Part 205.501 was based on ISO Guide 65. Validus, a division of 

Where Food Come From, is currently audited yearly by ANSI using the ISO 17065 as the baseline standard for 

the GFSI SQF requirement. 

USDA AMS L&P would also provide USDA PVP mandatory training to the private CB’s program 

representative(s) at least once per year. All marketing claims would be pre-approved by USDA AMS L&P as it 

currently is the practice. 

Changes requested in QAD documents: QAD 1012 and associated checklist would need to be updated to 

reflect these changes. QAD 1000 and 1001 would also need to be updated to allow the option for entities other 

than AMS L&P QAD to conduct the audits and make the certification decisions.

 
Changes that would need to be made in the 7 CFR Part 62 Quality Systems Verification Program. 7 CFR Part 

62 Quality Systems Verification Program are very minor. 

The definition in the rule lists 

Accreditation - The action or process of officially recognizing an entity as being qualified to perform a specific 

activity(s). 

This would allow an entity to conduct USDA Process Verified Program activities and should be expanded to make 

that statement. 

Auditor – Person authorized or accredited to conduct official audits or assessments. 

This should allow someone or an audit program that is accredited by AMS to conduct the audit.

I am commenting to oppose the proposed rule changes for asylum application. I believe that extending the wait period to apply for a work-permit would be detrimental to asylum seekers - who by definition are fleeing persecution - and cause further challenges for communities and local and state governments that support asylum seekers when they are unable to work.

Currently asylum seekers have to wait 150 days after their applications have been filed to apply for a work permit. I understand that under the proposed rule, the wait time would be a full year, and asylum seekers who do not enter through an official port of entry would need to wait until their asylum case is granted to work. The courts processing asylum cases are incredibly backlogged, and if asylum seekers had to wait until their cases were approved, they could be waiting years. How are they supposed to support themselves for a whole year, or for many years, if they cannot work? This would place additional hardship on people who fled violence and persecution and who are unlikely to have money to support themselves. I have known a few families of asylum seekers from Central America. They were fleeing death threats, and some had family members who had been killed or disappeared. They came to the U.S. out of fear and necessity. U.S. families helped to shelter and feed them until they obtained work permits. Obtaining work permits and subsequently work, enabled them to be independent. They have worked incredibly hard to support themselves. One has years of experience working with victims of human rights violations. She now puts that experience to use working at a shelter for migrant unaccompanied minors, helping others adjust to a new culture and life. 

The United States has a long history of protecting refugees and asylum seekers, and the right to work is
an important part of those humanitarian protections. Through the ability to work, refugees and asylum seekers are able to connect and give back to the communities that they are now a part of in the U.S. If they are not allowed to work, U.S communities lose out on much that asylum seekers and refugees have to offer.

I urge the USDA to adopt the strongest possible standards of care for birds used in commercial enterprises and for wild-caught birds used for research. It is unconscionable that for the past 50 years these animals have been denied coverage under the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) and that--even after a court ruled against this exclusion--the department dragged its feet for 20 years. The number of investigations by animal welfare organizations for cruel treatment by bird breeders and others during this time is only the tip of the iceberg of the suffering that could have been avoided had the USDA acted sooner. Now the USDA is finally initiating efforts to promulgate regulations to protect birds under the AWA.

Birds are disappearing more every year. Something needs too be done now.

There should be no double standard when it comes to protecting birds; they should receive the same level of oversight as other animals covered by the AWA, regardless of other laws that may apply to birds. Regulations regarding their welfare should include the following basic elements: 

1. No sale of unweaned or prematurely weaned baby birds. These young, fragile birds are at great risk of succumbing to disease, mishandling, and the extreme hazards of transport. 

2. Environmental enrichment for all birds. Achieving the AWA's goal of ensuring "humane care and treatment" requires that species-specific physical and psychological needs of birds be met. 

3. Health certificates and record keeping for all birds. Records (including but not limited to acquisition and disposition of the birds) and disease testing are essential to prevent disease transmission and illegal trade in wild-caught birds. 

4. Enclosures that enable the birds to express normal behavior, including flight. Confinement in cages causes poor welfare in birds and can lead to destructive habits, including feather plucking. Birds need to be able to fly and express other natural behaviors. The USDA should adopt enforceable standards that don't rely solely on subjective assessments. 

5. No painful physical mutilations. Pinioning (severing of wing muscles or amputation of wings), toe clipping, devoicing, and beak alterations are examples of painful procedures that are typically done for the convenience of keepers and are extremely detrimental to the welfare of the birds. 

6. Coverage of all bird species. There is no justification for exempting certain species because they are addressed in other laws such as the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Many animals covered by the AWA are regulated under state or other federal laws, and such laws do not nullify their protections under the AWA. The same should be true for birds. The ESA does not ensure humane care and treatment.

There are several good components to this proposal in addition to the noble goals:

1) The captitated payment for CKD stage 4 care recognizes the disparity between nephrologist compensation for clinic care (i.e. good nephrologists get paid the least) and inpatient/dialysis care. If done correctly, this should achieve several goals simultaneously: delaying progression of kidney disease, less "crash" hospital admissions, and more effort devoted to dialysis education and preparation which should lead to more home dialysis.
2) The recognition that nephrologist compensation plays a huge role in the current state of home dialysis in the US.
3) The recognition of the superiority of pre-emptive transplantation to our current practice and rewarding preemptive transplantation

However, I have some concerns about the implementation:

A. Not all of the stakeholders are held accountable in this model. 
 1. The OPOs and hospitals that perform transplants are not impacted by these rules. Transplant is enormously profitable to both. They have no incentive to change their behavior. Since many hospitals control the administration of the transplant programs, the transplant physicians often little direct input into decisions and allocation of resources. Subjecting their payment to a change with preemptive transplantation will help allocation of resources for physicians to achieve more preemptive transplant
 2. The ACGME has not held nephrology training programs accountable for their lack of producing nephrologists competent in home dialysis modalities. Many of these programs are major academic research institutions who have close relationships with CMS, NIDDK, ASN, etc. They do not view their role as training nephrologists competent in home dialysis therapies. CMS pays for post-graduate training and having some accountability to the practice of the nephrologists who training programs graduate may change this behavior
 3. It is extremely difficult to find a good surgeon to place PD catheters. Based on Medicare claims data, it appears that less than 80% of PD catheters actually work after placement (based on claims of catheter insertion, removal and repositioning). PD does not work without a functioning PD access. Giving interventional nephrologists an increased reimbursement for performing this procedure successfully may change behavior. Incentivizing interventional radiologists and laprascopic surgeons to successfully place PD catheters without complications will help also.
 4. It is extremely hard to compete as a smaller dialysis provider or a new dialysis provider. Innovation often comes from this type of competition. CMS has allowed dialysis to experience "regulatory capture." 
 5. New technology is extremely hard to introduce to the dialysis space. In order to achieve the goals of the executive order, we need new technology. Incentivizing this behavior will help.

 B. The idea of randomizing the 306 HRR for 6 years is a great idea. However, I think the methodology is too complex and the reward/penalty is probably not enough to significantly change behavior. I would simplify this: 1) put all of the risk/benefit on the nephrologist 2) Do a time-work study to figure out how nephrologists spend their time managing dialysis. So because of the allocation change, nephrologists in the larger city will be rewarded without actually changing their behavior.

The board and the membership of Little People of America (LPA), the world's oldest and largest dwarfism support organization for people with dwarfism and their families, is strongly in favor of the Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) of the United States Department of Agriculture's (USDA) proposal to revise the United States Standards for Grades of Shelled Pecans and Grades of Pecans in the Shell by subsituting the term "midget" with "extra small". 

On May 13, 2013, AMS received a letter from the Little People of America stating that we "are trying to raise awareness around and eliminate the use of the word 'midget'." The letter further stated that, "Though the use of the word midget by the USDA when classifying certain food products is benign, Little People of America, and the dwarfism community, hopes that the USDA would consider phasing out the term midget." We are thankful that the USDA, an institution of leadership, appreciates that using an insulting word as part of a description for a food product is never appropriate and is changing this long tradition. 

The word "midget" is used as a derogatory slur to refer to people of short stature. Whether or not the intention of using the word is to bully and to demean, or just as a synonym for small, the term has been deemed a slur. In a recent organizational statement, LPA put forward a call to action to eliminate this word from agricultural nomenclature and to replace it with synonymous designations. We are pleased that these changes have already been implemented in the standards for raisins. This proposal by the AMS for another food product further supports this call and is a model for other entities that use the word "midget" in their designations.

EPA can't approve the single source order into the state implementation plan because it does not comply with EPA's definition of Reasonably Available Control Technology. As laid out in the order, the limits the source is subject to are 2 lbs VOC/lb solids for topcoats, 2.3 lbs VOC/ lb solids for sealers, and 0.8 lbs VOC/ lb solids for strippable booth coatings. However, as laid out in the order the source is able to meet much lower limits. Table 1 of the order shows that the source has current emission rates of 1.1 lb VOC/ lb solids for topcoats. As defined by EPA, RACT is the lowest achieveable limit able to be met using technologically and economically feasible controls. In this case the source is able to meet a lower limit than that which is specified in the order. The source's emission rate is 1.1 lbs VOC/lb solid, but the RACT limit being set is 2.0 lbs VOC/ lb solids. This cannot be approved to meet RACT for this faciltiy because it is not the LOWEST emission limit. In addition EPA should not be approving sections of the order that involve SIP approved rules as these rules are already incorporated into the sip and are redundant. By allowing sip approved rules to be in the order epa will create a situation whereby the state will eventually change it's rules and thus the source will be subject to dueling requirements which will require the state and the source to undergo further SIP changes and regulatory uncertainty.

As to Env-A-900, EPA should not approve this rule into the SIP untill the state clarifies the applicability section of this rule. In sections 902.01 and 903.01, the state is setting the applicability of the rule to any "stationary source, area source, or device..." Further subsection 902.01(b) requires owners and operators of "stationary source, area source, or device," to maintain and keep records. By including "area sources" the state's applicability is exceeding all rational thought and is overly burdensome! According to EPA's NEI website, EPA lists examples of area sources as including things like residential heating, asphalt paving, and commercial and consumer solvent use. Additional research gives examples like consumer products like hair spray, spray paint cans, portable fuel containers, and dry cleaner shops. Requiring consumers to keep and maintain records of their hair spray usage or gas can MSDS sheets is completely ridiculous!

If EPA believes "area source" simply relates to hazardous air pollutant thresholds, that arguement is unconvincing. Small sources, typically called "area sources" in EPA's National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants would be covered under the "stationary source" definition and thus wouldn't be considered "area sources." 

EPA should not approve this rule untill the state fixes their rule!!

predicting age-related differences in beef tenderness and eating quality.

I write in opposition to this Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) proposed rule that would allow this administration to undermine the current protections outlined by the 1997 Flores settlement. The Flores decision sets clear guidelines that direct the government to reunite children with a parent or relative without delay and provides standards and protections for children while in government custody. The proposed rule seeks to weaken or remove those protections and allow children to be jailed indefinitely.

Experts in child development assert that detaining children in jails and camps for long periods of time is a form of punishment that may likely harm the developmental and mental health of the incarcerated children for years and perhaps for a lifetime. It takes little effort to look around the world to see the detrimental impacts on children incarcerated by other countries. Is this the model this administration wishes to follow?

Among many other concerning changes, this rule would:
- Give the administration the power to self-license and implement standards at detention centers at a time when reports that show that DHS is not capable of maintaining clean, humane and safe detention centers currently.
- Weaken protections for children as they undergo processing in detention facilities and make release from detention and reunification with family members a more difficult process. DHS would have increased authority to change the rules regarding when and how children can be reunified and with whom. DHS and HHS are also given the authority to declare an emergency and completely suspend protections for children.
- Reverses a child’s right to a bond hearing and instead creates an agency-run administrative process that poses threats to due process

This rule outlines a system where an avowedly anti-immigrant administration, responsible for separating over 2,000 children from their parents, is able to create and change the rules of immigrant enforcement, due process, and the already deplorable detention conditions for children as they see fit. This proposal emanates from an administration that declares a "national emergency" anytime it needs to score political points. It has no qualms about using children as pawns in its costly & damaging political games.

The changes proposed are unconscionable, inhumane and would directly harm children and families who have come to the United States to seek a better life.

I am mortified by my country's descent into hate and fear of immigrants and morally opposed to jailing children and families and believe that our government should focus on keeping families together, seeking alternatives to detention and providing full due process under the law.

It is beyond comprehension that during a pandemic our government would chose to create chaos in the medical field by changing the process for renewing a J-1 visa. 

It is during a pandemic that we need all hands on deck in the medical field. These highly trained doctors are crucial to the survival of Americans and they are not easily replaced. Many of these doctors are willing to work in rural or other underserved areas. These are often positions that US medical residents don’t want to accept. 

With 94% of US medical students receiving acceptance into a residency program, these foreign physicians are not taking positions away from US doctors. Any doctor complaining that they can’t get residency due to the position going to a foreign candidate, should probably re-examine their own qualifications. It’s likely that if a doctor can’t secure a residency position, it is a clue that they may not be competent. Accepting foreign applicants allows for institutions to have a larger pool to choose only the most highly qualified doctors. This is a boon to this country. If rules are changed and become complicated, the physicians will go to other countries. This will result in a brain drain in the medical field. For a Presidential administration that wants to be number one, this is not a step in the right direction. This proposed change into the renewal process for J-1 visas reeks of xenophobia. Unnecessary tariffs caused an entire market to be crushed almost overnight. A market that took American farmers years to cultivate and which will take decades to return to normal, if ever. Please do not create more bureaucracy. Consider the long term ramifications to this country.

Dear Federal Register:
As a research scientist who has been directly involved in both in vitro and in vivo 
experimentation and handling of Brucella spp for over 20 years, I strongly support
removing B. abortus, B. melitensis, and B. suis from the Select Agent list.
I am convinced that Brucella would make an ineffective Bioterror weapon. As has been 
described by other commenters, Brucellosis is rarely fatal and there are effective 
antibiotic treatments widely available. It is easily diagnosed and there is no evidence it 
spreads from human to human. This reasoning applies to any threat to animal 
agriculture as well. Herds are regularly monitored, and every state has a diagnostics 
lab (veterinary as well as human) to detect Brucella infection. In most cases, animals 
would be isolated and culled with minimal economic impact. Further, states have 
effectively monitored and, for the most part, controlled wild herds (Deer, Bison, Elk, etc.) 
known to have Brucella infections.
Yet the strongest argument for removing these Brucella species from the SA list is that
Brucella is endemic in many areas of the world that are known to be hubs of terrorism 
such as the Middle East. If the purpose of the formidable security, constant inventory 
inspections, and extensive bureaucracy involved in the Select Agent designation is to 
prevent access to or stealing of Brucella culture, it is completely impotent. A potential 
Brucella bioterrorist need only go to Africa, Asia, South America, or the Middle East 
where these Brucella species are endemic in the local animal agriculture, and scoop 
some in a tube. There would be no sense to suffering the risks of breaking in to a 
research laboratory in the United States.
Removing Brucella from the Select Agent list would not affect the ABSL3 status of the 
organism, and the biosafety practices used in handling the agent, but it would remove 
current restrictions on research of these species. These restrictions are due to research 
only being performed in SA approved spaces by SA approved personnel through an 
onerous process closely monitored by the CDC/APHIS. This process involves layers of 
bureaucracy that can be formidable to research scientists who also face the specter of 
grant loss or even prison by unwittingly breaking federal law.
