Thank you for this opportunity to provide comments on behalf of Empower Retirement regarding your 
proposed rule addressing the “one bad apple” issue in multiple employer plans (MEPs). Empower 
serves over 38,000 retirement plans and 9.2 million participants, including many MEPs. Our clients 
range from start up plans to plans with over 200,000 participants and we are very engaged in the small 
employer plan market where use of MEPs is most common. 
 
We commend the Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service for this effort to 
eliminate one of the obstacles that exists today in establishing MEPs. The risk of incurring plan 
disqualification or other adverse tax consequences through no fault of their own is a deterrent to many 
employers considering participation in a MEP. We believe the IRS’s general strategy of allowing MEP 
administrators to spin off and terminate non-compliant plans without creating risk for other employers in 
the MEP is an excellent solution to this problem. We do have a couple of comments, which are more 
fully described below. 
 
Notice Requirements 
 
The proposal requires that three notices be provided before action can be taken to initiate a spin-off 
with a 90-120 day period between each notice. In addition, before a participating employer is deemed 
an Unresponsive Participating Employer (UPE) (a determination needed before the initial notice is 
sent), they must have received and ignored requests from the MEP administrator for either data or 
actions necessary to address the compliance issue. This means that once a compliance issue has 
been identified by the MEP Administrator and the participating employer has been put on notice, the 
time period before a spinoff and termination can occur is seven months at a minimum and could be a 
year or longer. When an employer, particularly a small employer, is not complying with a tax code 
requirement and is unresponsive to attempts to correct the problem, they are often not complying with 
other requirements, such as the timely remittance of salary deferral contributions, that negatively impact 
plan participants. We believe that in order to protect the interests of the UPE participants the period 
between when a participating employer first receives a written communication that there is or may be a

 
qualification defect and when a spinoff of the portion of the MEP maintained by the UPE can be initiated 
should be no longer than four months (assuming the participating employer fails to respond). 
 
Treatment of Participant Accounts Not Attributable to Service with the UPE 
 
As noted in your request for comments, a participant in the portion of the MEP maintained by an UPE 
may also have established a rollover account representing assets rolled over from a different plan, or 
may have established an account with a different participating employer that is part of the same MEP. 
The question is whether the related rollover and the unrelated participating employer accounts should 
be treated the same as the UPE plan account (i.e. distributed as part of the spinoff and termination and 
eligible for rollover). 
 
We believe that an account held in the portion of the MEP maintained by a different participating 
employer should not be swept into the spinoff and termination process. In that circumstance the 
participant has chosen to keep their account with a former employer and that account is not jeopardized 
by the actions of the UPE so there does not appear to be any purpose served by including it in the 
spinoff. Forcing a distribution of that account may result in premature distribution of retirement assets if 
the participant does not elect a rollover of assets from the UPE Plan.

I oppose the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) proposed Modernization of Swine Slaughter Inspection rule, which would speed up pig slaughtering.

The proposed rule would expand a failed and unlawful pilot program, the Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point-based Inspection Models Project (HIMP), to pig slaughterhouses nationwide, creating the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System. 

Results of HIMP show that the proposed system is bad for pigs and for people. 

An undercover investigation of Quality Pork Processors, Inc. (QPP), which was part of HIMP and which is the exclusive supplier of Hormel Foods, revealed that high speed slaughter results in the abusive, painful slaughter of thousands of pigs. Allowing this high-speed model across the country would result in even more suffering.

Corporate profits, and/or cheaper meat do not justify this suffering

HIMP processing plants rack up more food safety violations than others. The most-cited plant in the country during a recent three year period with nearly 50% more citations than the slaughterhouse with the next highest number was a HIMP plant. This is because the proposed inspection system (which HIMP was testing) allows poorly-trained plant employees to act as on-line sorters, replacing The USDA's Food Safety Inspection Service (FISA) inspectors with expertise in pathology and decades of experience in inspection. Pressured to go faster, the new sorters miss or ignore dangerous and unsanitary contaminants, defects, and diseases.

Corporate profits, and/or cheaper meat do not justify this risk to human health.

It is telling that FSIS's own HIMP plant inspectors were so alarmed by the pilot program and by their leaderships repeated failure to heed warnings that they became whistleblowers. Citing abysmal results for food safety, slaughter plant workers, and the welfare of animals, a bipartisan coalition of members of Congress further warned FSIS not to proceed with HIMP, while over a quarter million people signed a petition opposing the plan.

Along with them, I urge the USDA not to adopt the Modernization of Swine Slaughter Inspection Rule.

I vehemently oppose the proposed rule, Apprehension, Processing, Care, and Custody of Alien Minors and Unaccompanied Alien Children. It's disgusting, it's wrong, it's immoral, it's against everything we as Americans stand for, and it absolutely must be stopped immediately.

The proposed rule perpetuates the cruel, horrific denial of basic human rights that every single person who ever steps foot in our country deserves without question - and is especially disgusting considering it's happening to THE MOST VULNERABLE people who are simply trying to escape from unspeakable violence and constant death threats that plague their homes. 

As a natural born U.S. citizen raised in a small conservative town in TN, I am personally traumatized by reading the stories, hearing the voices and seeing the pictures of what is happening to these families and children at the detention centers. This rule would:

I wish to comment on the proposed rule issued by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) that could jeopardize the ability of port authorities that have appointed board members from issuing tax-exempt bonds. As I understand it, the proposed rule would create a new definition of political subdivision for purposes of tax-exempt bonds, as it sets out a three-part test for an entity to qualify as a political subdivision which includes: (1) sovereign powers, (2) governmental purpose, and (3) governmental control. With regard to governmental control, a port or similar authority with an appointed board might not qualify as a political subdivision under the rule unless the appointing official or body retains the right to remove a majority of the governing board.

As the Chief Financial Officer of the Port of Los Angeles from 1989-1999, and the Chief Financial Officer of the Alameda Corridor Transportation Authority, since 2004, I have observed closely the public benefits tax-exempt bonds provide for development of public infrastructure facilities. Docks and wharfs, terminal, intermodal, and transportation corridor facilities are vital to the shipping and distribution needs of the public throughout the nation. For example, about a third of all cargo passing through the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach is destine for public consumers in areas hundreds of miles away from Southern California. Tax-exempt financing, as an option under existing tax regulation, is sometimes a crucial component of the financial viability of such public purpose shipping and distribution networks.

If the goal is to curtail certain limited property developer abuses, please consider other more specific thresholds and prohibitions. As proposed, the legislation would have unintended consequences, compromising vital infrastructure development and network maintenance.

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

Please re-establish federal charges for marijuana use due to marijuana's impact on air pollution. Three primary typologies of legal cannabis cultivation systems based on existing regulations: indoor, mixed-light, and outdoor. (8) These three production systems may impact the environment through different pathways (Figure 2). Indoor and mixed-light cannabis cultivation systems may require higher external inputs (e.g., energy (14) and fertilizer) but are also associated with higher yields and reduced concerns about ecosystem degradation. Outdoor farms may require fewer resource inputs, but poor management or siting can disrupt surrounding ecosystems. Both indoor and outdoor cultivation systems may be associated with air pollution risks from biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) that can be precursors to ozone formation. To date, these various concerns have not been systematically researched. Moreover, in practice, there are countless variations and combinations across production systems. For example, in a single farm, mother plants may be kept indoors, while cloning occurs in mixed-light environments, and full plants are grown outdoors. Primary air pollution impacts from cannabis appear to be different from these other agricultural air pollution pathways. Our review identified three recent studies that assessed the impacts of indoor cannabis cultivation on air quality. Wang et al. (62) measured biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) emitted by cannabis plants grown under conditions mimicking greenhouse cultivation. Despite author-acknowledged limitations related to small sample sizes, suboptimal growing conditions, and a lack of access to common cannabis strains for testing, the results suggested BVOC emissions from indoor cultivated cannabis in Colorado could contribute to ozone formation and particulate matter pollution. In a follow-up study, Wang et al. (63) estimated terpene emissions and regional ozone impacts from indoor cannabis cultivation in Colorado using the Comprehensive Air Quality Model. This approach was limited by the reliance on estimates and assumptions in the absence of data regarding emission capacity of most cannabis strains, the number of plants, and plant biomass. Nevertheless, preliminary findings predicted increases in hourly ozone concentrations, indicating that concentrated indoor cannabis cultivation could influence ozone pollution through BVOC emissions (including terpenes), particularly in areas where nitrogen oxides are not limiting factors in ozone formation. See https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.estlett.0c00844

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I have educated myself and only buy eggs that say "Certified Humane". Please don't encourage the misleading of the public by allowing producers to make claims that are less than truthful!

Thank you for considering my request.

I urge the USDA to adopt the strongest possible standards of care for birds used in commercial enterprises and for wild-caught birds used for research. It is unconscionable that for the past 50 years these animals have been denied coverage under the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) and that--even after a court ruled against this exclusion--the department dragged its feet for 20 years. The number of investigations by animal welfare organizations for cruel treatment by bird breeders and others during this time is only the tip of the iceberg of the suffering that could have been avoided had the USDA acted sooner. Now the USDA is finally initiating efforts to promulgate regulations to protect birds under the AWA.

Do the right thing NOW

There should be no double standard when it comes to protecting birds; they should receive the same level of oversight as other animals covered by the AWA, regardless of other laws that may apply to birds. Regulations regarding their welfare should include the following basic elements: 

1. No sale of unweaned or prematurely weaned baby birds. These young, fragile birds are at great risk of succumbing to disease, mishandling, and the extreme hazards of transport. 

2. Environmental enrichment for all birds. Achieving the AWA's goal of ensuring "humane care and treatment" requires that species-specific physical and psychological needs of birds be met. 

3. Health certificates and record keeping for all birds. Records (including but not limited to acquisition and disposition of the birds) and disease testing are essential to prevent disease transmission and illegal trade in wild-caught birds. 

4. Enclosures that enable the birds to express normal behavior, including flight. Confinement in cages causes poor welfare in birds and can lead to destructive habits, including feather plucking. Birds need to be able to fly and express other natural behaviors. The USDA should adopt enforceable standards that don't rely solely on subjective assessments. 

5. No painful physical mutilations. Pinioning (severing of wing muscles or amputation of wings), toe clipping, devoicing, and beak alterations are examples of painful procedures that are typically done for the convenience of keepers and are extremely detrimental to the welfare of the birds. 

6. Coverage of all bird species. There is no justification for exempting certain species because they are addressed in other laws such as the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Many animals covered by the AWA are regulated under state or other federal laws, and such laws do not nullify their protections under the AWA. The same should be true for birds. The ESA does not ensure humane care and treatment.

I'm pleased to provide comments as a grower, handler and Chairman of the ABC Board of Directors. The Federal Register notice focused on the April FY 16/17 BOD-approved budget which included expenditures totaling $69,897,626 based on a 1.873 billion pound crop. Program expenses are derived through a process by which multiple Committee meetings and planning sessions are held, attended by industry members who either serve on the Committees or who are attending the open sessions. This process begins as early as January. After reviewing projects and opportunities, the Committee members make their budget recommendations to the Board of Directors. In the April approval of the FY 16/17 budget, research efforts (production research, environmental research, AIM and Crop of Choice initiatives) constituted 14% of program expenses, while marketing (Nut of Choice initiatives, global market development, reputation management) constituted 65% of the program expenses. Market demand budgets normally constitute approximately 2/3 of program expenses or more.
 
Since the June 2016 Federal Register notification, there have been additional meetings by Committees, Finance & Audit, and the Board of Directors. Those meetings have had the benefit of knowing that the FY 16/17 crop is forecasted to be larger than originally included in the April budget - the objective forecast released in July is for a 2.050 billion pound crop. With that knowledge, the Committees and Board will be recommending additional funding for direct marketing activities. Several industry members have raised the possibility of "earmarking" a portion of additional assessment funds for marketing. While we fully anticipate the budget for direct marketing will increase, it would not be fiscally responsible for the Board of Directors to adopt a budget that includes additional program expenses until it is known if the $0.01 additional assessment will be approved.
 
The Board of Directors has always encouraged Committees to bring forward recommendations for programs that effectively utilize assessment dollars to generate more demand. If there is sufficient revenue, those opportunities are reviewed and approved by the Board, and recommended to USDA/AMS for funding. This same process will certainly be pursued should the $0.04 assessment be approved.
 
I support the unanimous recommendation put forward by the ABC Board of Directors to move ahead with a $0.04 assessment for the next 3 years.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Open Textbooks Pilot Program. I am involved in the LibreTexts Project which was the first funded award from this program but my comments do not represent LibreTexts or any other persons or organizations.

1. Award Size: Currently there are many small awards for OER construction and evaluation, from institutions of higher education and state governments. Therefore, to maximize impact I would suggest a minimum award of $1 million for four years with between three and six awards. Further as set forth in Proposed Priority 1, awards should involve a collaboration between diverse institutions where diversity describes the students and faculty served and the types of institutions. Since states have statewide programs, FIPSE should aim to fund collaborations that target regions or ones which reach many states.

2. Matching contributions: Experience shows that requiring matching contributions disadvantages worthy proposals from less well off institutions. I would strongly recommend that there be no matching contribution requirement, moreover that matching contributions should not be included in any proposal budget beyond release time to keep the playing field level.

3. High enrollment: There are a multitude of open textbooks for high enrollment courses. Where support is lacking is in ancillary materials, homework systems, test banks, presentation material, etc. Further, the area where textbooks are lacking is for advanced courses with lower enrollments. Rather than specifying high enrollment courses, it might be better to ask for open material supporting zero textbook cost curricula with emphasis on zero extra cost curricula including ancillary materials beyond textbooks.

4. Open Textbook: I recently received an Email which made the point about organizations providing educational materials: here is the open textbook, but there are features sitting on a commercial platform that students will have to buy to get the full benefit. This is the business model of several significant groups in the low cost educational materials market including variations on inclusive and equitable access and value added resellers. The costs of these offerings usually based on per course per student payment of small amounts adds up especially when money is tight.

OER is often defined by the 5Rs, Reuse, Retain, Revise, Remix and Redistribute, reflecting the origin of the movement by the creators of the material and the custodians. I suggest that there are two more important Rs that FIPSE should use to evaluate proposals: the right to reach materials and the right to be able to read them, the latter being not only accessibility. The COVID19 emergency has hammered home the fact that many students and informal users of OER do not have access to online materials because of poor connectivity, lack of equipment and lack of support for users. I suggest that the ability to reach and read the OER that is created be proposal priorities

Thank you again for this opportunity

Standardized Bycatch Reporting Methodology (SBRM). The Oceans program of the Environmental

internationally, working with local stakeholders and communities to achieve sustainable fisheries. 
The accurate assessment of bycatch is crucial to the health of our ocean ecosystems and for the 
sustainable management of our fisheries. Understanding the type and amount of bycatch is 
essential to prevent overfishing, to rebuild overfished stocks, and to protect threatened or 
endangered species. The incidental catch of non-target species remains a significant threat to many 
species across US fisheries, and the accurate characterization of bycatch is key to informing 
management. 
 
We appreciate NOAA’s effort to provide guidance and clarity for the Regional Councils and 
its own staff managing certain highly migratory fisheries to standardize the reporting of bycatch in 
fishery management plans (FMPs) as required by the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and 
Management Act (MSA). See 16 U.S.C. 1853(a)(11). Data on many bycatch species are lacking, 
especially for shark species, including those depleted species categorized as “prohibited” that are 
effectively bycatch-only. Some of these species experience high levels of fishing mortality resulting 
largely from bycatch, making bycatch data collection particularly important for their conservation. 
 
The proposed rule defines standardized reporting methodology as “an established 
procedure or procedures used to collect, record, and report bycatch data in a fishery or subset of a 
fishery.” See 81 Fed. Reg. at 9418. While this definition reflects the statutory language, we urge 
NOAA to direct managers to consider monitoring bycatch of fish caught as bycatch that are 
managed in separate FMPs and by different management entities. This is especially true for highly 
migratory species like sharks that are commonly caught in fisheries under the jurisdiction of 
different FMPs. 
 
For example, Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico sharks managed under the Highly Migratory 
Species FMP are caught as bycatch in snapper/grouper fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico and South 
Atlantic fisheries, which are managed under separate FMPs. See, e.g., U.S. National Bycatch Report 
First Edition Update 2 and NOAA Technical Memorandum NMFS-SEFSC-652. Currently,

 
understanding the sources of mortality associated with each fishery is a challenging task, as species

ongoing issue. Including a provision to require the movement to housing of data in a single source

sustainable management of shark species relies on a solid understanding of sources of mortality,

Currently, technical assistance on disproportionality, including significant disproportionality, is available to states through at least three OSEP funded technical assistance centers – IDEA Data Center (IDC), National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), and Center for Fiscal Reporting (CIFR). While additional availability of technical assistance around disproportionality may be needed, it would be best to keep the technical assistance under the existing centers rather than add another center. Adding an additional center is not a good use of taxpayer funds in that it is not an effective or efficient way to provide assistance to states or LEAs. Creating a new TA center requires funds for start-up and overhead; many of the existing centers already share personnel; and states will have to manage additional center contacts and webinars that overlap in both content and timing. As an example of the content overlap, it is impossible to separate the calculations for disproportionality from the data itself. IDC provides technical assistance to states on the collection, reporting, and use of child count, educational environments, and discipline data that are then used in the calculations for disproportionality. It would be a far better use of taxpayer dollars to expand the technical assistance on disproportionality currently offered by IDC, NCSI, and CIFR than to add on an additional center.

If an additional center is deemed necessary, their scope of work should include all areas of disproportionality, including SPP/APR indicators 4, 9, and 10. Confusion between the required methodologies would only be exacerbated by having one center focused exclusively on significant disproportionality.

The Directed Questions request information about common challenges or barriers experienced by SEAs and LEAs regarding significant disproportionality, and how the investment in a new center could address them. The basic challenge at both the SEA and LEA levels is the differences in requirements for SPP/APR Indicators 4, 9, and 10, and significant disproportionality. Existing centers have developed and disseminated technical assistance in this area. Again, more assistance would be helpful, but not to the extent of needed an additional center. 

The second and third directed questions ask about supports for conducting the review of policies, procedures, and practices in LEAs as well as the root cause analysis. Here again, existing centers have created toolkits and provided technical assistance to both SEAs and LEAs in these areas.

The fourth directed question asks about the supports needed by SEAs to conduct the analysis of significant disproportionality. Technical assistance has been available to states in many forms through the existing centers. 

Finally, the fifth directed question asks about supports needed regarding CCEIS. Again, technical assistance is currently available in this area through CIFR and other TA centers.

In summary, technical assistance is readily available through several existing centers, several of which already share personnel and/or collaborate on the creation and provision of assistance to states. The creation of a new technical assistance center would, in theory, consolidate the resources, but at the cost of the additional overhead of a new center, and additional contacts and possibly redundant offerings to states that can become burdensome to manage and coordinate.

Despite significant reductions in the number of children killed in motor vehicle crashes over the 

past decade, motor vehicle crashes remain the leading cause of death among children aged 4 

years and older. Children and adolescents represent approximately 15% of all people killed

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Please make sure the farmers are really adhering to the rules! Having an empty lot is not 'pasture raised.' 
Having a huge barn with animals being housed with an empty lot next to it doesn't qualify as 'pasture raised.'
It is the responsibility of the USDA to make sure these animals are really 'pasture raised.'

protective and implementable. 

Analytical method 

As detailed in EPA's Final Aquatic Life Ambient Water Quality Criteria for Aluminum, 2018, aluminum 

is the third most common element in the earth's crust, occurring predominantly in the form of 

aluminosilicate minerals, including clays. These clays are ubiquitous in the environment and are 

common as suspended load in the water column of surface waters. Aluminum in these forms is not 

biologically available and thus not toxic to aquatic life. Although other solid forms of aluminum can be 

toxic (supporting the expression of the aluminum criteria in terms of total aluminum), it is critical that 

aluminum in non-toxic solids not be part of the regulated total aluminum load. Unfortunately, the only 

EPA-approved analytical methods for total aluminum (EPA Methods 200.7 and 200.8) employ 

aggressive digestion techniques that dissolve these clays, releasing the aluminum that is otherwise 

tightly bound in their structure. The result is that non-toxic solid forms of aluminum are included in the 

total aluminum result. Although the discussion of the proposed criteria suggests that this inclusion "may 

be considered conservative," it is incorrect to count non-toxic forms of aluminum as toxic and doing so 

would lead to burdensome and unnecessary overregulation with no benefit to water quality.

Endangered and Threatened Species: Section 4(d) Rule for Sickle Darter [FWS-R4-ES-2020-0094-0001]

The evidence provided by the SSA report is sufficient to categorize the sickle darter as endangered. The future scenarios shown in Table 2 display a grim future for sickle darter populations. There are six locations where this species is known to currently exist. If the current trend of habitat degradation continues, half of these are expected to become extirpated by 2070. If the trend worsens, four or more locations will see the extirpation of the sickle darter in the same timeframe. NatureServe, a database with extensive conservation information, has the sickle darter listed as “presumably extirpated” in North Carolina, “critically imperiled” in Virginia, and “imperiled” in Tennessee (Hammerson, 2020). Major causes of the decline of this species include siltation, nutrient pollutants, and pathogens from animal waste runoff. Tennessee holds the majority of the populations of the sickle darter, and should not be expected to follow the improving trend scenario (as shown in Table 2) for these reasons: (1) The legalization of industrial hemp in 2015 has led to over 1,700 people obtaining hemp licenses, and (2) The 2018 amendment to Tennessee Code (Tenn. Code Ann. § 69-3-1) lessened restrictions on concentrated animal feeding operations. These changes are likely to result in increased nonpoint pollution from agricultural runoff.

The loss of even a few sickle darter populations would result in decreased gene flow, resulting in reduced genetic diversity throughout the species and higher vulnerability to environmental changes. The ultimate goal, as stated under the Recovery Planning section, is “the recovery of these listed species, so that they no longer need the protective measures of the Act”. It is much more effective to restore the population of a species early-- before the species is subject to genetic drift and loses genetic diversity. It is imperative to classify the sickle darter as an endangered species as it is in danger of extinction in a specific portion of its range.

The proposed changes to the Packers and Stockyards Act must include stronger protections for farmers. Farmers need the following:

3. The right to form and join farmer associations without suffering retaliation.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

Dear Administrator Oz,

I am writing to you as an interventional cardiologist at St. Thomas Hospital. With over 5 years of clinical experience specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of coronary artery disease (CAD), my practice focuses extensively on advanced catheterization procedures that improve patient outcomes. I am commenting regarding the complexity adjustment for CPT code 0523T related to angiography-based physiologic assessment technologies (commonly referred to as FFRangio solutions).

FFRangio solutions are innovative, angiography-based physiological indices that non-invasively assess the functional significance of coronary artery stenosis. They have been prospectively validated and shown to improve clinical outcomes by providing precise coronary physiology assessment without the need for pressure wires or hyperemic agents. This technology is valuable for millions of patients globally who suffer from CAD, as it optimizes decision-making for coronary revascularization.

Importantly, the recently released PIONEER IV trial (2025) has confirmed the non-inferiority of QFR-guided PCI compared to usual care—including FFR, iFR, IVUS, and OCT guidance—demonstrating that angiography-based physiologic assessment can safely and effectively guide revascularization decisions in real-world practice. These findings reinforce the growing body of evidence that FFRangio solutions represent an evidence-based, efficient, and patient-friendly alternative to invasive physiology testing.

Currently, CPT code 0523T—which covers the use of angiography-based physiology in interventional coronary procedures—has a complexity adjustment only associated with CPT code 93460 (simultaneous left and right heart catheter angiograms). However, the majority of patients (over 60%) undergo left heart catheterization alone (CPT code 93458), whereas only about 10% undergo both left and right heart catheterizations.

This disparity in the application of the complexity adjustment limits access to these technologies for the larger patient population undergoing left heart angiograms. CPT code 93458 involves substantial procedural complexity, making it equally deserving of the complexity adjustment currently assigned exclusively to 93460. Because these angiography-based algorithms are new, the early claims used in determining the complexity adjustments appear not to properly reflect the true cost and complexity of the service related to CPT code 93458.

Therefore, I respectfully request that CMS reassign CPT code 0523T with complexity adjustments to include both CPT 93458 and 93460 to more accurately reflect clinical practice and patient care realities. Including 93458 in the complexity adjustment will ensure equitable reimbursement, promote fair access to these innovative physiologic solutions, and ultimately benefit a broader patient base afflicted by CAD.

Thank you for considering this important issue, which affects patient access to innovative cardiovascular diagnostic modalities. If further information or discussion is needed, I am available to provide clinical insights or data supporting this request.

Sincerely,
Dr. Jimmy Kerrigan, M.D.
Interventional Cardiologist
Ascension St. Thomas Hospital

Every tax-exempt entity is required to file an annual return with the IRS, but the Code does

Congress expressly required more comprehensive reporting only for charitable entities organized

I, like many consumers, rely on on-package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised" I assume that there is value and meaning behind that claim and that is backed by a regulatory agency.

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. Companies will still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit.

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Industry has continuously shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating/policing itself. Companies are taking advantage of consumers, and grossly overcharging them, by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels to bring in more profits all the while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. We should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare.

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers.

FSIS owes it to the American public to set a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," take steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensure that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

I write on behalf of the City Colleges of Chicago to support the proposal of the US Department of Education Office of Postsecondary Education to waive the requirements in the Education Department General Administrative Regulations that generally prohibit project periods exceeding five years and project period extensions involving the obligation of additional Federal funds. This proposed waiver and extension would have considerable and measurable positive impact on furthering the goals and objectives of the projects funded under CFDA number 84.382A. Additionally, as a large, urban community college district comprised of both Predominantly Black Institutions and Hispanic Serving Institutions, the waiver would enable the City Colleges of Chicago to strategically align applications for and (if funded) execution of these related Title III, Part F projects.

In September 2015, the US Department of Education awarded the Predominantly Black Institutions grant to Malcolm X College, one of the City Colleges of Chicago. The focus of this project has been to enable and support African-Americans to matriculate through the health sciences programs and concurrently provide them with the opportunities to either transfer into four-year institutions or graduate with credentials of economic value. Three primary goals of the grant have guided the activities of the project. By carrying out these activities, the College has made substantial progress toward accomplishing the overarching strategic goals: (1) to increase the number of students earning college credentials of economic value; (2) to increase the rate of transfer to Bachelor's degree programs following CCC graduation; and, (3) to drastically improve outcomes for students needing remediation. In this most recent project year alone, Malcolm X College was able to serve over 500 African American males through its Black Male Institute Conference. We accomplished this by extending our outreach to cultivate relationships with approximately 30 low-income and/or minority-serving public schools throughout the Cityof Chicago, and provide STEM programming for 5th-8th grade students.

As indicated above, the City Colleges of Chicago's support of this waiver is twofold. First, the opportunity to continue PBI activities at the City Colleges of Chicago would allow us to continue to strengthen the pipeline of Black students enrolling in and successfully completing higher education in the City of Chicago. It will allow us to continue to build the capacity of our institutions to serve those students as we groom them for success in higher education and for entry into the workforce. Second, it would enable the City Colleges of Chicago - and other similar districts - to coordinate districtwide efforts to align applications for the Title III, Part F discretionary grant programs for which their colleges are eligible.

The Northeast Organic Producers Alliance (NODPA) request that the comment period for the above Proposed Rule be increased by 90 days from March 20th 2017 to June 19th, 2017.
NODPA is the largest organic dairy producer organization in the country with a membership of eight hundred and thirty six organic dairy producers in the Eastern US. NODPA's mission is to "enable organic dairy family farmers, situated across an extensive area, to have informed discussion about matters critical to the wellbeing of the organic dairy industry as a whole." NODPA is not aligned with any one processor or cooperative and therefore is able to represent the views and needs of many different farmers.
Our producer members are busy as we start to move out of the winter chores into the time of year with field work, including planting crops for feed and grazing; harvesting forage for the next winter; reseeding land that has become unproductive or too damaged by the harsh winter and the spreading of composted manure to fertilize the land. Of course, milking cows twice a day, 365 days of the year is part of the regular routine of our members. Many of our members have cultural and religious prohibitions on using the internet and therefore can only receive information on any proposed regulation by mail. The proposed comment period would disenfranchise those producers from being able to analyze a regulation that would require active participation on their part, either to annually ask for exemption or to pay into the Organic Checkoff. With the extra 90 days for a comment period we would be able to include an analysis of the regulations in our regular bi-monthly printed publication (the NODPA News) and solicit feedback from these producers.
This extra 90 days would allow all producers an opportunity to either contribute to NODPA"s written comments or to mail comments in themselves. This proposal by the Organic Trade Association has already split the organic community and appears to disenfranchise over 70% of organic producers. Our request for an extra 90 days for the comment period is a comparatively small amount of time in the decision making process but will allow for increased participation at this important stage of the process.

Dear Ms. Ryan and Ms. Hubbard: 

I’d like to share my opinion on Docket No. USCBP-2021-0030: Continuing Education for Licensed 

Customs Brokers. I’ve shared the same opinion on the blog at Flexport, where I serve as Vice 

President, Global Customs.  

Yes! I think continuing education is a great idea. More than that—I think it’s the future of customs 

brokerage.  

The stated intentions in the Customs rule proposal set the stage:  

• Brokers need to stay knowledgeable as trade advances.  

• Increased trade compliance will protect US revenue. 

But I see another angle. As we enter a more tech-driven economy, customs brokers will take on 

more important roles, advising clients on more advanced matters.  

It’s actually already happening.

 
Thus, continuing education uniﬁes the industry around pillars of client service and global trade 

growth. It’s an obvious yes.  

Shifting Demands for Brokers 

Typically, customs brokers engage in high volumes of clerical work, mainly data entry and 

document ﬁling. At some brokerages, they don’t even classify goods, because the clerical load is 

so heavy.  

But at companies like Flexport, much basic taskwork is achieved or supported by digitization—or, 

in some cases, by automation with humans in the loop to validate or handle exceptions.  

As a result, customs brokers are free to develop their knowledge and engage appropriately in 

greater trade advisory. They still primarily serve on the frontlines, but they can spot opportunities 

that may surface across a client’s larger transactional patterns.     

There’s a huge need for these bigger thinkers in today’s market. Trade acts and agreements have 

complex impacts. New classiﬁcations have cascading effects beyond just duty rates. CBP requires 

deeper supply chain tracing, and its enforcement is more precise.  

As supply chains evolve, customs brokers need to keep up with these shifting demands. 

Doing More with More Knowledge 

I’ve been a proponent of continuing education throughout my entire career. At Flexport, all of our 

brokers are required to take more training than the new regulation would require, anyway—20 

hours annually, compared to the 36 hours triennially the proposal puts forth.  

So I already know, ﬁrsthand, that continuing education is worth it.  

It also creates value for clients. I’ll give you an example of a tariff engineering solution. This may 

sound complex at ﬁrst, but it could easily be within the purview of a knowledgeable customs 

broker: 

A product ﬁnished and packaged in China would typically be subject to Section 301 duties.  

But if you’re building a product like a router or modem, the country of origin could be where its 

printed circuit board assembly (PCBA) is made.

AAL would also like to be advised on how to mark newer slides that do not fall within the serial number range on page 1, but have an older, modified regulator installed (Refer to step AC on page 11 of Ref (3) and step W on page 11 of Ref (4)).

Service Bulletin, Ref (3) Accomplishment Instruction 3, step N. on page 9 references a testing step out of CMM, Ref (5). The SB Ref (3) lists this step as "paragraph 7.B (Leak Test)," but the newest CMM revision Ref (5) has these steps located in paragraph 3.B.

Service Bulletin, Ref (3) Accomplishment Instruction 3, step Y. on page 10 references a testing step out of CMM, Ref (5). The SB Ref (3) lists this step as "paragraph 8, Charged Cylinder Assembly Leak Test," but the newest CMM revision Ref (5) has these steps located in paragraph 4. The SB Ref (3) should be updated with the correct step numbers out of the CMM Ref (5).

I am against the proposed reclassification of West Indian Manatees from Endangered to Threatened for many reasons. These animals are a treasure to the State of Florida, creating thousands of jobs in tourism across the state, and generating millions in tourism dollars. Unfortunately, many motor boaters do not seem to care about injuring them. Many boaters will follow laws to slow in manatee zones, but I have seen many that don't. Downgrading their status will likely result in fewer "slow" zones to protect them. Boaters will not voluntarily slow down in zones that are not marked as such. More manatees will be injured and die, and changing their status back to endangered at that point is likely to take far too long to save them from eventually extinction. In addition, all of these are valid reasons for keeping manatees classified as endangered:

The decision for the Antillean Manatee appears hinged on the number of individuals, which is buoyed by the Florida population. The number of manatees in the rest of the range (Greater Antilles, Mexico, Central America, and South America) is about equal to the number in Florida. Manatees in many areas are isolated from those in other locations, meaning Antillean manatees are not one large, interbreeding sub-species, but that there are smaller population segments. FWS acknowledges that the populations in most countries are declining or unknown. 

The FWS decision for Florida is largely based on a computer model that does not include recent, massive die-offs of hundreds of manatees from red tide, cold weather events, and an unusual mortality event on the state's east coast, the causes of which are still unknown. From 2010-2015, 3,217 manatees died in Florida waters, which is 53% of the highest minimum population ever recorded (6,063 in 2015). Breeding probability and survival rates would have been negatively affected by these events.The model that weighed heavily in the FWS decision, "predicts that it is unlikely that the southeastern U.S. population will fall below 4,000 total individuals over the next 100 years, assuming current threats remain constant indefinitely." But threats won't remain constant, they'll increase.

More than 60% of the manatee population in Florida is affected by the "pending" loss of artificial warm water when environmental regulations for discharges of heated water catch up with coastal power plants that for decades have provided winter habitat to the growing manatee population. There are no plans yet developed to determine how to replace lost warm water habitat, how to get manatees to transition to new sites, or how to minimize negative impacts to the manatee population in the process. 

Watercraft-related manatee injury and mortality is likely to increase as a result of an improving economy and lower gas prices. Florida law fails to reach the majority of boaters with education requirements and the state still lacks boater licensing. Compliance with existing speed zones averages only 54%.

Natural spring flows at many sites have been reduced from historic levels, human demands on Florida's freshwater supply continue to grow, and manatee access to other sites has been blocked by human alteration. FWS should be working to restore the Ocklawaha River, which would provide winter habitat for hundreds of manatees, and working closely with state water management districts to restore historic flow and water quality at springs throughout Florida. This includes not only sites already used by manatees, but sites that could be used in the future. FWS should also be working with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) to create manatee sanctuaries at a number of springs, including locations where manatee harassment is on the rise.

To Whom it May Concern in Our taxpayer funded Fish and Wildlife Service:
This Service stands for the people and by the people and for the interests of preserving the delicate balance of our fish and wildlife systems and habitats for future generations. The proposed revision seeks to redefine the word "habitat" that would radically limit the ability to protect land and waters that enable the recovery of imperiled species. I strongly oppose and object the this change which as a result would cripple further Environmental and Endangered Species Protection Acts. The proposed habitat definition is a departure from every administration that preceded it during the highly-successful tenure of the Endangered Species Act. It would require that habitats have an undefined number of necessary elements that support wildlife. This could allow this - or future - administration to deny habitat protections based on an arbitrary finding that the forest, river, or other space was somehow lacking.

The administration is even seeking to limit protections to currently-occupied land or waters. Meaning that forests and other wild areas that could support highly-endangered species can be developed or destroyed if the species has yet to recover sufficiently to expand to that space. For example, if a species must move to a higher elevation due to a warming climate, that habitat will not be protected under these new regulations. This would clearly limit the ability of those species to recover.

Dear Secretary Perdue, 
As a consumer, I have grave concerns about the proposed rule in its current state, as it fails to ensure a robust, meaningful labeling standard that provides confidence to producers and consumers alike. 
As a sustainable food advocate, I also think its important to highlight the sustainable agriculture perspective in this debate. This rule should help to provide consumers with information about the systems and processes that went into the production of the food, and to provide them with a very real opportunity to vote with their food dollars for the type of agricultural production systems they wish to support. 
Comment #1: the use of Bioengineered (BE) vs GMO
I disagree with AMS decision to forgo the use of any terms other than bioengineered (BE) as part of the rule. Congress gave AMS the authority to include additional terms, and urged AMS to utilize terms that are more commonly-used in the discourse around genetic engineering. Genetically modified (GMO) is the most widely used term in this national discussion. Relying entirely on BE, a relatively new term in this conversation, appears to obfuscate what the disclosure standard is intended to make transparent.
AMS should adapt the use of GMO to similarly reflect industry practices that are already in place. For example, the Non-GMO project reports that Non-GMO Project verified products have reached $22.3 billion in annual sales, with more than 50,000 verified products across more than 3,000 brands. 
Recommendation: I strongly recommend that AMS use the authority Congress granted it to use GMO in the disclosure standard as the primary term to mean bioengineered.

Comment #2: the thresholds within the proposed rule.
In the proposed rule, AMS requests comment on three options for a threshold. The proposed option that best satisfies this objective is Alternative 1-B, which would exempt from disclosure products that contain ingredients with GMO material that is inadvertent or technically unavoidable, and does not exceed 0.9 percent of the weight of the specific ingredient. 
As noted by AMS, this threshold aligns with some existing industry standards for the separation of GE and non-GE products as well as the thresholds established by some U.S. trading partners. Notably, both the Non-GMO Project and the European Union set their labeling threshold at 0.9 percent. 
It is also worth noting that Alternative 1-C subverts the intent of the law by allowing products that knowingly contain GMOs to avoid disclosure.
Recommendation: AMS choose Alternative 1-B for the rules threshold standard.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. (1) The way the regions are divided in this proposal splits States that have built relationships and work well together. The federal government has invested in these relationships over time and through various grant/agreement/contract relationships; therefore, it seems fiscally irresponsible to redivide states that have been working well together. And in some cases, it appears that the redivision is based on one common factor rather than a multitude of factors that influence SEAs and their relationships to LEAs and schools. For example, aligning Oklahoma, New Mexico, Arizona, and the BIE appears to be for the sake of their American Indian populations, which is one factor, albeit significant in these states, but the way in which the SEAs and BIE relate to LEAs and schools in these states is very different, so the alignment doesn't even necessarily help for this one demographic area. (2) The requirements for the Center to "be located in the region" and the Director to "be located in the region" do not seem to accomplish the goal. It appears that the goal for these requirements is to make Center staff and the Director either more knowledgeable of the region, more accessible to clients in the region, or both. Neither of these is accomplished by setting arbitrary geographic boundaries. In fact, it may do just the opposite, limiting Centers and Directors who already are knowledgeable of a State's needs from being able to serve that State. Further, accessibility in this modern era can be defined quite differently than it once was. Virtual accessibility can occur from anywhere. This regulation should protect consumers from unfair and deceptive conduct - namely, holding onto consumers' funds after a refund becomes due. 
The focus should be on inhibiting holding onto the money deceptively or unfairly and not turning Travel agencies into bridge loan providers for airlines OR consumers.

Consumer protection is of the utmost importance to Travel Agencies. 

The proposed rule has some excellent concepts but stands to (whether inadvertently or not) cause considerable and irreparable harm to Travel Agencies and, subsequently, the consumers who rely on travel agencies to advocate on their behalf and enforce consumers' rights.

Requiring Airlines to refund customers for cancelled flights within 30 days is a simple concept. The money was given to the airlines for a service; the service was cancelled - the funds should be returned promptly.

The flawed logic here is not following the money in relation to travel agents.

Travel Agents can book flights in multiple ways. Agencies usually book on the customer's card through their GDS or directly through the supplier or a vendor portal; the money doesn't even enter the travel agent's possession - and is immediately sent to the airline or supplier. A little while later, the vendor sends the airline a commission check - typically after the completion of the trip - or in the case of ARC, weekly. In the above case, the agent never holds the portion of the customer's money due to be refunded if the trip is cancelled.
In the current proposed rule wording, if the airline delayed the client's refund by one day, the Travel agent would be liable to refund the client out of their own pocket. The airline, the next day, would not even allow agents the option of receiving their reimbursement to the agency directly. 
This would leave agents scrambling to recoup funds from clients who were paid double.
In some cases, fares are NET fares or package trips where cash payment to the airline is the only acceptable form of payment. In those cases, while it is true that the agent collects the money first - they then pass on the portion of the payment for the flight to the airline. This rule would force agents to fork out a refund for consumers even if the airline that holds the money did not.
How can it be a fair practice to penalise a middle man who does not hold the funds and hold them responsible for reimbursing customers from their pocket? 
This would reward and encourage airlines to slack off on refunding travel agents since consumers get their refund, and the travel agents bear the burden of cash flow - not the airlines. In a pinch, airlines could delay travel agency ticket refunds without harming consumers. A truly deceptive scenario, and one the airlines employed against travel agencies during the covid pandemic.

I strongly urge the DOT to amend the blank slate proposed requirements for travel agencies to refund consumers within 30 days.
I propose The rule change to require travel agencies to refund consumers within 30 days of receipt of a refund from the airline or supplier.
If the airlines processed a refund to the agency within 24hrs of a flight cancellation, the consumer refund would be due from the travel agency to the consumer 31 days from the cancellation event. 
If the airline processed the refund on the 30th day, the latest a consumer would receive their refund from a travel agency would be 60 days later.
The average agent in the USA earns on average $40,000, from $800,000 in revenue sales per year.
If an airline delays the refund to the agent, there is little chance and a significant burden for an agent to cough up and refund business class tickets for a family of 4 - e.g. $40,000 in sales. 
Especially considering the money and refund is actually at and due from the airlines.
Please amend these regulations - to protect consumers, while focusing on eliminating the deceptive practices, and not creating undue financial burdens on travel agents.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

I buy only Organic food products. There is increasing knowledge of the benefits of local, organic food. This will lead to fewer products not certified as organic being purchased and profits from other producers will fall. So, this is an economic issue as well.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

I support the FDA in its effort to issue a Guidance for Industry (GFI) 273 that would set strong standards in durations of use for the medically important antimicrobials used in animal feed. 

Every year, 35,000 Americans die from antibiotic-resistant infections—and this number will only grow if we do not stop unnecessary antibiotic usage. Animal antimicrobial usage contributes significantly to this resistance, and not setting strong standards for duration of use on animal feed antibiotics can lead to prolonged and unnecessary use. 

Feed antimicrobials constitute approximately 63% of the antimicrobials given to food animals every year, so ensuring that these antimicrobials are given appropriately is crucial to public health. Durations of use on every label will help resolve this longstanding problem.

I urge the FDA to adopt a policy that will encourage veterinarians to use the shortest possible durations to achieve their desired clinical outcomes. These durations should not be set based on extreme or rare circumstances. Instead, drug manufacturers should be pushed to include evidence-based instructions on how long to use the drug under expected or common circumstances. These expected duration limits should be specific, offering a definite length of time such as, “use for 14 days.” Such limits should also take into account the risk of antibiotic resistance associated with the drug’s use.

Karen K Becker

Often the communities support the idea of an acquisition project, but are unable to administer it or provide the local match. Then it falls to the property owners, who are often impoverished themselves, so the grant never happens. The way the program is described here, I do have several concerns. In general, a lot of the details are poorly spelled out and leave room for dangerous interpretation.

My first concern is that there is no indication or explanation of how the community will be involved in this process. Its critical that the goals and future plans of the community be considered when implementing these grants. Additionally, many details of this potential grant were not addressed. If a property owner wishes to sell their property to the community, what happens if the community refuses to buy it? Can the property owner sell the land at a later date? If so, will the community receive a grant to buy the now vacant parcel? Purchase of vacant land, unless an adjacent parcel with a structure on it is also purchased, is not an eligible activity under the HMA grant programs. If the community purchases the land, will they be required to report that it is still in open space use every three years? If an owner opts to rebuild, can the community purchase the property with a new structure on it at a later date through one of the HMA grant programs? 

Im also opposed to the whole idea of a property owner keeping the land after demolishing the home. The language, allows a property owner to rebuild on the parcel up to local floodplain standards. They are then still in the floodplain and may receive more flood insurance payouts. Investing federal money into acquiring and demolishing the home should result in the property not receiving additional federal funds. Furthermore, if the community is not involved in the decision, the communitys first responders may be put at continued risk by attempting to rescue homeowners from flooded areas.

There has been considerable improvement in the quality of HbA1c testing since the NGSP was initiated back in 1996. I urge the USDA to adopt the strongest possible standards of care for birds used in commercial enterprises and for wild-caught birds used for research. It is unconscionable that for the past 50 years these animals have been denied coverage under the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) and that--even after a court ruled against this exclusion--the department dragged its feet for 20 years. The number of investigations by animal welfare organizations for cruel treatment by bird breeders and others during this time is only the tip of the iceberg of the suffering that could have been avoided had the USDA acted sooner. Now the USDA is finally initiating efforts to promulgate regulations to protect birds under the AWA.

Since other species do not belong to humans at all, the least we can do is assiduously try to protect them as much as possible, after all the harm people have inflicted on them.

There should be no double standard when it comes to protecting birds; they should receive the same level of oversight as other animals covered by the AWA, regardless of other laws that may apply to birds. Regulations regarding their welfare should include the following basic elements: 

1. No sale of unweaned or prematurely weaned baby birds. These young, fragile birds are at great risk of succumbing to disease, mishandling, and the extreme hazards of transport. 

2. Environmental enrichment for all birds. Achieving the AWA's goal of ensuring "humane care and treatment" requires that species-specific physical and psychological needs of birds be met. 

3. Health certificates and record keeping for all birds. Records (including but not limited to acquisition and disposition of the birds) and disease testing are essential to prevent disease transmission and illegal trade in wild-caught birds. 

4. Enclosures that enable the birds to express normal behavior, including flight. Confinement in cages causes poor welfare in birds and can lead to destructive habits, including feather plucking. Birds need to be able to fly and express other natural behaviors. The USDA should adopt enforceable standards that don't rely solely on subjective assessments. 

5. No painful physical mutilations. Pinioning (severing of wing muscles or amputation of wings), toe clipping, devoicing, and beak alterations are examples of painful procedures that are typically done for the convenience of keepers and are extremely detrimental to the welfare of the birds. 

6. Coverage of all bird species. There is no justification for exempting certain species because they are addressed in other laws such as the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Many animals covered by the AWA are regulated under state or other federal laws, and such laws do not nullify their protections under the AWA. The same should be true for birds. The ESA does not ensure humane care and treatment.

Cattle Empire is the largest family-owned and operated cattle producer in the United States, as such we unequivocally support modernizing the current U.S. standards for grades of carcass beef. The standards currently in use, rely solely on skeletal and lean (physiological) metrics, a method that unduly limits carcass grade classifications and results in the reduction of public perception in the quality of beef produced. We suggest that dentition or age verification should be used as methods to determine maturity groupings instead of relying solely on physiological maturity as a way to classify and grade beef carcasses.

Since 1993, cattle producers have invested well over 10 million checkoff dollars in the Beef Checkoff, research to better understand palatability as well as the characteristics that drive consumer demand for beef products. A recent study, funded by the Beef Checkoff, tested the eating quality of strip loin steaks produced by fed steers and heifers that had been classified as less than 30 months of age using dentition versus current USDA carcass maturity. Results of the study showed that sensory panelists were unable to detect any differences in tenderness, juiciness or flavor between steaks from carcasses classified by USDA graders using current skeletal and lean maturity observations. 

This alternate method of classifying beef carcasses into maturity groupings will allow more carcasses to qualify for the higher USDA grades of Prime, Choice and Select without significantly reducing the consistency of those grades that predict palatability and drive public demand for consumable, grain-fed beef. 
According to projections from the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, with this modernization producers would yield approximately $59 million in additional revenue by removing discounts for cattle identified as greater than 30 months of age. 

Due to the clear positive industry impacts associated with modernizing the ways in which USDA graders grade beef, Cattle Empire respectfully requests that USDA AMS add the following language to section 54.104, paragraph k, of the Standards:

Carcasses of grain-fed steers and heifers determined to be less than 30 months old either by dentition (assessed at the time of slaughter under the supervision of USDA-FSIS) or by documentation of actual age (verified through a USDA Process Verified Program or USDA Quality System Assessment) are included in the youngest maturity group for carcasses recognized as "beef" (A-maturity) regardless of skeletal evidences of maturity.

This is a request to modernize the beef grading system to take into account the most recent research available and more accurately assign carcass maturity based on available data. 

We respectfully ask AMS to modernize the current U.S. Standards for Grades of Carcass Beef to include the use of dentition or age verification. Such a change would have a profound economic impact on producers and would also clear the path for an increase in the availability of beef proven to contain characteristics that are important to the consumer.

Thank you for your consideration of this important change.

Sincerely,

Trista Brown Priest
Chief Strategy Officer
Cattle Empire, LLC

I wish to thank you for proposing to expand critical habitat for the Southern Resident killer whales (SRKW) to include marine waters from Monterey Bay in California through Cape Flattery in Washington State. I fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

I was able to see some orcas this summer with my Granddaughter who wants to be a marine biologist. We have to protect these amazing creatures.

Protecting this full range as critical habitat reflects new and best available science as new sightings and data show that SRKW regularly forage in the coastal waters off Washington, Oregon, and California and is essential to help get the southern resident orcas off the path to extinction and on the way to recovery.

The final rule designating critical habitat identified three essential habitat features essential to the conservation of the SRKW: (1) Water quality to support SRKW growth and development; (2) prey species of sufficient quantity, quality, and availability to support individual growth, reproduction, and development, as well as overall population growth; and (3) passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

However, the proposed rule exempts the Navy's Quinault Range Site off the coast of Washington from being designated as critical habitat due to national security. The Quinault Range Site includes part of two high-use foraging areas, as recognized by NMFS in the Biological Report, and completely bisects the proposed expanded critical habitat area. From the tagging data, about half the time that K and L pods spend in coastal habitat is in Area 1 (Washington and Northern Oregon inshore habitat). This exemption could impact their foraging ability in an area and season when nutritional stress is a significant concern and impact their ability to migrate up and down the coast. Therefore the exempted area is in conflict with the third essential habitat feature: passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

The proposed rule should include a narrow area sufficient in width between the shoreline and the eastern border of the Quinault Range Site to ensure orca migration along the coast and for foraging for limited prey. 

The science also shows that sound from vessels and other sources undermines orcas ability to echolocate to forage for salmon as well as to communicate and navigate. The Washington Governors Orca Recovery Task Force and the ESA Recovery Plan have noted that noise and disturbance are key threats hindering orca recovery and have recommended decreasing, not increasing, military noise. To sufficiently protect SRKW, NMFS must include sound as a fourth essential feature. Urge them to ensure that it is at least retained as an explicit factor in the prey and passage essential features. 

I am grateful that NMFS has engaged and consulted with Tribes to ensure that this rule does not impact Tribal Treaty rights and usual and accustomed fishing areas.

Again, fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.
