Considering the beating injured victims of the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon Fire have taken and the extended amount of time it has taken for the U.S. Government to get its act together to pass law and ramp up to begin reconciliation work, injuries from this catastrophe did not cease when the fire was extinguished and will not come to an end any time within the foreseeable future. Damage from post wildfire incidents such as flooding, landslides, mudslides, debris flows, access road degradation, etc. are obviously to be expected even if they cannot be accurately predicted and planned for ahead of occurrence. But there is more damage continuing to happen to injured victims each day on a level which cannot be seen, measured or described by any metric.

Negative mental and emotional impacts will continue for decades, if not through the remainder of their lives, for all injured victims as they slowly but surely, and repeatedly, recall every detail of every loss as time passes. These naturally stressful recollections cannot be suppressed or halted by any means or methods known, and they never should be. They have become part of every injured victim's make up now, both individually and collectively.

Taking into account this invisible, ongoing, never ceasing damage happening to injured victims on a daily, hourly, minute-by-minute basis no matter how stoic they may be, reconciliations should not only be applied to make all injured victims whole again, they should go well beyond that to provide recovery compensations which will improve their lives and livelihoods to an even greater degree than they were before this disaster destroyed them.

In other words, HPFAA reconciliations should go far beyond mere recovery to day-before-the-fire life conditions for every injured victim because the damage runs far deeper and much wider than what actually burned in the fire. Notably, the most severe threats are attributed to climate change which NMFS describes as creating a foreseeable likelihood and danger of extinction for these corals throughout all of their ranges. 

An estimated 50% of coral reefs worldwide have already been lost to climate change, and about one-third of reef-building coral species are at risk of extinction. Stressors and risks to threatened coral species include both climate related threats as well as ecological effects of fishing and land-based sources of pollution. 

Impacts of the climate crisis include ocean acidification, which hinders the ability of corals to grow, and ocean warming, which causes corals to expel the algae living in their tissues in a phenomenon known as coral bleaching. 

High-growth conditions for reef-building corals include clear, warm waters with abundant light, and low levels of nutrients, sediments, and freshwater. Critical habitat designations are necessary to reduce and remove threats to these conditions which foster growth and recovery of these threatened species

Coral reefs help support over 25% of all marine life, and designation of critical habitat for these coral species means a chance for recovery and the opportunity to save them from extinction.

Department of Transportation, Refunding Baggage Fees for Delayed Checked Bags
Docket No. DOT-OST-2016-0208

 Empirical evidence regarding the social science of consumer satisfaction counsels in favor of adopting an automatic refund mechanism for delayed baggage instead of requiring consumers to request and submit an additional form as is currently required under Regulation Z. Because negative experiences with service recovery can further worsen consumers' dissatisfaction, it is in the interests of both consumers and airline companies for the Department of Transportation to make the refund process for delayed baggage as efficient and painless as possible.
According to a study by Pezak and Sebastianelli, efforts to improve the quality of airline services, including baggage services, tend to boost overall customer satisfaction. L. Pezak & R. Sebastianelli, Service Quality in the U.S. Airline Industry: Factors Affecting Customer Satisfaction, 2013 Pa. Econ. Assoc. 143, 145. At the same time, since relatively few options are available to consumers choosing among airlines, poor customer service rarely harms the airlines' profitability. B.P. Waguespack & D.L. Rhoades, Twenty Five Years of Measuring Airline Service Quality, 10 Research in Transp. Bus. & Mgmt. 33, 37-38 (2014). In the present market, therefore, airline companies have little incentive to adopt fairer practices regarding delayed baggage. These findings imply that the proposed rule will improve the experiences of consumers beyond the level that would exist without regulation. 
 But while refunds are effective at improving customer satisfaction after a negative customer experience, a difficult or unpleasant service recovery process tends, for obvious reasons, to deepen consumers' antipathy. See A. Kau & E.W. Loh, The Effects of Service Recovery on Consumer Satisfaction: A Comparison Between Complainants and Non-Complainants, 20 J. Serv. Mkt. 101, 107-08 (2006). If consumers who are already frustrated by baggage delays can only obtain a refund through a needlessly slow and bureaucratic process, the proposed rule will likely yield more dissatisfaction, not less. The Department should ensure that the proposed rule avoids exacerbating consumers' frustrations by requiring that airlines automatically process the required refunds. And because favorable service recovery experiences also promote consumers' trust in the company and increase positive word-of-mouth behavior, see id. at 108, a simple automatic refund mechanism would serve the interests of both consumers and airlines.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

I hope you will consider labels that honestly portray the living conditions so people can make informed decisions. Consumers deserve honesty and accuracy!

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I am a family physician providing primary care at an urban FQHC and urban Indian Health program clinic in the heart of Silicon Valley, in San Jose, CA. I urge you to continue reimbursing audio-only telehealth visits beyond the pandemic. 

Our clinic's patients have benefited greatly from telehealth services, whether because traveling to our clinic requires multiple bus rides, because they are ill with COVID, or for a variety of other important reasons. Among our patients who use telehealth visits, my colleagues and I have found that even here in Silicon Valley, the digital divide keeps many of our clinic's low-income and elderly patients unable to access video visits. Many of our patients still lack high-speed internet access. Others, particularly our elderly patients including many Medicare patients, are unfamiliar or uncomfortable with the video technology. Audio-only visits have provided a critical lifeline for our patients for the past two years, and will continue to do so. 

Through audio-only phone visits, we are able to provide high quality visits that meet the needs of our patients. We provide care for acute illnesses, care for chronic illnesses such as diabetes and high blood pressure, pediatric visits, and more. For patients with a blood pressure cuff and a scale at home, we can provide preventive visits. We have used grants to fund home blood pressure cuffs for patients and have used audio phone visits to bring those patients' blood pressures down to goal levels, decreasing the patients' risk for heart attack and stroke. We keep patients with acute illnesses such as infections out of the hospital by providing treatment before the condition becomes severe, thus preventing costly emergency room visits and hospitalizations. We are even able to diagnose and treat dermatologic conditions via audio-only visits when patients send a photo of the skin issue before the visit. 

Audio-only care is equivalent to video-based care for many patients in many circumstances. Audio-only care has been crucial for many of our vulnerable patients, who would be at risk of deteriorating health and worsening health outcomes if they lost access to audio-only visits. I urge CMS to please continue reimbursing audio-only visits, for the health of our patients.

Sincerely,
Bridget Harrison MD MPH

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

People are interested in seeing our food animals treated in a humane manner. Also, I depend on the accuracy of labels to help me make purchasing decisions. Unfortunately there are always those that want to get around vague definitions which the USDA is so good at.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

As an organic business stakeholder, I strongly support the Organic Livestock and Poultry Practices (OLPP) Rule that strengthens the animal welfare standards for organic livestock production. Reinstating the OLPP Rule without further delay is critical to ensure continued consumer trust in the organic seal. 

The OLPP was finalized after years of public input and aligns with the clear intent of the National Organic Standards Board. Organic livestock producers strongly support this rule. Organic consumers support this rule.

Consumer willingness to pay the organic premium relies on a strong USDA Organic seal and having confidence that organic products meet rigorous standards. Animal welfare is an important part of consumer expectations for organic products. More broadly, the vast majority of dedicated organic shoppers identified dynamic progress and continuous improvement in the organic standards as important to them.

As demonstrated by the most recent consumer data, USDA's revised cost-benefit analysis on the OLPP rule wrongly estimates that the costs of higher standards outweigh the benefits. As a member of the organic business community, I know that the benefits of the OLPP rule and strengthened animal welfare standards outweigh the costs. The private sector works hard to uphold the integrity of the organic seal, but we need the government to keep up with us in setting organic standards that honor consumer trust in that seal. USDA's failure to implement the OLPP final rule jeopardizes consumer confidence in the organic label, and could cause catastrophic impacts that ripple throughout the organic industry.

One of the most important components of patient care is being able to provide adequate patient education. This is the key to empowering patients and their families to make healthy choices that ultimately result in better outcomes. When patients and their families are educated about their conditions and recommended care, the result is fewer complications, visits to emergency rooms or readmission to acute care facilities. The potential savings to the patient, the facility and the health care system are very significant. When the nurse staffing and skill mix is not adequate, appropriate patient education can not occur. 

Please support the adoption of two quality measures on nursing for inclusion in CMS quality reporting program in the Medicare Program; Hospital Inpatient Prospective Payment Systems (IPPS) for Acute Care Hospitals and the Long-Term Care Hospital Prospective Payment System (LTCH PPS) and Proposed Policy Changes and Fiscal Year 2018 Rates; Quality Reporting Requirements for Specific Providers. Specifically, please support: Nurse Staffing; and Staff Skill Mix, which refers to the combination or grouping of different categories of workers providing patient care.

Nurses are critical to patient safety in hospital settings and are the most trusted providers on the health care delivery team. Studies continue to find that inadequate registered nurse staffing is associated with increased mortality and multiple types of avoidable adverse events causing patient harm, reinforcing the need to match staffing and skill mix to patients need for nursing care. In fact, there is a direct correlation between nurse staffing, patient satisfaction, readmissions, and adverse events. 

Yet patients and their families are unable to access information on Hospital Compare about how many nurses are staffing the unit to which they may be admitted and the staff skill mix, both of which ultimately impact outcomes. Skill mix is part of the formula for appropriate staffing. Proper use of support personnel improves nurses workflow, permitting nurses to fully apply their professional knowledge and skill.

Dear Friends,

Please consider the following that I respectfully submit as both an owner and breeder of Scarlet macaws:

The Scarlet macaw is not endangered at all here in the US where it has become a very prolific exotic species with a relatively large captive bred population in every state of the USA. The Scarlet macaw is one of the most popular captive bred macaw species and has proliferated as a result of domestic husbandry. The Scarlet macaw is the 2nd most commonly kept pet macaw in the US following the Blue & Gold macaw. That alone speaks volumes for not listing it as endangered here in the US.

The Scarlet macaw was originally impacted due to deforestation and habitat loss in it's native environment, but conservation efforts in those countries have had a positive effect and the Scarlet macaw has proliferated as a result, and the population has recovered and is now considered stable. We have not imported Scarlet macaws since 1992 and the fact that they have produced so well domestically attests to their innate ability to adapt and survive in friendly & new environments and that they are not, in fact, an endangered species.

The Scarlet macaw is not endangered domestically, but it could become endangered in the US if listed on the ESA. There are 25 states where it is illegal to keep any species that is listed on the ESA, and pet owners & breeders in those states automatically become criminals unless they have a Captive Bred Wildlife Permit to breed and/or keep them. 

Listing the Scarlet macaw on the ESA is counter intuitive and counterproductive. Breeders will not be able to sell the offspring from their producing pairs across state lines without a CBW permit and prospective buyers will not be able to buy and keep them without the same. As it is right now, even conservation breeders of endangered species here in the US who do not approve of hybrids have turned to producing hybrids with their recently listed ESA species. Breeders of ESA listed species need a product that they can sell legally across state lines to the pet trade, breeders & private buyers that can be legally shipped and legally kept without restrictions, and without having to worry about criminal charges being filed against them. 

Breeders need a way to produce income to pay their bills and to feed and otherwise care for their flock. Some breeders with recently listed ESA species have already closed off nest boxes and shut down breeding pairs from future production. Many breeders can not afford to house and feed the extra birds that they are not able to sell. Others have already turned to producing hybrids with their recently listed ESA species, including the Buffon's, Military and Blue-throated macaws. This trend to create new hybrids will only increase, and could eventually worsen to extreme proportions, with the addition of the Scarlet macaw to the ESA since the Scarlet macaw is the 2nd most commonly produced macaw species here in the US. 

Many breeders are already producing hybrids with Scarlet macaws. The market for hybrid macaws in the US has become significant the last few years and nearly all of the hybrids sell for more than the pure species that they were originally produced from. Listing the Scarlet macaw on the ESA will decrease the demand for pure species Scarlet macaws, and eventually decrease their production, as well. If 50% of the nation can no longer legally keep them and they end up either confiscated with no place to house them, or in the hands of breeders that produce hybrids with them, what will become of the species? If this trend continues, the US will become the first country with nothing but hybrids available to the pet trade, and it's population of endangered species dwindling to just a few that conservation breeders, with the resources to do so, can afford to house and care to for. Do we really want to become a country that is to blame for endangering the Scarlet macaw species?

I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed Revised Definition of Waters of the United States. Reducing protection of our nations surface water will negatively impact sensitive species such as amphibians that rely on shallow, temporary surface water bodies for their survival and reproduction, but it will also negatively impact the 13 million households in the United States who rely on private wells as drinking water.
Isolated wetlands provide the same or greater function as adjacent wetlands and should be protected. Isolated wetlands filter surface water, recharge groundwater, provide breeding habitat for amphibians and insects and food and water for larger animals.
Requiring a direct hydrologic surface connection is not scientifically sound and goes against the definition of wetland hydrology set forth in Section 404 of the Clean Water Act and the 1987 Corps of Engineers Wetlands Delineation Manual. In these documents, wetlands are defined as areas that are inundated or saturated by surface or groundwater at a frequency and duration sufficient to support a prevalence of vegetation typically adapted for life in saturated soil conditions. Groundwater is a critical connection between wetlands and our planets groundwater that we cannot directly seem. According to the 2015 US Census, 13 million people, 10 percent of the United States, rely on groundwater from private wells for drinking water. Clean water is a human right and the United States should be protecting ephemeral streams and isolated wetlands to protect every persons right to clean drinking water.

Section 701 Rule – TRICARE SELECT - PRIME 
Comments Requested: November 28, 2017 
Comments provided in this document represent patient access issues as it relates to civilian 
providers providing patients and prescribers access to quality product, product education, 
including indication for use, proper function, and safe maintenance. 
According to the 701 rule, if an enrollee cannot access services within an acceptable period of 
time, they will be able to receive care from any authorized provider without having to pay the 
additional cost-sharing. 
The rule is simple and makes sense as it provides timely access to enrollees, when such care 
cannot be provided by the military installation, or by a contracted network provider. 
Our comments are regarding access to patients when bases/MTFs do not allow provider access. 
We are hopeful that our comments, based on 22 years of experience in the same field, will 
provide a productive perspective that will improve patient access to, not only care, but 
education – which is the cornerstone of an effective and compliant treatment plan. 
1) DME companies have limited access to some facilities due to a widely misinterpreted 
memo dated March 17, 2012 signed by the Assistant Secretary of Defense Health 
Affairs. The memo addressed a serious issue present in 25 MTFs where DME companies 
were engaging in what appeared to be irregular, and/or inappropriate billing practices. 
The Assistant Secretary called for this activity to immediately cease: “I am directing 
that the Deputy Director, TMA, shall immediately notify our MCSCs that their 
network DME providers are not to participate in these arrangements. Those DME 
providers that are involved will cease operations.” 
a. Unfortunately, this was interpreted by some to mean that all DME providers were 
no longer allowed on bases/MTFs. Those DME providers that were not in any 
way engaging in these questionable practices were banned from many bases. 
b. As stated above, patient compliance when using a medical device hinges on the 
understanding of its proper use, and its safe handling. When DME companies 
were not allowed on base/MTF, patients were no longer allowed this benefit in 
favor of a package in the mail, and the hope that they would understand the 
instructions. 
c. It would be helpful to the civilian providers if there were minimum standards to 
follow as it relates to base/MTF access. In the absence of guidelines, there are 
inconsistencies that have lead to issues, and ultimately, it is the enrollee that 
suffers the consequence. 
2) Fair & Equitable Form of Issue Resolution between provider and parties: It has been 
our experience that discord between providers, MTFs, and contractors are rare, and yet 
providers find themselves at a loss regarding issues brought up because there is no 
process by which a provider may defend a position, or present their own challenges. 
a. Contractors, although they have a dedicated team to maintain the provider 
network, they are largely not provider advocates. 
b. Provider questions go unanswered, and issues go unaddressed, unless they are 
brought by the base/MTF. 
 
When expanding the potential for civilian provider utilization, we feel it is important to clarify, 
and outline a framework for such providers to effectively deliver quality care and promote 
compliance and positive clinical outcomes.

It retains wide bipartisan support, including from 96 percent of people who commented on the recent rollback of the rule in Alaska. 

In the middle of multiple national crises, the Trump administration focused on finalizing its plan to remove crucial protections for Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, serving industry interests aiming to open the forests to clear-cutting. President-elect Biden promised bold climate action — and full protection of the Tongass is an integral part of that. It’s already stored over 3 billion tons of carbon — about 15% of what the United States produces in a year — and continues to store more and more each passing year. 

I urge you to fully reinstate the Roadless Rule protection to the Tongass National Forest and put the public interest, environmental justice, our public lands, and taxpayers above corporate profits. 

Thank you for considering my comments.

1. The new proposed rule adds several “factors” to the overall calculus of how FEMA will 
determine when to recommend an IA declaration. This is exciting because I really believe that it

the means in which FEMA anticipates this data to become available: 
a. As an example, insurance data will feature more prominently in the new analysis. While 
this is not inherently a bad idea, FEMA seems to believe that the Insurance

state, along with limits, exclusions and types of coverage, and this just is not the case.

stakeholders to support a framework now where the details are left to be determined 
later. 
 
2. The rule does not seem to do a good job in regard to differentiating between widespread 
events, and localized events that still may rise to the level of a major disaster. Throughout the

analysis (local vs. statewide) as the primary focus, and provide an exception to allow for the

As a U.S. government employee that serves my country overseas as a Foreign Service officer, I am committed to public service and share the CDC's mission to keep the United States safe. I have spent 17 years voluntarily moving around the world with my family and pets, at great financial expense, in the name of public service.

While the impact of these restrictions on the broader population is minimal, the negative repercussions are overwhelmingly placed on federal employees, who seek nothing but to advance the country's mission wherever and whenever is needed. On behalf of North Arkansas Regional Medical Center (NARMC), thank you for the opportunity to respond to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) request for comment on potential remedies for the nearly 30% reduction in reimbursement for certain 340B hospitals that a district court judge ruled were unlawful. Specifically, the agency seeks potential remedies for the calendar year (CY) 2018 and 2019 payments and for use in CY 2020 payments in the event the agency receives an adverse ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals. 

 

NARMC is a 501(c)(3) non-profit DSH serving a population of approximately 100,000 people spread over 5 counties (3500 mi2) in rural north-central Arkansas. 340B savings allow our health-system to provide rural health clinics, cancer treatment, emergency medical services, and obstetrics, among other services. Without the 340B program, tens-of-thousands of people would be at risk for losing vital basic healthcare services.

 

We believe the remedy should be as follows: Refund payments should be made to each affected 340B hospital and calculated using the JG modifier, which identifies claims for 340B drugs that were reduced under the 2018 and 2019 hospital outpatient prospective payment system (OPPS) rules, and others not adversely impacted by the reductions should be held harmless. This remedy would not disrupt the Medicare program and is consistent with those for past violations of law.

 

While the claims will be for different total amounts, the percentage of the claim that the hospital was underpaid is identical in each case. These calculations should be on a hospital-by-hospital basis. Once the total amount that each hospital was paid is calculated, that amount can be multiplied by a single factor, which will be uniform across hospitals, to determine how much should have been paid and thus how much the reimbursement was reduced. Each hospital can be compensated according to the amount that its reimbursements were reduced plus interest.

 

There is ample authority for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to remedy the underpayments caused by its unlawful rule, including: Cape Cod Hospital v. Sebelius, (D.C. Cir. 2011) (HHS corrected errors for the future and past claims for which hospitals had been underpaid), H. Lee Moffitt Cancer Ctr. & Res. Inst. Hosp., Inc. v. Azar, (D.D.C. 2018), (HHS may make a retroactive adjustment without applying the budget-neutrality requirement to cancer hospitals that received a statutorily mandated adjustment a year later than the law required), and Shands Jacksonville Medical Center v. Burwell, (D.D.C. 2015), (HHS compensated hospitals for three years of across-the-board cuts with a one-time, prospective increase of 0.6%). 

 

The authority the agency cites is not applicable because such expenditures would be required by a court decision in service of fixing a prior unlawful underpayment. The agency does not consistently apply budget neutrality to fix its missteps and in other relevant instances. For example, HHS allows for retroactive correction of the wage index without any budget-neutrality adjustment when it made the error. In addition, budget neutrality does not apply to changes in enrollment or utilization for drugs when the average sales price increases. 

 

There Is No Basis for Paying Hospitals Less than the Statutory ASP Plus 6%.The OPPS mandates HHS reimburse hospitals for covered outpatient drugs at ASP plus 6%. This was the methodology used from 2013 to 2017. HHS has now requested comment on adjusting the payment for 2018, 2019 and 2020 from ASP plus 6% to ASP plus 3%. Although the agency has some authority to deviate from this law, the agency is attempting to use a policy rationale that is inconsistent with the law itself and, therefore, it would be unlawful to reduce ASP to 3%.

The proposed rule expands the criteria under which children are required to provide biometric and DNA samples for immigration and asylum proceedings. I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

It is against the humanitarian values of our country to subject children to prolonged detention as part of a civil case. Many of the detained children will ultimately be found to meet the legal definition of refugees, and all of them have gone through displacement and upheaval to arrive on U.S. soil. They are a fragile group, many of whom have directly suffered violence and other trauma. Our nation should not welcome child refugees by incarcerating them for months on end. Children are not at fault for the world's problems, and children cannot thrive in detention. 

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Reinstate the Roadless Rule on the Tongass Dear Comment Period Alaska Roadless Rule, I pay my bills here in Southeast Alaska, at least in part, by having short and intense conversations on airplanes. I help wedge wadered clients from all over the globe into DeHavilland Beavers and we drop in on some of the most spectacular intact temperate rainforest habitat in the world, making intimate albeit brief connections with the salmon, char, and trout who thrive in this unique environment. If everything goes well, the airplane conversations are really prelude and d[eacute]nouement to the main act-it's not easy to talk over the throaty roar of a 450 horse radial engine-but the plane rides are nevertheless important moments to contextualize the experience for folks making brief visits to the Tongass National Forest. From our sub-2000' cruising altitude, it's so much easier to see connections between the glaciers, steep mountains, spruce and hemlock-clad hillsides, and our short high-gradient, salmon-producing streams Like any guide worth his salt, I want my clients to feel the tug, and to get their trophy shot for Instagram, but it's equally important to me that they understand that image's place in a much larger ecological drama. Rehearsing the details of their trip-sharing a run with a brown bear sow teaching her cubs to chase chum, rapidly retreating as a 22' tidal swing filled a thousand yards of tidal flat behind them in a matter of minutes, watching both salmon and dollies in the intertidal repeatedly slash at slowly stripped poppers-my hope is my clients could string the moments into a larger story about our day fishing. That they could readily tell you about how they got to play a small role in an ongoing Tongass narrative that carves out space for average Americans to enjoy amazing recreational opportunities on public lands. I don't make this final point explicit, but I also hope their experience in one small part of the nearly 17 million acres of the Tongass National Forest leads to an ethic of stewardship-and that they consider speaking up for conserving this national treasure so future generations can participate in this story, too. Another summer airplane conversation put the future opportunities to add to this Tongass story at risk, creating just such an opportunity to speak up for the forest. Perhaps you heard about the Air Force One confab between Alaska's governor and the president? The conversation is most famous for rekindling efforts to despoil Alaska's other world-class fishery. But while we were collectively digging out our No-Pebble-Mine gear and fighting again to save Bristol Bay's fisheries from this mega project, our Governor and Congressional delegation were quietly strongarming the USFS to roll back protections on the spectacular fisheries here in Southeast Alaska, too. The public lands story that emerges from this latter airplane conversation is less about meaningful connection to representative pieces of intact ecological beauty, and more about dollar signs produced on the heavy labor of miners and loggers. Here's the short version of the plan for the Tongass, hatched in that quick tarmac exchange just outside of Anchorage: under the President's direction, the USFS was forced to roll back protections for the Tongass in the form of a full exemption for Alaska from the 2001 Roadless Rule. This matters for anglers like me and my clients: simply put, the Roadless Rule has helped to conserve key areas of the Tongass from the predictable impacts of industrial old-growth logging, in the process supporting healthy habitat for salmon, trout, and steelhead and enabling guys like me feed my family as part of the $2 billion per year fishing and tourism industry. Dear USFWS and NOAA,

Despite the resounding success of the ESA, the proposed changes will make protecting endangered and threatened species more difficult. By defining habitat to exclude areas that currently cannot support a species, you would be foreclosing an important tool that has been used successfully in the past to promote species recovery. This change could preclude proactive and essential measures to establish an area as critical habitat and then restore that area for species recovery, a tactic thats been used from HawaiI to continental U.S. to help conserve the palila and other species trying to survive in degraded ecosystems. Introduction 

On behalf of its member companies, the Environmental Technology Council 

(ETC) respectfully submits these comments on EPA’s proposed rule entitled 

“Modernizing Ignitable Liquids Determinations” published in the Federal Register on 

April 2, 2019. 84 Fed. Reg. (FR) 12539. 

ETC is the leading trade association of commercial firms that provide 

technologies and services to customers for the recycling, treatment, and secure disposal 

of industrial and hazardous wastes. ETC member companies own and operate a wide 

variety of commercial operations, including spent solvent distillation, oil recovery 

facilities, metals reclamation units, mercury recovery from fluorescent lamps, 

photographic chemical and film recovery facilities, wastewater treatment plants, 

collection and transfer stations, secure landfills, high-temperature incinerators, and a 

variety of other types of facilities. 

Although the proposed rule identifies “generators and laboratories” as affected 

parties, 84 FR 12540 col. 3, EPA should be aware that commercial treatment, storage and 

disposal (TSD) facilities probably make more ignitability determinations on hazardous 

wastes than most other entities. TSD facilities perform the ignitability test methods and 

apply the regulatory exclusions in order to determine whether hazardous wastes they 

receive from customers exhibit the ignitability characteristic. The test methods and 

procedures are stipulated in their RCRA permits and Waste Analysis Plans (WAPs), 

which are the result of state permit proceedings with public participation. Changes to the 

ignitability test methods will need to be incorporated into their WAPs, which will impose 

additional costs and burdens on TSD facilities. As a result, ETC member companies are 

directly and substantially affected by the proposed rule. 

Comments 

1. Flash Point Test Methods 

The ETC supports the proposal to update the flash point test methods to use new 

technology and best practices developed by ASTM. 84 FR 12543 col. 3. We understand 

that EPA is proposing these newer test methods “as an alternative” to current methods, 

and not as a mandatory replacement. 84 FR 12544 col. 2. We agree with EPA that

 
current test methods still “provide accurate determinations” of whether a liquid waste is 

characteristic for ignitability, id., and therefore the newer test methods should be 

optional, not prescriptive. The cost of replacing all current equipment to conduct only the 

new test method(s) would be expensive and unnecessary. We anticipate and agree with 

EPA that TSD facilities will replace existing test equipment and install the new 

equipment as needed and based upon a typical upgrade cycle. Therefore, the final rule 

should make clear that the current flash point test methods in 40 CFR § 261.21(a)(1) may 

continue to be used so that all test methods are available. 

The same caveat applies to the phase-out of mercury thermometers. We support 

EPA’s proposal to remove the requirement to use mercury thermometers in the analytical 

methods, provided the use of non-mercury-containing temperature measuring devices is 

an option

It is also unfair to those passengers who would like to hear the safety announcements. Further, allowing calls on an airplane will have a negative affect on passenger interaction. I often ride the subways and buses in Chicago, and cannot begin to tell you how annoying these calls are to the general public. Dozens and dozens of people chatting about irrelevant matters because their cell phone is their new primary means of communication. It is very difficult for Flight Attendants to enforce "civility" and monitor "social interactions". We already have passengers asking us to "make the passenger put his seat up", or "tell those parents to control their children". I am a Family Nurse Practitioner student at Emory University’s Nell Hodgson Woodruff School of Nursing. At Emory, I have given presentations on the use of photography-based artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical dermatology, which has made me acutely aware of the ethical and technical challenges surrounding biometric imaging. 

After review, my first significant concern involves current accuracy gaps in facial recognition technology across age, gender, and racial groups. NIST’s Face Recognition Vendor Test reports false-match rates up to five times higher for Black and Native American females and substantially lower accuracy for children under 14. Without safeguards or significant improvement, these disparities could result in disproportionate secondary screenings, travel delays, and, most concerningly, leave the youngest and most vulnerable travelers (children < 14 years) exposed to undetected victimization and crime. I recommend that CBP publish public algorithmic performance data by demographic group and commit to ongoing third-party audits through NIST or comparable independent evaluators. 

Secondly, the privacy protections and data-retention policies should be reevaluated. Per this rule, non-citizen biometric data may be retained for up to 75 years, a clear deviation beyond the 15-year retention period that DHS and CBP currently apply to most travel-related records under their System of Records Notices (SORNs) and Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs), as outlined in the Federal Register pursuant to the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. § 552a). The 75-year retention period represents a significant and unnecessary extension, exceeding even the longest existing DHS retention framework for comparable administrative records, in addition to, far exceeding the global norm observed by fellow democratic nations of 3–15 years. I urge DHS to consider aligning its biometric retention policy with its existing travel-record standards by either (a) shortening the retention period to 15 years with case-based extensions, or (b) linking data retention to specific travel events (such as visa expiration or departure) rather than retaining every traveler’s biometric data for nearly three-quarters of a century. Keeping sensitive biometric data long after it serves its operational purpose magnifies privacy, security, and fairness risks without clear justification. 

Thirdly, unlike Canada, the U.K., and EU nations with established biometric monitoring systems, DHS currently lacks a mandate for recurring, independent privacy audits of the systems. The absence of regular external audits means there is no independent verification that the biometric data collected will be handled lawfully, ethically, and fairly. This gap undermines accountability, increases risk of misuse, and weakens public trust, especially when compared to peer nations that sustain robust biometric programs while successfully maintaining such oversight. Implementing independent privacy audits for DHS biometric systems would likely cost only $5–8 million per year, less than 1 percent of the program’s total budget. In exchange, such audits would elevate U.S. policy to alignment with international standards, strengthen public trust, and reduce long-term legal and reputational risks.

It is only clear that all non-citizens will undergo facial biometric screening. Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

Humane does not mean crammed into a small enclosed space in unnatural conditions. Free range should truly mean free to move about outdoors without having to b in direct contact with other animals.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

I support the call to protect the Tongass, to allow the Alaska Natives control this local forest as in the past. Only, fire prevention efforts should be the concern of the Government.

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

I support Stars and Stripes and oppose the rules that restrict the free flow of news and information because service men and women and their families deserve to be as fully informed as the rest of us. 

I hope the rules can be amended to remove the parts that:
• Restrict the filing of Freedom of Information requests.
• Prohibit the publication of classified and controlled unclassified information after it has been published by other media.
• Require Public Affairs escorts for Stars and Stripes reporters.
The mission of Stars and Stripes is to provide fair and impartial news and information to the military community. To do so, it is “governed by the principles of the First Amendment.” 
The Statement of Need for This Rulemaking spells out the mission very well: “Stripes provides a reliable source of commercially available U.S. and world news and original news stories developed through first-hand reporting by Stripes staff from bases around the world that is accurate, fair, impartial, credible, and editorially independent of the military chain of command and Public Affairs activities.”
The rules purport “to reaffirm (Stripes’) editorial independence” but, in fact, they fall short in three key areas. 
1. Stripes reporters cannot use the FOIA, which means they are not free to report the news. If they are restricted by a government rule, it is censorship. Even the proposed rules call for an ombudsman to ensure the newsroom is free from censorship. 
2. Stars and Stripes cannot republish some stories that have been published by other media, which means the paper is neither fully independent nor free from government control, as the rules purport to reaffirm.
3. Stars and Stripes reporters are often “escorted” to their assignments by Public Affairs officers, which means the reporters are not free of command interference or “Public Affairs activities.”
The proposed rules should be changed to allow Stripes editorial employees to use the FOIA and to report on the findings. 
The rules should be changed to allow the publisher to make the call on republishing stories that involve classified information or controlled unclassified information. 
And the rules should make clear that Public Affairs officers, as important as they are, do not need to shadow Stripes reporters. Stripes reporters are also DoD employees who have passed background checks and who carry Common Access Cards.
Much of this discussion is about matters of trust and control. In my opinion, it would help if more of the trust and some of the control were shifted to Stars and Stripes. 
Thank you for considering my proposals.
Reid MacCluggage
Chair, Publisher’s Advisory Board, Stars and Stripes

Re: 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule Dear USDA Forest Service, I am writing to request that you fully restore 2001 Roadless Rule protections on the Tongass National Forest and end large-scale old growth timber sales on the entirety of the forest. It is appalling to allow roads and/or logging in this National Forest! The Tongass is a key weapon for fighting climate change, with its old-growth trees effectively trapping and sequestering climate-warming greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Scientists have estimated that the forest accounts for about 8 percent of the carbon sequestered by all national forests. Protecting the Tongass from old-growth logging will not only preserve that capacity, but avoid releasing carbon currently sequestered in its trees. The Tongass is also the ancestral and contemporary homeland of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples, and they have been the driving force of the effort to protect the forest. Their way of life is inextricably linked with these lands and waters. They hunt, gather, fish and harvest medicines in the Tongass that their ancestors have stewarded for more than 10,000 years. Restoring full protections will allow their traditional use of the land to continue. As part of planning for a future beyond old-growth timber, please also make a sustained investment in the Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy. Operating in full consultation with Tribal governments and local communities, this program will help the region stoke the already robust fishing and recreation industries that are driving the economy. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Gale Luce -PII-

profitability, and focus on their core mission. Through a PEO, the employees of their small and mid-sized

regulation, specifically those which have been entrenched in an industry for years, it is understood these 

procedures have been a monumental undertaking. I must commend the Federal Aviation Administration 

(FAA) for your work towards consolidating standards which pertain to specific airworthiness regulations 

for transport category airplanes. In many instances regarding sweeping regulation reform, regardless if 

they are specific to fire, it is easy to add unnecessarily complex layers of regulation. For the proposed 

amendments to 14 CFR Parts 25, 27, 29, 91, 121, 125, and 135, it is clear the FAA is seeking to reduce 

burdensome requirements, going from prescriptive requirement to more performance-base standards 

which is an overall positive move. With that stated, I do not agree with all proposed changes. With this 

letter, I will outline a few specific personal positions which I hope will allow further discourse to occur. 

The Executive Summary of the proposed rule states, “This proposal would convert those 

flammability regulations from detailed, prescriptive requirements into simpler, performance-based 

standards. This proposal would divide these standards into two categories: Those designed to protect the

 
airplane and its occupants from the hazards of in-flight fires, and those designed to protect the airplane 

and its occupants from the hazards caused by post-crash fires.” In modern building design, performance 

based design regarding fire protection and life safety can often allow designers to “work within” the code 

to meet a minimum standard of life safety. Areas where allowances are easily understood are scenarios 

where the addition of automatic fire sprinkler systems allow for relaxed interior material use, increased 

height and area allowances, reductions in hourly ratings, etc. Additionally, based on computer aided 

modeling, alterations to exiting requirements found in NFPA 101 can be made or evaluations to smoke 

control systems can be provided. In both instances, where reductions or increases have been made, it is 

via the addition of an alternate means of protection, i.e., fire sprinkler systems, alarm and notification 

systems, smoke control. What are the alternate means of protection which would be provided for 

passenger life safety if regulations allow the move to performance based design? While I am a proponent 

of performance based design in modern building construction, I do not believe I am a full proponent of the 

performance based design approach outlined in the proposed rules to the aforementioned 14 CFR Parts.

would be deemed acceptable or safe based on passenger survivability. Looking specifically at proposed 

§ 25.853(c)(2)(i), it states the rule ”…would set the performance standard that extensively used parts, 

components, and assemblies must not propagate the largest fire that, by itself, would not be a hazard to 

the airplane.” Reading further through the document, I was unable to find a definition or a threshold to 

what would constitute a fire which would be “a hazard to the airplane.” This isn’t to say I don’t agree with 

the theory of the rule, however, there are much too many holes of undefined thresholds which must be 

addressed.

DRAWBACK AND TFTEA HISTORY 
 
Drawback dates to the Tariff Act of 1789, and its original purpose remains the same today: to 
promote U.S. exports, manufacturing capital investment, and job creation in the United States. 
Congress modified the original drawback provisions several times in the years to follow, 
ultimately including them in the Tariff Act of 1930. Since then, Congress has consistently acted 
to expand drawback rights, including these changes: 
 
• 1980: Congress added same condition direct-identification drawback.1 In expanding the 
program, Congress codified the right to claim drawback of 99% of duties, taxes or fees 
paid. 
 
• 1984: Congress added “same condition” substitution drawback.2 
 
• 1993: Congress expanded standards yet again with the Customs Modernization Act of 
1993.3 This included replacing “same condition” drawback with broader unused 
merchandise drawback. It also included easing the rules for substitutability to include 
“commercially interchangeable” goods, and added 8-digit HTSUS (Harmonized Tariff 
System of the U.S.) substitution for petroleum products. 
 
• 1999: Congress clarified the scope of drawback available to include “any duty, tax, or fee 
imposed under Federal law because of importation.”4 
 
• 2004: Congress amended the drawback laws again to reverse the Texport Oil5 decision 
and Customs’ rulings limiting drawback, confirming that Section 1313(j) allows for 
drawback of any duty, tax, or fee imposed under Federal law upon entry or importation.6 
 
• 2008: Congress broadened substitutability for wine if it is of the same color, with a price 
variation not over 50% between the imported wine and the exported wine.7 
 
• 2016: The President signed the Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015 
(“TFTEA”) providing numerous, significant enhancements to the drawback laws under 19 
U.S.C. § 1313, including broadened standard

Conservation Northwest respectfully submits the following comments on proposed rule changes. 

Regulation for Prohibitions to Threatened Wildlife and Plants

 Changes to Blanket 4(d) rule: We find this proposal very problematic. Having blanket protections for threatened species allows for immediate changes to be made after listing to decrease likelihood that a species will further decline to an Endangered status. The use of blanket protections also allows for protections when not at all stressors to a species can be identified. In a world of increasing interacting stressors and complexity, and intensity of pressures on the natural world, this change moves us in the wrong direction. Allowing for tailoring of take prohibitions through a specific 4(d) rule later is a more preferable and conservative approach. 

 Building a 4(d) rule from scratch without the backstop of blanket protections will take considerable time and effort. Congress has chronically underfunded the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to the detriment of proper implementation of the Act. This change would likely worsen the workload burden on staff while decreasing the ability of the listing process to deliver needed protections to threatened species. 

Finally, the goal of aligning the regulatory approaches of USFWS and the National Marine Fisheries Service seems irrelevant given they deal with very different species. In addition, the number of listings that USFWS has to process are far larger than what NMFS typically faces. The proposed change would, as noted above, cause burdensome workloads for staff. If alignment is desirable, we recommend that the NMFS adopt the practices of USFWS on the use of the blanket 4(d) rule until tailored rules can be developed. 

We therefore request that this rule change not be pursued. 

Thank you for considering our comments.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable. There have already been numerous news reports about detained children being sold, abused, and lost. Allowing this to continue indefinitely is unconscionable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

I am a law clerk at an immigration law firm and am currently in law school in Chicago. As a law clerk, I have worked with a number of immigrants who have founded extremely successful startup companies and contribute millions of dollars toward the U.S. economy. If the IER is rescinded, these individuals will have no viable alternatives to remain in the States. They will take their successful companies and move them elsewhere. Once the founders and the companies leave, thousands of Americans will lose their jobs. Similarly, these companies will not even consider moving from abroad to the U.S., where they could create hundreds of jobs and boost the U.S. economy, if their founders have no reasonable means of staying here.

The DHS claims that the IER does not sufficiently protect "U.S. workers and investors, and is not the appropriate vehicle for attracting and retaining international entrepreneurs."

This is completely false. The IER's requirements ensure that only those immigrants who can clearly demonstrate that their startup would have a significant positive impact on the U.S. economy and job market, are considered for the visa. The rule's other requirements disqualify most other potential applicants such as the requirement that significant U.S. capital be raised from qualified investors, that the startup has received significant awards or grants from certain government entities, etc. Because of its stringent requirements, the IER allows U.S. workers and investors to remain well-protected.

The elimination of the startup visa will be a devastating blow to the U.S. Over 50% of the most successful private companies in the U.S. have been founded by immigrants. Immigrant-founded businesses have higher survival rates than those of U.S.-born founders. The IER is estimated to create over 300,000 new U.S. jobs over the next 10 years. Furthermore, there is clear bipartisan support for the IER, and 90% of U.S.-born AND foreign-born company founders believe a startup visa for immigrant entrepreneurs would benefit the U.S. economy (according to the National Foundation for American Policy). 

In effect, getting rid of the IER is a serious mistake that will inevitably harm the U.S. economy. I sincerely encourage you to read all of the comments submitted in this forum and take notice of the concerns of the American public. We want you to read the facts and listen to the advice of the company founders who advocate for saving the IER. We need immigrant entrepreneurs in this country and want the IER to be saved.

The American Property Casualty Insurers Association, the National Association of Mutual 
Insurance Companies and the Reinsurance Association of America (the “Trades”) represent the 
great majority of insurance and reinsurance companies underwriting property and casualty 
insurance throughout the United States. 
The Trades commend IRS/Treasury on the clarification provided by the proposed regulations 
addressing the changes to the Net Operating Loss deduction of Code §172 by Pub. L. 115-97, 
known as the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) and the Coronavirus Aid, Relief and Economic 
Security (CARES) Act, Pub. L. 116-136. These regulations provide guidance on the application 
of the special rules for “nonlife” or property and casualty (P&C) companies to consolidated groups 
that include both P&C companies and other companies that are subject to the post-2017 rules (after 
the CARES Act, the post-2020 rules). 
The Explanation of Provisions in Section II, B, 2 of the Preamble notes that the application of the 
80% limitation depends on the status of the entity whose income is being offset, rather than on the 
status of the entity whose loss is being absorbed. The Explanation then sets out a two-factor 
computation for groups that consist of both P&C insurance companies and non-P&C companies 
(the most common arrangement for P&C groups consists of several P&C insurance companies 
held by a noninsurance holding company). 
Subsection (f) of section 172 provides that the deduction allowed under subparagraph (a) for 
nonlife insurance companies is the aggregate of the NOL carried forward or back to the taxable 
year and provides that the 80% limitation of taxable income in the carryback or carryforward year 
does not apply. The language in subsection (a) and (b)(2)(C) of section 172 was modified by the 
CARES Act to focus the 80% limitation on taxable income.

As an independent community pharmacy owner, I care for many Medicare patients. My staff and I provide patient services beyond filling prescriptions. We counsel our patients on the proper use of their medications to promote proper adherence, which leads to better health outcomes and reduces costs to the health care system. 

 

 I urge CMS to require all pharmacy price concessions, or DIR fees, to be reflected at point of sale, as the proposed rule suggests, rather than assessed retroactively. I urge CMS to promptly make this a final requirement. For pharmacy owners such as me, this would provide some predictability as to my minimum reimbursement amounts and better facilitate planning business operations. Moreover, pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and Part D plan sponsors (PDPs) would still be able to offer performance incentives to pharmacies that achieve contractual goals. 

Furthermore, CMS has determined that accounting for pharmacy DIR at point of sale would create significant net savings for Medicare beneficiaries and make vital prescription medication more affordable overall, even after considering any potential increase in monthly premiums.
 
I also commend the proposed rule for creating a definition of mail-order pharmacy. Pharmacies that mail a prescription to a patient who may be temporarily out of the vicinity risk being classified as a mail order pharmacy by some PBMs, even if the patient is paying the retail, and not the mail order, cost-sharing amounts. This can lead to pharmacies being removed from networks. The proposal would bring greater clarity as to what constitutes a mail order pharmacy. 

The proposed rule also reinforces existing "any willing pharmacy" regulations as they pertain to base pharmacy networks. I strongly support this reinforcement. Many independent pharmacies offer services such as compounding or care for patients on specialty medications in addition to retail offerings, but, because of these additional services, PBMs sometimes preclude us from participating in base networks. Moreover, the proposed rule establishes a date when the terms and conditions of the base network must be readily available and would require they be promptly provided at the request of a pharmacy. Thus the rule provides necessary clarifications to the "any willing pharmacy" provisions. While the proposed rule did not expand "any willing pharmacy" provisions to preferred pharmacy networks, I am hopeful future rulemaking will address this.
 
CMS in its proposed rule also expressed disapproval of current PDP sponsor or PBM-specific credentialing criteria in order to participate in a network or dispense certain medications. PBM-specific credentialing is both costly and duplicative of other recognized credentials, and I strongly support CMS' efforts to ban this extra credentialing.

State of Ohio Notification to Consumers of Motor Vehicle Recall 

Let this serve as notification that the Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles (BMV) would like to be considered for 

any/all Federal funding opportunities with regards to BMV recall notifications. Ohio BMV personnel have 

already begun exploratory phases for implementing such a program and are hoping to have a pilot project 

operational by January 1, 2020. 

The Ohio BMV issues approximately 13 million vehicle registrations annually. This number is comprised of 

both new and renewal issuances. For all vehicle registrations approaching their renewal date, a notification is 

sent via mail, email, or text message 45 days prior to the date of expiration. The BMV intends to include 

applicable recall information with customer registration renewal notices. Information provided will, at a 

minimum, notify the vehicle owner of a safety recall and request the customer contact an appropriate 

dealership to have the necessary repairs performed. 

Business rules are very broad in spectrum, which allow for implementation flexibility. In an effort to be 

financially conservative, we have chosen an in-house created process opposed to outsourcing to a third party 

vendor. After action reviews will be conducted when the initial pilot is completed to determine whether an in-

house operation is most efficient or if a third party should be utilized. After initial phases are proven successful, 

it is our hope to begin cross-referencing recall data with notices sent to verify which vehicles had the recall 

repairs performed and which vehicles did not. Automation of this process is currently not in the scope or 

budget for the Ohio BMV’s current recall notification program, nor are any further communication outside of the 

original registration renewal notification. 

Increased costs will be incurred for IT programming, printing, and mailing/electronic transmission of recall 

notifications. While we believe that we have identified a cost-effective way to begin a recall notification program 

internally, there will be manual processes involved. The long-term feasibility of the notification program, and 

identification of rates of completion for recall fixes, may be dependent on the availability of Federal funds. 

Additional details on the Ohio BMV’s current plan and potential enhancements with Federal funds can be 

provided upon request.

Subject: Comments on Proposed Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat 

The Institute for Policy Integrity at New York University School of Law1 submits these comments on the 

Fish and Wildlife Service’s (FWS’s) proposed amendments to its regulations for designating critical 

habitat.2 Policy Integrity is a non-partisan think tank dedicated to improving the quality of government 

decisionmaking through advocacy and scholarship in the fields of administrative law, economics, and 

public policy. Policy Integrity’s amicus brief in Weyerhaeuser Co. v. U.S. FWS, 139 S. Ct. 361 (2018)—

which we attach and hereby incorporate into these comments—focused on the reasonableness and 

necessity of considering indirect benefits and unquantified benefits in weighing the costs and benefits of 

including or excluding areas as critical habitat. 

The proposed rule makes several changes that are inconsistent with the best practices for weighing the 

costs and benefits of agency action. Consequently, the proposed rule is unreasonable and arbitrary as 

drafted and, therefore, should not be finalized. In particular, these comments focus on the following 

proposed changes: 

• The proposed rule wrongly casts doubt on the consideration of indirect benefits, and more 

generally focuses disproportionately on economic costs while paying relatively little attention 

to, and offering little advice on, the possible benefits of designating critical habitat. 

• The proposed rule wrongly defers to regulated entities, lessees, and private landowners on the 

weighing of costs, ceding FWS’s discretion in ways inconsistent with the best practices for 

vetting economic information. The proposed rule also wrongly constrains FWS’s discretion on 

the ultimate decision whether to exclude areas from designation. 

• The proposed rule arbitrarily reverses the agency’s prior position on the treatment of federal 

lands, and in particular highlights potential costs relating to federal leases and permits but fails 

to consider how substitution may offset such costs. 

• The proposed rule makes unreasonable changes with respect to public notice of excluded areas. 

I. The Endangered Species Act Requires Full Consideration of Direct and Indirect Benefits

There are several ways in which the proposed rule wrongly casts doubt on indirect benefits or minimizes 

the potential for a critical habitat designation to result in economic benefits at all.

As a homeowner in Gallatin Gateway, Montana and a regular visitor and recreational user of Yellowstone National Park and the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, I am submitting comments on the Select Agent status of Brucella abortus. I support the removal of B.abortus from the select agent list. My background and connection to this issue is that I am a strong advocate for wild, free-roaming bison (buffalo).

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

Thank you for this opportunity and your consideration of my comments.

Sincerely,
Pamela Sieck
