In selecting which studies to review, the authors of this evidence review committed a error which renders their findings irretrievably flawed: they conflated idiopathic chronic fatigue with ME/CFS. The hallmark symptom of ME/CFS, as evidenced by the CDC's own definition, is post-exertional malaise (PEM). The review includes studies on chronic fatigue and studies which use a case definition which doesn't require PEM, such as Fukuda and Oxford criteria. 

You cannot use evidence of what therapeutic approaches work on idiopathic fatigue as a basis for recommending treatment of ME/CFS. That would be like using a study cohort of people with any sort of cough as a basis for judging whether a particular chemotherapy is an effective treatment for lung cancer. 

The inclusion of people who don't have PEM and therefore don't have ME/CFS renders any conclusion about treatments for ME/CFS invalid. 

The review also doesn't address harm that GET and CBT can do to ME/CFS patients. When is it ever appropriate to recommend a treatment for any illness without considering its potential harm? Apparently the review committee assumes that because exercise is generally benign, it would be benign for ME/CFS patients, since they didn't include evaluation of harm in their selection criteria for which studies to review. But in a disease with PEM, "the worsening of symptoms following even minor physical or mental exertion, with symptoms typically worsening 12 to 48 hours after activity and lasting for days or even weeks" as its hallmark symptom, how can exercise be assumed to be harmless? 

When I was first diagnosed with CFS (as it was called then), I followed the CDC's recommendation for GET. In spite of my careful efforts, it repeated caused PEM and my condition gradually deteriorated until I became housebound. It wasn't until I stopped PEM and relied on pacing that my illness stabilized. I was very relieved when the CDC removed the recommendation of GET from its website, so that what happened to me wouldn't happen to others. 

Exercise is not harmless for people with ME/CFS and there are empirical studies which demonstrate that. 

This review is fundamentally flawed because it looks at studies of fatigued people and incorrectly applies their findings to people with ME/CFS. That is scientifically invalid and should not be published. Nor should any treatment guidelines be based on it. 

The CDC took careful stock of the evidence when it removed GET and CBT as treatments for ME/CFS. It was the correct decision. That decision shouldn't be reversed based on this fundamentally flawed review.

Please find attached the oral testimony of Kyle Isakower on behalf of the American Council for Capital Formation, delivered July 1, 2020.

 
 
Oral Testimony of Kyle Isakower, Senior Vice President for Regulatory and 

Energy Policy, American Council for Capital Formation on EPA Proposed Rule: 

“Increasing Consistency in Considering Benefits and Costs in the Clean Air Act 

Rulemaking Process” 

July 1, 2020 

Good morning, my name is Kyle Isakower, Senior Vice President for Regulatory 

and Energy Policy at the American Council for Capital Formation. ACCF is a 

nonprofit, nonpartisan economic policy organization dedicated to the advocacy of 

pro-growth tax, energy, environmental, regulatory, trade and economic policies 

that encourage investment in the US economy. ACCF appreciates the opportunity 

to provide comment to EPA on its proposed rulemaking to increase consistency in 

considering benefits and costs in the Clean Air Act rulemaking process. 

ACCF supports EPA’s efforts to standardize and add transparency to benefit-cost 

analyses in the Clean Air Act regulatory process, and offers the following specific 

comments:

 
Since 1981, Presidents of both parties have issued multiple Executive Orders and 

OMB Circulars calling for the use of benefit-cost analysis for significant agency 

actions. This proposal simply makes this a regulatory requirement. 

The proposal calls for use of the best available scientific information, and "best 

practices" across multiple fields of science. All stakeholders in the regulatory 

process should be able to rely on EPA to use "best practices" regardless of which 

party controls the Oval Office. 

The proposal would also require EPA add transparency by publishing their 

benefit-cost analyses in a manner that is objective, comprehensive, and 

reproducible. Similarly, the data and analytical conclusions must be presented in a 

manner that is easily understood. To the extent possible, EPA must make public 

all the data and models that were used in the analysis to reach their conclusions. 

Further, the final rule must make clear that uncertainties in data or modeling are 

made transparent to stakeholders. Stakeholders on both sides deserve to know 

the data, models, and assumptions our government uses to make regulatory 

decisions, and the uncertainties associated with them.

 
This transparency should clearly identify what are targeted benefits and what are 

non-targeted co-benefits. Importantly regarding co-benefits, the benefits of 

reducing non-targeted compounds should be considered in benefit-cost analyses. 

However, co-benefits should not be the primary driver in regulatory decision-

making! If a benefit-cost analysis demonstrates that this is the case, then the rule 

is targeting the wrong compound and should not move forward! 

In conclusion, ACCF supports this proposal because it will: 

• Require that EPA adopt best practices in how it assesses risks, benefits 

and costs; 

• Ensure that EPA conducts more systematic reviews of existing studies 

and models using clear criteria; 

• Provide stakeholders with a greater understanding of how EPA will 

estimate benefits and costs, enhancing their ability to more effectively 

participate in the rulemaking process; 

• Enable greater public involvement resulting in more complete and 

accurate analysis of the benefits and costs; and

 
• Acknowledge key uncertainties in the benefit or cost estimates that may 

be critical in final decision-making. 

Thank you again for the opportunity to present to you today.

As consumers, we rely in large part upon information on food packaging to inform our purchase decisions. The new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by creating whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. Companies will still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. This simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit. 

What the public needs and wants is a set of minimum standards to apply to the words "humanely raised" and the like. This should include NOT being raised on a factory farm; it is about each individual animal or bird having free and unfettered access to a minimum outdoor square footage that is perhaps 15 to 20 times the size occupied by the animal's/bird's body so that the animal or bird can move about in the fresh air as nature intended and graze or eat or walk normally. Animals crammed into a building with one small opening that perhaps a few individual animals can enter or exit through does not qualify as humane by anyone's standards other than the industry's, and the industry appears to be concerned only with profit and not with the welfare of the animals it raises for their meat.

Research has shown that the flesh of animals and poultry raised in CAFOs is much less nutritious than that of animals allowed to freely roam outdoors and consume the types of foods that that animal was intended by nature to eat, i.e., grass for beef, insects and various seeds and grains for poultry, etc. Reasonable regulations, therefore, governing "humanely raised" helps not only the animals in question but the health of the public as well.

As the Nurse Administrator for Columbia surgical Institute, I am writing in opposition to CY 2018 OPPS/ASC Proposed Rule for the following reasons with regard to the CAHPS:

1. The cost of having to pay the "approved" vendor. Since ASCs have been doing patient satisfaction surveys for over 20 years, they are more than capable of handling this important aspect of patient care, themselves, and don't need to pay an extra $500- $900/ month for this service. The cost associated with this program will most certainly be a hardship on the bottom line of most facilities, and unlike most businesses, a surgery center cannot pass the increased cost of doing business along to its customers because we get a facility fee and nothing more.

2. The length of the survey. We feel that this lengthy questionnaire will be too long for many of the patients, and that only the patients with negative comments will take the time to respond. If fewer patients reply then the negative replies will impact what appears to be the center's satisfaction rate in a very negative way. For example, if a center has a 60% return rate on their questionnaires with a 97% positive feedback rate currently, this rate would be greatly skewed with fewer patients replying if an automated-type survey was put in place such as the ones being proposed. This will also decrease the level of respect in the community for the ASC since these skewed results will be public record. 

3. Loss of personal touch. We believe that with a 3rd party vendor survey, we will experience the loss of feeling in touch with the patient's concerns. Patients look forward to hearing from us, personally rather than a random call from a "stranger" which is invasive and impersonal. Please consider allowing us to continue handling our patient satisfaction surveys in house, and we are more than willing to share all of our results/ statistics with CMS for your records. In addition, we are prepared with Patient Satisfaction Survey results to present to every CMS surveyor as part of our required, now bi-annual inspections. We recognize the need for transparency for the patients to be able to make a proper choice, but feel this will have the opposite effect. We have a very personal relationship with our patients, and we look forward to personal follow up after every procedure. If required to utilize a third party vendor, we will lose that personal touch.

RE: Docket No. FDA-2013-D-1543 Nonproprietary Naming of Biological Products: Update 

Dear Sir or Madam, 

The National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) submits this letter to the Agency in 

response to a request for comments on ways to balance development of biosimilars and 

interchangeable biologics with innovation of new therapeutic proteins. 

NCPDP is a not-for-profit ANSI-Accredited Standards Development Organization (SDO) consisting 

of more than 1,500 members. The organization provides a multi-stakeholder forum of high-level 

expertise and diverse perspectives for developing and promoting industry standards and business 

solutions that improve patient safety and health outcomes, while also decreasing costs. 

NCPDP is committed to furthering the interoperable electronic exchange of information among a 

wide array of healthcare stakeholders. To assist in consistent and accurate identification of drugs, 

NCPDP’s Work Group 2 Product Identification deals with product identification systems and data, 

including naming, that serve to uniquely identify a product with the intent of establishing 

standards for product identification to avoid ambiguity in distinguishing one product from 

another. NCPDP is central to developing standards by which biologic and biosimilar products are 

distributed and recorded, 

including 

identification of products 

for 

the purpose of 

pharmacovigilance. 

NCPDP has already commented that, in our opinion, biosimilars and interchangeable biologics 

should carry the same nonproprietary names as their respective reference products, without 

modification. We incorporate by reference our submission of August 20, 2012 to Commissioner 

Hamburg in which we stated the INN “should not be redesigned to respond to concerns about 

pharmacovigilance and drug tracking.”1 

NCPDP continues to disagree with FDA’s recently adopted approach to naming biologics whereby 

nonproprietary names (“proper names”) include unique meaningless 4-letter suffixes which are 

1 https://ncpdp.org/NCPDP/media/pdf/20120820-NCPDP-Ltr-to-FDA-Biosimilars.pdf

 
unlikely to be recalled reproducibly by prescribers, pharmacists, patients, and others. NCPDP 

remains hopeful the agency will eventually recognize the application of such suffixes is an 

approach that is unnecessary, unproven, burdensome, and ineffective at substantially improving 

the accurate identification of unique products that share the same unmodified nonproprietary 

name (“core name”). 

NCPDP applauds Health Canada’s recent decision to implement a biologics naming policy that is 

brand name-centric rather than adopt the aforementioned suffix application to the 

nonproprietary name. In Canada, a biologics naming convention that applies both nonproprietary 

(with no suffix) and brand names will be used throughout the medication use process, including 

prescribing, dispensing, and pharmacovigilance settings. In this manner, biosimilars, reference 

biologics, and innovator biologics that share the same nonproprietary name would be 

distinguished by their unique brand names. 

In commenting about their decision, Health Canada indicated this approach achieved the 

pharmacovigilance objective of clearly distinguishing unique products with the same 

nonproprietary name without imposing an unnecessary regulatory burden, and avoided the 

complexity associated with implementing a suffix-based naming convention. 

Evidence from adverse drug event reporting in both Canada and the US has shown reporting by 

brand name is largely successful in achieving accurate product-level attribution of spontaneously 

reported adverse effects for suspected biologics. Analy

Comments of the United Mine Workers of America 
On The 
Proposed Rule for Examinations of Working Places in 
Metal and Nonmetal Mines 
 
 
It pleases us to hear that the agency has decided to take steps into 
reviewing its current rules and regulations pertaining to workplace exams at 
Metal Non Metal mines. 
 
 
We believe that the current federal law is nowhere near stringent enough 
to adequately protect miners from hazards that can adversely affect their health 
and safety. Proper workplace exams are extremely important and have a vital role 
in preventing accidents and injuries. Proper workplace examinations by a 
competent person that has the proper experience and training in recognizing 
hazardous conditions, violations of mandatory safety standards, imminent 
dangers, and adverse conditions is vital to the safety of the miners working at that 
mine. The proposed revisions to the current rule are simple and easy to apply but 
can make a huge impact on improving the health and safety of miners. 
 
 
Making the examinations prior to someone working in that area just seems 
like common sense. This gives the miners coming into the next shift knowledge of 
what conditions and hazards may be present before they arrive. The United Mine 
Workers of America suggest that the examinations be performed as close to the 
start of the next shift as possible but no more than 2 hours prior to. We would 
also suggest that the person performing these exams have a mine foreman or 
assistant mine foreman certification as well. This would ensure that they have the 
experience and knowledge in recognizing hazards that could adversely affect the 
health and safety of miners. 
 
 
The requirement to record the location, hazards found, corrective action 
taken, and the date action was taken must be required to ensure proper

 
documentation as well as ensure the hazard was corrected. This would also help 
make the operator as well as the miners more aware of the hazards so that they 
cannot say that they were not aware of a hazard and not correct it. Many hazards 
will be able to be corrected during the time of the exam but some will require 
time and man power to correct and this requirement will show what progress is 
being made on a particular area and hazard. It’s also important for miners and 
their representatives to have access to these records to see what hazards they 
may encounter and what actions are/were being taken to correct those hazards. 
 
 
One thing that may be a concern for some is the fact that the person 
performing the examination must sign and date in the examination book. The 
only people who have to worry about this requirement are the people who cut 
corners while making their exams or who turn a blind eye to certain things that 
may be too expensive or time consuming to fix. Or people who don’t report and 
record hazards because of pressure from their employer. Honest people who try 
to follow the law will have nothing to worry about. This rule will also keep people 
accountable and more alert to hazards. 
 
 
The proposed rules and regulations are common sense revisions to the current 
examinations rule and quite frankly should have been made years ago. These are 
much like the rules and regulations used in coal. We are aware that MNM mines 
are not exposed to the same hazards that present itself from coal dust and 
methane. However, aside from that, most if not all other hazards can be found in 
both coal and MNM mines and these miners deserve the same protections.

FEMA proposes two changes regarding publication requirements regarding community eligibility requirements:

1. Change the notification of community loss of eligibility of the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) from the Federal Register to online publication
2. Change the maintenance of the list of communities eligible for flood insurance from the Code of Federal Regulations to an online method

These requirements are outdated and were made prior to the widespread use of the internet. Though not mentioned in the docket, this proposed rule also aligns with memorandum M-19-21 issued on June 18, 2019, from the Office of Management and Budget and the National Archives Records and Administration to Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies regarding a transition to electronic records. While this memorandum may not apply nor be directly related to these proposed rule changes, it is illustrative of the overall concept that it is increasingly effective and efficient for government agencies to move to electronic documentation if feasible. 

The benefits of the proposed changes are increasing public visibility to the notices, increasing public access to the notices, reduced costs to the agency, reduce the burden to the agency, allow the agency to be more agile in making and publishing updates. 

An example of the burden experienced by FEMA to produce these reports is evidenced by the fact that FEMA has not updated the eligible community list since August 28, 2006, because of the list's overlap with the Community Status Book and the costs of publishing the updated lists in the Federal Register. 

This proposed change moves these notices to FEMA's website. Whether or not this proposed change becomes effective, I strongly recommend a major revision the FEMA's website to improve the user experience. The current home page currently has 136 topics in the navigation bar. These topics are not listed in any logical order and are overwhelming to the user. While there is a search feature in the navigation bar, it is not effective. For example, if I type in "cov" attempting to pull up COVID-19 topics, I receive 7 topics. However, if I type in "coro," I only receive 4 topics, thus the end-user is not receiving all the information available from the search menu. The docket mentions a website re-design is in the works that will include a more versatile search functionality. They should also consider consolidating many of the topics into major topics to create a more user-friendly experience in addition to improving the functionality of the search feature.

I am concerned about the lack of regulation for vehicles to determine the maximum speed that may be safely traveled under any given circumstances. For autonomous vehicles, this must be defined by a mathematical equation, not a speed limit sign. Please remember that speed limit signs only post the theoretical maximum speed that can be safely driven by humans under ideal conditions. Even then, reading posted speed limits does not improve safety even for human drivers, as proven by the mortality rate of Montana's highways before and after speed limits were posted. 

The maximum safe speed may be determined by the time it would take to brake, but how can a reasonably safe braking time be defined? There are many safety variables to consider such as visibility, room to maneuver (e.g. empty four-lane highway vs crosswalk with people on both sides), setting (highway vs rural vs urban), presence of construction, people, etc. At the very least, these factors need to have scales defined, so a mathematical equation can legally define what the expected time to be able to brake would be. Ideally, in addition, AI trained by X number of hours of real-world data would analyze the behavior of nearby vehicles and people to better define their risk factors. Although it is impossible to perfect such AI, or even define exacting standards, demonstrable software may be required to show that a bonafide attempt was made and supported.

With the expected braking time in place, the vehicle can then be expected to factor in environmental variables such as road curvature, surface conditions, and weather against its own capacity to calculate what its maximum speed should be. Posted speed limit signs should be irrelevant to autonomous vehicles - rather, they should be tested to show that they will meet expected braking times under various circumstances.

Dear APHIS,
I have the privilege of being a member of the training team at Dolphin Research Center in Grassy Key, Fl. I can assure anyone reading this that DRC is always thinking of our dolphins well being in every way possible and that we go above and beyond regulations in their care every day. 
 When it comes to interactions with guests, programs are tailored to what the animals enjoy and only those that demonstrate an interest and excitement about those sessions are asked to participate. It isn't enough for the animals to simply do the programs safely, they need to enjoy them and find them enriching. Our trainers build incredible bonds with our animals and they are skilled at interpreting behavior and responding to our animals' needs. It is DRC's philosophy that every session between a trainer and animal is a partnership, one in which communication is a two way street. Our animals have choices. It is up to them whether they want to participate, not just in programs, but in any session.

 3.111 Interactive Programs: Based on the safety record of these programs for 30 years, it is not necessary to have an additional layer of regulations governing them. 
 
Definition of Interactive Program: If the participant does not enter the water, a cetacean's primary enclosure, by the agency's own proposed definition, it is not an interactive program. 
 
Sanctuary Area: I suggest this be changed to Public Free Area. The word "sanctuary" implies that the animals need a refuge or escape from something and that something negative is happing. Nothing could be further from the truth, as evidenced by our 30-year safety record for the animals as well as the guests. We frequently see dolphins who are not participating in an interactive program choose to swim over to that dock and join in. This is the opposite of seeking sanctuary. The dolphins chosen to participate in our interactive programs at DRC find them entertaining and enriching.
 
3.111(b) Water Clarity: Over years of both conducting and observing thousands of interactive programs and other training sessions, I know the animals do not have to be visible at all times in a program to ensure safety. At DRC the dolphins and guests interact at or above the surface of the water. For 30 years trainers have been able to safely supervise these interactions. There is no need to have perfectly clear water to see the dolphins. Additionally, the water depth provides them respite from the sun, which is important and another concern APHIS is addressing in these proposed regulations. 
 
3.111(d)(4) One trainer/ One animal ratio: I strongly disagree with this recommendation. By restricting this, APHIS takes away the ability of professional behaviorists to create enriching and variable experiences for the animals in their care. These animals are social and enjoy having other animals as partners in their training sessions. Interactive programs are no different. This rule is detrimental to their welfare. Experienced trainers are more than capable of working in partnership with more than one animal at a time to conduct safe interactive programs. 
 
 
3.111(d)(8) I strongly disagree with APHIS providing specific language to define "unsafe" behavior. Behavior must be interpreted by experienced animal care and training staff. They are experts at knowing each animal's history and personality, and reading all aspects of each situation. I also disagree that APHIS should require written criteria of the "retraining of such an animal". Animal training teams at each facility have successful management plans for the safety of our programs, as is evidenced by our 30 year record of conducting them. 
 
In closing, I would like to ask that APHIS proceed with careful consideration of the facts and choose regulations that make sense based on the science and professional experience of those that work with and observe these animals each day. Please do not regulate these amazing opportunities out of existence. There is no need,

However, much of the growth in the industry has been usurped by industrial scale operations gaming the system. The resulting psychological damage to families in rural communities is almost incalculable.

Marine life in New York has always been important to me. I attend the Harbor School on Governors Island because of my interest in protecting our ecosystem. Putting limits on these species allows for long-term sustainability in the north-east waters. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, they state, “The number of overfished stocks globally has tripled in half a century, and today fully one-third of the world's assessed fisheries are currently pushed beyond their biological limits.” This regulation, though a small step in the entire issue, moves to help this ongoing problem. In addition, National Geographic claims “Fishers remove more than 77 billion kilograms (170 billion pounds) of wildlife from the sea each year. Regulations such as this one should be expanded to more species to protect the overall health of our environment. For example, the shortnose sturgeon is currently endangered according to the New York Department of Environmental Conservation. Rules should be expanded to include more species for increased biodiversity within our habitats. Therefore, this regulation has my full support for being passed, but more species of fish that are being harmed by overfishing should be included in regulations such as these. Long-term sustainability should be a goal that everyone reaches for, and small steps like this continue to push us in the right direction.

Dear USCIS,
I'm writing simply to let you know that I oppose these efforts to make the Asylum Application process more restrictive for asylum seekers approaching our country for safety. 
One issue that I am growing more concerned about is how difficult we as a country are making it for people to actually apply for asylum. I spent time at the Arizona/Mexico POE in Nogales, AZ, so have seen those who are seeking asylum. The wording in the Executive Summary under the heading "Revised Eligibility for Employment Authorization" disqualifies people who have tried to enter the country outside of official POE. I would agree with that under normal circumstances, but from what I observed personally in my time at the border is that we as a people are severely limiting the number of people allowed to apply for asylum at our POE. As vulnerable people become more desperate I as a citizen do not want us to look for more ways to punish them for their vulnerable circumstance. I request that we as a people build up systems that grant asylum based upon a spirit of compassion and generosity, not a system of punishment and restriction.
Also, I oppose the regulations extending the length of time that asylum seekers must wait in order to receive Authorization for Employment. 365 days will motivate more asylum seekers to work without authorization, which will put them at risk and also keep us as a community from receiving taxes from their labor. We want those seeking asylum to feel welcomed and allowed to participate in our economy and democracy. The underlying assumption of this proposed modification seems to be based on a belief that the vast majority of those seeking refuge and safety in our country are coming with "frivolous, fraudulent, or otherwise non-meritorious asylum requests". As one who has volunteered at a shelter for asylum seekers, and has observed the conditions in which those waiting for their chance to request asylum are living, I reject this extreme assumption. I am very willing to accept that there are some who will apply in a frivolous and fraudulent manner, but from what I have seen the vast majority are fleeing violence and oppression that is legitimate. 
I so valued the work that I saw border patrol agents doing at our border. However, I am concerned about the culture that the underlying assumptions of these suggested modifications are creating within our government organizations such as USCIS and CBP. I ask that we adopt a more compassionate and nuanced approach to this humanitarian crisis.

I am a private small midwestern grower, and this goal is ludicrous, exorbitant, untenable, and cumbersome. I do NOT agree with this proposal. DO NOT PLACE THIS into law. DO NOT have a "trial group". Please DO read on. It places additional burden of time, cost, and accounting squarely on the farmer, and undue additional stress on the animals, not to mention the dreaded "red tape" effect, which slows the productivity of everything it touches. 

There are relied-upon methods to account for one's stock; ear tags, brands, segregated groups; the list goes on. These previously listed identifiers can all be seen by the naked eye. Howr many shysters will claim that their stock is "e-tagged", when they are not? There are just too many opportunities for obfuscation and misleading. 

This proposed identification would put undue strain on an already fragile supply chain. What happens when it is the allotted time to "chip" your stock, but the chips are on backorder? How often has THAT happened to you in the last two years? It took my neighbors 22 weeks to get a couch. Really. And these are electronic devices, which can break, cease to function and be counterfeited, never mind having (and not losing) a correctly functioning reader. Would this require a USDA annual inspection and seal? Any implanted device carries the inherent risk of concomitant infection. 

In order to accurately position such a device the animal would need to be "handled", which, when in large groups, requires infrastructure, multiple people multiple hours to coordinate, with typically heavy machinery. If you think this is "no big deal", see what it takes for a bison rancher to place ear tags and give a vet exam. Have you ever had a bison burger? It is totally delicious. 

Now on the other end of the spectrum, when would every rabbit produced also be required to have this tagging method? They are a livestock species that is farmed and consumed. The idea of, "where we go one, we go all", is ringing in my head, and the slippery slope that is being proposed is very dangerous. Livestock is different than a treasured pedigreed dog that could be lost. 

My sister breeds pedigreed dogs. They are "tagged" prior to sale. It is not a small process. Besides placement of this chip, there is an electronic "back end" component to this. She is placed as primary and the purchaser is placed as secondary on the chip memory, which requires computer programming. All these steps have a cost; money and time. This is where a cost-benefit analysis for a litter of 8 puppies makes sense, but for a herd of hundreds, or even thousands, is ludicrous. 

Once an animal is processed, would these "e-tags" be removed and recycled? Would they be placed back into circulation? Yet another step and more costs, which sounds like an impending problem for the leather industry. 

Do not underestimate the "average" farmer's intelligence in comprehending the behemoth that this law would create. 

This idea has been adopted by people who are disconnected from their food sources, and have no idea the volume of animal stock that is required to feed such a large populace. I wonder if any person drafting this proposal has been to a CAFO lot? I highly doubt it. I wonder if any farmer was part of drafting this proposal? I very much doubt that. 

I will reiterate that I do NOT support this proposal.

Dear Ms. Penna, 
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) offers comments regarding the 
proposed rule on Measures to Keep Fishery Impacts within the Conservation Objective 
for the California Coastal Chinook Salmon, as published in 89 FR 30314. The proposed 
revisions represent a significant step forward in the sustainable management of 
California salmon fisheries, and we commend NOAA for its collaborative efforts with 
CDFW and other stakeholders in developing this framework. 
CDFW supports the transition to inseason harvest management of California 
commercial ocean salmon fisheries by utilizing caps on allowable harvest and 
establishing vessel-based landing and possession limits. In the years preceding the 
2023 and 2024 ocean salmon fishery closures for the California coast, CDFW 
expressed concern over recent trends in escapement and harvest and advocated for an 
inseason management system that would help ensure harvest to stay within pre-season 
projections for target and non-target stocks. The proposed framework was designed to 
improve fishery performance relative to the conservation objective for California Coastal 
Chinook salmon, which has been substantially exceeded in recent years. As described 
in NMFS’ 2024 Guidance Letter to the Pacific Fishery Management Council, the harvest 
rate in ocean salmon fisheries from 2018 through 2022 considerably surpassed the 
California Coastal Chinook salmon conservation objective of a 0.16 ocean harvest rate 
on age-4 Klamath River Fall Chinook, averaging 0.28. 
The concept of utilizing inseason management to keep salmon catches within 
projections has also been highlighted as a goal in the Governor of California’s Salmon 
Strategy for a Hotter Drier Future. CDFW wishes to acknowledge the shared vision on 
this approach, which should substantially reduce the potential to overharvest California 
Coastal Chinook, other ESA and CESA listed runs, and target stocks.

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

Why is it that the consumers are always misled? USDA , please revise your new guidance document to align animal raising standards/awareness with consumer expectations.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation.

As a frequent airline passenger, I strongly support a continued ban on voice calls while in flight. Being forced to listen to voice calls would be a hardship, since people talk louder on the phone and, unless the cost is prohibitive, are likely to have long and/or multiple conversations. If many people are using their phones at once, they will speak even louder than usual in order to be heard. Thus the European experience, which is based on expensive, infrequent calls by passengers, is not a good guide for US policy. On the other hand, if a practical way can be found to allow only "listen-only" calls (using a headset), that would be unobjectionable. 

The proposed rule states, "Here, we particularly solicit comment on whether there is any market failure or other reason to support a Federal ban on voice calls during flights." The proposal suggests an alternative, market-based mechanism, which is for airlines to disclose their policy of allowing phone calls so that consumers can make purchasing decisions based on this information. However, this mechanism is unlikely to protect consumers, because a) there is often not a choice of carriers for a given flight and b) the carriers tend to adopt similar policies (as we have seen with baggage fees), so being informed of an airline's policy does not mean that one can avoid it. Likewise, it seems impractical to have a "voice call free zone" on an aircraft unless that zone constitutes a large percentage of the seats. Nothing short of a ban would realistically protect consumers. 

Thank you.

The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (WDNR) submits the following comments regarding the U.S. 

Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) proposed Fuels Regulatory Streamlining rule, as published in the 

Federal Register on May 14, 2020 (85 FR 29034). In this action, EPA is proposing to update and streamline its 

existing gasoline, diesel, and other fuels programs. These changes include several proposed changes to EPA’s 

reformulated gasoline (RFG) requirements. WDNR recommends a few clarifications to facilitate implementation 

of the proposed RFG program changes. 

Clean Air Act (CAA) Section 211(k)(10)(D) mandates RFG use in the six-county Milwaukee-Racine area.1 This 

area must use RFG because it was among the areas with the nine highest 1-hour ozone design values from 1987-

1989 that also met a specific population threshold. The CAA did not define a way for RFG programs in these 

areas to be terminated, modified, or replaced with other emissions control programs in the future. 

In this proposed rule, EPA is for the first time offering a way for states to request removal of these RFG programs 

in areas like Milwaukee-Racine. Specifically, EPA is proposing that such programs can be removed when the 

most recent and prior ozone national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS) have been attained in these areas, 

and if the state can demonstrate that the removal of the RFG requirement would not interfere with reasonable 

further progress requirements, continued maintenance of the NAAQS, or any other CAA requirement. 

EPA proposes to address the CAA’s requirements for RFG areas by providing a pathway out of that requirement 

in a way that continues to ensure attainment and maintenance of air quality and the protection of public health. As 

EPA notes, it is important that states use their limited resources for programs that are necessary for attainment, 

rather than require the implementation of an RFG program indefinitely simply because a covered area had the 

highest ozone design values thirty years ago. It is important to note that states would still need to demonstrate, in 

an approved maintenance plan, that the NAAQS would be maintained without the emissions reductions 

attributable to RFG. EPA’s proposal sensibly allows states the option to pursue emissions reductions programs 

other than RFG should those alternatives be more cost-effective or otherwise better reflect state-specific goals or 

circumstances.

One key inconsistency relates to the Proposed Policy’s requirement for onsite avoidance 
before compensatory mitigation. This requirement cannot apply to ESA programs because 
neither ESA Section 7 nor Section 10 requires that impacts be avoided except in the narrow 
circumstance where the continued existence of the species would be jeopardized and other forms 
of mitigation would not alleviate jeopardy. 
 
Under Section 7, the Service has authority to require that federal agencies and applicants 
minimize, but not avoid, incidental take provided that the minimization measures involve only 
minor changes to the project. The Section 7 Consultation Handbook describes this authority as 
follows: 
 
Section 7 requires minimization of the level of take. It is not appropriate to 
require mitigation for the impacts of incidental take. Reasonable and prudent 
measures can include only actions that occur within the action area, involve only 
minor changes to the project, and reduce the level of take associated with project 
activities. These measures should minimize the impacts of incidental take to the 
extent reasonable and prudent. . . . Measures are considered reasonable and 
prudent when they are consistent with the proposed action’s basic design (e.g., 
narrowing of disturbed right-of-way at known species locations), location (e.g., 
temporary storage of equipment or other materials), scope, duration, and timing. 
The test for reasonableness is whether the proposed measure would cause more 
than a minor change to the project. 
 
Section 7 Consultation Handbook at 4-50 (Mar. 1998) (emphasis in original). 
 
Under Section 10, applicants for a Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) must minimize and 
mitigate impacts to the maximum extent practicable. Avoidance is not mandatory. 16 U.S.C. 
§ 1539(a)(2)(B). The Service has a non-discretionary duty to issue an incidental take permit 
where the applicant adequately addresses the permit issuance criteria under Section 10 even if 
avoidance is not proposed. See Center for Biological Diversity v. U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 
202 F. Supp. 2d 594, 624 (W.D. Tex. 2002). 
 
Another inconsistency relates to the Proposed Policy’s goal of “net conservation gain.” 
The Proposed Policy aims for all compensatory mitigation to “maximize the benefit to impacted 
resources.” 
 
Even if a mitigation ratio of more than 1:1 meets the goal of net conservation gain, 
requiring compensatory mitigation to result in a net benefit or maximum benefit conflicts with 
ESA standards. Under Section 7, compensatory mitigation can be required to remove jeopardy, 
but there is no requirement for a net conservation gain. Under Section 10, mitigation must be 
commensurate with the impact and no more. The Habitat Conservation Planning Handbook 
notes: “No explicit provision of the ESA or its implementing regulations requires that an HCP 
must result in a net benefit to affected species. ” Habitat Conservation Planning Handbook

I am a seasonal farm worker at Milwaukee County Zoo. I have been in the zookeeping field for three years and have been an animal training professional the entire time. I am a member of AZA, AAZK and ABMA. Prior to my zookeeping career, I was a practicing attorney. After reviewing the proposed legislation, I have the following comments for your consideration. These comments are my own.

I feel that many of the proposed changes are not based on peer-reviewed scientific data or professional observations or experience, especially the following:

-Interactive programs: This seems unnecessary given the strong history of safety records of these types of programs. I know of no existing research that shows a need for further regulation of these programs. It seems more appropriate to address any problems on a case by case basis instead of an overbroad new regulation. I fail to see how adding this regulation will be of benefit to marine mammals. I also feel the definition of interactive programs is problematic. If the definition is to be: "any human-marine mammal interactive program where a member of the public enters a primary enclosure for a marine mammal with the intent of interacting with the marine mammal(s)", then there needs to be an explicit exception made for guest programs that involve guests sitting or standing on a floating platform or shallow ledge or poolside and trainers that bring the animals into a public area under stimulus control.

-Time limits for sessions: Limiting sessions to a total of 2 hours per day seems totally arbitrary, without consideration of each animal's best interests and is in my opinion completely unnecessary. Every animal is an individual and as such each has it's own level of interests and capabilities. Decisions on length and frequency of training sessions should be left up to the trainers and caretakers and made in the individual animal's best interest. Training sessions provide a great deal of enrichment value to individual animals. There is no scientific data that I am aware of that supports this limit. In my experience, a blanket rule arbitrarily limiting the amount of time spent in training sessions is unnecessary and not supported by the requirements of animal welfare.

-Trainer to animal ratios: Requiring a trainer/attendant for every animal is unnecessary and burdensome. The number of trainers in relation to the number of animals should be dependent upon the situation, the animals, the trainers and the type of session. A blanket rule is arbitrary, unnecessarily limiting and unsupported by my professional experience. There is great enrichment value in varying the conditions of training sessions - including the number and orientation (single or teams) of the trainers. Limiting the flexibility of trainers to vary the conditions of training is very likely to actually decrease the welfare of the animals in question.

-Undesirable behavior: As a professional, I do not favor the language used to describe "unsatisfactory" or "undesirable" behaviors. Using a broad definition including a "not limited to" category is likely to cause confusion and unnecessary restrictions. Behavior should always be assessed in individual animals on a case by case basis - behaviors deemed undesirable in one animal in one situation may in fact be desirable in another individual in another circumstance. Professional trainers are in the best position to evaluate an animal's behavior in the specific situation and determine if it is unsafe. If so, the trainer is in the best position to decide how to address the behavior through behavior managment techniques. This is not a one size fits all kind of situation.

I appreciate APHIS's continuing commitment to improving animal welfare. I am also grateful that APHIS recognizes the general excellence of care and public education in US marine parks (and zoos) and the restraint shown in not changing or adding regulations unnecessarily.

Members of the Patient, Consumer, and Public Health Coalition strongly support the up-

classification of influenza detection devices. We support moving the devices from class I to class 

II with special controls and into a new device classification regulation (from 21 CFR 866.3330 to 

21 CFR 866.3328). We agree with the FDA that “the accuracy of these devices has serious 

public health implications,” since influenza can cause serious illness and death.1 

Many of the rapid influenza antigen detection tests or RIDTs (also referred to as antigen tests) 

that were cleared since 1998 have had performance problems (good specificity but low 

sensitivity).2 The 2009 flu pandemic underscored that RIDTs “performed poorly resulting in 
misdiagnosed cases.”1 

On June 13, 2013, the Microbiology Advisory Panel met to discuss performance problems with 

RIDT systems. The panel noted that “poor sensitivity of RIDTs has always been a concern,”2 and 

they raised concerns that influenza viruses mutate quickly. Fast changing viruses “may cause the

 
functional components of influenza diagnostic devices not to recognize current influenza 

strains,” which will lead the devices to provide inaccurate results.2 

Panel members indicated that putting RIDTs into Class II with special controls was needed to 

mitigate the risks of false positive and false negative results. We strongly agree. 

In the past, FDA has cleared these less-than-effective RIDT devices as class I 510(k) devices. 

This allowed the devices to be used as predicates for new 510(k) submissions, which “promotes 

further clearance of devices that do not meet the needed performance for detection and 

management of infection by novel strains of influenza.”2 Reclassifying RIDTs as class II will 

better ensure that ineffective devices are no longer cleared on an ineffective class I RIDT 

predicate. Devices that were cleared as class I RIDTs will have to meet the class II special 

controls to remain on the market, which will better protect patients and public health. 

We agree with FDA’s proposed order that RIDTs regulated under 21 CFR 866.3330 be 

reclassified into Class II with special controls under the new device name “influenza virus 

antigen detection tests system”(21 CFR 866.3328). Section 866.3328 specifically states, 

“Because influenza is highly contagious and may lead to an acute respiratory tract infection 

causing severe illness and even death, the accuracy of these devices has serious public health 

implications.”1 The regulation also lists precise special controls for these devices including 

sensitivity and specificity performance characteristics.

failure of the device to perform accurately could harm patients. For example, a false negative

After reviewing this notice made by the FDA, I am in accordance with their effort to transform naloxone from a prescription drug to a nonprescription drug in order to increase access. As mentioned in the notice, the opioid epidemic in the United States has worsened, where more than 80,000 people died due to an opioid related death from January 2021 to January 2022. This demonstrates the need for an accessible and effective product that has the potential to avert these deaths in the future and save many lives. Currently, there are Naloxone access laws in all fifty states but they vary. These laws may include allowing a provider to prescribe naloxone to someone who is not directly at risk for an overdose (such as a caregiver, family member) and criminal immunity to prescribers and those who dispense this drug. Although these laws are effective in increasing the distribution of naloxone and reducing deaths, there are still many ways that people cannot access this drug. This includes some pharmacies not being fully educated on what their state laws allow and they are not willing to dispense naloxone without a patient specific prescription, when in fact their state allowed this. Additionally, some providers are hesitant on prescribing naloxone because of liability issues. Also, some people feel scared or that they are being judged when trying to obtain naloxone from a healthcare professional. Overall, changing naloxone into a nonprescription drug can overall remove these barriers and allow for more individuals to access it when needed. Another aspect that the FDA should consider are drug shortages as mentioned in the article. They expect with this change, there will be more of a demand for this drug which causes drug shortages to occur. In understanding this, the FDA can anticipate this and possibly incentivize drug manufacturers to make this nonprescription drug. Additionally, the cost and ability to ensure this product gets to the most affected communities is of concern. These high priority areas should be taken into consideration if this change gets approved. The most at risk areas deserve access to these products and should not be ignored, especially since these areas would produce the most opioid related deaths. I also do agree that more research needs to be done in order to gather more data as to how the labels and directions affect the administration of naloxone in a community setting. They want to ensure that if individuals are provided with this product, the directions and labels are functional in communicating the information necessary to use the product. This is especially true considering that currently naloxone is provided by a healthcare professional who can provide instructions to individuals when prescribing or dispensing it. Similarly, in community based settings, they may provide naloxone with additional products or instructions so that individuals understand how to use the drug. I think it would be important for the FDA to consult these community organizations when creating the label so they can gain some insight as to how best to write these labels and instructions. Overall, I also understand that there will always be risks associated with taking a drug and there were many outlined in the notice. But, I do agree that the benefits outweigh the risks in this situation. Naloxone is an effective drug and by removing the need to obtain a prescription, more people will have access to this drug and more lives can be saved. It is imperative that if the FDA approves this change, they make it accessible for the most at risk communities, via distribution and cost. This has the potential to make an impact on the opioid epidemic and save so many lives that I hope it comes into fruition.

I agree with NOAA's proposed changes to the duration of certain permits and letters of confirmation under the MMPA. I have been significantly involved in marine mammal research permits as a CI for more than 30 years and a permit holder for more than 20 years. I have worked closely with the NMFS Office of Protected Resoures on many permit related issues, and have spent a great deal of time over the years on applications, modifications, reports, and other communications with the OPR Office. I strongly believe that NOAA should be able to consider various factors when determining the appropriate duration of a given permit permit. These include the experience and track record of the applicant, the type of research to be conducted, the self-evaluation conducted during annual reports, the support of an institutional animal welfare or research committee to oversee the activity, and more. In particular, the current 5 year permit review cycle does not make sense for marine mammals that participate in long-term research programs that extend beyond the duration of the permit, or research programs that primarily conduct low-impact, behavioral studies. I have found the personnel at the Office of Protected Resources to have considerable and valuable expertise in marine mammal science and welfare. The OPR program is capable of using that expertise to make reasonable decisions about the appropriate duration of various permits. Anyone who has received a marine mammal research permit will acknowledge that it is an aurdous process with many checks and balances. Once issued, permits are updated continuously with annual reports and detailed modifications that account for any needed changes to the original permit. There is an extremely rigorous system for confirming the qualifications and experience of all personnel involved, and personnel changes are kept updated through regular modification requests. To receive a permit, input is provided from a variety of internal references and external groups including the Marine Mammal Commission, participating native co-management organizations, attending veterinarians, government partners, and other stakeholders. For many purposes including long-term research programs, it simply does not make sense to restart this process from scratch every 3-5 years. Increasing flexibility in permit durations would lower the administrative burden on scientists and increase resources available for research and education. In a research program like mine, this could amount to saving many weeks and months of time over the duration of the activity. NOAA's OPR Office has an organized and effective process for evaluating marine mammal research permit applications. This process already ensures meaningful outcomes for animal welfare under the MMPA. Increasing flexibility in the maximum duration of marine mammal research permits given by NMFS makes complete sense and I support this proposed change. Time currently spent in taxing administrative cycles with a small number of scientists can be better spent protecting marine mammals from harm at larger scales.

Amending fish habitats to enable mass death due to wind turbines is short sighted and violates the Endangered Species Act. Whistleblower Speaks Out: Offshore Wind Will Drive Whales to Extinction. The critically-endangered North Atlantic right whale, one of the most imperiled mammals in the world, seemed until just a few years ago to be on a path to recovery. It was our nation’s energy policy in the 18th century to kill the right whales for their oil, but the species was recovering after the 1982 ban on whaling took effect.

Today, the whale is in more danger than ever. An “unusual mortality event” beginning in 2017 has reduced the population by 30 percent. The North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium’s October 2022 count estimates that only 340 individuals survive, with fewer than 70 breeding females and an overall decline in body size. Major sources of stress today include fishing gear entanglements, vehicle collisions, and climate change. 

But one source of danger to the right whale is rarely discussed: the industrialization of their habitat by offshore wind companies, enabled by two government agencies, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries (NOAA Fisheries) and the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM). The head of New England Aquarium’s whale impact monitoring program has openly stated that the first offshore wind projects will serve as a “test bed” to study their impacts on the whale. A recently-surfaced letter from a whistleblower indicates that BOEM and NOAA were aware in May 2022 that offshore wind construction and operation posed a direct danger to the North Atlantic right whale. 

The author, NOAA’s own Chief of Endangered Species, Dr. Sean Hayes, bravely sounded the alarm, noting that not only the construction but also the operation of wind turbines could result in extinction. 

Yet these agencies have failed to put in place any meaningful measures to protect this critically endangered species from extinction.
By NOAA Fisheries’ own admission, “The potential biological removal (PBR) level for the species, defined as the maximum number of animals that can be removed annually while allowing the stock to reach or maintain its optimal sustainable population level, is less than 1.” In plain language, this means the death of a single whale could make the difference between extinction and recovery.

Recent data collection finds the whales are increasingly relying on the southern Massachusetts wind lease area as a last refuge for foraging and raising their young. Because the federally-designated critical right whale habitat is out of date, these very same areas have been approved by the federal government for industrialization by offshore wind companies.

But all to often, I have witnessed first hand abuse of the allowance simply because a person wants a pet and wants to bring them into an environment that may not be suitable whether it be housing that doesn't allow pets, restaurants, airplanes, etc. My father in law's girlfriend is guilty. ESA's are not supposed to be pets but rather provide support for a specific disability. CITES provisions and status of implementing legislation in range states 
The Atlantic humpback dolphin, Sousa teuszii, is listed under Appendix I of the Convention on 
International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).1 CITES Appendix I 
species can not be traded internationally for primarily commercial purposes.2 International trade, as 
defined under CITES includes “introduction from the sea”3. When conducted for non-commercial 
purposes, the export of a species listed under CITES Appendix I requires that such trade not be 
detrimental to the survival of the species in question, that the specimen not be obtained in contravention 
of national laws, that any such living specimen be transported with minimum risk of injury, damage to 
health or cruel treatment, and that an import permit be granted for the specimen.4 Comparable 
safeguards are in place for the import, re-export, and introduction from the sea5 of Appendix I 
specimens.6 
Under the CITES National Legislation Project,7 a Party is classed as a Category 1 State if its 
legislation is believed generally to meet the following requirements for the implementation of the 
Convention: the State has designated at least one Management Authority and one Scientific Authority; 
it has legislation that prohibits trade in violation of the Convention; it penalizes such trade; and provides 
for the confiscation of specimens illegally traded or possessed.8 Parties are classed as Category 2 if 
their legislation is believed to only partially meet CITES implementation requirements, and as Category 
3 if their legislation is believed generally not to meet the requirements for the implementation of the 
Convention.9 
 
Some range states of S. teuszii, including longstanding Parties to CITES,10 currently fall under 
Category 3 (see table 1), meaning that they are believed to not have the legal framework in place to 
effectively implement the CITES provisions above. While the status of a country’s legislative progress 
is not species-specific, it may serve as a preliminary proxy for the robustness of its CITES-listed species’ 
protections. A more detailed legal analysis should, nevertheless, follow this exercise (see table 2).

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

On behalf of the USDA, an independent agent should personally visit every site where animals are being used and make sure proper descriptions are used by exploiters to describe living conditions for animals.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The Black-capped vireo, like many other neo-tropical migrant bird species faces threats on both it's
breeding and wintering grounds. This species' specific habitat requirements require continual proactive
management to maintain the vegetation structure required for successful breeding. This species has
increased in numbers, but this is exclusively due to very dedicated efforts by federal, state,
non-governmental entities and private land owners within the species range.

guarantee of funding for this activity.

The FWS should only delist the Black-capped vireo when there is a long-term (25-50 year) monitoring and habitat
management plan with the funding in place to carry out the necessary work uninterrupted.

The signs of improvement for the Black-capped vireo should be reason to ensure that the measures
which have been effective are continued.

It would be much wiser to list the species as Endangered or at the very least Threatened under the
ESA while it's population dynamics are studied and monitored further. This would ensure that the funding and legal structure that has supported the maintenance and creation of suitable habitat will continue.

this unique species.

The Canadian Consensus Criteria (CCC) is a more specific definition of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME/CFS) than the older Oxford case definition used in many GET/CBT trials (as acknowledged in the draft evidence review). Use of the Oxford case definition is problematic as it has been found to diagnose 14 false-positive ME/CFS cases for every 15 individuals when compared with the CCC [1]. Since GET as a form of physical exertion can incur a post-exertional malaise (PEM) response in ME/CFS patients, use of the Oxford definition is especially troublesome for GET studies since the definition does not require PEM for a diagnosis of ME/CFS. This is likely to lead to the underestimation of harms. 

ME/CFS diagnosed under the CCC possesses a biomedical basis that leaves a clear and measurable molecular signature in blood-derived cells. This is evidenced by published work wherein we observed diverse cellular abnormalities in blood-derived cells from people with CCC-compliant ME/CFS which accurately discriminated them from healthy control cells [2, 3, 4]. This pattern of abnormalities is distinct from those observed in other neurological conditions such as Parkinson's Disease or Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome using similar investigative methods [5, 6]. We see no reason why this would be the case for a condition that could supposedly be reversed with GET/CBT. The experience reported by patients diagnosed under the CCC is clear and should be accepted. 

Relevant professional expertise: This comment was co-authored by Mr Daniel Missailidis (doctoral candidate), Professor Paul R. Fisher and Dr. Sarah J. Annesley. Off-Label use of current HCV RNA molecular assays

One immediate area we would like to bring to your awareness is the gap between the proposed 

recommendation and existing diagnostic solutions. To our knowledge, there are no HCV molecular assays 

currently on the market that have US IVD approval as a standalone diagnostic; instead, the intended use 

for these products is in anti-HCV positive persons. Therefore, to immediately implement this perinatal 

HCV recommendation, laboratories would have to validate the off-label use of their molecular HCV 

assays - which many US clinical laboratories still need to do. Although this is a significant barrier, we are 

confident that this limitation can be overcome through a strong public-private partnership.

Evidence of Transient Suppression of Viremia in Acute HCV

We encourage you to consider addressing false negative HCV RNA that could occur because of transient 

viremia. The current recommendation states that infants with an undetectable HCV RNA result do not 

require further follow-up (page 20, line 8). Some studies have shown up to 50% of infants could 

spontaneously clear viremia during early life1. However, a recent case report indicated a recurrence of 

viremia in later years following seroconversion suggesting a closer look to the management of these cases

serology testing recommendations to include upcoming solutions such as the Elecsys(R) HCV Duo*, a

Elecsys® HCV Duo would be sufficient to aid in the diagnoses of active HCV infection and initiate 

treatment. Antibody-antigen dual testing could help address several rationales for recommending early 

HCV RNA testing. Most importantly, the number of laboratories that could complete acute HCV 

diagnostic algorithms in exposed infants would increase significantly.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

FSIS' policy of approving "humanely raised" labels for varying standards of care creates consumer confusion and it dilutes the meaning and value of the humanely raised label.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

As a resident of Washington and one who is concerned about the declining orca population, I want to thank you for proposing to expand critical habitat for the Southern Resident killer whales. I fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

Protecting this full range as critical habitat reflects new and best available science as new sightings and data show that SRKW regularly forage in the coastal waters off Washington, Oregon, and California and is essential to help get the southern resident orcas off the path to extinction and on the way to recovery.

The final rule designating critical habitat identified three essential habitat features essential to the conservation of the SRKW: (1) Water quality to support SRKW growth and development; (2) prey species of sufficient quantity, quality, and availability to support individual growth, reproduction, and development, as well as overall population growth; and (3) passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

However, the proposed rule exempts the Navy's Quinault Range Site off the coast of Washington from being designated as critical habitat due to national security. The Quinault Range Site includes part of two high-use foraging areas, as recognized by NMFS in the Biological Report, and completely bisects the proposed expanded critical habitat area. From the tagging data, about half the time that K and L pods spend in coastal habitat is in Area 1 (Washington and Northern Oregon inshore habitat). This exemption could impact their foraging ability in an area and season when nutritional stress is a significant concern and impact their ability to migrate up and down the coast. Therefore the exempted area is in conflict with the third essential habitat feature: passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

The proposed rule should include a narrow area sufficient in width between the shoreline and the eastern border of the Quinault Range Site to ensure orca migration along the coast and for foraging for limited prey. 

The science also shows that sound from vessels and other sources undermines orcas ability to echolocate to forage for salmon as well as to communicate and navigate. The Washington Governors Orca Recovery Task Force and the ESA Recovery Plan have noted that noise and disturbance are key threats hindering orca recovery and have recommended decreasing, not increasing, military noise. To sufficiently protect SRKW, NMFS must include sound as a fourth essential feature. Urge them to ensure that it is at least retained as an explicit factor in the prey and passage essential features. 

I am grateful that NMFS has engaged and consulted with Tribes to ensure that this rule does not impact Tribal Treaty rights and usual and accustomed fishing areas.

Again, fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

Dear Dr. Engeljohn,

Please raise the standards for companies labeling. VAGUE OR LOWER standards obviously do nothing but encourage most producers to stay right exactly at that standard level, and they STILL get the benefit of charging the consumer a premium price. The farmers who actually invest the money to TRULY treat animals humanely are quickly bankrupted since they cannot compete with the majority of producers who get away with murder by having much lower costs and STILL being allowed to charge a premium. This is obviously not fair to the consumer OR the animals. Thank you for your efforts!! 

- Chris Felton

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.
