Regulatory Review 
 
Vault Health Workforce Screening is a provider of DOT-regulatory compliance services to companies nationwide. 
We provide a range of services to a diverse client base including Fortune 500 companies, trucking companies, 
state and municipal governments and many small employers. In our role, we provide Third-Party Administrator 
and Medical Review Officer Services for companies in every DOT agency. Our MROs review over 500,000 drug 
tests annually. 
Vault Health supports the need and benefit of inclusion of oral fluid specimens as an alternative method under 
Part 40 for use by DOT regulated employers. We do not believe it should be mandatory for any circumstance or 
testing reason. However, prohibiting it for a return to duty or follow up test should be considered. Donors taking 
either of these tests have had a positive test or a reason to refuse testing. The longer detection times of urine 
testing will help deter the continued use of controlled substances. The shorter detection windows for oral fluid 
testing are better suited for post-accident and reasonable suspicion testing. However, to mandate it may cause 
problems in completing the testing especially in areas where there are fewer collectors. Employers often rely on 
the collectors to bring all the collection supplies to these emergency tests. Expired or no available devices could 
prevent the testing from being completed when it would be possible to get a urine test done in the same 
situation. The employer should be allowed to use either urine or oral fluid but should be uniform in handling the 
testing whenever possible. 
Our MRO team believes the oral fluid detection windows listed in the NPRM are too long. Their training lists 
detection times of up to 48 hours for all drugs. We believe the detection times chart should be updated to allow 
employers to make an educated decision on which specimen type to use for their testing. 
The decision on which specimen type to use initially should be made by the employer. The decision on which 
specimen type should be used for any additional collections should be determined by the employer and/or the 
MRO. The collector should not make this decision. Not all employers will choose to use oral fluid testing so while 
the collector might choose to run an oral fluid test, there is no contract between the employer and a lab and an 
MRO to process the test. The employer should inform the collector if they do utilize oral fluid testing either in 
the company protocols when contracting with the collector, or at the time of the collection. If the collector is 
not provided this information, they should contact the DER for authorization to change to an alternative 
specimen type when the situation occurs. Many employers use multiple collection sites and collectors. If the 
collector would make the decision, there is nothing to ensure that an employer program is handled the same for 
all employees. One collector may handle the process one way because they are trained in both oral fluid 
collections and urine collections. Another collector may handle the process differently because they are only 
trained to collect urine specimens. The MRO should make this decision when they are directing the employer to 
send a donor for a collection following a canceled-invalid result.

substantial equivalence. For example, there are both special and general controls that are part of the 

processes. The general public and non-medical device experts often are under the mistaken belief that one 

only has to show substantial equivalence in order to have a cleared 510(k) and that the 510(k) process

510(k) process involves much more than simply showing substantial equivalence.

concerns with the proposed demonstration by the Centers for Medicare and 

Medicaid Services (CMS) to alter the Medicare Part B program.

treatment for our most critically ill patient populations. Not only does the

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

The animals, who give us life, deserve respect. They should have a good life while they are here. The people who pay money for the product should know exactly what they are eating and putting in their bodies.

Thank you for considering my request.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I want to be able to trust that what I am purchasing and consuming is actually what you say it is.

I am writing to express my support for the proposed priority and definition for Transitioning Gang-Involved Youth to higher education (TGIY).

The Priority

Clarification is needed. Regarding the proposed priority, particularly for the Invitational Priority:
Invitational Priority: Under an invitational priority, we are particularly interested in applications that meet the priority. However, we do not give an application that meets the priority a preference over other applications (34 CFR 75.105(c)(1)).

The second sentence under the Invitational Priority negates the preceding statement. Clarify the other applications. For example, "However, we do not give an application that meets the priority a preference over non-priority applications." Distinguishing the difference in applications prevents the reader from making inferences.
Additionally, when prioritizing the associated TGIY projects, it is important to consider limiting absolute priority. Several organizations can provide additional youth services and should have the opportunity to expand such programs with TGIY funding. For instance, Resettlement Agencies, whose primary focus is to aid refugees with reception and placement, also offer youth mentoring programs for children aged 15-24. During activities, mentors may identify youth affiliated with gangs who need additional support. Therefore, organizations that provide other services unrelated to gang-involved youth should be allowed to apply for absolute priority projects, provided their proposals meet the statement of needs for TGIY funding.

The Definition

The proposed definition allows for seamless integration of services among gang-involved youth by aligning criteria with the U.S. Department of Justice's Gang Center. Consistent with the resettlement agency example, immigrant/refugee youth are often resettled in diverse communities such as Clarkston, Georgia. Families from the same country or countries with discordance may live within proximity. A broad definition of gangs enables supporters and grant recipients of TGIY to increase the number of youth involved in at-risk behaviors, including those associated with less visible gangs/groups that do not have a dominant presence in Western culture.

The time limit for submission of the declaration should be further harmonized with other 

applicable import regulations. 

Proposed 7 CFR § 357.2 defines import as ``To land on, bring into, or introduce into, any place 

subject to the jurisdiction of the United States, whether or not such landing, bringing, or 

introduction constitutes an importation within the meaning of the customs laws of the United 

States." 

Proposed 7 CFR § 357.5 states that the declaration must be submitted within 3 business days of 

importation. The deadline for a majority of submissions required by other agencies that 

regulate imports into the United States is the time of entry. Setting the deadline for submission 

of the Lacey Act declaration measured from the time of import rather than at the time of entry 

creates the potential for disruption in the entry process and an undue burden on commerce. We 

suggest that the declaration deadline be set as the time of entry as defined by Customs in 19 

CFR § 141.68 rather than after a time period measured from importation. Alternatively, setting 

the deadline for submission at fifteen calendar days after import, as defined by proposed 7 CFR 

§ 357.2, would correspond with the Customs requirements regarding general order 

merchandise.

I am writing to express my firm opposition to the newly published BLM Proposed NPR-A Rule. These regulations, in their current form, present a significant threat not only to the delicate balance of natural resource development and conservation but also stand in violation of the legal requirement to consult with the indigenous communities affected.

The rushed and inadequate consultation process is deeply concerning. It is evident that key stakeholders, especially Alaska Native communities residing in the vicinity of NPR-A, were not appropriately consulted, as mandated by law. The failure to engage Alaska's federally Recognized Tribes and Native Corporations in the formulation of these regulations is a stark oversight. The abrupt notification provided just seven business days before the rule's publication severely undermines the rights and input of these communities whose livelihoods and lands are directly impacted.

Moreover, the economic ramifications resulting from the proposed regulations pose a significant threat to the well-being and prosperity of Alaska Native communities. The dismissal of critical benefits such as the NPR-A Impact Mitigation Grant program, which substantially aids local communities with revenues for public services and essential resources, is alarming. Any impedance or cessation of project development due to these rules would directly strip these communities of crucial funds, impacting vital services like health facilities and education.

Additionally, the adverse effects on oil production from the NPR-A will inevitably lead to a decline in revenue for both the State of Alaska and local governments, thereby restricting their capacity to provide essential services to Alaskans. This financial strain further exacerbates the challenges faced by these communities and the state at large.

The strategic importance of NPR-A in supporting national energy security cannot be overstated. At a time when energy prices are escalating and global oil supply remains susceptible to external disruptions, domestic oil production stands as a critical pillar for safeguarding our nation's energy independence. Furthermore, these regulations would likely contribute to increased energy prices for working-class families across the country, exacerbating the burden of rising inflation.

It is important to acknowledge that the current regulatory framework adequately balances oil and gas development with the protection of vital surface resources, as established by the 2013 NPR-A Integrated Activity Plan. This plan, issued during the Obama-Biden Administration, already imposes stringent environmental protection requirements and delineates specific areas available for oil and gas development, rendering the proposed regulations redundant.

In conclusion, I strongly advocate for an extended and comprehensive consultation process with the impacted indigenous communities and key stakeholders to ensure their voices are heard and their concerns addressed. The Department of the Interior should reevaluate the proposed regulations, considering the far-reaching impact on the Alaskan Native communities, the state's economy, and our national energy security.

Thank you for considering my comments.

I strongly oppose the alterations to the process of designating critical habitat that are proposed in this rule. These changes expand the USFWS's ability to exclude areas essential to the conservation of threatened and endangered species from designation as critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act. Among other problematic provisions, it states that the USFWS must exclude such areas if the economic benefits of using the land for development, such as for oil and gas extraction, grazing, and logging, are greater than those of protecting the area for wildlife (except in cases where extinction will result). These changes would grant economic considerations outsized weight in decisions about habitat, which is inconsistent with the ESA's intent that species' recovery needs should be prioritized and should be determined using the best available science.

Designation of critical habitat is a vital tool available under the Endangered Species Act to help conserve species. Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors. 

The exclusion of areas that do not meet the new standards for the designation of critical habitat could significantly decrease the amount of habitat that can be protected. This would represent a severe setback to conservation, because critical habitat is vital for stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species that have protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species without it. Designation of critical habitat is more important than ever as species face increasing habitat loss due to conversion, pollution, and climate change.

We highly appreciate and fully support the proposed changes. Modifying several genes to enhance plant breeding is an important step to address global changes in food security. We and others have demonstrated the ability to make multi-gene edits to reveal hidden traits (Hu et al., Nature Plants, 2023, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-023-01374-4).

However, limiting the edits to 4 will not allow the community to reveal the full potential of crop breeding. We would like to recommend that the upper limit of four multiplex edits be increased to up to six. In several cases, it has been shown that more than four genes are needed to expose a genetically hidden phenotype or modify an agricultural trait. For example, Chen et al. 2023, EMBO reports (https://www.embopress.org/doi/full/10.15252/embr.202256271) edited five genes simultaneously to reveal and characterize five novel auxin transporters. In addition, Wang et al. 2014 Nature Biotechnology (https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.2969) simultaneously edited three homoeo-alleles in hexaploid bread wheat to confer heritable resistance to powdery mildew. This research was followed by additional genetic modifications to generate wheat resistance to powdery mildew without growth penalties. This work demonstrates the ability to stack genetic changes to rescue growth defects caused by recessive alleles, which is critical for developing high-yielding crop varieties with robust and durable disease resistance (Li, S., et al. 2022, Nature. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04395-9).

Emerging approaches such as BREEDIT: a multiplex genome editing strategy to improve complex quantitative traits in maize, present the gene discovery pipeline, which combines multiplex genome editing of whole gene families with crossing schemes to improve complex traits such as yield and drought tolerance (Damian Lorenzo et al., Plant Cell 2023, https://doi.org/10.1093/plcell/koac243).

Administrator, I am writing in response to the APHIS proposal published January 19, 2017, to amend the 

APHIS regulation 7 CFR Part 340 for the importation, interstate movement, and environmental release 

of certain genetically engineered organisms, a regulation that first was promulgated almost exactly 30 

years ago today. 

I appreciate having the opportunity to provide some brief comments as someone who has followed the 

regulations closely as a plant scientist over the past decades. I have had the privilege over the years of 

hearing APHIS personnel give talks about the origin and evolution of these regulations. 

In particular I recall hearing the former Director of the Biotechnology Permits Unit, Dr. Arnold Foudin, 

talk about the APHIS rationale for setting up the regulations in 1987 (primarily so there would be a 

Federal system for field testing GE plants), as well as the original intent of the Agency to have the 

regulations sunset or expire after several years once it was clear that it was further proven in field tests 

that the use of recombinant DNA techniques were not likely to pose safety risks in and of themselves. 

He told about the blue-ribbon scientists of the National Research Council that had already reached this 

conclusion, but that it might take some time before others saw it with their own eyes in research labs 

and field tests. He emphasized that it was the phenotype of the organism, the way it appeared and 

behaved, that made the difference in evaluating safety, not the techniques used to modify the plant or 

microorganism. 

The original 1987 version of this regulation and its subsequent revisions in 1988, 1989, 1993, 1997, and 

2005 are not without substantial shortcomings, and it is time for APHIS to reconsider whether the path 

of these regulations is worn out, and a new, more adaptable approach might be a better match for the 

circumstances. 

If there is one over-riding theme to my criticism of this 2017 proposed revision, it is that APHIS has not 

followed the general maxim for regulators around the world to use the regulatory approach that is least 

restrictive yet still achieves the objective. The United States and other members of the WTO captured 

this in Article 2.2 of the Sanitary and Phytosanitary Agreement of 1995, which states that "Members 

shall ensure that any sanitary or phytosanitary measure is applied only to the extent necessary to 

protect human, animal or plant life or health, is based on scientific principles and is not maintained

drinks, water beverages, 100 percent juices, fruit drinks, and soft drinks.

healthful diets. It is critically important, however, that as FDA engages in additional research on front-

utility. FDA’s ultimate goal in pursuing FOP labeling is to enable consumers to obtain useful

This Missouri Biotechnology Association's (MOBIO) mission is to advance and champion the life sciences across Missouri by accelerating bioscience comprehension throughout our state's elected leadership and citizenry. MOBIO supports investing in innovation, entrepreneurship and capital formation policies to enhance the state's role in creating a place that encourages the development of bioscience. 

I am writing on behalf of MOBIO to express the concerns we have regarding the Centers of Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) policy on payment for biosimilars, which currently includes blended reimbursement. The issue that members of MOBIO have with this policy is that it deters innovation in the biosimilar field. This field of biosimilar manufacturing is just opening up across the United States, and we should be developing reimbursement policies that encourage this venture, and recognize the complexity of the entire process, only as more competition is generated will price efficiencies be passed to the consuming public.
 
The CMS reimbursement policy for biosimilars is that all biosimilars related to a reference product are given a shared HCPCS code. MOBIO is asking that CMS reverse this policy and instead of blending prices, provide each biosimilar with a unique HCPCS code for billing and payment. Placing all biosimilars for a reference biologic into one HCPCS code creates considerable risk for biosimilar manufacturers, discouraging investment in biosimilar development and deterring innovation. Biosimilar progression is important to the overall development of bioscience. 

The Missouri Biotechnology Association is hopeful that CMS changes their reimbursement policy in context of the 2018 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule final rule.

Thank you for your attention.
The Missouri Biotechnology Association

Celiac Disease is a serious autoimmune disease affecting millions of Americans, where the ingestion of gluten leads to damage in the small intestine. People with Celiac Disease have a 2x greater risk of developing coronary artery disease, and a 4x greater risk of developing small bowel cancers as compared to the general population. Those with non-Celiac gluten sensitivity also require a gluten-free diet. It has been estimated that gluten consumption affects between 10-16% of the population to some degree. Many with non-IgE-mediated medical conditions including but not limited to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, Type 1 diabetes, autism and schizophrenia, also benefit from a gluten-free diet. All of the above amount to a significant portion of the American population who need to be considered stakeholders. I am a parent to a child with Celiac, aunt to a child with Celiac, aunt to a child with diagnosed non-Celiac gluten-sensitivity, godchild to an adult with Celiac, camp counselor for a child with Celiac and neighbor to a child with Celiac, to name only a few in my own sphere. It is important for the FDA to recognize that gluten, not just in the form of wheat, significantly influences their long-term health. As the caregiver to a number of children and some adults, I rely heavily on food labeling and the regulations that govern them.

According to the Celiac Disease Foundation, "The treatment burden of Celiac Disease is comparable to end-stage renal disease, and the partner burden is comparable to caring for a patient with cancer. Untreated Celiac Disease can lead to the development of other autoimmune disorders like Type 1 diabetes and multiple sclerosis (MS), and many other conditions, including dermatitis herpetiformis, anemia, osteoporosis, infertility and miscarriage, neurological conditions like epilepsy and migraines, short stature, heart disease, and intestinal cancers." Currently, the only treatment for Celiac Disease is lifelong adherence to a strict gluten-free diet. People living gluten-free must avoid foods with wheat, rye, and barley.

All of the above are serious medical conditions, however most if not all do not cause IgE-mediated reactions and acute and life-threatening responses. It is this distinction in the proposed FDA guidelines that I am requesting be reevaluated and reconsidered, as well as the distinction of (or definition of) gluten to include ALL its components, and therefore be included in the guidelines..

FALCPA protects the above consumer populations to a limited extent. It is only in cases where manufacturers choose to voluntarily label certain products “gluten-free.” For other products not voluntarily labeled “gluten-free,” consumers currently have no way of knowing if these foods contain gluten-containing grains other than wheat, which is covered by FALCPA labeling regulations. Because FALCPA does not cover the gluten-containing grains barley and rye as it does for wheat, manufacturers in the U.S. are not currently required to alert consumers of the presence of other gluten-containing ingredients in their foods such as malt, malt extract, malt syrup, malt vinegar, malt flavoring, "natural smoke flavor", yeast extract, and "natural flavors".

FDA’s draft guidance limits citizen petitions regarding foods that cause *any* immune-mediated adverse reactions, and limits its review to only foods causing IgE-mediated reactions and acute life-threatening responses. This ignores a significant portion of the stakeholder population who nonetheless have been shown to have longer term life-threatening responses to the consumption of gluten in forms other than wheat.

Comments of the South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association on the Animal and Plant Health 

Inspection Service Process for Establishing Rates for Veterinary Services User Fees 

The South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association (SDCA) appreciates the opportunity to submit 

comments in response to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), Animal and 

Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) proposed rule to amend the regulations for establishing 

rates for veterinary user fees for veterinary diagnostic services and for certain import-related and 

export-related services for live animals, animal products and byproducts, birds, germplasm, 

organisms, and vectors. Our members are committed to ensuring the health and well-being of the 

cattle under their care and to producing high quality, safe, and wholesome beef. 

Changes to the Veterinary User Fee Process 

 USDA, APHIS, Veterinary Services (VS) is proposing to amend the regulations in 9 CFR part 

130 to provide for a set of standardized formulas by which import/export and veterinary 

diagnostic user fees would be calculated. The proposed regulations would specify the 

methodology used to calculate and implement the user fees and would remove tables showing 

specific fees. USDA, APHIS, VS would post fee rates on its website and annually issue a notice 

providing all fees calculated for the upcoming year using the formulas contained in the 

regulations and request public comment. 

Since fiscal year 1992, APHIS has received no directly appropriated funds to cover the cost of 

certain veterinary diagnostics or to provide import/export related services for animals, animal 

products and byproducts, birds, germplasm, organisms, and vectors. In the past, the agency’s 

rulemaking established user fees for five-year periods of time. 

Under the proposed rule, APHIS, VS would update user fees each calendar year thorough 

publication of a notice in the Federal Register and accept public comment. We understand that 

USDA, APHIS must compensate the Treasury General Fund for these imputed costs, so the costs

 
are not borne by the taxpayer. Directly charging the users of the veterinary services internalizes 

these costs to those who require the service and benefit from it. At the same time, with the 

current extreme volume of cattle movement and beef trade, user fee consistency is vital to 

maintaining continuity of business and the continued promotion of beef trade. While the 

proposed veterinary user fee methodology seeks to provide transparency and predictability to the 

industries served, it is important that the annual reevaluation of veterinary user fees by the 

agency does not result in burdensome or onerous fees that discourage continued business. 

Conclusion 

SDCA understands that user fees for veterinary services, not covered by appropriated funding, 

are necessary to recover the costs of the agency for inspection and certification services for 

imports and exports of live animals and animal products and for providing veterinary diagnostic 

goods and services. It is our hope that the proposed changes to the process for establishing 

veterinary user fee rates will be organized to allow cattle producers to better anticipate any 

possible increases in user fee rates, provide comments for consideration regarding user fee 

changes, and be better informed to prepare future business planning and decision-making. 

Sincerely, 

Eric Jennings, President

Dear Director Stone-Manning,

Thank you for initiating a plan to elevate conservation and bring balance to how the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) manages America’s public lands. As an outdoor enthusiast and responsible recreationist, I support the Public Lands Rule and encourage you to strengthen it to help ensure a vibrant future for western communities' water supplies, wildlife and way of life that make the region unique. 

America's public lands offer some of the most readily available, fiscally responsible solutions to address drought, storm impacts, catastrophic fire and nature loss that are causing rapid changes in the West. They are also drivers of the $862 billion outdoor recreation economy, which provides sustainable economic benefits to surrounding communities. For more than 40 years the BLM has prioritized resource extraction over other uses on public lands that are home to over 3,000 species, many of which inhabit no other places in the country. 

It's time to balance BLM's approach and elevate conservation and responsible recreation to help sustain the nation's iconic open landscapes of the West that drive tourism, offer refuge for wildlife, provide greater public access to nature, and safeguard innumerable stories of human experiences on the land. Expanding co-stewardship with Tribal Nations will bring traditional knowledge and incorporate Indigenous expertise to decision-making to ensure these lands remain healthy and support us in the future. 

While the draft rule is an important step forward, I believe it will need strengthening prior to its finalization. In particular, the rule should: 
•Require the identification and protection of habitat connectivity areas. 
•Facilitate ecological integrity and climate resiliency across all forest-types by conserving old and mature forests from logging, wildfire and climate change, informed by the best available science and Indigenous knowledge. 
•Ensure that, prior to approving any development, the BLM has conducted an inventory of intact natural landscapes, including lands with wilderness characteristics, and determined that the action will not degrade any intact natural landscape. 
•Ensure that all eligible areas that meet the criteria are designated as Areas of Critical Environmental Concern and are properly managed. 
•Require the BLM to consult with Tribes to ensure it fully advances opportunities for co-stewardship, incorporation of Indigenous Knowledge, respect for Tribal sovereignty and treaty rights, protection of Tribal cultural sites, and carrying out Tribal consultation in ways that honor the unique historic and current connections of Native Americans to public lands. 
•Ensure that responsible recreation, as a low impact and compatible use, is further integrated in an appropriate manner into conservation planning, as greater access to recreation helps bring more people from all backgrounds into the conservation movement. 

I'm grateful for this Administration's commitment to conserving and restoring America's public lands and supporting the communities that depend on them. Now is the time to act for the critical places that are the backbone of the West. Please strengthen the Public Lands Rule and work swiftly to bring balance to BLM-managed landscapes.

Sincerely,
Daniel Bunker
New York, NY 10025

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. As a school psychologist, I have seen firsthand the damage that sustained childhood trauma can do. Often profound and long-lasting, the effects of childhood trauma can interfere with normal and healthy childhood growth and development. 
 Unnecessarily sustaining traumatic separation of children from their families is tantamount to child abuse. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

As a mental health professional, I implore you to consider the damage that the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement would do to innocent children. For the above reasons, I oppose the proposed regulations.

obligation to inform the City if a private service line is replaced. Accordingly, the City will likely 

need to identify private service lines as being of “unknown material.” Although the intent is to 

provide the utility with time to obtain data on the privately-owned pipes, publication of the

I believe that vehicle's safety ratings should reflect not only how safe the vehicle is to passengers, but how a vehicle affects a streets overall safety environment. 

Many deadly crashes involve large SUVs and Trucks particularly when they strike a smaller vehicle, pedestrian, or cyclist. Additionally these same large vehicles often have large blind spots, that inhibit the drivers ability to operate the vehicle safely. High hoods limit visibility of pedestrians, particularly children, and provide hazards in tight spaces such as driveways or parking lots, both places where pedestrians are likely to be present. Lifted vehicles and high hoods also affect the likelihood a pedestrian or cyclist will go under the vehicle in the event of a crash.

While many large vehicles provide safety for the passengers of the vehicles when in a crash, they create a hazardous safety environment for pedestrians and cyclists. I strongly urge the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to consider these factors when rating vehicles on their safety.

After pre-viewing the four alternative plans and attending meetings in the Upper Keys, I appreciate the Advisory Councils opportunity to comment. As a local living here for the past 19 years and a member of the working community in the SCUBA diving industry, I find several areas of concern with the restorative blueprint. I spend an average of 300 days on the waters in the Sanctuary earning my living taking our local and visiting divers out to our reef. I have my greatest knowledge of the KEY LARGO area, and my comments are reflected to this. The first topic of concern with Alternative 2,3,4 is the:

CLOSING OF ANCHORING AREAS in the KEY LARGO EMA: To close off these areas will restrict access to our favorite patch reefs and fringing barrier reefs. To restrict the usage of these smaller, quieter, out of the way places would not only change our business model, but take away the reason as to why we live here in the first place. If these Alternatives are enacted, you would no longer be able to go to your favorite diving, snorkeling, fishing, recreational areas that we enjoy. These areas are also what our business is founded upon. This would turn the entire KEY LARGO area into a no use zone. This cannot happen.

WHITMORE BIGHT: In the Upper Keys Alternative 2,3,4 would in essence, turn this into a no use zone. Trying to troll / pole such great distances would not only require the strength of Hercules but also the battery power of a battleship.

SPA IDLE ZONES: This is one area I believe will be beneficial to the safety of the diving community. Common sense would dictate this to be a prudent mode of vessel operation. Is this not already in place?

EDUCATION: With these gross alternative plans, 2, 3, 4, education will be key to success. I recommend that all boat operators be certified with the Sanctuary Blue Star program. This program is already in place and easily implemented. The recreational boat operator takes the course once, receives a card / placard such as a driver's license. A small fee ($20) would cover the cost of issuance. On the federal level there's already a entrance fee into the Everglades National Park as well as a Everglades National Park Boater Permit, (which is free) 

CARYSFORT REEF SPA: Changing this reef to a commercial Blue Star Operator program only, while leaving the recreational boater 'as is' makes no sense (alt 3). If the commercial operators have to be Blue Star so should the general public. Changing the status to ALT 4 making this area a idle zone from the shore line out to Sanctuary boundaries is crazy.

ENFORCEMENT: This is the biggest problem of them all. As of now there is very little to no patrols from FKNMS Sanctuary Patrol as well as from FWC. You people can't enforce what you already have in place, let alone taking on the responsibility of a much larger and broader area. I see violations in the SPA's on a daily / weekly basis and when reported to the appropriate phone numbers, there's no action. The violators know this, which offers no deterrent to their actions. It's turned our waters into a Wild West state of mind. Without additional enforcement, officers, staffing, this practice will continue.

MOORING BUOYS: I've heard comment at the Key Largo meeting's concerning the additional placement of mooring balls in the KEY LARGO EMA. I spend a lot of my time and days in the SPA's and see first hand the condition and maintenance (or lack of) the buoy's in place. If the Mooring Ball team already has a hard time replacing and maintaining the mooring ball's already in place, how are they going to keep up with additional mooring balls? This was a question asked at the Key Largo meeting and the answer was vague. I believe this would just add to a team that is already underfunded and understaffed. 

 Common sense and good judgement is what's needed for the sanctuary instead of radical change.Eliminating and restricting use will not make the sanctuary waters better. EDUCATI

Two years and three days ago, my family and I were hit head on by an oncoming car. A distracted driver slid across a lane, rounded a corner, and found our car ten feet ahead. 

My intestine instantly ruptured, although we would not find out for hours. My mom suffered a fractured sternum, tailbone, and concussion. Thankfully, we are all okay today. My family is lucky to be alive, healed, and together. 

A simple mistake should not have such dire and traumatic consequences with the advanced technology of today. Yet one reason remains – cars do not care about women.

This is not to say that cars care particularly about any man. These masses of steel and power throttle to their destiny no matter the passenger. The same is not true, however, for their designers and regulators. It is not true for the ones who are supposed to protect us from the cars themselves. 

The government has known since the 1980s that cars are not designed equitably. Women, being of a different sex, are different. Variations in mass distribution, skeletal formations, and stature relative to seat positioning all contribute to a more dangerous vehicular structure for women. The famous statistics published by UVA, and validated by NHTSA, show that women are 17% more likely to be killed and 73% more likely to be injured in a frontal belted crash. VerityNOW estimates 1,300 women’s lives would be saved each year with more equitable safety measures. The cause is the design of the cars themselves – designed to fit a safety standard in which women are not accounted for. The safety standard, as implemented through the New Car Assessment Program, only requires male drivers. The results of these tests determine a car’s safety score and are displayed on the Monroney label. Thus, consumers unknowingly proceed in their purchases based on faulty and untrue data. 

Some kinds of crashes are inevitable. Drivers will get distracted, an animal will jump in the road, or a tire will skid on a patch of black ice. The difference, however, between a simple accident and a life-altering injury or death is enormous. If cars were designed with female dummies, I could drive without remembering the pressure against my chest of a seatbelt not supposed to fit a women’s chest, without the echo of a searing tear in my abdomen. 

The Monroney label should represent an accurate and reliable measurement of the cars’ protection for its passengers. Instead, it boasts an inconsistent and biased calculation, willingly endorsed by the government and misleading consumers. Any ongoing assessments, and advancements based on these, will be wholly unjust should they proceed in the same inequitable manner. I hope the government does not willfully and knowingly continue to deceive and endanger consumers, particularly women.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. 

The Flores Settlement is necessary to protect vulnerable children from tremendous harms, and by protecting those children the Settlement does better by America: it supports resilient young people, some of whom may ultimately become U.S. citizens, and it supports American values of fundamental fairness, due process, and moral decency. 

The proposed regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

When airlines began charging for checked luggage in 2008, they raised customer 
expectations that luggage would be delivered reliably and upon arrival.1 Yet, it is procedurally

This shorter timeframe best serves the act’s underlying purpose. The FAA Extension 
Act’s refund provision seeks to promptly reimburse the customer for the inconvenience of 
delayed luggage. Its goal is plainly customer protection. However, a rule longer than 12 hours is 
unlikely to generate greater convenience for passengers. 
First, it takes an average of 31.2 hours for a passenger to be reunited with their misplaced

notified within 4 hours, state the reason for the delay.”5 This suggests that the statutory minimum 
of 12 hours is rational and feasible for domestic flights.

The rule should minimize the procedural hurdles customers might face in obtaining the 
refund.

determination. The proposed rule would also establish the general procedures FDA intends

addition, the proposed rule is intended to provide both industry and FDA with more certainty 

about the content and format of SE Reports with the goal of supporting efficient and 

predictable reviews of SE Reports. FDA has invited comments on various aspects of the 

proposed rule.

burden on Agency and industry resources and better carry out its public health mission.

Dear Mr. Rauch, and Mr. Barnette,

I am writing today to support the National Marine Fisheries Services advance notice of proposed rulemaking, which proposes to expand the requirement to use Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs) on vessels less than 40 feet in the southeast U.S. shrimp fisheries and requests public input on impacts. The Fisheries Service should expand the TEDs rule to require 3-inch bar spacing TEDs on all trawls in the shrimp fisheries of the Southeast Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico.

All six sea turtle species found in U.S. waters are listed as endangered or threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Sea turtles face significant threats from commercial fishing. Sea turtles, which require air to breathe, can get caught in fishing nets as bycatch, non-target catch, and be harmed or even drowned. According to the Fisheries Services own estimates, under the rules currently in place, Southeast U.S. shrimp trawl nets come into contact with endangered or threatened sea turtles over half-a-million times a year, resulting in as many as 50,000 sea turtles deaths. If used properly, TEDs provide an escape hatch in the fishing nets that can reduce sea turtle bycatch by as much as 97 percent. And, narrower, 3-inch bar spacing TEDs protect small, juvenile sea turtles. At least 50 percent more sea turtles could be saved with the expansion of the TEDs rule to all shrimp trawling vessels in the Southeast.

In addition to saving sea turtles, TEDs have been proven to reduce bycatch of other marine life, including recreationally and commercially valuable fish. Moreover, expanding use of TEDs is beneficial to shrimp fishers, who will likely spend less time sorting out the targeted shrimp from non-target species, may have reduced fuel costs due to reduction of drag, and will likely benefit from broader markets if the Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch removes the red-listing for the fishery.
With more sea turtles alive and well due to expanded TEDs use, locals and tourists in the Southeast region can observe sea turtles on land through guided nesting walks and rehabilitation release events as well as in the water through scuba diving. Coastal economies in the Southeast benefit from sea turtle tourism, which attracts over 500,000 visitors annually.

Expanding 3-inch bar spacing TEDs to all trawls in the U.S. southeast shrimp fishery not only provides necessary protections for endangered and threatened sea turtles, as required by the Endangered Species Act, but also benefits fishers, coastal communities, and visitors to the Southeast region. I urge you to fully and effectively implement this common-sense, win-win solution: expand the TEDs rule to require 3-inch bar spacing TEDs on all trawls in the shrimp fisheries of the Southeast Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico.

Sincerely,
Mary Shea

I appreciate the fact that USDA moved quickly to create hemp production regulations; certain provisions, however, will be detrimental to farmers and the industry and are of great concern to me.

Measurement of Uncertainty
I appreciate the flexibility USDA provides in allowing an acceptable hemp THC level to fall within the range of a testing methods measurement of uncertainty (MU). I am concerned, however, that measuring of sampling uncertainty was not included in the IFR and hemp-testing laboratories will have insufficient insight into the crop sampling process and genetic variation in the crop to properly calculate total uncertainty, resulting in potentially severe economic harm to hemp producers mistakenly found to have produced a non-compliant crop.

I recommend that USDA amend the MU provision of the IFR to require the measurement and inclusion of sampling uncertainty.

Sampling Procedure
The Sampling Guidelines require that Sampling Agents collect samples from only the top one-third of the plant. That is odd, as the upper portion of the plant is not the only part of the plant that is used in the manufacturing of hemp products. Moreover, the highest concentration of THC is found in this top portion of the plant, which will result in an inaccurate measurement of THC in the plant. Without all flowering portions of a hemp plant, the sampling has a high likelihood of causing farmers to lose their crop because of incomplete and invalid samples.

I recommend that Sampling Guidelines be amended to require samples taken and homogenized from all parts of the plant.

Sampling to Harvest Window
I feel that allowing only 15 days between sampling and harvest is inadequate and unworkable. Farmers have to depend on hand labor to harvest and bring in crops. Weather conditions also must be right during harvest and precipitation could delay the harvest process. There is also an insufficient numberof DEA-registered laboratories to perform testing on all producers during such a small window. Finally, if I were a farmer, I would want to know if my crop is considered hot or not before beginning the harvest because the cost of harvesting would be an added burden if the crop is later determined to be non-compliant and ordered to disposal.

I recommend that USDA revise the regulations to allow for 45 days between sampling and harvest to take into account all these factors.

Disposal of Non-Compliant Plants
The IFR requires all non-compliant plant material to be destroyed pursuant to DEA regulations. The complete destruction of a non-compliant hemp crop poses a great risk of economic hardship on hemp farmers, who invest tens of thousands of dollars per acre for planting. Re: 2020 Alaska Roadless Rule Dear USDA Forest Service, Please fully restore 2001 Roadless Rule protections on the Tongass National Forest and end large-scale old growth timber sales on the entirety of the forest. The Tongass is a key weapon for fighting climate change, with its old-growth trees effectively trapping and sequestering climate-warming greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Scientists have estimated that the forest accounts for about 8 percent of the carbon sequestered by all national forests. Protecting the Tongass from old-growth logging will not only preserve that capacity, but avoid releasing carbon currently sequestered in its trees. The Tongass is also the ancestral and contemporary homeland of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples, and they have been the driving force of the effort to protect the forest. Their way of life is inextricably linked with these lands and waters. They hunt, gather, fish and harvest medicines in the Tongass that their ancestors have stewarded for more than 10,000 years. Restoring full protections will allow their traditional use of the land to continue. As part of planning for a future beyond old-growth timber, please also make a sustained investment in the Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy. Operating in full consultation with Tribal governments and local communities, this program will help the region stoke the already robust fishing and recreation industries that are driving the economy. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Rob Williams - PII -

I strongly urge USDA-APHIS to deny the petition to deregulate the genetically engineered Darling 54 American chestnut. This tree is flawed both in design and intent, and its release into the wild would pose unacceptable risks to forest ecosystems!

A Defective Tree with Unstable Traits

The tree suffers from a serious genetic defect: the unintended deletion of the SAL1 gene. This has resulted in weakened growth, high mortality, and unreliable blight resistance. These are not isolated issues—they are fundamental problems that render Darling 54 unfit for any restoration effort.

Misleading Science, Misidentified Tree

SUNY-ESF mistakenly provided the wrong GE pollen for over a decade of research. The data that USDA is relying on comes from an entirely different tree than originally described. The American Chestnut Foundation, once a key partner, has withdrawn support due to these scientific missteps and a disturbing lack of transparency.

Ecological Recklessness

If deregulated, Darling 54 trees could reproduce in the wild and permanently alter native chestnut populations. These long-lived trees could spread engineered genes across forests without adequate understanding of the consequences. There is no precedent—and no justification—for such ecological gambling.

Corporate Control of Conservation

SUNY-ESF has signed a commercialization deal with a private company to sell these GE seedlings. What began as a conservation project funded by public money is now being turned into a biotech business venture, despite unresolved health and environmental concerns—including a wheat gene with unknown allergenicity.

There are safer, proven alternatives. USDA must reject this flawed petition and invest in restoration efforts that prioritize ecological health, scientific integrity, and public trust.

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

200 Bennett Ave.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

Summary: The North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality (department) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed revision to the Clean Water Act Section 401 Certification Rule (Certification Improvement Rule 2022). The department has Clean Water Act Section 401 authority for the state of North Dakota (state). These comments are aligned with the objectives of cooperative federalism and supported by President Biden’s Executive Order 13990. 

Comment 1: Pre-Filing Meeting Request: 
The department supports the proposed change to the pre-filing meeting request. The proposed language replaces an arbitrary time burden with the flexibility to customize the time-period needed for review based on project complexity and potential to discharge to waters. 

Comment 2: Request for Certification:
The department supports clearly defining the steps to request certification.
 
Comment 3: Concurrent federal permit and certifying application:
The department finds this portion of the 2020 rule effective at ensuring transparency and cooperation between the applicant, the federal agency and the certifying authority. It is the departments request that this requirement remain part of the Certification Improvement Rule 2022. 

Comment 4: Reasonable Period of Time:
The department supports coordination between the federal permitting/licensing and state certifying agency in deciding the reasonable period of time and agrees that a 60-day default is functional if agreement cannot be reached.

Comment 5: Scope of Review: 
The department supports: (1) Review the certifying authority has indicated the nature of the certification decision (i.e., grant, grant with conditions, deny, or waive); (2) the proper certifying authority issued the decision; and (4) the decision was issued within the “reasonable period of time”.

The department does not support the federal agency review of (3) The certifying authority provided public notice on the request for certification. 

The department does not believe the reach of the federal agency extends to overseeing state public notice policy. 

In 33 U.S.C.A. § 1341 the exact language is: “Such State or interstate agency shall establish procedures for public notice in the case of all applications for certification by it and, to the extent it deems appropriate, procedures for public hearings in connection with specific applications”. Note that Federal oversight is not mentioned or implied.

Conclusion: The department appreciates the opportunity to be involved with process of reviewing and editing the Certification Improvement Rule 2022 to best fit the needs of the state. These comments, in combination with the proposed changes has the potential to help protect the aquatic environment while also reducing permitting time and project costs by setting in plain language the steps needed to comply with Standards of Quality of Water Quality of the State, North Dakota Administrative Code Chapter 33.1-16-02.1 as intended by the clean water act and 40 CFR part 121.

To: Secretary John Kelly

From: Americans for Tax Reform

Re: Oppose EB-5 Midnight Rule

Dear Secretary Kelly,

I am writing to you today to ask for the reconsideration of Obama's EB-5 "midnight rule" that would compromise the integrity of the program. The EB-5 visa program has been an important source of investment for the American economy. Changes to the program should be handled in the legislative branch, where democratically elected representatives can best represent their constituent's priorities. 

The EB-5 regulation proposed by the Department of Homeland Security's U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on January 13 (see 82 Federal Register 4738) should be pulled from consideration like the rest of the previous administration's 11th hour rules.

The regulation aims to increase the financial burdens of obtaining the visas, putting the entire program at risk. The new rule would increase the lower visa cost from $500,000 to $1.35 million and the high end from $1 million to 1.8 million. Simply put, this will discourage investment in American job markets that need it most. Investors will have the option of going to Australia, or Canadahigh income countries with lower visa monetary requirements.

The Commerce Department has recently conducted a study of the job-creating impact of the investor visa program. In just one year 11,000 immigrant investors provided $5.8 billion in capital for FY2012 and FY2013 to support an estimated 174,039 thousand jobs in the United States. Much of it in construction and infrastructure. USCIS has been unable to determine the possible impact of the new rules. DHS should not put 174,000 American jobs at risk for an Obama administration holdover.

Instead, DHS should wait for the legislative branch to act. Such a sudden change to the program would send the wrong message to companies and investors, possibly chilling investment in American jobs and the economy.

Congress should also work to reauthorize the EB-5 regional centers program before its expiration this month. Given the consistent backlog on visa requests, and the global demand from investors for these visas, Congress and DHS should be looking at ways to safely expand the program, not shrink it. The influx of capital could help spur the private market towards infrastructure investment. 

I encourage you to take a close look at this program and its well-documented benefits for the economy and rescind this Obama regulation. To remain competitive, America needs to welcome investments that employ more workers and improve infrastructure.

Regards,
 
Grover G. Norquist

We, the undersigned organization, represent or have represented clients facing indefinite immigration detention in Southern California. We submit this comment urging the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw these proposed rules in their entirety. 

On November 19, 2020, DHS published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) that, among other things, drastically restricts eligibility for employment authorization documents (EADs) pursuant to 8 C.F.R. 274a.12(c)(18). The proposed rule, which was announced during the ongoing and unprecedented global health crisis, serves only to significantly reduce the availability of EADs for people living under orders of supervision (OSUP). If the proposed rule is finalized and takes effect, the harm that it will wreak on indigent individuals living under OSUP and their families cannot be overstated. 

DHS seeks to eliminate EADs for individuals with final orders of removal with only one narrow exception. DHS proposes to allow individuals with final orders of removal to seek EADs when DHS has determined that their removal is impractical because all countries for whom travel documents have been requested by DHS have affirmatively declined to issue a travel document. Not only does the proposed rule exclude tens of thousands of individuals presently dependent on EADs, but the exception renders the likelihood of individuals successful application for EADs virtually impossible. 

By DHSs own estimate, the rule will result in lost labor wages of upwards of 1.5 billion dollars in its first year alone. This loss will be exacerbated by the devastation that the COVID-19 pandemic has left in its wake, leaving many OSUP individuals homeless, re-confined in ICE detention, or entirely dependent on personal support networks of family members and social services organizations. DHS has failed to adequately consider all of these social costs. 

Moreover, the proposed ban on EADs for individuals with final orders of removal does not accomplish its stated goal. DHSs stated intentions for this rule are (1) to reduce the incentive for individuals to remain in the U.S. after receiving a final order of removal and (2) to strengthen protections for U.S. workers. As explained below, the agencys incentive to remain analysis does not meet its defined objectives and inaccurately characterizes the present OSUP requirements prior to an individuals request for EADs under 8 C.F.R. 274a.12(c)(18) (hereinafter referred to as (c)(18)). Additionally, the benefits allegedly conferred on U.S. workers by implementation of this rule are ill-defined and insufficient. 

For all these reasons and because the rule changes will irreversibly harm those living under OSUP and their communities, the proposed rule should be rejected in its entirety.

I grew up on an avocado ranch in southern California in the fifties and sixties. My father was president of Calavo (an avocado-growers cooperative) during some of that time. For ten of the last twelve years I have lived in cattle ranching country in southeastern Arizona. For the last eight years I have done extensive volunteer work on a permaculture farm. So I know a fair amount about the subjects my comments address.

I strongly support USDA’s proposed rule “Inclusive Competition and Market Integrity Under the Packers and Stockyards Act” for the following reason(s): 

Farmers and ranchers must be able to participate in producer organizations and associations, such as coops. Being able to do so can help their businesses in many ways; industry retaliation against such participation is harmful to their businesses and livelihoods, and reduces competition. Both producers and consumers lose out substantially when producers are prevented from full and free participation in their respective associations.

Farmers and ranchers must also be permitted to serve as witnesses in any proceeding relating to violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act, without fear of intimidation or retaliation. The ability to speak out without fear of reprisal is essential to promoting fair and competitive markets in the livestock and poultry industries. If farmers and ranchers cannot speak up freely, consumers cannot be honestly informed about the products they purchase and feed to their families.

Discrimination and retaliation result in greater profits for the industry, at farmers' and consumers' expense. Further, farmers who complain about their pay or the fairness of their contracts run the risk of losing those contracts, putting their livelihoods at risk. The 23 million total acres of the Western Arctic Reserve (which also bears the unfortunate title National Petroleum Reserve Alaska) represent our nations largest single parcel of public land. Maximum protection for Special Areas in the Reserve must include prohibiting future oil and gas leasing and any industrial development. 

Alaska Native communities across the region rely on these lands and resources and have resided in this region since time immemorial. These protections are critical for saving wildlife habitats that are home to grizzly and polar bears, caribou and millions of migratory birds. 

Development and extraction in the Western Arctic not only impact local wildlife and people, but also our global climatewe need to stop the expansion of oil and gas extraction in this region.

I ask that your administration take the strongest possible measures to protect the Western Arctic Reserve and advance Americas global climate leadership. A first action might be to simply rename the 23 million acres to better reflect the incredible wilderness legacy it represents, and how important it is to the Arctic's ecosystem. A second move might be to permanently end all leases for oil and gas exploration and extraction in the region. Third, craft a rule that prevents end-runs around these extraction processes to ensure future generations of informed American citizens don't have to fight the dying oil and gas industry in near perpetuity to protect the marine ecosystem from likely catastrophic damage if drilling is permitted anywhere near or on the waters of the Arctic Ocean.

Thank you, again, for taking direct, clear, and complete action to protect one of America's most pristine and important wilderness heritage areas.

individual air waybill or individual bill of lading for the processing of airway bills for shipments

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. REVISION OF TESTING STANDARD
For
FMVSS 138
Tire Pressure Monitoring System
Comment for
Docket ID: NHTSA-2020-0109

This comment suggests the revision of the testing location requirement for this standard. This comment is submitted by NAVTA, the North American Vehicle Trade Associates.

The only location at which the regulations allow testing certification is on the Southern Loop of the Treadwear Test Course near San Angelo, Texas.

This comment does not suggest any change to the temperature or pavement condition requirements of this regulation, merely to allow certification testing on any suitable roadway.

There is no justification found as to why this location was deemed the sole acceptable location on the planet to conduct this test. There is no specialized equipment required, nor is there any reason that the road surface of the Treadwear Test Course provides a unique surface for the tests.

Basically the test involves verification that the system functions as required, with a low pressure and malfunction segment. Pressure is pressure and a road is a road. 

ECONOMIC IMPACT:
Obviously there is a significant cost to certification of conformity for this standard. The vehicle must be transported to San Angelo and the testing conditions must be within the parameters. These costs impact small manufacturers more than large volume manufacturers. Additionally, Registered Importers who wish to import vehicles without a U.S. certified TPMS are required to transport and test individual vehicles to this site in order to document compliance.

REPEATABLE RESULTS:

The important variables which could affect the test are ambient temperature and roadway humidity. Temperature changes would affect tire pressure. However, the regulations specify the parameters of these variables. So long as the testing conditions are within those parameters the roadway should not make a difference. The road surface should be well maintained and paved.

NHTSA may, at its option, conduct confirmatory tests at San Angelo, or at another location.

EFFECT OF CHANGE:
Should NHTSA adopt the suggestion of this comment, manufacturers will be more likely to conduct additional tests of their products. 

This will streamline the compliance process and enable small manufacturers and importers to economically compete.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

As a veterinarian, I am fully aware of the importance of animal welfare and the need for major improvement in the labeling of products.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

Dear Officials,
 I am writing to comment on the proposed rule changes to the user fees regarding Agricultural and Quarantine Inspection Services. The Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service is proposing to eliminate the user fee exemption for small commercial passenger aircraft on June 2nd 2025. This rule change will effectively eliminate a vital air transportation link to a border community in western Lake Erie know as Pelee Island, Ontario. 
 Pelee Island has many multigenerational American property owners such as myself that rely on daily small aircraft service from Port Clinton, Ohio. This service is provided by a multigenerational small family business know as Griffing Flying Service in Port Clinton. The Griffing family has been dedicated to serving Pelee Island with small 4 to 8 passenger aircraft year round. The average passenger count per flight is usually 3 to 4 passengers. These aircraft make many trips per day over the same short route. The flight time to Pelee Island is approximately 12 minutes and travel distance to Pelee Island is approximately 20 miles. The passengers carry only personal belongings to their seasonal cottages on Pelee Island, enjoy their stay on Pelee Island and return with their personal belongings to Port Clinton, Ohio. There is no cargo on board to pose a risk of contamination. 
 There are many islands in western Lake Erie. These islands are only a few miles apart and only a few miles from the shorelines. They all share the same lake geography and environment. Given the close proximity and environmental similarity of these islands, there is nothing unique about Pelee Island that would pose a contamination risk. 
 We feel that the longstanding user fee exemption should remain in effect for this air service based on the very low risk. These are short flights flown multiple times per day with low passenger counts and no cargo. This is the only air service from the Ohio mainland to Pelee Island, Ontario. It is critical to American property owners. Without the continuation of the fee exemption, the cost per passenger on these small planes will be unsustainable. This would be an unnecessary hardship on the property owners and and the small flying service business and will effectively eliminate the air service that we have come to rely on for generations.
