This comment pertains to the treatment of interest during the SAVE forbearance as well as increasing Buyback efficiency and transparency.

The Buyback provision does not quite hold all borrowers harmless from the effects of the preliminary injunction (which occurred as a result of what ED has stated is the "unlawful" nature of the SAVE program--for which ED is responsible) because now that the SAVE litigation has dissolved without a court's declaration of SAVE's illegality, borrowers will have missed out on its interest subsidy from Aug. 1, 2025 onward. This accrued interest encouraged some borrowers to leave SAVE and enter repayment, particularly those for whom an increased loan balance was judged to impact their ultimate total repayment amount. For the majority, that accrued interest is purely psychological as payments will be based on income and be finished at the completion of the applicable forgiveness period regardless. However, the harm is material for some borrowers in the following ways:

- Increased loan balance for anyone that decides to pay off their loans without using forgiveness, i.e. by standard repayment plan or lump sum.

- Increased loan balance increasing the cap on monthly payments under IBR (or PAYE).

- Increased amount forgiven under IDR plans resulting in increased tax bills

Thus, eliminating the interest that has accrued since August 1, 2025 for SAVE borrowers, or at least the amount in excess of what their SAVE payments would have been during this period, would psychologically comfort many borrowers without any actual reduction in revenue and prevent undue material harm to a few.

ED is already inundated with Buyback requests. Borrowers are depending on this program being there for them in the future but are anxious about it in the setting of the backlog. Because the SAVE forbearance has affected millions of borrowers in the same way, it would be inefficient to process the Buyback requests for this situation individually. I suggest informing these borrowers that the entire SAVE forbearance may be bought back at a monthly rate that is the lesser of their IDR payment entering the forbearance or leaving it, unless they wish to submit additional income information for a lesser amount. Then, perhaps, the process could be automated and these borrowers would be able to elect to make the Buyback payment soon, before the 10 years has been reached, with the appropriate warnings.

The proposed rule puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. Dear Mr. Pentony: 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed 2023 recreational Gulf of Maine 
(GOM) haddock measures. As a partner in sustainable management of our shared stocks, the Massachusetts 
Division of Marine Fisheries (MA DMF) intends to continue to enact complementary recreational groundfish 
measures in the Gulf of Maine. However, MA DMF has concerns about NOAA Fisheries’ proposal to adopt 
split mode regulations in the recreational GOM haddock fishery, in stark juxtaposition to both the 
Recreational Advisory Panel and Council recommendation for a singular set of regulations across all modes. 
 
No recreational management action is complete without a discussion about catch estimate uncertainty. 
While the Marine Recreational Information Program (MRIP) was designed to provide precise coast-wide 
estimates of recreational catch, managers are increasingly faced with demands for variable angler access by 
season, by mode, and by state. However, the precision level of estimates often does not support such 
surgical management measures. Moreover, non-uniform measures impede our ability to evaluate catch and 
the impact of rule-changes in the aggregate which provides for the best precision levels. 
 
Disparate bag limits and minimum sizes can also create a situation for rampant confusion, misunderstood 
rules, and at worse illegal fishing. Non-compliance, whether willful or accidental, increases management 
uncertainty. Split mode management is not a robust regulatory approach given the realities of our joint 
enforcement resources and that this particular stock is able to be filleted at sea. Most charter and private 
boat anglers fillet their haddock at-sea and therefore whole fish are unavailable for measurement by a 
shore-based sampler. Even if implementation was perfect, the catch estimates provided by MRIP to 
subsequently evaluate split mode performance are likely to feature unacceptably high PSEs. 
 
MRIP does not provide robust length-frequency analysis by mode to evaluate the proposed split mode 
approach. This is due to a differential in observations quantity skewed towards the for-hire mode and in 
particular headboats. From 2019-2021, observations on headboats appeared about 4 times higher than on 
charter boats and about double the observations on private vessels. In 2022, observations were almost

 
2 
 
equal across for-hire modes, driven primarily by an increase in charter observations in NH. For a species with 
a high bag limit, like haddock, the number of length observations can be somewhat misleading. For example, 
in Maine the mean length of haddock caught by private vessels was much larger than other modes in 2020 
and 2021, but this is likely because these fish came from 1-2 intercepts, where the effect of a few large 
haddock could skew the results. 
 
Utilizing the available scientific observations nonetheless, MRIP data suggest there is very little difference in 
size distribution of landed haddock across modes. This is not surprising given anglers generally use similar 
tackle and fish in similar areas (i.e., no shore-based catch), reducing the potential size selectivity.

Scientists have estimated that the forest accounts for about 8 percent of the carbon sequestered by all national forests. Protecting the Tongass from old-growth logging will not only preserve that capacity, but avoid releasing carbon currently sequestered in its trees. Re: Event Data Recorders Proposed Rule, Agency/Docket Number: Docket No.

Dear Administrator Cliff, 

On June 22, 2022, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) published in the 

Federal Register a Proposed Rule on Event Data Recorders (the “Proposed Rule’). The National 

Association of Mutual Insurance Companies (NAMIC) welcomes the opportunity to respond to this 

request for comments. 

NAMIC is the largest property/casualty insurance trade group with a diverse membership of more 

than 1,500 local, regional, and national member companies, including seven of the top 10 

property/casualty insurers in the United States. NAMIC members lead the personal lines sector 

representing 55 percent of the auto market. Through our advocacy programs we promote public 

policy solutions that benefit NAMIC member companies and the policyholders they serve and foster 

greater understanding and recognition of the unique alignment of interests between management and 

policyholders of mutual companies. 

The Proposed Rule would amend NHTSA regulations regarding Event Data Recorders (EDRs) to 

extend the EDR recording period for timed data metrics from 5 seconds of pre-crash data at a 

frequency of 2 Hz to 20 seconds of pre-crash data at a frequency of 10 Hz (i.e., increase from 2 

samples per second to 10 samples per second). The Proposed Rule begins the process of fulfilling 

the mandate of the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act), Public Law 119-14 

(Dec. 4, 2015), to establish the appropriate recording period in NHTSA's EDR regulation. 

As detailed in the Proposed Rule, Section 24303 of the FAST Act requires NHTSA to conduct a 

study “to determine the amount of time event data recorders installed in passenger motor vehicles 

should capture and record for retrieval [of] vehicle-related data in conjunction with an event in order

 
to provide sufficient information to investigate the cause of motor vehicle crashes,” and to submit a 

report containing the findings of this study to Congress. Further, within two years of submitting this 

report to Congress, NHTSA “shall promulgate regulations to establish the appropriate period during 

which event data recorders installed in passenger motor vehicles may capture and record for retrieval 

vehicle-related data to the time necessary to provide accident investigators with vehicle-related 

information pertinent to crashes involving such motor vehicles.” 

Based upon a study to determine the frequency with which EDRs with a 5-second recording duration 

fail to record a sufficient duration of pre-crash data to determine crash causation for rear-end, 

intersection, and roadway departure crashes, NHTSA concluded that in many cases, the 5-second 

recording duration may not be sufficient to determine the factors that led to the crash or the pre-crash 

actions taken by the driver to avoid the collision, meaning that EDRs currently would not always 

provide investigators crash-related information that could assist in the determination of crash 

causation. 

Based upon a further study to determine an appropriate EDR recording duration to provide crash 

investigators with sufficient data to determine crash causation, the results of this analysis supported 

that a recording time of 15 seconds would capture approximately 50 percent of the total intersection 

event time, and 18.6 seconds would capture 90 percent. The study concluded that a recording time of 

20 seconds would capture approximately 99 percent of the total intersection event time. Based on the 

studies, NHTSA believes it is reasonable to propose requiring a minimum of 20 seconds of pre-crash 

data.

We at the North Shore Land Alliance urge you to allow this outstanding work to proceed, so that disease-resistant seedlings can be planted across the 200 million acres the American chestnut once thrived on, including at several of our Long Island (where the blight likely started!) nature preserves, home of a number of mother trees.

I believe that opening of the Upper Kenai River and Russian River corridors to firearm use and hunting will create a lot of user conflict and the potential for human injury and or death. The Upper Kenai River has seen a dramatic increase in use by the general public especially sport fishing during my 18 years of guiding. You will find people fishing in the Kenai National Wildlife refuge ever month of the year. The Upper Kenai River use to close to all fishing after October 31st until June 11th. The regulations changed and now the river is open from June 11 thru April 30th .The amount of users fishing in October thru December has dramatically increased along with use during the Spring months of February March and April. Having large caliber rifles being discharged along the river corridor while other users groups are using the river could be a lethal combination.

The regulations have opened a brown bear season in areas on the Kenai Peninsula. The Kenai National Wildlife Refuge allowed brown bear hunting the first year of this opening. This created numerous user group conflicts on the Upper Kenai River.. Numerous bears were shot right off the highway, and on the Upper Kenai river banks and the shores of Skilak Lake. There were numerous conflicts between hunters fisherman and tourists during this time. For example there were 3 groups of tourists taking pictures of a bear from the Kenai River Bridge on the Sterling highway. A hunter also stopped on the bridge and proceeded to shoot the bear from right off the bridge. Another group rafting down the Upper Kenai River were floating by a brown bear taking pictures when someone unseen in the bushes shot the bear right in front of them, what if the hunter missed or there was a ricochet that would have hit one of the rafters? What if someone is hunting bear on the Russian River, shoots at a bear but only injuries it and it runs off. Meanwhile a group of hikers is enjoying the Russian River boardwalk or a hike to the Russian River Falls. They come across the bear who is injured and very upset who then mauls a members of the hiking party? Are these the types of conflicts that we want to have within the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge? The KNWR stopped participating in this hunt after that first year. Reopening the refuge to Brown Bear hunting will create major user group conflicts again. 

The surrounding Chugach National Forest still allows brown bear hunting. The study before the bear hunting opening stated that they estimated the Kenai Peninsula brown bear population to be around 650 bears. The study also concluded that the Brown bears have a large range and go back an forth between the Chugach National Forest land and Kenai National Wildlife Land. They allocated 70 bears a season for hunting or for defense of life or property. They have met or exceeded 70 bears a year since that regulation change. I believe that open of more brown bear hunting in the Kenai National Wildlife Refuge could decimate the current stock of bears do to over harvesting or from a population crash once there are not enough bears to sustain the population.. 

There has been a dramatic decrease in the amount of bears in the Upper Kenai River and Russian River corridors since bear hunting has been instituted. We would not want to lose such an amazing species do to over harvesting or from thinning the bears out to much so that the population crashes. We have already seen what happened to brown bears in the lower 48, lets learn from our mistakes and not allow that to happen in Alaska. The Kenai National Wildlife Refuges mission has been to protect the wildlife of the refuge first and foremost. Lets not forget this mission and make mistakes

Diseases (NLRAD) to further strengthen the country’s ability to detect, respond to and control animal 

diseases. 

1. Notifiable diseases in wildlife: This proposal does not include the reporting of notifiable diseases in 

wildlife. However, the occurrence of notifiable diseases and emerging diseases in wildlife should be 

addressed within the NLRAD because disease can be bi-directionally transmitted at the wildlife-

livestock interface. Recognizing that B. abortus is endemic in elk and bison in the Greater Yellowstone 

Area, B. suis is endemic in feral swine populations, and that Bovine Tuberculosis is endemic in the 

Modified Accredited Zone in Michigan, it is suggested that these and other endemic notifiable 

diseases should be considered as “Monitored” in wildlife especially when reservoirs of a notifiable 

disease are determined to exist in wildlife within a State. We believe that all domestic animal disease 

control and eradication programs should be under the direction and supervision of veterinarians, 

especially if a wildlife specialist is not readily available. Any listed disease found in wildlife should be 

reported to APHIS and the state animal health official using the same protocol as would be followed 

for reporting domestic animal disease. 

2. Timing of reporting: We recommend inclusion of an unambiguous written definition of “immediate 

reporting” of a notifiable disease, such as “within twelve (12) hours of a suspected FAD or knowledge

12.75 million men and women, contributes $2.33 trillion to the U.S. economy annually, has the 
largest economic impact of any major sector, and accounts for more than three-quarters of all 
private-sector research and development in the nation. The NAM is the voice of the manufacturing 
community and the leading advocate for a policy agenda that helps manufacturers compete in 
the global economy and create jobs across the United States. 
Duty drawback has long been a critical tool to promote U.S. exports to grow U.S. 
manufacturing, well-paying jobs, and stronger communities across the United States. Given the 
importance of these goals, Congress has repeatedly expanded the scope of duty drawback from 
its origins in the Tariff Act of 1789. Most notably for the manufacturing sector, Congress expanded 
drawback to include “substitution” drawback as part of the Omnibus Trade and Tariff Act of 1984.1 
In doing so, Congress substantially boosted the export promotion benefit for manufacturers in the 
United States by enabling manufacturers to claim a drawback for “any duty, tax, or fee” paid on 
an imported product when it exports a similar product manufactured in the United States. 
Congress has subsequently clarified the substitution drawback rule in 2004 and most recently as 
part of the Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015, Pub. L. No. 114-125, § 906, 
130 Stat. 122, 226–234 (TFTEA), to make these provisions usable by all industries. 
The full implementation of a robust duty drawback program, including substitution 
drawback for all industries and “any duty, tax, or fee” not only promotes the growth of exports, it 
incentivizes export-oriented U.S. and foreign direct investment that supports and expands U.S.-
based manufacturing production and well-paying American jobs. The importance of export 
promotion for the manufacturing sector cannot be understated. Exports have helped drive major 
growth in U.S. manufacturing. Approximately half of the record $2.33 trillion in output is exported.

We also believe that any new regulation or standard should be carefully considered for

Advisors, has reviewed the National Marine Fisheries Service’s (NMFS) proposed amendment to 
regulations implementing the Atlantic Large Whale Take Reduction Plan (ALWTRP) to expand the 
boundaries of the Massachusetts Restricted Area (MRA) to include the so-called ‘wedge’ area 
between the MRA and Massachusetts State Waters Trap/Pot Closure (MSC) (88 Fed. Reg. 63917; 18 
September 2023). The Commission agrees with NMFS’s assessment that this rulemaking is 
consistent with the exception set forth under section 101(b) of the right whale provisions of the 
Consolidated Appropriations Act 2023 (Pub. Law 117-73) because it pertains to an extension of a 
final emergency rule affecting the lobster and Jonah crab fisheries that was in place at the time the 
rule was enacted. 
Due to the presence of significant numbers of North Atlantic right whales during the late 
winter and spring in and around Cape Cod Bay, Massachusetts, the MRA and MSC are closed to 
lobster and other pot/trap fishing from February 1 to April 30 and May 15, respectively. The Federal 
Register notice and associated draft Environmental Assessment (DEA) provide detailed 
documentation of the ― 
1. critical conservation status and extinction risk of the North Atlantic right whale, 
2. presence of significant numbers of right whales in Cape Cod Bay, Massachusetts Bay, 
and the ‘wedge’ from February through April, and 
3. presence of high densities of fixed-gear buoys in the ‘wedge’ during the same period, 
 
thus creating substantial co-occurrence of pot/trap gear and right whales, and therefore significant 
entanglement risk. 
 
The DEA provides strong support for the need to close the ‘wedge’ at the same time that 
the MRA and MSC are closed, and offers two alternatives for the closure, in addition to the ‘no 
action’ alternative. NMFS’s preferred alternative (Alternative 2) would close the ‘wedge’ from 
February 1 to April 30. NMFS estimated this would reduce the risk of mortality and serious injury 
due to entanglement relative to all pot/trap fisheries in the Massachusetts portion of Lobster 
Management Area 1 (LMA1) by 13 to 17 percent, with the range reflecting the degree to which gear 
would be relocated and fished elsewhere or brought ashore, respectively. Alternative 3 would, in 
addition to closing the ‘wedge’ over the same period, close areas north of the MRA and the ‘wedge’

DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002 - Public Comment Opposing Proposed Rule
I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. The FSAs purpose is that detained immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law.

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This proposed regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. The traumatizing effects of detention on children has been amply documented, causing considerable and lasting harm on childrens physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable and unnecessary because the government can continue to release detained immigrant families under safeguards such as ankle bracelets.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed removal of state licensing requirements for DHS facilities holding immigrant would also allow the government to bypass state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children and without adequate oversight of these facilities, detained children will be further traumatized by inadequate facilities.

ore than 30 years ago, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and its partners began efforts to reintroduce the endangered red wolf into the wild in North Carolina. While many of the captive-bred wolves adapted well to a wild environment, the program faced unforeseen challenges, including hybridization of wolves with coyotes and conflicts with humans. After initially increasing, the population plateaued and then declined. Today, only approximately 35 wild wolves remain, with a further 200-plus wolves in captive breeding facilities.

In an effort to adaptively manage to the challenges confronting the red wolf, the Service is proposing a rule that would remove management efforts from existing private lands and instead focus continuing efforts on certain public lands in Hyde and Dare counties, North Carolina. The new proposed rule is based on a comprehensive four-year evaluation of the nonessential experimental population (NEP) of red wolves designated under section 10(j) of the Endangered Species Act.

By restricting management to Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge and the Dare County Bombing Range, we will ensure we can better reduce external threats and monitor the environments surrounding these wild wolves, said Greg Sheehan, the Services Principal Deputy Director. A recent Species Status Assessment informed us that past strategies were not effectively leading to recovery, so we believe that a concerted effort in a managed area will help.

The Services role outside the proposed management area would be limited to providing technical assistance if requested by landowners.

Under this new proposal, there would be no prohibitions on the take of red wolves on non-federal lands outside the NEP area, provided the take occurs in conjunction with an otherwise lawful activity.

I read the comments from the industry, and I can understand the position. The issues as I read them are; distance learning, competency based training, and eliminating national passing norms. 

The distance learning issue the FAA has to address the comments appropriately, and I have no further comment. My concern is that what the commentators wanted to allow what would be a giveaway to large chain schools. The commenter implied that there would only be one manual for all with a single CHDO office approval. The FAA response was to have still local CHDO manage and approve each separately, which I feel would maintain the current level of oversite required. 

Eliminating national passing norms would be a bad idea in that there is not another reliable and consistent method that could be used to determine the quality of instruction. One solution for passing norms is not to publish the FAA written questions. Dear Assistant Director, Office of Policy Debbie Seguin,

You have to be out of your mind if you think Americans want refugees held indefinitely in cages or think that that makes us safer in some way. We need immigrants in this country as much as we always have. Why are you making it more difficult for people who are fleeing for their own safety to come here and start a new life? Indefinite detention for what is essentially a misdemeanor is wrong and is a human rights abuse. This is not how this country is supposed to be.

I write in opposition to this Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) proposed rule that would allow this administration to undermine the current protections outlined by the 1997 Flores settlement. The Flores decision sets clear guidelines that direct the government to reunite children with a parent or relative without delay and provides standards and protections for children while in government custody. The proposed rule seeks to weaken or remove those protections and allow children to be jailed indefinitely. 

Among many other concerning changes, this rule would:
- Give the administration the power to self-license and implement standards at detention centers at a time when reports that show that DHS is not capable of maintaining clean, humane and safe detention centers currently.
- Weaken protections for children as they undergo processing in detention facilities and make release from detention and reunification with family members a more difficult process. DHS would have increased authority to change the rules regarding when and how children can be reunified and with whom. DHS and HHS are also given the authority to declare an emergency and completely suspend protections for children.
- Reverses a child�s right to a bond hearing and instead creates an agency-run administrative process that poses threats to due process

This rule outlines a system where an avowedly anti-immigrant administration, responsible for separating over 2,000 children from their parents, is able to create and change the rules of immigrant enforcement, due process, and the already deplorable detention conditions for children as they see fit. These changes are unconscionable, inhumane and would directly harm children and families who have come to the United States to seek a better life. 

I am morally opposed to jailing children and families and believe that our government should focus on keeping families together, alternatives to detention and full due process under the law.

Sincerely,

Dear DOT - My home based travel agent business, my livelihood, depends on clear terms, conditions, and doing right by my customers, suppliers and myself. However, I am VERY concerned about the wording in the proposed rule regarding airline ticket refunds. At NO point does my agency ever take money from clients for airline tickets. My agency acts as the 'booking agent' only, and no money passes into my accounts for this transaction. Therefore, it is critical that the wording is clear for 'Ticket Agents' - this is NOT a travel agent!

On behalf of my business and the more than 160,000 Americans who work at travel agencies in the U.S., I urge you to remove from this proposed rule the provision that would require "ticket agents" to issue refunds to consumers for cancelled or significantly changed airline flights, regardless of whether the agency controls the funds in question. 

In air bookings, it is exceedingly rare for a travel agency to be in possession of consumer funds for any meaningful period of time and thus be in a position to issue a prompt refund. It would be difficult if not impossible for me to pay requested refunds when I don't have access to the funds - not to mention profoundly unfair. 

If adopted in the final rule, this proposal could prove extremely disruptive to the airline distribution system because the obligation to issue refunds in these circumstances represents a financial risk that many agencies may be unwilling to accept. That, in turn, would deprive consumers of the valuable consolatory services travel advisors provide and negatively impact a critical distribution channel for the airlines. 

I urge the Department in the strongest possible terms to eliminate from this proposal any obligation of a ticket agent to issue a consumer refund when the agency does not possess or have control over the funds in question. 

Thank you for considering my views on this important topic.

Hello, my name is Ryan Furrow and I am currently a student at Virginia Tech in the Aerospace Engineering department. As a current student, but mostly as someone who is about to enter the professional engineering world, I am writing this comment to express some concerns about the V2V communication rule that is being proposed. 

The main issue that I see with the V2V system is the fact that your personal data my not be completely safe. I know that in the rule they state that "V2V devices would transmit safety information in only a limited geographical range" but what kind of range does this entail? This range could be 500 feet which would only allow the vehicle to see the immediate surroundings but it could also mean a range of a couple of miles. As this limited geographical range gets larger and larger there are more people who are in that range and could be affected by this system. One example is in the video on the NHTSA website that shows a couple of bikers within this range. It does not state whether or not these bikers are affected but they very easily could be and it could happen without their knowledge. This would be a severe breach of privacy and they would have no way of consenting because they would have no way of knowing that the vehicle that was next to them was equipped with the V2V system.

The next major concern that I can see is who would have access to the data that the V2V system creates. Would it be the car manufacturers, car dealerships, yourself, or maybe even the government? There can be pros and cons to each but until it is known exactly where this data is going and what that entity is doing with it then this is a really big problem. Not every consumer that has a car with a V2V system equipped in it may agree to what is being done with that data and there may be no way to opt out of this. However, there is some trade off going on because if you want a car with a V2V system equipped then they may have to forfeit some of their privacy rights. 

The third thing that seems to jump out at me is what kind of cars will have this system, where will they be able to drive, and what kind of testing has been done on them. The main thing about this is whether or not this V2V system will be exclusive to new cars that are coming out or will it be adaptable to some of the older cars that are on the road. Also, with this new technology coming out it may not be safe to have some cars with the V2V system and others without it on the same road because the ones that do not have it have no way of controlling whether or not someone else has it. This can become a problem because it could end of causing accidents or be a hindrance to the flow of traffic. 

In regards to the testing aspect of this V2V system, I think there needs to be extensive tests that occur both in a controlled environment and out in the public. There is no way of knowing whether or not this would truly work without fully testing the product. I think initially it needs to be done in a controlled environment so that everything can be looked at carefully and if something happens it can be handled safely and efficiently. However, there eventually needs to be public testing because something may always work in a controlled environment but the true test is when unknown variables are input and you can see how that system reacts to those. 

Overall, I think that a V2V communication system can end up being a beneficial thing that can help the safety of cars. However, many issues still need to be addressed before this can be something that is widely used by everyone.

“In the presence” of BSAT is ambiguous and should be defined. This could mean 
a torn glove while working with agent in the biosafety cabinet, or it could mean 
safety glasses slipping down one’s nose while someone else is working with 
agent in a biosafety cabinet across the room without incident. It could include 
fully contained BSAT (e.g. docked ventilated cages, frozen inventory samples) or 
it could only apply to “open vessels”. It could include fully contained BSAT only 
if an individual is within a certain distance of the BSAT. As written, this 
statement does not provide clarity. 
(5) the failure of biosafety procedures such that it is reasonably anticipated that a select 
agent or toxin was outside of containment. 
“Outside of containment” is also ambiguous and should be defined. 
“Containment” can be used to mean an immediate primary containment vessel 
or to mean the containment envelope of a laboratory suite into non-
containment space. The industry uses the terms in both contexts and, if clarity 
is the goal, the use of the word “containment” should be clear in every instance.

 
These suggested statements do not clarify what a release is, they redefine it. The SAR exist for a 
very specific purpose – to prevent bad actors from obtaining agents that could be used as 
biological weapons. The SAR currently define a reportable release in 73.19(b): “…a release of an 
agent or toxin causing occupational exposure or release of a select agent or toxin outside of the 
primary barriers of the biocontainment area”. This describes the big picture of what the SAR is 
for: Ensuring agent is not released into the environment or into the hands of someone not 
authorized to possess it. People should not be exposed so that they do not release the agent 
from containment within their own bodies. Of course we don’t want our workers to fall ill, but

I am an avid birder and conservationist, and a strong supporter of the United States National Wildlife Refuge System. I buy Duck Stamps regularly and encourage other birders to do so. I also salute the historical and ongoing contribution of hunters to conserving our wildlife heritage, including game and non-game species, and view members of the sporting community as allies. 

That said, I have serious misgivings about this "secondary species" proposal, especially as stated. What I find most troubling is that there appears to have been no study done to support the notion that this approach, if adopted, will actually increase sales and thus acres of habitat conserved. And acres of habitat conserved should indeed be the bottom line, not what any of us, however impassioned and well-intentioned, thinks or feels about this proposal.

I can't imagine any for-profit company taking such a chance and seriously tinkering with one of its most successful and beloved products without doing significant market research first. Even then, mistakes can be made, sometimes on a spectacular "New Coke" scale. 

Before this change is made, it should be tested on actual and potential Stamp buyers: hunters, birders, other outdoor recreationists, and stamp collectors. What is the likely impact on total sales? Is that impact worth it?

Another approach that should be tested is creating additional stamps, modeled on the Duck Stamp, but specifically targeting different user groups such as birders, anglers, and other wildlife fans. Clearly, there is an appetite for this approach among many non-hunting refuge supporters, but again, would likely sales justify the expense of setting up such a program?

Until this very basic legwork is done, I don't see a good justification to add a secondary species to the Stamp. I believe many of the intentions here are good, even excellent; I just would like to see a little bit of data to back things up.

I greatly appreciate that the Service is trying to recognize and attract birders and other refuge supporters, and to increase acres of habitat conserved. I also very much appreciate the opportunity to comment here.

Thank you for your hard work on behalf of our birds and wildlife.

On behalf of the Hep B United coalition and the undersigned 28 organizations, thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the draft CDC recommendations for hepatitis B screening and testing. We appreciate and commend CDC’s leadership in this undertaking to update and expand hepatitis B screening and testing recommendations. 

Overall, we are pleased to see the expansion of hepatitis B screening to a universal recommendation for adults 18 and older. Additionally, we strongly support the recommendation to provide hepatitis B screening with the 3-part panel for all adults including pregnant persons, providing a more complete picture of potential infection and clear steps for clinical management. The addition of risk factors to include persons currently or formerly incarcerated, with current or past STIs or multiple sex partners, with current or past HCV infection and anyone who requests a hepatitis B test, regardless of disclosure of risk, are reflective of the current trajectory of hepatitis B epidemiology in the United States and will be supportive of the work of hepatitis B service providers to reach all highly impacted populations. We believe these new recommendations will greatly increase access to hepatitis B screening and testing, removing barriers such as individual and community stigma and anxiety related to hepatitis B risk factors, and improve testing rates.

Additionally, we appreciate the timeliness of the expanded screening recommendations to align with the recent decision by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to recommend all adults aged 19-59 years be vaccinated against hepatitis B infection. We believe it is critical to coordinate clinical guidance for screening and vaccination. We believe screening for hepatitis B infection, with the 3-part panel, is primary and essential to finding susceptible persons and preventing new infections and agree that offering a first dose of the vaccine at the same time as screening to the hardest to reach populations is beneficial.

While the key updates to the hepatitis B screening and testing recommendations are clear, we believe certain components of the recommendations can be strengthened to avoid any confusion and provide health care providers the most specific guidance for implementation. We offer the following suggestions, listed by section titles of the draft recommendations document, for consideration.

adverse economic impacts coastal fishing communities and compromise sustained participation
of those communities. 
HMS tournaments that are dedicated to, or include bluefin tuna represent a significant
financial contribution to their respective coastal communities. The Casco Bay Bluefin Bonanza
alone contributes approximately $300,000 to its community annually. It is one of at least 7 other
bluefin tournaments in the New England region. That means actions that affect these tournaments
could have adverse economic impacts on a $2 million contribution to coastal fishing
communities.
Furthermore, these impacts would be additive to what has already occurred as a result of
previous imposition of RFDs that include Friday and Saturday - days that traditionally represent
the foundation of tournaments dates. The tournaments were forced to adapt, in some cases
experiencing negative financial impact. All of these tournaments are scheduled a year or more in
advance. Forcing them to alter or modify schedules or postpone or cancel events because of a
change in the RFD schedule at this point would necessarily represent a significant adverse
economic impact not only on the tournaments, but on their respective fishing communities. 
2) I do not support extending RFDs through the December subquota period and I offer the
following rationale.
The currently existing framework for December has been deemed consistent with
conservation requirements and management objectives for the fishery, but changing it to add
RFDs in December does not promote the safety of human life at sea. Participation in the fishery
is at its lowest level. Adding RFDs at this time would not substantially extend fishing
opportunities through this relatively minor portion of the relevant General category time periods
and the fishing season overall. Nor would it have any substantive impact on supply chains and
distribution as supply is low while demand is high due to higher fat content. Meanwhile, weather
in December can be highly variable and often dangerous. Restrictions on fishing days at this time
could limit or prevent access to the resource, and would encourage fishermen to take greater risks
by fishing during hazardous conditions.

the following rationale.

extend fishing opportunities through a greater portion of the relevant General category time
periods and the fishing season overall, consistent with management objectives for the fishery.
These restrictions have already been imposed in traditional bluefin fishing areas of the northeast.

March period and the relatively recent southeast fishery. Furthermore it would represent a more
fair and equitable allocation of the resource among residents of different states.

Automotive aerodynamics play a large role in energy efficiency, and when it comes to mirrors specifically, they require constant adjustment and add drag to the vehicle. They also are limited in their field of view.

Camera-based systems can be used to improve not only the aerodynamics of a vehicle, but also can be strategically placed in the vehicle so as to eliminate traditional blind spots. A fender-mounted camera looking down the side of the car and out at a 60 degree field of view eliminates side blind spots inherently. This also benefits the task of parking, making curbs and ground markings much easier to see in relation to the vehicle.

Cameras can also benefit from high dynamic range, offering the driver a clearer picture at night than mirrors alone can. Tesla's Autopilot cameras have much better night vision than any human being does.

Another benefit: screens showing each camera feed can be placed closer to the driver, requiring less "head on a swivel" action for monitoring their surroundings.

Private citizen response to the USDA ANPR: Labeling of Meat or Poultry Products Comprised of or Containing Cultured Animal Cells

Docket FSIS-2020-0036

October 15, 2021

 

Dear Sir/Madam,

 

I am writing in response to the ANPR related to the labeling of cultivated (cell-based) meat and poultry products published on Sept 3, 2021 (FR86.169). First, thanks for taking the time to ask for public opinion on this new technology. These products have the potential to significantly reduce the adverse effects of industrial farming while even reducing the cost of animal products. 

This is critical -- as the world population rises, high protein food alternatives should be a core focus of the USDA. Cultivated meat and poultry products will in time significantly supplement traditional meat and poultry products, so this won't displace the existing industry and shouldn't be seen as threatening. 

Regarding how these meats should be labeled, I support using the term ‘cultivated’ for these new products as it is sufficient to describe and to convey meaningful information to consumers like myself. For example, ‘cultivated beef’ or ‘cultivated chicken’ is a good word to distinguish these new products from conventional slaughtered meat products. I also support the use of cultivated beef or cultivated chicken in ingredient labeling as this would be seen as definitely different from traditional meats for consumers.

I feel it would be inappropriate and cast a negative light over this new industry if terms like ‘fake meat’, ‘synthetic meat’ or other obviously demeaning terms were approved by the FSIS.

Finally, the USDA should make it easy to use these new meat and poultry products in traditional foods. If regulations and standards need to be modified to facilitate these new ingredients the USDA should put enough resources into these needs to prevent unnecessary delays in getting these products to consumers.

Best,
Dan Sachs

I am writing in support of the US Department of Agriculture's proposed Horse Protection Act rulemaking, which was published in the Federal Register on August 21, 2023 (Docket No. APHIS-2022-0004). These reforms would do much to curb the rampant and horrific abuses associated with "soring." An upgrade to the HPA is desperately needed as horses continue to suffer under a status quo that allows that industry to police itself despite the obvious conflict of interest. 

According to the USDA's own review of data in recent years, there remains a persistent and vast discrepancy between violations found by industry-appointed inspectors vs. USDA inspectors (who attend only a small proportion of shows). Unfortunately, it is clear that the industry continues to turn a blind eye to evidence of soring.

The nearly finalized 2017 HPA regulations, which the prior administration froze and which the USDA moved to formally withdraw in July, were widely supported by the public and lawmakers in Congress, as well as by animal protection, veterinary, and major equine industry groups. I am heartened to see that rather than simply discard the hard work that went into developing the 2017 regulations, the department is proposing to implement a similar rule that prohibits ankle chains and other "action devices" associated with soring and eliminates the failed industry-run self-enforcement system.

The HPA rule could be strengthened, however, by including spotted saddle horses in addition to the covered Tennessee walking and racking horses, since this breed is also victimized by soring. A clear prohibition on the heavy weighted shoes that are used to cause pain is also needed. Furthermore, the USDA should reevaluate its proposal to delay the ban on hoof pads for 270 days after finalizing the regulations. As the proposed rule states, pads can induce pain by "caus[ing] a horse's foot to strike the ground at an unnatural angle." And USDA "inspections at flat-shod events in which horses do not wear pads and action devices rarely find soring violations," further underscoring the importance of implementing this ban without delay. Finally, the proposed rule appears to allow show management to select which USDA-authorized inspector(s) will examine horses; further clarity is needed concerning this point and how it will work in practice. Ideally, the department should directly assign USDA-licensed-and-trained inspectors to shows.

Congress enacted the Endangered Species Act (ESA) for three purposes: to conserve

agreements.1 The strength of the ESA was well-expressed by U.S. Supreme Court Justice Burger 

in the seminal ESA case of Tennessee Valley Authority v. Hill in his statement that “[t]he plain 

intent of Congress in enacting this statute was to halt and reverse the trend toward species 

extinction, whatever the cost.”2 

Because the law is designed to prevent the extinction of species, and the science of extinction is 

not always certain, the ESA takes a precautionary approach to the conservation of threatened 

and endangered species. This can be seen in the terminology of key provisions of the ESA, 

which use risk assessment rather than certainty as operative mechanisms. For example, an 

endangered species is one that is “in danger of” extinction, while a threatened species is one 

that is “likely to” become an endangered species.3 Federal actions cannot proceed if they are 

“likely to” jeopardize the continued existence of any listed species or result in the destruction

that federal agencies implement measures to protect listed species and their habitat even if 

there is not full scientific consensus on the cause and effect of covered actions on listed species 

or their habitat.

the benefit of the doubt in favor of listed species. As detailed below, the three proposals fail to

The Association of Transportation Safety Information Professionals (ATSIP) thanks the National Highway 

Traffic Safety Administration for the opportunity to comment on a revision of the Traffic Records 

Program Assessment Advisory (Advisory). 

ATSIP members include data collectors, managers, and users and many come from State Highway Safety 

Offices (SHSO) so are directly affected by the Advisory. The current assessment process, like the former 

process, has both positives and areas that could use improvement. 

The iterative nature of the online assessment allows for the assessor to ask for clarification and provide 

guidance to the State. This process gives both sides opportunity for communication. It would be an 

improvement for States to be able to skip questions in the second and third rounds that didn’t “Meet 

Ideal” but the State has nothing further to add. 

As assessors, we applaud NHTSA’s decision to allow equivalent evidence as a move in the right direction. 

States sometimes have documentation that serves the same purpose but is not identified as such from 

the requirements in the Advisory. Another advantage to the current system is the use of more than one 

assessor per module who must reach consensus on the ratings. 

One module that should be changed is Injury Surveillance. This section is over-burdensome and out of 

line with the other sections. Although Traffic Records includes all the systems surveyed in the Advisory, 

DOT’s Performance Measures are based on Crash Data. It seems unrealistic to have 31% of the 

questions pertain to Injury and only 11% to Crash. 

The final report received by the State could be made more useful. The former assessment process often 

produced dozens of highly specific recommendations and was too much. The current version offers only 

generic recommendations that are not very useful. There is an opportunity here for middle ground. 

Many States miss the human interaction of the former process, but the current process gives assessors 

more time to be thoughtful in their assessments. Perhaps there is room for a hybrid assessment where 

the draft report is discussed in person with the State Stakeholders. 

States that put in the effort to provide detailed documentation are left with a very useful repository of 

information that can guide the Traffic Records Coordinating Committee to identify gaps and solidify 

improvement targets. 

As always, ATSIP and our members would like to help NHTSA through the process in any way we can. 

Kathleen Haney 

ATSIP President

include a requirement to remove the washers at the scheduled 3000 Hour Special Inspection for a detailed

As an Owner, Breeder and Exhibitor of the Tennessee Walking horse, for 35 years, I feel that experience is on my side to submit the following points about the TWH. There is no need to replace a law (HPA) that has done the job it was designed to do. The rule is just a method to insert animal rights beliefs into the law. This language has been rejected by Congress FOUR times. That should be the full answer, Congress said they do NOT see a need to enact any further changes. 
 
Tennessee Walking Horses and Racking Horses are already the most regulated breeds of show horses in the United States and in the past decade our compliance rates have consistently been above 90% each year.
 
The recently conducted study by the National Academies of Science, funded in part by USDA, pointed out the flaws in the inspection process as well as those persons conducting the inspections. In particular, the NAS found that the current scar rule is “unenforceable as written” and made suggestions with how to better enforce the scar rule. The USDA has not done those studies needed and has put forth a modified scar rule that will continue to permit arbitrary disqualifications of horses.
 
The current proposed rule is that it does not correctly evaluate the economic impacts. This rule would have devastating economic impacts and deem thousands of show horses virtually worth nothing as their show division would be eliminated. In addition, the impact on small businesses, which make up the majority of the show horse industry, would be devastating and leave thousands of people unemployed and faced with major economic hardships. 
 
In addition, the USDA is also proposing to eliminate industry Horse Industry Organizations and screen, train and authorize qualified persons to conduct inspections at horse shows. Currently, the USDA has been unable to secure qualified equine experts to conduct inspections as part of their system of using Veterinary Medical Officers. The American Association of Equine Practitioners and US Census Bureau has already pointed out the severe shortage of equine veterinarians that currently exists and is expected to worsen over the coming years. The USDA proposed rule ignores this fact and relies on a system that will be very difficult and expensive, if not impossible, to implement. The backbone of the show circuit for Tennessee Walking Horses and Racking Horses continues to be middle class Americans who show their horses in small communities, often at competitions hosted by local civic groups as a source of fundraising for various philanthropic initiatives. It is imperative that any regulations are capable of being carried out extensively at a variety of venues without being cost prohibitive or placing an unnecessary burden on competitions or exhibitors.

DNREC-DOW commends the goals of this rulemaking to update existing regulations to 
be more consistent with the statutory text of the Clean Water Act (CWA) and to support an 
efficient and predictable certification process that is consistent with the water quality protection

focus on the relationship between the water quality certification and the Coastal Zone 
Management Act (CZMA) federal consistency review processes. 
 
Scope of Review 
 
DNREC-DOW appreciates and supports the proposed return to the “activity as a whole” 
approach to scoping water quality certification review. Delaware relies on the Section 401 WQC 
process in addition to state regulatory authority to comprehensively protect and steward wetlands 
and subaqueous lands within the state.

 
Additionally, DNREC-DOW supports the proposed provision allowing certifying 
authorities to define the necessary information for a “request for certification” required for the 
section 401 review. This provides certifying agency the necessary data to better assess water 
quality impacts specific to the state. These proposed provisions will align the requirements of 
water quality certifications and federal consistency review processes, achieving shared statutory 
goals of efficient permitting and comprehensive resource conservation and management. 
 
DNREC-DOW supports the ability of the states to waive the requirement for a pre-filing 
meeting request. Delaware provides a pre-application consultation process through the joint 
permit process meeting. The final rule and accompanying guidance should make clear that states 
have the option to waive the requirement entirely for all projects, and the flexibility to adopt or 
modify applicable submission procedures to fit with existing state procedures, such as changing 
which agency should receive the request or allowing other existing pre-application consultation 
processes to fulfill the requirement.

We have a cow/calf operation including 120 cows, calves, 6 bulls and horses. We own private pastures joining Forrest and BLM land that we run our cattle on in the summer. We had to haul water to our herd last summer due to the drought. We supplied much needed water in amounts that not only supported out cattle but local wildlife as well. We saw evidence of Bear, Elk, deer, Moose, turkeys and large coyotes utilizing our water resources. We realized they need help as well.
Several years ago we had several what looked like very, very large coyotes eating our calves right as they were being born. We could not get close enough to confirm, but they sure looked like wolves. We are a small ranching family and depend on the sale of our calves each year to pay the ever increasing cost of ranching. 
 We support the EIS for wolves in Colorado to focus on the impacts of a statewide 10(j) status for the species. Alternative Concept 1 would provide this flexibility and allow for the best chance of success for the species and those communities and individuals who will inevitably experience negative impacts from the introduction. Only through impact-based management will Colorado be able to successfully balance the needs of wolves, prey species, and social/cultural/economic impacts. To allow for true impact-based management, wolves must be recognized as a non-essential, experimental population across the entire state. 

The 10(j) status will allow for the greatest range of management tools for Colorado Parks and Wildlife to ensure a healthy introduction of a species that has been absent from the range in Colorado for more than 75 years. This will help protect other sensitive species of interest to FWS that will bear the brunt of depredation from introduced wolves, including moose. And it will allow for close management of a species that will significantly impact individuals, businesses, and the communities that benefit from those businesses. 

The other proposed alternatives for introduction in Colorado will result in failure of the program and environmental and economic damage to the state. I urge the FWS to study the impacts of a statewide 10(j) designation for wolves introduced into Colorado.

market failure, where no such failure exists, would be an over reach by the Department. The

The proposed rule has serious problems.

The relationship between the excellence of the US and foreign students needs to be clearly stated and sufficiently supported by statistics and evidence. If foreign students stop coming to the US, how will it influence the academic institutions and cutting-edge technology, as mentioned by the proposal?

2. This rule disguises the incompetence of the department by blaming foreign students. With modern technology, especially the use of big data, locating a person can be extremely simple. Thank you for taking the time to read my comments. With regards to the USDA's proposed regulations, I have several concerns. These regulations: 

Fail to require a large enough space for birds to be able to fly, the most natural and fundamental behavior of almost all bird species. Failing to provide birds who fly with enough space to do so takes away much of what gives their lives meaning

They fail to prohibit mutilations, including pinioning (the surgical removal of the outermost bones in a bird’s wing, equivalent to removing a human hand, to prevent flight permanently, often performed without pain medication).

They fail to prohibit public contact with birds, including wrangling, mounting, and riding them, such as in ostrich racing.

They fail to prohibit or require a time limit on tethering birds, which severely restricts their mobility.

They fail to recognize parrots and other species as exotic animals, meaning that retail pet stores would be allowed to confine and sell them without obtaining a license or adhering to even the most basic welfare standards.

In terms of proposed changes that I would like to see, I suggest that the regulations: 

Require a large enough space for birds to be able to fly, which is the most natural and fundamental behavior of almost all bird species.

Prohibit licensees from mutilating birds, including pinioning, which is completely unnecessary and cruel.

Prohibit public contact with birds, including riding birds such as ostriches, which causes stress and puts them at risk of injury.

Prohibit the tethering of birds, which severely limits their mobility and doesn’t allow them to express normal, natural behavior.

Wild and exotic animals, including parrots and most other bird species, should never be kept or sold as pets. At the very least, the agency should include definitions of “pet animal” and “retail pet store” that explicitly provide all wild and exotic bird species with protection.

Thank you again for your time and consideration.

Discrimination against Deaf individuals is widespread and created a lot of frustration and anger, especially as it has a direct impact on their employment and life goals. During the past year, many individuals in the Deaf community have channeled their frustration by organizing through peaceful Deaf Grassroots Movement (DGM) rallies at state capitols in all 50 states. The need for DSAT is more apparent than ever before and the requests I have been getting for Deaf Self-Advocacy Training (DSAT) training has more than doubled recently.

While the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and other laws exist to provide Deaf individuals with rights more than 25 years ago, the impact that it has had on reducing discrimination has not been as effective as we hoped. The main reason for this is most individuals are not as knowledgeable about the existing laws and how to use them effectively to advocate for themselves. Entities and other individuals exploit this lack of knowledge and view Deaf individuals as a liability, creating barriers and hardship for Deaf individuals to achieve equal access. When discrimination happens, Deaf individuals often do not have a strong enough case to file a complaint because of a lack of documentation and not first exhausting all possible channels. DSAT training is necessary to help the ADA and other laws to become more effective by empowering consumers to use them better.

As one of the Deaf trainers for Deaf Self-Advocacy Training (DSAT), I can attest to the effectiveness of the curriculum in sharing tools and strategies that empower Deaf individuals to self-advocate more effectively. Bringing in Deaf trainers to facilitate DSAT has several benefits: 
1) creating a process for Deaf individuals to share both positive and negative experiences with self-advocacy, 
2) providing a safe space for individuals to heal from negative advocacy experiences and build self-esteem, 
3) sharing information about rights, resources, and support to achieve equal access to employment and other life goals, 
4) empowering individuals to decide for themselves what they need and to be assertive in asking for it, 
5) understanding strategies for interacting effectively with individuals, interpreting professionals, and the system to get what they need to have equal access to employment and other life goals, and 
6) building a network of Deaf individuals who can support each other when facing discrimination and other challenges for gaining equal access.

As a Deaf DSAT trainer, I provide consumer trainings and train the trainer seminars, which has become a means for me to earn income. I believe this would become a great opportunity for other trainers to have a way to use their skills to earn a living by becoming a specialist. However, from time to time, I also volunteer to provide free consumer trainings as a way to give back to the Deaf community. For example, last year I volunteered to provide consumer training at a school for the deaf to juniors, seniors and transitional students. The result has been more students being better self-advocates and having a greater role in transforming their own school to meet their needs. The expectation is that they will graduate from the school having tools they need to achieve access to employment and other life goals.
 
Funding for DSAT needs to continue because the Deaf community has witnessed significant transformation during the past 5 years with new ideas such as Deafhood and Deaf Gain that promote a positive view of being Deaf and the contributions Deaf people make to society. DSAT can benefit from further revisions that keep up with the more positive, transformative view of what it means to be Deaf. For example, Deaf trainers and consumers would increase their self-esteem and self-determination, which is necessary for effective self-advocacy, by changing a deficit view of themselves and viewing their place in humanity in an affirming way.

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

Forests are of major importance to human society, contributing several crucial 

ecosystem services. Biodiversity is suggested to positively inﬂuence multiple services 

but evidence from natural systems at scales relevant to management is scarce. Here, 

across a scale of 400,000 km2, we report that tree species richness in production 

forests shows positive to positively hump-shaped relationships with multiple ecosystem 

services. These include production of tree biomass, soil carbon storage, berry 

production and game production potential. For example, biomass production was 

approximately 50% greater with ﬁve than with one tree species. In addition, we show 

positive relationships between tree species richness and proxies for other biodiversity 

components. Importantly, no single tree species was able to promote all services, and 

some services were negatively correlated to each other. Management of production

We are graduate nursing students from San Diego State University who are all Registered Nurses
currently working at the bedside in acute and critical care settings. We are writing to express our
support of the proposed priority and requirements for training of interpreters for individuals who
are deaf or hard of hearing and individuals who are deafblind.
We feel the U.S. Department of Educations proposal of a priority and regulations for the training
of interpreters for the deaf, hard of hearing and deafblind addresses a critical need. As health care
professionals, we are familiar with the importance of precise translation of medical information.
Study has shown that deaf patients experience difficulties such as accessing healthcare and
communicating with staff related to interpreter barriers (Schniedewind et. al, 2020). Establishing
guidelines for initial and ongoing training for interpreters should be a priority in order to address
such barriers. Research has also shown that “trained ASL interpreters can help bridge the
disparity gap through improving provider-patient communication” (Hommes et. al, 2018). In our
experience and with evidence cited, it is clear that we need to address this problem and improve
the quality and availability of interpreter services. Higher quality interpreter services are going to
improve the patient experience and outcomes by fostering better communication between
patients and their providers not only in preventative care but also in acute care settings.
Currently, in the setting of COVID-19, we are seeing an impact in communication with our
patients who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deafblind. These issues include the elimination of
lip-reading as an adjunct to communication, and muffling of healthcare workers’ speech due to
PPE constraints. Further, due to masking, another critical method of communication, facial
expressions, is also extremely limited. This has only highlighted the need to address the quality
and availability of interpreter services to these individuals. In the already difficult situation of
needing healthcare, compromised communication between a patient and their medical team can
feel lonely, frustrating and frightening.
We agree that appropriately training and adequately preparing post-graduate interpreters to assist
with communication with patients who are deaf, hard of hearing, or deafblind will greatly
improve quality of life.
Once again, we all are in support of the proposed priority and requirements for training of
interpreters for individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, and deafblind.

This is Yasmin Ibrahim, MD, PhD. I work as a Public Health Program Manager at the Hepatitis B Foundation. 

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the draft CDC recommendations for hepatitis B screening and testing. I appreciate and commend CDC’s leadership in this undertaking to update and expand hepatitis B screening and testing recommendations. 

Overall, I am pleased to see the expansion of hepatitis B screening to a universal recommendation for adults 18 and older. Additionally, I strongly support the recommendation to provide hepatitis B screening with the 3-part panel for all adults including pregnant persons, providing a more complete picture of potential infection and clear steps for clinical management. The addition of risk factors to include persons currently or formerly incarcerated, with current or past STIs or multiple sex partners, with current or past HCV infection and anyone who requests a hepatitis B test, regardless of disclosure of risk, are reflective of the current trajectory of hepatitis B epidemiology in the United States and will be supportive of the work of hepatitis B service providers to reach all highly impacted populations. I believe these new recommendations will greatly increase access to hepatitis B screening and testing, removing barriers such as individual and community stigma and anxiety related to hepatitis B risk factors, and improve testing rates.

Additionally, I appreciate the timeliness of the expanded screening recommendations to align with the recent decision by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to recommend all adults aged 19-59 years be vaccinated against hepatitis B infection. I believe it is critical to coordinate clinical guidance for screening and vaccination. I believe screening for hepatitis B infection, with the 3-part panel, is primary and essential to finding susceptible persons and preventing new infections and agree that offering a first dose of the vaccine at the same time as screening to the hardest to reach populations is beneficial. I also encourage the CDC to take this opportunity to recommend making HBV rapid testing available in the United States, to enhance the reach-out efforts to those hard-to-reach populations, and facilitate linking them to care. 

I also believe the expansion of the recommendations for hepatitis B screening and testing is an opportunity to promote awareness and screening for hepatitis delta infection. There are very low levels of awareness and knowledge about hepatitis delta in the U.S. among the persons at risk for infection and health care providers. Given the promising treatments currently in clinical trial and anticipated dissemination of research related to hepatitis delta prevalence, I encourage the CDC to take the opportunity to include a statement on hepatitis delta.

The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) needs a solution. Whether its surface mining or coal mining, the dangers are constant. Poisonous gases, explosions, roofs caving in, or rocks falling from above are all dangers miners face daily. Companies need to take action to improve working conditions and training so fatalities diminish.
In an effort to address these issues, the MSHA held six meetings with stakeholders across the country. The purpose of the meetings was to acquire data and information on mobile equipment and conveyor belts. They understand what parts of the equipment need improving and that input is vital.

The Southeast Alaska Sperm Whale Avoidance Project (SEASWAP) is an unusual collaboration 
between scientists, fishermen and fishery managers. SEASWAP has worked since 2003 to 
understand sperm whale interactions with sablefish longline gear and to develop strategies that 
minimize sperm whale depredation on longline gear. We submit these comments based on our 
collective experience studying sperm whale interactions with the Gulf of Alaska sablefish 
longline fleet, which includes hundreds of hours on and off the water and multiple published 
articles (see http://seaswap.info/research/publications/). 
 
We have reviewed the Proposed Rule (NOAA– NMFS–2017–0031) to elevate the Gulf of Alaska 
sablefish fishery from a Category 3 to a Category 2 fishery, and we object to that proposed 
change. We do not dispute that sperm whales interact with longline gear. We do dispute the 
Serious Injury/Mortality (SI/M) classifications that leads to NOAA’s decision to re-categorize the 
sablefish fishery. We do not believe the interactions described in the report resulted in either 
serious injury or mortality, as defined by NOAA, nor do we believe the pro-rating to be 
appropriate. Our conclusions are based on reading the observer notes, our own experiences 
with Gulf of Alaska sperm whales, and our knowledge of their behavior and biology, as well as a 
cross reference to NOAA’s classification of fishery interactions with other large cetaceans. Our 
rationale is provided below. 
Background 
Over 50 sablefish fishermen have participated in SEASWAP research over the past 14 years. 
During this time, 123 individual sperm whales have been sighted 480 times near vessels, with 
one to ten whales observed near a vessel at any one time. Despite these extensive sperm 
whale sightings, fishermen participating in SEASWAP research have never witnessed sperm 
whale entanglement and have heard anecdotally of only one entanglement—and that one was 
known to be temporary. Our experience, including video captured by SEASWAP 
(http://seaswap.info/media/), documents that sperm whales are dexterous and highly 
proficient at both targeting prey and avoiding entanglement.

 
SEASWAP has documented that all sperm whales do not behave similarly near fishing vessels. In 
fact, sperm whales sighted near fishing vessels exhibit a broad range of behaviors. A relatively 
small number (n= 12) of the whales sighted near vessels remove substantial numbers of 
sablefish. Other sperm whales eat offal and discarded grenadier. A NOAA analysis released in 
October 2016 estimated that 5-10% of longline sets are depredated by sperm whales and, 
based on visual evidence of torn or partially torn fish, that 2.2% of total sablefish catch is lost to 
sperm whales.1 Some whales sighted by fishermen are naturally foraging and never interact 
with deployed longline gear. 
 
To provide greater detail, from SEASWAP data: 
• 123 individual Sperm whales have been identified, which were sighted 480 times. 
• 30 individuals have been seen 5 or more times (making up 298 sightings, or 62% of all 
sightings). 
• 12 individuals have been seen 10 or more times (making up 174 sightings, or 36% of all 
sightings). 
In short, 
• A substantial number of whales have been sighted 1-4 times and are not considered by 
the SEASWAP Team to be significant depredators. These whales are likely opportunistic 
feeders, or passing through but not spending a lot of time near boats. 
• 30 individuals have been sighted over 5 times around boats. These whales appear 
slightly more interested in boats as a food source. 
• Of these 30, 12 have been seen around boats more than 10 times and seem to be 
focused on depredation as a foraging method.

The proposed rule to implement Amendment 33 to the Pacific Coast Groundfish Fishery Management Plan (PCGFMP) is a well-considered response to the urgent need to rebuild the California quillback rockfish population and manage shortspine thornyhead allocations more effectively. The rebuilding plan for the quillback rockfish is essential given its overfished status, as declared by the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) in December 2023. By adopting a rebuilding strategy that targets a recovery by 2060, the Council is taking a balanced approach that considers both the biological status of the species and the socio-economic needs of the fishing communities. This plan is grounded in scientific analysis and incorporates parameters such as Tmin, Tmax, and Ttarget, ensuring that the stock is rebuilt in a sustainable and timely manner.
Furthermore, the proposed changes to the allocation framework for shortspine thornyhead are both necessary and pragmatic. The current allocation method, based on outdated data, has led to inefficiencies and constraints that negatively impact both trawl and non-trawl sectors. By establishing a coastwide annual catch limit (ACL) and harvest guideline (HG), the new framework allows for more flexible and efficient management of the stock. This change will not only help prevent overfishing but also provide equitable fishing opportunities across different sectors and regions. The shift to a 2-year allocation specified in regulation rather than in the PCGFMP itself reflects a forward-thinking approach that can adapt to future stock assessments and management needs. The proposed rule demonstrates a commitment to sustainable fisheries management and should be supported for its comprehensive and science-based approach.
