I am a practicing allergist and my practice of Board-Certified Allergists has been preparing allergen extracts in our office for our patients using aseptic technique for many years. The FDA Draft Guidance would require that allergen extracts now be prepared in an ISO Class 5 environment. Meeting this standard would be prohibitively costly and would make it impossible for us to continue to provide allergy immunotherapy to our patients. In all the years that I have been practicing I have seen no incidence of infections or other problems associated with allergen extracts prepared in our office. The Draft Guidance goes beyond what is necessary to ensure patient safety and would threaten patient access to care. I strongly urge the FDA to create an exception for allergenic extracts prepared by physicians for their own patients as requested in the comments submitted by the Advocacy Council of the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology.

I am writing in support of making NO changes to the current NEPA. The Forest Service Draft NEPA rule will prevent local communities' ability to weigh in on decisions impacting citizen's health and environment. I want my voice and every American citizen's voice to be heard in decisions. Public scoping is an integral part of NEPA. It needs to remain in place unchanged.
 I do not want "extraordinary circumstances" changed. I want sensitive species included as constituting an extraordinary circumstance. I want the current "likelihood of adverse effects to the listed resource condition" to remain the same and not have the weakening word "substantial" added to the threshold of determination. I want environmental analysis and public oversight to remain.
 I do not want to add or expand Categorical Exclusions (CEs). This is an obstruction tactic to circumvent environmental review and public input. 
 Multiple CEs should NOT be used to carry out land management decisions. I do not want the Forest Service to be able to forego NEPA analysis, using the tactic of separating various project elements and allowing the Forest Service to pick and choose CEs to cover elements. This is disingenuous and subverts the intent of NEPA.
 I do NOT want "determinations of NEPA adequacy" adopted. DNAs allow the DOI to avoid adequate analysis of needed assessment for every new or different proposed action. An EIS or EA needs to be required for each new proposed action.
 Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) and potential wilderness areas must be included in classes of action that now require preparation of an EIS. The proposed rule is an attack of IRAs and of potential wilderness areas identified in Forest Service wilderness inventories. Public scrutiny and environmental analysis of any projects that impact these areas must remain and, if anything, be strengthened. 
 There should be no "condition-based management" adopted. The Forest Service should NOT be about to authorize land management activities without obtaining information about all resources that would be affected on the ground. The public must keep the fundamental right under NEPA - the chance to speak up for specific places when they are proposed for logging. 
 I am especially concerned about the misnomer "ecosystem restoration and/or resilience activities" on up to 7300 acres, which includes commercial logging on up to 4200 acres, needing simply a restoration add-on. This is again duplicitous and MUST have public input and/or environmental analysis.
 What I find especially unconscionable is allowing illegal off-road vehicle routes to be changed to official Forest Service System roads or trails. Historic Forest Service travel and transportation management policy has been designed to ensure ORV route designations minimize impacts to resources. This policy also included making the Forest Service's transportation system ecologically and fiscally sustainable. 
 Long-standing policy that the Forest Service is not in the business of building permanent system roads. That should be maintained. 

 NEPA should remain as is. Weakening this law with the proposed Forest Service draft Rule is unacceptable and should be abandoned.

When first learning to drive at 16 years of age with my Dad providing me guidance, one thing he mentioned was to never trust your mirrors...it's always better to confirm by looking over your shoulder to make sure the next lane is clear to move to. His process was to first look at the sideview mirror, and then continue your glance to over your shoulder, in one smooth head movement.

Practicing this in the many (more than 32) years of driving has saved me more than a few times where cars were in my blind spot, and had I relied solely on my side mirrors, I would have surely hit those cars.

That being said, I currently drive a Model 3 Tesla which was recently enhanced with an OTA (Over The Air) update to now include a live image of your side view on the computer screen whenever your turn signal is activated. The location of the side camera is on each front fender of my Tesla.

When first using this new feature, it took some getting used to. However, after a few days, I have found it exceptionally beneficial. So much so that now, because of the enhanced and better view of the side, I have all but abandoned the use of my side mirrors. But yes...Dad is still guiding me with his ways, and I still do a glance over my shoulder when switching lanes.

That being said, I completely support the idea to replace the side view mirrors on US vehicles with cameras. I believe they offer a much better view of the side, eliminating any blind spots, while also eliminating many negatives with side mirrors (glare from cars behind you, fogging/misting of the glass, cost associated if the mirrors get damaged, etc.

Thank you,

Captive birds deserve, at the very least, humane treatment. These birds aren't able to live their lives in their natural environments, so we need to require that they be treated humanely in captivity at a minimum. 

Almost 20 years ago, Congress amended the federal Animal Welfare Act to include birds, but the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) never established standards to ensure the welfare of birds confined in U.S. facilities. As a result, birds have been suffering in unimaginable ways. They are used for unnecessary and painful research in laboratories, endure frustration and self-mutilation at roadside zoos, and live in squalid conditions at countless other facilities. 

Thank you for recently drawing up proposed standards for captive birds, but some of them still fall short of what is necessary to ensure these animals’ health and welfare. 

The proposed standards fall short in the following ways:

They fail to require a large enough space for birds to be able to fly, the most natural and fundamental behavior of almost all bird species. Failing to provide birds who fly with enough space to do so takes away much of what gives their lives meaning.
They fail to prohibit mutilations, including pinioning (the surgical removal of the outermost bones in a bird’s wing, equivalent to removing a human hand, to prevent flight permanently, often performed without pain medication).
They fail to prohibit public contact with birds, including wrangling, mounting, and riding them, such as in ostrich racing.
They fail to prohibit or require a time limit on tethering birds, which severely restricts their mobility.
They fail to recognize parrots and other species as exotic animals, meaning that retail pet stores would be allowed to confine and sell them without obtaining a license or adhering to even the most basic welfare standards.

The following requirements need to be implemented immediately:

Require a large enough space for birds to be able to fly, which is the most natural and fundamental behavior of almost all bird species.
Prohibit licensees from mutilating birds, including pinioning, which is completely unnecessary and cruel.
Prohibit public contact with birds, including riding birds such as ostriches, which causes stress and puts them at risk of injury.
Prohibit the tethering of birds, which severely limits their mobility and doesn’t allow them to express normal, natural behavior.
Wild and exotic animals, including parrots and most other bird species, should never be kept or sold as pets. At the very least, the agency should include definitions of “pet animal” and “retail pet store” that explicitly provide all wild and exotic bird species with protection.

Thank you for helping captive birds, let's get this right for them!!

EPA is proposing a complete overhaul of its longstanding regulations, which serve as the 
“umbrella” regulatory framework to implement Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (“CWA” or 
“the Act”). EPA’s proposal drastically undermines the tenets of cooperative federalism in the 
CWA and inappropriately encroaches into authority expressly reserved to the states and 
authorized tribes (hereinafter referred to as “certifying authorities” or “states”) under 
Section 401, 33 U.S.C. § 1341. As recognized by Congress, states are in the best position to 
protect their waterways through their own individualized water quality certification processes 
that are tailored to work within their own legal frameworks, especially when certifications 
cross into the realm of water allocation and management. See 33 U.S.C. § 1251(b); 33 U.S.C. 
§ 1341; 33 U.S.C. § 1370. Colorado is concerned about the impacts that EPA’s proposal, if 
finalized, will have on our ability to protect the quality of Colorado’s valuable water 
resources in the context of essential water storage and supply infrastructure projects. We 
want to ensure that EPA considers the implications of the proposed rule changes for these 
critical water supply projects, which are somewhat unique to Colorado, and which are very 
different from the energy infrastructure projects that are a main driver of EPA’s proposal per 
the directives in Executive Order 13868, Promoting Energy Infrastructure and Economic 
Growth. 84 Fed. Reg. 15,495 (Apr. 15, 2019).

 
2 
The principle of cooperative federalism and the primary authority of states to manage and 
protect their water resources are paramount concepts reflected in numerous provisions of the 
CWA. For example, Section 101(b) confirms Congress’ overarching policy “[T]o recognize, 
preserve, and protect the primary responsibilities of the States to prevent, reduce and 
eliminate pollution [and] to plan the development and use … of water resources….” 33 U.S.C. 
§ 1251(b). Section 510(1) further emphasizes the central role of states under the Act, 
providing that “nothing in this chapter shall preclude or deny the right of any State … to 
adopt or enforce (A) any standard or limitation respecting discharges of pollutants, or (B) any 
requirement respecting control or abatement of pollution….” so long as they are at least as 
stringent as any federal counterpart. 33 U.S.C. § 1370(1). Section 510(2) goes on to say that

I remember a time when air travel was fun. Now it's more of an endurance test--a means to an end--what with the endless fees, smaller cabins, loss of leg room, etc. 

As if flying weren't stressful enough, now there is consideration of allowing cell phone calls on flights. The thought of being surrounded by a plane full of chatty Cathys sets my teeth on edge, and I can only imagine the dread and anger this would inspire in my fellow travelers.

A plane cabin is a confined space, and there is only so much one can block out with noise-cancelling headphones. Getting up and leaving the room is not an option. 

It is unrealistic to expect that folks' understanding of basic decorum will encourage them keep their cell phone calls brief, quiet, and to a minimum. If you've traveled on Amtrak's Quiet Car, you know that conductors must remind passengers to respect the rules. It is unfair to expect airline attendants to police when calls are too loud or too long or inappropriate, which is something they will certainly be called upon to do. It is also unfair to expect the flying public to grit their teeth for the duration of a flight.

For the health, sanity, and safety of all involved, I implore you to ban cell phone calls on flights.

Thank you.

I, like many consumers, rely on on-package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised" I assume that there is value and meaning behind that claim and that is backed by a regulatory agency. 

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. Companies will still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit. 

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Time and time again industry has shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating/policing itself. Companies are taking advantage of consumers, and grossly overcharging them, by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels to bring in more profits all the while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare. 

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers. 

FSIS owes it to the American public to set a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," take steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensure that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

III. E.Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small Community Water Systems and Non-Transient, Non-Community Water Systems

I agree with the implementation of cost efficient alternatives for small Community Water Systems since this will allow small/low income communities with fewer financial resources to still minimize the impact of lead exposure. However, the recommendation system in which the small CWS's need approval by the state on the implementation of their preferred alternative is flawed. Under the current proposed regulation should the lead action levels exceed in a water system within the six month period after the initial lead trigger level, the small CWS must implement the State-approved compliance option. Having to resort to a State-approved compliance option may not be in the best interest of a small CWS which might not have the resources available to implement a general State-approved compliance option in time to prevent a crisis. One solution might be to empower these small CWS's to implement their preferred alternatives of CCT, POU, or a LSLR after at most two months of the initial lead trigger level. Giving states a large window of six months to approve a recommendation may result in the needs of a small community being ignored for half a year which is enough to negatively impact a community even with simply exceeding the lead trigger levels.

2022 National Strategy to Support Family Caregivers

Cancer Moonshot

Overall, HHS and CMS serve a critical role in ensuring that the federal government achieves the ambitious, but essential, goals included in myriad national commitments to caregivers. The annually updated Physician Fee Schedule provides an ongoing opportunity to identify, implement, and improve policies to support caregivers.

Caregivers are essential participants in a patient’s care team, but have historically been unrecognized and unsupported

Unfortunately, according to the same report, fewer than three in 10 caregivers surveyed (29 percent) said they have had general conversations with health professionals

Furthermore, only seven percent report receiving any training related to tasks they perform. Black and Latino American caregivers (67 percent each) more often help with medical/nursing tasks than do White caregivers (52 percent). While four in 10 caregivers are in high-intensity caregiving situations (40 percent) the proportion of caregivers (31 percent) who reported difficulty in coordinating care among health care providers is growing.

Demographics portend that absent significant and cross-cutting action from federal policymakers, these challenges will become more acute. The population of older adults—the majority of Medicare beneficiaries needing care—is growing at an historic rate, necessitating the support of increasing numbers of family caregivers. In fact, between 2015 and 2020, the number of unpaid family caregivers increased by more than 10 million, to 53 million family caregivers according to research from NAC and AARP. Dear Mr. McNally: 

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on EPA’s proposal to revoke the existing tolerance exemption 

and establish specific tolerances for the biofungicide banda de Lupinus albus doce (BLAD), as described 

in notices published on May 29, 2015, February 11, 2020, and April 21, 2020 in the Federal Register. We 

appreciate that EPA afforded stakeholders several opportunities to comment on the proposed action, and 

we also thank EPA for its consideration of the comments that USDA previously submitted in July 2015 

(USDA, 2015). 

USDA continues to be concerned that the proposed action is not sufficiently supported by the available 

evidence, and appears to be based on a presumption of hazard rather than on the identification of risk. In 

particular, we do not believe that EPA has assigned adequate weight to a factor that is fundamental to the 

assessment of risk: exposure. 

We respectfully disagree that the existing tolerance exemption for BLAD “on its face, permits unlimited 

residues of BLAD in or on all food commodities” as asserted in the proposed rule. In response to 

concerns raised by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and in accordance with EPA 

requirements, the registrant conducted field trials using exaggerated application rates of 5X the maximum 

label allowance, as well as maximally conservative preharvest intervals ranging from 1 hour to 1 day. 

Pursuant to the objectives outlined in 40 CFR §180.34, these data establish the residues that may remain 

when BLAD is applied according to directions registered under the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and 

Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), and further establish the residues that may remain under conditions most likely 

to result in high residues on the commodity (i.e., the worst-case scenario). Based on these “worst-case” 

data, EPA concluded that “there will be no residues of BLAD above the level of detection, if any remain 

at all, when commodities are treated in accordance with the label.” EPA further notes that trials could not 

be conducted at higher exaggerated application rates (i.e., 10X rates, as initially requested by EPA), as 

these rates would be phytotoxic to target plants. Consequently, USDA contends that the theoretical 

presence of “unlimited residues,” or any detectable residues for that matter, is precluded (and essentially 

self-regulated) by the intrinsic properties of BLAD itself. 

Like EPA, USDA places tremendous value on FDA’s expertise for issues related to allergenicity. 

However, the initial concern expressed by FDA—and the question that USDA believes is most relevant to 

EPA’s proposed rulemaking—is whether, absent an explicit tolerance limit, use of BLAD would result in 

“clinically relevant levels” of BLAD in food. Based on the evidence provided by EPA in support of the 

proposed rulemaking, this does not appear to be the case. 

The proposal to revoke a previously granted tolerance exemption and establish specific tolerances for a 

biopesticide with no toxicological endpoints and negligible exposure appears to be somewhat

Dear Administrator Andrew Wheeler,

I am writing to strongly oppose the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) proposal to restrict the science that is used in its decisionmaking processes.

In issuing this proposed rule, the EPA claims that it would be making science more transparent. But it instead would put researchers in the difficult position of choosing between protecting privacy and security versus allowing their work to be used in EPA decisionmaking. It would excessively burden EPA staff with reanalyzing data from each study used to support a rulemaking which is not only pointless as peer review already is a check on the work of researchers, but it would be resource intensive and time consuming.
 
The EPA's proposed rule has three fundamental flaws that render it unfeasible. 

First, the agency provides insufficient justification and analyses to support the rule. The proposal includes no analyses of the rule's effect on the EPA's mission-related work, the costs or benefits of such a move, and the problem that such a rule is addressing.

Second, the proposal would restrict the agency's ability to implement and enforce mission-critical laws by blocking the EPA from using many kinds of scientific studies vital to its decisionmaking, including studies that rely on personal health data, confidential business information, intellectual property, or older studies for which the authors or data sources may not be accessible. 

Finally, the rule would grant the EPA administrator broad authority to exclude individual studies or entire decisions from being subject to its provisions on a case-by-case basis, giving the administrator unprecedented power to decide what the best available science is. 

The rule does nothing to advance the cause of transparency in the broader scientific community. This issue is best addressed with the full involvement of scientists, science advisors, and scientific institutions, not designed solely by political appointees. this rule deviates away from open-minded rigorous analysis required for science to be valid, and to me this indicates that EPA is moving away from prioritizing what a democratic government would prioritize---activities in the best interests of the electorate--not the corporations.

The EPA must not move forward with this rulemaking as it would undermine science-based decisionmaking at the agency, and limit its ability to protect public health and the environment.

Sincerely,
susan michetti
Mount Horeb, WI 53572

Dear Ms. Wayson:

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce submits these comments in response to the USDA 

Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS or the Agency) Notice of Proposed 

Implementation of Revised Lacey Act Provisions, 85 Fed. Reg. 17,849 (Mar. 31, 2020) (the 

Notice). The Canadian Chamber of Commerce is Canada’s largest industry association, 

representing businesses of all sizes across all sectors and regions of the country. Our members 

rely on the movement of wood pallets for the functioning of cross-border supply chains. For the 

purpose of this document, we will use the term “wood packaging” when describing articles 

affected by the proposed Lacey Act revisions.

This proposed rule to include HTS code 4415 in the scope of the Lacey Act will cause significant 

hardship on those shipping wood packaging to the United States. Preliminary estimates of the 

economic impacts on the Canadian economy are significant. We also understand from our 

members that this rule’s potential impact on the US economy will be more than $100 million. 

The view of our members is that there is no connectivity with a measure such as this, and the 

overarching goals of the Lacey Act. We have consulted with the Canadian Wood Pallet and

Container Association (CWPCA) and support their position that HTS code 4415, and more 

specifically wood packaging moving between Canada and the United States should be removed 

from scope, or receive a special classification.

Whether traversing borders underload or as a commodity, wood packaging’s purpose is 

singular. It is a material handling device used as a platform to move goods. Understanding 

how the North American supply chain works is key to understanding the role of wood packaging. 

Once wood packaging enters the supply chain, it moves freely about, carrying goods to 

consumers. Rarely is wood packaging repurposed for anything but a material handling device 

during its useful life and therefore it is essentially always an implement of trade. 

The North American supply chain is interconnected and should therefore be considered as a 

whole. In fact, the North American supply chain is so interconnected it can be argued that wood 

packaging in any form can be considered as an implement of international trade, which under 

the Lacey Act rule, is exempt from scope. The free flow of goods must be encouraged and 

supported. Wood packaging enables the functionality of the supply chain, and any 

encumbrance in getting wood packaging to market cripples that functionality. This has taken on 

added importance as our economies need to have tools at our disposal to recover from COVID-

19.

 
As wood packaging serves only one purpose, which is to move goods, and the supply chain in 

North America is all encompassing, it is our recommendation that HTS code 4415 is removed 

from the scope of inclusion. Barring that, we would propose that all wood packaging moving 

between Canada and the USA be considered as IIT and therefore exempt from Lacey Act rule.

This comment is related to proposed changes to "Evaluation & Management (E/M) Guidelines and Care Management Services".

Generally, I support modifying the guidelines to place emphasis on medical decision making and to reduce the required documentation burden for History and Physical Exam for coding purposes. My comment is specifically in response to the following request: "While we believe MDM guidelines may also need to be updated, we believe in the nearer term it may be possible to eliminate the current focus on details of history and physical exam, and allow MDM and/or time to serve as the key determinant of E/M visit level. We are seeking public comment on this approach. We are also seeking comment on how such reforms may deferentially affect physicians and practitioners of different specialties, including primary care clinicians, and how we could or should account for such effects as we examine this issue."

I would like to provide an opinion as a dermatologist who has closely analyzed the E/M guidelines and has detailed knowledge of the Marshfield Scale for scoring medical decision making.

In my opinion, a move towards using medical decision making as a primary determinant of coding could be challenging for dermatologists and may discourage thorough, quality skin examinations if performance of such examinations is not appropriately valued. In my experience, many melanomas have been identified incidentally on examination and have been in areas normally covered by clothing in which a detailed or comprehensive examination was required. Perhaps this issue could be solved - at least partially - by appropriately weighting high risk patients (i.e. those with a history of skin cancer or those who are immunosuppressed at increased risk of melanoma) within the medical decision making component as a population that increases the complexity of the visit, as it not only increases risk but also requires greater scrutiny of skin lesions during the examination.

Since there is a certain degree of subjectivity regarding scoring complaints/problems using the Marshfield scale, I am also concerned that there could be confusion about the level of complexity that a visit meets (straightforward vs low vs moderate vs high). In speaking with other dermatologists, it is often challenging to decide what makes a problem "minor" (and therefore only worth 1 point in the scale, with a maximum of 2 points and therefore maximum of low complexity regardless of the number of minor problems addressed), versus what makes a problem "not minor" (e.g. "chronic stable") and therefore worth more points in the scoring scale. Either more clarification, additional guidance, or a specialty-specific scale on medical decision making could help alleviate this problem for dermatologists.

Ecological Consequences Could Be Permanent

This would be the first GE tree deregulated for wild release and unchecked spread. The risks are irreversible: pollen from Darling 54 could alter wild American chestnuts for generations, with no way to recall or contain it once it's released.

Public Resources, Private Profits

The nuts contain a gene from wheat, yet there's been no allergen or toxicity testing.

Dear Secretary Mayorkas:

The Northwest Horticultural Council (NHC) writes today to provide comment regarding the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule entitled “Modernizing H-2 Program Requirements, Oversight, and Worker Protections,” published in the U.S. Federal Register on September 20, 2023, under DHS Docket No. USCIS-2023-0012.

The NHC is a trade association that represents the growers, packers, and shippers of apples, pears, and cherries on federal, as well as international trade, policy and regulatory issues. Our growers produce approximately 70 percent of the apples (supplying 80 percent of the U.S. fresh market), 84 percent of the fresh pears, and 73 percent of the fresh sweet cherries grown in the United States.

The NHC represents growers with farms of all sizes. With many current workers reaching retirement age and few new domestic workers entering the workforce, more and more growers have turned to the H-2A program to secure the workforce they need to grow and harvest their crops – in spite of paying a wage that is 19 percent or more above the state minimum wage, plus the substantial costs of providing benefits like housing and transportation. The number of H-2A workers brought to Washington state alone increased by a third in just one year, from nearly 18,800 in 2017 to approximately 25,000 in 2018. The number has continued to rise substantially even through the COVID-19 pandemic, with approximately 30,000 worker positions being filled in 2021, a reported 34,661 in 2022, and a reported 38,664 in 2023. In Oregon, the number of H-2A workers jumped by one-third between 2018 and 2021. Numbers are also increasing in Idaho. 

Unfortunately, during this same period in which use of the H-2A program has grown so substantially, we have seen multi-generation family farmers lose their operations at an alarming rate, causing unprecedented consolidation within the industry. With labor constituting 60-70 percent of a grower’s input costs, the single biggest contributor to these growers losing their farms is the significant, non-market-based increases to the cost of labor driven by the terms and conditions of the H-2A program. Making the H-2A program more accessible and workable for growers of all sizes is paramount to halting this trend. 

Treating workers with dignity and respect is critical to retaining a knowledgeable and productive workforce. It is telling that the vast majority of H-2A employers in the Pacific Northwest tree fruit industry report seeing 90 percent or more of their workers continue to return to the same employer year-after-year. Of those that do not return, it is often because that worker has made enough money to invest in a business at home and therefore no longer needs to work away from their families for much of the year. 

The NHC recognizes the need for rigorous enforcement of the existing requirements of the H-2A program regarding protection of workers. Our organization has advocated with Congress to increase funds for states for this purpose through the Office of Foreign Labor Certification’s (OFLC) state grants program. We believe that bad actors who are violating the terms and conditions of the program should be punished. However, the NHC is concerned that this rule goes too far in imposing extreme penalties – to the point of preventing access to the program, which is a death knell for farms that are unable to secure the workforce they need domestically to grow and harvest their crops – on good actors who are attempting to navigate an extremely complex program.
 
While some of the provisions in this proposed rule are positive changes to the program, the NHC encourages DHS to reevaluate aspects of this proposed rule to better focus extreme penalties like debarment, or denial or revocation of an H-2A petition, on bad actors who are knowingly and willingly violating the terms and conditions of the H-2A program in a manner that jeopardizes the health and safety of workers. Current detention policies regarding housing assignments for transgender detainees are also extremely concerning and likely increase the risk of violence and assault. as described in the Pacific Halibut Catch Sharing Plan (CSP). 
Public Input on 2023 California Season Dates 
Following the completion of the International Pacific Halibut Commission’s Annual 
Meeting, CDFW conducted an online public survey to gather input on preferred season 
dates for 2023. The survey was open for ten days and 207 responses were received. 
Forty-seven percent of the respondents indicated a preference for a May 1 – November 
15 season structure, which is the status quo. Thirty-one percent of respondents 
indicated a preference for a June 1 – November 15 season structure. Other minority 
preferences were to include one or more time block closures during peak months to 
spread fishing effort over a longer period. 
 
Recommended Season Dates 
Given the size of the California recreational quota (39,520 net pounds) and the results 
of the public survey, CDFW recommends the California recreational season for 2023 be 
set as open May 1 through November 15, or until the quota has been met, whichever is 
earlier. CDFW expects that with this continuous open season structure the quota will be 
fully harvested, and potentially will need to be closed inseason even earlier than August 
7, the closure date in 2022. 
 
CDFW notes that catch projections cannot account for the unpredictability of fishing 
effort, changes in catch rates, availability of alternative targets, weather, and other 
factors that may affect angler behavior and/or catch. CDFW plans to continue the 
daily and weekly catch tracking of the fishery as in prior years. This will allow for

The proposed new regulations will, in my opinion, create unintended consequences within the horse industry adversely affecting horse owners, competitors, the livelihood of thousands of members of many different horse-related associations and the overall health and viability of the horse industry. I also believe, if implemented, the new regulations will create a glut of neglected horses resulting from unnecessary over-regulation, a misinformed and under-manned bureaucracy and the lack of opportunity for owners to enjoy, show and compete with their horse or horses. 
My personal experience follows; I am a competing member of the NRCHA and a local affiliated association. In my close to 20 years of association with the stock horse and reined cow horse world, I have NEVER witnessed any "soring", nor am I aware of anyone being suspected of or proven to have "sored" a horse. Both the NRCHA and our local affiliate have enforceable and effective rules applying to abuse of horses shown and present during competitions. What I have witnessed are horse owners taking better care of their horses than themselves, judges with a sharp sense of a healthy, useable horse, and show management that cares deeply about the providing a safe environment for horses to be shown in. Can anyone, any bureaucrat, or any politician effectively promote the welfare of horses any better? I say, "NO".
Generally stating, the proposed regulations are unnecessarily broad in its bureaucratic reach in that it applies to ALL horse breeds when only a small niche of the horse industry has an alleged "soring" problem. This "if one suffers, they all must suffer" rule-making mentality simply is not acceptable. If a niche of the horse industry is of concern, then they should be approached about cleaning up their act. The whole industry should not suffer because of an under-performing member. 
Having dealt with the governmental agencies and the bureaucratic state for most of my professional like, I recognize and firmly believe these rules will create a bloated enforcement division within the USDA which will ultimately create enough havoc in the horse industry to irreparably damage it over the coming months and years. I also believe the on-site cost to enforce these rules will significantly and adversely affect the horse industry along with costing the taxpayers millions of dollars, which in itself should be a budgetary concern for USDA.
I believe the proposed rules are an over-reaching solution to an isolated problem. The isolated problem should be treated as such and a whole industry should never suffer because of it.

To: Division of Dockets Management, Food & Drug Administration 

From: Shannon Clancy, J.D. Candidate 2017, University of Baltimore School of Law 

Date: March 9, 2017 

RE: Use of the Term “Healthy” in the Labeling of Human Food Products 

Docket No.: FDA-2016-D-2335 

I. Introduction 

This comment is in response to the Food and Drug Administration’s request for comments 

on the Use of the Term “Healthy” in the Labeling of Human Food Products. This comment poses 

a response to the questions: “What is consumers' understanding of the meaning of the term 

“healthy” as it relates to food” and “would this change in the term “healthy” cause a shift in 

consumer behavior in terms of dietary choices?” As a result of my research, I do not feel the term 

“healthy” should be added to food labels. 

II. Background 

The authority in this area comes from section 403(r)(1)(A) of the Federal Food, Drug, and 

Cosmetic Act (the FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 343(r)(1)(A)). More specifically, the definition in 21 

CFR 101.65(d) provides the parameters for use of the implied nutrient content claim of “healthy” 

or related terms on the label or in labeling of a food to suggest that a food, because of its nutrient 

content, may be useful in creating a diet that is consistent with dietary recommendations, if the 

food meets certain nutrient conditions, and the claim is made with an explicit or implicit claim or 

statement about a nutrient. 

The certain nutrient conditions discussed above vary from the amount of total fat, saturated 

fat, or sodium included, to the elements in the Nutrition Facts label and serving size. The 2015–

2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans discusses what individuals should look for in creating 

“healthy eating patterns,” including the following: (1) focus on variety, nutrient density, and 

amount; (2) limit calories from added sugars and saturated fats and reduce sodium intake; (3) shift 

to healthier food and beverage choices; and (4) support healthy eating patterns for all. 

1

 
III. Discussion 

As a law student currently enrolled in administrative law at the University of Baltimore 

School of Law, I have developed an interest in current administrative affairs. More specifically, I 

find the development of the food-labeling term “healthy” in today’s society extremely prevalent, 

as there are continuous debates as to what constitutes being “healthy.” “As individuals, we are 

bombarded with suggestions that we should adhere or aspire to any number of things preceded by 

the adjective ‘healthy.’” Rob Smythe, Americans Have Forgotten What the Word ‘Health’ Means, 

FORBES (Oct. 1, 2015, 12:43 PM), https://www.forbes.com/sites/roysmythe/2015/10/01/what-is-

health/#4da12f4e6b97. 

While the media floods our television screens with new “healthy tricks” to lose weight or 

slim down, it is evident that the term “healthy” does not mean the same thing for every single 

American consumer. According to Webster’s Dictionary, “healthy” is defined as: “(1) free from 

disease or pain; (2) showing physical, mental, or emotional well-being; or (3) beneficial to one’s 

physical, mental, or emotional state.” Healthy, MERRIAM-WEBSTER, https://www.merriam-

webster.com/dictionary/healthy (last visited Mar. 8, 2017). As a consumer, when I think of the 

term healthy, I think about exercising daily and moderating my sugar intake. However, when I 

asked my dad the same question, he said he thinks of keeping his blood pressure low and staying 

active. While we have completely different understandings of the word healthy, both are 

acceptable as the term “healthy” is not just one-dimensional. 

The goal of placing the word “healthy” on certain food labels is “to provide consumers 

with information and tools to enable them to easily and quickly make food choices consistent with 

public health recommendations and to encourage the development of healthier foods by the 

industry.”

Here are some of my questions and concerns. We really need more protection of our reefs. This blueprint should be more encompassing than what is currently included. Our ecosystem is in total danger of collapse. We have been diving here for 25+ years and wow, the changes over the last 10 years have been saddening.

1. Can we please add more officers for enforcement at Hens and Chickens and Alligator Lighthouse, especially on busy days? More officers are needed at lots of our reefs to prevent damage before it happens and to issue fines so guests follow the rules. These areas have many boaters who anchor on the coral and would be a great place to start due to high volume of improper anchoring. 

2. Can you add more Mooring Balls, no anchor areas, dinghy moorings (the BVI uses these)? At Alligator, boats shouldn't be allowed to anchor so close to the Lighthouse where the corals are shallow. No anchor areas are critical when boaters can’t/won’t anchor without dropping on coral. No anchor mooring balls can be a different color, without lines, and say NO ANCHORING.

3. Can you increase education in English and Spanish at all boat ramps, parks, points of entry, boat dealers? To include proper anchoring technique, fishing line removal, take your trash home. 

4. Can you increase fines for violations, strengthen laws for reef damages? If there is little penalty enforcement people are not as likely to comply.

We just returned from Bonaire and all users of the marine park pay a tag price to utilize the waters. This is paid on line or at the commercial operator before entry. The government uses this fee for enforcement, moorings, education, orientations. Divers wash gear in different barrels for different areas that are or are not effected by disease to prevent spreading. Windsurfers, kiteboarders, fishermen, snorkelers all pay this fee.

Just in the last two weeks we’ve been diving on Sand Island #3, Crocker Shallows, and Conch Reef. Sand Island has a nice new mooring line. During our time on the boat before and after dives we saw other boaters not boating properly. One threw their anchor under power. One was fishing at Sand Island. One was moving fast through boats with dive flags. Underwater the landscape we saw was under stress. Small coral heads were not only diseased but also being smothered by Christmas tree worms, lots of fishing line entangled, brown sponges bleached white, sick looking soft corals and fans, and more. We did see underwater life working to adapt which made me feel we really need to fight for them. 

I would like to see maximum growth in education/advertisement on how to properly enjoy our reefs, new no anchor areas and anchor rules to protect more reefs, and a lot more enforcement/creation of rules with penalties. I think these steps can help reduce the human caused damage/stress. 

Please expand your goals as much as possible. The next time you consider upgrades this eco system could literally be gone. It really feels like the time is now. 

I am a photographer and have photos/videos over time if you are in need of any proof for comparisons please contact me.

Bless you as you work on this most important project.

I am commenting on the Proposed Rule "Clarification of When Products Made or Derived From Tobacco Are Regulated as Drugs, Devices, or Combination Products; Amendments to Regulations Regarding 'Intended Uses'"(Docket No. FDA-2015-N-2002)

 I quit smoking three years ago using e-cigarette products. I now vape alone. It is important that these products remain in charge of their own production, manufacturing, and product descriptions. As a member of CASAA, I already have a source for quality information on vapor products. I do NOT need the government involved in or attempting to influence my decisions. Being able to visit retailers and get their honest, unadulterated opinion on various products is extremely important to the vaping community. 

Please, let the industry stand and evolve on its own. No one vaping thinks it's "healthy" - just a 'healthier alternative' to smoking. 

The more regulations placed on the products, the fewer the number of creators and manufacturers will exist. This you may think is a good thing. Fewer would be easier to control. It would also mean fewer small start-ups, more money in the hands of fewer and fewer - greedier and greedier - individuals; individuals who care more about their profit margin than they do their customers. Beginning to sound like a Big Tobacco to anyone else?

And it all starts with regulation - regulation choking the life out of small mom-and-pop companies who are only out to sell a good product, and make a living doing it. So keep in mind, these regulations sought to protect good people from bad people may very well end up creating the bad people from whom others need protection. 

So in this, I ask you: do not require product information or warnings of any kind on e-cigarette products. 
 Enforce the rules already in place, and leave the 18 and older to determine for themselves what is the truth about the product. 

Thank you.

The argument behind the removal of regulations that they are ineffective and as a result unnecessary is fundamentally flawed. There is no denying that quarantine is not as effective as desired, but the proposed rule itself states that there is no way to determine the full effects of removing quarantines on emerald ash borer. The Nebraska State Forestry Service has come out against the removal of federal quarantines, arguing that the benefits to the quarantine are undeniable. In particular, they point out that while quarantine does not completely stop the spread of emerald ash borer, it slows the spread, allowing communities to prepare for the arrival of emerald ash borer and extending the lifespan of ash trees. Without the quarantine, emerald ash borer would have spread faster than it did (https://journalstar.com/news/local/govt-and-politics/state-forestry-experts-oppose-proposal-to-end-federal-emerald-ash/article_369226bc-9a19-5a8c-aee8-a4c4b79ee819.html).

The proposed rule also focuses heavily upon the efficacy of biological controls to solve the emerald ash borer problem. Initial studies have shown promise, and lent credence to the opinion that biological controls are the best method of controlling emerald ash borer. However, these studies are still in their infancy (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112717301081), and in some cases, such as a study done by the USDA Forest Service, have yet to produce results (https://www.nrs.fs.fed.us/disturbance/invasive_species/eab/control_management/biological_control/).

Finally, the proposed rule acknowledges two caveats. First, it only applies to the removal of federal quarantines. States will have the opportunity to impose their own quarantines on emerald ash borer. However, the loss of federal quarantines could hurt individual states attempting to export to Canada and Norway, something the proposed rule itself acknowledges. Those states which have not had emerald ash borer spread to them yet could still be prevented from exporting, as there is no federal regulation preventing the ash borer from spreading within their borders. Second, Native American tribes, who the proposed rule acknowledged as being potentially affected by the loss of federal quarantines, are urging APHIS to delay in this deregulation. Their pleas will be taken into account when deciding to finalize the rule, as they rightly should. Native American traditions that rely upon ash trees could be lost, due to the spread of emerald ash borer (https://www.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/pubs/55528). 

Until there is a method to tackle the problem of emerald ash borer head-on, the methods that reduce its spread should not be removed. Deregulation should be done because the regulations are no longer needed, not just for sake of deregulating. The evidence does not support the removal of emerald ash borer quarantines, and as a result, Subpart Emerald Ash Borer in 7 CFR Part 301 should remain. At the very least, it should remain until biological control studies have yielded a surefire method of eradicating emerald ash borer, so that its spread no longer needs to be slowed.

I agree everything FARFA says about labeling lab raised meat substitutes. These products need to be labeled in a way that clearly describes them as being produced in a lab. 

As stated by FARFA:

Cells grown in a petri dish on artificial nutrient solutions are not meat. They are legitimate food items that businesses can manufacture and that consumers can choose to buy. But labels that imply in any way that these products are equivalent to meat from livestock are false and misleading.
 
1. Consumers should be clearly informed that a product was derived from cell cultures grown under artificial conditions rather than from live animals fed whole foods. Numerous scientific studies show that a live animals’ diet significantly changes the nutrient profile of its meat. Given that, it is certain that raising isolated cells on synthetic nutrients and added chemicals “alters the biological, chemical, nutritional, or organoleptic properties of meat or poultry to the extent that the resulting product no longer aligns with consumers’ expectations.” These lab-raised foods are fundamentally different from what normal people consider “meat.”
 
2. In describing these products, the agency should not use the word “cultured.” In the context of food, the word “cultured” has been used to describe fermented foods, which takes a naturally grown or raised agricultural product (such as a vegetable or dairy) and uses a low-tech process to increase its nutritional value, flavor profile, and storability. This is both a completely different process and a completely different result from lab-based animal cell products. Using the term “cultured meat” would mislead many consumers who may believe that this is analogous to things such as “cultured dairy products” (e.g. sour cream) or “cultured vegetables” (e.g. fermented carrots).
 
Other terms would be clearer, such as “lab raised” or “cell cultivated.”
 
As a consumer, I urge the agency to either prevent these foods from being labeled as “meat” at all or, at a minimum, to require clear terminology that provides consumers with unambiguous information as to the source of the product.

I am a respiratory therapist, and I run a pulmonary rehabilitation center for chronic lung disease patients (specializing in COPD & sarcoidosis patients waiting for lung transplantation)

Both the National Action Plan and the GOLD strategy report place a great deal of emphasis on the outpatient management of COPD. Increasing exercise tolerance, improving adherence with medication plans, and generally enhancing a patient's self-efficacy and ability to self-manage are cornerstones of treatment. Many patients receive the knowledge and training they need to effectively control their symptoms and slow the progression of COPD through the use of pulmonary rehabilitation programs.

Unfortunately, access to these programs has been declining in recent years. Due to a variety of factors (such as a lack of sufficient advocacy and awareness and a poor understanding of the role of pulmonary rehabilitation), Medicare reimbursement for these programs has been repeatedly cut. These cuts have severely limited the viability of many programs, because they simply weren't a good return on investment. Quality pulmonary rehabilitation programs require significant resources, in terms of both equipment and personnel, to effectively educate and prepare patients for 'graduation.'

Due to the efforts of several advocacy and pulmonary professional groups, CMS reversed this trend and in 2016, significantly increased reimbursement levels by reassigning pulmonary rehabilitation codes to status 'Q1'. This was a boon to facilities and patients alike, as more people were able to take advantage of one of the few interventions we have that has been clinically proven to improve quality of life and prevent things like disability payments. Much work remains, as we also know that the benefits of pulmonary rehabilitation, like most exercise, wane over time without maintenance programs, and these programs are not covered under the Medicare benefit (and are unfortunately cost-prohibitive for many patients on Medicare and/or Social Security payments). However, this move was widely hailed as a step in the right direction.

However, the proposed re-classification to status 'S' reverses all of that progress. The net effect of this re-classification will be to cut reimbursement for pulmonary rehabilitation below (in some cases SIGNIFICANTLY below) FY2016 reimbursement levels. These cuts will be devastating to current pulmonary rehabilitation operations, and instead of increasing access, will instead serve to restrict it even further.

The GOLD strategy report states, "The benefits to COPD patients from pulmonary rehabilitation are considerable, and rehabilitation has been shown to be the most effective therapeutic strategy to improve shortness of breath, health status, and exercise tolerance." In addition, the report goes on to state, "Pulmonary rehabilitation also ranks as one of the most cost-effective treatment strategies, with an estimated cost per quality-adjusted life year of GBP2,000-GBP8,000," which translates to approximately $2,500-$9,950. This compares favorably with common pharmaceutical therapies, which START at the high end of that range and can cost orders of magnitude more to create the equivalent benefit.

It defies logic and fiscal sense to continue to push pulmonary rehabilitation to the sidelines. This is a well-established, highly effective therapy modality that improves lives and saves money, both in direct costs (medications, hospitalizations, etc.) and indirect costs by keeping patients engaged and healthier. In an era where healthcare continues to look for practices based upon value and evidence, pulmonary rehabilitation stands as a leader in both. I strongly urge CMS to reconsider this proposed rule change, which conflicts with upcoming US healthcare policy (the COPD National Action Plan), international standards (the GOLD strategy), and evidence-based medical practice.

As an dedicated organic foods consumer, I strongly support the Organic Livestock and Poultry Practices (OLPP) Rule that strengthens the animal welfare standards for organic livestock production. Reinstating the OLPP Rule without further delay is critical to ensure continued consumer trust in the organic seal. 

It's simple. The OLPP rule expands and clarifies existing requirements for livestock care and production practices; it is not government overreach. Previous public comment periods showed nearly universal support among organic businesses and consumers for the rule, with 99 percent in favor of the rule becoming effective. 

89 million U.S. adults purchase organic on a regular basis. Consumer willingness to pay the organic premium relies on a strong USDA Organic seal and having confidence that organic products meet rigorous standards. Animal welfare is an important part of consumer expectations for organic products. In fact, a recent consumer insights study found that more than 70% of shoppers who regularly purchase organic dairy products such as eggs cited animal welfare as a leading motivator for purchasing organic. Additionally, 61% of Millennials - are the largest demographic of organic consumers - cite animal welfare as a key component of organic. More broadly, the vast majority of dedicated organic shoppers identified dynamic progress and continuous improvement in the organic standards as important to them.

As demonstrated by the most recent consumer data, USDA's revised cost-benefit analysis on the OLPP rule wrongly estimates that the costs of higher standards outweigh the benefits. As a member of the organic business community, I know that the benefits of the OLPP rule and strengthened animal welfare standards outweigh the costs. Underestimating the economic benefits and value that consumers place on strong, consistent and clear standards such as the OLPP harms the entire organic market.

The private sector works hard to uphold the integrity of the organic seal, but we need the government to keep up with us in setting organic standards that honor consumer trust in that seal. USDA's failure to implement the OLPP final rule jeopardizes consumer confidence in the organic label, and could cause catastrophic impacts that ripple throughout the organic industry.

From 2010-2015, 3,217 manatees died in Florida waters, which is 53% of the highest minimum population ever recorded (6,063 in 2015). Breeding probability and survival rates would have been negatively affected by these events.The model that weighed heavily in the FWS decision, "predicts that it is unlikely that the southeastern U.S. population will fall below 4,000 total individuals over the next 100 years, assuming current threats remain constant indefinitely." But threats won't remain constant, they'll increase.

Florida law fails to reach the majority of boaters with education requirements and the state still lacks boater licensing. Compliance with existing speed zones averages only 54%.

FWS should be working to restore the Ocklawaha River, which would provide winter habitat for hundreds of manatees, and working closely with state water management districts to restore historic flow and water quality at springs throughout Florida.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I strongly support humane care and access to free range pasture for all our farm animals

Thank you for considering my request.

I am writing on behalf of Taxpayer Advocacy Services, Inc. to provide professional comments on the proposed regulations relating to the establishment and administration of Trump accounts under Section 530A. While the objective of fostering early-life savings is commendable, several technical and administrative aspects of the proposed rules present significant concerns for taxpayers and tax practitioners.

1. Verification Risks for "Authorized Individuals"
Under Proposed § 1.530A-1(c)(1)(i)(B), the IRS establishes an ordering rule for who may open an account (guardian, parent, sibling, grandparent). Relying solely on a "penalty of perjury" representation without documentary proof creates a high risk of intra-family litigation and "account poaching" in fractured households.

Recommendation: The IRS should provide a "Safe Harbor" for trustees and tax preparers who rely on these representations and clarify the specific documentation required to "prove" a higher-priority individual is "unavailable."

2. Barriers to Entry for Nonbank Trustees
Proposed § 1.530A-1(b)(2)(iii) automatically approves nonbank trustees active before 2026 but requires a rigorous new application for others. This "grandfathering" could create a market monopoly, leading to higher fees for low-balance accounts.

Recommendation: Lower the net worth requirements for new nonbank trustees specifically for Trump accounts to encourage competition and ensure that fee structures do not erode the $1,000 pilot program contribution.

3. Lack of a "De Minimis" Error Correction Window
The "growth period" rules are exceptionally rigid. A single "prohibited transaction" or an ineligible investment could lead to the total disqualification of the account's tax-exempt status.

Recommendation: We urge the inclusion of a "Self-Correction" period (similar to the Employee Plans Compliance Resolution System) allowing responsible parties to reverse inadvertent errors—such as exceeding the $5,000 contribution limit—within 90 days without penalty.

4. Privacy and Opt-Out Design (Section 6103)
The preamble notes that Section 6103 prevents the IRS from automatically opening accounts (an "opt-out" design). This significantly disadvantages children of taxpayers who lack the digital literacy or professional help to navigate Form 4547.

Recommendation: The IRS should explore a "Conditional Opening" process where the Secretary initiates the account, but the "Responsible Party" is finalized only upon the first tax return filing, bridging the gap between privacy and participation.

5. Succession of the Responsible Party
The proposed rules are vague on what happens if the "Responsible Party" dies while the beneficiary is still a minor. Relying on "State law" (Proposed § 1.530A-1(d)) creates a patchwork of 50 different standards.

Recommendation: Establish a uniform federal standard for "Successor Responsible Parties" to prevent accounts from being frozen during probate.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important regulations. Taxpayer Advocacy Services, Inc. remains committed to ensuring the tax code is administrable and fair for all Americans.

I have been using event data recorder (EDR) data to help investigate and reconstruct vehicle crashes since the early 2000s. EDR data is immensely valuable to properly and thoroughly understanding a crash event. It has great value whether it is used for criminal prosecution (or defense), civil lawsuits or to help better understand vehicle crashes. For all of those reasons, I applaud and support NHTSA's proposed rule here. Having 20 seconds of pre-event data, recorded every 0.1 of a second, would allow me to better understand the entire crash event. This additional data is valuable in all aspects of crash reconstruction and analysis. I use EDR data regularly for both criminal justice purposes and for my private crash investigation company. The addition of 15 seconds of pre-crash data would give me more confidence in my analysis of what are often complex crash events.

Although I do support this proposed rule wholeheartedly, I would strongly implore that NHTSA make other minor changes to this rule. The rule was last changed almost a decade ago, and the amount of data that a vehicle captures about a crash event has grown exponentially during that time. NHTSA should consider expanding this rule to cover all newly manufactured vehicles (without limiting them to passenger vehicles under a certain weight). New electric vehicles, such as the Rivian R1T, are over the 5500 pound limit mentioned in the current rule, exempting them from the rule. (Rivian apparently does not plan on voluntarily complying with Part 563 as of today.) Surely a vehicle such as that was meant to fall under the umbrella of 'passenger vehicle'. I also think that NHTSA should expand the data tables in part 563.7 and 563.8 to include new, emerging data elements. Any video or photographs captured by the vehicle should also be stored in a crash event and available for retrieval.

The Minnesota Disability Law Center (MDLC) is Minnesota's Protection and Advocacy (P&A) system and includes the Client Assistance Program (CAP). Acting through our CAP, MDLC informs and advises people with disabilities of services and benefits available to them through programs authorized under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, as amended, and helps people with disabilities in their relationships with such programs. 

With respect to Proposed Priority 1, entitled "Innovative Rehabilitation Training Project, Client Assistance Program," We do not believe the approach in Priority 1, which is similar to that in Priorities 2 and 3 governing the vocational rehabilitation training program, will adequately meet the specific needs of our CAP staff. The needs of CAP personnel are significantly different from the targeted beneficiaries of the other proposed priorities. 

For example, the proposal focuses on developing a proscribed training curriculum in the first year, with a focus on training within an academic setting. Re: Comments on NOAA-NMFS-2020-0057 
Subject: Proposed Rule to Modify North Atlantic Swordfish and Shark Retention 
Limits 
 
 
To Whom It May Concern, 
The Delaware Nature Society (DelNature) appreciates the opportunity to 
comment on the above referenced project. We have several comments regarding 
this project: 
 
North Atlantic Swordfish (Xiphias gladius) rely on external reproduction 
and water temperature is thought to play an important role in hatching 
success. As ocean temperature grow warmer it is unknown how this will 
affect Swordfish (SF) populations. Tiger Sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) are 
ovoviviparous, so consequently their eggs are less vulnerable to 
temperature change. However, overall reproductive biology of Tiger 
Sharks (TS) is not well understood. Due to the uncertainties of 
reproductive needs of these species, DelNature urges caution in 
raising retention limits for these species. 
 
SF and TS are large carnivores and sit atop the oceanic food chain. 
Consequently, overfishing of these species may have deleterious effects 
as species lower on the food chain as herbivorous species become 
overabundant, leading to denuding of critical nursery sites such as coral 
reefs and beds of sea grass. 
 
The Proposed Rule change would allow for in-season adjustments of 
retention and take limits. Likely the data for these adjustments would be 
gathered from catch and bycatch reporting gathered by commercial 
fishermen incidental to their harvest activities. These data would not be 
gathered in a scientifically rigorous manner and should not be used to 
determine TS and SF bag limits. 
 
Alternative B3 of the Proposed Rule Change would allow for a bag limit of 
up to 18 SF per trip, three times the current limit. This increase appears 
excessive and flies in the face of caution. 
 
Several dockside studies of Caribbean fishing crews covered by the three 
permits to be modified showed that many were not aware that the 
permits existed. Although NOAA’s data suggest that SF quotas are 
currently not reached in the North Atlantic, given the dearth of oversight 
and harvester’s lack of knowledge regarding permitted take, it is likely 
that current surveys undercount the number of SF taken. 
 
Given the uncertainty of future stresses on these species and current lack 
of comprehensive knowledge of their current status, DelNature 
requests NOAA refrain from increasing take limits for SF and TS.

 
Thank you for your consideration of DelNature’s comments on this proposed 
rule. We are not requesting a Public Hearing.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most effective conservation laws in the United States. Ninety-nine percent of listed species have been saved from extinction, including iconic species such as the bald eagle. The law is also widely popular; polling shows that 90 percent of voters across the political spectrum support the law. The proposed changes to the statute will weaken the law and put thousands of plants and animal species at risk. 

Proposed changes will allow federal agencies to not acknowledge the broad consequences of their actions through changes to the consultation requirements of Section 7 of the Act. Section 7 consultations require that a federal agency that is funding, authorizing, or conducting an activity to consult with the Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service to ensure that the activity does not jeopardize the existence of endangered or threatened species or destroy their critical habitat. The proposed changes will reduce the effects of agency actions required to undergo consultations. For example, the proposed rule seeks comment on changes that would stop consultation for effects like climate change that are manifested through global processes. The changes proposed will also make it harder to protect critical habitat that is being impacted by development. The protection of even small sections of habitat is crucial for species conservation. The proposed changes would allow death by a thousand cuts by ignoring impacts to species critical habitats unless they impacted the entire habitat at once. If the mechanisms for enforcement of the protection of endangered and threatened species and their critical habitats are weakened, species will be put at greater risk. 

I urge you not to move forward these proposed changes and leave the regulations to one of our most effective and popular conservation laws untouched. Please withdraw the proposed changes to section 7 (Interagency Cooperation) rule. CFR Citation: 50 CFR Part 402 / Docket ID: NOAA_FRDOC_0001

Dear Secretary McCaffery: 
 
The National Military Family Association has long been an advocate for improving the quality of life 
of our military family members, who have sacrificed greatly in support of our Nation. We believe it 
is vital to protect the health and safety of service members, retirees, their families and survivors 
while ensuring they can access high quality medical care. For that reason, we appreciate the 
opportunity to provide comments on the Interim Final Rule (IFR) addressing TRICARE coverage 
and payment for certain services in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. 
 
As the novel coronavirus spreads across the United States and around the world, military families, 
like other families, are following the guidelines set by the Centers for Disease Control and 
Prevention (CDC) and staying home as much as possible. While limiting travel is essential to 
controlling the spread of the virus, it has led many military family members to delay essential 
medical care. Up to 50 percent of available appointments at Military Treatment Facilities (MTFs) 
have gone unused since the declaration of the national emergency, and civilian providers are also 
reporting lower numbers of patients. 
 
These statistics are concerning. We fear for military families’ long-term health outcomes if they 
continue to defer essential care. However, it’s also crucial to limit the number of patients in MTFs 
and providers’ offices, in order to reduce the risk of infection to both health care workers and 
beneficiaries. Increasing the use of telemedicine is one answer to this problem. We commend the 
Defense Health Agency (DHA) for taking steps to expand access to and coverage of telemedicine. 
The measures included in the IFR – allowing telemedicine to be provided via audio-only devices, 
loosening licensure requirements and waiving cost shares and co-pays for telehealth – are 
important steps to protect the health and safety of military families and health care workers. 
 
While these steps are essential during the current national emergency, we encourage DHA to 
consider making the expanded coverage of telehealth permanent. As patients and providers 
become more accustomed to and comfortable with telemedicine, we expect demand for this method 
of providing health care will only increase. In addition, as the pandemic eases, MTFs and network 
providers are likely to see a surge of patients seeking treatment that had been delayed. This 
anticipated demand surge is even more worrisome given the financial pressures on the civilian 
health care system; we must expect that some network providers may not be able to remain viable. 
Continuing the expanded coverage of telemedicine that has been allowed during the emergency 
may ease some of the stress on the system by allowing providers to treat patients more efficiently 
and expanding the pool of available providers.

 
We are pleased the IFR notes plans to review the costs and benefits of audio-only telehealth; we 
hope that review also includes a study of patient and provider satisfaction and health outcomes. We 
also encourage DHA to explore ways to maintain less restrictive licensure requirements for 
providers after the end of the national emergency. In particular, we urge DHA to review its
