I rely on on-package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised" I assume that there is value and meaning behind that claim and that is backed by a regulatory agency.

Imagine my surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allowmeat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS, and these companies will maintain the right to use those labels through self-regulation. Companies will still be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit.

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Time and time again industry has shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating/policing itself. Companies are taking advantage of consumers, and grossly overcharging them, by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels to bring in more profits all the while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare.

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers.

I respectfully submit the following comments concerning the proposed rule from the Departments of Homeland Security (DHS) and Health and Human Services (HHS) on the care of immigrant children (Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002).

I am concerned that the proposed rule is contrary to the language and underlying purpose of the 1997 Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA) to ensure that all children in the government's custody are "treated with dignity, respect, and special concern for their particular vulnerability as minors." I am concerned that the proposed regulations will undermine necessary safeguards protecting children in DHS and HHS custody, exposing them to harm. I urge DHS and HHS to revise the proposed regulations so that they adhere to both the language and purpose of the FSA.

Detention of Minors

I am opposed to the proposed rule providing for the indefinite detention of minors, including in family detention. As the rule acknowledges, the federal court has made clear that children in family units are covered by the FSA, including its limitations on holding children in detention for more than 20 days. 
Researchers, doctors, and mental health professionals have pointed to overwhelming evidence indicating that children held in immigration detention suffer significant, often permanent, psychological harm.
I favor maintaining the existing limitations on detaining children, including children held in immigration detention with family members.
Cost-Benefit
I believe that the cost-benefit analysis undertaken in the proposed rule is incomplete and fails to consider the substantial fiscal costs of family detention. As the proposed regulation notes, various changes in the proposed regulations concerning long-term family detention, the alternative federal licensing process, and parole determinations "may increase variable annual [Family Residential Center] costs paid by ICE." The proposed rule further notes "DHS acknowledges that this rule may result in additional or longer detention for certain minors." However, it declined to specify the additional potential costs because of DHS's uncertainty over how many individuals may be detained in family detention facilities.
The failure to consider these additional costs of detention undermines the cost-benefit analysis, particularly considering the availability of cheaper, effective alternatives to detention.
In addition, if there are any benefits of detaining children with their families for long periods of time or indefinitely, these will likely be outweighed by the costs.
Licensing
I am concerned about the new federal licensing framework in the proposed regulations. Consistent with the FSA, the proposed regulations require that facilities holding children are licensed. And, as the proposed rule notes, many states do not have existing licensing frameworks for family detention facilities, making it virtually impossible to license such facilities.
While the creation of an alternative federal licensing scheme helps fill these gaps, it leaves oversight to unspecified third-parties, which would audit such facilities. This leaves many unanswered questions: What third-parties will be conducting audits of such facilities? What standards will be applied by those third-parties? How will DHS and HHS provide oversight over the third-party auditors? I would favor modifications to the proposed regulations to answer these concerns and spell out the federal licensing scheme in greater detail to ensure that children are adequately protected and that the facilities are held to high standards related to the care of children.
Relaxing standards
I am concerned that the proposed regulations provide for broad exemptions to existing child protections by expansively defining the terms "emergency" and "influx." Existing conditions along the border likely would meet these standards, and would permit DHS and HHS wide discretion to be exempted from meeting established standards of care.

Darling 58 is enhanced with an added gene for an enzyme called oxalate oxidase (OxO) which neutralizes or detoxifies oxalic acid produced by an invasive fungus, Cryphonectria parasitica (C.parasitica), introduced to the United States in the early 1900s and responsible for killing over three billion American chestnut trees throughout their natural range. This OxO gene is naturally-occurring in wheat and other grain species, and allows the Darling 58 tree to coexist with C.parasitica, minimizing harm to the tree. It does not kill the fungus, nor does is have the potential for direct or indirect injury to, damage to or disease (7 CFR 340.3 plant pest risk) the fungus. 

I am strongly in support of APHIS granting non-regulation status (per 7 CFR part 340) to the Darling 58 transgenic tree based on the fact that it is not lethal or damaging to the fungus, and based on extensive study, it is unlikely to pose a plant pest risk.

This proposal focuses on what is best for the manufacturers, not the public who will have to pay for devices that have little perceived value. Page 3858 in the section titled "Estimated Costs and Benefits" indicates that the breakeven point would not occur until 5 to 10 years after the start of this program. In addition, the proposed standard indicates in the future this V2V technology will be required "on vehicles produced during earlier model years." Consumers will not be pleased paying higher prices, repairs, and back-fitting their older vehicles with no foreseeable near-term benefits. Therefore, this mandate will probably fall into the same category of "if ever". 
A critical mass does not need to be huge. A few thousand vehicles properly prototyped could refine the technology, plus demonstrate that driverless cars can and will dramatically reduce the vehicle accident rate. The focus should be on reducing accidents in the most effective way that meets the needs of society, not industry. 1, Consumers should not have to pay for V2V communication technology and the costs to maintain the ancillary sensors and dashboard displays;

A prototype test facility would replicate, in an area of about 2 to 4 square miles, the configuration and conditions that drivers encounter when traveling in and between small cities. Dear Members of the Review Committee: 
 
As Chief of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at Northwestern and an esophagologist who has advocated for 
patients with complex esophageal diseases requiring esophageal function testing, I strongly encourage CMS to 
reconsider the proposed APC assignment for CPT code 91040 in the 2026 HOPPS rule. 
 
Mucosal-attached telemetry pH monitoring (CPT 91035) and impedance planimetry (CPT 91040)—are clinically 
homogeneous in their procedural intensity, diagnostic purpose, and patient population. Both are performed 
during upper endoscopy, require similar technical expertise, and are used to evaluate esophageal function in 
patients with dysphagia, non-cardiac chest pain, or suspected motility and reflux disorders. The two approaches 
provide a patient focused approach that removes painful catheters and the anxiety and trauma associated with 
these tests. They are both extremely accurate in defining various components of esophageal function and are 
used to guide therapeutic decisions and surgical planning, particularly in complex cases such as achalasia or post-
fundoplication assessment. 
 
It is therefore concerning to see CPT 91035 assigned to APC 5724 while CPT 91040 is placed in APC 5723. This 
discrepancy does not reflect the clinical similarity or resource utilization of these procedures. Aligning their 
placement in APC 5724 would better support the integrated, physiologic approach we now take in esophageal 
diagnostics—an approach that prioritizes precision, efficiency, and patient-centered care. I urge CMS to 
reevaluate this classification to ensure reimbursement accurately reflects the value and complexity of these 
complementary technologies.

This is my formal notice of objection to the proposed regulation that prohibits pack llamas (camelids) in Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR). I request that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service refrain from identifying camelids (pack llamas) as a disease threat and remove all reference in the proposed regulations and planning documents that implicate them as a disease threat, especially on page 20084:

 36.39 Public use.
 (d) Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
We prohibit all domestic sheep, goats, and camelids on the refuge.

Pack llamas are a historical user group in the ANWR. However, we were not informed of the 2015 public review process. We should have been included in the discussion that resulted in losing our access to this public land.

Last fall, the Chugach National Forest Land Management Plan included language that banned pack llamas. Our community raised objections, and the reviewing officer, David E. Schmid, Regional Forester, responded by removing the ban. Furthermore, he wrote:
"I am also instructing Forest Supervisor Schramm to remove references to llamas (or lamas) as potential vectors for the transfer of pathogens to Dall sheep or mountain goats from the FEIS."

The CNF reviewing officer recognized that there was no scientific basis for the ban. The idea that camelids are a disease threat to wildlife is scientifically untenableas our community has proven, time and time again and to every division of our public land managers. This current attempt to prohibit a historical user group from recreating on the ANWR is arbitrary and has no scientific basis. It does not align with the recommendations of the Western Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (WAFWA) and does not match the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) regulations, neither of which prohibits the use of camelids in Alaska. And yet, not only did the USFWS, in this current proposal, fail to provide credible scientific evidence that implicates camelids as a disease threat in ANWR or prove that camelids pose a greater disease transmission risk than horses, but the document instead included wild speculations about theoretical dangers posed by camelids (see page 20033).

The fact that alternative pack animals were banned in a document overwhelmingly focused on opening up hunting and fishing opportunities also seems disingenuous. If domestic livestock are considered to be such a risk to the wild animals to which you are opening access, then horses and mules should logically also be banned from the ANWR. And if those wild populations are so threatened by livestock, perhaps they are not robust enough to warrant this document's main priority in the first place: to open up National Wildlife Refuges to hunting.

I have been a recreational llama packer in the state of Colorado since the age of 4 and my family has been in the pack equipment manufacturing business since 1985. I have been the editor of Pack Animal Magazine, a publication highlighting the use of alternative pack animals, since 2013. I am well acquainted with llamas as pack animal and we, as an industry, would be happy to provide the Objection Reviewing Officer with further documentation regarding the lack of risk posed to wildlife by pack llamas. Extensive documentation can also be found on the website www.packllamas.org.

Please remove any accusations of camelids as being a disease threat from this document. Thank you for your consideration of this objection.
Sincerely,
Alexa Metrick, Editor
Pack Animal Magazine

My name is April Tovar, and I am a student at Oregon State University working toward my undergraduate degree in Natural Resources Policy and Management. Throughout the last 4 years at this university, I have come to appreciate maritime history throughout the world. That is why I am writing in support of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) proposal to designate 1,724 square miles of New York’s eastern Lake Ontario as a National Marine Sanctuary. Designation of this site would preserve thousands of years of history dating back to the settlement of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, which consisted of five different indigenous tribes, to the most recent European settlers. This site was collectively nominated by community-based initiatives in several counties including, Oswego, Jefferson, Cayuga, and Wayne. 

This historic site houses 43 known shipwrecks and one aircraft. Additional research from NOAA suggests that there could be additional shipwrecks and aircrafts still to be discovered. Lady Washington, a sailing vessel from the late 1700’s to the early 1800’s, is located within the proposed area in Lake Ontario. Lady Washington was the first American-flagged vessel to visit Japan, Honolulu, and Hong Kong in the late 1700’s. This sailing vessel also aided the maritime trade with indigenous people and trades of tea and porcelain in China. It is important to keep these artifacts intact to provide education for communities and protect the area's long cultural history. Designating this area would not only provide protection to these maritime artifacts, it would also allow us to explore, learn from and share the history that is rooted in Lake Ontario. 

Thank you for allowing public input and taking the time to consider designating Lake Ontario as a National Marine Sanctuary. Implementing this protection will ensure that important history is protected while still allowing for recreation activities such as diving and fishing to occur in the sanctuary. I encourage NOAA to establish Lake Ontario as a National Marine Sanctuary to allow for further exploration, recreation and preservation of hundreds of years of history. 

Sincerely, 
April Tovar

My name is Laura Deehan, Public Health Advocate with CALPIRG. 

As a statewide consumer group, our message is simple: A rollback of money-saving national fuel economy standards and the rights of states to set greenhouse gas emission standards would hurt the health and finances of hard working California families.

We support the current national vehicle fuel economy and emissions standards and the rights of states to lead on vehicle emissions reductions. 

Today, 13 states and DC, over one third of the automotive market, have chosen to exercise their right to bring cleaner, more efficient vehicles to their communities. 

A rollback of national standards and the rights and freedom of these states to adopt their own clean air standards means Californians, who have the second highest cost of gasoline in the country will be saddled with more polluting, less efficient cars, trucks and SUVs that will cost them more at the pump.

Right now, the national and state vehicle emissions standards are improving public health and protecting consumers pocketbooks across the nation. The Consumer Federation of America, of which were a member, has been tracking the benefits of fuel economy standards for more than a decade, as cars have become more efficient, consumers save money at the pump. Someone who bought a new car in 2017 is saving on average about $220 a year right now. Since the standard was put in place, it has saved Californians almost $4 billion. 

And, savings will continue to grow if we simply leave the standards alone. In addition to direct savings at the pump, adding in the larger economic benefits, spurred by consumers spending money saved on fuel on other goods and services, helping the environment and reducing pollution, the total is over $1 trillion. 

By 2030, that translates to an additional $3,550 in the bank account of each California household. We will reap these benefits so long as policy makers stay the course.

The fact is that we are enjoying the cleanest, most fuel efficient and safest cars, trucks and SUVs in history. Recent research from Consumer Federation of America found that the average number of advanced safety features in new vehicles is increasing as fuel economy technologies are also added. The fuel saving technologies pay not only for themselves, but for these safety advancements and new high-tech features as well.

The financial health of consumers is often tied to physical health. This rollback threatens both.

At CALPIRG, we stand up to the powerful interests that threaten the livelihoods and well-being of Californians. The evidence shows that oil companies - arguably one of the most powerful interests in the world - would be the only ones to benefit from this rollback.
 
There is no reason to throw these standards in reverse. Doing so would force Californians into less efficient cars that cost them more money at the pump. We want a future of safer, cleaner and more fuel efficient cars, trucks and SUVs. We want families to be able to breathe clean air and free up that money for other needs, not burn it at the pump, where its sent out of our state and overseas. 

To ensure this, we strongly urge the Environmental Protection Agency not to roll back or weaken common sense fuel economy and emissions standards that are helping millions of Americans breathe easier and save money at the pump. We also ask that state authority to lead on these standards, now and in the future, be protected.

Thank you again for the opportunity to speak here today.

I respectfully ask that you please help protect the Banggai Cardinalfish. I support an immediate ban, under the Endangered Species Act, on the U.S. import and sale of Banggai cardinalfish.
 
This species has been heavily exploited for the past three decades to supply the aquarium trade. But the science is clear: It can’t survive the constant barrage of collection from the wild. Several populations have been extirpated, and the ones that remain are small and isolated. Banggai cardinalfish have already declined by up to 90% and continue to decline today.

These fragile swimmers, who reproduce slowly, are particularly ill suited for trade. About 75% to 80% of individuals collected from the wild die before being exported. This necessitates taking large quantities from their habitat to have enough living fish to meet demand. 

NOAA Fisheries has determined that cardinalfish are at risk of extinction — but this extinction is preventable. As a leading importer, the United States can take an important step by banning their import and sale under the Endangered Species Act.

There’s no time to waste. Please act swiftly to extend Endangered Species Act protection to this imperiled species.

As patient advocacy organizations, we are writing to comment on the above-captioned payment rule (CY 2018 MPFS Final Rule). We oppose the CMS policy on Payment for Biosimilar Biological Products that assigns shared codes to multiple distinct biological products. We believe this Rule to be inconsistent with efforts to ensure the safety of all biologic medicines, and likely to result in fewer treatment options and higher costs to patients. We urge CMS to reconsider this policy, and instead assign each and every biologic and biosimilar medicine its own distinct payment code. 

Biosimilars offer new treatment options and lower costs to the patients we represent. But the CMS Rule as it stands undermines this shared goal: 

First, it disproportionately prioritizes cost among the many factors that go into making a treatment decision. These include whether or not a biosimilar was approved for a particular indication; whether its comparability to the reference product was ever demonstrated by studies in that indication or whether its effects were merely extrapolated from studies in different indications; whether the FDA determined the biosimilar is "interchangeable" with its reference product (producing the same effects without additional risks); product features such as ease and frequency of administration; the quality of patient support programs; the degree of discomfort associated with injections; whether it can it be administered at home; and whether it will be consistently available (not subject to shortages). These are important patient considerations above and beyond the simple price paid. 

Second, the use of a shared identifier for multiple different biologic products implies an identicality between them which does not exist and an interchangeability between them that may or may not have been demonstrated. For this reason, both the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and World Health Organization (WHO) have recognized the need for clear product identification among biologics and biosimilars, and have proposed differentiating them with a four-letter suffix. The CMS Rule stands in stark contrast to the policies of these regulators. Its merging of distinct products into a single payment code could put patients at increased risk of adverse reactions and/or suboptimal treatment.

The National Family Farm Coalition, representing thousands of family farmers, ranchers and fishermen and farmworkers, disagrees with the statement: "The Agency's evaluations to date have provided evidence that most genetic engineering techniques, even those that use a plant pest as a vector, vector agent, or donor, do not result in a GE organism that presents a plant pest risk."

For a time, Bt corn was considered a means for killing the corn rootworm. However, it has also been linked to the deaths of livestock, humans and beneficial insects, including ladybugs and honeybees, while becoming less effective over time.

Meanwhile, farmers have cumulatively lost millions of dollars due to cross-pollination and contamination of their non-GM crops by GM varieties. There are even instances when APHIS knew of GMO outbreaks and failed to contact the farmers who would be impacted negatively. 

The herbicides that are sold with herbicide-resistant GM seeds have become increasingly deadly, particularly as they are applied more and more regularly in combinations of two or three. This has led to more than 100 superweeds and reduced biodiversity among wildlife and heirloom or indigenous crops.

It is time for the US Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service to take the roles of importation, interstate movement and release of genetically modified organisms much, much more seriously, not less. The safety of our food supply, the health of our environment and the wellbeing of our rural communities - where most GMOs are grown and harvested - depend on careful and stringent assessment and oversight.

I reside in Ohio. My family has owned a seasonal cottage on Pelee Island, Ontario for more than 80 years. These flights typically carry 2-6 passengers and no cargo. Eliminating the fee exemption enjoyed previously by small air carriers will make it prohibitively expensive for Americans, like myself, to access their properties and will irreparably harm small businesses like Griffing Flying Services.

All of the islands in the Western Basin of Lake Erie (most of which are located in the U.S. side of the lake) share a common ecosystem. Invasive species introduced into this area have come from ocean-going freighters emptying ballast water into the Great Lakes, not from Americans traveling to and from their cottages on Pelee Island. Fees to fund agricultural quarantine and inspection services should be borne by the commercial vessels and aircraft most likely to introduce invasive species into the U.S. – commercial shipping, trucking, railroad, and air cargo carriers – not small passenger carriers making short trips within a single ecosystem. Accordingly, the exemption from fees for small commercial passenger aircraft should not be removed from the rule.

I am an American citizen studying as a PhD student in the Philosophy department at Princeton University. Many of my colleagues (about 40%) are international students and scholars, and many of them would be immediately affected by this rule. Furthermore, this rule would have an immediate impact on our ability to recruit the best philosophers from abroad. Philosophy PhDs as currently constructed in the US currently take at least five years for almost all students. People simply won't be drawn to Princeton, even with its generous funding package, if they have no guarantee that they will be able to finish out the program when they enter.

At present, the 3 places generally considered the best places to do philosophy graduate school are all in the US, and indeed are all within about an hour's drive of each other--NYU, Rutgers, and my own Princeton. Much of the best philosophy in the world is done within this small radius, because the best students from all over the world see that these are the places where they will best be able to develop their talents. As a coordinator for pro bono legal services representation for detained immigrants in CA, I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Docket: AMS-NOP-19-0053, NOP-19-02, and/or Regulatory Information Number (RIN) 0581-AD83
Subject: 205.605Nonagricultural (Nonorganic) Substances Allowed as Ingredients in or on Processed Products Labeled as "Organic" or "Made With Organic (Specified Ingredients or Food Group(s))"
Pullulan

Comment: 
It would be much more accurate to describe pullulan as an agricultural substance (nonorganic) allowed as ingredients in or on Processed Products Labeled as "organic" or "made with organic".

Reasons:
Pullulan is an intracellular adhesive produced by fungi Aureobasidium pullualn and Aureobasidium melanogenumto for binding their cells together. Pullulan producing fungi exist naturally in soil and orchard trees. 

Although fungi are not "crops" in scientific term, but for practical reasons, they are treated as "crops" by regulatory bodies worldwide as humen harvest and grow mushrooms (fungi) as foods for a long time. 

The practices of growing pullulan producing fungi is not different than proactices of producing mushrooms such as Agaricus bisporus, the common white mushroom. The only difference is we harvest the caps and stipe of the white mushroom as food and harvest intracellular adhesives of fungi Aureobasidium pullulans as food. 

To enhance the efficiency of growing Aureobasidium pullulans, we innoculate the fungi on substrates of starch, sugar and nitrogen containing substance instead of on its naturally growing environment of soil and orchard trees, same as we grow edible mushrooms on manure, rye meal, vermiculite and sawdust. 

Some may argue that pullulan is produced in an stainless steel vat instead on s growing bed for mushrooms. The reasons to grow fungi Aureobasidium pullulans in vats are: 1) the necessity of constant agitation that providing oxygen to the fungi growth. Without agitation, the fungi Aureobasidium pullulans will either not grow or die off quickly due to lack of oxygen; 2) containment of the spores of the fungi. For similar reasons, we grow edible mushrooms on various artificially growing enviornments to enhance its growth and containing its spores.

As to harvest pullulan, you just add water into the growth substrate to dissove pullulan, then separate pullulan from fungi cells and unutilized substrates. The extraction of pullulan from its fungi cells is almost same as we extract sugar from beets and sugar cane.

Therefore, growing fungi Aureobasidium pullulans is still an agriculatural production in essence. 

To organically produce pullulan, we grow fungi Aureobasidium pullulans on certified organic starch, sugar and nitrogen souce and use only NOP organic allowed substances and practices. The nonorganic pullulan is produced on non organic substrate and use substances that best fit for their commerical production. 

Therefore, it is more accurate to decribe pullulan powder as an agricultural and nonorganic substance instead of a nonagricultural and nonorganic substance.

I have read the proposed rule to de-list Borax Lake Chub published in the Federal Register (FR) 

on February 26, 2019 and the Post-Delisting Monitoring Plan (PDMP). 

I am in general agreement that some threats have been reduced or eliminated and some excellent 

recovery work has occurred. However, I have major concerns about delisting, described below, 

and do not support the decision to de-list at this time. These concerns can be grouped as: 1) 

inadequate understanding of population age structure; 2) inadequate understanding of 

mechanisms influencing recruitment and survival; 3) an illogical conclusion that although high 

temperatures are hypothesized to negatively influence population size, a 2.4˚C increase in 

temperature from global climate change is not a threat; and 4) no acknowledgment that the 

biogenic mound supporting Borax Lake is susceptible to slope failure during seismic events. 

There is discrepancy in the literature regarding age and spawning between Williams and Bond 

(1983), which is mostly cited in the FR on these subjects, and Scoppettone et al (1995). 

According to Scoppettone et al (1995), females live to 10 years and males to 6 yr (Figure 1).

probability bias against larger (and smaller) fish - which “has important implications for age‐

structure and demographic studies” (Peterson et al 2015 North American Journal Fish manage 

35: 491-502). Small fish (<35 mm TL) were three times less likely and large fish (>60 mm TL) 

were two times less likely to be captured than medium sized fish (35-59 mm). These biases need 

to be accounted for when statements are made about age or size structure of a population. Based 

on Table 1, the three size classes used in recent studies equate to: small= Age 0, medium=Age 1 

(mostly) or Age 2, and large=Age 2-10. In 2015 and 2016, large, Age 2-10, fish made up 38.4%

with slower growth after maturation. Why is the population apparently resilient? If these fish live

To whom it may concern: 

Please consider these comments in further rulemaking decisions regarding the computation of 

Total Potential THC (TP-THC) as well as other total potential cannabinoids measured using 

Liquid Chromatography (LC) methods. 

I applaud efforts to achieve a more accurate and fair computational method of determining TP-

THC when tested with LC methods. Historical conversion factors presume 100% of the molar 

mass of each acidic cannabinoid is converted to its non-acidic for, which has been shown to be 

flawed in multiple cannabinoid decarboxylation studies. However, there are several important 

implications the USDA should consider before making a final determination on this subject 

matter. 

First, Mei Wang, Yan-Hong Wang, Bharathi Avula et al. (2016) and other researchers provide 

some evidence that less than 100% of the molar mass of acidic (carboxylated) cannabinoids will 

convert to the non-acidic (decarboxylated) forms of their respective counterparts. Wang, Wang, 

Avula et al. (2016) studied THCA to THC, CBDA to CBD, and CBGA to CBG in multiple 

samples. 

That said, there is also some evidence that conversion occurs at different rates where the amount 

of mass converted may depend on time, energy constants, and other factors not well documented. 

Much research to date was done with a very small number of samples of less than statistically

 
significant size (n<30). Furthermore, the proposed conversion factor of 52.62 percent both 

understates the estimates found by current research and is overly-optimistic at best. In fact, it 

appears to underestimate the highest document conversions by about 17%. 

A rulemaking with implications of this magnitude should not be done without further study, and 

there does not appear to be evidence that I am aware of that supports the proposed conversion 

factor of 52.62 percent. The USDA should commission a larger, controlled study of conversions 

before making any final decisions. 

Second, the DEA, FDA, and USDA should all agree on the conversion factors for TP-THC as 

well as conversions for CBCA to CBC, CBDA to CBD, CBDVA to CBDV, CBGA to CBG, 

CBNA to CBN, THCA to THC, and THCVA to THCV. All three of these regulatory agencies 

have some oversight with cannabis and cannabis-derived products, and a common set of rules for 

all agencies is beneficial to the agencies and the industry as a whole. 

Third, we have particular interest in conversion and recording of total potential CBD since CBD 

toxicity is well documented in animal models and we are focused on hemp-based animal 

nutrition. Therefore, whatever decisions the USDA makes have implications on the animal feed 

industry as it relates to hemp.

Science has made tremendous advances because theories (about disease, cures, and behaviors of living things) have been tested through scientific research, both through surveys and through experiments. We know one research study of a matter is never enough. Studies need to be repeated by other scientists and submitted to expert review to see if the studies are comparable in method and to what extent one study confirms the findings of the first. Knowledge is developed and advances are made by constant study and review of the same. Society and science have made amazing progress in healing our people and planet over the years by these methods.

 Free scientific access to and use of pertinent research data is essential to these studies. I am writing in opposition of the proposed rule change by the Homeland Security Department.

If the goal is to truly harmonize fees and application procedures then the time has come to fold Global Entry and SENTRI into one program. As explained in the supplementary information, there are only a few differences between these two programs and it would make sense to combine it into one under one fee structure. This could, at the very least, help eliminate some of the cost concerns and help justify the additional proposed cost for Global Entry members.

Secondly, I propose DHS update its definition of a family pulled from PORTPASS to be inclusive of LGBTQ families. Most states along the southern border have legalized same-sex marriage. Should this change go forward, it would be prudent to allow same-sex couples with children to enjoy the same privileges.

Finally, I am strongly opposed to the fee structure proposed by DHS. I will reserve my specific comments about the massive increase for NEXUS users for the separate federal register. However, the government notes here that the NEXUS Program exempts all minors from payment of the application fee. If CBP and its Canadian counterpart, the Canadian Border Services Agency, can process applications for an individual for $50 and a family for just $100 while also splitting revenue then CBP should be able to do the same for Global Entry and SENTRI users.

CBP and DHS go to lengths to point out the cost to administer these programs. It seems to forget that it also receives cost savings from users of this program. A CBP officer can screen more people who participate in these programs than people who do not. Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Although I eat meat, dairy, and eggs, I try to consider humane practices when choosing food. I try to eat "clean" to avoid pesticides and herbicides, but I also I would like to know that my choices are not causing undue harm and distress to animals and that they live as naturally as possible. I would like to know that the standards that are in place are meaningful..

Thank you for considering my request.

This comment applies to the informed consent for all drug-test recipients as required for pre-employment, random testing, or after an incident/accident. The test administrator MUST have the recipient read and sign an electronic form that fully explains the purpose of the test in accordance with DOT Rule 49 CFR Part 40 Section 40.193, the shy-bladder procedures, and that a refusal, as defined in the regulation, will mean likely revocation of the recipient's DOT/FAA/USCG certificates. 

In my current role as vice-chairman of the NTSB where Board members serve as appellant judges for airmen and mariners facing certificate revocation, we see too many cases where the test recipient is either poorly informed or does not understand the ramifications of a refusal. This should be rectified by having both test administrator and recipient sign an electronic form that clearly shows that the proper procedures were followed. The benefits to the recipients is obvious and for the government, it should significantly reduce the number of emergency revocation cases that are contested.

These comments are based on my observations during my four years on the Board and do not represent the official view of the NTSB. Thank you for the consideration.

Please take into account the damage done to fisheries by Chinese fishing fleets and offshore wind, and levy sanctions and/or fines accordingly. China has emerged as the world’s largest exploiter of fisheries on a global, not just regional, scale. Chinese fleets are active in waters far from China’s shores, and the growth in their harvests threatens to worsen the already dire depletion in global fisheries. China leads the world in seafood production from aquaculture, inland (freshwater) fisheries, and marine fisheries. The expansion and modernization of fisheries is a key part of China’s broader industrial policy goals 
of upgrading their agricultural industries and improving domestic food security. China has developed the world’s largest fishing fleet of vessels operating in domestic and neighboring coastal inshore and offshore areas, as well as a distant-water fleet (DWF) active in many parts of the world. China is a major hub for value-added processing in seafood supply chains and it is the world’s largest seafood processor. The magnitude of China’s seafood production and consumption has implications for international trade, fisheries conservation and management, and allocation of fishery resources among 
fishing and coastal nations. Many in Congress are interested in China’s involvement in fisheries around the world because of efforts to conserve marine resources globally, and the fishing industry’s intersection with regional conflicts and transnational criminal activities that impact U.S. national security. 
National and international efforts to manage fisheries are weakened by Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated (IUU) 
fishing, both within Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) and on the high seas. IUU fishing may diminish the benefits 
of fisheries management and contribute to overfishing. IUU fishing generally refers to fishing activities that violate 
national laws or international fisheries conservation and management measures. For example, licensed vessels may 
operate in violation of national laws within EEZs, misreport harvest, or not comply with regional fisheries 
management organization (RFMO) measures in high seas areas outside of national EEZs. Unlicensed vessels may 
operate illegally within EEZs, or participate in unregulated fishing in areas managed by RFMOs (Figure 1). IUU 
operations may violate basic safety standards and deny crew members’ fundamental rights, such as agreed-on 
terms and conditions of their labor. IUU fishing is also sometimes associated with other illegal activities such as 
drug trafficking, labor exploitation, and organized crime. However, the United Nations Food and Agriculture 
Organization and U.S. definitions of IUU fishing are specific to fisheries laws and resources while other types of 
illegal activities are subject to other national laws and international agreements. 
According to the National Intelligence Council, IUU fishing, along with surging worldwide demand for seafood and 
declining ocean health, pose an existential threat to global fisheries.7 Precise estimates of the global scale of IUU 
fishing are difficult to quantify in financial terms, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration 
recognizes that “there is little disagreement that it is in the billions, or even tens of billions, of dollars each year.”8 
One recent study estimated that gross revenues associated with unreported fish catches worldwide potentially 
generate $9 billion to $17 billion in illicit proceeds annually; the study further estimated corresponding economic 
impact losses due to the diversion of fish from the legitimate trade as costing $26 billion to $50 billion annually 
and potential losses to countries’ tax revenues worth approximately $2 billion to $4 billion annually. Please review the 2022 congressional report on this and levy sanctions against China accordingly, as well as grant bills of marque to offshore fishermen who destabilize Chinese fleets: https://www.congress.gov/crs_exte

As an instructor for a CBP Broker exam preparation course for the past 9 years, I would like to submit my 
comments in regards to the proposed rule published on September 14, 2016. In my opinion, there are 
several proposed changes that should be reviewed more closely by CBP prior to issuance of a final rule. 
 
First, with regards to the change in exam date from the first Monday in April and October to the last 
Monday in April and October, I do not see this as being a problem for the industry. 
 
Second, with regards to moving the current written examination to an electronic version, I believe that 
this is a positive step by CBP and will be welcomed by the trade. However, there are several concerns 
with this move. Primarily, it is in the best interest of the trade community that a practice exam be given 
to a select group prior to going “live” with the exam. This group should consist of individuals familiar 
with the test who would be available to provide feedback to CBP concerning the format, environment, 
etc. I also noted that another commenter suggested providing a sample electronic exam on the CBP 
website for potential test takers which would allow them to maneuver through the exam and become 
comfortable with the program prior to taking the actual exam. I support this suggestion. 
 
Third, concerning the proposed exam increase, I believe that this is an unrealistic increase which will 
deter individuals from taking the exam. It is noted in the FR Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that most 
customhouse brokerage businesses would not feel the effects of the increase. It is important for CBP to 
understand that the vast majority of individuals taking the exam pay for the exam personally and are not 
reimbursed by their company. I have been teaching an in person course in the Boston area for 9 years 
and can attest to the fact that the majority of the students pay individually for the exam. In fact, given 
the low pass rates for the exam, most individuals take the exam more than once. At a cost of $200, 
individuals are inclined to take the exam multiple times. However, at the proposed increase to $390, 
the students I spoke with indicated that they would be reluctant to take the exam multiple times. 
 
Fourth, with regards to amending the regulations to not include the option for a special examination, I 
do not believe that this is in the best interests of the trade. There should continue to be the regulatory 
option for allowing a special examination in the case of extenuating circumstances, including weather 
issues, technological issues or a specific event at a certain port that could result in the examination not 
being held on the appropriate day in April and October.

I believe that one of the biggest changes that will help is the tailored dosing. When I was prescribed opiates in the past I was lucky to have the benefit of knowing how addictive it is to not feel pain and that there is not one dose that works for everyone. This is something that plagues the entirety of our healthcare system. For example, if I go into the hospital with nausea I am given a 25 mg tablet of promethazine yet, I only generally take half of a tablet . I have taken them before and a whole tablet was not needed and just adds to the side effects, the same is true with opiates, even the Dr looks at you funny if you crack apart a pill in the Emergency Room. 

 People often take their medicines as prescribed by the Doctor, because they trust them to be correct. If they are told they need 5 mg of hydrocodone they take 5 mg, instead of tapering up from 1/2 a tablet or 1/4 of a tablet at a time until the pain is manageable. Also, one of the other issues I have seen is that alot of people have no idea what PRN means. When a person sees that they should take a one Vicoden every X amount of hours PRN they believe it is the same as being told to take Amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hrs. Sure, in the office the Doctor may tell them as needed but when they read the bottle to them it says something different because of the way it is worded. I have seen alot of elderly patients get confused by this especially when taken multiple medicines.

 I believe that instead of turning opiates into this evil thing if we can just tailor doses and still prescribe them frequently in small amounts at small dosages we would do a world of good in helping to treat pain while still trying to control the potential for addiction as opposed to looking at them as if they are evil or even a last resort in most cases. 

 My biggest problem with the last resort method is it puts a stigma on something that truly can help and sometime forces people to have to take pain relievers that do more harm than good like prescription NSAIDS for those with stomach issues or steroids for people who are diabetic. We have reduced our arsenal of helpful drugs and are now prescribing things that may be more dangerous. Also, when we remove those two there are very few medications left to actually treat pain. 

 In conclusion, I believe we should keep opiates fairly accessible but in small doses, with alot of information on what is "As needed", change the labeling, and use them for as short a time as we possibly can and make sure that people are doing therapies while on these medications. Opiates are not the problem our inability to properly administer the medication and monitor the patient is. We hand them the medication and throw them out the door, when they come back as an addict we then wondered how this happened and then point the finger at a medicine. 

 With smaller doses and fewer pills and proper patient monitoring and repeat visits for pain management instead of assembly line doctoring we could prescribe opiates quite often and still see a major reduction in addiction.

As an education researcher working with school and district leaders, I know firsthand the advantages of having access to data provided by the Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC). The CRDC is the nations largest and most comprehensive source of education data, and one of the most actionable sets of data collected by the U.S. Department of Education. Districts and schools often do not have the human or financial capacity to collect school and student data, hindering their ability to make targeted resource decisions, see how they compare to peers, and measure progress over time.

The data points the department proposes to eliminate (e.g. school finances, whether teachers are in their first few years on the job, student discipline) are needed to help educators, researchers, and advocates enforce civil rights laws and ensure we are building more equitable schools. The CRDC is the only data source that shows school level expenditures across the country. Funding disparities across school districts continue to persist. Nationally, districts serving the most students of color receive about 13% less per student than districts serving the fewest. In most states, children who live in low-income neighborhoods attend the most under-resourced schools. School financing data is crucial because research confirms that school spending matters more money leads to better outcomes, especially if spent well and spent in schools serving students with the highest needs. 

We also know from research that low-income and students of color have less access to experienced teachers. According to the Learning Policy Institute, in schools with high enrollments of students of color, nearly one in every 6 teachers is just beginning his or her career compared to one in every 10 teachers in schools with low enrollment of students of color. Without tracking first-year teachers, it will be much more difficult for districts to assign and support novice teachers. This is important, because teachers with stronger qualifications (content knowledge, certification in the field taught, experience) produce higher student achievement. 

Without tracking data on out-of-school suspensions by demographic subgroup, it will be much more difficult to calculate inequalities in discipline. Discipline data has consistently shown that Black students are more likely to be disciplined than their peers. They are suspended or expelled three times more frequently than white students. These disciplinary actions result in missed instructional time and disengagement, leading to lower academic performance. They also put students at higher risk for negative life outcomes, including involvement in the criminal justice system. Recent literature suggests that the disproportionately negative outcomes of discipline policies for students of color directly contributes to their overrepresentation in the justice system - youth of color make up over 60% of children detained by juvenile justice systems.

It is clear that we have far to go in regards to building a more equitable education system. These are just three areas in which we see persistent disparities in terms of race and ethnicity in our education system. This is why it is absolutely critical that the U.S. Department of Education continue to collect this information. The department was created in part to "collect data on America's schools" and "prohibit discrimination and ensure access to education." Please ensure that the department continues to deliver on that promise.

• 

Integrity – Integrity of the USDA organic seal is important. We strongly urge USDA to ensure organic products of 

American origin and their foreign counterparts are produced and sold under the same strict standards. Provisions of 

the proposed rule aim to do this, in exchange for increased monitoring. We hope that these new requirements result 

in fewer fraudulently-labeled products sold in the United States. 

• Education and Time – New requirements come with a learning curve. As a result, it is important that USDA provide 

growers impacted by this rule sufficient time, guidance and education to ensure that the regulated community 

understands the changes, and have time to comply, prior to the final rule going into effect. 

• Exemptions – We support the proposed rule change which narrows the list of entities not required to hold organic 

certification. These exemptions should be limited, and based on activities where there is a low risk of compromising 

organic integrity. 

• Minimizing Fraud – We appreciate the proposed provision to require the mandatory use of National Organic 

Program Import Certificate. We recommend that the 30-day timeframe for certifiers to issue certificates be 

shortened to maximize the potential for successful traceability. It also makes sense to align the import certification 

with the Customs and Border Protection deadline for uploading to the Automated Commercial Environment system.

the overall goal of the new provisions. We support improving current recordkeeping requirements as a way to 

prevent organic fraud. Foreign producers selling organic products in the U.S. must meet equivalent record keeping 

standards just like our domestic producers.

fraud to occur is important to making sure that American producers, operating in accordance with strict organic standards, 

will not be disadvantaged by those who are not.

Animals living in institutional settings like a commercial breeding facility or research lab are at high risk in the event of an emergency or natural disaster, and it is vital that these animals are considered in disaster preparation. There is currently no federal requirement for facilities regulated under the Animal Welfare Act (AWA) to have emergency response plans in place to care for their animals in case of emergency. I strongly support the USDA’s proposal to move forward with implementation of this requirement for facilities regulated under the AWA to have contingency plans ready to protect the animals in their care.

Overall, this is a great proposal, and long overdue. As a frequent flyer, it has been frustrating to see the proliferation of poorly behaved pets presented as emotional support animals in recent years. To be clear, I believe emotional support animals can and do provide legitimate health benefits, but it is troubling and confusing that, with respect to air travel, they are afforded the same accommodations as service animals without being subject to similarly rigorous training, behavioral, and documentation requirements. Once on board an aircraft, the ability for airline personnel and passengers to manage an aggressive, disruptive, destructive, or sick animal is limited. In that context, it's important that reasonable risk mitigation steps are taken before boarding. 

In particular, I support the proposals to:

- No longer consider an emotional support animal to be a service animal - lumping these two distinct groups together is misleading and poses a safety hazard, as airline crew and passengers may be under the mistaken impression that emotional support animals are appropriately trained and medically necessary
.
- Consider a psychiatric service animal to be a service animal and require the same training and treatment of psychiatric service animals as other service animals 

- Continue to allow airlines to require that service animals be harnessed, leashed, tethered, or otherwise under the control of its handler - this precaution helps protect the health and safety of passengers and flight crews

- Continue to allow airlines to refuse transportation to service animals that exhibit aggressive behavior and that pose a direct threat to the health or safety of others - it is reasonable to subject all animals, including service animals, to common sense behavioral, health and safety restrictions similar to those imposed on passengers.

I believe improvements could be made to the proposals to:

- Define a service animal as a dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability - limiting service animals to dogs may unduly restrict disabled individuals with legitimate service animals of other species. Any service animal that meets the training, behavioral, and health requirements should be considered a service animal regardless of species. 

- Allow airlines to require a service animal to fit within its handler's foot space on the aircraft - again, this may unduly burden some individuals with legitimate service animals. I support the AFA's comments that airlines should be allowed to limit the size (or weight) of service animals based on aircraft type, but I also suggest that airlines should be required to accommodate passengers with larger service animals if the passenger has purchased additional seating sufficient to keep the animal out of other passengers' space.

The proposal appears to be silent on this issue, but I believe that airlines should be expressly permitted to require passengers with service animals to have a means of containing or restraining the animal if it becomes necessary for the health and safety of others on board.

The Automotive Safety Council (ASC) is an industry trade association of 48 of the world’s leading 

suppliers of Autonomous, Crash Avoidance and Occupant Protection automotive safety systems to the 

automobile industry. The mission of the Automotive Safety Council is to improve the safety of people 

through-out the world through the development, production and implementation of the latest automotive 

safety equipment by preventing accidents, protecting occupants and pedestrians when in a collision and 

to notify emergency responders after the collision when necessary.

The ASC is providing comments to the recently published RFC document requesting comments 

pertaining to Shoulder Belt Requirement for Side-Facing Seats on Motorcoaches. The ASC appreciates 

the opportunity to comment on this topic.

 
Overall Comments:

We fully support the goal to provide the same level of crash protection to all vehicle occupants. In this 

spirit there is concern whether adequate protection is provided for occupants in side-facing seats when 

compared to the protection for occupants in forward-facing seats. As demonstrated in the tests 

referenced in the August 18, 2010 NPRM (Docket NHTSA-2010-0112) “The unbelted dummies and lap 

belted dummies generally exhibited higher injury values than dummies secured with lap/shoulder belts” 

for forward and oblique loading conditions. For side facing seats the NPRM proposed to “permit lap 

belts in side-facing seats because we are unaware of any demonstrable increase in associated risk”. 

In the absence of any significant epidemiological research done to improve our understanding of the 

injury risks and countermeasure needed to protect occupants in side-facing seats, we are not confident 

that either lab belts, or lap/shoulder belt systems alone provide adequate protection for side-facing 

occupants. Regardless of whether these petitions for temporary exemption are granted, we urge the 

NHTSA to promote further research toward understanding injury risk in side-facing seats, and to 

establish performance based safety standards to ensure adequate occupant protection - not only side-

facing seats in motorcoaches, but also future passenger cars:

 Passenger vehicles with side-facing seats (one of several unconventional seating configurations 

anticipated for highly automated vehicles) are generally subjected to more severe crash pulses 

than motorcoaches and will likely be produced in larger volumes. 

 Limousines – which may in the future, be subject to the same Federal standards for safety belts, 

seats, and seat assemblies as other passenger cars (ref. House Bill H.R.2 Moving Forward Act, 

Sec. 32006).

Specific Comments:

1. To consider the level of protection offered by shoulder belts for side-facing seats, it is necessary 

to also consider the location of the D-Ring with respect to the occupant. The D-Ring location 

dictates how the shoulder belt is routed across the thorax of the occupant. A D-Ring located 

toward the rear of the vehicle from the occupant positions the shoulder belt such that it may slip 

off the occupant in a frontal crash, providing little (if any) additional restraint in a frontal crash 

from what is offered by the lab belt alone. Likewise, a D-Ring located toward the front of the 

vehicle from the occupant places the shoulder belt in a more favorable position to provide 

additional restraint, but also could introduce added injury risk.

As an advocate who is directly impacted by a neuromuscular disease, I am writing regarding the Department of Transportation's recently published Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on proposed regulations that will make lavatories more accessible on single aisle aircraft (Docket ID: DOT-OST-2021-0137-0003).

Overall, I am happy DOT is finally proposing rules that will make lavatories more accessible on single-aisle aircraft. It's long overdue. Currently, many individuals living with a neuromuscular disease face significant challenges when travelling, including around issues with inaccessible lavatories. Some people living with a disability have no choice but to dehydrate themselves in preparation for flying because existing aircraft bathrooms are wholly inaccessible, or they may simply forego traveling altogether due to the myriad challenges presented by air travel. Having an accessible restroom, including allowing space for a care attendant, on these airplanes will remove this major hurdle for the disability community and make traveling easier. I applaud these proposed changes! 

In saying that, I urge DOT to speed up the deadline airlines have to make these necessary changes to single aisle airplanes. In the proposed rule, the Department will mandate airlines begin providing an accessible lavatory on aircraft ordered 18 years after implementation or delivered 20 years after implementation. This would result in the disability community waiting almost two decades for an accessible bathroom on single aisle aircraft. This is unacceptable. Those living with a disability have waited long enough. 

Thank you again for this historic, proposed rule. It will go a long way in making air travel more accessible for the disability community. I hope the final rule, when published, will include a quicker deadline for implementation.

Dear CMS,
We greatly appreciate being allowed to comment on the proposed rule as well as anything else we feel will enable us to care
for our patients.

In response to the non-hospice spending section of the proposed rule, if hospices will be expected to manage medications and
other non-hospice related costs, this should be reflected in the calculation of the rate of reimbursement. Adding maintenance
drugs could be especially burdensome for hospices.

In response to the data gathering at admission as well as the current face to face visit requirements, it is currently our practice
to gather sufficient data from referral sources to demonstrate appropriateness for certifying the terminal illness. However, as
had been pointed out in previous comments, it is common practice for medical decisions to be made based on the RN assess-
ment and documentation everywhere in healthcare, but oddly enough not in hospice. The Registered Nurse, experienced in
hospice, knows more about what constitutes a terminal prognosis than most general practice physicians or hospitalists.
Hospice RNs are able to assess a multitude of signs and symptoms, as well as take history that would support a terminal 
prognosis. In thinking about our own practice in particular, our physicians are working long hours as it is, and it would be pretty
much impossible for them to have to take time out for being on call for our 50 to 60 hospice patients, in addition to their 
general practice patients, to make a face to face visit for a possible new admission. In regards to the current face to face 
policy, it is unnecessarily burdensome as well, because, once again, a pre-admission evaluation (which is not billed for under
the hospice benefit) by the RN should be sufficient to support a terminal prognosis if that evaluation so indicates, and the 
practice of relying on RN documentation to make medical decisions is followed.. Plus the requirement to have a completed 
face to face visit within 24 hours on an emergency admission for a patient that would be entering their 3rd benefit period or 
later, does not seem to be a reasonable amount of time. The patient, if needing an emergency admit, must be actively dying 
or in some severe distress that needs controlled. If the patient dies before the face to face is completed, that would show that
certifying them as terminal was appropriate. If the patient stabilizes, then this would permit time for the face to face to be 
completed.

I think we all expected the development of an assessment tool that would impact payment similar to the OASIS to happen 
eventually. HEART looks to be a good idea, but we would want to make sure that the data collected would accurately reflect 
the patient acuity and cost to the hospice. Hopefully this tool will not add too much to the burden of the admitting nurse, so it 
would either need to stand alone as an admission assessment, or be streamlined and not take an undue amount of time if it is
to be in addition to an admission assessment.

Introduction. 
General Motors LLC (“GM”) submits these comments in response to the National 
Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s (“NHTSA” or the “agency”) Supplemental 
Initial Decision (“SID”), dated August 5, 2024, that Certain Frontal Driver and Passenger 
Air Bag Inflators Manufactured by ARC Automotive, Inc. (“ARC”) and Delphi 
Automotive Systems LLC (“Delphi”) Contain a Safety Defect.1 The SID contemplates 
ordering a sweeping recall of approximately 51 million frontal driver- and passenger-side 
hybrid toroidal air bag inflators manufactured by ARC and Delphi from 2000 through June 
2018. The SID contends that an entire population of inflators, manufactured over nearly 
20 years, contains a defect related to motor vehicle safety under the National Traffic and 
Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, see 49 U.S.C. § 30101 et seq. (“Safety Act”), based on 
seven airbag inflator ruptures that occurred over the span of several decades. Those 
ruptures have no systemic common cause and involve inflators that were manufactured on 
over 20 different production lines. The SID further contends that the purported defect 
presents an unreasonable risk of harm even though the agency itself predicts that only one 
future rupture will occur in the inflator population over the next few decades and makes no 
effort to assess the countervailing costs of a recall. 
Styled as a “supplemental” decision that “confirms” the conclusions in NHTSA’s 
September 8, 2023 Initial Decision (“Initial Decision”),2 the SID is—in almost every 
way—a fundamentally different decision. The agency’s proposed recall scope has changed 
for a third time, once again by millions of inflators, and a new vehicle manufacturer that 
was not included in the Initial Decision has been added.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

The labeling must be and accurate and truthful !

Thank you for considering my request.

I am writing in support of the proposed rule 2021-25467, revoking the exemption of the roadless rule for the Tongass National Forest, and restoring the roadless rule to the Tongass. 
The proposed action should be regarded not only in the local context, but in the context of all North American forests. I grew up in central Indiana, where forests in virtually the entire state were eradicated 200 years ago. In 1967, I went on a fishing trip by float plane in Ontario, 200 miles north of the Minnesota border. I clearly recall the broad landscape of forest and lakes, stretching to the horizon. In 1999, I took my own sons to the same lake, flying over the same terrain. I was shocked to see that the entire forest had been clear-cut over the 200 miles from International Falls to Lake Latreille, leaving only a thin rim of trees around each lake. Whatever habitat and whatever wildlife had existed there was destroyed. The long post-glacial forest succession of the past 10,000 years was abruptly interrupted. The ecosystem that will now develop after the logging will be different, with deciduous trees replacing pines. All of the life adapted to the pine forest, from bacteria to insects, birds and bears will also be radically changed. The Great North Woods is gone forever. During my own lifetime, the forests of Michigan and Minnesota were also cut down. The economy of paper mills and trucking companies briefly flourished, then shut down when the trees were gone. Human demand for wood and paper greatly exceeds the capacity of nature to replace what has been cut.
The Tongass is the largest remaining island of pristine American forest. The area at issue in the National Forest is large, at about 17 million acres. But much of that area is rock and ice; only a fraction is forest. A smaller fraction is old-growth forest, and an even smaller fraction is large-tree old-growth forest, which is the most productive biological habitat and the most desirable forest for logging. (1) Over one-quarter of the large-tree old growth forest in the Tongass has already been cut. Over one-third of the karst forest has been cut, and two-thirds of the landscapes with continuous stands of trees have been cut (2). Recent biological research has emphasized the importance of continuity of habitat for ensuring the health of an ecosystem. Further logging in the Tongass would create isolated islands of habitat, insufficient for biological diversity and interbreeding for long-term health of wildlife. 
It takes about 300 years to restore a clear-cut forest to an old-growth condition.(1) Even at that, the disruption and introduction of new species virtually guarantees that the former condition is never restored. Roads, by themselves, allow migration of invasive species and pests. Roads also allow legal and illegal human development and interference with wildlife, particularly in the form of hunting and poaching. (1)
The number of jobs maintained by logging in the Tongass is trivial, only a few dozen. And these jobs have only been economically viable due to Federal subsidies to build and maintain logging roads and infrastructure. The American taxpayer has literally been paying to destroy wilderness habitat in the Tongass. (1) It would be a better use of the taxpayer dollar to simply give the money to the loggers and sawmill workers, instead of building roads. 
The Tongass is the last remnant of North American forest that once covered much of the continent. For the sake of future generations, for recreation, for subsistence, for biological knowledge and for nature’s own sake, we should protect what remains of this forest. I strongly urge Secretary Vilsack to restore the roadless rule to the entire Tongass National Forest. 
D. R., Anchorage, AK
