To whom it may concern:
RE: Comments on Proposed Legislation 

I am submitting this comment in support of AMS-NOP-0065. I have a solid understanding of this area of law, as I am a second-year law student at the University of Mississippi who comes from an agricultural background, grew up in a rural community, and have worked for organizations that had to meet legislative health and compliance standards. 

The proposed rule has many benefits, the most impactful in my opinion being the heightened scrutiny this piece of legislation will require inspecting agents to use in ensuring compliance by organic operations of the federal organic standards. 

While I am in full support of the proposed legislation, I have two recommendations:

 1. Section 204.403(b)(1) of the proposed legislation states, "A certifying agent must, on an annual basis, conduct unannounced inspections of a minimum of five percent of the operations it certifies, rounded up to the nearest whole number." While I agree with the substance and overarching goal of this proposed section, personal experience working for agencies subject to unannounced inspections has shown me that with such a low percentage of required unannounced inspections, operations may be tempted to "take the gamble," as even if 5% of all operations are subject to unannounced inspections, that leaves very good odds for the other 95%. I would propose that the number be raised to 10%. For an inspector with 20 operations, that is 2 unannounced inspections per year instead of 1. For the inspector with 100 operations, that is 10 unannounced inspections instead of 5. While this may seem insignificant, it doubles the number of unannounced inspections per year, while also not over-burdening the inspector. This would reduce the operations' potential desires to "risk the odds," but would not be overly burdensome to the inspectors responsible for conducting the unannounced inspections. 

 2. 205.406(b) of the proposed legislation states, "The certifying agent must arrange and conduct an on-site inspection, pursuant to § 205.403, of the certified operation at least once per calendar year." While this is an excellent and necessary piece of legislation to dispel any uncertainties found in the vagueness of our current legislation, and it ensures that each certified operation gets inspected at least once a year, I would argue that once a year is not enough to ensure adequate compliance. If an operation knows that their inspector is coming on "x" date, then they do not necessarily have to keep their organization strictly "by the books" if they can tweak how they operate closer to time in order to pass the compliance test. I have seen this first-hand, and while we would hope that our farmers and producers hold the same values as we do, many individuals are swayed by greed and slothfulness and will opt for the easy way out, even if it means bending the rules at the detriment of others. As such, I propose that the legislation be changed to say "twice per calendar year" instead of "once per calendar year." Inspections every six months, along with the chance of unannounced inspections, would greatly increase the odds of operations' compliance with the legislative standards, which in turn would ensure quality organic products for the American public. Integrity must be upheld among our farmers and producers, not just for the safety and trust of the American people, but also to preserve the sanctity and reputation of our nation's agricultural industry. 

Sincerely, 
Jacob D. Hamm

I support the removal of Brucella abortus from the select agent list. My background and connection to this issue is that I am a strong advocate for wild, free-roaming bison (buffalo).

The last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

There is currently no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

Thank you for your consideration of my comments.

On behalf of the Division of Lands and Forests at the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), we submit this comment in strong support of the petition for nonregulated status of the blight-tolerant Darling 54 American chestnut (Castanea dentata), developed by the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry (SUNY ESF). 
 
The Darling 54 tree represents a promising opportunity to restore a foundational species that was once dominant in the forests of New York and the eastern U.S. Chestnut blight devastated ecosystems and economies, and we view this biotechnology-driven restoration approach as both scientifically rigorous and ecologically responsible. 

We appreciate that SUNY ESF has invested considerable effort not only in developing blight tolerance, but also in maintaining genetic diversity in the chestnut trees they propagate – an essential component of long-term forest resilience. Their transparency, commitment to conservation, and history of collaboration on other forest health efforts give us confidence in their work. 
 
We also support USDA-APHIS’s preliminary finding that Darling 54 does not pose a plant pest risk. The OxO gene does not provide a competitive advantage beyond what pre-blight chestnuts possessed and is already common in the environment. There is no indication that this tree would behave invasively or disrupt natural systems. 
We believe Darling 54 could play a valuable role in forest restoration across New York, especially in areas where other canopy species have been lost due to invasive pests and pathogens. We are eager to facilitate experimental plantings and long-term use of a chestnut as a restoration tool on public and private lands. 
We encourage USDA-APHIS to move forward with granting nonregulated status and appreciate the opportunity to comment.

flood-prepared communities, I thank you for the opportunity to offer comments on FEMA’s proposed 
rulemaking, “Factors Considered When Evaluating a Governor’s Request for Individual Assistance for a Major

The Disaster Relief Fund (DRF) created under the authority of the Stafford Act has long served as an important 
safety net, offering assistance to individuals and communities dealing with the consequences of severe weather 
events and other types of disasters. Whether used for Individual Assistance or Public Assistance, the Fund was 
created as a complement to state and local resources in cases which clearly exceed local and state capacities for 
response. In our view, the proposed criteria, which consider the level of damage as well as the level of effort 
and state capacity, will allow FEMA to make well-reasoned spending decisions at a time when pressure to 
reduce federal expenditures is strong. 
 
While the current rulemaking is focused solely on Individual Assistance (IA), as required by Section 1109 of 
the Sandy Recovery Improvement Act of 2013, we were pleased to see that FEMA also intends to propose 
changes to the factors used for consideration of Public Assistance (PA) requests. We believe that reasonable 
updates to both sets of factors will help to address the growth in federal disaster spending and, at the same time, 
create incentives for states and local communities to prepare for extreme weather events and invest in flood 
mitigation. 
 
As you know, the language from Congress called on FEMA to revise the current factors related to level of 
“trauma” and other conditions that FEMA assesses in making recommendations to the President regarding the 
severity and magnitude of a disaster and the need for Individual Assistance Funding from the DRF. While 
Congress specifically called on the Agency to make changes that would provide “more objective criteria,” 
clarify thresholds for eligibility, and speed declaration decisions, it did not alter the Stafford Act’s prohibition 
against denial based solely on the use of an arithmetic formula on income or population. Nor did Congress 
change the Act’s overall objective of offering federal financial assistance as a complement, rather than 
supplement, to state and local resources. 
 
We see the Agency’s proposal as a reasonable balance of these multiple objectives, and we strongly support the 
consideration of state and local response capability via the Total Taxable Resources or State Gross Domestic 
Product factor, data on the “Cumulative Effect of Recent Disasters,” and information on “Planning After Prior 
Disasters.” Taken together, these data points will help the Agency to consider the expense of a given disaster 
within the broader context of ongoing state efforts to prepare for and mitigate against disaster damage. We 
understand that the Total Taxable Revenue indicator is not, of itself, a perfect indicator of response capacity but

The main factor that has affected the Monito Gecko is the introduced and invasive population of black rats that was discovered in the early 1980s. While rats are known to be predaceous feeders on both lizards and lizard eggs, there is no conclusive evidence provided in the supplementary information that suggest it is truly the cause of Monito gecko population decline. It should also be considered that the effect of black rats on geckos on nearby Mona and Desecheo Islands has not been well studied. 

Original population studies conducted in 1983 by Dodd and Ortiz and in 1984 by Hammerson failed to recognize the nocturnal behavior exhibited by Monito Geckos which resulted in lower counts per unit area. The 2016 systematic gecko survey, which involved observation of 40 random plots covering a 16,000 m^2 conducted at night, yielded a much higher gecko count and may have been a more accurate representation of actual population size. Because of the possible gap in available data of accurate population counts over time, it may be harder to track whether the the Monito gecko has truly recovered and if the removal of the rats from the island had statistically significant effects on population size. 

While the removal of the Monito Gecko from the Federal List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife may be justified, it is important to recognize these uncertainties and approach this bureaucratic action with caution. Assuming that recovery has truly been achieved, Monito Island should continue to be protected by the Puerto Rico Department of Natural and Environmental Resources as a nature reserve with tight restrictions on who is allowed to visit to prevent the reintroduction of the black rat. If the correlation of black rat introduction and decline of the Monito gecko is correct, its return could mean 30 years of conservation work down the drain.

Subject: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002 - Public Comment Opposing Proposed Rule

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed regulations relating to the implementation of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), DHS Docket No. ICEB-2018-0002. In short, the regulations contravene the principles driving the FSA - that immigrant children should be released from immigration detention as quickly as possible and that immigrant children are uniquely vulnerable and therefore deserve special protections and treatment under law. 

Indefinite Detention of Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would lead to the indefinite detention of children and would directly contravene a core principle of the FSA - that immigrant children must be released from detention as "expeditiously" as possible. The FSA calls for the release of a child from immigration detention within days, stating that the government must generally release a minor "without unnecessary delay." This regulation, however, would allow children to be detained with their parents through the entirety of their removal proceedings, which could mean children are detained for months or even years in immigration detention facilities. Volumes of evidence show the traumatizing effects of detention on children, and the considerable and lasting harm it has on their physical and mental health. Allowing indefinite detention of children is unacceptable.

Removal of State Licensing Requirements for DHS Facilities Holding Immigrant Children

The proposed regulations would also allow the government to sidestep state-licensing requirements of detention facilities holding children, leading to the removal of critical oversight over the conditions in these facilities. The FSA requires the government to expeditiously release children to a parent or other family. If neither is available, the government must release the child to a program licensed by a state child welfare agency program. The government seeks to avoid this requirement by self-licensing the facilities that would hold children and parents together, called Family Residential Centers or FRCs, rather than requiring that they be licensed by a state child welfare agency. Such a self-licensure is tantamount to the fox guarding the henhouse. The government lacks the impartiality and expertise to ensure compliance with basic standards relating to the care and custody of migrant children.

Sincerely, 

Susan Fernandois

Creating robust domestic and international marketing opportunities for U.S. producers of California walnuts and other specialty crops is under the direct administration of the Agricultural Marketing Service through regulation. 

The proposed rule in 7 CFR Part 984 allows that growers, handlers and the public continues to have a reliable supply and demand for walnuts especially under Marketing Order No. 984. The proposed reporting of nuts sold but not shipped monthly may bring into account unanticipated consequences.

The shipping point spot market traditionally purports that first handlers offer California walnuts in good quality and condition. The addition of nuts sold but not shipped creates wholesale lots of stock that may or may not be in good merchantable condition. Also, when there are time lapses without seller shipping the commodity, implied warranties may allow for orders to be automatically canceled thus erroneously maintained as part of the reporting inventory. It would behoove the AMS to consider a category such as "awaiting seller to ship" until the indicated shipping time (month) has passed. The reporting data could also be skewed because backorders represent any amount of commodity a grower or producer customer has ordered but has not yet received because it currently isn't available in inventory. Of course, just because there may be a lack of supply of inventory doesn't mean farm growers, handlers and others can't operate on backorder. In fact, many companies can still do business even it they don't have inventory on the books. The AMS needs to keep in mind that keeping products on backorder - such as product sold but not shipped monthly -does help boost demand, retain and increase the customer base and creates value for the commodity but it may also create a false inventory management analysis.

When growlers, handlers and the public are confronted with two equally good options, many struggles to decide, even though there is a possibility that both options are equally good. The AMS should proceed with caution and understand that the options here may or may not be equal when considering this rulemaking.

There are currently a number of federal technical assistance centers providing assistance to States on disproportionality, including significant disproportionality: IDEA Data Center (IDC), National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), and Center for Fiscal Reporting (CIFR). 

Adding an additional center is not a good use of taxpayer funds in that it is not an effective or efficient way to provide assistance to states or LEAs. Creating a new TA center requires funds for start-up and overhead; many of the existing centers already share personnel; and states will have to manage additional center contacts and webinars that overlap in both content and timing. As an example of the content overlap, it is impossible to separate the calculations for disproportionality from the data itself. IDC provides technical assistance to states on the collection, reporting, and use of child count, educational environments, and discipline data that are then used in the calculations for disproportionality. It would be a far better use of taxpayer dollars to expand the technical assistance on disproportionality currently offered by IDC, NCSI, and CIFR than to add on an additional center.

If an additional center is deemed necessary, their scope of work should include all areas of disproportionality, including SPP/APR indicators 4, 9, and 10. Confusion between the required methodologies would only be exacerbated by having one center focused exclusively on significant disproportionality. 

The biggest challenge at both the SEA and LEA levels is the differences in requirements for SPP/APR Indicators 4, 9, and 10, and significant disproportionality. Existing centers have developed and disseminated technical assistance in this area. Again, more assistance would be helpful, but not to the extent of needed an additional center. 

The second and third directed questions ask about supports for conducting the review of policies, procedures, and practices in LEAs as well as the root cause analysis. Here again, existing centers have created toolkits and provided technical assistance to both SEAs and LEAs in these areas.

The fourth directed question asks about the supports needed by SEAs to conduct the analysis of significant disproportionality. Technical assistance has been available to states in many forms through the existing centers. 

Finally, the fifth directed question asks about supports needed regarding CCEIS. Again, technical assistance is currently available in this area through CIFR and other TA centers.

In summary, technical assistance is readily available through several existing centers, several of which already share personnel and/or collaborate on the creation and provision of assistance to states. The creation of a new technical assistance center would, in theory, consolidate the resources, but at the cost of the additional overhead of a new center, and additional contacts and possibly redundant offerings to states that can become burdensome to manage and coordinate.

This proposed rule would create a significant burden on walnut handlers by requiring them to report purchase commitments. Although this requirement would provide more accurate information about supply and demand to industry, it would be creating an unnecessary barrier between walnut handlers and their supplier. A requirement to report purchase commitments is intrusive and although this can help provide more accurate information about supply and demand to industry, I do not think it helpful enough on its face to justify this rule being made into law. Before this proposed rule, it was only required that reports of shipments and receipts be filed by handlers on CWB Form No. 6 no later than the 5th day of the month following such shipments or receipts. This proposed change is said to be expected provide more timely information about supply and demand for walnuts, however I do not think the trade-off of requiring all purchase commitments to be reported to the agency justifies the mandate. Purchase commitments can be misleading because sometimes the actual shipments of walnuts can vary in quality and even sometimes quantity. Because of these factors, requiring walnut handlers to report their purchase commitments seems to be a waste of resources both of the citizen and the AMS that will not achieve the goal of being able to better predict supply and demand to industry.

Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Dear Administrator Andrew Wheeler,

I am writing to strongly oppose the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) proposal to restrict the science that is used in its decisionmaking processes.

In issuing this proposed rule, the EPA claims that it would be making science more transparent. But it instead would put researchers in the difficult position of choosing between protecting privacy and security versus allowing their work to be used in EPA decisionmaking. It would excessively burden EPA staff with reanalyzing data from each study used to support a rulemaking which is not only pointless as peer review already is a check on the work of researchers, but it would be resource intensive and time consuming.
 
The EPA's proposed rule has three fundamental flaws that render it unfeasible. 

First, the agency provides insufficient justification and analyses to support the rule. A rule change should be supported by facts, which this obviously is not. A rule change should bring about increased public health and safety. The proposed change will only weaken rules that keep the public safe.

Second, the proposal would restrict the agency's ability to implement and enforce mission-critical laws by blocking the EPA from using many kinds of scientific studies vital to its decisionmaking, including studies that rely on personal health data, confidential business information, intellectual property, or older studies for which the authors or data sources may not be accessible. Limiting the ability of the EPA to make informed decisions harms the public health and safety.

Finally, the rule would grant the EPA administrator broad authority to exclude individual studies or entire decisions from being subject to its provisions on a case-by-case basis, giving the administrator unprecedented power to decide what the best available science is. Giving the EPA administrator the proposed power will lead to corruption and destruction of best practice in determining EPA rules.

The rule does nothing to advance the cause of transparency in the broader scientific community. This issue is best addressed with the full involvement of scientists, science advisors, and scientific institutions, not designed solely by political appointees who have demonstrated far too little concern for the health and safety of the American people.

The EPA must not move forward with this rulemaking as it would undermine science-based decisionmaking at the agency, and limit its ability to protect public health and the environment.

Sincerely,
Carol Gocken
Edwardsville, IL 62025

Funding for High-Quality Dual Language Instruction Schools

We recommend that the Secretary establish a competitive preference priority for the replication and expansion of high-quality dual language instruction schools and improve access to facilities for such schools, provided support to such dual language immersion schools shall include distinct attention to schools taught primarily through the medium of a Native American language as established under the Native American Languages Act of 1990, Sec. 104 and 105.

In the context of Dual Language Immersion, high quality programs are those which ensure that at least half of the instructional day is taught in a language other than English, and furthermore, which use methodologies, program designs, and curricula which have been shown to foster better outcomes for students, especially low income or at-risk students. Factors to consider in assessing high-quality should include higher graduation rates and college attainment; improvements in academic achievement test scores; increases in retention rates, school attendance, well-being, self-esteem and resiliency to addiction and the prevention of other risky behaviors. At the same time, dual language immersion presents a host of challenges for all types of schools, including charter schools. Institutions of higher education located in the area may be uniquely suited to help address some of these challenges, including working closely with immersion charter schools to help facilitate early college enrollment of students. The Committee encourages the Department to consider these factors in granting awards. 

In response to a bipartisan and bicameral request by members of the Congress, the Commission on Language Learning of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences studied the status of language learning in the United States. The report, Americas Languages, outlines capacity building goals and important language education investments needed to ensure that our nation can compete in an increasingly demanding, diverse and complex global environment. Key findings identified in this 2017 report include:
 
 The United States lags behind most nations of the world, including European nations and China, in the percentage of its citizens who have some knowledge of a second language.
 Fluency in world languages, in addition to English, is critical to success in business, research, and international relations in the twenty-first century.
 Improved learning outcomes in other subjects, enhanced cognitive ability, and the development of empathy and effective interpretive skills have all been linked to the study of a second language.
 Delays in certain manifestations of aging have also been linked to the use of a second language.
 Native American languages are distinct in political status and history, and immersion schools are a best practice for educating Native American students.

This priority supports the 2017 Secretarys Final Priorities for Discretionary Grant Programs (Federal Register, v83 n42, pp. 9128ff) as follows:

Priority 1: Dual Language immersion programs support English Learner communities and Native American, Alaska Native, and Hawaiian learners directly. More importantly, extensive research evidence shows the differential benefit of immersion, with students who participate in immersions typically scoring a full year ahead of their peers, when SES and other factors are statistically controlled. (See for example, the research summary prepared for the Commission on Language Learning of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences: https://www.amacad.org/multimedia/pdfs/KrollDussias_April%205.pdf). Therefore, Dual Language Immersion supports sections (a) (iii), (iv), (v), (vii), (ix), and (x) specifically.

Concomitantly, the proven higher outcomes of high quality Dual Language Immersion Programs directly support Priority 2(d); as noted above, ample research evidence demonstrates improved educational outcomes for Dual Language Immersion.

To whom it may concern: 

I write to you regarding my concern that CPT 50590 (SWL) was removed from APC 

5375 and placed in APC 5374 in CMS's 2019 Final HOPPS/ASC Rule. There are multiple 

reasons why I find the CMS decision impacting Medicare patients and being potentially costly 

for Medicare's economics. 

As a practicing urologist, I operate on patients with kidney stones. The two procedures 

that I use most often are SWL and CPT 52356 and CPT 52353 (URS). They are clinically 

homogeneous and each has its following. My patients, however, generally favor the non-

invasive aspect of SWL and their ability to immediately return to normal activities post-SWL. 

With URS, on the other hand, most of my patients have a ureteral stent placed inside of them 

after their treatment. It hurts as bad as it sounds, most tolerate it poorly and it creates the need 

for an additional procedure or visit for its removal. 

In addition, URS patients have a higher rate of unplanned admissions after treatment than 

do SWL patients. With a higher complication rate than SWL and at least one study showing that 

10% of URS procedures fail because the stone cannot be found, why would CMS create a $1093 

disparity in reimbursement for the two procedures most similar in use? 

If your answer is "costs explain a justification for the difference," I would have to 

respond that hospital charges are not costs. As widely acknowledged, they are a fiction based on 
a charge master. What I do know is that a SWL machine costs around $500,000 and can be used 

on one procedure: 50590. My ureteroscope is less than $10,000 and can be used on many 

different CPT cases and the unintended costs to Medicare associated with unplanned admissions, 

complications, and stenting of URS are not insignificant. Perhaps hospital charges do not 

accurately capture SWL costs.

Re: Support for CMS-1716-P 

Dear Administrator Verma: 

I write today to thank you and express strong support for the Medicare Area Wage Index 

provisions included in the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Fiscal Year (FY) 2020 

Medicare Hospital Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS) and Long Term Acute Care Hospital 

(LTCH) Prospective Payment System Proposed Rule and Request for Information (CMS-1716-P), dated 

April 23, 2019. 

Under the current wage index, all 95 counties in Tennessee fall among the very lowest 

reimbursement rates in the U.S. The wage index has created a challenging environment that has 

negatively impacted the health care system in Tennessee. In fact, Tennessee has the second highest 

hospital closure rate in the United States. The fundamentally flawed wage index has played a key role in 

these closures. Without the relief CMS has proposed, Tennessee hospitals will continue to suffer and 

more may be forced to close their doors to the many Tennesseans who need care. 

Additionally, because the wage index is statutorily budget neutral, a self-perpetuating cycle has 

developed that has sharply driven down Tennessee's reimbursement rate over the last 15 years. Certain 

states are able to record higher wages resulting in higher payments, providing those states with more 

resources to increase wages, driving its wage index higher. Then, because of budget neutrality, 

resources get pulled from low wage index states like Tennessee to "par for high wage index states, 

meaning that Tennessee hospitals lose the ability to hire staff or increase wages in order to increase our 

wage index. This is a self-perpetuating cycle. Moreover, the wage index covers less each year despite 

ever-rising costs and declining revenues, further crippling Tennessee hospitals resources and ability to 

recruit staff. 

CMS proposed rule CMS-1716-P offers a constructive way to address these wage index 

disparities for those hospitals with a wage index value below the 25th percentile. The proposed rule also 

seeks to curb the manipulative hospital practice in certain states that abuses the "rural floor calculation 

provision to inappropriately influence the rural floor wage index value; in turn, this affects 

reimbursement rates everywhere else, like Tennessee. 

Thank you for acknowledging the wage index problems and including reforms to return a more 

equitable Medicare Area Wage Index reimbursement rate to hospitals like those in Tennessee. Your 

proposal offers a lifeline, and I hope you include it in the final rule. 

Sincerely_

Also, a logo with "BE" and a smiley face doesn't communicate well at all that the food was produced with genetic engineering-- it's very misleading and biased. Restore the Roadless Rule for the Tongass National Forest, Docket #FS-2021-0007-0006 Dear Secretary Tom Vilsack, I strongly support restoring full Roadless Rule protection to the Tongass National Forest. The Tongass is America's wildest national forest, with more than 9 million acres of roadless areas. It provides habitat for a wide range of wildlife, including Alexander Archipelago wolves, grizzly bears and salmon. And it's the ancestral homelands of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. The Tongass stores a vast amount of carbon, with its centuries-old trees serving as a carbon-reserve life raft in this time of climate change. Logging would release most of that carbon into the atmosphere. Closing the door to clearcutting and bulldozing roads will protect the forest's many values. The Tongass belongs to everyone and shouldn't be sacrificed to the timber industry, which provides a small fraction of the jobs and income in Southeast Alaska compared to tourism and fishing - both of which rely on intact forests to thrive. Further, I urge you to swiftly implement your "Southeast Alaska Sustainability Strategy" announced last year, which for the Tongass would end large-scale old-growth timber sales on roadless and roaded lands, focusing forest management on restoring lands degraded by logging and roads, as well as on recreation, climate health, wildlife habit, and watershed improvement. For wildlands, wildlife, people and our future, the Service should restore full Roadless Rule protection to the Tongass and end commercial old-growth and mature forest logging there. Thank you for this opportunity to comment. Sincerely, Calum Mackay -PII-

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

Consumers concerned with the origins of the foods they consume deserve the right to accurate information. Conservatives often state that transparency is all that is required for public choice in a free market. Logic thus indicates that for labelling to be factual, industry can not be permitted to promote claims utilizing its own standards, and based solely on self-inspection. Please impose stricter guidelines, and enforce them.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

When they compared the climate in their model with and without extremely large wind farms (large enough to generate about twice the world's total present electrical demand), they found that in addition to climate effects in the immediate vicinity of the wind farms, there were changes in climate all around the world. Vautard's study agrees with this earlier work, in finding that the climate impacts of wind farms extend beyond the farms themselves and are caused by changes in the flow of the atmosphere that bring warming and cooling to different regions around the wind farms.

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

Might does not make right.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

My name is Brian Beech and I am a backyard beekeeper. I've been following the labeling of honey for a while and I find it to be confusing already, without adding this additional layer of confusion to it.

I believe the confusion with requiring 'Added Sugars' would make the label-conscious consumer believe the honey has been adulterated - or enhanced.
As stated in 21 US Code 342 (b)(4), "A food shall be deemed to be adulterated... if any substance has been ADDED thereto or mixed or packed therewith so as to...make it appear better or of greater value than it is."

For many of us, we take pride in the fact that there has been nothing added to, or removed from, the honey we're packaging. Requiring this would not allow the consumer to easily tell what honey is actual pure honey versus a mis-marketed brand that actually adds corn syrup or some other fructose to the honey.

I would appreciate a clarification for honey and the labeling on this.

Wolf, is not actually the acting DHS Secretary). It should not be finalized, and if finalized, should be rescinded before it becomes effective.

If DHS cannot remove an alien, and the alien lacks the financial ability or travel documents to leave the United States under his or her own power, then denying the alien the ability to work and earn the means to feed himself or herself is gratuitously cruel. There is no point in forcing aliens to starve, or forcing public entities or charities to support them so that they do not starve.

Restricting employment authorization to a case in which the relevant foreign government or governments have affirmatively declined to grant travel documents does not make logical sense, because the distinction between an affirmative declination and a refusal through silent non-cooperation is completely arbitrary in this context. A foreign country should not be deemed more cooperative, or more likely to eventually allow effectuation of removal, because it does not deign to respond to DHS's inquiry at all. If anything, the existence of an open line of communication might be deemed some evidence that there is hope of convincing a country to grant travel documents in the future. Complete failure to communicate, on the other hand, does not tend to hold out such hope. Nor is it apparent, even in the case of an open channel of communication, why a repeated series of noncommittal statements from a country that travel documents might be forthcoming someday would justify refusal of employment authorization to that country's nationals.

The prospect of an alien starving on the streets because the government of his or her country of nationality has refused to respond to DHS inquiries regarding necessary travel documents, or has given an unending series of noncommital responses, serves no U.S. policy interests and lacks any apparent purpose other than cruelty. If it is impossible to remove an alien, and the alien requires employment authorization as a matter of economic necessity, then the precise form of communication that the alien's country or countries of nationality have employed in declining to actually produce the required travel documentation is not material. Whether the answer is no, or there is no answer, or the answer is "maybe later" for months on end, the fact remains that if the absence of travel documentation renders removal impossible, then it makes no sense to deny the alien the means necessary to survive.

The proposal to require employers of aliens with this type of work authorization to be active participants in the e-Verify program, while it (unlike the main proposal) at least has some semblance of logic behind it, is legally dubious. E-verify is supposed to be a voluntary pilot program. It contradicts Congressional intent for the federal government to coerce participation in e-Verify.

As you write the regulations for the new ESSA for states to follow, I ask you to avoid repeating those past mistakes by not over reaching again with federal power into what should be the purview of the states. Local families, educators and community members must have input into and control over what happens in the schools that are funded by their taxes if any educational reform efforts are to work in our democratic society. It is particularly important to have educator voice at all levels of policy discussion, as teachers and principals who are actually on the ground implementing policy will have great insight into what some of the unintended consequences of such policy might be that may not be evident to those who have not been inside a public school other than as a student or visitor in many years, or perhaps ever. Top down mandates have not worked for the past 15 years and they will not work in the future. The law allows for over a year for states to develop a plan for what works best for their children in their local area. The federal government should not do anything to try to either rush nor impede that process. 

I also urge you to honor the diversity of our student population and to respect other laws that were hard fought for and won when setting regulations. IDEA is an example of such a law. It protects the rights of children with disabilities to a free and APPROPRIATE education. An appropriate education may look different for many children with disabilities in the ways that goals are set and in how instruction is delivered and progress assessed. Our students who are on Individual Education Plans have a right to have those plans, which are determined with the collaboration of teachers and parents who know the children best, kept as a focus of their instruction. 

Our students who are English Learners and Emergent Bilinguals must be allowed the time they need to develop their new English language as well as their native languages fully without pushing for acquisition of English at a speed that is developmentally unreasonable for the vast majority of these students or devalues or denies their opportunity to maintain and improve their native languages. Just as we cannot push a child to learn to walk or talk before the child is ready, we cannot force quicker English acquisition. The average amount of time necessary for a student to acquire academic English has been determined by researchers to be an average 5 to 7 years. That trajectory may be longer when students' native language is being maintained and improved as well. I also urge you not to inappropriately require English Learners to be rated on their academic attainment by assessments given to them in English until they have acquired a level of English proficiency that is comparable to their peers for whom English is a native language. Assessing students in that way violates their civil rights, as does denying them access to some programs unless and until they reach a certain level of English proficiency.

Accountability cannot rest with teachers and schools alone. We must all work to ensure that children's basic needs are met so they can learn. 

Insisting that all children must be at the same place at the same time has been very damaging to individual students. It has labeled them failures before they have had time to show what they can ultimately achieve. Clearly we want all our children to be successful, but we must allow for student and family voice regarding what "successful" means and how students move along their different paths to reaching their own individual goals. I am a marine mammal trainer at Blank Park Zoo and have been a professional animal trainer for more than five years. I hold memberships in the following professional organizations: International Marine Animal Trainers Association (IMATA) and American Association of Zoo Keepers (AAZK). I have had the opportunity to review the proposed changes to the regulations and would like to submit the below comments for consideration.
 
IMATA members care for and train marine mammals in a wide variety of physical settings, from inland habitats to ocean enclosures, and engage with the animals in an even wider variety of contexts: everything from dynamic stadium performances to intimate interpretive chats, from in-water guest interactions to educational presentations for schoolchildren, from peer-reviewed research designed to enhance understanding of ecosystems and species to veterinary care focused on the welfare of an individual patient. No matter the context, the one constant we believe is essential to ensure the health and welfare of marine mammals in any managed setting is providing them the opportunity for robust, diverse, and positive interaction with a qualified, professional staff with knowledge in best-practices and expertise in state-of-the-art animal training and care.
 
After having the opportunity to review the proposed changes to the APHIS regulations related to marine mammals, the additional components specific to marine mammal interactive programs seem unjustified based on the strong safety record of these types of encounters. To my knowledge, there is no peer-reviewed scientific data that demonstrates a need for additional regulation or how further regulation would be a benefit to marine mammals. 
 
If interactive programs are defined as "any human-marine mammal interactive program where a member of the public enters a primary enclosure for a marine mammal with the intent of interacting with the marine mammal(s)" - I believe that the definition should explicitly exclude guest contact programs in which the participants may sit/stand on a floating platform or shallow ledge, or remain poolside, as well as programs in which trainers bring marine mammals into a public area under stimulus control.
 
Additionally, I cannot support the proposed rule which stipulates that interactive sessions must not exceed 3 hours per day per animal. Based on my professional experience, I believe that the amount of daily interactive time should be based around the best interests and capabilities of the animals as determined by the caregivers that know them best. In general, training sessions have proven to be a very enriching part of an animal's day - providing physical/mental stimulation. The notion that somehow limiting or reducing this interaction would provide some benefit to marine mammals is not data-driven and has no scientific basis. Any changes to the management of the marine animals in our care should build on the high quality of our existing animal care and training programs, and provide additional opportunities for the animals to engage and interact with the professionals to whom their care has been entrusted. At its core, an interactive program session is simply a training session - which is a highly beneficial and important component of an animal's day. I'd like to express my sincere appreciation to Secretary of the Interior David Bernhardt for his ongoing efforts to make the interests of sportsmen and women a top priority. The historic undertaking to open an unprecedented number of national wildlife refuges to new hunting opportunities is just one example of Secretary Bernhardt's unwavering commitment to enhancing and expanding opportunities for American taxpayers to access the public lands and waters they own.

I am also writing to respectfully request that, as Interior and the Fish and Wildlife Service continue to open national wildlife refuges to additional hunting access, that they make addressing the overwhelming demand for additional public waterfowl hunting opportunities in California a priority.

Unlike many other states, there are simply not enough quality public waterfowl hunting opportunities in California to always meet hunter demand. This leads to frustration for many hunters and results in reduced hunter participation.

Drawing a waterfowl hunting reservation has become extremely difficult at many California refuges and wildlife areas, particularly in the Sacramento Valley and Southern California, with some odds as high as 138:1. For those who are not drawn, they must undertake considerable additional efforts for the chance to hunt. Sportsmen and women will oftentimes go through the rigors of preparing to hunt, traveling several hours to a public area at night in order to enter a lottery, waiting for a drawing, returning to the refuge in the early morning before shoot time and, after all of that, ending up waiting hours in line throughout the morning or early afternoon before they can access the refuge.

Public refuges in California typically offer only three hunting days per week, some even fewer.

Those who try to hunt California refuges without a reservation can find themselves among 200-300 other people waiting in line for an opportunity to hunt that may never come.

Public lands and waters are typically where new hunters are recruited into waterfowl hunting in California, in part because the costs of joining a private club are simply too high for most new hunters to invest in.

Since 2012, duck stamp sales in California have been steadily declining. Lack of sufficient access to productive waterfowl lands is a primary reason people are hunting less or quitting altogether.

California represents the most significant opportunity to enhance and expand waterfowl hunting opportunities on national wildlife refuges in a manner that will address overwhelming demand while also reversing declining trends in hunter participation and the resulting loss of license, duck stamp and federal Pittman-Robertson excise tax revenue, all of which is vital to continuing the North American Model of Wildlife Conservation in our nation's most populous state.

Thank you, 

Jeff

As a senior citizen with health issues I am constantly checking the sodium content of foods that I purchase. I am astounded by the high levels in so many foods. If I am having trouble and watch what I eat I can't imagine how those folks who don't read the nutrition labels stay healthy at all. Action by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to support industry-wide sodium reduction is crucial for Americans’ health, and I support the agency’s efforts with its draft guidance on Phase II voluntary sodium reduction targets for commercially processed, packaged, and prepared foods. 

However, the FDA must be more aggressive with its sodium reduction efforts. Given the life-saving potential of sodium reduction, the FDA should set more aggressive Phase II targets to more quickly reduce consumption to recommended levels. 

The FDA should also do more to hold food companies accountable for meeting these targets. Specifically, the agency’s monitoring and evaluation of Phase I and II targets must be timely, transparent, and methodologically rigorous. The FDA should also secure public commitments from industry to meet these targets and publicize companies’ progress to highlight those that are leading and those that are falling behind. Finally, if the agency’s evaluations find that industry is failing to meet the voluntary targets, the FDA should consider setting mandatory targets. 
 
The FDA has an obligation to protect Americans’ health by ensuring that industry reduces sodium. I urge the FDA to act quickly on these recommendations to ensure a safer U.S. food supply.

Sincerely,
Mary Moore

I agree with FEMA that establishing criteria is important. However, I recommend that FEMA consider implementing criteria based on numerical data. 

First, FEMA should consider a 50% numerical benchmark (i.e. the median). By using numerical benchmarks approximating where it can be estimated that half of all requests are granted and denied, FEMA can establish criteria that in past disasters has shown Federal assistance is not likely needed, and criteria where States cannot respond by themselves.

Since this is subjective, not objective, and is the general policy, notice and commenting on the objective thresholds are not needed. 

Second, FEMA should also consider publishing the first and third quartiles (25% and 75%) for key criteria. For example, if $50 million of economic harm is the median, and $40 million and $60 million are the first and third quartiles, it is unusual for damages of $25 million to get assistance (or $75 million not to). FEMA does not need to be precise with these values, however.

Third, FEMA should value criteria that represent harm. I understand why FEMA does not want to use certain criteria, such as buisness losses, or insurance damages. However, in questionable disasters, using such proxies is faster than engaging in a time sensitive process of survaliance. 

Putting strong reliance on faith / community / volunteer organizations shows self sacrifice, not how much everyone needs assistance. Insurance costs, business losses, foreclosures, and unemployment all are easier to estimate than cost benefit analysis. 

For these reasons, FEMA should rank criteria in terms of most to least important.

Fourth, State by State analysis should be retained. It is not exceedingly diffucult to tell which State was hardest hit in interstate disasters, and normally, only one State should be questionable. Nevertheless, the amount of damage matters more than the size of a State. For example, a lower threshold is needed for territories other than Puerto Rico, with populations under 200,000 people.

Fifth, regulatory criteria should also be mentioned. There are a few that I believe need to be reconsidered.

(A) The Paperwork Reduction Act should be strongly considered, but should exclude information which does not affect how long it takes to submit and determine whether to grant an emergency regulation. In a disaster, time manners more than money.
(B) Enviromental justice should be considered as an important factor, even though not major.

FDA’s GRAS notification process provides a framework that proponents2 use to ascertain the safety of a 

substance for proposed uses and use levels in foods using established guidelines. In providing guidance 

about how a substance may be determined to be generally recognized as safe, FDA states, “General 

recognition of safety requires common knowledge throughout the scientific community knowledgeable about the 

safety of substances directly or indirectly added to food that there is reasonable certainty that the substance is not 

harmful under the conditions of its intended use.”3 Additionally, in order for a substance to be determined to 

be GRAS, data must meet two criteria related to the common knowledge element: data and safety 

information must be generally available and there must be a basis to conclude that there is consensus 

exists (but not unanimity) among qualified scientists about the safety of the substance for its intended use, 

and this is established by relying upon secondary scientific literature such as published review articles, 

textbooks, or compendia, or by obtaining opinions of expert panels or opinions from authoritative bodies,

An emotional support animal is an animal that provides a therapeutic benefit to a person diagnosed with a psychological disorder, as anxiety, depression, or PTSD, and that is allowed to accompany to the person in certain public places where pets are not allowed to accompany the person in certain public places where pets are not allowed, as the cabin of an airplane. Unlike service animals, ESA requires certification and a letter from a licensed therapist. Airlines can require this documentation before an animal can be taken on an airplane. If anxiety prevents you from traveling, for example., an ESA can provide the comfort you need to make it through a long flight.

During NOAA’s public information meetings in March, 2017, several private property owners 
questioned how using the Ordinary High Water Mark (OHWM) as the sanctuary’s shoreward 
boundary may or may not impact their riparian rights. Riparian rights may include beach 
maintenance, shore protection, dredging, piers, groins and trespassing. NOAA collaborated 
with the State of Wisconsin and drafted an appropriate response as follows. 
“NOAA’s proposal to designate a national marine sanctuary in Wisconsin would not change 
riparian rights as defined by the State of Wisconsin, nor would it change state law regarding 
public access to the area in which shoreline property owners have exclusive access. The 
proposal recognizes the state’s sovereignty over its waters and submerged lands, and would 
not extend Federal jurisdiction beyond the Ordinary High Water Mark (OHWM). 
Under Wisconsin law, riparian owners have the exclusive right to use the exposed bed of the 
lake in front of their property when the water level is low. That right extends to the 
OHWM. The State of Wisconsin holds the beds of all lakes, ponds, and navigable rivers beyond 
the ordinary high-water mark in public trust, and the public has the right to use the water for 
activities like fishing. 
The proposed landward boundary of the sanctuary is the state-designated OHWM. This 
boundary was chosen because it is a current, known regulatory boundary. Under State of 
Wisconsin regulation, the OHWM is defined as “The point on the bank or shore up to which the 
water, by its presence, wave action or flow, leaves a distinct mark on the shore or bank.” The

from participants’ own contributions. Our comments focus on two areas:

The term “pre-service” may be limiting to bi/multilingual people working in schools who may have teaching credentials but may not have a license/certificate to teach bilingual learners in their state. While I certainly agree that pre-service programs need to be diversified, this is certainly not the only pathway for diversifying the teacher pipeline.
 
I would recommend removing the term pre-service so that multiple pathways (including master’s programs) might be able to be envisioned for anyone seeking to become a licensed/certified bi/multilingual teacher. Narrowing the funding priority to pre-service teachers limits possibilities at a time when we need to think more expansively and creatively about how to leverage the rich bi/multilingualism that exists in this country toward diversifying the teacher workforce.

Dear Sir or Madam:

Please do not downlist the West Indian (Florida) manatee from its current Endangered status. I believe that the proposal to downlist from Endangered to Threatened status is premature and is based on numerous faulty assumptions. My personal experience has offered me a broad perspective on this issue. 

I live on Merritt Island, Florida, in the heart of the Indian River Lagoon Estuary (IRL), and have had extensive experience with manatees and manatee habitat over the past several decades. I have also personally witnessed the degradation and elimination of manatee habitat across Florida for the past 40 years, as a professional pilot and aerial photographer. 

I have personally witnessed the widespread loss of sea grasses and other manatee food stocks as a Keep Brevard Beautiful river clean-up scuba diver in the IRL, and recreational diver in various springs in central and northern Florida. I've been physically immersed in the toxic anaerobic "muck" that has increasingly covered the bottom of the IRL, and smothering its seagrasses. I've been tangled in the growing masses of discarded monofilament fishing line and cast nets that routinely ensnare manatees in our turbid waters. As an avid boater and kayaker, I have seen the widespread encroachment of human development and activities that have included direct and indirect harassment of these gentle creatures.

I was a delegate to the most recent Indian River Lagoon Action Assembly at the Florida Institute of Technology, and have studied the decline of the IRL for years. For the past several years, I have extensively participated in oyster restoration work, under the auspices of the University of Central Florida and the Brevard Zoo, in large portions of the IRL - both in Volusia and Brevard Counties.

From that perspective, I was disturbed to learn that the downlist proposal relies on the Runge et al. model, which assumes "stutus quo", and fails to take into account several critical issues:

 Threats to manatees and their habitat increase with the steady increase of the human population living and vacationing in Florida. The human population living along the IRL has increased 300 fold since WW II!
 Florida's spring flows are decreasing across the state, and this trend is likely to continue for many years.
 Manatees have suffered from significant mortality events since 2009, especially the 2009-2010 die off, the 2010-2011 die off and the unexplained "Unusual Mortality Event" of 2013.
 The dramatic 2011 "brown tide" algae super bloom, destroyed up to 70% of the sea grass beds in the IRL. Although sea grasses have begun to recover over the last few years, a new, 2016 brown tide super bloom is currently ravaging the IRL with a density and extent that has never been witnessed before. The 2016 super bloom is forecast to persist or re-occur as water temperatures warm from Spring into Summer. It is reasonable to expect that sea grasses (the primary manatee food source in the IRL) will be degraded to a much larger extent than was experienced in 2011.
 Manatee mortality from red tide in southwest Florida in 2013 resulted in record - never before seen - kill numbers.

None of these issues are accounted for in the Runge model! This fact alone invalidates the current proposal to downlist the Florida manatee.

Habitat loss, food source destruction, spring flow degradation, and increasing pollution and harassment from an incessantly increasing human population have combined to create unsustainable pressure on the Florida manatee. 

I spent the first 8 years of my 40-year flying career as an aerial photographer and photo mapping pilot. I can attest that aerial population estimates of in-water marine mammals are notoriously difficult. Two or three years of increased (and likely inaccurate) aerial manatee population estimates must not be used to justify downlisting!

Our other concern with the paragraph (h)(2) requirements is Limitation No. 4 – Engine Nacelle Maintenance Errors. Protecting wildlife is more important then ever, I go hiking almost every weekend and the mountains and nature bring me peace. There is land the must remain untouched to preserve its natural beauty and safety for all of the animals that inhabit it. 

My name is Cecily Board and I am opposed to the U.S. Forest Services proposal to cut out public participation from the vast majority of its decisions. I have commented on forest plans, projects, or policies affecting national forests in the past. The current proposal would fundamentally change the relationship between the U.S. Forest Service and the public, cutting our voices entirely out of how to manage these special places.

I often visit our national forests to appreciate nature, spend time in the outdoors, create memories with my family and friends, hike, swim, fish, explore new places, relax, enjoy the scenery, watch wildlife, and enjoy access to public lands. A subset of this NPRM which is specifically designed to address the ability of a pilot act as a safety pilot while operating under Basic Med provisions is one that I fully support (Quote 1 below). This effort is one that should be expanded to allow the same provision to be utilized by FAA designated examiners but is currently prohibited.

Under current provisions of 14 CFR § 183.23 DPEs are authorized to conduct practical tests. However a this is also subject to a DPE requirement to maintain at least a third class medical in accordance with the following: "14 CFR § 61.23 (a) (3) Must hold at least a third-class medical certificate”...”(iv) When performing the duties as an Examiner in an aircraft when administering a practical test or proficiency check for an airman certificate, rating, or authorization." This requirement prohibits a DPE from acting in that capacity without a Third Class or greater medical certificate. The current NPRM language does not contemplate this additional change.

Designated Pilot Examiner Reforms Working Group Final Recommendation Report as of June 22, 2021 included recommendations that regulations be altered to allow a DPE act as a DPE while maintaining medical compliance using the Basic Med option. Specifically, in this report recommendation #11 indicated that "Designees should be allowed to perform examinations with an equivalent level of medical certification that would be necessary for that designee to act as PIC of that aircraft (i.e., if you can act as PIC in the aircraft, then you should be qualified as an examiner (medically)." (The report can be found at: https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/rulemaking/committees/documents/media/ARAC%20DPEWG%20Final%20Recommendation%20Report%20June%202021.pdf).

Modifying 14 CFR § 61.23 to remove or modify the requirement for a DPE to be required to hold at least a third-class medical certificate would be a change in accordance with that recommendation and allow greater utilization of DPEs who could otherwise act as a CFI (a requirement for a DPE) but are prohibited from acting as a DPE due to this regulatory constraint.

I strongly encourage the modification of this regulation while this regulatory effort is engaged.

Respectfully,

Jason Blair

Dear USFWS:

I’m a lifelong supporter of wildlife and strongly support the Endangered Species Act. I’ve been appalled at the USFWS’s policies regarding wolves, particularly the horrible 2015 changes to its 10(j) management rule regarding the Mexican gray wolf; it was anti-wolf, anti-science, and violated the ESA. Now that the USFWS is being forced to correct its wrongs via a court order, I am submitting these comments on the proposed “Revision to the Nonessential Experimental Population of the Mexican Wolf” (Docket #: FWS-R2-ES-2021-0103-0001). 

The USFWS must rectify all the failures specified in the court order. Therefore, the revisions to the 2015 10(j) Rule must incorporate the following provisions:

Geographic Boundaries: The new rule must eliminate artificial boundaries that prevent dispersal. USFWS’s own appointed scientists emphasized that the Mexican gray wolf’s long-term survival requires connected habitats north of Interstate 40, including the Grand Canyon region and portions of southern Utah and Colorado.

Isolated Population: The USFWS must be proactive in support of establishing two additional subpopulations of Mexican wolves. Scientists recommend a minimum of three naturally connected subpopulations of at least 200 individuals each, collectively comprising a meta-population of at least 750 wolves in identified areas of suitable habitats in the U.S. Southwest, north of I-40. Scientists warn that this meta-population structure and geographic distribution is essential to the success of the Mexican wolves. 

Wolf Removal Orders: Lethal control must be narrowly restricted to cases in which a wolf poses a likely threat to human health or safety. The new rule must also include higher thresholds for initiating wolf removals. Public land grazing permittees must practice basic animal husbandry and remove livestock carcasses or render them inedible to prevent savaging by wolves. If livestock carcasses on public land attract wolves who subsequently prey on livestock in the vicinity, those wolves shall not be removed from the wild. Public land grazing permittees must also be required to take non-lethal measures to prevent conflicts to protect livestock. If wolves pretty on livestock when the permittee is cognizant of the nearby presence of wolves but fails to take measures to protect the livestock, wolves shall not be removed from the wild. Any permittee found guilty of the illegal killing or injuring of a Mexican wolf shall have their livestock grazing permits revoked.

Genetic Health: The Mexican wolf’s genetic imperilment requires an active program of releasing more genetically diverse wolves into the wild to capitalize on the remaining genetic potential available in the captive population. The USFWS’s dedication to cross-fostering is helpful, it should not be the only strategy used to increase genetic diversity in the wild population. Given the severity of the wild Mexican gray wolf population’s genetic crisis, USFWS should also resume releasing pair-bonded adult male and female Mexican gray wolves with pups into the wild – the means by which reintroduction was initiated in 1998 and successfully undertaken until abandoned under political pressure in 2007.

Replacement Release Objective: The final rule should include a RRO, which would allow the USFWS to release wolves from the captive breeding population into the existing wild wolf population to replace wolves that have been removed from the wild population due to illegal killings or mortality caused by USFWS management activity. Replacement wolves from the more genetically diverse captive population would maximize genetic diversity of the wild wolf population. 

The USFWS has the opportunity to right the wrongs of the past by taking the necessary steps to ensure the long-term recovery of this important species. 

Thank you.

This rule has a reason for being, although for many it may sound counterproductive at this moment, regarding to timing and or efficiency in the use of resources, and that is because it has not been an easy time for the industry in question. There have been diseases such as Greening (Huanglongbing or HLB) that have been attacking since 2005 and that, to date, have reduced citrus production in the state by around 50%. 1 (Blake, T. Some years later, the COVID-19 pandemic arrived, with a particular effect in Florida, coinciding with the peak date of the harvests, and where both consumer behavior (due to the lockdowns), and availability of labor (due to travel restrictions for temporary agricultural workers) were totally altered, resulting in entire crops that could not be harvested or marketed. 2 (Court, Christa D. et al.2.3). A year later, hurricane Ian generated around 550,000,000 USD in losses 3 (UF/IFAS Food and Resource Economics Par.10), and let us not forget the frosts on flowering period, which also caused a significant decline in the production yield last season; producers are exhausted and finally, they see some relief considering that this year the USDA projects that numbers for producers will be a little more auspicious. 

Greening has been devastating for this field, and if the fee augmentation is partly allocated on the research and development of citrus resistant species to it, ways to deal with it, as well as ways to face other challenges of the industry; then the fee augmentation it is important to contribute to the joint effort at all level of alliances between private - state - federal entities, in order to confront this devastating plague that has put one of Florida’s main industry at the very edge.

My comments are directed to the breast density notification portion of the proposal. Id like to thank the FDA for taking the steps to update the MQSA standards which have not been updated for 20 years. Since updates do not happen frequently, it is important to consider the completeness and clarity of information for patients and ordering physicians, as well as to consider how the healthcare providers will implement these changes. 

I have the unique advantage of working with breast centers as part of my job. I know that even in states that have been informing women of their breast density, there is still much confusion on behalf of patients and referring physicians. Lack of education after patients are informed of their breast density is a cause of low compliance to additional screening today. Patients need simple, clear language. The information about breast density needs to be at the top of the letter. Once women read that their mammogram is normal, they often do not read much further. Also, direct information that dense tissue may hide cancer on a mammogram, and that additional imaging may increase cancer detection must be clearly stated. Directing patients to their referring physicians for more information is not always helpful depending on the bias or lack of education of their physician. My recommendation is to include a resource in the letter for patients to independently learn more about breast density and additional imaging options. The patient may not get appropriate information when directed only to a referring physician. A resource such as DenseBreast-info.org or a web page on the Cancer Society or Society of Breast Imaging would be potential resources to direct patients to. Mammography reporting language for referring physicians also needs to be simple and clear as they are often confused about what to do with a normal mammogram report and may not be concerned about dense tissue or have knowledge of additional imaging options.

Additional updates that would be helpful for implementation would be to create a screening code for dense breast imaging, a specific BI-RADs ranking to identify normal but dense to referring physicians to indicate additional imaging is warranted, and the creation of a self-referral for supplemental screening so that women can order the exam if they want it. Same day supplemental imaging for women with dense breast tissue achieves the highest compliance.

This is a great opportunity to increase education about what it means to have dense breast tissue and make it clear that more cancers can be found with additional imaging. Patients should receive education so they will have the facts to be able to make an informed decision to seek additional screening for peace of mind.

The FDA proposal clearly shows with the research that is cited that supplemental screening finds more cancers, and finds them at early stages. The research cited also indicates that supplemental screening will save the health system money because cancers will be found early and there will be less severe treatments needed. The FDA cited research needs to be widely shared to educate the naysayers on this topic.
