Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

It's about time that you started actually earning the tax dollars I spend by enforcing the law for a change.

Thank you for considering my request.

The proposed information request should be amended to include information on the effectiveness of passenger vehicle crash avoidance technologies in tests with the sides and rear of commercial motor vehicles.

Crash avoidance technologies rely upon sensors to detect the presence of a threatening obstacle. If the sensors fail to detect the obstacle, they fail to trigger other aspects of the technology, such as automatic emergency braking, and the crash occurs. Failure to detect the presence of a threatening obstacle can happen if the line of sight of the crash avoidance sensor lies below the threatening obstacle, such as the high open spaces along the sides and between the axles of commercial motor vehicles. 

The intent of NCAP information and the proposed information collection is to inform consumers about the presence and effectiveness of safety technologies in passenger vehicles.

These technologies work as intended only in crashes with other passenger vehicles and stationary objects. They may not work in crashes with the sides and rear of commercial motor vehicles which may be undetectable by the passenger vehicle’s crash avoidance sensors. 

Consumers deserve to know, and automobile manufacturers should disclose, the effectiveness of crash avoidance technology in protecting consumers in crashes with commercial motor vehicles. This disclosure will likely alert consumers to the dangers they continue to face after crash avoidance technologies are fully deployed. It will also alert vehicle manufacturers to the limits of the protective value of their technologies.

Consuming gluten, even in small amounts, causes my immune system to attack my small intestine for months. This causes me to have uncontrollable diarrhea and abdominal pain, which lasts for multiple weeks and makes it difficult to function away from home. Technically that's not the only problem with consuming gluten: it causes damage to the small intestine which becomes permanent if it occurs often enough. This increases the risk of bowel cancer, and also affects how your body absorbs nutrients. It even causes long lasting brain fog which affects the ability to remember important upcoming events and even affects daily life! Currently, there can be hidden gluten in products that contain barley, rye, triticale, and other grains that contain gluten. This is because they can hide behind labels like "natural flavors" and "natural smoke flavor". As a result, it is a guessing game every time I go to the store, unless I pay to test every product each time I buy it, which is prohibitively expensive. By changing the labeling laws and requiring gluten containing grains be declared on product packaging, and the sources of natural flavors to be announced, it would take away the guessing game and make shopping easier and safer.

Even people who do not suffer from this disease would benefit from knowing what is in their food. It allows consumers to make informed decisions on what they put their own bodies and gives them the freedom to choose between brands based on accurate information.

This is why I support updating our outdated labeling laws. As we continue to advance our research into understanding these conditions and the benefits of a gluten free diet, it is only appropriate to make the use of gluten containing grains labeled on product packaging. We need to make sure everyone can make informed decisions about their food and improve safety for those suffering from autoimmune conditions. Particulate matter (PM) harms our health. PM, especially the fine particles known as PM2.5, not only affects the lungs; it also enters the blood stream and is carried to other tissues and organs. Because of this, PM2.5 has been linked directly to leading causes of mortality including cardiovascular diseases including stroke and cancer, as well as, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases and asthma.

The standards for PM should be set at levels that protect our most vulnerable populations - children, the elderly, and those with chronic medical conditions,

At a time when Covid-19 is affecting millions of Americans and over 120,000 have died, EPA should take every step possible to clean the air and protect our lungs and our health from harm. Strengthening the air quality standards for PM is essential.

I am in opposition to the EPA's proposal to retain, without revision, its current inadequate standards for PM.

I urge the EPA to pursue its mission to protect human health and well-being and the environment, by reviewing and revising its PM standards.

As a private pilot with formation time, I’m glad to see that some common sense is being applied to 

formation operations and ADS-B transmission. The constant “traffic!” warnings were getting annoying. 

But I find it ironic that, with less than six months to go before the mandated 2020 deadline, someone in 

the government is finally waking up to the realization that broadcasting identification and position data 

in the clear might just represent some form of security risk, too. Unfortunately, this only seems to be

And although I broadly agree with AOPA’s comments, I struggle to see how these privacy concerns could 

have been “unforeseen” until now, unless there’s just nobody within the FAA’s regulatory branch 

playing the role of “red team” and meaningfully asking the question “what could go wrong?” However, 

it’s never too late to start doing the right thing. 

Imagine for a moment what would happen if anyone with an internet connection could look up license 

plate information and cross-reference it to a driver’s license (and all the information therein, like home 

addresses). That alone represents a huge personal security risk. In fact, easy availability of that 

information in the past led to stalking, burglary, and at least one high-profile murder (and that was 

before the internet!). Eventually this led to the passage of the Drivers Privacy Protection Act of 1994. 

Now imagine if all of this information was once again public—but also every vehicle was equipped with a 

GPS tracker, broadcasting position and identification to the internet at large, in real time, and linked to 

an automatic traffic ticket generator. It would be a boon to burglars and extortionists, a godsend to 

speed trap towns (but I repeat myself), and a stalker’s dream come true. Lawyers would be dueling 

each other on the steps of the Supreme Court for the honor and prestige of arguing such an open-and-

shut privacy case. The safety and privacy implications are clear and scarcely need explaining, except 

apparently when airplanes become involved. 

Yet this is exactly the situation that presents itself within aviation. The database of aircraft registration 

is public—anyone with an internet connection (and that’s pretty much everyone in the US today) can 

look up tail numbers--and at least for the vast majority of light aircraft which typically aren’t obfuscated 

through LLCs or holding companies, find the owner’s full name and home address. Cross-referencing 

that to the pilot certificate database is trivial. And now with ADS-B and the proliferation of websites 

displaying tracking data, past flight history, real-time tracking data, and even push notifications of 

activity are available at anyone’s fingertips. By this point we are all familiar with the internet 

phenomenon of “doxxing” and the havoc it can wreak on anyone’s personal and family life; surely we 

don’t need to be serving that information up in a nice gift-wrapped box sealed with government 

approval? It’s already considered good advice not to post on social media that one is out of the house 

or on an extended trip, yet the government happily serves up information that says “this guy’s not 

home!” with ADS-B tracking data.

The undersigned organizations collectively represent individuals, caregivers, family members and 

healthcare professionals attempting to manage serious, complex, life-threatening conditions each 

day. As such, we understand the profound impact that biologic medicines have had on the lives of 

many Americans and it is our hope that as biosimilars enter the marketplace, they will provide 

additional treatment options by being both affordable and accessible. 

It is our view as patient and provider stakeholders that all policy regarding biosimilars must 

recognize and reflect their unique nature. Unlike chemical generics, biosimilars are not exact 

copies of their reference products, but instead created from different materials and processes to 

mimic the therapeutic properties of the reference product. Variances will always exist between 

a biosimilar and its reference product, as well as between two or more biosimilars to a shared 

reference product, and may cause unexpected effects including immunogenic responses. A 

biosimilar may not be approved for all disease indications of the originator product, and approval 

for an indication may have been based on extrapolation, rather than on clinical research. 

For these reasons, we support the FDA’s leadership in creating a system of distinguishable names 

for all biologic medicines, including biosimilars. Distinct naming helps ensure a patient receives 

the intended medicine and allows for accurate designation of any adverse events to the correct 

product, aiding in pharmacovigilance while promoting manufacturer product accountability. 

Furthermore, a four-letter structure makes it potentially compatible with the WHO’s Biological 

Qualifier system, which will extend these protections to patients worldwide. 

It is our position regarding the structure of the distinguishing suffix that meaningful suffixes such 

as the FDA used with its first biosimilar approval, for Zarxio (filgrastim-sndz), are preferable to the 

random suffixes described in the FDA’s Draft Guidance and used in its second approval for Inflectra 

(infliximab-dyyb). 

1

 
Meaningful suffixes are easier for patients, providers and pharmacists to both recognize and 

remember, thus facilitating accurate association between adverse events and specific products. 

A suffix based on the manufacturer name, as was used in the Zarxio approval where ‘-sndz” refers 

to “Sandoz”, also promotes manufacturer accountability. A survey of 400 prescribers of biologics 

revealed that they prefer meaningful suffixes over random by a six-to-one margin, and a survey of 

401 US pharmacists showed 77% prefer manufacturer-based suffixes over random. 

Biosimilars hold great promise for millions of individuals living with debilitating, life-altering 

diseases and we appreciate your ever-vigilant efforts to promote access to these treatments. 

We believe that by the FDA instituting a distinguishable naming system for biological medicines 

that incorporates meaningful, memorable suffixes will achieve these goals by providing strong 

patient protections, critical transparency and promoting pharmacovigilance, resulting in greater

I am in support of the proposed Borrower Defense to Repayment rule Docket ID ED-2018-OPE-0027. I am a Financial Aid 
Administrator at Triangle Tech-Greensburg. I have been working at Triangle Tech for twenty years caring for our 
students. I have counseled my boyfriend’s three children in understanding their student loan obligations and the 
importance in completing their education. One of his children is in deferment and the other two are currently in 
repayment. I am happy that I have been given the opportunity to share my opinion on the Borrower’s Defense to 
Repayment Notice of Proposed Rule Making because it will affect those I care about. 
In regards to the Affirmative Claims, I feel that both defensive and affirmative claims should be allowed if there is a clear 
and convincing evidentiary standard required for both. I feel that it is important that a claim cannot be made without 
strong evidence. Accusing any school of misrepresentation is serious and could do significant damage to the school, even 
if the school is found not guilty. I also feel a three-year time limit is fair and needed for students that have defaulted and 
also for those current in repayment for the Time Frame for Filing. 
I agree with the new definition of “misrepresentation,” included in this new rule. Triangle Tech is a great school and is 
always striving to serve their students the best ways possible. I believe a clear definition of what misrepresentation 
means and consideration of the intent of the misinformation is needed. I believe all schools should be held accountable if 
they knowingly provide false, misleading or deceptive information to students. However, if it is not an intentional act to 
misrepresent, then I don’t think we should have a process that could hurt all of the other students who benefit from the 
school’s academic programs. 
I support the section Evidence of Misrepresentation. A clear list of communications where a student can justifiably make 
a misrepresentation claim against the school is essential. Considerations should be made to accommodate for 
circumstantial changes out of the school’s control that change the original information provided to students, to no fault 
of the school. The list for a student to make a claim against a school appears reasonable with the considerations I 
mentioned. 
Teach-Out Safe Harbor proposed rule would no longer provide for closed-school loan discharges if the student’s school 
provides a full completion of the program through a teach-out plan approved by their accreditor and state licensing 
agency. I support this provision of the rule. With a fully-approved teach out plan, faculty and staff often go above and 
beyond to serve students through completion of their program. Students will leave with their planned credential, and a 
loan discharge is not needed in these cases. 
I feel we should always try to resolve disputes between a student and the school if possible. We do not need to send 
them to Washington to drag out disputes and potentially add more cost to both parties, if they can be solved locally more 
efficiently. This is why I support the Arbitration and Class Action Waivers. The Department’s proposed rule restores the 
ability of schools to establish a Binding Arbitration Process between the students and the school. If a student feels they 
were the victim of misrepresentation or fraud, we want a process that is clean, clear and fair to both the student and the 
school. Arbitration can be a good option for both parties, as long as the students are properly informed of the option and 
given the necessary information on how to proceed. 
 
I appreciate the opportunity to express my opinion on the proposed Borrower Defense to Repayment rule 
(Docket ID ED-2018-OPE-0027). 
 
Thank you, 
Jennifer Lynch 
Financial Aid Administrator

Position Statement on USDA Proposal to Remove Phytosanitary Inspection Fee Exemption for Small Aircraft

As a small commercial airline operating 9-passenger aircraft between South Florida and the Bahamas, we strongly oppose the United States Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) proposal to eliminate the long-standing exemption from phytosanitary inspection fees for aircraft with 64 passenger seats or fewer.

This proposal—though likely aimed at standardizing procedures across the aviation industry—fails to recognize the dramatic disparity between large international carriers and small, regional airlines in both scale and economic viability. The proposed $300 inspection fee per arrival would be imposed uniformly, regardless of aircraft size or passenger count. As a result, a Boeing 767 carrying over 300 passengers would pay the same fee as a 9-passenger Cessna Caravan. This one-size-fits-all approach is not only inequitable, it is unsustainable for small carriers.

Disproportionate Economic Impact
Small airlines like ours operate with narrow margins and serve niche routes that are vital to regional mobility and economic development—particularly between South Florida and neighboring island nations. Applying a $300 fee every time an aircraft returns to the United States constitutes a disproportionate economic burden on our operations. For a single flight, this could add an effective cost of $33 per passenger just for inspection—before accounting for fuel, crew, maintenance, and other fees. In contrast, for a large carrier operating a 300-seat aircraft, the same fee equates to just $1 per passenger or less. This fundamental imbalance unfairly penalizes smaller operators for participating in the same inspection process.

Capricious and Rash Policy Change
The long-standing exemption for smaller aircraft was not arbitrary; it was based on operational realities and economic prudence. Smaller aircraft pose a significantly reduced risk in terms of volume and variety of agricultural contaminants, and they carry far fewer passengers, cargo, and consumables. The USDA’s proposal to remove the exemption without considering the scale of operations or associated risk lacks rational basis and appears capricious.

Threat to Viability of Regional Air Service
This proposed change threatens the very viability of regional air service to island communities and small destinations. Operators may be forced to raise fares, cut routes, or even exit the market altogether, resulting in reduced connectivity, diminished tourism, and negative economic consequences for both U.S. and Bahamian communities that rely on small-scale air transport.

Call for Proportionality and Dialogue
We urge the USDA to reconsider this proposal and engage with stakeholders in the small aircraft community to develop a more proportionate and risk-based fee structure. A sliding scale or exemption threshold that takes into account aircraft size, passenger capacity, and actual risk would achieve the USDA’s goals without undermining the small carriers that form the backbone of regional international travel.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I strongly support and greatly appreciate this proposed rule. It is reasonable, necessary, and timely. As President Biden and Interior Secretary Haaland have accurately described, the climate and extinction crises are real, connected, pose an existential threat to humanity, and are rapidly getting worse. Bold and innovative reforms are urgently needed. 

This proposed rule properly recognizes that environmental conditions are changing fast. Many Endangered Species Act (ESA) listed, proposed, and candidate species are likely to be significantly affected by these changes. 

For example, the ESA threatened Mojave desert tortoises, which are seriously declining over much of their historic range, are likely to need to move both northward and to higher elevations to escape increasing heat and exceptional drought conditions. This means that FWS should be proactive in identifying where tortoises will be in the foreseeable future, not just where they occur now. Wherever possible, these future habitats should be protected from harmful human uses so that those habitats are viable when tortoises arrive. 

The worst drought in the West in 1,200 years also means that many existing aquatic, wetland, and riparian critical habitats for ESA species are already under severe stress. When these habitats are lost or seriously degraded due to prolonged drought and excessive human water uses, it will be necessary to translocate species to similar habitats that may occur outside of their historic ranges. 

For millions of years, species were able to move as most environmental changes slowly occurred. Unfortunately, humans have greatly altered the natural environment and seriously fragmented habitats such that many species no longer can move on their own. They will need human help to do so. This proposed rule would facilitate that help. I urge FWS to adopt and implement this proposed rule as soon as possible. 

Thank you very much for your consideration.

Now is the time for action to protect our iconic orcas. I support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take immediate action to finalize the proposed rule.

Thank you for proposing to expand critical habitat for the Southern Resident killer whales (SRKW) to include marine waters from Monterey Bay in California through Cape Flattery in Washington State. 

Protecting this full range as critical habitat reflects new and best available science as new sightings and data show that SRKW regularly forage in the coastal waters off Washington, Oregon, and California and is essential to help get the southern resident orcas off the path to extinction and on the way to recovery.

The final rule designating critical habitat identified three essential habitat features essential to the conservation of the SRKW: (1) Water quality to support SRKW growth and development; (2) prey species of sufficient quantity, quality, and availability to support individual growth, reproduction, and development, as well as overall population growth; and (3) passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

However, the proposed rule exempts the Navy's Quinault Range Site off the coast of Washington from being designated as critical habitat due to national security. The Quinault Range Site includes part of two high-use foraging areas, as recognized by NMFS in the Biological Report, and completely bisects the proposed expanded critical habitat area. From the tagging data, about half the time that K and L pods spend in coastal habitat is in Area 1 (Washington and Northern Oregon inshore habitat). This exemption could impact their foraging ability in an area and season when nutritional stress is a significant concern and impact their ability to migrate up and down the coast. Therefore the exempted area is in conflict with the third essential habitat feature: passage conditions to allow for migration, resting, and foraging.

The proposed rule should include a narrow area sufficient in width between the shoreline and the eastern border of the Quinault Range Site to ensure orca migration along the coast and for foraging for limited prey. 

The science also shows that sound from vessels and other sources undermines orcas ability to echolocate to forage for salmon as well as to communicate and navigate. The Washington Governors Orca Recovery Task Force and the ESA Recovery Plan have noted that noise and disturbance are key threats hindering orca recovery and have recommended decreasing, not increasing, military noise. To sufficiently protect SRKW, NMFS must include sound as a fourth essential feature. Urge them to ensure that it is at least retained as an explicit factor in the prey and passage essential features. 

I am grateful that NMFS has engaged and consulted with Tribes to ensure that this rule does not impact Tribal Treaty rights and usual and accustomed fishing areas.

Again, fully support the proposed critical habitat expansion and urge the government to take expedient action to finalize the proposed rule.

Proposed Organic Check-off Voting Rules Would Harm American Organic Farmers, 

Favor Importers 

By Jim Riddle, Organic Independents LLP 

A new proposed rule, released by the Obama administration during their final days 

in office, would favor importers of organic products at the expense of America’s 

certified organic farmers. 

Under the proposed voting procedures, only domestic certified organic producers 

who sell over $250,000 of organic products per year would be eligible to vote on 

whether or not an organic check-off program should be created. According to 

USDA’s calculations in the proposed rule, 76% of the certified organic farmers in the 

United States would not be eligible to vote in the referendum, unless they choose to 

be “voluntarily assessed.” 

On the other hand, importers of organic products, both foreign and domestic, would 

be allowed to vote, even though they are not required to be certified. To make 

matters worse, importers who have multiple “business entities” would be allowed to 

cast multiple ballots. 

The proposal would also allow foreign certified organic handlers to decide if a 

check-off, or tax, will be imposed on organic sales in the United States. 

As proposed, the voting procedures would tilt power away from America’s organic 

farmers towards importers of organic products by the allowance of multiple votes, 

and by not requiring compliance with U.S. organic regulations. The proposal would 

allow voting by operations that comply with an “authorized international standard” 

without defining the international standard; describing the requirements for 

authorizing the approval of such a standard; or even requiring that such a standard 

comply with U.S. organic requirements. 

If adopted, the proposed referendum procedures would undermine domestic 

organic producers and handlers, who are required to comply with NOP Regulations, 

by forcing their votes to be counted as equal to those cast by non-certified importers 

and by foreign operations that are certified to an unspecified “authorized 

international standard.” 

A fair system of participation would be for every domestic certified organic 

operation to have one vote per domestic certificate. This would ensure that every 

American certified organic producer and handler would be given an equal voice in 

whether or not a tax is imposed on the U.S. organic sector. It would also link the 

referendum directly to National Organic Program regulations, which require that all 

producers and handlers of organic products, who sell more than $5000/year in 

organic products, must be certified in order to label their products as “organic.”

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

Please make companies providing animals for consumption provide proof when they label products humanely raised, free range etc, as the current system has few checks and balances with consumers being over charged and the poor animals not being raised humanely. Thank you!!!!??

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

Medicines (Docket No. RIN 0938-AV09) 

Dear Administrator Brooks-LaSure, 

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on CMS’s proposal for potential IPPS payment for 

Establishing and Maintaining Access to Essential Medicines. We commend CMS for proactively engaging 

in the drug shortage crisis affecting highly vulnerable hospital patients. 

We agree that maintaining sufficient inventory is one way to make drug supply chains more resilient to 

shocks. We are concerned, however, that the proposal will not have the effect on shortages where it is 

most needed. In addition, some provisions may inadvertently result in increased levels of waste, fraud, 

and abuse. 

Our comments are based on over a decade experience studying drug shortages. One of us is a 

healthcare economist focusing on economic drivers of drug shortages, the other one is an industrial 

engineer who studies vulnerabilities of drug supply chains, including vulnerabilities in inventory 

systems. 

In this comment letter we explain our concerns about the CMS buffer inventory proposal and identify 

improvements to some elements of that proposal. We propose to extend the buffer to six months, 

narrow down the proposal to third-party options only, switch from a submit-a-bill to a fixed payment, 

and be more explicit when inventories are to be build up and drawn down. 

We are, however, unable to provide a CMS solution to the drug access disparities that we expect will 

continue to exist under any proposal that does not explicitly tackle panic buying. We do think 

mechanisms like that exist, but within powers of other HHS Agencies. In turn, we believe that CMS’s 

greatest contribution would be in encouraging hospitals to buy from reliable manufacturers. 

The buffer inventory proposal may not have impact where it is needed most 

According to the proposed rule, CMS looks to establish an IPPS payment for the IPPS share of the 

reasonable costs of establishing and maintaining access to a three-month buffer stock of one of more of 

the 86 essential medicines on the ASPR list. There are three options that CMS offers: maintaining 

inventory directly at the hospitals, arranging contractually for a distributor or wholesaler to hold, or 

arranging contractually for a manufacturer to hold. The cost of establishing or maintaining inventory 

would not include the costs of the medicine itself. 

1

 
To assess whether this proposal would be an effective buffer, it is important to understand what drives 

current shortages, how hospitals currently respond to shortages, and how that response differs across 

hospital types. This will give indication of the likely impact of creating incentives for a buffer inventory. 

Currently, most shortages of the generic sterile injectable drugs heavily used in hospitals are caused by 

manufacturing quality problems that lead to production disruptions. When supply shocks occur, 

shortages are then exacerbated by panic buying by hospitals. When panic buying, hospitals try to rapidly

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

For heaven's sake, can't we let the animals and poultry that we raise for food have a short life of peace, compassion, humane treatment and proper food and medical care? It is the least that we can do for those innocent beings that give their lives for us.

Thank you for considering my request.

There are still only ~700 grizzly bears in Yellowstone, and I see no reason for de-listing the species, which will continue to be in a fragile state because of factors beyond our control, namely climate change and all the changes within the Yellowstone ecosystem that follow from it.

Worryingly, the FWS and states are clearly at odds on how the grizzly population should be maintained post-delisting. 

How will "secure" habitat be protected within the Primary Conservation Area when mortality rates are allowed to range up to 10% for female bears and 22% for male bears? This proposal does not contain adequate regulatory mechanisms to ensure secure habitat remains and that hunting will not disrupt National Park Service resources. 

How will the proposed mortality thresholds affect population numbers, dispersal, and connectivity?

If counting methodologies change in the future, mortality thresholds and the calculation of a stable population must be recalibrated. The proposed rule does not ensure this will occur. 

A final rule must commit to connectivity and coordinated management. The long-term viability of Yellowstone's grizzlies, especially in a time of climate change, depends on their ability to connect with other bear populations in the Northern Rockies - without human intervention. The grizzly bear is a conservation-reliant species that requires this coordinated management to continue into the foreseeable future.

Directed Question 1: Considering a requirement that would limit the reimbursement of indirect 
costs based on the grantee’s modified total direct cost (MTDC) base. 
 
Comment: It is not completely clear why the Department is considering a limit on the 
reimbursement of indirect costs based on a MTDC base for this particular Center application. 
The stated rationale is to make more grant funds available for technical assistance, but 
reimbursement of indirect costs has not been an issue historically in other technical assistance 
cooperative agreements or contracts, including the current Comprehensive Centers Program 
for ESSA, comprised of a National Comprehensive Center and nineteen (19) Regional 
Comprehensive Centers. Reimbursement of indirect costs to grantees in the Comprehensive 
Centers Program is based on Provisional Indirect Cost Rate Agreements reviewed, negotiated, 
and approved by the Office of Finance and Operations – Office of Grants Administration, 
Indirect Cost Division. Presentation of an Applicant’s most recent Negotiated Indirect Cost 
Rate Agreement is typically a requirement in any application. Those rates are approved by the 
Division based on reviews of actual costs—the costs that have been determined to be essential 
to sustaining that entity as a viable, operating business. 
 
Placing an arbitrary cap (35%) on Indirect Costs rather than using Negotiated Rates may 
prevent some organizations from applying for the Center, either as a Prime, or from 
participating as a subcontractor, if they will not be able to recover all of their negotiated 
Indirect Costs. 
 
The document’s references to Indirect Costs are not consistent. In some instances, the 
reference is about capping all Indirect Costs and in others it refers to a cap on “those 
administrative costs that are indirect costs for grantees”. It would be helpful to know how 
“administrative costs” are being defined. Are these the costs typically found in General and 
Administrative (G&A) indirect, for example, rather than administrative costs within an 
approved Overhead rate? 
 
Variations in the definition of Indirect Costs (Overhead – with or without Fringe Benefits; 
General & Administrative (G&A) etc.) and how/where an entity applies those indirect costs in 
a budget makes calculating a fair, reasonable “cap” very challenging. Not all organizations 
define Indirect Costs in the same manner or apply those rates in the same way in their 
budgets, which underscores the challenge of determining a cap percentage and the importance 
of the review and approval of Indirect Cost rates by the Department’s Indirect Cost Division.

should be conducted by the Center. Paragraph (C) of the proposed priority outlines the proposed

National Comprehensive Center on Improving Literacy for Students with Disabilities”, 
document is identical or very similar to that used in the recent Comprehensive Centers

Comprehensive Centers Program is funded and administered by OESE. The proposed

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Dear Dr.Miceli, 
 
These comments are being submitted on behalf of the IDEA Infant & Toddler Coordinators 
Association (ITCA). The ITCA represents states and other jurisdictions implementing the 
Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) Part C for infants and toddlers with and at 
risk for developmental delays and disabilities and their families. These comments relate to 
the U.S. Department of Education’s (ED) notice to establish a Technical Assistance (TA) center 
to improve states' capacity to collect, report, analyze, and use high-quality IDEA data. 
 
ITCA has two specific areas in the proposed priority on which we will comment: 
 
I. 
Proposed Priority and Expected Outcome: While the statutory language and the 
appropriations report language are clear that these TA funds are to be targeted to states to 
assist them in the collection, reporting, analysis and use of high-quality IDEA data, both 
Part B and Part C, this proposed priority only addresses Part B. Although, other data 
from general education, early childhood and Title 1 are mentioned specifically, there is 
no mention of Part C data. Including Part C data is necessary if a state is preparing a 
complete data picture of services and outcomes through these efforts. 
 
Recommendation: ITCA strongly recommends that the priority and expected outcomes 
included in the proposal be revised to add specific language supporting the inclusion of 
Part C and Preschool 619 data and the state lead agencies administering these programs. 
States are currently using these data to enhance their ability to answer critical questions 
that help evaluate and improve early childhood programs and services. Linking data 
across sources both vertically (Birth to 21 years and beyond) as well as horizontally 
(across programs such as IDEA, Head Start, Pre-K, child care, child welfare, health, Title 
1, etc.) can provide powerful information about the value of all these programs as they 
work to improve outcomes for children and families. Data from Part C and Preschool

 
619 are needed to create complete information about services provided under IDEA and 
by collaborating partners. Other data TA centers funded through the Department of 
Education are logical partners in this work. 
 
II. 
ED asked whether the establishment of two centers (i.e., one Center addressing the needs 
of Developed Capacity States, and another Center addressing the needs of Developing 
Capacity States) would be an efficient and effective approach to meeting the diverse 
needs of states in integrating, reporting, analyzing, and using high-quality IDEA Part B 
data? 
 
ITCA believes there is no need to establish two data management centers and that ED 
should respond to the TA goals and priorities to support states through one data center. In 
the experience of our members, states do not easily fit into one of the two categories 
described in the draft priority (i.e. Developed Capacity and Developing Capacity) to 
receive TA. States are in different places regarding these activities including in data 
quality and in the status of collaboration with partners. Individual state progress evolves 
as states work on priority activities and components necessary to linking and integrating 
data. These multiple activities do not always allow categorization of states to fit easily 
into these two categories. 
 
Additionally, creating two centers will generate unnecessary redundancies and result in 
inefficiencies. State staff often express the value of opportunities to learn from each 
other. If states are divided between two centers, it will be more difficult for state staff in 
various stages of data integration, to learn from their colleagues.

It’s not just trespass grows causing environmental issues. Since Colorado stores started legally selling recreational cannabis in 2014, emissions from the 600-plus licensed cultivation facilities in Denver have sparked concerns over air pollution.

William Vizuete, associate professor at the University of North Carolina’s Gillings School of Public Health, is working on an air quality model to better understand how commercial cannabis cultivation could affect the atmosphere. His research showed that cannabis plants produce volatile organic compounds or VOCs that can produce harmful pollutants.

“If plants produce VOCs, there is a high possibility that under certain conditions, cannabis cultivation could impact the ozone,” Vizuete explains. Cannabis emits potent VOCs called terpenes that, when mixed with nitrogen oxide and sunlight, form ozone-degrading aerosols. In a high desert zone like Denver, where normally there are few sources of VOCs, any new source of such pollutants will likely lead to ground-level ozone production, Vizuete notes. He worries that the significant numbers of cannabis plants being grown will become the regular source of VOCs, exacerbating the issue by combining with the manmade nitrogen oxide spewed from the many cars in that urban environment. Vizuete worries that the significant numbers of cannabis plants being grown in an urban area could exacerbate the issue. (High concentrations of VOCs have been linked to a range of human health issues, from nausea and fatigue to liver damage and cancer).

To test the potential effects, Vizuete grew four strains of cannabis (from among the 600-plus strains available in Colorado): Critical Mass, Lemon Wheel, Elephant Purple, and Rockstar Kush—for 90 days and measured the terpenes at each stage of growth. The results showed that in Denver, assuming a concentration of 10,000 plants per cultivation facility, cannabis could more than double the existing rate of annual VOC emissions to 520 metric tons and produce 2,100 metric tons of ozone.

Vizuete believes his estimates might be conservative, explaining, “We picked four [cannabis] strains based on their popularity, and their VOC emissions might not be representative all of the strains. Additionally, in commercial facilities, where conditions are optimized for growth, emissions may be even higher.” In California, the water-hungry crop is often grown in remote, forested watersheds and requires almost 22 liters of water per plant a day during the growing season, which adds up to three billion liters per square kilometer of greenhouse-grown plants between June and October, according to some research. During the low flow period, irrigation demands for cultivation can exceed the amount of water flowing in a river, leaving little water to sustain aquatic life.

Some of the biggest environmental offenders are cultivators operating unpermitted farms on public lands. These “trespass grows” are often in national forests or on tribal lands where water is diverted from streams to irrigate acres of plants. In 2018, there were an estimated 14,000 trespass grows on federal and private lands in Humboldt County, California, alone. See https://daily.jstor.org/the-environmental-downside-of-cannabis-cultivation/

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

Three specific restrictions in the proposed Defense Department regulation would undermine Stripes' reporters and editors as they work to provide reliable, impartial and independent news to the military community. These restrictions must be changed into permissions.
The regulation would prohibit Stripes from republishing news stories based on classified information already published elsewhere. It would impose a blackout on stories from wire services or other newsrooms about classified leaks, questionable secret operations, etc. – even if the security was already blown in print, online or broadcast around the world. That's absurd on its face – and the essence of censorship. The regulation should say that Stripes is authorized to exercise its own editorial judgment about republishing news reports already available to the public elsewhere based on classified or controlled unclassified information.
Weak language in the regulation would allow Pentagon Public Affairs offices to require that Stripes journalists be escorted on bases, even though they have already been vetted for security and authorized for access as DoD employees. You've probably been there – official escorts impede newsgathering and chill open interviews. The regulation should say that Stripes journalists are authorized access to otherwise unrestricted areas of military installations.
The regulation would allow the Pentagon to continue its practice of prohibiting Stripes reporters from using the Freedom of Information Act. The regulation should forbid DoD from rejecting Stripes reporters' FOIA queries on the basis of their status as government employees.

EXPAND THE CRITICAL HABITAT DESIGNATION FOR SOUTHERN RESIDENT KILLER WHALES TO INCLUDE THEIR ACTUAL HABITAT.

I support the proposed critical habitat expansion to include marine waters from California through Washington for Southern Resident killer whales because they're headed for extinction unless we do more to protect them.
The designation of marine coastal areas as critical habitat for these West Coast orcas is long overdue. I urge the government to finalize the rule as soon as possible. This orca population has dropped to just 73, the lowest level in over 30 years, and they urgently need more protected habitat.
Southern Residents have been starving because of depleted Chinook salmon runs and are also harmed by pollution that leads to toxins accumulating in their bodies over their long lives. In addition, vessel noise and disturbance interferes with their communications, resting and foraging.
Southern Resident critical habitat protections are currently limited to the Salish Sea, but orcas forage in the winter and spring from Canada to Monterey Bay in Northern California. Protecting this full range as critical habitat can mean cleaner water and fewer disturbances for orcas. For example, this means that federally permitted activities - like water pollution permits, military sonar activities, and offshore drilling - won't be allowed to damage their habitat.
Because critical habitat pertains to federal actions only, this rule will not burden local governments. Fishing for salmon is already undergoing review by the federal government to protect orcas; this process could restrict fishing in areas of proposed critical habitat, depending on the best available science available at the time of the decision.
We know the Endangered Species Act works to protect animals. Over 99 percent of those listed do not go extinct. Further, those listed animals with critical habitat protection are twice as likely as those without it to be recovering.

I support the proposed rule to list the Queen Conch as a threatened species. This plays a critical role in the conservation of the species and is a way to ensure that it does not become an endangered species in the future. 

Queen Conch can live up to thirty years and play an important role in the ecosystem. Queen conch are marine snails, and they require direct contact to mate. Therefore, without a stable adult population, they cannot reproduce. Queen conch are benthic-grazing herbivores that feed on algae, epiphytes, diatoms, and seagrass. Without Queen Conch the health of seagrass beds would rapidly decline. If Queen Conch become endangered a trophic cascade would occur and there would be an imbalance in the ecosystem. Queen Conch are also an important food source for larger predators and without them predators would have to turn to an alternate food source which could increase competition.
Queen Conch are threatened by overharvesting and illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. How much we harvest effects how fast or slow a population can grow. Overharvesting results in slow population growth. The maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is how much you can take without compromising future availability and right now we are over the MSY which is resulting in slow population growth. Competition and niche differentiation allow complete competitors to co-exist but fishing pressures are already driving Queen Conch out of their preferred habitat which creates unwanted competition. This skews habitat, resource, and predator partitioning not allowing competitors to exist in harmony.

Queen Conch need to be protected before it is too late. The species and ecosystem as a whole are fragile and Queen Conch should not only be listed as a threatened species but protected and regulated until it is of little concern.

The drawback committees of the industry associations cited submitted various comments on the proposed drawback regulations. We contributed to these comments and are in full agreement with the recommendations with made therein. 

We offer the following supplemental comments: 

Drawback on Federal Excise Tax: The extensive policy position outlined in the NPRM suggests that CBP is engaged in policy making instead of implementation of the TFTEA statue and ensuring the intent of Congress is accurately represented in drawbacks regulatory framework. CBPs argues that allowing exportation of merchandise that is free of excise tax results in a double benefit. It proposes eliminating drawback on exported merchandise filed under 19 USC 1313(J)(2) that is free of tax. By logical extension, if this same rule where applied to regular duty in addition to excise tax, then the effect would be the elimination of a claimants ability to substitute domestic merchandise for the imported duty paid merchandise. Why is the type of fee or tax a determining factor in eligibility under the statue? CBP has clearly substituted its authority for that of Congress. Given the amount of potential recovery to various industries, the issue is destined for costly and time consuming litigation. 

Agriculture Fees: The Drawback CATAIR includes requirements related to the electronic submission of drawback against various agriculture fees. As the eligibility of such fees has been a previous point of contention between CBP and the Trade, the regulations should make the eligibility of such clear by including a specific citation of the drawback eligibility of fees collected at the time of importation. 

First Filed Rule: Customs should designate a transition period from CORE from TFTEA that allows for a solution to what appears to be more of a systems issue, in that entries designated both at the HTS line using averaging as and those based the invoice line appear to be incompatible in ACE. The NCBFAA suggested using invoice value only during this transition. There are other possible solutions. CBP should work with Trade industry representatives to fashion a workable solution. 

Specific Manufacturing Drawback Rulings: The elimination of the need for time consuming specific manufacturing drawback rulings was thought to be one of the clear benefits of HTS level substitution. The primary purpose of the specific ruling was the establishment of manufacturing substitution parameters specific to a claimants manufacturing operations necessitated by the fact that its operations fell outside the scope of an existing general ruling. TFTEA HTS level substitution makes the need for such a determination moot. the United States. Farmworker Justice works with migrant and community health centers, 
farmworker community-based organizations and farmworker advocates to improve 
farmworkers’ health and safety and to ensure greater access to healthcare. 
 
IRS asks for comments on how the quality, utility, and clarity of information collected 
under section 6055 may be enhanced. Section 6055 requires issuers to report certain 
information of covered individuals to the IRS, including tax identification numbers 
(TINs). The proposed regulations clarify the provisions related to the proper solicitation 
of TINs. 
 
The proposed regulations make it clear that reporting entities must report a TIN or date of 
birth, if a TIN is not available. To ensure that farmworkers are encouraged to provide 
their TINs to issuers, in compliance with section 6055, we encourage IRS to further 
clarify that TIN solicitations from issuers must refer to all TINs, not just social security 
numbers (SSNs). Issuers who request only SSNs in their solicitations discourage workers 
from enrolling in health insurance. Enrolled farmworkers and their family members may 
not have an SSN. Instead, they may have an Individual Tax Identification Number 
(ITIN). Some may not have any form of TIN, especially family members who may also 
be covered under an employer or other private health insurance plan. 
 
Further, we recommend that IRS clarify in its final rule that entities cannot charge a fee 
or transfer a penalty to the consumer for failure to provide a TIN. The proposed 
regulation makes it clear that reporting entities will not be penalized for not collecting

 
TINs, rather they will be penalized for not making a good faith effort to collect TINs. 
However, we are concerned that issuers and other reporting entities may use TIN 
solicitation under section 6055 to collect fees from individuals. For example, some 
workers have reported receiving notices from issuers indicating that they will be assessed 
a fine for not providing an SSN. Since the solicitation satisfies a good faith effort to 
collect TINs under the regulations, it is not appropriate for entities to threaten fines to 
consumers who fail to provide an SSN or other TIN. These types of letters, rather than 
encourage the provision of TINs, creates a chilling effect, deterring others from enrolling 
in health insurance Further, seeking payment from consumers without SSNs could be 
seen as charging non-SSN/TIN holders higher rates for health insurance, which is not 
allowed under the ACA’s market reform.

reporting under section 6055. Thank you for your attention.

Thank you to DOT for these long awaited rule making next steps. Having oral fluid testing added to the very limited only option of urine testing is long overdue, and greatly needed by many companies and providers in our industry. It will add an invaluable new method to the tool-chest of testing options not only for the DOT market and customers, but it will expand testing options for non-regulated customers who tend to use the DOT guidelines as their gold seal of approval. Oral fluid provides a tool that is harder to beat, making drug testing more reliable; it will expand testing by given us options to test in circumstances where it is next to impossible to collect urine, adding to safer workplaces; it will provide a solid way to detect recent use which is greatly needed today in our industry; it will save costs particularly where collections can be done directly in the workplace; finally it will eliminate unintentional effects (invalid samples) from over-hydrating in markets where workers need to consume large quantities of liquids to stay hydrated since oral fluid cannot be diluted. We submit just a few comments about the oral fluid collection device we think are important: 
 
We believe a split sample for DOT testing can be achieved using two swabs simultaneously as per the HHS guidelines. This has been done for many years effectively by our customers with no issue even when challenges have occured. It is easy, straightforward and accomplishes the intent of having an A & B sample. From our perspective and information, 2 samples taken this way from the mouth at the same time are so closely similar, no method would detect any differences given they all have their own inherent variability. This could be left side, right side of the mouth, or both under the tongue...again, very much the same sample. We are not in support of 2 samples taken separately with a wait time in between. Oral fluid content/components tend to change every 5 to 10 minutes so a sequential type collection could in effect produce differing samples. 

- We also believe single devices should be allowed that have two pads together in the same unit, either side by side or back to back, thereafter separated into 2 samples, A & B. 

- We would also support a single device, such as a funnel type device that is spit into, collecting a sample that is then sub-divided into an A & B sample on the spot should be allowed. It is unclear how well the drug testing market will adapt to such a device, however, given the launch of similar devices for COVID testing, it is possible that an openness to this method could evolve. However, it should not be our only choice.
- It is also advised that in order to anticipate future developments and advances in oral fluid collection device design, language should be added that would provide a mechanism for the review of said future designs for inclusion in the DOT guidelines of new devices that may not be described herein.

- Regarding expiration dating of devices and transparency of devices, having the collector document the expiration date of the device should be a "must". Without the expiration date being on the chain of custody form, there is a risk of an expired device being sent to the lab. This will cause problems both from a logistics perspective and a legal perspective should the test result go to court. The laboratory should not need to be concerned about the expiration date of a device since it was sent a valid dated device from the point of collection. Also the expiration date on the vial may be covered by the CCF seal making it VERY difficult for the lab to read that date. This would cause rejection of a perfectly valid sample causing delays for recollection, costs and loss of the original sample integrity which could be a big issue in the case of a post-accident test that would have been positive but is now negative due to the second collection being at a later time. This comment is submitted on behalf of Open Oregon Educational Resources, the program 
designated by the state of Oregon to support open education and textbook affordability in our 
colleges and universities. Open Oregon Educational Resources promotes textbook affordability 
for community college and university students, and facilitates widespread adoption of open, 
low-cost, high-quality materials. We applaud the congressional appropriation for the Open 
Textbook Pilot Program, and hope that our recommendations will be helpful as the Department 
considers how to implement the program to best support its intent to achieve savings for 
students, while maintaining or improving instruction and student learning outcomes. 
Purpose of Program 
The purpose of the Open Textbook Pilot Program can be clarified in order to receive 
submissions that are in line with the intent of the program. As written, it is both too broad and 
too narrow - a Goldilocks problem. At issue is this phrase: “create new open textbooks or 
expand the use of open textbooks.” 
 
Too narrow: “textbooks.” A textbook is widely understood to be an authoritative book by subject 
matter experts with the primary purpose of supporting curriculum, available in print or online. 
While ebooks may include interactive and multimedia elements, a textbook is, in essence, a 
book. Seeking to create or expand the use of open textbooks does not take into account the 
very wide range of openly licensed resources already in use that could be creatively deployed 
by applicants. A broader term should be used, and that term is Open Educational Resources 
(OER). Open textbooks are a subset of OER and will be understood to be a relevant format for 
development by grant applicants.

Proposed rule § 656.22(b)(1) would require applicants for an undergraduate Center to demonstrate that the institution or consortium of institutions primarily serves undergraduate students through educational programs as an outgrowth of the institution's mission and identity as an institution focused predominantly or even exclusively on undergraduate education. In this context, an institution “predominantly” serves undergraduate students when baccalaureate or higher degrees represent at least 50 percent of all degrees but where fewer than 50 master's degrees or 20 doctoral degrees were awarded in the most recent year preceding the application deadline for which data is available. 

As a faculty director of a current undergraduate NRC (Asian Studies), I believe this proposed rule is much too narrow for the purposes of the NRC program. The NRC program is intended to contribute to the national interest through training of students in foreign languages and area studies. The proposed criterion of The criterion of fewer than 50 awarded master's degrees or 20 doctoral degrees would effectively exclude most major research universities, particularly the flagship public R1s, from becoming undergraduate NRCs. My university, for example, produces many doctorates and master's degrees, but not in Asian studies per se. Our center serves faculty, students, and staff, but its curricular offerings are focused on undergraduates. Federal grants are our major source of funding because foreign language and area studies are not a priority for university administrations focused solely on enrollments. At a time when the US is desperately in need of specialists in foreign area studies, this seems like an unnecessary and counterproductive change to the very successful NRC program. Instead of this, the program should allow for a diversity of institutions to be competitive for NRCs, including research universities and land grant institutions, smaller state universities, and a variety of other categories of institutions as well.

 I ask you to permit the disposal of non-compliant hemp in farming or fuel, and eliminate the requirement that all such material must be destroyed. This is not only contemplated by the Farm Bill, but it would be an invaluable resource and cost-savings for farmers.

 I encourage you to extend the 15-day sampling period to 30 days in order to prevent testing bottlenecks and be consistent with a number of current state laws.

communications. We write to express concerns about the implementation of DSRC as currently 

detailed in the NPRM. Specifically, we raise concerns regarding the potential for non-safety uses 

of DSRC spectrum and radios, cybersecurity, and privacy risks associated with DSRC, and the 

implications this mandate may have for ongoing efforts to find ways to share the 5.9 GHz band 

with non-DSRC unlicensed users. Commenters urge that, as NHTSA considers moving forward,

vehicle safety,” specifically by “reduc[ing] the number and severity of motor vehicle crashes, 

thereby reducing the losses and costs to society that would have resulted from these crashes.”2

ANPRM record, and throughout the public debate on the DSRC issue, is unanimous. It is 

worrying, however, that in pursuing this laudable goal, the door remains open to 

commercialization3 of the DSRC service. The FCC’s service rules do not presently prohibit 

commercialization of DSRC technology, though a Petition for Rulemaking submitted by 

Commenters to that body remains pending.4 NHTSA’s NPRM neither mandates nor prohibits

Every year, our lives become more connected to and dependent on the digital world. Products and 

services that once only existed in the physical world are now part of our connected society. 

Automobiles are no exception. 

As physical machines evolve into increasingly software-dependent and connected platforms, technology 

is reshaping the relationship between vehicles and their users. In the past, the main, or only, external 

input for a vehicle was the driver or occupants of the vehicle. That is no longer the case. Innovative 

vehicle technologies - combined with the integration of vehicles into a broader ecosystem of connected 

infrastructure, devices, features, and stakeholders – can unlock a wide range of benefits in safety, fuel 

efficiency, and convenience. This transformation also provides consumers with new - and, increasingly, 

remote - ways of interacting and engaging with vehicles, opening doors to innovative businesses, 

technologies, and services.

electrification, automation– may also introduce new threats and risks. These increasingly digital, rather

has relied on robust risk management standards and practices to develop and deploy life-saving safety

industry is adapting cybersecurity risk management strategies to meet the challenges and complexities of 

the modern vehicle.

I agree with this proposed regulation on the need to expand shark handling/release rules to include more types of fishing vessels/methods than purse seine, such as longline fishing. This ensures that there is no longer the issue of imperfect/asymmetrical information that could allow longline vessels to get away with potentially harmful practices regarding the incidental catch and release of sharks. In particular, making sure that incidentally caught sharks stuck in the branchline should have the line cut close to the hook, at no more than a meter of line remaining, is needed to maintain the safety of the sharks and their place in the ecosystem as shorter line remaining causes less problems. I will add, though, that there is research (such as that described in “Quantitative estimates of post-release survival rates of sharks captured in Pacific tuna longline fisheries reveal handling and discard practices that improve survivorship” by Hutchinson, et al., 2021) that suggests it is healthier for the shark to have the hook removed, as when a hook remains in the shark it increases the chance of infection and mortality. I believe it should be encouraged to first remove the hook if it is safe for the vessel operator/crew to do so, and not only focus on cutting the branchline (though that is, of course, still important). 

Though catching sharks is not the actual “purpose” of these fishing vessels, sharks play an integral role in regulating the populations of tuna and tuna-like (and other commercial fishing) species. Their preying on the weaker tuna allows for the healthier/stronger tuna populations to survive, and their populations can be a good indicator of the health of the marine environment where they live. By ensuring the safety of sharks, it prevents a “tragedy of the commons” type of situation. At first, a reduction in shark populations could be seen as beneficial for commercial fishing, as it will allow the tuna populations to grow due to lack of predation. However, eventually the greater population (and overfishing) will lead to decline with the competition for resources. 

In “Banning is not enough: The complexities of oceanic shark management by tuna regional fisheries management organizations,” from Tolotti et al. (2015), they describe that the act of banning the retention and trade of caught sharks is often not enough to establish safe shark populations. Even without keeping/trading sharks, the approach to shark catch and release was still harmful, with many sharks dying while being caught or shortly after being released. I believe that this aspect of the proposal’s goal to further implement safe release practices of incidentally caught sharks will be a good way to remediate the effects of unsafe release practices. 

Thank you for your time and allowing for the submission of comments from the public.

I respectfully submit this comment to strongly oppose USCIS's NPRM, USCIS-2020-0019; RIN 1615-AC61. This misguided rule, which dramatically alters the way in which H-1B registrations are selected for the annual H-1B statutory cap, is inconsistent with Congressional intent, is in violation of the statute, and will undermine our nation's pipeline of global talent we need to drive innovation and foster economic growth.

As an immigration attorney who represents employers in healthcare, tech, finance, manufacturing, and other industries, I can tell you this new rule will hurt U.S. employers by adding yet another obstacle to their ability of employers to attract talent and grow.

This Proposed Rule is a Clear Violation of the Statute and Congressional Intent:

The H-1B program was established by Congress to provide an avenue for employers to hire a foreign worker in a specialty occupation. This proposed rule is a clear violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which prioritizes the selection of H-1B cap-subject petitions in the "order in which they are filed" and does not limit who is selected for the H-1B cap to those employers who pay the most. USCIS lacks the statutory authority to make such a change and cannot use the statute's silence as an invitation to adopt criteria, such as wage level or skill level, to prioritize the selection of H-1B cap subject visas. 

This Proposed Rule is Based on a False Premise That Salary Alone Equates with Value: 

This proposal, which is based on the false premise that individuals who earn more in their profession contribute more to the economy or society, is yet another misguided and illegal attempt by the Trump administration to weaken our legal immigration and promote falsities about the workers who, contrary to what this rule implies, strengthen our economy.

If implemented, this rule will have a direct and negative impact on U.S. employers and college-educated foreign-born professionals by dramatically reducing access to the H-1B visa program for early-career professionals, including those completing Master's or Doctoral degrees at U.S. colleges and universities. Indeed, USCIS has acknowledged that if this new regulation is implemented, no individuals who are paid a Level 1 wage would be selected to submit a H-1B cap-subject petition for the annual H-1B cap. These proposed changes would effectively eliminate the H-1B program as an available visa option for new graduates seeking employment in an entry-level position.

USCIS Should Refrain From Implementing this Rule For the FY2022 H-1B Cap Filing Season:

Many U.S. employers and immigration attorneys start preparing for the H-1B cap filing season months in advance, in some cases as early as August depending on the industry. Any changes by USCIS to the H-1B cap filing process this late in the year would have an adverse impact on U.S. employers, immigration attorneys and individuals, as hiring decisions and filing processes and procedures have already been put in place by many employers and immigration law firms. Thus, if USCIS finalizes this illegal and misguided rule, USCIS must refrain from implementing it for the upcoming FY2022 H-1B cap filings season in order to allow U.S. businesses, immigration attorneys and individuals sufficient time to adapt to the new wage-based selection process.

 For communities of color and low-income people living in areas burdened by air pollution from coal-fired electric power plants., they bear the brunt f the health effects.

I am a DACA recipient who has resided in the United States for more than 20 years. For instance, DACA has allowed its recipients to pursue higher education, access more and better job opportunities, deepen their social ties in the US, serve in the front lines as essential workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, and simply participate more fully in their communities. - Ninety-five percent is employed.
- Eighty-eight percent speaks English well, very well, or only English. 
- The great majority speaks at least two languages: 94 percent speaks a language other than English at home. 
- DACA recipients participate in the US labor market at high rates. Eighty-three percent is in the labor force. From this pool, 95 percent is employed. Five percent of those in the labor force (or 27,100 DACA recipients) is self-employed."
