I am a former over-the-road tractor-trailer driver with several years' experience who was never involved in an accident in which someone was injured. Nor was I ever cited for speeding. I believe I am qualified to comment on this issue. I am passionately opposed to the speed limiter mandate. I wish to state:

1. This proposal would effectively reinstate a federal limitation on speed. Many states, if not most, have been setting speed limits in accordance with sound principles of traffic engineering since the NMSL was repealed and the NHTSA has no business butting in now. Should the NHTSA do so, it will be up to the Republican Congress to reaffirm the gift they gave to the American motorist in 1995 and intervene on his behalf. I will be contacting my congressman and holding him to account on this issue.

2. Trucking companies championing speed limiters claim this mandate will "level the playing field." Even assuming this is a valid need, it can be accomplished without the heavy hand of government by their simply speeding up. Using the NHTSA to gain a competitive advantage is crony capitalism at its worse.

3. They claim their effort is all about safety. Frankly, I am tired of hearing about safety. Motor travel is far safer than ever before. As far as I am concerned, the goal of safe roads has been achieved. Any further improvement can only come about with ever more severe restrictions on drivers' liberty. Man is imperfect and as long as he is free there will be property damage, injuries and fatalities when he chooses to travel at a pace greater than nature provides. "Vision Zero" and similar efforts should be seen for what they are: a utopian fantasy. They are a serious threat to individual liberty. At this point, I choose liberty over safety.

4. Given the goal of safe motor travel having been achieved, agencies such as the NHTSA have outlived their usefulness and should be abolished or relegated to data collection. 5. The companies also complain of a chronic driver shortage. There are many ways in which their treatment of drivers contributes to this. One is speed limiting their trucks. I will never drive any vehicle speed limited by government decree. Except under very limited circumstances, I will never again knowingly drive any other speed limited vehicle. Comment to the Fish and Wildlife Service regarding “Endangered and Threatened Species: Revision to the Nonessential Experimental Population of the Mexican Wolf”:

Contrary to the position implied by the title of this proposed rule, Mexican gray wolves are essential. Zoos and captive breeding facilities in the Mexican Wolf Species Survival Plan could not replace the nearly 200 wolves in the wild, particularly with respect to genetic diversity. The need for genetic diversity to sustain a healthy and stable Mexican gray wolf population also requires the existence of several population zones, including the Grand Canyon ecoregion and Southern Rockies in addition to existing populations in the designated Mexican Wolf Experimental Population Area and Mexico. Further, arbitrary population boundaries such as the proposed I-40 boundary, restrict the natural dispersal of individuals which helps to maintain genetic diversity of the greater population.
With respect to the I-40 boundary in particular, suitable wolf habitat exists north of Interstate 40 and FWS should be pursuing recovery in this expanded area. Although FWS acknowledges that territory north of I-40 will likely be required for future recovery and recognizes the importance of natural dispersal and expanding the species’ range, it nevertheless imposes a hard limit on dispersal north of I-40. The realities of climate change predict that wildlife species will shift their ranges in response and Mexican gray wolves will likely move further northward into the Grand Canyon region if allowed to do so. FWS must adequately address the potential changes in wolf habitat, prey species, water and vegetation distribution, and wolf movements due to the impacts of climate change in the revised Mexican Wolf 10(j) Management Rule. 

While I am grateful to FWS for agreeing to limit certain kinds of Mexican gray wolf “takes”, FWS must do more to limit human-caused mortality, including illegal killing. Proposed limits on taking wolves should be made permanent, not temporary. If Anubis were better protected, he might be alive today to lead the way toward Mexican gray wolf recovery in suitable wolf habitat.

Finally, I beseech FWS to meaningfully include indigenous voices in Mexican gray wolf conservation. There are diverse perspectives on wolves amongst tribes in and around the Mexican Wolf Experimental Population Area. Incorporation of their knowledge derived from centuries of coexistence would greatly benefit the development of this rule change. These indigenous perspectives should be uplifted as part of an inclusive and transparent rule change. 

Thank you for your careful and thoughtful consideration,

Thanks to FDA for keeping patients safe from hospital acquired infection.

 Section VII "Summary of Data Upon Which the Reclassification Is Based," details cases of infection transmission. These involve hundreds of patients around the world over three decades. In many situations, human error facilitated infection transmission.

 As well as the cases cited in this FDA guidance, other evidence points to additional cases of disease transmission. In diabetes, notably glucose meters and other materials can transmit infection. FDA has raised concern over clinical use meters. CDC has detailed that test strip containers are one such other means of passing infection from one patient to another. FDA should consider the total risk, not piecemeal responses.

 ALL of the evidence presented in the docket is of transmission in professional care facilities. It is clear that healthcare facilities are where FDA should address the problem of lancets infection transmission. Don't fix what isn't broken. The draft presents no evidence to support the proposed up-regulation of personal lancet devices.

 I appreciate FDA efforts to protect people in the clinical setting. That is a setting where we, as patients, have no way of knowing if we are getting fresh blades and disinfected devices. In some cases, we may not even be conscious to ask.

 FDA's 2013 draft meter guidance is instructive to this docket. While the final guidance is not yet out, the draft made a clear distinction between the setting of professional use and individual over the counter home use. Separating devices based on these environments is a logical precedent to follow with lancets.

 FDA should be addressing documented problems. All of the evidence FDA presents is in clinical settings. Therefore, FDA should be using guidance and labeling to address the clinical setting where we need protection and device design that can minimize human factors that contribute to risk.

 Section VII shows that multiple patient devices in-clinic use are a particular risk. The proposed up-regulation to class III of such devices is an indication of FDA's appreciation of that risk. FDA should be clear how unique device identifiers will usefully implement with replaceable blade devices and how both components will be tracked.

 I support FDA taking reasonable regulatory precautions and labeling steps to guide health care providers to use single patient, one-time use, disposable devices. Specifically, those that have blade protection as outlined in section V part B. Multi-patient devices should discourage through regulatory and labeling measures. FDA should address the real risk of transmission and create a clear delineation that safe, single-use, disposable lancets are the best practice.

 Labeling is a tool FDA can use to differentiate between use devices intended for home use and professional settings.

 Devices for a single patient, over the counter, with replaceable blades, should carry a black box label NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. One time use disposable lancets, with blade protection as outlined in section V part B, should be labeled APPROVED FOR CLINICAL USE.

 Price is a driver of purchasing behavior. Third party purchasers, other than the caregiver and patient, may assume that any FDA-approved device is safe in all settings. Clear labeling, as suggested above, will create an economic liability for clinical purchasing agents and insurance payers who require anything for clinical use but lancet devices explicitly approved for clinical use.

 Price driven purchasing is a documented source of safety disruption related to blood testing. The Journal Diabetes Care recently detailed the disruption of testing supplies as a source of increased hospitalization and mortality in diabetes patients served by Medicare. I fear a similar economic driven disruption will occur with lancet access driving use of less expensive devices not intended for clinical settings. FDA labels can protect patients with labels.

The welfare of animals raised for food is important to me, and misleading label claims used to market foods to the public need to be meaningfully addressed. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range," "humanely raised," or similar animal-raising claims, because the FSIS fails to adequately regulate the use of such claims.

When I see the claim "free range," I understand it to mean more than limited access to a barren outdoor area. When I see the claim "humanely raised," I expect it to mean that the animals received significantly better care than the baseline industry standard.

Third-party certification for animal-raising claims must require verification not just encourage it. Encouragement alone is like asking companies to voluntarily police themselves - i.e., like putting a fox in the henhouse.

Over the past decade, the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) has investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims and nearly 100 approved labels containing "humanely raised," "sustainably farmed," or similar claims. Among AWI's findings:

• Although "free range" and "range grown" claims ostensibly require "outdoor access," the FSIS defines that term so broadly that consumers are likely to be misled about what access, specifically, the animals received.

• For "humanely raised" and "sustainably farmed" labels, 85% of applications lacked adequate substantiation.

I am disappointed by these results and FSIS's revisions to its label approval guidelines fail to correct these issues. The agency must require--not merely encourage--producers to obtain third-party certification for animal-raising claims. Crucially, this certification must verify that the level of animal care provided significantly exceeds that of conventional industry standards. And for "free range" claims, the agency must make it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient.

Thank you for considering my request.

The IFR notes in a number of locations that the FAST Act made limited administrative 
changes to the Section 402 program, no substantive changes to existing Section 405 
grants, and no changes to the contents of the Highway Safety Plan. In reality, the IFR 
made a number of substantive changes that place an unrealistic and unnecessary 
administrative burden on states already under pressure to deliver proven, effective 
countermeasures to reduce death and injury on roadways across the nation. To wit: 
 1300.11(b) Performance Report—requiring a state to include specifics related to 
how the state will adjust to better meet HSP performance goals. This information

provide program level information. This regulation requires project level 
information with additional elements that were not requested by Congress or

PLAN for the coming year than is produced up-to nine months in advance.

project level information be required, every change and amendment would require 
information so detailed that states and regional offices would be unduly burdened 
by administrative requirements. The IFR also states that the HSP must include

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

Mercyhurst University strongly opposes changes to Duration of Status (D/S) for international students and exchange visitors contained in a proposed rule published in the Federal Register Sept. 25 by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). If adopted, this rule would have wide-ranging detrimental effects for international students in the United States and in our own Laker community.

For decades, most international students have been allowed to remain in the United States for the full length of their program, otherwise known as Duration of Status (D/S). The proposed rule seeks to effectively eliminate D/S, and instead replace it with fixed terms of admission, ranging from 2 to 4 years. If this rule is finalized, our students' ability to complete their program of study will be severely impeded.

The proposed rule argues that the elimination of Duration of Status is necessary to safeguard national security by reducing overstays. However, it fails to establish with compelling evidence that overstays happen with any statistically significant frequency. Moreover, the published rule links to a DHS report published in March 2020 that shows an overwhelming majority of students and exchange visitors, 98.79%, follow our nation's immigration laws and depart or change status within the time frame required. To fundamentally change a system that has been in place for decades to reduce an already minimal (less than 2%) number of students who fail to comply is overly punitive and counterproductive.

As stated by Esther Zimmer, Executive Director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, "This proposal sends another message to immigrants, and in particular international students and exchange visitors, that their exceptional talent, work ethic, diverse perspectives, and economic contributions are not welcome in the United States."

The Open Textbooks Pilot Program is a valuable and much needed initiative for reducing students' post-secondary educational costs. As the Department of Education moves forward with setting definitions and establishing parameters for this grant cycle, it is imperative that this be kept at the forefront when making the final decisions. Emphasis and priorities should be in supporting innovative ideas that will result in long-term sustainable student learning outcomes and will continue to lower costs for students well past this grant cycle. With this in mind, the following suggestions are offered:

Defining Open textbooks: Much more goes into a student's education than just reading the textbook. Homework, assessments, and a host of other ancillary materials contribute significantly to student learning and success. These should definitely be included in the definition of an open textbook. 

Matching Contribution: A matching contribution should not be a requirement of this program. It would be unfortunate if a great idea was excluded because the contributor's institution did not have the resources to provide a matching contribution.

Inclusion of non-profits: There a lot of non-profits whose missions reflect increasing the success of post-secondary students, especially students from under-served populations. Their efforts towards improving student learning outcomes tend to align very well with the spirit of this program. Non-profits have a lot to contribute to post-secondary education and should definitely be eligible for grant awards.

Number of Collaborating Institutions: There should be no restrictions on the number of institutions collaborating on a grant project. The number of institutions involved in a grant project should not be a determining factor in awarding funds. What's important is the quality of the proposed project and if it has the potential to contribute to lowering post-secondary education costs beyond the scope of the grant project. If a single institution has a great idea, it deserves funding, as does a collaboration of multiple institutions. Likewise the entities submitting proposals need not already be involved in OER. This program offers a great way for "non-OER" institutions to get involved.

Award Size: The Department of Education needs to strike the right balance with respect to the number of awards granted. While there needs to be multiple awards granted, there should not be so many awards that the funds are diluted to the point of being ineffective. One possibility is having a single large award of up to two million dollars, two awards not to exceed 1.5 million dollars, and the remaining funds distributed to some or all of the remaining proposals. This would result in at the very least four awards being made, but could be more.

High enrollment courses: While targeting high enrollment courses would have a greater impact on the number of students benefiting from the program, a proposal targeting students in a low enrollment course should not automatically be excluded from funding consideration. If the proposal has merit and the rationale for targeting a low enrollment course is sound (e.g., the students are from a marginalized population), then the proposal should be given full consideration.

I agree that we need to extend protections for the Red Grouper, however I don’t think the 
rule being proposed is strict enough. An update to the previous amendments passed should be 
obvious as these Red Groupers are still being overfished. Amendment 24 was not strict enough 
in it’s rebuilding plan and we need to make sure we forge a proper plan this time so we’re not in 
the same place in another ten years. I don’t agree with the plan’s decision to not add the month of 
May to the offseason for Red Grouper as I do believe a more aggressive plan should be in place. 
Red Groupers also spawn from February to June so making another month during their spawn 
season off limits would have a direct impact on improving population among the species. I also 
think the 200lb limit for commercial fishing is too high and might not even have any effect on 
the Grouper’s population. As is said on this website historical fishing trips for grouper usually 
come in at under 200lbs so what’s the point of imposing a limit if it’s never going to be met? 
Whatever amount of red grouper that has been fished commercially, is clearly leading to 
overfishing and a decrease in population, so we need to have a study on what the average for 
these commercial trips have brought back and make the limit below that in order to stop over 
fishing. Red Grouper are not only for us to eat, but play a vital role in our ecosystems as well. 
Red Grouper are among the top predators in reef community food webs and play in an important 
part in controlling the community balance in reef systems. They are also food for larger predators 
such as jacks, groupers, sharks, barracudas, and morays, all who depend on them for food. 
Another role the Red Grouper plays in our ecosystems is that they actively remove sediment and 
other debris from the limestone holes they occupy. By doing this they create settlement sites for 
sponges, corals, anemones, and other species while creating a refuge for others. The mass

 
removal of these groupers of recent years have not only impacted the red grouper but it’s 
surroundings as well for they’re an integral part to their ecosystem in many ways. This proposal 
is the right step but is not nearly strict as it should be, and I would encourage policy makers to 
take a second look at this proposal and come back with something that will be more supportive 
in helping the red grouper population recover. An extended offseason and lower commercial 
limit are necessary for the red grouper nots to be overfished.

As a clinician who cares for patients who receive important care at rates determined by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, I am greatly disappointed to see CMS reduce work RVUs for cardiac ablation, pulmonary angiography, and pulmonary revascularization services below the values recommended by the American Medical Association/Specialty Society RVS Update Committee (RUC) in the 2023 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule proposed rule. I urge you and the staff at CMS to reconsider the proposed work RVU reductions to these services in the 2023 rulemaking and implement the RUC-recommended values. After a year of devastating cuts to CV services, further cuts for 2023 are simply indefensible. We are currently facing record inflation, a continuation of the nationwide public health emergency, and significant challenges retaining our workforce. We urge CMS to re-evaluate their position and its harmful impact on patient access to care. We cannot sustain continued cuts, especially cuts that go beyond the RUC recommendations.

Beyond the troubling trend of ongoing reductions via conversion factor cuts (proposed -4.5% in CY2023), statutory cuts from sequestration and PAYGO rules, and a flat annual payment update that fails to account for significant inflation in practice costs, these specific reductions are an alarming and significant departure from the RUC recommended values. The RUC survey and evaluation process, in which practicing physician feedback is used to create recommended relative values for services, was in these instances disregarded by using comparator codes which are in no way comparable to the services in question. Despite the RUC process taking great lengths to recognize and adjust to the new efficiencies of these codes due to advanced technology that increases complexity and risk, CMS further reduced the RUC proposed values. 

After the large reductions ablation services underwent in 2022 resulting from bundling of services and subsequent refinement of the work RVUs by the RUC based on a second work RVU survey for 2023, further reductions at the scale proposed are unfounded. Doing so will harm patients' access to care and the clinicians who serve them. RVUs for these services were reduced 26% from 2021 to 2022 through bundling. Phasing-in of these reductions should have taken place in 2022, but did not occur. CMS's proposal for 2023 would reduce the same codes another 10% within a 12-month period, based solely on a desire to see greater reductions in RVUs commensurate with time that ignore the intensity and risk inherent in these services. 

While still a reduction, the RVUs from the April 2021 RUC recommendations, which reflect survey data from electrophysiologists who perform these services, should be used to establish their value. Because of the issues noted above, the survey median values, which are above the RUC recommendations, better reflect the skill, intensity, complexity, and risk of these services. These values appropriately capture reductions in time while also reflecting the intensity that remains in these services. To make the work of ablating tissue inside the heart to control chronic rhythm disorders equivalent to the work of revascularization of a lower extremity vessel, as CMS proposes, would be improper and a distortion of the relativity of these procedures.

Pulmonary services suffer a similar outcome, where CMS seems to consider time without regard to intensity or complexity. In some instances, this was done when submitted materials included compelling evidence the services had changed from their prior work valuation and are now more intense. With new codes, the rule repeatedly states that values appear high compared to codes with similar times, making reductions appropriate. However, this fails to account for the increased intensity and work of these services versus the services CMS identifies, all of which are performed primarily in pediatric populations for congenital heart disease.

Dear Dr. Engeljohn:

I am pleased to see that the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service is updating its label approval process. However, I am dismayed that the new animal raising claims guidance (Docket No. FSIS-2016-0021) does not address several concerns that have been brought to your attention. For instance, the Animal Welfare Institute exposed weaknesses--vague definitions and insufficient evidence to verify claims--within the label approval process in two reports: "Label Confusion: How 'Humane' and 'Sustainable' Claims on Meat Packages Deceive Consumers" and "USDA Gives Producers Free Reign Over 'Free Range' Product Labels."

You, the US Department of Agriculture are charged with ensuring that animal raising label claims on meat and poultry products are truthful and not misleading. Yet, the USDA's current approval process for claims such as "humanely raised," "free range," and "pasture raised," allow practices that are a far cry from consumer expectations and are dishonest, misleading and misrepresentative. A producer may keep animals crammed in barren sheds by the thousands, with no natural light, and ammonia-soaked litter that burns their eyes and skin, yet still slap a "humanely raised" label claim on the package. Wrong! 

In your new guidance document please align label claim requirements with consumer expectations and be truthful instead of giving fraudulent information. It continues to allow producers to define claims however they like, and puts the onus on consumers to decipher the meaning of label claims.

The new guidance actually discourages producers from providing higher welfare for animals, because producers can maintain the status quo and still receive a premium for claiming that the animals were raised in a more humane manner.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should: 

- Require third-party certification for animal welfare and environmental stewardship claims. In several surveys, large majorities of consumers have said that a "humanely raised" claim should not be allowed on products unless verified by an independent third party. Consumers also believe that the claim should not be used unless producers exceed minimum industry standards.
- Define animal living claims, such as "free range" and "pasture raised." Producers should only be allowed to use these claims if they meet established standards, including minimum space allowances and access to vegetation for animals. 
- Prohibit the use of feedlots for the "grass-fed" claim. Producers are only required to provide grass-fed animals with access to pasture for the growing season. When not on pasture, producers can keep animals in barren, cramped feedlots. 
- Require more documentation to substantiate claims. When third-party certification is not required, producers using animal raising claims should submit a detailed animal care protocol and photographic documentation. 

As it stands, the guidance document does not align animal raising claims with consumer expectations. It also harms farmers who do provide higher-welfare for animals. They incur higher costs in maintaining systems that go beyond conventional production standards in terms of animal welfare and environmental stewardship, but must compete with those who use label claims without actually committing to high-welfare production. 

I urge you to make the above changes to the new animal raising claims guidance. Doing so will help consumers, farmers, and animals. Thank you for your time, and for taking my concerns into consideration.

Culverts and wildlife corridors must be included as a minimal performance measure for the State Highway Safety Grant Program. Wildlife move both daily and seasonally to survive. However, the habitats animals rely on continue to be fragmented by housing, roads, fences, energy facilities, and other man-made barriers. As a result, animals are struggling more and more to reach food, water, shelter, and breeding sites. One million animals are killed each day on American roads, and the car insurance cost to Americans is in the billions. Habitat connectivity is defined as the degree to which the landscape facilitates or impedes animal movement and other ecological processes, such as seed dispersal. And climate change is fundamentally altering landscapes, forcing many animals to relocate. As habitat continues to be fragmented, degraded, and lost to development, the need for a coordinated connectivity network is growing. Better habitat connectivity will allow wildlife to migrate and disperse throughout the country with the changing seasons, boost biodiversity and resilience in degraded ecosystems, safeguard genetic flow between populations, and ensure species are better able to adapt to our changing climate. This work is an important and long overdue investment in the long-term health of wildlife populations and ecological processes.The following are examples of current and proposed wildlife corridors:

Elk and bighorn sheep: In the Upper Rio Grande Valley, the National Wildlife Federation is working with the New Mexico Wildlife Federation, Colorado Wildlife Federation, and other partners to establish federal protections for wildlife habitat connectivity across three national forests (the Carson and Santa Fe in New Mexico, and Rio Grande in Colorado) and the Rio Grande del Norte National Monument. This corridor would help species like elk, bighorn sheep, mule deer, pronghorn, lynx, black bear, mountain lions, and the rare Rio Grande cutthroat trout.
Migrating birds and monarch butterflies: The Burnham Wildlife Corridor is a 100-acre landscape within Chicago’s Lakeshore Park featuring the prairie and woodland ecosystems that are native to this part of the Central U.S. The corridor runs right through the heart of the city. It is mainly used as a refuge for the three million migratory birds that pass through the Windy City each year, but also creates valuable butterfly habitat.
Mule deer: In Wyoming, the Red Desert to Hoback mule deer corridor supports the longest mule deer migration in the U.S.
Pronghorn and greater sage-grouse: The Northern Great Plains, which extend from Montana into Canada, support the longest pronghorn and greater sage-grouse migrations for both species. Taking a holistic approach to conservation, collaboration continues across the patchwork of public and working lands to sustain connectivity.
Enhancing Habitat Connectivity Through Wildlife Crossings
In addition to identifying and prioritizing corridors across the landscape, the National Wildlife Federation also supports infrastructure that enhances these efforts. This work consists of building overpasses and underpasses across highways that block mule deer and pronghorn migrations and creating culverts (pathways for water to flow under infrastructure) that allow turtles and amphibians to cross barriers safely.

Models for Connectivity Banff: A system of wildlife crossings in Banff National Park across the Trans-Canada Highway has reduced ungulate-vehicle collisions by approximately 80 percent.
Montana: A network of 81 wildlife crossings over and under U.S. Highway 93 in Montana, combined with more than nine miles of fencing, reduced deer-vehicle collisions by over 90 percent.
California mountain lions: By creating a safe passage for wildlife near Highway 101, the Liberty Canyon Wildlife Crossing in California will be the largest wildlife crossing in the world, and a global model for urban wildlife conservation.

I agree that 1996 amendment to 8 CFR 212.1(g) should be reinstated. The current penalty system, based on whether or not a passenger receives a post-entry waiver due to an unforeseen emergency, has resulted in inconsistent application. While the Carriers are opposed to this proposed rule because of financial concerns, the rule makes the most sense, especially compared to the two latter alternatives which are to 2) waive the penalty for small carriers, and 3) keep the system the way it is. It might seem unfair to fine a carrier for bringing a passenger who later receives a waiver based on the unforeseen emergency provision of the INA, but the INA also specifically states that it is illegal to bring anyone into the US without a valid passport and/or visa. I am also unpersuaded by the Carriers' economic burden. A mere $4,300 per passenger fine is not enough to convince me that they should not be required to pay a fine for a passenger who later receives a waiver. It could also be dangerous to allow an inconsistent application, especially when dealing with "unforeseen emergencies." It would be extremely undesirable to put Carriers in a position in which they can determine who they think would qualify as having faced an unforeseen emergency. Carriers do not have the expertise or the practical knowledge necessary to make these judgement calls. This decision should rest solely with the district director at the port of entry. 
 
Along those lines, it is especially important for carriers to stay out of the decision-making process because there is such ambiguity concerning what constitutes an "unforeseen emergency." The 1996 amendment does not define "unforeseen emergency," nor does it give any guidance to those who are deciding who qualifies for such a waiver. The proposed rule to reinstate the 1996 amendment also does not add any more detail. Because the waivers are meant to be decided on a case-by-case basis, such ambiguity could lead to inconsistent application of the waiver itself, and that power should never be placed in the hands of the Carriers. The Carriers should be solely focused on adhering to the INA Section 273, especially when the threat of terror particularly high. Mandating a fine, regardless of the waiver outcome, would provide an economic incentive for Carriers to adhere to Section 273, and stay out of the decision-making process surrounding "unforeseen emergency" waivers. This strict application of penalties dissuades Carriers to consider passengers' arguments about "unforeseen emergencies" and therefore lowers the level of possible abuse of the provision. 
 
There is another level of danger in not clarifying the terms of what constitutes an "unforeseen emergency." Aside from the issue of Carriers and penalties, the amendment should provide more detail on the criteria to meet the "unforeseen emergency" provision. Clarity and/or criteria would help in deciding the cases and would result in a fairer outcome in most cases. Considering the many humanitarian crises, civil wars, and conflicts the world currently faces, I wholly support "unforeseen emergency" provision, but I simply worry about its vagueness.

As one of the 1233 individuals who has received a Daylight Waiver under part 107, I agree that this can be done safely. I do agree with the overall plan to allow "night" flights, provided that the anti-collision lighting and training requirements are fulfilled. ...over moving vehicles.
I will say that this is one aspect of 107 that has puzzled me. In general, I do not see where operation directly over a moving vehicle poses any significant risk to the public. Certainly, the individuals inside are protected from impact by the fact that they are in a shelter (vehicle). And in fact when "directly over" a vehicle with an sUAS, whether the vehicle is moving or not has relatively little effect on the forces experienced by a falling drone. Yet, we are currently allowed to operate directly over a stationary vehicle. The distractions are more of an issue when off to the side or in front of vehicles. Generally, my sUAS is rarely noticed when it is significantly above a moving vehicle, and would be even less so if it were truly directly above. Additionally, the likelihood of an impact with the vehicle it is over, if my sUAS stopped operating and fell, is extremely unlikely based on the dynamics of both systems, both moving differently. I think operation over moving vehicles should be allowed.

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service officials, 

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on portions of your existing Mitigation Policy and 

Endangered Species Act Compensatory Mitigation Policy (ESA-CMP). The Olympic Forest 

Coalition and the West Coast Action Alliance join the Washington Forest Law Center in 

submitting comments on these important policies. Our organizations work to protect the forest, 

watersheds, wildlife and associated marine waters of the Olympic Peninsula in Washington 

State. We are writing to request that you retain all of the fundamental principles (a-h) for guiding 

mitigation as defined in the 2016 policies across all Service programs, especially the goal of “net 

conservation gain”. 

Effective mitigation is a powerful tool for furthering the Service’s mission to conserve, protect, 

and enhance fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats to the continuing benefit of the American 

people for current and future generations. Mitigation, as broadly defined in current policy, as 

“measures to avoid, minimize, and compensate for impacts” is an essential means of achieving 

the overarching purpose of the ESA (to conserve listed species and the ecosystems upon which 

they depend), and the current mitigation policies provide guidance for doing so most effectively. 

The changes made to these mitigation policies in 2016 were based on numerous growing 

conservation challenges and practices, including accelerating loss, degradation, and 

fragmentation of habitats; effects of climate change, human population growth and other new 

threats; and advances in fish and wildlife conservation science. These challenges and practices 

remain today and are expected to persist well into the future. Designing mitigation that ensures a 

‘‘net conservation gain’’ in the status of affected resources is imperative to address the additive 

impacts that lead to significant deterioration of resources over time, to foster recovery of listed 

species, and to avoid listing of additional species. This is an obligation of the Service as an 

administrator of the ESA. 

As of the end of 2016, more than 1,500 species listed have been listed under the ESA since its 

inception. Without a commitment to responsible and implementable standards and polices for 

accomplishing effective, sustainable mitigation that more than fully offsets the adverse impacts 

of actions to listed species and other resources of concern, these species and resources are 

unlikely to recover and persist. Mitigation with a “net conservation gain” is necessary because 

an accurate accounting of the functions and services lost at impact sites and gained at mitigation

Dear Ms. George:
 
For two decades, we have been dedicated to representing military families all around the country and the world. Typically, this has involved injuries to veterans and their family members at Department of Veterans Affairs and military hospitals and clinics. 
 
There are two primary concerns we wish to raise regarding the Department of Defense’s interim rule governing tort claims by active duty servicemembers.
 
1. Prohibition on Wrongful Death Claims
 
First, section 45.3(b) appears to prohibit wrongful death and survival claims by a deceased servicemember’s estate or surviving family members. 
 
DoD’s own Background section of this interim rule, however, specifically notes that the “2020 NDAA allows members of the uniformed services or their authorized representatives to file claims for personal injury or death caused by a DoD health care provider in certain military medical treatment facilities.” As such, the interim rule’s interpretation does not appear to have any rational basis derived from the 2020 NDAA legislation and, indeed, appears to be in direct contravention of the law.
 
Further, this is a particularly harsh and punitive prohibition that will disproportionately impact those families of deceased servicemembers who have young children or several dependents. Indeed, the death of the servicemember may mean that the family’s primary source of income is no longer available. While there may be certain death benefits that are paid to the surviving family, it is unfair to prohibit the estate or family from pursuing a wrongful death or survival claim for the very same cause of action that the servicemember could have pursued had he or she lived. This interpretation also provides a perverse incentive in which DoD’s potential liability is absolved if the servicemember dies, but not if he or she lives. 
 
2. Off-Sets Unrelated to Malpractice Injury
 
Second, section 45.11 appears to consider as off-sets several items that have nothing to do with the medical malpractice or related injury at issue for which the servicemember would be compensated. 
 
For example, items like active duty pay, housing allowance, and TRICARE coverage are unrelated to a servicemember’s medical malpractice claim or injury. Using such items as off-sets against a medical malpractice tort claim settlement is unfair and not a good faith solution to Congress’s directive to compensate servicemembers for such injuries. 

Indeed, as a practical matter, using TRICARE coverage as an off-set would, by itself, likely mean that the vast majority of settlements would result in no payments by DoD to the servicemember. That is certainly in contravention of the spirit and intent of the legislation giving servicemembers this new remedy.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments and please do not hesitate to contact me if you have any questions or concerns, or need any additional information.

In addition to strengthening the climate analysis, an economic analysis should be required and the economic boosts claimed by the industry compared with the negatives which will be generated to our economy, such as climate disasters generated by greenhouse gases from the burning of fossil fuels from these Arctic areas, the health costs which will result, businesses and homes destroyed, hits to agriculture and other industries and businesses, and worker losses.
Further oil & gas development will be incompatible with meeting urgently needed commitments to address the climate crisis. To demonstrate climate leadership and meet our commitments, the nation needs to move rapidly away from burning fossil fuels. There is no room for expansion, particularly in the Arctic, where oil would not come to market for years. The huge infrastructure build-out required would lock us into reliance on fossil fuels, while bringing further stress to a region feeling climate effects even more acutely than lower latitudes. I urge the administration to take measures to bring its management of the Western Arctic in line with its commitment to address the climate crisis. 

The proposed regulations are a step in the right direction but do not go far enough. They offer important incremental protections for some of the Western Arctic’s most ecologically and culturally important areas, such as Teshekpuk Lake, an internationally vital wetland critical for birds from around the globe and for caribou herds that are integral to Alaska Native communities in the region. However, they do not do enough to address the most imminent threat to the region and the planet—the over two million acres of existing oil leases in the Western Arctic that this administration inherited. Development on these existing leases—like Willow—threatens the sensitive habitat of the Western Arctic and the nation’s ability to meet its climate goals. 

The current environmental analysis of the Western Arctic, written in the previous administration, fails to study the impact oil development in the region would have on the climate and the nation’s ability to rapidly reduce its reliance on fossil fuels to meet climate goals. We urge the administration to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the climate impacts of Western Arctic oil development, and to bring its management of the region in line with climate policy by expanding its proposed regulations to require limits on drilling on the millions of acres already leased to oil companies to protect the climate and the fragile resources of the region already under severe strain from climate change.

According to the International Labor Organization around 313 serious injury incidents occur each year due to work hazards that result in disabling injuries and economic burden of 4% on global gross domestic product. The U.S Bureau of Labor Statistics states that employers record more than 3 million occupational injuries annually (Frumkin, 2016). The CDC's mining facts report of 2014, for MNM mines, states that fatality rate was 12.5 per 100,000 FTE employees and the rate of nonfatal lost-time injuries was 1.8 per 100 FTE employees, which resulted in 56,633 days lost from work. Since mining is one of the most hazardous occupations in the nation, more light should be shed on this issue. 
The international labor organization estimates the cost of occupational injury to be $1.25 trillion per year (Camm et al). There are many factors that we should consider when looking at workplace injuries; there are economic consequences that include direct, indirect and productivity costs and social consequences that include stress, anxiety and group conflict. Direct costs include medical and compensation expenses, indirect costs include the cost of injury on the community that is due to the change in economic circumstance in the family (Camm et al). For example, increased need for social and economic support to the family due to increased need for care and decreased ability to work. As for the social consequences, the American Institute of Stress estimated costs of stress and ills to an injury, whether it was physical, mental or behavioral, to be $300 billion a year (Mine safety and health program technical staff, 2011). 
Inspecting the workplace and documenting the inspection not only benefits the worker but the managers as well. It saves the workers from work hazards and harmful incidents and it saves the employer the amount of incidental compensation he has to pay. Inspection resources at most agencies tend to be limited and there are roughly seven inspectors for every million covered workers for federal and OSHA programs (Frumkin, 2016). This is an important factor for teaching and training an on-site employee to perform daily worksite inspections. According to the American Society of Safety Engineers, "every $1 spent on prevention can lead to $3-6 in loss avoidance" (ASSE, 2010). Sierra Club on delisting-
"Grizzly bears are an essential piece of the American West, a wildlife icon that has been integral to the Yellowstone region for centuries. Each year, visitors spend millions of dollars hoping to catch a glimpse of a grizzly bear in the wild. As a top predator, grizzly bears play an important role in keeping the whole natural system healthy, and protecting the large wild areas they need to survive also protects habitat for many other species.
Thanks to 40 years of Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections, grizzly bears in the Yellowstone region have made a comeback - but they are still vulnerable and need protection. The growth rate of the population has been flat since the early 2000s and could be declining, fewer cubs are surviving to adulthood, bears have lost key foods due to climate change, and Yellowstone grizzly bears are still completely isolated from other grizzly bears, which threatens their long-term survival.
Despite all this, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has released a proposal to remove federal ESA protections and turn management over to the states, who want to immediately begin sport trophy hunting of grizzly bears and who refuse to let grizzly bears access prime, biologically-suitable habitat on federal public lands.
Sierra Club believes that it's too soon to remove Endangered Species Act protections from this still-vulnerable population and hand the management keys over to the states."

I am urging you to withdraw the proposed rule to 'modernize' swine slaughter inspection and issue a new proposal that prioritizes food safety.

The proposed rule puts consumers at risk of foodborne illness by removing important microbiological testing requirements for Salmonella and generic E coli that have been at the core of efforts to modernize food safety since the 1990s. In place of these requirements, slaughterhouses will be allowed to design their own individualized testing programs, making it impossible to compare performance or spot the worst performers industry-wide.

When the USDA implemented the New Poultry Inspection System in 2014, it maintained a maximum line speed and kept in place updated microbial performance standards. Even with these additional measures, contamination rates do not appear to have gone down.

The goal of modernizing inspections should be to make food safer, and this proposal will not achieve that. Instead, it has the potential to make food less safe by de-regulating swine inspection, handing important government duties to industry while removing microbial standards needed to verify that industry is performing those duties effectively.

We urge you to withdraw the proposed rule and design a new rule that prioritizes food safety through enhanced microbial testing and the implementation of pre-harvest pathogen reduction requirements that will significantly reduce contamination and foodborne illness.

supporting and following policies and regulations rooted in sound science and

The Meat Institute appreciates the Agricultural Marketing Service’s (AMS or 

the agency) outreach to the industry to solicit input regarding changes to the beef 

carcass grading standards to allow for dentition and documentation of age to be 

used to classify beef carcass maturity and eligibility for quality grade classification. 

The proposed changes are aligned with current scientific thinking. 

The reason beef is graded for quality grading is to separate carcasses into 

homogeneous groups based on palatability traits. Carcasses with similar quality 

characteristics, including lean color, skeletal ossification or skeletal maturity, and 

marbling score, are combined and then carcasses are placed into ranked groups and

classified as USDA Prime, Choice, Select, Standard, Commercial, Utility, Cutter, or 

Canner. Skeletal ossification or maturity classification (A, B, C, D, or E), is the 

method AMS has used to determine age of an animal at slaughter. Carcasses 

classified as A-maturity are supposed to be 9-30 months of age (MOA). However, 

approximately 7.2% of carcasses from cattle slaughtered at 30 MOA or younger 

possess a skeletal maturity of B or older and are therefore ineligible to be 

considered A-maturity and receive a discount.1 

Recent peer-reviewed science evaluated the effect of USDA skeletal maturity 

classification applied to carcasses in two groups, over 30 MOA and under 30 MOA 

(classified using dentition) on beef palatability attributes. Results showed that 

USDA skeletal maturity classification (A versus B, C, or D maturity) had no effect 

(P > 0.05) on tenderness, juiciness, or flavor of longissimus dorsi (LD) steaks from 

carcasses slaughtered less than or over 30 MOA. 2 However, LD steaks from cattle 

slaughtered at over 30 MOA, were associated with greater (P < 0.05) incidence of 

grassy and livery flavors.3 In addition, dentition interacted with marbling score to 

affect LD steak tenderness.4 Among LD steaks with Slight marbling scores, those 

originating from carcasses slaughtered at less than 30 MOA were more tender (P < 

0.05) than LD steaks from carcasses slaughtered at 30 MOA or older.5 Dentition 

did not affect (P > 0.05) LD steak tenderness within the Small and Modest-

Moderate marbling score categories.6 Similarly, no difference (P > 0.05) was found 

in LD steak tenderness, juiciness and flavor between carcasses slaughtered at 30 

MOA or younger with different skeletal ossification classifications (A, B, or C).7 

This scientific evidence demonstrates that dentition and documentation of age is an 

accurate tool to help predict acceptability of eating experience.

Acting Secretary de la Vega, 

Thank you for the opportunity to provide scientific comments on the ‘‘MBTA Rule’’, 

which redefines the scope of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) to protect birds only 

if a business or individual intentionally injures or kills birds protected by the MBTA 

(https://www.fws.gov/regulations/mbta/), and on the supplementary information as 

published in the Federal Register (50 CFR Part 10, Docket No. FWS–HQ–MB–2018–

0090; FF09M22000–201–FXMB1231090BPP0], RIN 1018–BD76, Regulations 

Governing Take of Migratory Birds; Delay of Effective Date). As North American 

representatives of the IUCN Species Survival Commission (SSC) Swan Specialist Group, 

we have significant concerns about the “MBTA Rule”, not only for migratory swans 

(particularly Trumpeter Swans Cygnus buccinator, which recovered from near-

extinction following protection under the MBTA) but for all migratory birds of 

conservation concern in North America. With this letter, we therefore provide comment 

on two issues regarding the reinterpreted “MBTA Rule”: (1) intentional take as 

stated/implied in the MBTA and its effects, and (2) our treaty obligations and 

responsibilities. 

1. Intentional/Unintentional Take Provision of the Migratory Bird Treaty 

Act (MBTA) 

The original provision of the MBTA, Section (2a) of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act 

(MBTA) states: 

“unless permitted by regulations, it is unlawful: at any time, by any means or in any 

manner, to pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, attempt to take, capture, possess, offer for 

sale, sell, offer to barter, barter, offer to purchase, purchase, deliver for shipment, ship,

 
export, import, cause to be shipped, exported, or imported, deliver for transportation, 

transport or cause to be transported, carry or cause to be carried, or receive for 

shipment, transportation, carriage, or export, any migratory bird, any part, nest, or 

egg of any such bird, or any product, whether or not manufactured, which consists, or 

is composed in whole or part, of any such bird or any part, nest, or egg thereof.”

breeds and disciplines, the amendments would both fulfill Congressional 
intent and limit any regulatory overreach that would not only be taxing for

February 1, 2026, and, at the very least, supports extending the 
postponement until January 2027. Any implementation should be delayed 
until listening sessions and discussion groups with industry stakeholders 
have been held so APHIS Animal Care fully understands how the final 
rule significantly impacts the equine show industry.

without guidance to the industry, leaving stakeholders with many 
unanswered questions. A new rule should be communicated well in 
advance of implementation with easy-to-understand resources for 
stakeholders.

HPA violations within 5 days post event, provide access to all records and 
an area for APHIS officials to review records is very onerous for show 
managers who are mostly volunteers. AQHA believes that any 
requirement for event notification should be restricted to events in which 
an altered gait due to limb hypersensitivity would be advantageous.

NOAA Fisheries mission is to be responsible for the stewardship of the nation's ocean resources and their habitat. This should not include any ability to manipulate the market of any specific fishery.

Proposed Rule: DOD-2020-OS-0095-0001. Privacy Act; Implementation
Issue- Privacy Act Exemption/amendment to 32 CFR part 310
The core purpose of the DoD is to provide the military with the strength needed to deter war 
and promote the security of our nation. I understand that this goal is unattainable if classified 
information may be leaked to the public, which in the modern atmosphere of terroristic warfare would 
be a national security nightmare. The proposed rule and modification of 32 CFR part 310 would be a 
reasonable request if the DoD were specific in how it defined classified information before proposing a 
rule to help shield that information. Currently the DoD reserves the right to determine what information 
is in the interests of national security and deserves protection against unauthorized disclosure. 
My intent for this comment is to encourage the DoD to be more clairvoyant and honest about 
what determines something to be classified. Details and disclosure of the item in question is certainly 
not an option. However, requesting that something remain classified because it is immaterial under 
Public Law 96-354 while also significant enough to be protected under subsection (c)(3) (accounting of 
disclosures) seems rather suspicious on the surface. I am sure that there is a reasonable justification for 
the suppression of the information pursuant to § 310.13 but the verbiage of the request and the 
proposed rule stands to be improved. A revision in the phraseology of the DoD’s request could 
contribute to a more honest and transparent environment for future requests propositions. 
The current verbiage of the request does not include the function or directive that the DoD is 
striving to protect: “DoD is proposing to claim an exemption from the access and amendment 
requirements of the Privacy Act, pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 552a(k)(1), to prevent disclosure of any 
information properly classified pursuant to executive order”. The justification of asking for an exemption 
is because properly classified information could be leaked. I suggest a revision to this proposition to 
include what function (in vague terms) the DoD is seeking protect and what public interests are 
involved. The DoD must be able to expect a reasonable degree of confidentiality, but likewise the public 
deserves verification that the information the DoD is withholding is in their best interests. A financially 
immaterial action, as defined in the proposition, should not necessitate a restructuring of section 310.13 
without a reasonable justification.

Attachment 1 
 
Biological Charateristics of Scirtothrips dorsalis 
 
The life cycle of S. dorsalis comprises the following stages: egg, two active feeding larval 
instars, a prepupa and a pupa, both of which are relatively inactive, and a winged, feeding 
adult stage. The feeding stages are usually found on the green parts of the plant, as thrips 
feed mainly on actively growing plant tissues (EFSA Journal, 2014). 
Its eggs are laid in the youngest tissues of plants, and feeding by adults and larvae can 
result in extensive cell damage to these developing tissues, leading to leaf and fruit 
distortion, and flower fall (CABI, 2016). 
The first and second larval stages are found on the green plant parts from which the second 
stage larvae seek out some sheltered place (leaf litter or crevices of bark) and then pass 
through two resting stages called propupa and pupa, respectively. Rarely, these occur 
beneath the calyces of fruits. Winged adults, male and female, are found normally on the 
green plant parts, where they feed. The two feeding larval stages are yellow to orange, 
cigar-shaped and just visible to the naked eye (Bert Vierbergen & Dirk Jan van der Gaag, 
2009).

Today I am submitting comments on the Select Agent status of Brucella abortus. I support the removal of B.abortus from the select agent list. My background and connection to this issue is that I am a strong advocate for wild, free-roaming bison (buffalo).

Apparently the last known reservoirs of B.abortus exist within the Greater Yellowstone ecosystem, and decades ago, both bison and elk were exposed to this livestock disease. The cattle industry maintains a position of fear that wild bison may pose a brucellosis threat to cattle, though not a single case has ever been documented. Regardless, the wild bison of Yellowstone country the last continuously wild herds continue to be a target of the livestock industry, and thousands have been slaughtered, quarantined, hazed, excessively hunted, experimented on and otherwise harmed because of this perceived threat. Elk have been implicated in transmitting B.abortus to cattle in Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho more than 27 times since 1998. While elk are rightly free to roam, there is an ongoing war waged against wild, migratory bison in the name of brucellosis. Both important wildlife species, however, are unfairly targeted by the livestock industry due to brucellosis.

At this time there is no safe or effective brucellosis vaccine for livestock. Cattle ranchers should be required to vaccinate their livestock against brucellosis. Many in some Montana counties surrounding Yellowstone - within the Brucellosis Designated Survellience Area) are required to do so. But the vaccine they are using does not work. Currently, ranchers are using RB 51, which does not offer full protection against brucellosis.

Clearly, delisting B.abortus from the Select Agent List is important so that effective research can be conducted towards the development of improved vaccination for livestock, diagnostics, and other livestock management options.

I am commenting today in support of the proposed priority to enhance the capacity of SEAs and LEAs to implement positive and safe school environments, and effectively support and respond to students’ social, emotional, behavioral, and mental health needs to improve their learning, by implementing evidence- based practices within a Multi-Tiered System of Support / Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) framework in educational settings. I would like to share how PBIS has made an impact on both my personal life (as a parent) and professional life (as a teacher). 

As a parent of an elementary school student, I have experienced first-hand how implementing the PBIS framework supports students’ needs; in kindergarten, my child’s school did not practice PBIS schoolwide, but now in 4th grade the school does utilize the framework schoolwide. Witnessing the effects of this transformation over the past five years has been helpful to see the effects of implementation from a family perspective. Namely, teacher retention rate has increased, with more teachers continuing to remain part of the school community. From a parent perspective, this promotes a safe, positive, predictable, and culturally and linguistically inclusive learning environments where students feel a sense of belonging. I believe this is a direct result of the school’s administration and staff committing to use the PBIS framework. The school’s social worker had a large role in leading the PBIS efforts and we are grateful to have her as a resource! Retaining specials teachers is particularly importation, because they have a unique opportunity to see student growth year after year, and for our family have been a consistent support for our child. 

As a former middle school teacher, I have experienced how implementing the PBIS framework impacts teachers and their relationships with students, school families, and community. We are often reminded that utilizing the PBIS framework is not about changing student behaviors, it is actually about changing adult behaviors and expectations, to best support their students’ needs. As a first-year teacher in an urban area, I was fresh out of graduate school and excited to start my teaching career. In hindsight, no amount of student teaching in various settings could have fully prepared me for being the only adult in a class of 30 middle school students. My district provided in-service training around a few different classroom behavior strategies, and I tried them all in that first year. The strategies that impacted me the most were those based around and nested in the PBIS framework. Creating an inclusive environment, versus using exclusionary practices, supported my students’ desire to be present each day and participate in my class, resulting in a culture of respect and belonging. I joined our school PBIS team, helping with universal celebrations, and became the teacher liaison for the PTA where I got to better understand families’ concerns. After a few years, I moved to a new district, and again became part of the PBIS team. We met monthly to look at our discipline data, and used it to inform our decision-making which, in turn, resulted in us identifying any disproportionalities that needed to be addressed. With PBIS in place, we were focused on improving our school climate, to support and
respond to students’ needs. 

I am in favor of the proposed priority, and feel its advancements in the field would continue to positively impact my personal and professional experience along with continuing to support students in all school settings.

The Animal Welfare Act is important and should be enforced through a reasonable, reliable licensing process.

"...the current regulations do not require the applicant to demonstrate compliance before APHIS renews his or her license. The current regulations also do not require a licensee to demonstrate compliance when the licensee makes any subsequent changes to his or her animals or facilities, including noteworthy changes in the number or type of animals used in regulated activity." 

1) All licensees should be required to demonstrate compliance with the AWA before their license is renewed. 

2) All licensees should be required to demonstrate compliance when the licensee makes any subsequent changes to his or her animals or facilities, or at least when they make noteworthy changes in the number or type of animals used in regulated activity. 

As a licensed attorney I am familiar with administrative law and the loopholes through which motorcades can be driven, but there is a purpose to this law, and reasonable, realistic enforcement is necessary to honor that purpose. The same way polluters won't regulate industry without government enforcement, businesses who make their money from animal abuse aren't going to blink an eye before signing a form that says they aren't abusing animals. There are never going to be enough boots on the ground checking for compliance on a day-to-day basis, especially when it comes to animal welfare, so I would hope the government would invest the necessary time and money into regulating this industry through a reasonable and reliable licensing process. We can't be rubber stamping the licenses of people and businesses who aren't obeying the law. That's just not right, and it removes any incentive to obey the law. 

Maybe, as some sort of compromise, you could have the licenses of new applicants be seriously reviewed and renewed every 2-3 years for 6-9 years, and then for companies/individuals who have never had any complaints filed or any problems with their licenses during that probationary period, they only have to go through the more rigorous process every 5-6 years after that (but they would still be required annually to sign the form and pay whatever fee is necessary). 

Thank you for your diligent review of these comments and thorough consideration of these issues.

Animal welfare is important to me. According to numerous polls, it is also important to a majority of consumers who purchase meat and poultry products. Unfortunately, consumers who want to support higher-welfare farmers cannot rely on "free range" or similar claims, because the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service fails to adequately regulate the use of these claims.

When I see the claims "free range" and "pasture raised," I understand them to mean more than just limited access to the outdoors. These animals should have consistent, easy access to range that includes soil, vegetation, and plenty of room to roam, as well as shelter from extreme weather events and protection from predators. I also believe that the FSIS should not allow producers to define these claims themselves.

In 2015, the Animal Welfare Institute investigated the FSIS's label approval process for more than 100 approved labels containing "free range" claims. AWI found that
 - for "free range" and "range grown," the FSIS applied an overly permissive definition that allows consumers to be misled about the quality of the products they are purchasing; and
 - the FSIS is approving some label applications despite little or no evidence for the particular animal production claim being made. 

I was disappointed to see these results, and hope that the USDA will work to improve its label approval process. It can do this by strengthening the "outdoor access" requirements for animal products marketed as "free range" and "pasture raised." These similar (though not equivalent) claims represent far more than simple access to the outdoors. The FSIS should establish minimum standards for such claims, making it clear that limited access to gravel and concrete lots is insufficient, and that free access to soil and vegetation throughout the growing season is required.

I, like many others, are willing to pay more for products that I know are from animals humanely cared for. If animals aren't cared for then we are being deceived.

Thank you for considering my request.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed airworthiness directive. Based on 

my research I’m going to break this response down to comment points as follows: 

1. A comment involving ambiguity regarding using 100-hour inspections to define “factored 

service hours,” as defined in the NPRM 

2. A comment involving the necessity of incorporating the requirements of Piper Service 

Bulletin (SB) 1244C, dated December 3, 2018, titled Aft Wing Fitting Inspection 

Requirements into the NPRM since wear allowing movement of the wing at the aft wing 

attachment joint would subject the main wing spar attachment to additional stresses that 

are not included in the “factored service hours” formula. 

a. For further information on wear in this fitting refer to 14 CFR Pt 141 “Safety 

Summit “Maintenance” PowerPoint presentation, dated May 10,2018 by Tony 

Alfaya, Program Manager, Orlando FSDO FAASTeam. 

3. A comment comparing real world labor reports to the estimate of labor man-hours to 

replace a wing spar in the NPRM. 

Discussion No. 1 

The NPRM suggests that 100-hour inspections are the “rate-determining step” in determining 

when an aircraft needs to be inspected. There is a loop hole here. What about the airplane 

that flies 300 hour a year in a flight training or for-hire operation and the third inspection is 

signed off as an “annual” inspection? The way the NPRM is written the “factored service 

hours” for that airplane would be off by a third. 

For example, let’s create a PA-28 that had flown 4660 hours. If the annual were counted as a 

100-hour inspection, it’s factored service hours would be 4603.5. If the annual were not 

counted as a 100-hour inspection, the factored service hours would be 3285, or 29 percent 

less. 

I recommend that this ambiguity be addressed by adding the following to the AD: 

“Airplanes on 100-hour inspection schedules must treat each “annual inspection” sign off as 

a 100-hour inspection to arrive at the “N” total in the “factored service hours” equation.” 

Discussion No. 2 

The main spar of PA 28 wings supports vertical positive and negative loads; a steel stub spar 

that is bolted to a steel fuselage fitting (Aft Wing Spar) is designed to prevent any pivoting of 

the wing around the main spar. Piper issued Service Bulletin (SB) 1244C, dated December 3, 

2018, titled Aft Wing Fitting Inspection Requirements. 

This bulletin requires the inspection of the aft side of the aft wing spar for corrosion and for

This comment has to do with the regulatory status of containers in aerosol can puncturing operations. 

Containers attached to aerosol can puncturing systems should be exempt from the RCRA container 

standards because they are part of an exempt recycling process. In guidance EPA said “…since the 

process of emptying the aerosol cans is part of a recycling process (i.e., scrap steel recycling), this 

activity would be exempt from RCRA regulation under 40 CFR 261.6(c).” (RO 11782) 

An aerosol can puncturing process usually consists of three parts; a container (typically a 55-gallon 

drum), a puncturing device and a filter to control hazardous air emissions. The puncturing device and 

filter are attached to the two bungs on the top of the drum. All parts are needed for safe puncturing 

operations to take place; that is, the container is an integral part of the puncturing process (which is the 

first step in the metal recycling process).

Because all parts are needed for this exempt recycling activity to take place, the container in aerosol 

puncturing service should enjoy the RCRA exemption afforded to other recycling units (e.g., solvent 

recycling stills). While the container is in aerosol puncturing service the handler should have the option 

of managing the container as an exempt recycling unit. If the agency disagrees, it is requested the 

agency clarify why a container attached to the puncturing system should be subject to the SAA or CAA 

container standards and not be an exempt recycling unit.

Dear Acting Director Rauch,

As someone who cares deeply about sharks and all ocean life, I commend the National Marine Fisheries Service for proposing to protect the oceanic whitetip shark as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). I urge the agency to finalize this rule at the earliest possible date.

"Our duty to the whole, including to the unborn generations, bids us to restrain an unprincipled present-day minority from wasting the heritage of these unborn generations. The movement for the conservation of wildlife and the larger movement for the conservation of all our natural resources are essentially democratic in spirit, purpose and method."
-- Theodore Roosevelt

Based on the latest scientific data, the oceanic whitetip shark (Cacharhinus longimanus) is in desperate need of the protections of the Endangered Species Act. The species is deliberately targeted for its large and distinctive fins, which command high prices in the lucrative shark fin trade. It also suffers significant losses from incidental bycatch in many fisheries. Once one of the most abundant and ubiquitous shark species in tropical seas, the oceanic whitetip has suffered significant global population declines of as much as 70% in recent years. In certain areas, the declines have been much greater. In the Mediterranean, for example, the species has undergone a 98% population loss.

"Nothing is more priceless and more worthy of preservation than the rich array of animal life with which our country has been blessed."
-- Richard Nixon, on signing the Endangered Species Act on December 28, 1973

In recognition of these steep population declines, the species was listed in 2013 on Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna, an action co-proposed by the United States. But as the proposed ESA listing rule recognizes, the oceanic whitetip shark is still not receiving adequate legal protections to halt its decline. In the Eastern Tropical Pacific, regulatory bodies have been unable to put in place adequate rules to prevent a noted decline as a result of longlining, purse seining, and other industrial fishing practices targeting tuna species.

"What is the nature of a species that knowingly and without good reason exterminates another?"
-- George Small

The cruel trade in shark fins has been a major economic force in the decline of this species. Listing the species under the ESA could impede the transport of shark fins through US ports and undermine the economic forces that allow this trade to continue.

"Every man who appreciates the majesty and beauty of the wilderness and of wild life, should strike hands with the farsighted men who wish to preserve our material resources, in the effort to keep our forests and our game beasts, game-birds, and game-fish--indeed, all the living creatures of prairie and woodland and seashore--from wanton destruction. Above all, we should realize that the effort toward this end is essentially a democratic movement."
-- Theodore Roosevelt

However, simply listing the oceanic whitetip shark as threatened is not enough. A threatened listing alone won't give this species any protections under the Endangered Species Act at all without a species-specific rule establishing which ESA protections will apply. Therefore, I urge your agency to take immediate action to list the oceanic whitetip shark as threatened and to put into place rules to give this species the full benefit of legal protections under U.S. law.
