The FWS bears the burden of establishing a rationale for altering the current regulations regarding threatened species under the Endangered Species Act and enabling regulations. 

Executive Order 13777 provides authority to address "unnecessary regulatory burdens placed on the American people."

The ESA Section 4(D) provides some discretion regarding regulations for threatened species. 50 CFR 17.31 currently applies default regulations when a species becomes threatened. Nothing in the statutes or code appears to preclude a special rule (see 17.31(c) in fact recognizing the authority of special rules).

The FWS suggests, without support, that the current regulation, per Executive Order 13777, somehow represents an unnecessary regulatory burden." Furthermore, the FWS fails to establish that the proposed regulation, dropping the default treatment under threatened species, will meet any of the objectives under Executive Order 13777(2)(d). As the FWS admits, the FWS can still create special rules. Furthermore, the proposed regulation applies only prospectively--raising questions regarding whether the current rule represents ANY burden. As the FWS also admits, the question of whether species-specific shall issue with a determination remains open.

We need not consider the perverse results because the basis for the proposed revision appears ultra vires. Yet, the proposed rule, standing alone, strips newly listed threatened species on ANY protections--conflicting with Congressional intent Section 4(d). The proposed rule also necessitates a special-rule simultaneous proceeding with listing. Nowhere does the FWS establish how the bifurcation, already possible under current rules, reduces regulatory burdens. In fact, a plain reading suggests just the opposite--triggering additional regulatory hurdles to threatened species. Under the new rule, Section 4(a)(1)(D) creates duplication because the Secretary must already consider regulatory burdens--again, conflicting with the apparently limited authority granted by Executive Order 13777 and expressly cited in the notice by the FWS as support for the change.

Thus, I ask that the FWS reject the proposed rule.

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

I strongly oppose the definition of "habitat" that is proposed in this rule. Designation of critical habitat is a vital tool available under the Endangered Species Act to help conserve species. Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors.

This change would result in the exclusion of areas that do not meet the new, narrower definition of habitat, thereby decreasing the amount of habitat that can be protected. This would represent a severe setback to conservation, because critical habitat is vital for stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species that have protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species without it.

modification” or whether the designated habitat is essential

I strongly oppose the definition of "habitat" that is proposed in this rule. Designation of critical habitat is a vital tool available under the Endangered Species Act to help conserve species. Critical habitat is specific geographic areas that contain features essential to the conservation of a threatened or endangered species, including shelter, water, food, and other nutritional requirements; areas for breeding and raising young; and adequate space for animals to engage in normal growth and behaviors.

This change would result in the exclusion of areas that do not meet the new, narrower definition of habitat, thereby decreasing the amount of habitat that can be protected. This would represent a severe setback to conservation, because critical habitat is vital for stabilizing populations of threatened and endangered species. Listed species that have protected habitat are more than twice as likely to move toward recovery than species without it.

I am a person who eats meat, eggs, and dairy products. I do not object to quickly and humanely killing an animal to eat. I do not object to humanely hunting. However, I am against making an animal suffer before or during the process of dying. 

Thus, I look for products that do NOT involve such cruelty in the animal's living condition. If I cannot find such, I do without. (I even use locally sourced meats that I know are from humanely treated animals.) I am willing to pay more for such products. (Note that local laws involve criminal prosecution of those treating their pets in the manner that many -most?- farm producers treat their animals. Thus, it is strange to me that conditions allowed for a commercial pig would get me hauled to court if I subjected a pet pot-bellied pig to those same conditions.)

What is bad about the process now and as it is proposed, is that FSIS is supporting the label "Humanely Raised" even if the farm is a standard factory process. To me this is my government (employees I pay with my taxes) to engage collusion in fooling people into paying a higher price for nothing. Moreover, it fools us into doing something we do not want to do: support animal cruelty.

And what about the producer who cares about animals and/or wants to market to me and incurs a higher cost to truly "humanely raise" animals? You are really torpedoing them as their truly labeled higher priced product cannot compete with a misleadingly (falsely) labeled "standard" product sold at a lower cost. Allowing a seller/producer to make up own definitions will not fix the problem.

Since I am willing to pay for humane treatment, I and the producers of truly humanely raised animals should not be subjected to false advertising and false labeling. That is, a seller/producer should NOT be allowed to make up its own definition of the term "Humane" or "Organic" , etc. and to let me remain unaware of that definition at the moment I buy the product. There are 2 solutions--(1) to require in large print the producer/seller definition used, thus probably taking up the whole label on a package, or (2) to standardize definitions to a few clear legal ones.

I suggest solution (2) is clearly the more efficient and effective for all involved, including the animals. Then there needs to be an transparent process of verification that the product satisfies the definition.

In summary, FSIS should set a clear legal definition for a term/phrase/clause. As an example, let's consider "humanely raised." That phrase should mean the same thing regardless of the product to which the label is affixed. Also the process used to approve the label should be transparent and easily accessible by the public via a prominent place (with many references) on the FSIS website. For example, if I see on special at the local Food Lion, "Perdue Skinless Boneless Chicken Breats Humanely Raised", I should be able to quickly locate via the internet (on my Smart Phone or Computer) the FSIS page that allows me to look up the definition and to look up that particular product and see the documentation and approval process used to determine that "Humanely Raised" does indeed honestly apply to that product. In this way we all benefit: the honest producer, the consumer, and the animals. 

On a philosophical note: Why not spend money and time that creates a win-win-win outcome, instead of a win-lose-lose outcome?

Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

L3Harris Commercial Aviation has reviewed Docket No.: FAA-2023-2270 regarding 25-hr CVR. and notes that the forward fit mandate for 25-hour CVR as a good first step. But also recommends that FAA should follow NTSB’s recommendations to include retrofit aircraft to maximize the effectiveness and ensure that CVR data is available during incidence/accident investigators.

 
 
L3Harris Comments on FAA proposed NPRM 
FAA–2023–2270; Notice No. 24–0 
02 February 2024 
Page 1 of 9 
 
1. Background 
The Federal Aviation Administration published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) that 
states in the Executive Summary section A: 
This rulemaking effort proposes to amend the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) regulations to 
increase the recording duration of CVRs. Currently, CVRs are required to retain the last two 
hours of recorded information. Once this 2-hour limit is reached, a CVR overwrites the oldest 
data to maintain a rolling 2-hour recording. This proposal would increase the minimum 
duration of CVR recordings to 25 hours. The proposed change would affect all newly 
manufactured aircraft operating under title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) 
parts 91, 121, 125, and 135, one year after the effective date of the final rule. 
 
Aircraft accidents and incidents continue to occur where the current 2-hour recording 
requirement has been insufficient to retain audio recording data to support regulatory 
investigations. A recent example of this is the Alaska Airlines flight 1282 incident in which a plug 
door in the fuselage of the 737 MAX 9 aircraft detached at 16,000 feet shortly after taking off 
from Portland Oregon. 
 
In issuing this NPRM, the FAA noted several other cases - near misses - where vital information 
was overwritten, including the January 2023 runway incursion at JFK airport. 
 
It's worth noting that the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) adopted 25-hour 
recorders as an international standard with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency 
(EASA) adopting a 25-hour rule 3 years ago. 
 
Also noteworthy is that the FAA is only proposing this new requirement for newly manufactured 
aircraft; there is no retrofit requirement. Though it is consistent with EASA and ICAO's rules, 
L3Harris believes that the FAA should adopt the NTSB recommendations that were provided in 
their 2018 safety study and, more recently highlighted on ‘missing’ or overwritten data from 
recent incidences that continue to hamper safety investigations. 
 
L3Harris believes the benefits of including retrofit upgrades outweighs the incremental costs. In 
fact, we believe that the costs are overstated and, additional financial benefits have not been 
considered in the analysis. The benefits of retrofit along with forward fit mandates are as follows:

25-Hr CVR provides complete Audio data critical to investigators during the incidence 
window

alone

Financial benefits to analyzing the safety improvements to equipment, pilot-crew

My name is Milda Begovic and I am opposed to the U.S. Forest Services proposal to cut out public participation from the vast majority of its decisions. I want to have the ability to comment on decisions affecting places I care about in the future. The current proposal would fundamentally change the relationship between the U.S. Forest Service and the public, cutting our voices entirely out of how to manage these special places.

I often visit our national forests to appreciate nature, create memories with my family and friends, enjoy the scenery, swim, bike, paddle, fish, backpack, rock climb, camp, explore new places, relax, watch wildlife, picnic, and enjoy access to public lands. My uses of national forests could be harmed by large logging projects, new roads, pipeline and utility rights of way. The public deserves the chance to raise issues or concerns so that those harms can be avoided. 

I am most alarmed that the rule proposes to cut public participation from the vast majority of Forest Service decisions. The Forest Service should strengthen public involvement and focus on broadly supported work rather than attempting to bypass accountability for decisions that sacrifice the overall wellbeing of our national forests.

I rely on on-package labels to inform my purchasing practices. When I purchase a package with the claim "humanely raised" I assume that there is value and meaning behind that claim and that is backed by a regulatory agency. 

I am surprise to find out that the new rules proposed by the U.S. Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), would allow meat and chicken producers to use slogans like "Raised With Care" or "Humanely Raised" simply by making up whatever standards they want and submitting their own definitions to FSIS. Companies will be allowed to set their own definition for animal welfare and the only verification their labels will receive is a few signed pieces of paper. A written and signed document simply isn't enough to validate industry claims of animal welfare and environmental stewardship. We have already seen companies falsify these claims for their own economic benefit when actual standards exist. 

In fact, in a statement to the Huffington Post, the FSIS acknowledged that under its new proposed rule, products could be labeled "Humane" even if animals were raised on standard factory farms, where animals are commonly subjected to prolonged extreme confinement and horrific body mutilations including unanesthetized castration, debeaking, and dehorning.

Time and time again industry has shown us that it is not capable of self-regulating/policing. Companies are taking advantage of consumers, and grossly overcharging them, by using animal welfare and environmental stewardship labels to bring in more profits all the while failing to change their practices and address major issues in the supply chain. Consumers should be able to purchase products that are in line with their values and concerns for the well-being of animals and the environment and be assured that those purchases live up to genuine standards regarding animal welfare. 

FSIS is supposed to ensure transparency and ensure that meat and poultry labeling is "truthful and not misleading." The proposed guidelines fail to ensure the integrity of on-package labels. In fact, they simple perpetuate business as usual allowing corporate control of our food system and failing to hold companies accountable for the baseless claims and misleading consumers. 

FSIS owes it to the American public to set a clear legal definition for "humanely raised," take steps to ensure that this label means producers verify their compliance with specific requirements, and ensure that inspections are done periodically to ensure that these procedures continue to be followed.

These comments are in support of removing Coxiella burnetii from the DHHS select agent list and to request that this pathogen NOT be added to the USDA select agent list. Although this agent is an important zoonotic pathogen in man, it is a ubiquitous organism that is endemic in the U.S. and can be found in many species of animals and in many countries of the world. (Kirsh 2010; NASPHV NASAHO report 2013)

From the perspective of a veterinary laboratory epidemiologist and diagnostician, the classification of Coxiella burnetii as a select agent impedes the completion of diagnostic necropsy testing needed to work up complex herd problems, and limits the development of better methods to prevent and diagnose disease caused by Coxiella burnetii. In the diagnostic laboratory setting, once the select agent Coxiella burnetti has been demonstrated, all materials from the infected animal are collected and destroyed because of the select agent classification, though the diagnostic work on the case may not have been completed. This prevents an accurate diagnosis from being made when Coxiella is part of a multifactorial herd problem. 

Perhaps more importantly, the classification of C. burnetii as a select agent limits the ability of researchers/research facilities to conduct research on ruminant coxiellosis, which is greatly needed advance diagnostic testing and to develop or evaluate vaccines for C. burnetii. The need for Coxiella burnetti vaccines to prevent shedding in small ruminant vaccines for sheep and goats, and the need for a U.S. vaccine for high risk humans were identified by the U.S. Animal Health Association as a 2014 resolution and are urgently needed. (USAHA Res 2014)

Additionally, the classification of C. burnetii as a select agent compromises our ability to diagnose it accurately. Without samples available from known infected animals, we are unable to use standard quality assurance methods to ensure that our diagnostic methods are performing consistently over time. A cornerstone of quality assurance is repeatability, whereby the same test produces the same result on the same sample when run at different times. When we are unable to store samples from animals known to be infected with C. burnetii, we are unable to assess the repeatability of our test methods to detect this important pathogen.

Epidemiologist and Serology Section Leader
California Animal Health and Food Safety Laboratory

I support the proposed amendment to 8 CFR 212.1(g) to allow DHS to impose carrier fines on airlines that transport nonimmigrant aliens without a valid passport or visa into the United States. As the proposal suggests, the current regulation has created an inconsistent system that penalizes carriers based on whether CBP has granted a waiver to an alien and not based on actual carrier conduct (81 FR 12035). As a result, the current system appears inequitable; however, an even more alarming problem is that the current system fails to provide a sufficient economic incentive to prevent airlines and other small entity carriers from transporting undocumented aliens into the U.S., thus posing a serious safety issue, especially during a time when the threat of terror is very high.

 Expanding DHS's ability to assess carrier fines for such transportation violations will undoubtedly force airlines and other small entities to implement more stringent practices regarding whom they transport into the United States. Ensuring that every individual who enters the United States, from no matter what country, has a valid passport and visa is a vital necessity to protect American citizens. We should not allow carriers to make the judgment call with respect to whom to transport into the U.S. based on whether carriers think they may be at risk for a $4,300 penalty (81 FR 12034). Carriers should be aware that whenever they transport an undocumented alien into the United States, regardless of whether that individual may be granted an "unforeseen emergency" waiver, they will face a penalty of up to $4,300 per individual. Furthermore, because 8 CFR 212.1(g) does not define "unforeseen emergency," carriers can attempt to interpret that exception on their own and, assuming that they expect CBP to apply a broad reading to the exception, could feel motivated to transport a large number of undocumented aliens into the U.S. with the expectation of being exempt from the penalty.

 Approving the proposed rule would greatly strengthen the economic incentive of carriers to comply with 273 of the INA. Unless a carrier will receive more than $4,300 to transport an alien into the U.S. without proper documentation, that carrier will be unmotivated to provide such transportation due to the expectation of having to pay a $4,300 fine. Arguably, the money that an airline receives per individual for the cost of transportation is so minimal (The average international airfare price was $1,004 at the start of 2015. (Ann Rivall, Airfaire Trends on the Rise in 2015, U.S. News Travel, Jan. 21, 2015)), particularly in comparison with the potential to receive a $4,300 penalty, that carriers will not face significant economic hardships from the barrier against transporting nonimmigrant aliens who do not have the necessary documentation.

 In addition, the potential to assess fines of more than $1 million should greatly exceed the costs of hiring new government employees to cover the increased workload of assessing additional penalties. To cover approximately 2,375 hours of penalty administration per year (81 FR 12035) would arguably require the hiring of only two additional employees, whose salaries would clearly not consume the entirety of the fines assessed of the carriers. As a result, in the case that carriers continue to violate the documentation requirements, DHS will have additional funds which could be put toward increasing American security.

 Finally, I support Alternative 1, the chosen proposal (81 FR 12038). Making an exception for small entities as provided in Alternative 2 (81 FR 12038) is unjustified; this alternative would remove the economic incentive to comply with 372 of the INA and could create an unnecessary safety risk. The costs to the few small entities that this rule may affect do not outweigh the overall benefits of ensuring that nonimmigrant aliens have both a valid passport and visa upon entry into the United States.

After reviewing the proposed AD and the comments to date, I have the following comments.

I purchased a Navworx ADS600 EXP unit for my experimental EAB Vans aircraft on September 4, 2016. My unit was supposed to go into production on the 09/14, and I was making plans to install it while performing my aircraft's condition inspection. Thanks to this proposed AD, that will probably not happen.

The proposed remedy to require removal of all units affected will only serve to create additional collision hazards in the NAS. The FAA should be working with Navworx to work out a solution to this problem, not threatening to require removal of the equipment and scrapping it!

Navworx states that the units in question are using a GPS position source which satisfactorily met CFR 91.227(c) 3 years ago. After reviewing many reports from current users of the Navworx units going back at least 3 years, I have found no faulty position reports as a cause for a failing report.

Navworx was told by FAA at the time of testing the GPS source to use a SIL of 0 despite the acceptable performance of the GPS source. This was OK until the FAA changed their system's response to deny TIS-B data to those users reporting SIL 0.

I do not see any way a faulty ADS-B position report could create a collision. ADS-B just gets a pilots attention to look outside for an aircraft when one is close by. So even if the GPS position was in error to show a proximate target, the only adverse effect is a pilot looking out the window. If the GPS position was in error to simulate a distance target (when the target is truly proximate) then the system is no less safe than it was before ADS-B. In other words, removing the system creates the very safety concern under discussion!

Also, even if the position is incorrect, the altitude should still be correct, since that is based on barometric pressure. Aircraft that are separated vertically (not in the same horizontal plane) cannot collide. So even if the GPS is as bad as the FAA thinks, having this system installed is STILL a safer condition than not having it installed (or having it removed).

The Atlantic humpback dolphin is found on the west coast of Africa, and it is one of four coastal humpback dolphin species (Fisherman et al., 2023). This species has been confirmed in 13 of the countries from Western Sahara to Angola; however, there is little known about this species (Fishman et al., 2023). Their populations are heavily fragmented as this species lives in small pods in warm, coastal waters (NOAA Fisheries, 2023). Due to their limited range and trivial numbers, they are severely impacted by different anthropogenic factors such as coastal development and noise (NOAA Fisheries, 2023). 
Despite not being listed under the Endangered Species Act, the Atlantic humpback dolphin is already considered critically endangered by the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature) (Fishman et al., 2023). It is estimated that there are less than 3,000 individuals left in the entire population (NOAA Fisheries, 2023). Since Atlantic humpback dolphins live in extremely shallow waters, they are heavily influenced by tide patterns (NOAA Fisheries, 2023). Since their habitat is close to shore, they are often bycatch in fisheries, further reducing their small populations (NOAA Fisheries, 2023).
A recent assessment determined that the Atlantic humpback dolphin was at a “high risk of extinction throughout its range and warrants listing as an endangered species” (Fishman et al., 2023). Though marine protected areas have been used as a conservation technique, these efforts have not been made in all 13 countries (Fishman et al., 2023). Additionally, the lack of information on this species has prevented targeted regulations that could aid in the species' survival (Fishman et al., 2023). Therefore, the Atlantic humpback dolphin should be placed under the Endangered Species Act so conservation efforts can be put in place to save this species from extinction.

Residents of the Dallas area are consistently exposed to some of the highest ozone levels 
in the Central United States. Indeed, air quality monitors in the area consistently exceed the

I support the FDA moving forward with a Guidance for Industry (GFI) 273 to set strong durations of use for medically important antimicrobials used in animal feed. 

I am concerned that each year 35,000 Americans die from antibiotic-resistant infections and that this number will only grow if we do not stop unnecessary antibiotic usage. Animal antimicrobial usage contributes to this resistance and not having durations of use on animal feed antibiotics can lead to unnecessary use. 

Feed antimicrobials are approximately 63% of the antimicrobials given to food animals every year, so ensuring that these antimicrobials are given appropriately is crucial to public health. Durations of use on every label will help with this.

Yes, it's a hassle, but we have to be careful about medications losing their effectiveness.

I urge the FDA to adopt a policy that will encourage veterinarians to use the shortest possible durations to achieve their desired clinical outcomes. These durations should not be set based on extreme or rare circumstances. Instead, drug manufacturers should be pushed to include evidence-based instructions on how long to use the drug under expected or common circumstances. These expected duration limits should be specific, offering a definite length of time such as, “use for 14 days.” Such limits should also take into account the risk of antibiotic resistance associated with the drug’s use.

Sincerely,
Kathryn Burns

I am writing to express support for the U.S. Forest Service's proposal to restore the Roadless Rule to the Tongass National Forest in Southeast Alaska. America's remaining ancient forests are precious, and it is critically important we safeguard them from logging and road building.

Roadless area protections sustain southeast Alaska's ancient forests including thousand-year-old Sitka spruce, western hemlock, and western red cedar. Tribal communities currently rely on the Tongass for traditional uses that date back thousands of years and support communities' essential food security. The Tongass is also home to endemic species including brown bears, wolves, eagles, black-tailed deer, and world-class salmon habitat that support commercial and recreational fisheries.

The Tongass produces 25% of the entire west coast annual salmon harvest. The Forest Service estimates that the salmon industry generates $986 million annually.

As you know, during the 2019 Alaska Roadless Rule comment period more than 95% of responses favored keeping the National Roadless Rule intact on the Tongass National Forest. These comments came from salmon fishermen, indigenous people, local Alaskan communities, Alaskan tourism industry representatives, climate activists, and more. 

I appreciate the U.S. Forest Service -- with direction from President Biden -- is beginning to take the right steps to correct the devastating decision made in 2020 to eliminate Roadless Rule protections for the Tongass. More must be done to safeguard our remaining forests -- especially the old growth and mature forests -- for their natural values. 

Please fully reinstate the 2001 National Roadless Rule in Alaska and protect the Tongass National Forest!

Dear Ms. Verma:
Novo Nordisk is pleased to provide the following comments on CMS' proposed changes to the Quality Payment Program (QPP). Headquartered in Denmark, and with more than 6,000 U.S. employees, Novo Nordisk is a global health care company with 90 years of innovation and leadership in diabetes, obesity, hemophilia and growth hormone disorders. Novo Nordisk is committed to the goal of ensuring patients have access to high-quality, affordable health care. As a life sciences company with a focus on diabetes care, we support the Agency's continued efforts to develop policies that are reflective of system capabilities and grounded in core strategies to drive progress and reform efforts.
We are encouraged by CMS efforts to ensure the QPP is driving toward the stated program aims to (1) support care improvement by focusing on better outcomes for patients, decreased clinician burden, and preservation of independent clinical practice; (2) promote adoption of Alternative Payment Models (APMs) that align incentives for high-quality, low-cost care across healthcare stakeholders; and (3) advance existing delivery system reform efforts, including ensuring a smooth transition to a healthcare system that promotes high-value, efficient care through unification of CMS legacy programs. In particular, we are hopeful that the QPP can improve care for chronic health conditions, especially patients with diabetes.
We support the CMS activities focused on improving the QPP related to the measure portfolio and options for eligible clinicians, as well as continued efforts in exploring the best mechanisms and timing for scoring of the cost performance category. Specifically, we support the timeline proposed and attention to retiring topped out measures. We think it is important to ensure there is a trend in the high performance of measures over multiple years and then thoughtful consideration for replacement measures to sustain focus on those clinical areas where improvement opportunities exist. We support the proposal to weight the cost performance category at zero percent of the final score for the 2020 MIPS payment year in order to improve clinician understanding of the measures and continue development of episode-based measures that will be used in this performance category. At the same time, it is important for CMS to consider and prioritize the need for exploration and development of new episode-based measures for the QPP. We believe a continued effort to reduce costs incurred by patients is an important goal and appreciate CMS' broadened efforts to work with stakeholders to advise and revise program requirements to continue to move toward an overall goal of improving quality of health. 
Based on our commitment to improving the lives of people with diabetes and encouraging quality improvement in the health system, we are supportive of the inclusion of new measures to broaden some specialty sets (e.g., Nephrology, Mental/Behavioral Health, Urology, Podiatry, Preventive Care, Ophthalmology, Cardiology and Internal Medicine) and increase the focus on obesity and related comorbidities. Measures promoting both evidence-based processes of care and those focused on communication and coordination of care are particularly important for the diabetes community. Finally, we support the inclusion of the two new Quality Improvement Activities focused on glycemic screening and referral services.

Director Ashe,
The recovery of grizzly bears in Greater Yellowstone is one of our country's greatest conservation success stories and delisting bears must continue this legacy. We are concerned that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) is considering regulatory mechanisms that are inadequate and the process the Service has taken to request public comment and peer review is seriously flawed.
These key pieces are missing:
 The Service must commit to a stable population. The FWS and states are clearly at odds on how the population would be maintained post-delisting. The Service must provide the public a full analysis of how the proposed mortality thresholds will impact population numbers, dispersal, and connectivity.
 If counting methodologies change in the future, mortality thresholds and the calculation of a stable population must be recalibrated. The proposed rule does not ensure this will occur. 
 How will "secure" habitat be protected within the Primary Conservation Area when mortality rates are allowed to range up to 10% for female bears and 22% for male bears? This proposal does not contain adequate regulatory mechanisms to ensure secure habitat remains and that hunting will not disrupt National Park Service resources. 
 A final rule must commit to connectivity and coordinated management. The long-term viability of Yellowstone's grizzlies, especially in a time of climate change, depends on their ability to connect with other bear populations in the Northern Rockies - without human intervention. The grizzly bear is a conservation reliant species that requires this coordinated management to continue into the foreseeable future.
 The Conservation Strategy hasn't been finalized, yet the agency is asking for comments on a proposed rule. How can the public meaningfully comment on delisting without first finalizing the guiding document for future grizzly bear management? The Service and partner agencies must release the revised Conservation Strategy for public comment before proposing a final delisting rule.
 The peer reviewers raised substantive concerns regarding the regulatory mechanisms and the ability of the Service to ensure that the population would remain stable and connect to other populations. The reviewers were asked to review state regulatory mechanisms that have been significantly modified and a Conservation Strategy that will be significantly different than the document they reviewed. The peer-review must be repeated with the actual management framework for grizzly bears that will be signed and finalized and their concerns must be addressed in the final rule.
 Key regulatory mechanisms for habitat protections are still missing. The Forest Plan Amendments have not been revised to reflect the current planning rules or opened to public comment. Grizzly bear habitat must receive protections post-delisting on National Forest and Bureau of Land Management lands to ensure the continued recovery of bears. 
 
Please stop this delisting process and withdraw the proposed rule until these critical flaws have been addressed. This process and proposal is fraught with errors and inaccuracies. To comment on fluid and unfinished regulatory mechanisms is an insult to the public process and decades of efforts of all of the partners involved in the recovery of bears. The FWS must pause and work with the National Forests, National Park Service and the three states to ensure that all of the pieces of the Conservation Strategy are complete, accurate and consistent. This process and rule will erode decades of efforts that have gone toward ensuring a coordinated recovery of bears.

I am writing to urge you to reject the proposed rul-e to downlist West Indian manatees to threatened under the Endangered Species Act. Please keep this species listed as endangered.

I have lived off the Homosassa river and have watched people blatantly speed in no wake areas 'people are always in a hurry' and touch and ride manatees while in the water with them. We must protect them or they will not survive what humans are doing to them. A five year status revie-w must be done before any thing is done to their endangered status.Only the most current scientific information must be used to make any decision since it is imperative to their survival.

Manatees were originally listed as endangered in 1967 due to the threats they faced from boat strikes, habitat loss, and pollution. These threats have not decreased, in fact, they have increased. Within the last two years, at least 1,200 Florida manatees have died from boat strikes, the effects of algal blooms, and other threats. In the first three months of 2016 alone, the number of watercraft mortalities was double the previous five-year average. Compliance with existing speed zone restrictions averages only 54 percent.

I am also concerned about the 'evidence' that USFWS is relying on for the proposed downlisting. The USFWS is proposing to undertake a reclassification of the species without first conducting the required five-year status revie-w under the Endangered Species Act. The last status revie-w for West Indian manatees took place in 2007. This revie-w has been questioned by numerous scientists, as it appears to be ba-sed on one computer model 'the Core Biological Model' which failed to take into account recent massive die-offs of hundreds of manatees from prolonged cold snaps and toxic red tide blooms between 2010 and 2013. It also did not take into account habitat loss due to waterfront development and the anticipated loss of artificial warm water. Without incorporating the full data set, it is impossible to assess the long-term viability of the Florida manatee population. 

In sum, the USFWS is proposing to undertake a downlisting without basing it on concrete scientific studies that demonstrate that the manatee population has recovered sufficiently. Before such a move is even considered, the USFWS needs to put together a viable plan to reduce mortality and establish achievable recovery benchmarks. Specifically, the agency should account for the increase in boating hours, algal blooms, loss of artificial warm water, Lake Okeechobee discharges, and state speed zones. 

After losing over 3,000 manatees in Florida waters alone between 2010 and 2015, there is no evidence that they are ready for downlisting. Please keep them listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act.

Allied Pilots Association (“APA”) is the authorized representative of the more than 16,000 pilots 
of American Airlines, the world’s largest airline with daily flights to 350 destinations in more 
than 50 countries. As a steadfast advocate for aviation safety, APA supports the role of cockpit 
voice recorders (CVRs) in enhancing aviation safety through their original intended purpose, as a 
tool to be used during incident or accident sequence reconstruction. Because the adoption of a 
25-hour CVR requirement does nothing to advance that purpose and does not lower aviation 
safety risks, APA opposes any change to the current CVR requirements. 
A 25-hr CVR would be continuously recording flight deck conversations during as many as four 
or five flights before an “incident” flight. This extended recording of crew communications 
during non-event flights does nothing to advance safety or enhance incident or accident 
investigation and reconstruction. There is simply no logical justification for why crew 
communications which occurred as much as a day prior to an incident or accident would have 
any relevance on the investigation or reconstruction of such event. By contemplating such a 
drastic change in the duration of CVR recordings, with no demonstrable evidence to support how 
it advances safety, the proposal simply seeks an extended duration for the sake of being able to 
say such exists. 
The use of CVR data was originally intended for situations where direct crew accounts are not 
available after a catastrophic accident. It was not intended for intrusive assessments of intra-
cockpit communications for incidents as minor as display failures and the like. If the 25-hour 
CVR is passed, then section 49 CFR 830 must be updated and expanded to precisely limit how 
such recordings can be used. While there currently exists a prohibition against the public 
disclosure of cockpit recordings by the NTSB, Part 830 does not contain any specific language 
addressing the preservation and permissible use of extended CVR recordings. As noted above, a 
25-hour recording will inevitably contain hours of irrelevant communications between crew 
members from non-event flights. Should the 25-hour proposal be advanced, it must be 
accompanied by a corresponding regulation limiting the ability to review crew communications 
from uninvolved flights, irrespective of whether such recordings exist. A 25-hour CVR should 
not be an invitation to go on a fishing expedition to review crew communications during non-
event flights. 
Further, because there are no clear statutory protections for flight crew from the misuse of CVR 
data by an air carrier or others, CVR data could be used for other purposes such as disciplinary 
actions against pilots. Extending the CVR duration to 25-hours increases the possibility for 
misuse of CVR data. Such an extension will create an environment in which pilots will have 
their interactions continuously recorded while in the privacy of their workplace. While there are 
established protections in place regarding use of CVR data in connection with governmental

Dear Tracy Stone-Manning, Director, Bureau of Land Management,

I hope this letter finds you well. I am writing to express my support for the proposed rule that aims to include conservation as a vital goal for the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). It is encouraging to see the BLM taking steps towards managing public lands with a focus on resilient ecosystems, wildlife habitat, and the challenges posed by a changing climate. However, I would like to address some concerns regarding the proposed rule's insufficient emphasis on biodiversity and the need for clearer definitions and regulations.

Biodiversity, the protection and restoration of which are essential for the health of our ecosystems, appears to be overlooked in the current version of the proposed Public Lands Rule. Biodiversity loss is a significant global issue that requires urgent attention, and it should be a primary consideration in any framework governing our public lands. I urge the BLM to integrate the concept of biodiversity explicitly into the rule, ensuring that its conservation becomes an inherent objective.

Additionally, the definition of "restoration" is crucial and needs to be clarified. The BLM's current perspective, which considers the replanting of invasive non-native species favored by grazing livestock as restoration, is concerning. True restoration should encompass the return of an area to its natural, native ecological state, promoting native plant species and supporting a diverse array of wildlife. It is imperative that the BLM revises its definition of restoration to align with this broader conservation objective.

The introduction of 10-year "conservation leases" to businesses, individuals, non-governmental organizations, and Tribal entities is a noteworthy initiative. However, the potential ambiguities surrounding these leases raise concerns about their long-term impact on our public lands. What happens to the leased land after the 10-year period expires? Could oil, gas, and mining industries exploit these leases as a means of mitigating damage they cause elsewhere on public lands?

Furthermore, the BLM's classification of livestock grazing as a "restoration tool" raises eyebrows. The ecological damage caused by grazing is evident, and it contradicts the principles of conservation and restoration. Allowing ranchers to obtain conservation leases and utilize the land for grazing undermines the purpose of such leases. It is essential to assess the long-term consequences and ecological costs of such practices. Additionally, clarity is needed regarding responsibility for funding restoration activities: should it be borne by the leaseholder or the BLM?

In conclusion, I commend the BLM for recognizing the importance of conservation and including it as one of the agency's goals. However, it is essential to address the issues I have outlined to enhance the proposed Public Lands Rule's effectiveness. I urge the BLM to prioritize biodiversity protection, revise the definition of restoration, address the potential pitfalls of conservation leasing, and better address climate protection, to safeguard the integrity of our public lands.

I am commenting on the Noise Exposure Maps and the Noise Compatibility Program for the Ted Stevens International Airport and the Lake Hood Seaplane Base. My wife and I have lived near both airports for 28 years and I participated in the Part 150 process as the representative of the Spenard Community Council. 
My primary objection to this process is the way that the future noise exposure map was calculated. Currently, the airport operates under a preferential runway use program, and most flights take off on the north/south runway, where they go over water and not neighborhoods. This program has been amazingly successful, as demomstrated in the Land Use Analysis Chapter, where it states that only one home with two people are currently within the 65 DNL. However, that increases to three residential units with 8 people in 2020 and 15 residential units with 36 people within the 65 DNL by 2030. 
The Land Use Analysis Chapter states that this increase is due "an increase in aircraft operations forecast to be operating in the year 2030." (E.5) It is not. It is primarily due to the airport's intention to abandon the preferential runway use program during "daylight" hours, i.e., between 7am and 10am (15 hours a day). This will lead to an increase in flights using the east/west runway, which goes over the city. 
So the increase in incompatible uses in the future will be due to the airport's abandonment of a successful noise mitigation program, not to increased operations. It does not make make sense for the FAA to approve this map and consider noise compatibility programs when it is an abandonment of a current program which will create the excess noise in the first place. The future map should be recalculated on the assumption that the preferential runway use program will be in place until 2030.

As an HR professional I am in full support of a permanent change to the I-9 document verification procedures, allowing employers to verify documents remotely using digital means. This flexibility has been crucial in employers' ability to operate normally during the COVID-19 pandemic; additionally, many employers have learned since 2020 that remote work is both a viable operational model for their business and a valuable benefit for their employees. Data shows that employers plan to allow fully remote work long-term even following the end of the pandemic, and so it appears that this is a permanent development in the world of work.

The cost of digital document retention would be minimal for most employers would would utilize the remote verification option. Any company properly equipped to operate with a remote workforce must necessarily have digital tools in place to enable the quick and secure storage and sharing of information across work locations. It's reasonable to assume that most of these employers are already utilizing HR software or other digital tools that enable employee file storage, and so the additional burden in connection with remote I-9 verification would be minimal.

I am supportive of mandatory fraudulent document detection training for employers (the designated individuals in each company who are ultimately responsible for ensuring I-9s are completed properly and on time). However, I believe that mandating training for all authorized representatives outside of the company would prohibit many employers from being able to utilize this method of verification. It places an undue burden on individuals that might never need to verify another I-9 in the future, and creates an obstacle for the verification of I-9s for already disadvantaged individuals who may not have the means to easily submit digital copies of documents using a digital camera, scanner, or webcam. If the goal of this exercise is to add flexibility for employers to both verify work authorization and remain compliant with federal regulations, mandatory training for authorized representatives would negatively affect the outcome.

E-Verify as a pre-requisite for remote I-9 document verification is a reasonable requirement in order to minimize any additional risk of fraud or non-compliance. Additionally, because the e-Verify service is available to employers free of charge and is already required for employers in multiple states, it is not an undue burden to implement and manage the system. The downside of e-Verify as a requirement is that it would effectively limit the list of acceptable List B documents to only those documents that include a photo, which could lead to discrimination against individuals who need to verify work authorization using something such as a Native American tribal document.

In summary, I believe there are ample controls in protections available to allow employers to verify I-9 documents remotely using digital means. Whether by implementing mandatory training, requiring e-Verify, or some other parameter, this is a necessary and reasonable change to I-9 requirements that will better enable businesses across the US.

To protect consumers, farmers, and animals, I would like to see several changes to the guidance document. FSIS should:

Subject: Comments from Wisconsin Trout Unlimited on the U.S. Forest Service’s Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Oil and Gas Resources Regulations (RIN 0596-AD33).

Please accept the following comments from Wisconsin Trout Unlimited on the potential impacts of the proposed changes to the U.S. Forest Service’s Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Oil and Gas Resources Regulations.

Wisconsin Trout Unlimited is not opposed to the concept of updating and clarifying regulations dealing with the development of oil and gas on Forest Service lands. Our concern would be the strong possibility that changing the regulations for oil and gas development may not take into account the current best practices for managing fish and wildlife habitat, or if new regulations would move the USFS away from its mandate under the Multiple Use Sustained Yield Act of 1960 to recognize watershed protection as one of the five co-equal purposes of National Forests nationwide.

Wisconsin Trout Unlimited also supports the preparation of an Environmental Impact Statement over an Environmental Assessment to thoroughly provide a complete analysis of the impacts that changing rules for oil and gas development would have on the nation’s National Forest Lands.

Wisconsin Trout Unlimited urges the USFS to not transfer to BLM its vital discretionary role in deciding whether USFS landscapes will be open or closed to leasing or whether or not to offer specific leases. Currently USFS has the authority to identify stipulations needed to protect resources. Our desire is that current USFS authority remain in place.

The proposed rule changes appear to prioritize streamlining regulatory measures to speed up oil and gas development without regard for other National Forest resources and uses, including fish and wildlife habitat, outdoor recreation, and the security of fresh water supplies. The practice of multiple use management should be continued, protected, and not be weakened for the benefit of the oil and gas industry.

Wisconsin residents are frequent and numerous users of western National Forests. I strongly object to the proposal to include nursing degrees (bachelor's and up) in the CLIA high complexity testing personnel requirements. This proposal severely minimizes the skill level required to perform high and moderate complexity testing performed by qualified laboratory professionals. If the tables were turned, then a proposal adding laboratory professionals as personnel qualified to perform nursing duties such as administer medications, start intravenous lines, and many other nursing duties would be appropriate. Laboratory professionals are required to have additional training in the clinical laboratory prior to licensure that is invaluable to their skill level and cannot be negated or replaced by academic courses. 
 Nurses simply do not have the skill set to perform high and moderate complexity testing nor do they have the critical thinking skills that can only be developed and mastered with appropriate training in the clinical laboratory. Nursing degrees provide only a fraction of the academic science and little, if any, of the clinical training in non-waived laboratory testing that is required to qualify laboratory professionals. Bachelor's degrees in medical laboratory science, biology, and chemistry generally require at least 35-45 semester hours of academic science, with significant upper-level coursework. Bachelor's degrees in nursing often require less than 14 semester hours in biology and/or chemistry, and usually only at the introductory level.

In the proposed rule, CMS states that nurses perform the majority of point-of-care (POC) testing, and therefore it does "not have any reason to believe that nurses would be unable to accurately and reliably perform moderate and high complexity testing." But most POC tests are simple CLIA-waived for which there are NO CLIA personnel requirements. Given the significant leap in test complexity from waived to high complexity, it is reckless to believe this won't affect patient care. If CMS's concern is with POC testing, then this proposal should be limited to POC testing only. Otherwise, CMS should require these degree holders to meet a minimum coursework requirement, clinical training, and certification.

If adopted, CMS's proposal would undermine the ability of the CLIA regulations to protect patients from poor quality testing, which can result in significant delays in treatment, patient injury, and increased healthcare costs. This proposal should be withdrawn or revised.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed Seafood Import Monitoring Program. 
The Global Food Traceability Center (GFTC) is pleased to provide its comments on the seafood 
import monitoring program. This briefing is one of a series of commentaries that the GFTC has 
delivered to the Presidential Task Force on Combating Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated 
(IUU) Fishing and Seafood Fraud and to the National Ocean Council (NOC) Committee. 
GFTC (www.globalfoodtraceability.org) is a science-based, non-profit initiative within the 
Institute of Food Technologists (IFT) which focuses on providing research insights, education 
and training, as well as pragmatic guidance on food traceability. It is the global resource and 
authoritative voice on food traceability. 
In 2014 and 2015, the GFTC undertook a project on behalf of seafood stakeholders to examine 
the importance and impact of traceability as a means for the industry to more effectively manage 
the dramatically changing nature of its business. This year-long research study provided the 
foundation for our previous comments to the Presidential Task Force and NOC Committee. 
The GFTC has continued to advance on its study of seafood traceability, embarking on a broad 
international project to design a common ‘technology architecture’ or blueprint for a global, 
interoperable seafood traceability system. Early findings from that project help to inform this 
briefing. 
GFTC COMMENTS 
GFTC supports the inclusion of all seafood within this monitoring program thereby reducing 
redundant and sometimes conflicting requirements for stakeholders that handle multiple types of 
seafood. We also request that the requirements set forth under this proposed rule be aligned with 
the additional record-keeping requirements for food traceability being developed by the U.S. 
Food and Drug Administration under Section 204 of the Food Safety Modernization Act. 
We commend the Committee on proposing the implementation of an electronic reporting 
mechanism through the single window International Trade Data System for the purposes of 
collecting recordkeeping information. Due to the large amount of data that flows through global 
seafood supply chains, moving to an electronic data management system will eventually reduce 
costs and improve reliability of data for the industry as well as regulatory agencies. At the same 
time, provision of adequate data during import should not imply legality of catch. Verification 
processes need to be enforced to ensure validity of the data through rigorous inspections, audits 
and data analytics. As technology evolves, there may be new and novel methodologies for 
verification of data as well as authentication of foods. An iterative approach to incorporating 
these advances in software and hardware technologies will ensure cost and operational 
effectiveness when dealing with eliminating IUU fishing.

I am submitting comments from the perspective of a large public water system as defined by the Rule:

Water has become expensive for customers of many water systems, particularly large systems, where regulatory agencies continue to add regulatory requirements without additional funding. Every new regulatory requirement is an unfunded mandate. While water quality is important water supply has become a critical issue as well, increasing the cost of water as wells are drilled deeper and communities litigate over water rights. Water Systems are overburdened and customers are having trouble paying their water bill. Water professionals and local governing bodies are well acquainted with this serious problem. If EPA plans to double the cost of the Lead and Copper Program with the proposed Rule there needs to be associated funding from outside of the water system.

The Rule should not require Community Water Systems to collect samples from schools and childcare facilities. This is an unfunded mandate and creates an unnecessary burden. Schools and Childcare facilities should be required to sample for lead and copper as part of renewing a license or continuing to receive funding or approval to operate. They can use an approved lab and the lab can send the results directly to the regulatory agency. Advice and assistance with corrective action should be provided by the EPA, State, or licensed plumber. Most water systems have exceeded their ability to handle existing mandates and still provide water to customers at affordable rates. Unless we are taking some requirements away please do not add more .

Promoting the use of phosphate/phosphorous based corrosion control inhibitors can negatively affect wastewater treatment plants that have phosphorous reduction requirements in their permit. Promoting the use of phosphate/phosphorous based corrosion control inhibitors can also impact receiving waters for those plants that have no reduction requirement. An increase in phosphorous in receiving waters has the potential to create algal blooms and algal toxins. Phosphate/phosphorous also has been shown to promote bacterial growth in water distribution systems. The proposed rule requires evaluating 1.0 and 3.0 ppm of orthophosphate for all corrosion control studies. Will the use of higher levels of phosphorous containing corrosion control inhibitors promote biofilm development and increase the populations of pathogens such as MAC, Pseudomonas, and Legionella that have been shown to be present in premise plumbing? Has EPA considered "unintended consequences" to assure that more problems are not being created by this "solution".

The proposed rule requires water systems to replace customer portions of service lines and perform investigation of the source of lead in private residences where individual results exceed 15 ppm for lead. Replacement of customer/private plumbing and fixtures should not be required of the water system. This requirement is costly to other rate payers and carries with it liability for the water system. Customer claims for damages and repairs not done to the satisfaction of customers can cause undue financial hardship. Those having experience with customer complaints can easily forsee issues as small as scratches on countertops or the unintentional killing of a favorite shrub consuming valuable resources. Private plumbing issues are not and should not be the responsibility of the water system.

The proposed rule requires water systems that add a source of water such as a new well to complete additional monitoring. This is unnecessary if the new well is equivalent to existing system wells - same aquifer, same pumping level, water quality results are similar. The provision to demonstrate equivalence should be included in the proposed rule.

The Benefit Practice (TBP) is submitting this letter in response to the request for 
comments on the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) changes suggested in its Proposed Rule REG-
131643-15. TBP is a Third Party Administration firm providing consultative and administrative 
services for approximately 1,300 employer sponsored retirement plans, of which nearly 1 ,000 are 
defined contribution plans. A great majority of these plans contain a Cash or Deferred 
Arrangement (CODA) and/or matching contributions under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) 
§§401(k) and (m). These comments are presented to voice TBP's support for the proposed 
changes to Regulation Sections 1.401(k)-1, 1.401(k)-6, 1.401(m)-l , and 1.40l(m)-5, having the 
effect of allowing plan sponsors to use previously forfeited amounts under a plan to pay Qualified 
Nonelective Contributions (QNECs) and Qualified Matching Contributions (QMACs). 
As currently worded, § 1.401 (k)-6 requires that QNECs and QMACs meet the "vesting" 
requirements of 1.401 (k)-1 (c) at the time "when they are contributed to the plan." Since forfeiture 
money, by definition, includes funds that were not vested at the time of the plan contribution, 
current IRS interpretation of § 1.401 (k)-6 has provided that forfeiture money may not be used to 
fund QNECs and QMACs. We respectfully disagree that the current interpretation is appropriate 
even if the existing language were to remain in effect; in our opinion, no funds of any sort are truly 
nonforfeitable at the time they enter the plan, but only at the point they are allocated to a 
participant's account and fully vested forthwith. For that reason, whether the source of funds for a 
QNEC and/or QMAC comes from a direct plan sponsor contribution or allocation of a previously 
forfeited amount should not be material, and we believe that the current interpretation draws a 
distinction without meaning. 
However, as the proposed language clarifies this provision and 
eliminates any confusion as to the ability to use forfeiture amounts for this wholly legitimate 
purpose, we applaud the proposed change. 
Further, our understanding is that the IRS has on occasion approved plan documents which 
have provided for the use of forfeitures to reduce any employer contributions, including safe 
harbor contributions, QNECs, and QMACs, in direct contradiction to the current guidance 
prohibiting the use of forfeitures to reduce these same contributions. This has then raised the

De Minimis Exception for Minimal Amounts of Plant Material: NCBFAA has long supported an 

exception to the Lacey Act declaration requirement for products containing only a minimal 

amount of plant material, such as a sweater with a wooden button, dried soup (cellulose), 

machinery with a rubber gasket, or a tube of lipstick (wax from carob tree). When such products 

are highly processed and incorporate small amounts of plant material, combined with many other 

non-plant inputs, the importer cannot realistically provide meaningful information as to the 

specific identity of an incorporated harvested plant. Nor does it significantly further the purposes 

of the Lacey Act to require this information for minimal amounts of plant material. Creating this de 

minimis exception allows APHIS to better target its resources on products containing greater 

amounts of plant material and ensures that importers will not be burdened with unreasonable

appropriate for determining if the exception applies depending on the characteristics of their

straightforward, allowing importers to choose a method established by APHIS (whether based on 

weight, volume or value) most appropriate for their product and which can be readily and cost-
